posts.title: 5-Fluorouracil (injection + topical)
posts.summary: V Immunosuppressants · Pyrimidine analogue antimetabolite (antineoplastic)
posts.body:
_Injectables · V Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Pyrimidine analogue antimetabolite (antineoplastic)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate, which inhibits thymidylate synthase → no thymidine → no DNA synthesis
- Also incorporated into RNA
- In keloids: inhibits fibroblast proliferation and TGF-β-driven collagen production

## Pharmacokinetics
- IL use gives minimal systemic levels; systemic drug is metabolised by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intralesional: keloids and hypertrophic scars (alone or mixed with triamcinolone), warts, keratoacanthoma, small BCC (selected)
- Vitiligo (with microneedling/dermabrasion, off-label)
- Topical 5% cream for actinic keratosis, Bowen disease, superficial BCC (topicals slot)

## Dose & formulations
- Supplied as 50 mg/mL injection
- Keloids: 50 mg/mL alone, or mixed with triamcinolone (e.g. 0.9 mL 5-FU + 0.1 mL triamcinolone 40 mg/mL); 0.2–0.5 mL per cm² of lesion; total usually under 2–3 mL per session; every 1–4 weeks
- Keratoacanthoma: 50 mg/mL, 0.1–1 mL weekly

## Adverse effects
- IL: pain, burning, ulceration, purpura, hyperpigmentation
- Systemic (rare with IL): myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhoea; severe toxicity in DPD deficiency
- Systemic 5-FU skin effects: hand–foot syndrome, serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation, photosensitivity

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Known DPD deficiency; bone marrow suppression; infection at site

## Drug interactions
- Warfarin effect increases
- Sorivudine/brivudine (antivirals): fatal DPD inhibition

## Monitoring
- CBC if large or frequent doses are used

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D/X depending on form).

## Viva points
- Thymidylate synthase inhibitor
- 5-FU + TAC combination for keloids reduces atrophy and recurrence
- DPD deficiency → severe toxicity
- Supravenous serpentine hyperpigmentation with IV use

## Topical form: Topical 5-fluorouracil (5%, 0.5%)
_Topical antimetabolite (5% cream; 0.5% cream; 4% cream)_

**Mechanism**
- Thymidylate synthase inhibition in rapidly proliferating dysplastic cells

**Indications**
- Actinic keratoses (field therapy), Bowen disease, superficial BCC (5%), warts (off-label, under occlusion), vitiligo (after dermabrasion — off-label), disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis

**Dose & how to apply**
- AK: 5% twice daily for 2–4 weeks (or 0.5% once daily); sBCC/Bowen: twice daily for 3–6 weeks

**Adverse effects**
- Intense inflammation, erosion and crusting (expected), photosensitivity, pigmentary change; toxicity in DPD deficiency (rare)

**Contraindications**
- Pregnancy; DPD deficiency

**Pregnancy:** Contraindicated.

**Viva points**
- Field therapy for AK; inflammation is expected; combine with calcipotriol for better effect

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.47 (Topical and intralesional chemotherapeutic agents); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents); Khopkar ch.28; Wolverton 4e ch.47. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Abacavir + Lamivudine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors)

## Mechanism of action
- Both are nucleoside analogues, phosphorylated inside cells to active triphosphates
- They compete with natural nucleotides for HIV reverse transcriptase and cause chain termination of viral DNA
- Abacavir is a guanosine analogue (active form carbovir triphosphate); lamivudine is a cytidine analogue that is also active against hepatitis B

## Pharmacokinetics
- Both are well absorbed with or without food
- Abacavir: metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase and glucuronidation (no CYP); lamivudine: excreted by the kidneys
- Long intracellular half-lives allow once-daily dosing

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Backbone of first-line ART in children (with dolutegravir) under the national (NACO) programme
- Adults when tenofovir cannot be used (e.g. renal disease, osteoporosis)

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: abacavir 600 mg + lamivudine 300 mg once daily
- Children: weight-band dosing with dispersible tablets (abacavir 120 mg + lamivudine 60 mg) as per NACO tables

## Adverse effects
- Abacavir hypersensitivity syndrome (about 5–8%, usually in the first 6 weeks): fever, rash, GI symptoms, malaise, cough or breathlessness
- It is strongly linked to HLA-B*57:01. Rechallenge after a reaction can be fatal, so never restart
- Abacavir: possible increase in myocardial infarction risk
- Lamivudine: very well tolerated; pancreatitis in children; flare of hepatitis B when stopped
- NRTI class: lactic acidosis and hepatic steatosis (rare with these two)

## Contraindications
- HLA-B*57:01 positive (test before use where available)
- Previous abacavir hypersensitivity (lifelong contraindication)
- Moderate–severe liver impairment (abacavir)

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol raises abacavir levels
- Lamivudine: co-trimoxazole raises levels slightly; do not combine with emtricitabine (same drug class and target)

## Monitoring
- CD4 count and viral load as per programme schedule
- Hepatitis B status before starting (lamivudine stopping can cause a flare)
- LFT; lipids; cardiovascular risk

## Pregnancy & lactation
Both can be used in pregnancy; the national programme prefers TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) for pregnant women.

## Viva points
- Abacavir hypersensitivity = HLA-B*57:01 — never rechallenge
- Lamivudine also treats hepatitis B; stopping it can cause a hepatitis flare
- Current NACO preferred first-line for adults is TLD; ABC + 3TC + DTG is used in children

## Note on sources
Wolverton covers ART only briefly (HLA associations and a list of drugs), so Khopkar and NACO were the main guides here. Regimens change often — please confirm with the latest NACO guidelines.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Antiretroviral drugs); Wolverton 4e ch.3 (HLA-B*57:01 pharmacogenetics) and ch.11; check against current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Acitretin
posts.summary: I Retinoids · Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid; active metabolite of etretinate
posts.body:
_Oral · I Retinoids_

**Class:** Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid; active metabolite of etretinate

## Mechanism of action
- Binds nuclear RAR and RXR receptors and changes gene transcription
- Normalises epidermal proliferation and differentiation
- Anti-inflammatory: reduces neutrophil migration (hence its good effect in pustular psoriasis)
- Not immunosuppressive — useful in HIV-associated psoriasis and in transplant recipients

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 60%, better with food; 95% albumin bound; half-life about 50 h
- With alcohol it is re-esterified to etretinate, which is stored in fat and has a half-life of 80–160 days
- This is why contraception must continue for years after stopping

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis: pustular (generalised and palmoplantar) and erythrodermic respond best to monotherapy
- Plaque psoriasis: modest alone; much better combined with phototherapy (Re-PUVA, Re-NB-UVB), which also lowers UV dose
- Disorders of keratinisation: ichthyoses (lamellar, epidermolytic), Darier disease, PRP, palmoplantar keratoderma
- Hypertrophic and palmoplantar lichen planus; hypertrophic lupus erythematosus
- Chemoprevention of squamous cell carcinoma in organ-transplant recipients

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 25–50 mg once daily with the main meal (start at 25 mg; avoid high starting doses)
- Lower doses (10–25 mg) are often enough when combined with phototherapy
- Children (keratinisation disorders): about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, using the lowest dose that works
- Capsules 10, 25 mg; full response in psoriasis may take 3–6 months

## Adverse effects
- Mucocutaneous: cheilitis, xerosis, 'sticky' skin, peeling of palms and soles, retinoid dermatitis, paronychia, pyogenic granuloma
- Hair loss (telogen effluvium, dose-related) is commoner than with isotretinoin
- Raised triglycerides and cholesterol; raised transaminases (rarely toxic hepatitis)
- Bone: DISH-like hyperostosis, extraspinal calcification, premature epiphyseal closure in children on long courses
- Pseudotumor cerebri, night blindness, myalgia
- Teratogenic (long-lasting because of etretinate formation)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, and women who may become pregnant within 3 years of stopping
- Breastfeeding; severe liver or kidney disease; chronic alcohol use; marked hyperlipidaemia
- Concurrent methotrexate (risk of hepatitis) or tetracyclines (pseudotumor cerebri)

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol → conversion to etretinate (long-lasting teratogenicity)
- Methotrexate: severe hepatotoxicity — avoid
- Tetracyclines: pseudotumor cerebri
- Progestin-only pill becomes unreliable
- Vitamin A: additive toxicity; phenytoin displaced from protein binding

## Monitoring
- Pregnancy tests: before, monthly during treatment, and periodically for 3 years after stopping
- Lipids and LFTs at baseline, then every 1–2 weeks for the first 1–2 months, then every 3 months
- Children on long courses: watch growth; X-ray only if bone symptoms appear

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Contraception from 1 month before, throughout, and for 3 years after stopping. No alcohol during treatment and for 2 months after. No blood donation for 3 years.

## Viva points
- Best indications are pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis; for plaques, combine with UV (Re-PUVA)
- Alcohol turns acitretin into etretinate — hence 3 years of contraception
- It is not immunosuppressive, so it is safe in HIV and in transplant recipients
- Never combine with methotrexate

## Note on sources
Some Indian and European texts give 2 years of contraception after acitretin; Wolverton (US label) gives 3 years, which we follow.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22; Khopkar (Oral retinoids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Acridine dye antiseptic (yellow)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Acridine dye antiseptic (yellow)

## Mechanism of action
- Intercalates DNA of bacteria — bacteriostatic against Gram-positive organisms

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Infected wounds, burns dressings (acriflavine emulsion/gauze), minor skin infections (largely historical)

## Dose & formulations
- 0.1% solution or emulsion on dressings

## Adverse effects
- Yellow staining, photosensitivity, contact dermatitis, delays healing

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal data.

## Viva points
- Yellow acridine dye — historical wound antiseptic

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Acriflavine). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Acyclovir (oral/IV + topical)
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes · Synthetic acyclic guanosine (nucleoside) analogue
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes_

**Class:** Synthetic acyclic guanosine (nucleoside) analogue

## Mechanism of action
- Phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase (so it is activated only in infected cells), then by host kinases to acyclovir triphosphate
- Acyclovir triphosphate competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is incorporated into viral DNA → chain termination
- Active against HSV-1 and HSV-2 (most), VZV (needs higher doses); weak against EBV and CMV

## Pharmacokinetics
- Oral bioavailability only 15–30% → frequent dosing
- Half-life about 2.5–3 h; excreted unchanged by the kidneys (glomerular filtration and tubular secretion)
- Reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Genital herpes: first episode, recurrences, suppression
- Herpes labialis (severe or frequent), eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow
- Herpes zoster (start within 72 h) and varicella in adolescents/adults or complicated cases
- HSV-associated recurrent erythema multiforme (suppression)
- Severe or disseminated infection, encephalitis, neonatal herpes (IV)

## Dose & formulations
- First-episode genital herpes: 400 mg three times daily (or 200 mg five times daily) × 7–10 days
- Recurrent genital herpes: 400 mg three times daily × 5 days, or 800 mg twice daily × 5 days, or 800 mg three times daily × 2 days
- Suppression: 400 mg twice daily
- Herpes zoster: 800 mg five times daily × 7 days
- Varicella: 20 mg/kg (max 800 mg) four times daily × 5 days
- Severe/disseminated HSV or VZV: 10 mg/kg IV every 8 h (neonatal herpes 20 mg/kg every 8 h)

## Adverse effects
- Oral: nausea, diarrhoea, headache (generally very safe)
- IV: crystalline nephropathy (keep well hydrated, infuse slowly), phlebitis at the drip site
- Neurotoxicity (confusion, tremor, hallucinations) in elderly or renally impaired patients

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to acyclovir or valacyclovir
- Dose reduction (not contraindication) in renal impairment

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid and cimetidine reduce renal clearance
- Mycophenolate: both drugs' levels rise
- Other nephrotoxic drugs (with IV acyclovir)

## Monitoring
- Renal function with IV use or in the elderly

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe (old FDA category B); used for first-episode and late-pregnancy suppression of genital herpes. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Needs viral thymidine kinase for activation → selective for infected cells
- Resistance (TK-deficient mutants) occurs in the immunocompromised → foscarnet or cidofovir
- Zoster needs about 4 times the HSV dose
- Hydrate patients on IV acyclovir

## Topical form: Acyclovir 5% cream
_Topical guanosine analogue_

**Mechanism**
- Same as oral acyclovir; limited penetration through intact skin

**Indications**
- Recurrent herpes labialis (start at prodrome) — modest benefit (shortens episode by about half a day)
- Not useful for genital herpes, zoster or primary infections — use oral drugs

**Dose & how to apply**
- 5 times daily for 4–5 days

**Adverse effects**
- Burning, stinging, contact dermatitis (propylene glycol)

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity; not for eyes/mucosa (ophthalmic ointment is separate)

**Pregnancy:** Safe.

**Viva points**
- Topical acyclovir has minimal benefit — oral therapy is preferred

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.11 (Systemic antiviral agents); Khopkar ch.3; Khopkar ch.20 (Topical antivirals); Wolverton 4e ch.43. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Adapalene gel (0.1%, 0.3%)
posts.summary: VII Anti-acne — Retinoids · Third-generation (polyaromatic) topical retinoid — naphthoic acid derivative
posts.body:
_Topicals · VII Anti-acne — Retinoids_

**Class:** Third-generation (polyaromatic) topical retinoid — naphthoic acid derivative

## Mechanism of action
- Selective for RAR-β and RAR-γ → comedolytic, normalises keratinisation
- Strong anti-inflammatory action (inhibits neutrophil lipoxygenase, AP-1, TLR-2)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris — first-line (0.1% gel, available OTC in the USA; 0.3% for more severe)
- Fixed combinations: adapalene 0.1%/0.3% + BPO 2.5%; adapalene + clindamycin
- Maintenance after oral therapy or isotretinoin; PIH, keratosis pilaris, Darier disease (off-label)

## Dose & formulations
- Pea-sized amount once daily at night (can be applied in the morning — chemically stable)

## Adverse effects
- Dryness, redness, stinging — less irritating than tretinoin or tazarotene
- Photosensitivity (mild)

## Contraindications
- Eczema, sunburn; pregnancy (precaution)

## Drug interactions
- Stable with BPO and in light — can be combined in one product

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in pregnancy (precaution).

## Viva points
- Most tolerable topical retinoid
- Light-stable and BPO-stable — combined in one gel
- RAR-β/γ selective

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.46; Khopkar ch.24. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Adrenaline (epinephrine) injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · Endogenous catecholamine; α and β adrenergic agonist
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** Endogenous catecholamine; α and β adrenergic agonist

## Mechanism of action
- α1: vasoconstriction → raises BP, reduces mucosal oedema
- β1: increases heart rate and contractility
- β2: bronchodilation; also stabilises mast cells (less mediator release)

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM into the anterolateral thigh gives faster, higher peak levels than SC
- Onset within minutes; short action (5–10 min) — repeat dosing may be needed
- Concentrations: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) for IM; 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) for IV in cardiac arrest

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Anaphylaxis — the first-line, life-saving drug
- Cardiac arrest (IV/IO)
- Severe angioedema with airway involvement
- With local anaesthetics (1:100,000–1:200,000) to prolong action and reduce bleeding

## Dose & formulations
- Anaphylaxis: 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM in the anterolateral thigh — adult and child over 12 years 0.5 mg (0.5 mL); 6–12 years 0.3 mg; under 6 years 0.15 mg
- Repeat every 5 min if no improvement
- Refractory anaphylaxis: IV infusion by experienced staff only (never give 1:1000 IV bolus)
- Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV (1:10,000) every 3–5 min
- Autoinjectors: 0.3 mg (adult), 0.15 mg (child) — prescribe for patients with previous anaphylaxis

## Adverse effects
- Tremor, palpitations, anxiety, pallor, headache
- Tachyarrhythmias, hypertension, myocardial ischaemia (mainly with IV use or overdose)
- Tissue necrosis with accidental injection into digits (rare) or extravasation

## Contraindications
- None in anaphylaxis — always give
- Caution with local anaesthetic use: uncontrolled hypertension, severe heart disease, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma

## Drug interactions
- β-blockers: anaphylaxis resistant to adrenaline → give glucagon 1–5 mg IV; non-selective β-blockers may cause severe hypertension
- Tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, cocaine: exaggerated pressor effect
- Halothane: arrhythmias

## Monitoring
- BP, pulse, SpO₂, ECG; observe for at least 6–12 h after anaphylaxis (biphasic reaction)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use without hesitation in anaphylaxis in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM in the thigh — repeat after 5 min
- Antihistamines and steroids are only add-ons
- Glucagon for patients on β-blockers
- Every dermatology procedure room should have adrenaline ready

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (local anaesthetics) and anaphylaxis sections; Resuscitation Council / WAO anaphylaxis guidance. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Albendazole
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Benzimidazole anthelmintic (broad spectrum)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Benzimidazole anthelmintic (broad spectrum)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds parasite β-tubulin → inhibits microtubule polymerisation → impaired glucose uptake and energy depletion → death of worms (larvicidal, some ovicidal action)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Poorly absorbed; a fatty meal increases absorption (needed for tissue infections); active metabolite albendazole sulfoxide

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous larva migrans (drug of choice with ivermectin): 400 mg daily for 3–7 days
- Cysticercosis (including cysticercosis cutis and neurocysticercosis — with steroids and anticonvulsants)
- Gnathostomiasis, larva currens (strongyloidiasis — ivermectin preferred), hookworm, ascariasis, hydatid disease
- Lymphatic filariasis mass drug administration (with DEC ± ivermectin)
- Deworming before starting long-term systemic steroids/immunosuppressants in endemic areas

## Dose & formulations
- Single dose 400 mg (worms; 200 mg in children 1–2 years)
- CLM: 400 mg daily × 3–7 days
- Neurocysticercosis: 15 mg/kg/day (max 800 mg) in 2 doses for 8–30 days, with steroids
- Gnathostomiasis: 400 mg twice daily for 21 days

## Adverse effects
- Single dose: GI upset, headache
- Long courses: raised transaminases, reversible alopecia, bone marrow suppression (rare)
- Neurocysticercosis: seizures/raised ICP from dying cysts (cover with steroids)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (first trimester) — teratogenic in animals; ocular cysticercosis (treat surgically first)

## Drug interactions
- Dexamethasone and praziquantel raise albendazole levels; carbamazepine/phenytoin lower them

## Monitoring
- CBC and LFT every 2 weeks on long courses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in the first trimester; single doses in 2nd/3rd trimester allowed in deworming programmes.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for CLM (with ivermectin)
- Take with fatty food for tissue parasites
- Steroid cover in neurocysticercosis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5 (Table 5.1); Wolverton 4e ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Allopurinol
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Xanthine oxidase inhibitor
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Xanthine oxidase inhibitor

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits xanthine oxidase → lowers uric acid; also inhibits Leishmania purine salvage (allopurinol riboside is toxic to parasite)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Gout and tophi; prevention of tumour lysis
- Dermatology (off-label, historic): cutaneous leishmaniasis (with antimonials), sarcoidosis, reactive perforating collagenosis, granuloma annulare

## Dose & formulations
- 100–300 mg/day (start low, especially in renal impairment)

## Adverse effects
- Severe cutaneous adverse reactions: DRESS, SJS/TEN — allopurinol is the commonest cause of SJS/TEN in many countries; strongly linked to HLA-B*58:01 (screen in Han Chinese, Korean, Thai patients)
- Rash, hepatitis, interstitial nephritis, vasculitis

## Contraindications
- Previous allopurinol hypersensitivity; HLA-B*58:01 positive (if tested)

## Drug interactions
- Azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine: severe myelosuppression — reduce azathioprine to 25% or avoid
- Ampicillin/amoxicillin: more rash; thiazides (hypersensitivity); cyclophosphamide (marrow toxicity)

## Monitoring
- Renal function (start low), CBC, LFT; warn about rash in the first 8 weeks

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid unless essential.

## Viva points
- Top cause of SJS/TEN and DRESS — HLA-B*58:01
- Allopurinol + azathioprine = severe marrow suppression

_Sources: Khopkar (Allopurinol); Wolverton 4e ch.66 and ch.67. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Aluminium chloride hexahydrate (15–25%)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous topicals & wound care · Antiperspirant metal salt
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Antiperspirant metal salt

## Mechanism of action
- Forms aluminium hydroxide plugs in eccrine ducts → obstructs sweat outflow; long-term atrophy of secretory cells

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Focal hyperhidrosis — axillary (first-line), palmoplantar; bromhidrosis; haemostasis after biopsy (20–35% solution)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply to completely dry skin at night (6–8 h), wash off in morning; nightly until controlled, then once or twice weekly

## Adverse effects
- Irritation, stinging, itching (apply on dry skin; use hydrocortisone if needed); staining of clothes

## Contraindications
- Broken/shaved skin (wait 24 h after shaving)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Apply to dry skin at night — first-line for axillary hyperhidrosis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.28 (Antiperspirants); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Aminoglycosides: gentamicin (systemic + topical) & amikacin
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Aminoglycoside antibiotics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Aminoglycoside antibiotics

## Mechanism of action
- Bind 30S ribosomal subunit → mRNA misreading → bactericidal (concentration-dependent; oxygen-dependent uptake, so inactive against anaerobes)
- Amikacin is resistant to most aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes — the most broad-spectrum

## Pharmacokinetics
- Not absorbed orally; IV/IM; renal excretion — dose by renal function; once-daily dosing exploits post-antibiotic effect

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Gentamicin IV/IM: serious Gram-negative infections (Pseudomonas), with β-lactams in endocarditis; donovanosis (adjunct); plague, tularaemia
- Gentamicin topical 0.1% cream/ointment: impetigo, infected wounds, Pseudomonas-infected toe webs/nails (resistance and sensitisation limit use)
- Amikacin: actinomycetoma (Welsh regimen — amikacin 15 mg/kg/day in cycles with co-trimoxazole), rapid-growing NTM, MDR-TB (older regimens), Nocardia

## Dose & formulations
- Gentamicin 5–7 mg/kg IV once daily (adjust to levels)
- Amikacin 15 mg/kg/day (e.g. 500 mg twice daily) IM/IV; Welsh regimen: 3-week cycles with 2-week gaps, up to 3–4 cycles, with co-trimoxazole
- Topical gentamicin 3–4 times daily, short courses

## Adverse effects
- Nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis, reversible)
- Ototoxicity — cochlear (amikacin) and vestibular (gentamicin, streptomycin); often irreversible; mitochondrial gene variant increases risk
- Neuromuscular blockade (avoid in myasthenia)
- Topical: contact allergy (cross-reacts with neomycin/framycetin)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (fetal ototoxicity); myasthenia gravis; pre-existing hearing loss
- Topical on large raw areas or perforated tympanic membrane

## Drug interactions
- Loop diuretics, vancomycin, amphotericin B, cisplatin, cyclosporine: additive oto/nephrotoxicity
- Neuromuscular blockers potentiated

## Monitoring
- Renal function, trough levels, audiometry (baseline and during long amikacin courses — mycetoma)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D).

## Viva points
- Welsh regimen for actinomycetoma — amikacin + co-trimoxazole
- Ototoxicity: amikacin cochlear, gentamicin/streptomycin vestibular
- Topical gentamicin sensitises and cross-reacts with neomycin

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Aminoglycosides, Amikacin) and ch.18 (topical gentamicin); Wolverton 4e ch.9 and ch.41. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) — photodynamic therapy
posts.summary: Miscellaneous topicals & wound care · Porphyrin precursor photosensitiser (5-ALA 20% solution/10% gel; methyl aminolevulinate 16% cream)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Porphyrin precursor photosensitiser (5-ALA 20% solution/10% gel; methyl aminolevulinate 16% cream)

## Mechanism of action
- Taken up preferentially by dysplastic/neoplastic and sebaceous cells → converted to protoporphyrin IX
- Light activation (blue 417 nm or red 630 nm, daylight) → reactive oxygen species → selective cell death

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Approved: actinic keratoses (blue light/red light/daylight PDT), superficial BCC and Bowen disease (MAL red light, Europe)
- Off-label: acne, photoageing, sebaceous hyperplasia, warts, actinic cheilitis, field cancerisation in transplant patients

## Dose & formulations
- Apply under occlusion for 1–3 h (incubation), then illuminate (blue 10 J/cm² or red 37 J/cm²); daylight PDT: 30 min incubation then 2 h daylight

## Adverse effects
- Pain/burning during illumination (main limitation), erythema, oedema, crusting, pigmentation; photosensitivity for 24–48 h (avoid sun)

## Contraindications
- Porphyria, photosensitive disorders, allergy to ALA/MAL (peanut/almond oil in MAL cream)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- ALA → protoporphyrin IX → light → ROS
- Blue 417 nm (superficial) vs red 630 nm (deeper)
- Pain during illumination

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.25 (Photodynamic therapy); Khopkar (Photodynamic therapy — blue and red light). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ammonium lactate 12% lotion
posts.summary: VI Keratolytics & emollients · α-hydroxy acid (lactic acid neutralised with ammonium hydroxide)
posts.body:
_Topicals · VI Keratolytics & emollients_

**Class:** α-hydroxy acid (lactic acid neutralised with ammonium hydroxide)

## Mechanism of action
- Humectant (lactic acid is part of natural moisturising factor) and mild keratolytic (reduces corneocyte cohesion)
- Buffered (pH about 4.5–5.5) → less stinging than plain lactic acid

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Xerosis, ichthyosis vulgaris (FDA approved), keratosis pilaris, cracked heels, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis

## Dose & formulations
- Apply twice daily, rub in thoroughly

## Adverse effects
- Stinging and burning on fissured or inflamed skin; erythema
- Photosensitivity — sun protection advised

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; face (relative); broken skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Buffered lactic acid — approved for ichthyosis vulgaris and xerosis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.52 and ch.55; Khopkar ch.27. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Amorolfine (0.25% cream, 5% nail lacquer)
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Other · Morpholine antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Other_

**Class:** Morpholine antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits two steps of ergosterol synthesis: Δ14-reductase and Δ7–Δ8 isomerase → ergosterol depletion and toxic sterol build-up
- Fungicidal against dermatophytes; also active against Candida and some moulds

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- 0.25% cream: tinea corporis, cruris, pedis; cutaneous candidiasis; pityriasis versicolor
- 5% lacquer: distal and lateral onychomycosis without matrix involvement (up to 2 nails / under 80% nail area), and with oral antifungals for more severe disease

## Dose & formulations
- Cream: once daily (evening) for at least 2–3 weeks, continue 3–5 days after cure
- Lacquer: file the nail, clean with alcohol swab, apply once or twice weekly — 6 months for fingernails, 9–12 months for toenails

## Adverse effects
- Mild burning, itching, erythema
- Lacquer: nail discolouration, brittleness

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; children (limited data for lacquer)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (limited data).

## Viva points
- Morpholine — two enzymes in ergosterol pathway
- Lacquer once weekly (vs ciclopirox daily)
- Not available in the USA; used in India and Europe

_Sources: Khopkar ch.19; Wolverton 4e ch.42 (brief). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Amphotericin B
posts.summary: Other antifungals · Polyene macrolide antifungal (from Streptomyces nodosus); also antileishmanial
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antifungals_

**Class:** Polyene macrolide antifungal (from Streptomyces nodosus); also antileishmanial

## Mechanism of action
- Binds ergosterol in fungal (and Leishmania) membranes → forms pores → leakage of ions → cell death (fungicidal)
- Some binding to human cholesterol → toxicity
- Lipid formulations (liposomal, lipid complex) deliver drug to tissues with much less nephrotoxicity

## Pharmacokinetics
- Not absorbed orally; IV only; long tissue half-life; poor CSF penetration but effective in cryptococcal meningitis

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Life-threatening deep fungal infections: mucormycosis (drug of choice, liposomal), cryptococcal meningitis (with flucytosine), disseminated histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, disseminated sporotrichosis, invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis, penicilliosis (talaromycosis)
- Leishmaniasis: visceral (kala-azar — India's programme uses single-dose liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg), post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (alternative to miltefosine), mucosal and refractory cutaneous leishmaniasis

## Dose & formulations
- Conventional (deoxycholate): 0.5–1 mg/kg/day IV in 5% dextrose over 4–6 h (test dose 1 mg historically)
- Liposomal: 3–5 mg/kg/day (mucormycosis 5–10 mg/kg/day)
- Kala-azar (India): liposomal 10 mg/kg single infusion

## Adverse effects
- Infusion reactions: fever, chills, rigors, hypotension (premedicate with paracetamol, antihistamine, hydrocortisone)
- Nephrotoxicity (dose-limiting with conventional form) — saline loading helps
- Hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, renal tubular acidosis
- Normocytic anaemia (reduced erythropoietin), thrombophlebitis

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution with renal impairment (prefer liposomal)

## Drug interactions
- Nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cyclosporine, vancomycin); corticosteroids and diuretics worsen hypokalaemia (digoxin toxicity)

## Monitoring
- Daily renal function, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ initially; CBC; LFT

## Pregnancy & lactation
Drug of choice for serious fungal infections in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Binds ergosterol → pores
- Liposomal form for mucormycosis and single-dose kala-azar
- Nephrotoxicity and hypokalaemia

_Sources: Khopkar ch.2 and ch.5 (antileishmanial); Wolverton 4e ch.10 and ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Antimalarials: hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, quinacrine
posts.summary: Immunomodulators · 4-aminoquinolines (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine) and acridine (quinacrine/mepacrine)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Immunomodulators_

**Class:** 4-aminoquinolines (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine) and acridine (quinacrine/mepacrine)

## Mechanism of action
- Weak bases that accumulate in lysosomes and raise their pH → impaired antigen processing and MHC-II presentation
- Inhibit endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR7, TLR9) → less type I interferon (key in lupus)
- Absorb UV light, bind melanin, stabilise membranes; mild anti-platelet and lipid/glucose-lowering effects
- In porphyria cutanea tarda: form water-soluble complexes with porphyrins in the liver that are excreted in urine

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; huge volume of distribution; very long half-life (40–50 days) → takes 2–3 months to work
- Bound to melanin (skin, retina) — basis of retinopathy and pigmentation

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous lupus (DLE, SCLE) and SLE (first-line; reduces flares and thrombosis)
- Dermatomyositis skin disease, Sjögren, rheumatoid arthritis
- Photodermatoses: polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria (adjunct), lymphocytic infiltrate of Jessner
- Porphyria cutanea tarda — low dose (HCQ 100 mg or chloroquine 125 mg twice weekly)
- Others: lichen planopilaris and frontal fibrosing alopecia, morphoea, sarcoidosis, granuloma annulare, chronic urticaria (refractory), oral lichen planus
- Quinacrine: added to HCQ in refractory cutaneous lupus (no retinal toxicity)

## Dose & formulations
- Hydroxychloroquine: ≤5 mg/kg real body weight/day (usually 200–400 mg/day)
- Chloroquine: ≤2.3 mg/kg real body weight/day (usually 250 mg/day)
- Quinacrine: 100 mg/day
- Never combine HCQ with chloroquine (additive retinal toxicity)

## Adverse effects
- Retinopathy ('bull's-eye' maculopathy) — related to daily dose per kg and duration; risk higher with chloroquine, renal disease, tamoxifen
- Skin: blue-grey/black pigmentation (shins, face, palate, nails), bleaching of hair (chloroquine), exacerbation of psoriasis, AGEP (HCQ is a classic cause), SJS/TEN, lichenoid eruptions
- Quinacrine: diffuse yellow skin discolouration, aplastic anaemia (rare)
- GI upset, headache; myopathy and cardiomyopathy (long-term); haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; hypoglycaemia; QT prolongation
- Accidental overdose in children is often fatal (chloroquine)

## Contraindications
- Pre-existing maculopathy; hypersensitivity; caution in psoriasis, G6PD deficiency, porphyria (except low-dose regimen), epilepsy, long QT

## Drug interactions
- Tamoxifen (retinopathy risk), QT-prolonging drugs, digoxin (levels rise), antacids (separate by 4 h), cyclosporine levels rise, smoking reduces efficacy in lupus

## Monitoring
- Baseline eye examination (fundus) within the first year; annual screening (OCT and visual fields) after 5 years on HCQ (earlier with risk factors)
- CBC and LFT periodically

## Pregnancy & lactation
Hydroxychloroquine is safe and recommended to continue in pregnancy (reduces lupus flares, congenital heart block risk in anti-Ro mothers); compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Mechanism: lysosomal pH, TLR7/9 inhibition
- Dose by real body weight: HCQ ≤5 mg/kg, chloroquine ≤2.3 mg/kg
- Bull's-eye maculopathy; AGEP; psoriasis flare
- Low-dose twice-weekly regimen in porphyria cutanea tarda
- Smoking reduces response in cutaneous lupus

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.21 (Antimalarial agents); Khopkar (Antimalarials in LE and porphyria cutanea tarda). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Apremilast
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (small molecule)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (small molecule)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits PDE4 → raises intracellular cAMP in immune cells
- Higher cAMP lowers pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-γ) and raises anti-inflammatory IL-10
- Immunomodulatory rather than immunosuppressive — no lab monitoring needed

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; metabolised by CYP3A4; half-life about 6–9 h

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Approved: moderate–severe plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, oral ulcers of Behçet disease
- Scalp, nail, palmoplantar and genital psoriasis
- Off-label: atopic dermatitis, lichen planus, hidradenitis suppurativa, alopecia areata (limited)

## Dose & formulations
- Titration pack over 5 days (10 mg → 20 mg → 30 mg) to reduce GI side effects, then 30 mg twice daily
- Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min): 30 mg once daily

## Adverse effects
- GI: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting (mostly in the first 2 weeks)
- Headache, upper respiratory infection
- Weight loss (about 5–10% of body weight in some patients)
- Depression and suicidal thoughts (rare) — ask about mood

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity
- Caution in depression or suicidal ideation, low body weight, severe renal impairment

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin) lower levels — avoid

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests
- Weight and mood at follow-up visits

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited human data; animal studies showed pregnancy loss at high doses — avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- PDE4 → ↑cAMP → ↓TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23, ↑IL-10
- No lab monitoring; no TB screening required
- Start with a titration pack to limit GI side effects
- Watch weight and depression

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.18; Khopkar edition predates apremilast. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Atropine sulphate injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) belladonna alkaloid
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) belladonna alkaloid

## Mechanism of action
- Competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
- Heart: blocks vagal tone → raises heart rate and AV conduction
- Also reduces secretions, relaxes smooth muscle, dilates pupils

## Pharmacokinetics
- IV onset within 1 min; IM within 15 min; half-life about 2–4 h

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Symptomatic bradycardia — including severe vasovagal reaction during dermatological procedures
- Organophosphate/carbamate insecticide poisoning (large repeated doses)
- Pre-anaesthetic to dry secretions; reversal of neuromuscular block (with neostigmine)

## Dose & formulations
- Bradycardia: 0.5–0.6 mg IV every 3–5 min, up to a total of 3 mg
- Organophosphate poisoning: 1.2–2.4 mg IV, doubled every 5 min until the chest is clear and the heart rate is over 80/min
- Children: 0.02 mg/kg (minimum 0.1 mg)
- Ampoule 0.6 mg/mL

## Adverse effects
- Dry mouth, flushing, hot dry skin, fever (especially children)
- Tachycardia, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation
- Confusion, delirium in the elderly ('mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, hot as a hare')
- Doses under 0.5 mg in adults can cause paradoxical bradycardia

## Contraindications
- Angle-closure glaucoma, obstructive uropathy, paralytic ileus, myasthenia gravis (relative), tachyarrhythmias
- No absolute contraindication in life-threatening bradycardia or poisoning

## Drug interactions
- Other anticholinergics (TCAs, first-generation antihistamines, phenothiazines): additive effects

## Monitoring
- Heart rate, BP, ECG

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta; use when needed in emergencies.

## Viva points
- Vasovagal attack during a procedure: lie flat, legs up; atropine if bradycardia persists
- Minimum dose 0.5 mg in adults to avoid paradoxical bradycardia
- Signs of atropine toxicity (anticholinergic toxidrome)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (vasovagal reactions); ACLS/resuscitation guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Azathioprine
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Purine analogue (antimetabolite); prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Purine analogue (antimetabolite); prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted non-enzymatically to 6-MP, then to 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN)
- 6-TGN are incorporated into DNA and inhibit purine synthesis → T and B lymphocytes (which rely on de novo purine synthesis) are suppressed

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; 6-MP is broken down by three enzymes: TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase), xanthine oxidase and HGPRT (which makes active 6-TGN)
- Low TPMT activity → more 6-TGN → severe myelosuppression
- Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) greatly increases toxicity

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Immunobullous diseases: pemphigus (steroid-sparing; paired with steroids as first line in the Derma Desk ladder), bullous pemphigoid
- Chronic actinic dermatitis, airborne contact dermatitis (Parthenium — weekly pulse), atopic dermatitis
- Dermatomyositis, cutaneous lupus, vasculitis, Behçet disease, pyoderma gangrenosum

## Dose & formulations
- Dose by TPMT activity (Wolverton): under 6.3 U/mL → do not use; 6.3–15 U/mL → 1 mg/kg/day; 15.1–26.4 U/mL (normal) → up to 2–2.5 mg/kg/day
- Without TPMT testing: start 50 mg/day and increase slowly with close CBC checks
- Usual 1–3 mg/kg/day; takes 6–8 weeks for full effect
- Parthenium dermatitis (Indian practice): weekly pulse of 300 mg once a week (as in the Derma Desk ladder)
- Tablets 50 mg

## Adverse effects
- Myelosuppression (leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, macrocytosis) — acute (low TPMT) or chronic
- GI: nausea, vomiting (commonest reason to stop); take with food or in divided doses
- Hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, shock) in the first weeks
- Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis
- Infections; non-melanoma skin cancer (especially SCC) and lymphoma with long-term use

## Contraindications
- TPMT activity absent/very low
- Pregnancy (relative — see below), active serious infection, malignancy
- Previous treatment with alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) — higher malignancy risk

## Drug interactions
- Allopurinol/febuxostat: block xanthine oxidase → severe toxicity — avoid, or reduce azathioprine to 25% of dose
- ACE inhibitors, co-trimoxazole: added myelosuppression
- Warfarin effect reduced
- Sulfasalazine and mesalazine inhibit TPMT

## Monitoring
- Baseline: TPMT, CBC, LFT, renal function, hepatitis B/C, HIV, pregnancy test
- CBC every 2 weeks for 2 months, then every 1–3 months; LFT every 1–3 months
- Annual skin examination for skin cancer; sun protection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category D, but widely used in pregnancy in transplant and inflammatory bowel disease patients with acceptable outcomes; decide case by case. Low levels in breast milk.

## Viva points
- TPMT testing before starting — key exam point
- Allopurinol interaction (xanthine oxidase)
- Slow onset (6–8 weeks), so start steroids alongside
- Long-term risk of SCC and lymphoma

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.15 (Azathioprine), Box 15.4; Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Azelaic acid 20% cream
posts.summary: VII Anti-acne — Others · Naturally occurring saturated dicarboxylic acid (from Malassezia furfur)
posts.body:
_Topicals · VII Anti-acne — Others_

**Class:** Naturally occurring saturated dicarboxylic acid (from Malassezia furfur)

## Mechanism of action
- Antibacterial against C. acnes and staphylococci; normalises keratinisation (comedolytic)
- Competitive inhibitor of tyrosinase and toxic to abnormal (hyperactive) melanocytes → treats hyperpigmentation without affecting normal skin
- Anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidant (reduces reactive oxygen species, KLK5/cathelicidin in rosacea)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (mild–moderate), especially with PIH
- Papulopustular rosacea (15% gel — approved)
- Melasma, PIH, lentigo maligna (historic)
- Safe option in pregnancy

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily; results by 4–8 weeks (acne), 2–3 months (melasma)

## Adverse effects
- Transient burning, stinging, itching (common at start)
- Rarely hypopigmentation in dark skin (watch)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity (propylene glycol in gel)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding (old FDA category B).

## Viva points
- Tyrosinase inhibitor that acts only on hyperactive melanocytes
- Acne + rosacea + melasma in one drug
- Pregnancy-safe acne treatment

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.57 (azelaic acid); Khopkar ch.26 (Demelanizing agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Azithromycin
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — b) Macrolide · Azalide (15-membered macrolide)
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — b) Macrolide_

**Class:** Azalide (15-membered macrolide)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA) and blocks translocation → stops protein synthesis
- Bacteriostatic; can be bactericidal at high concentrations
- Also anti-inflammatory (reduces neutrophil activity and cytokines)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Acid-stable; very high tissue and intracellular levels (concentrated in phagocytes, which carry it to infected sites)
- Very long tissue half-life (about 68 h) → single-dose or short-course regimens
- Mostly excreted unchanged in bile; little CYP3A4 inhibition (fewer interactions than erythromycin)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- STIs: chlamydia/NGU, chancroid, donovanosis, gonorrhoea (with ceftriaxone in some guidelines), early syphilis in special situations
- Skin and soft tissue infections; pyodermas in penicillin allergy
- Acne (pulse regimens) — used in India, but no better than doxycycline and promotes resistance
- Rosacea; trachoma; scrub typhus

## Dose & formulations
- Chlamydia/NGU: 1 g single dose
- Chancroid: 1 g single dose
- Donovanosis: 1 g once weekly, or 500 mg daily, for at least 3 weeks and until healed
- Early syphilis: 2 g single dose (resistance is common — penicillin remains first choice)
- Skin infection: 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily on days 2–5
- Children: 10 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- GI upset (less than erythromycin), diarrhoea
- QT prolongation and arrhythmia (caution in heart disease or with other QT drugs)
- Cholestatic hepatitis (rare), hearing loss with long high-dose courses
- Rash, rarely SJS/TEN; C. difficile colitis

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to macrolides
- History of cholestatic jaundice with azithromycin
- Caution: long QT, hypokalaemia, severe liver disease

## Drug interactions
- Other QT-prolonging drugs (fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, hydroxychloroquine)
- Antacids reduce peak levels
- Warfarin and digoxin levels may rise (less than with erythromycin or clarithromycin)

## Monitoring
- None routinely; ECG if cardiac risk factors

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B); used for chlamydia in pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Long tissue half-life makes single-dose STI treatment possible
- Least CYP3A4 inhibition among macrolides
- Part of the NACO STI kits (e.g. kit 1 with cefixime) — check the slot-2 STI kits post
- Azithromycin-resistant Treponema pallidum is widespread, so it is not first-line for syphilis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1 (Macrolides). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: B-complex vitamins (riboflavin, niacin, pyridoxine, biotin, folic acid, B12)
posts.summary: Vitamins & trace elements · Water-soluble vitamins
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements_

**Class:** Water-soluble vitamins

## Mechanism of action
- Coenzymes in energy metabolism (B2, B3), amino acid metabolism (B6), carboxylation (biotin), one-carbon and DNA synthesis (folate, B12)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Riboflavin (B2) deficiency: angular cheilitis, glossitis (magenta tongue), seborrhoeic-like dermatitis, scrotal dermatitis
- Niacin (B3) deficiency — pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis (Casal necklace), diarrhoea, dementia; seen with alcoholism, isoniazid, carcinoid, Hartnup disease — treat with nicotinamide (see nicotinamide post)
- Pyridoxine (B6): prevent isoniazid neuropathy; deficiency causes seborrhoeic-like dermatitis, cheilitis
- Biotin: biotinidase/holocarboxylase deficiency (periorificial dermatitis, alopecia); popular for brittle nails (2.5 mg/day — limited evidence)
- Folic acid: with methotrexate; megaloblastic anaemia; pregnancy
- B12 (cyanocobalamin/methylcobalamin): pernicious anaemia, hyperpigmentation of knuckles and nails, glossitis; neuropathy

## Dose & formulations
- Riboflavin 5–10 mg/day; nicotinamide 100 mg every 6 h for pellagra; pyridoxine 10–25 mg with INH; biotin 2.5–5 mg/day; folic acid 1–5 mg/day; B12 1000 µg IM daily × 1 week, then weekly, then monthly (deficiency)

## Adverse effects
- Nicotinic acid (not nicotinamide): flushing, pruritus, hepatotoxicity, acanthosis nigricans
- High-dose B6: sensory neuropathy; B12 injections: acneiform eruption, rosacea flare
- Biotin interferes with laboratory immunoassays (thyroid, troponin) — stop 2–3 days before tests

## Contraindications
- Folic acid alone in B12 deficiency (corrects anaemia, neuropathy progresses)

## Drug interactions
- Isoniazid/penicillamine deplete B6; methotrexate/co-trimoxazole antagonise folate

## Pregnancy & lactation
Folic acid 400 µg–5 mg recommended in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Pellagra 4 Ds (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death); Casal necklace
- B12 deficiency → knuckle hyperpigmentation
- Biotin interferes with lab tests

_Sources: Khopkar (Water-soluble vitamins — riboflavin, niacin, biotin, folic acid); Wolverton 4e ch.40. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: BCG vaccine
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (Bacille Calmette–Guérin) vaccine
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (Bacille Calmette–Guérin) vaccine

## Mechanism of action
- Induces cell-mediated (Th1) immunity to mycobacteria
- Protects children against severe TB (miliary TB, TB meningitis); variable protection against pulmonary TB and some protection against leprosy
- Non-specific immune stimulation (trained immunity) — basis for use in warts and bladder cancer

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.1 mL intradermal (0.05 mL in infants under 1 month) over the left deltoid insertion
- Papule → pustule → ulcer → scar over 6–12 weeks

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Routine at birth in India (national schedule; up to 1 year of age)
- Dermatology: immunotherapy for warts (intralesional or intradermal), leprosy contacts (some programmes)
- Intravesical BCG for superficial bladder cancer

## Dose & formulations
- 0.1 mL intradermal (0.05 mL under 1 month)
- Warts (off-label protocols): 0.1 mL intradermal/IL every 2–4 weeks for a few sessions

## Adverse effects
- Normal: local papule, ulcer, scar
- Complications: large ulcer, abscess, suppurative lymphadenitis (BCG adenitis), keloid
- Cutaneous TB at the site: lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma; tuberculids (lichen scrofulosorum, papulonecrotic)
- Disseminated BCG infection (BCGosis) in immunodeficient children (SCID, chronic granulomatous disease, IFN-γ pathway defects, HIV)
- Flare (redness) of an old BCG scar in Kawasaki disease (a diagnostic clue)

## Contraindications
- Immunosuppression (primary immunodeficiency, symptomatic HIV, steroids, biologics, chemotherapy)
- Pregnancy; generalised skin disease or infection at the site; active TB

## Drug interactions
- Antituberculous drugs inactivate the vaccine
- Immunosuppressants increase the risk of disseminated infection

## Monitoring
- Check the site at follow-up; investigate persistent ulcer or adenitis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (live vaccine).

## Viva points
- Live vaccine — intradermal, left deltoid
- Cutaneous complications include lupus vulgaris and scrofuloderma at the site
- BCGosis signals immunodeficiency
- BCG scar reactivation in Kawasaki disease

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (IL immunotherapy for warts — brief); national immunisation schedule; Khopkar (Immunobiologicals). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Benzathine penicillin G
posts.summary: III Antibiotics · Long-acting depot form of penicillin G (natural β-lactam)
posts.body:
_Injectables · III Antibiotics_

**Class:** Long-acting depot form of penicillin G (natural β-lactam)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits transpeptidation of the bacterial cell wall → bactericidal (needs actively dividing bacteria)
- Treponema pallidum divides slowly (every 30–33 h), so long, steady penicillin levels are needed — the benzathine salt gives low levels for 2–4 weeks

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM depot slowly releases penicillin G over 3–4 weeks
- Does not reach treponemicidal levels in CSF — not suitable for neurosyphilis
- Excreted by the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Syphilis: primary, secondary, early latent (first choice); late latent and tertiary (non-neuro)
- Syphilis in pregnancy (the only adequate treatment; desensitise if allergic)
- Contacts of early syphilis; NACO white kit (kit 3, genital ulcer disease)
- Rheumatic fever prophylaxis; streptococcal pharyngitis; yaws, pinta, bejel

## Dose & formulations
- Early syphilis: 2.4 million units (MU) deep IM single dose (1.2 MU into each buttock)
- Late latent/unknown duration, tertiary (non-neuro): 2.4 MU IM once weekly × 3 weeks
- Congenital syphilis (asymptomatic infant, selected cases): 50,000 U/kg IM single dose
- Rheumatic fever prophylaxis: 1.2 MU every 3–4 weeks
- Reconstitute as per vial, inject deep IM with a wide-bore needle; observe for 30 min

## Adverse effects
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (fever, chills, myalgia, worsening rash) within 2–24 h — from release of treponemal lipoproteins; commonest in secondary syphilis; manage with antipyretics; in pregnancy may cause preterm labour
- Anaphylaxis (rare; have adrenaline ready); urticaria, serum sickness
- Injection-site pain; accidental intravascular injection → Hoigné syndrome (with procaine penicillin) or Nicolau syndrome (embolia cutis medicamentosa — painful livedoid necrosis)

## Contraindications
- Penicillin allergy (in pregnancy or neurosyphilis → desensitise, do not substitute)
- Not for IV use; not for neurosyphilis

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid raises penicillin levels
- Tetracyclines (bacteriostatic) may antagonise

## Monitoring
- Non-treponemal titre (VDRL/RPR) at 3, 6, 12 (and 24) months; a four-fold fall (two dilutions) by 6–12 months shows adequate response
- Test for HIV and other STIs; trace and treat partners

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe and essential in pregnancy (old FDA category B). Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for all stages of syphilis except neurosyphilis (needs aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV)
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction vs drug allergy
- Nicolau syndrome — inadvertent intra-arterial injection
- Pregnant women with penicillin allergy must be desensitised
- Skin sensitivity testing is still commonly done in India before injection (keep adrenaline ready)

## Note on sources
Skin testing before benzathine penicillin is routine in many Indian hospitals; international guidelines (WHO/CDC) do not require it but stress readiness for anaphylaxis.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1; NACO STI guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Benzoyl peroxide (2.5–5%)
posts.summary: VII Anti-acne — Others · Oxidising agent; bactericidal, keratolytic
posts.body:
_Topicals · VII Anti-acne — Others_

**Class:** Oxidising agent; bactericidal, keratolytic

## Mechanism of action
- Releases free oxygen radicals inside the follicle → kills C. acnes (bactericidal)
- Bacteria cannot develop resistance (non-specific oxidation)
- Mild comedolytic and anti-inflammatory effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris — in nearly every regimen; combine with topical/oral antibiotics to prevent resistance
- Pitted keratolysis, folliculitis, decolonisation (washes)

## Dose & formulations
- 2.5–5% gel once or twice daily (2.5% is as effective as 10% with less irritation)
- Washes 4–10%: short-contact for chest/back
- Fixed combinations: BPO + clindamycin, BPO + adapalene

## Adverse effects
- Dryness, peeling, redness, burning
- Bleaches hair, clothes, towels and bed linen
- Allergic contact dermatitis (about 1%)

## Contraindications
- Known allergy; acutely inflamed skin

## Drug interactions
- Oxidises tretinoin (apply at different times) — adapalene is stable
- Combined use with dapsone gel can cause temporary orange-brown skin discolouration

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe (minimal absorption).

## Viva points
- No antibiotic resistance — the reason it is combined with antibiotics
- 2.5% works as well as higher strengths with less irritation
- Bleaches fabrics — counsel patients

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.41 (BPO) and ch.46; Khopkar ch.18. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Benzyl benzoate (25%)
posts.summary: Scabicides & pediculicides · Ester of benzyl alcohol and benzoic acid; scabicide
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Scabicides & pediculicides_

**Class:** Ester of benzyl alcohol and benzoic acid; scabicide

## Mechanism of action
- Neurotoxic to mites (kills mites; ovicidal partly)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Scabies (cheap alternative where permethrin is unavailable), pediculosis

## Dose & formulations
- Adults 25% emulsion; dilute to 12.5% for children (and 6% for infants, if used); apply neck down after bath, repeat next day without bathing, wash off 24 h after second application (regimens vary)

## Adverse effects
- Burning and irritation (common, especially on excoriated skin), irritant dermatitis; conjunctivitis if it reaches eyes

## Contraindications
- Infants (irritation, benzyl alcohol toxicity), face and eyes

## Pregnancy & lactation
Has been used; permethrin preferred.

## Viva points
- Burning sensation limits use; must be diluted for children

_Sources: Khopkar ch.21 (Benzyl benzoate); Wolverton 4e ch.44. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Beta-carotene
posts.summary: Photoprotective agents · Carotenoid (provitamin A); systemic photoprotective
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Photoprotective agents_

**Class:** Carotenoid (provitamin A); systemic photoprotective

## Mechanism of action
- Quenches singlet oxygen and free radicals generated by light-activated porphyrins
- Deposits in skin → carotenodermia (yellow-orange colour)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Erythropoietic protoporphyria (classic indication; modest benefit — afamelanotide is newer)
- Polymorphous light eruption, solar urticaria, hydroa vacciniforme (limited evidence)

## Dose & formulations
- Adults 60–180 mg/day (children 30–90 mg/day), aiming for blood carotene of 600–800 µg/dL; protection begins after 1–2 months

## Adverse effects
- Carotenodermia (palms, soles, nasolabial — sclera spared, unlike jaundice)
- Loose stools; increased lung cancer risk in smokers and asbestos workers at high doses

## Contraindications
- Smokers (lung cancer risk)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe.

## Viva points
- Carotenaemia spares the sclera
- Used in erythropoietic protoporphyria
- Avoid in smokers

_Sources: Khopkar (Systemic photoprotective agents); Wolverton 4e ch.40. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Betamethasone (oral)
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist like prednisolone, but much more potent and longer acting
- No mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 0.6 mg betamethasone ≈ 5 mg prednisolone (about 25 times hydrocortisone)
- Crosses the placenta (not inactivated by 11β-HSD2) — used to mature fetal lungs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Oral mini-pulse (OMP): progressive/unstable vitiligo, spreading alopecia areata, extensive lichen planus
- General systemic steroid indications (less often than prednisolone)

## Dose & formulations
- OMP (Pasricha regimen): 5 mg betamethasone (or dexamethasone) as a single morning dose on 2 consecutive days per week (adults); children 0.1 mg/kg on the same schedule
- Continue OMP for about 3–6 months for vitiligo, then taper
- Tablets 0.5 mg (and 1 mg in some brands)

## Adverse effects
- Same as systemic steroids; with OMP mainly weight gain, acne, insomnia, menstrual disturbance, mild Cushingoid features
- Long-acting steroids suppress the HPA axis more than prednisolone if given daily

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- As for prednisolone

## Monitoring
- Weight, BP, glucose during OMP

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta (used deliberately for fetal lung maturity); avoid for skin disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- OMP — pulse dosing on 2 days a week reduces side effects but still stops disease activity
- Long-acting: more HPA suppression if given daily
- Not inactivated by the placenta (unlike prednisolone)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (Table 8.2, OMP indications); Wolverton 4e ch.13. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Bexarotene (oral + topical gel)
posts.summary: Retinoids · Third-generation retinoid (rexinoid) — selective RXR agonist
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Retinoids_

**Class:** Third-generation retinoid (rexinoid) — selective RXR agonist

## Mechanism of action
- Binds retinoid X receptors → induces apoptosis and inhibits proliferation of malignant T cells

## Pharmacokinetics
- Take with a fatty meal; metabolised by CYP3A4

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Oral: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) refractory to at least one systemic therapy (approved)
- 1% gel: early-stage (IA/IB) mycosis fungoides lesions (approved)
- Off-label gel: hand eczema, lymphomatoid papulosis, alopecia areata

## Dose & formulations
- Oral: 300 mg/m²/day (start at 100–150 mg/m² and increase)
- Gel 1%: every other day at first, increasing up to 2–4 times daily as tolerated

## Adverse effects
- Central hypothyroidism (almost universal — suppresses TSH) → levothyroxine needed
- Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (risk of pancreatitis) → fibrate/statin often started with it (avoid gemfibrozil — raises bexarotene levels)
- Leucopenia, headache, mucocutaneous dryness, photosensitivity
- Gel: irritant dermatitis, pruritus

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (teratogenic); pancreatitis risk; uncontrolled lipids

## Drug interactions
- Gemfibrozil and CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels; reduces efficacy of hormonal contraceptives

## Monitoring
- Fasting lipids weekly at start, free T4 (not TSH), CBC, LFT

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (category X); two contraceptive methods (one non-hormonal).

## Viva points
- RXR-selective 'rexinoid'
- Central hypothyroidism — monitor free T4
- Hypertriglyceridaemia — avoid gemfibrozil

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22 and ch.37; Khopkar (Retinoids; topical retinoids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Bleomycin (intralesional)
posts.summary: III Antibiotics · Glycopeptide cytotoxic antibiotic (from Streptomyces verticillus); antineoplastic
posts.body:
_Injectables · III Antibiotics_

**Class:** Glycopeptide cytotoxic antibiotic (from Streptomyces verticillus); antineoplastic

## Mechanism of action
- Binds DNA and iron; produces oxygen free radicals that cause single- and double-strand DNA breaks (G2 phase specific)
- In warts: kills HPV-infected keratinocytes and damages capillaries → haemorrhagic necrosis and eschar
- Skin and lung lack bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates it — hence toxicity in these organs

## Pharmacokinetics
- Intralesional use gives very low systemic levels
- Systemic drug is excreted by the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Recalcitrant viral warts (palmoplantar, periungual, common warts)
- Keloids and hypertrophic scars (alternative/adjunct)
- Vascular malformations (sclerotherapy), cystic lymphatic malformations
- Systemic (oncology): squamous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma (intralesional too), germ-cell tumours

## Dose & formulations
- Warts: 1 U/mL (dissolve a 15 U vial in 15 mL normal saline or lignocaine); inject 0.1–0.2 mL into the base of each wart until it blanches
- Keep total dose low per session (usually 1–2 U, a few units at most); repeat every 2–4 weeks if needed
- Vascular malformations: weaker solution 0.2–0.4 mg/mL (Wolverton), every 2–4 weeks for 4–10 sessions
- Reconstituted solution is stable in the refrigerator for some weeks (check local pharmacy guidance)

## Adverse effects
- Pain during and after injection (use lignocaine as diluent or a digital block)
- Black eschar/haemorrhagic crust, then healing in 2–4 weeks
- Periungual/digital injection: nail dystrophy or loss, Raynaud phenomenon, digital necrosis (rare)
- Systemic use (not with IL warts): flagellate hyperpigmentation, pulmonary fibrosis (cumulative over 400 U), Raynaud, scleroderma-like changes, fever, alopecia

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Peripheral vascular disease, Raynaud phenomenon (especially for digital warts)
- Immunosuppression with infection at site; children (relative)

## Drug interactions
- Cisplatin reduces bleomycin clearance (systemic)
- High oxygen concentration (anaesthesia) increases lung toxicity in patients who had systemic bleomycin

## Monitoring
- Review at 2–4 weeks; watch digital circulation after periungual injection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D).

## Viva points
- Works via DNA strand breaks from free radicals
- Flagellate pigmentation and lung fibrosis — systemic use only
- Skin and lungs lack bleomycin hydrolase
- IL warts: 1 U/mL, inject until blanching

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.47 (Topical and intralesional chemotherapeutic agents); Khopkar (intralesional agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Botulinum toxin type A
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Neurotoxin from Clostridium botulinum (onabotulinum-, abobotulinum-, incobotulinumtoxin A)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Neurotoxin from Clostridium botulinum (onabotulinum-, abobotulinum-, incobotulinumtoxin A)

## Mechanism of action
- Heavy chain binds cholinergic nerve terminals; light chain (zinc protease) cleaves SNAP-25 → acetylcholine cannot be released
- Result: temporary chemodenervation of muscles (3–4 months) and eccrine sweat glands (6–9 months or longer)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Hyperhidrosis: axillary (approved), palmar, plantar, craniofacial, compensatory
- Aesthetic: glabellar lines, crow's feet, forehead lines, platysmal bands, masseter hypertrophy, gummy smile
- Others: Hailey–Hailey and Darier disease (reduces sweating-triggered flares), rosacea flushing, keloids (adjunct), Raynaud phenomenon, Frey syndrome, anal fissure
- Microbotox/mesotherapy (intradermal dilute injections) for skin texture and sebum

## Dose & formulations
- Axillary hyperhidrosis: 50 U onabotulinumtoxin A per axilla intradermally (after starch–iodine test)
- Glabellar lines: 20 U (5 sites × 4 U)
- Reconstitute with preservative-free (or preserved for less pain) saline; units are not interchangeable between brands (abobotulinum ~2.5–3 × onabotulinum units)

## Adverse effects
- Injection pain, bruising, headache
- Spread to adjacent muscles: ptosis (eyelid — use apraclonidine drops), brow ptosis, asymmetric smile, hand weakness (palmar injections)
- Antibody formation (non-response) with frequent high doses
- Distant spread (rare): dysphagia, breathing difficulty — boxed warning

## Contraindications
- Neuromuscular disorders (myasthenia gravis, Lambert–Eaton, ALS), infection at site, pregnancy and breastfeeding, allergy to albumin

## Drug interactions
- Aminoglycosides, quinine, calcium-channel blockers, other neuromuscular blockers potentiate effect

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (insufficient data).

## Viva points
- Cleaves SNAP-25 → blocks acetylcholine release
- Sweat effect lasts longer than muscle effect
- Brand units are not interchangeable
- Ptosis — treat with apraclonidine eye drops

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.60 (Botulinum toxin injections); Khopkar ch.35 (Botulinum toxin; mesotherapy). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Burow's solution (aluminium acetate)
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Astringent solution (aluminium subacetate/acetate, usually diluted 1:20–1:40)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Astringent solution (aluminium subacetate/acetate, usually diluted 1:20–1:40)

## Mechanism of action
- Aluminium salts precipitate proteins → astringent (shrinks and dries weeping skin), mildly antibacterial; evaporation cools

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Wet compresses for acute weeping eczema, contact dermatitis (poison ivy), pompholyx, infected eczema, otitis externa
- Soaks for bullous and erosive lesions

## Dose & formulations
- Dilute 1:20 to 1:40; apply compresses for 15–20 min 2–4 times daily for 2–3 days

## Adverse effects
- Over-drying with prolonged use; irritation

## Contraindications
- Prolonged use on dry skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Wet compress for weeping dermatitis — 'if it's wet, dry it'

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Burow's solution — aluminium subacetate solution). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Butenafine & naftifine
posts.summary: Topical antifungals · Benzylamine (butenafine) and allylamine (naftifine) antifungals
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antifungals_

**Class:** Benzylamine (butenafine) and allylamine (naftifine) antifungals

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibit squalene epoxidase → fungicidal against dermatophytes; anti-inflammatory (naftifine)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea pedis, corporis, cruris; pityriasis versicolor (butenafine)

## Dose & formulations
- Butenafine 1% once daily for 2 weeks (corporis/cruris) or 4 weeks (pedis); naftifine 1–2% once daily for 2–4 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Burning, irritation, contact dermatitis (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Acceptable.

## Viva points
- Same target as terbinafine (squalene epoxidase) — fungicidal

_Sources: Khopkar ch.19; Wolverton 4e ch.42. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Calamine lotion
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Shake lotion (zinc oxide with a small amount of ferric oxide) — soothing, drying, mildly astringent
posts.body:
_Topicals · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Shake lotion (zinc oxide with a small amount of ferric oxide) — soothing, drying, mildly astringent

## Mechanism of action
- Zinc oxide/calamine powder suspended in water: water evaporates → cooling, antipruritic effect
- Powder remains on the skin → drying and protective; mildly astringent and antiseptic
- Ferric oxide gives the pink colour

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acute itchy rashes: varicella, insect bites, miliaria rubra, sunburn, urticaria (symptomatic), mild contact dermatitis
- Weeping lesions (drying)

## Dose & formulations
- Shake well; dab on 2–4 times daily; allow to dry

## Adverse effects
- Dryness with prolonged use; caking on hairy skin
- Phenol-containing versions — avoid in infants and pregnancy

## Contraindications
- Very dry or chronic lichenified eczema (too drying)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe (plain calamine).

## Viva points
- Classic example of a shake lotion (powder + liquid)
- Cooling by evaporation; drying for weeping lesions

_Sources: Khopkar ch.28 (Miscellaneous topical agents); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Calcium dobesilate
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Vasoprotective (angioprotective) agent
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Vasoprotective (angioprotective) agent

## Mechanism of action
- Reduces capillary permeability and fragility, improves blood viscosity and lymphatic drainage; inhibits VEGF and FGF signalling (anti-angiogenic) — also studied topically in rosacea

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic venous insufficiency, stasis dermatitis (adjunct), haemorrhoids, diabetic retinopathy (Europe)
- Pigmented purpuric dermatoses (limited evidence)

## Dose & formulations
- 500 mg two to three times daily

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, skin rash, arthralgia
- Agranulocytosis (rare but serious) — stop if fever, sore throat

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; history of agranulocytosis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (limited data).

## Viva points
- Venotonic for capillary fragility; agranulocytosis is rare but important

_Sources: Khopkar (Calcium dobesilate). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cantharidin (0.7%)
posts.summary: Wart & antiviral agents · Vesicant terpenoid (from blister beetle, Cantharis vesicatoria)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents_

**Class:** Vesicant terpenoid (from blister beetle, Cantharis vesicatoria)

## Mechanism of action
- Activates neutral serine proteases → breaks desmosomal plaques → intraepidermal acantholysis → blister lifts off the lesion; painless at application

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Molluscum contagiosum (0.7% topical solution approved in USA 2023 for age ≥2 years)
- Common and periungual warts (with podophyllin and salicylic acid in some formulations)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply a small drop to each lesion in clinic; wash off after 4–6 h (molluscum: 24 h per label for the approved product); repeat every 3 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Blistering (expected), pain, burning, ring warts (annular recurrence), scarring, pigment change; toxic if ingested

## Contraindications
- Face, genitals, mucosa; diabetes/peripheral vascular disease (feet)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Painless at application, blister in 24 h
- Ring warts after treatment
- Now approved for molluscum

_Sources: Khopkar ch.20 (Cantharidin); Wolverton 4e ch.43. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Castellani's paint (carbol-fuchsin paint)
posts.summary: Topical antifungals · Magenta dye (basic fuchsin) + phenol + resorcinol + boric acid in acetone/alcohol
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antifungals_

**Class:** Magenta dye (basic fuchsin) + phenol + resorcinol + boric acid in acetone/alcohol

## Mechanism of action
- Antifungal, antibacterial, drying and mildly keratolytic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intertrigo, interdigital tinea pedis and candidiasis, weeping toe webs, chronic paronychia, napkin dermatitis (colourless versions)

## Dose & formulations
- Paint once or twice daily; let dry

## Adverse effects
- Red-purple staining (colourless variant available), irritation; phenol toxicity if used on large areas in infants

## Contraindications
- Large areas, infants (phenol absorption)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Small areas acceptable.

## Viva points
- Traditional drying antifungal paint for macerated toe webs

_Sources: Khopkar ch.19 (Traditional antifungal remedies — Castellani's paint). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ceftriaxone
posts.summary: III Antibiotics · Third-generation cephalosporin (β-lactam)
posts.body:
_Injectables · III Antibiotics_

**Class:** Third-generation cephalosporin (β-lactam)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits cell-wall synthesis → bactericidal
- Stable against many β-lactamases; good Gram-negative cover (Neisseria, Haemophilus ducreyi, Enterobacteriaceae) with streptococcal cover

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM or IV; long half-life (6–9 h) → once-daily dosing
- Good CSF penetration with inflamed meninges
- Dual excretion (bile ~40% and urine) — no dose change in renal failure alone

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Gonorrhoea (uncomplicated: urethral, cervical, rectal, pharyngeal) and disseminated gonococcal infection
- Chancroid; PID (with doxycycline + metronidazole)
- Neurosyphilis (alternative when penicillin cannot be used); early syphilis alternative
- Lyme disease (late/neurological), cellulitis, severe skin and soft-tissue infections, meningococcaemia, typhoid

## Dose & formulations
- Uncomplicated gonorrhoea: 500 mg IM single dose (1 g if over 150 kg) — CDC 2020; some guidelines (WHO 2024) use 1 g IM
- Chancroid: 250 mg IM single dose
- Disseminated gonococcal infection: 1 g IV/IM daily
- Neurosyphilis (alternative): 1–2 g IV/IM daily × 10–14 days
- Skin infections: 1–2 g IV daily
