- Reconstitute IM dose with 1% lignocaine to reduce pain (never give lignocaine-mixed solution IV)

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain, phlebitis
- Hypersensitivity (rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis); cross-reactivity with penicillin is low (about 1–2%)
- Diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis
- Biliary pseudolithiasis (reversible sludge), especially in children with high doses
- Immune haemolytic anaemia (rare); SJS/TEN (rare)

## Contraindications
- Severe immediate hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis) to penicillins or cephalosporins
- Neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia (displaces bilirubin → kernicterus)
- Neonates receiving IV calcium-containing solutions (fatal calcium–ceftriaxone precipitates)

## Drug interactions
- Calcium-containing IV fluids (Ringer lactate) — do not mix in the same line
- Warfarin effect may increase

## Monitoring
- Test of cure for pharyngeal gonorrhoea (7–14 days); test for HIV, syphilis and chlamydia; treat partners

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B) — the gonorrhoea treatment of choice in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for gonorrhoea (single IM dose)
- Dual excretion — no renal dose adjustment
- Calcium precipitate risk in neonates
- Biliary sludge (pseudolithiasis)

## Note on sources
Gonorrhoea dose differs between guidelines (CDC 500 mg, older guidelines 250 mg, WHO 2024 1 g). Please use whatever dose your department or NACO follows.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1; CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cetirizine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (piperazine; carboxylic acid metabolite of hydroxyzine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (piperazine; carboxylic acid metabolite of hydroxyzine)

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist
- Some anti-inflammatory effect: reduces eosinophil migration and late-phase reactions

## Pharmacokinetics
- Rapid onset (within 1 h); half-life about 8–10 h; once daily
- Excreted mostly unchanged in urine — halve the dose in renal impairment
- Levocetirizine is the active R-enantiomer (5 mg = 10 mg cetirizine)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic spontaneous and inducible urticaria (first line)
- Allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis itch (limited), insect bite reactions, mastocytosis

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10 mg once daily; in urticaria may be increased up to 4 times (40 mg/day) per guidelines
- Children 6 months–2 years: 2.5 mg daily; 2–6 years: 2.5 mg twice daily or 5 mg daily; over 6 years: 10 mg daily

## Adverse effects
- Mild sedation (more than fexofenadine and loratadine; about 10%)
- Headache, dry mouth, fatigue

## Contraindications
- Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance under 10 mL/min)
- Hypersensitivity to hydroxyzine or piperazines

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol and CNS depressants (mild additive effect)

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
One of the preferred antihistamines in pregnancy (with loratadine); compatible with breastfeeding (watch infant drowsiness).

## Viva points
- Metabolite of hydroxyzine
- Renally excreted — adjust in kidney disease
- Most sedating of the second-generation group
- Updosing up to 4 times in urticaria

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32; Khopkar (Antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cetrimide
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Quaternary ammonium cationic detergent antiseptic
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Quaternary ammonium cationic detergent antiseptic

## Mechanism of action
- Disrupts microbial membranes; detergent cleansing action (removes crusts and debris)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Wound cleansing (often with chlorhexidine — e.g. Savlon), seborrhoeic dermatitis/dandruff shampoos, cleansing crusted lesions

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5–1% solution for cleansing; rinse off

## Adverse effects
- Irritation and burns with strong solutions; contact dermatitis

## Contraindications
- Eyes and body cavities (strong solutions)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe for cleansing.

## Viva points
- Cationic detergent — inactivated by soap (anionic)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Cetrimide). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Chlorhexidine (0.5–4%)
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Bisbiguanide antiseptic
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Bisbiguanide antiseptic

## Mechanism of action
- Cationic molecule binds and disrupts bacterial membranes; residual (persistent) activity on skin for hours

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pre-operative skin preparation (with alcohol — preferred), hand hygiene, body washes for MRSA decolonisation and recurrent furunculosis, mouthwash (0.12–0.2%), umbilical cord care (7.1% gel)

## Dose & formulations
- Body wash 4% daily for 5 days (with nasal mupirocin) for recurrent boils

## Adverse effects
- Irritation, contact dermatitis, contact urticaria and anaphylaxis (an increasingly recognised allergen)
- Ototoxicity if it enters the middle ear; keratitis (eyes); tooth staining (mouthwash)

## Contraindications
- Eyes, ears (perforated drum), meninges

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Persistent activity — preferred pre-op antisepsis with alcohol
- Can cause anaphylaxis (chlorhexidine-coated catheters)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Chlorhexidine). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Chlorpheniramine maleate
posts.summary: Antihistamines · First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine — alkylamine
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine — alkylamine

## Mechanism of action
- H1 inverse agonist; crosses blood–brain barrier; anticholinergic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acute urticaria, allergic reactions, itch, insect bites; adjunct (IV/IM) in anaphylaxis

## Dose & formulations
- Adults 4 mg every 4–6 h (max 24 mg/day); injection 10 mg IM/IV; children 0.35 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- Sedation (milder than other first-generation drugs), anticholinergic effects, paradoxical excitation in children

## Contraindications
- Neonates; caution in glaucoma, prostatism, epilepsy

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol and CNS depressants; MAO inhibitors; phenytoin levels may rise

## Pregnancy & lactation
Widely used in pregnancy (long safety record).

## Viva points
- Alkylamine — least sedating first-generation antihistamine; long pregnancy safety record

_Sources: Khopkar (First generation H1 antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ciclopirox olamine (1% cream, 8% nail lacquer)
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Other · Hydroxypyridone antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Other_

**Class:** Hydroxypyridone antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Chelates trivalent metal ions (Fe³⁺, Al³⁺) → inhibits metal-dependent enzymes (catalase, peroxidase, cytochromes) needed for fungal metabolism
- Different from azoles and allylamines — no cross-resistance
- Broad spectrum: dermatophytes, Candida, Malassezia, non-dermatophyte moulds, Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria; anti-inflammatory

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- 1% cream/gel: tinea, candidiasis, pityriasis versicolor, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- 1% shampoo: seborrhoeic dermatitis of scalp
- 8% nail lacquer: mild–moderate onychomycosis without matrix involvement (also in children), and as adjunct to oral therapy

## Dose & formulations
- Cream: twice daily for 2–4 weeks
- Lacquer: apply daily to the nail and 5 mm of surrounding skin; apply new layers over old; remove all layers weekly with alcohol; trim/file the nail; continue up to 48 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Cream: mild burning, itching
- Lacquer: periungual redness, nail discolouration, ingrown nail (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; avoid unless needed.

## Viva points
- Metal chelator — unique mechanism
- 8% lacquer daily; remove weekly with alcohol; 48 weeks
- Antifungal + antibacterial + anti-inflammatory

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42; Khopkar ch.19. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cidofovir (systemic + topical/intralesional)
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (cytosine nucleotide analogue)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Acyclic nucleoside phosphonate (cytosine nucleotide analogue)

## Mechanism of action
- Already carries a phosphonate group, so needs only host kinases (no viral TK) → cidofovir diphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase
- Broad DNA virus activity: CMV, HSV (including acyclovir-resistant), VZV, HPV, poxviruses (molluscum, orf), adenovirus
- Very long intracellular half-life → weekly/fortnightly dosing

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- IV: CMV retinitis in AIDS; acyclovir- and foscarnet-resistant HSV
- Topical 1–3% (compounded gel/cream): acyclovir-resistant HSV ulcers, recalcitrant warts (anogenital, periungual) and molluscum in immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant), recurrent respiratory papillomatosis
- Intralesional: recalcitrant warts (case series)

## Dose & formulations
- IV: 5 mg/kg once weekly × 2, then every 2 weeks — always with probenecid (2 g 3 h before, 1 g at 2 and 8 h after) and 1 L normal saline
- Topical 1–3% once daily, 5 days a week, for several cycles

## Adverse effects
- IV: dose-limiting nephrotoxicity (proximal tubule — Fanconi syndrome), neutropenia, ocular hypotony/uveitis, metabolic acidosis
- Topical: local erosion, ulceration, burning (inflammation is common); absorption from large areas can cause renal toxicity

## Contraindications
- Renal impairment (creatinine >1.5 mg/dL or proteinuria), concurrent nephrotoxic drugs, probenecid/sulfa allergy (for IV)
- Pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, foscarnet, NSAIDs, tenofovir)

## Monitoring
- Creatinine and urine protein before each IV dose; CBC; eye exams

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (carcinogenic/teratogenic in animals).

## Viva points
- Nucleotide analogue — TK-independent
- Topical cidofovir for warts/molluscum in HIV and acyclovir-resistant HSV
- IV always with probenecid and saline (nephrotoxicity)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.3 and ch.20 (Cidofovir); Wolverton 4e ch.11 and ch.43. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clarithromycin
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Semisynthetic 14-membered macrolide
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Semisynthetic 14-membered macrolide

## Mechanism of action
- 50S ribosomal inhibitor; bactericidal against M. leprae; active against many atypical mycobacteria

## Pharmacokinetics
- Acid-stable; active 14-hydroxy metabolite; potent CYP3A4 inhibitor

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Atypical mycobacterial infections (backbone drug): M. marinum, M. chelonae/abscessus/fortuitum, MAC, M. ulcerans (with rifampicin)
- Leprosy (second-line, rifampicin-resistant regimens)
- Skin infections in penicillin allergy, acne (alternative), H. pylori (associated urticaria)
- Bacillary angiomatosis

## Dose & formulations
- 250–500 mg twice daily (NTM: 500 mg twice daily for months)

## Adverse effects
- Taste disturbance (metallic), GI upset
- QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity
- Possible increase in long-term cardiac mortality in heart disease patients (FDA advisory)

## Contraindications
- With colchicine in renal/hepatic impairment (fatal toxicity), simvastatin/lovastatin, ergot, pimozide; long QT

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: colchicine, statins, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, carbamazepine, warfarin, rifampicin (reduces clarithromycin; rifabutin uveitis)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid unless necessary (animal teratogenicity; old FDA category C).

## Viva points
- Key drug for NTM skin infections
- Colchicine + clarithromycin = fatal toxicity

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 and ch.6; Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clindamycin + Nicotinamide gel
posts.summary: II Antibacterials · Combination: lincosamide antibiotic + vitamin B3 (anti-inflammatory)
posts.body:
_Topicals · II Antibacterials_

**Class:** Combination: lincosamide antibiotic + vitamin B3 (anti-inflammatory)

## Mechanism of action
- Clindamycin: 50S protein-synthesis inhibitor (anti-C. acnes)
- Nicotinamide 4%: anti-inflammatory (inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis, IL-8, mast cells), reduces sebum, improves barrier
- Nicotinamide is non-antibiotic, so the combination may reduce reliance on the antibiotic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Mild–moderate inflammatory acne

## Dose & formulations
- Usually clindamycin 1% + nicotinamide 4% gel once or twice daily; combine with BPO or a retinoid; limit antibiotic use to about 12 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Dryness, irritation, burning

## Contraindications
- As for clindamycin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Acceptable.

## Viva points
- Nicotinamide 4% gel alone is comparable to clindamycin 1% in some trials
- Combination still needs BPO to prevent resistance

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.41 and ch.57 (nicotinamide); Khopkar ch.28 (topical niacinamide). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clindamycin (topical gel + oral)
posts.summary: II Antibacterials · Lincosamide antibiotic (topical)
posts.body:
_Topicals · II Antibacterials_

**Class:** Lincosamide antibiotic (topical)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit → inhibits bacterial protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)
- Reduces C. acnes and the free fatty acids it produces; anti-inflammatory (reduces neutrophil chemotaxis)
- Phosphate ester is inactive until hydrolysed in the skin

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Inflammatory acne vulgaris (papules, pustules) — always combined with benzoyl peroxide (BPO) to prevent resistance
- Folliculitis, hidradenitis suppurativa (mild, Hurley I), rosacea (alternative), pitted keratolysis, erythrasma
- Also in the anti-acne list (group VII)

## Dose & formulations
- Thin layer once or twice daily
- Fixed combinations: clindamycin 1% + BPO 2.5–5%; clindamycin 1.2% + tretinoin 0.025%; clindamycin + adapalene; clindamycin + nicotinamide
- Do not use as monotherapy and limit to about 12 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Dryness, peeling, irritation
- C. acnes and staphylococcal resistance with monotherapy
- C. difficile colitis is very rare (case reports)

## Contraindications
- History of inflammatory bowel disease or antibiotic-associated colitis
- Hypersensitivity to lincomycin/clindamycin

## Drug interactions
- Erythromycin topical — antagonism (both act at 50S)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy (preferred topical antibiotic with BPO).

## Viva points
- Never use topical antibiotics alone for acne — always with BPO (resistance)
- Safe in pregnancy
- Rare pseudomembranous colitis — ask about bowel disease

## Oral form: Clindamycin oral
_Lincosamide (oral/IV)_

**Mechanism**
- 50S ribosomal inhibitor; also suppresses toxin production by staphylococci and streptococci (useful in necrotising infections)

**Indications**
- Hidradenitis suppurativa: clindamycin 300 mg + rifampicin 300 mg twice daily for 10–12 weeks
- Staphylococcal/streptococcal skin infections in penicillin allergy; community MRSA (if sensitive)
- Necrotising fasciitis and toxic shock syndrome (with penicillin — antitoxin effect); anaerobic infections; BV (oral/vaginal)

**Dose & how to apply**
- 150–450 mg four times daily (adults); children 10–25 mg/kg/day

**Adverse effects**
- Diarrhoea and C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis (classic association)
- Rash, metallic taste, hepatitis (rare)

**Contraindications**
- History of antibiotic-associated colitis

**Interactions**
- Neuromuscular blockers (potentiated); erythromycin (antagonism)

**Pregnancy:** Acceptable in pregnancy.

**Viva points**
- Clindamycin + rifampicin for hidradenitis
- Antitoxin effect in toxic shock
- Classic cause of C. difficile colitis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.41 (Topical antibacterials); Khopkar ch.18; Khopkar ch.1; Wolverton 4e ch.9 and ch.41. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% (ointment, lotion, solution)
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Super-potent fluorinated steroid (US class 1; UK 'very potent')
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Super-potent fluorinated steroid (US class 1; UK 'very potent')

## Mechanism of action
- Most potent glucocorticoid receptor agonist used on skin — strong anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic plaque psoriasis (body; scalp — lotion/solution/shampoo), palmoplantar psoriasis and eczema
- Lichen planus (hypertrophic), lichen simplex chronicus, discoid lupus
- Lichen sclerosus (first-line, including genital — even in children under specialist care)
- Localised bullous pemphigoid (whole-body clobetasol is as effective as oral steroids)
- Alopecia areata (under occlusion), vitiligo (limited areas, short pulses)

## Dose & formulations
- Once or twice daily; maximum 50 g per week; usually no more than 2 weeks continuously, then taper or use pulsed/weekend therapy
- Bullous pemphigoid: 10–40 g/day initially over the whole body (except face), then taper over months
- Lichen sclerosus: once daily for 1 month, alternate days for 1 month, twice weekly for 1 month, then as needed

## Adverse effects
- All topical steroid side effects — most likely with this agent: atrophy, striae, purpura, telangiectasia, steroid rosacea, tinea incognito, HPA suppression with large areas, Cushing syndrome
- Commonly misused in India in fairness and 'itch' creams — leading cause of topical steroid-damaged face

## Contraindications
- Face, flexures, genitals (except lichen sclerosus), children under 12 (except specialist use)
- Rosacea, acne, perioral dermatitis, untreated infection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid large areas/long courses (association with low birth weight).

## Viva points
- Most potent topical steroid: max 50 g/week, 2 weeks
- First-line for lichen sclerosus and localised bullous pemphigoid
- Ointment more potent than cream; lotion/solution for scalp

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clobetasol + Salicylic acid
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Combination: super-potent steroid (clobetasol 0.05%) + keratolytic (salicylic acid 3–6%)
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Combination: super-potent steroid (clobetasol 0.05%) + keratolytic (salicylic acid 3–6%)

## Mechanism of action
- Salicylic acid removes scale (desmolytic), allowing better steroid penetration

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Thick plaque and scalp psoriasis (lotion/ointment), palmoplantar psoriasis, hyperkeratotic hand eczema, lichen simplex chronicus

## Dose & formulations
- Once or twice daily for up to 2 weeks; maximum 50 g/week; then switch to a maintenance regimen

## Adverse effects
- Steroid atrophy, striae, HPA suppression; salicylic acid irritation; salicylism over large areas

## Contraindications
- Face, flexures, genitals, children; large areas; infection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid large areas.

## Viva points
- Same principle as halobetasol + SA
- Avoid on more than about 20% of body surface (salicylism and steroid absorption)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45 and ch.55; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clofazimine
posts.summary: Antileprosy drugs · Riminophenazine dye; antimycobacterial and anti-inflammatory
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** Riminophenazine dye; antimycobacterial and anti-inflammatory

## Mechanism of action
- Binds guanine bases of mycobacterial DNA → inhibits replication; generates reactive oxygen species (weakly bactericidal)
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits neutrophil motility and lymphocyte proliferation; stimulates phagocyte activity
- Very lipophilic — accumulates in fat and macrophages (crystals in tissues)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Variable absorption, better with food; very long half-life (about 70 days); stored in fat and reticuloendothelial system

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Leprosy — part of MB-MDT (and now 3-drug PB regimen)
- Erythema nodosum leprosum (steroid-sparing for chronic/recurrent ENL)
- Off-label: discoid lupus, pyoderma gangrenosum, granulomatous cheilitis (Melkersson–Rosenthal), granuloma annulare, Sweet syndrome
- MDR-TB (newer regimens) and Mycobacterium avium complex

## Dose & formulations
- MDT adult: 300 mg once a month (supervised) + 50 mg daily
- ENL: 100 mg three times daily (300 mg/day) for no more than 12 weeks, then taper to 100 mg/day; takes 4–6 weeks to act — combine with steroids initially
- Capsules 50 and 100 mg, with food

## Adverse effects
- Reddish-brown to purple-black skin pigmentation (dose-related; most marked in lesions; fades over months to years after stopping) — may cause social stigma and depression
- Red-brown discolouration of conjunctiva, tears, sweat, urine, sputum, breast milk
- Ichthyosis/xerosis (especially legs)
- GI: abdominal pain, diarrhoea; crystal-deposition enteropathy with high doses (can mimic acute abdomen — splenic infarction rare)
- QT prolongation

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in pre-existing GI disease and long QT

## Drug interactions
- QT-prolonging drugs (bedaquiline, fluoroquinolones, macrolides)
- May reduce the effect of rifampicin slightly (not significant clinically)

## Monitoring
- Weight, abdominal symptoms on high doses; ECG if other QT drugs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy within MDT (WHO); infants may be born with pigmentation (reversible).

## Viva points
- Pigmentation is the main side effect — counsel before starting
- Anti-inflammatory action used in ENL (300 mg/day max 3 months)
- Crystal enteropathy with high-dose use

_Sources: Khopkar ch.6; Wolverton 4e ch.40 (Miscellaneous systemic drugs — clofazimine). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clotrimazole + Beclomethasone cream
posts.summary: V Steroid combinations · Combination: imidazole antifungal (clotrimazole 1%) + potent fluorinated steroid (beclomethasone dipropionate 0.025%)
posts.body:
_Topicals · V Steroid combinations_

**Class:** Combination: imidazole antifungal (clotrimazole 1%) + potent fluorinated steroid (beclomethasone dipropionate 0.025%)

## Mechanism of action
- Clotrimazole: ergosterol synthesis inhibitor
- Beclomethasone: rapid relief of itch and inflammation

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Limited valid use: short-term (under 1–2 weeks) for highly inflamed candidal intertrigo or dermatophyte infection, under a doctor's supervision
- In practice it is heavily misused (OTC) in India for any itchy rash

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily for a maximum of about 1–2 weeks; then continue plain antifungal

## Adverse effects
- Steroid-modified tinea (tinea incognito) — extensive, atypical, chronic, recurrent dermatophytosis
- Atrophy, striae (especially groin and thighs), telangiectasia, topical steroid dependence
- Majocchi granuloma (deep fungal folliculitis), treatment failure, increasing antifungal resistance

## Contraindications
- Tinea when used for more than a short period; children, face, flexures (steroid absorption)
- Not for self-medication

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Irrational/misused FDC — a key driver of India's chronic dermatophytosis epidemic
- Many steroid–antifungal–antibiotic FDCs were banned by the Indian government in 2018; IADVL campaigns against steroid misuse
- Treat tinea with antifungal alone

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42 and ch.45 (misuse of combinations); Khopkar ch.19 and ch.22; IADVL taskforce on steroid abuse. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Clotrimazole (cream, solution, dusting powder, paint, soap)
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Azoles · Imidazole antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase → ergosterol depletion; fungistatic (fungicidal at high concentration)
- Broad spectrum: dermatophytes, Candida, Malassezia; some Gram-positive bacteria

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous candidiasis (intertrigo, napkin candidiasis, paronychia), tinea corporis/cruris/pedis, pityriasis versicolor
- Dusting powder: prevention in moist areas (groin, toe webs, folds) after the cream clears infection
- Mouth paint 1%: oral thrush; vaginal tablets/cream: vulvovaginal candidiasis
- Solution: hairy areas, nails folds, ear (otomycosis)
- Soap: adjunct only (short contact time)

## Dose & formulations
- Cream 1%: twice daily, continue 2 weeks after clinical cure (usually 2–4 weeks)
- Powder 1%: once or twice daily on dry skin
- Mouth paint 1%: 3–4 times daily for 1–2 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Burning, irritation, rare contact dermatitis

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe — preferred topical azole for vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Workhorse imidazole for candidiasis
- Powders are for prevention, not treatment of active infection
- Clotrimazole + steroid combinations are widely misused (see the combination post)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42; Khopkar ch.19. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole)
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Fixed combination of a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor (trimethoprim) and a sulfonamide (sulfamethoxazole) in 1:5 ratio
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Fixed combination of a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor (trimethoprim) and a sulfonamide (sulfamethoxazole) in 1:5 ratio

## Mechanism of action
- Sequential blockade of bacterial folate synthesis: sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
- Together they are bactericidal and slow resistance

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Community MRSA skin infections (abscess, furunculosis — after drainage)
- Actinomycetoma (Nocardia): with dapsone or amikacin (two-step and Welsh regimens) — long courses
- Nocardiosis, M. marinum (limited disease), donovanosis (alternative), chancroid (older regimen)
- Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis: HIV (CD4 under 200) and patients on high-dose steroids, rituximab, cyclophosphamide
- Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis, UTI, Whipple disease

## Dose & formulations
- Double-strength tablet (160/800 mg) twice daily for skin infections
- Actinomycetoma: 160/800 mg twice daily (or 8–10 mg/kg/day trimethoprim component) for many months
- PCP prophylaxis: one double-strength tablet daily or three times weekly

## Adverse effects
- Skin reactions are frequent: morbilliform rash, fixed drug eruption (a classic cause), SJS/TEN (sulfonamides are among the highest-risk drugs; much higher in HIV), DRESS, photosensitivity
- Bone marrow suppression (folate antagonism), megaloblastic anaemia; haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
- Hyperkalaemia (trimethoprim blocks ENaC), raised creatinine; hepatitis; aseptic meningitis
- Kernicterus in newborns (sulfonamide displaces bilirubin)

## Contraindications
- Sulfonamide allergy; severe liver/kidney disease; megaloblastic anaemia
- Late pregnancy and neonates under 6 weeks; G6PD deficiency (caution)

## Drug interactions
- Methotrexate: severe, sometimes fatal pancytopenia — avoid
- Warfarin (INR rises), phenytoin, sulfonylureas (hypoglycaemia)
- ACE inhibitors, spironolactone: hyperkalaemia; dapsone: more methaemoglobinaemia

## Monitoring
- CBC and potassium on long courses (mycetoma); stop at first sign of rash with mucosal involvement

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in first trimester (folate antagonist) and near term (kernicterus) unless essential (e.g. PCP prophylaxis in HIV).

## Viva points
- Sequential block of folate pathway
- Never combine with methotrexate
- Common cause of FDE and SJS/TEN, especially in HIV
- Drug of choice backbone for actinomycetoma

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Cotrimoxazole, Sulfonamides); Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Coal tar (crude coal tar, LCD)
posts.summary: Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics · Distillation product of coal (crude coal tar 1–5%; liquor carbonis detergens 5–20%)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics_

**Class:** Distillation product of coal (crude coal tar 1–5%; liquor carbonis detergens 5–20%)

## Mechanism of action
- Aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist → normalises keratinocyte differentiation (restores filaggrin), antiproliferative, anti-inflammatory, antipruritic; photosensitises to UVA

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic plaque and scalp psoriasis, palmoplantar psoriasis, atopic dermatitis (lichenified), lichen simplex, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Goeckerman regimen (crude coal tar + UVB, inpatient)
- Tar baths (Ingram regimen)

## Dose & formulations
- Crude coal tar 1–5% in petrolatum or zinc paste; LCD 5–20% in creams, shampoos and bath additives; apply at night

## Adverse effects
- Smell, staining, folliculitis (tar acne), irritant dermatitis, phototoxicity ('tar smarts'), keratoacanthomas/carcinogenicity (occupational, theoretical with therapy)

## Contraindications
- Erythrodermic/pustular psoriasis, infected skin, pregnancy (relative)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (theoretical carcinogenicity).

## Viva points
- AhR ligand; Goeckerman regimen (tar + UVB)
- Tar folliculitis and phototoxicity

_Sources: Khopkar ch.28 (Coal tar); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Coal tar + Ketoconazole scalp lotion/shampoo
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Other · Combination: keratoplastic/antiproliferative tar + imidazole antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Other_

**Class:** Combination: keratoplastic/antiproliferative tar + imidazole antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Coal tar: antiproliferative (activates aryl hydrocarbon receptor → normalises keratinocyte differentiation), antipruritic, anti-inflammatory
- Ketoconazole: reduces Malassezia load
- Together they treat scaling, inflammation and the yeast driver in scalp disease

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff of scalp, especially thick scaling
- Scalp psoriasis (mild) and sebopsoriasis

## Dose & formulations
- Lotion: apply to scalp at night, wash next morning (or as directed) 2–3 times weekly
- Shampoo: lather, leave 3–5 min, rinse; 2–3 times weekly, then weekly for maintenance

## Adverse effects
- Tar: odour, staining of hair (especially grey/blonde) and fabrics, folliculitis, irritation, photosensitivity
- Ketoconazole: irritation, dry hair

## Contraindications
- Acutely inflamed or broken scalp skin; infected scalp
- Avoid tar in pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Coal tar: avoid in pregnancy (theoretical carcinogenicity); ketoconazole topical safe.

## Viva points
- Tar = AhR agonist (normalises differentiation), ketoconazole = anti-Malassezia
- Tar shampoos may stain grey hair yellow

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.51 (Therapeutic shampoos) and ch.57 (Miscellaneous topicals — tar); Khopkar ch.28. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Coal tar + Salicylic acid
posts.summary: VI Keratolytics & emollients · Combination: tar (antiproliferative, antipruritic) + salicylic acid (keratolytic)
posts.body:
_Topicals · VI Keratolytics & emollients_

**Class:** Combination: tar (antiproliferative, antipruritic) + salicylic acid (keratolytic)

## Mechanism of action
- Coal tar activates the aryl hydrocarbon receptor → normalises keratinocyte differentiation, reduces proliferation (antimitotic), anti-inflammatory, antipruritic; also photosensitises (UVA)
- Salicylic acid removes scale and helps tar penetrate

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic plaque psoriasis (body and scalp), palmoplantar psoriasis
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff (shampoo), lichen simplex chronicus, chronic eczema
- Goeckerman regimen: crude coal tar followed by UVB

## Dose & formulations
- Ointment/lotion: apply at night, wash off in the morning; shampoo 2–3 times weekly
- Crude coal tar 1–5% or liquor carbonis detergens (LCD) 5–20%

## Adverse effects
- Odour, staining of skin, hair and clothes
- Tar folliculitis (tar acne), irritation, contact dermatitis
- Phototoxicity ('tar smarts' — burning on sun exposure)
- Carcinogenicity in occupational exposure; risk from therapeutic use is not proven

## Contraindications
- Acute, pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis; infected or broken skin
- Face, flexures, genitals (relative); pregnancy (relative)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (theoretical carcinogen/mutagen).

## Viva points
- Tar = AhR ligand
- Goeckerman regimen: tar + UVB
- Tar folliculitis and 'tar smarts'

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.57 (tar) and ch.55; Khopkar ch.28. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Colchicine
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Alkaloid from Colchicum autumnale; anti-mitotic, anti-inflammatory
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Alkaloid from Colchicum autumnale; anti-mitotic, anti-inflammatory

## Mechanism of action
- Binds tubulin and prevents microtubule polymerisation
- This blocks neutrophil migration, adhesion and degranulation, and inflammasome (NLRP3) activation
- Also an anti-mitotic (metaphase arrest) at higher concentrations

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorbed in the gut; enterohepatic circulation; metabolised by CYP3A4 and pumped out by P-gp
- Narrow therapeutic index

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Behçet disease (mucocutaneous ulcers, erythema nodosum)
- Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (chronic cutaneous), urticarial vasculitis
- Recurrent aphthous stomatitis, Sweet syndrome, erythema nodosum leprosum (adjunct)
- Dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, linear IgA, palmoplantar pustulosis
- Familial Mediterranean fever, gout

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5–0.6 mg once to three times daily (usually 0.5 mg twice daily; Wolverton lists 0.6 mg twice daily)
- Reduce dose in renal/hepatic impairment or the elderly

## Adverse effects
- GI (the commonest, dose-limiting): diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain — start low
- Myelosuppression, myopathy and neuropathy (especially with renal impairment or interacting drugs)
- Overdose is often fatal (above 0.8 mg/kg): multiorgan failure, alopecia in survivors
- Reversible azoospermia

## Contraindications
- Severe renal or hepatic impairment
- Combination with strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors in patients with renal or hepatic impairment

## Drug interactions
- Clarithromycin, erythromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, cyclosporine, verapamil, diltiazem: raise colchicine levels → fatal toxicity reported
- Statins and fibrates: myopathy

## Monitoring
- CBC, renal function, LFT and CK periodically on long-term use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Can be continued in pregnancy for familial Mediterranean fever (old FDA category C); generally avoid for skin disease. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Microtubule inhibitor → neutrophil inhibitor
- Main use: Behçet and cutaneous vasculitis
- Diarrhoea is the dose-limiting side effect
- Clarithromycin/cyclosporine interaction can be fatal

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40; Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.summary: Miscellaneous topicals & wound care · Enzymatic debriding agent (clostridial collagenase from Clostridium histolyticum)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Enzymatic debriding agent (clostridial collagenase from Clostridium histolyticum)

## Mechanism of action
- Digests native collagen in necrotic tissue → selective debridement without harming viable tissue

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Debridement of chronic dermal ulcers and severe burns (necrotic/sloughy tissue)
- Injectable collagenase: Dupuytren contracture, Peyronie disease (systemic forms)

## Dose & formulations
- Once daily to the wound bed (2 mm layer), covered with moist dressing; stop when wound is clean

## Adverse effects
- Local erythema, burning

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Inactivated by silver, iodine, hexachlorophene, heavy metals and acidic solutions

## Pregnancy & lactation
Acceptable.

## Viva points
- Selective enzymatic debridement; incompatible with silver/iodine

_Sources: Khopkar ch.32 (Collagenase); Wolverton 4e ch.54. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Combined oral contraceptives (in dermatology)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Oestrogen (ethinylestradiol) + progestin combinations
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Oestrogen (ethinylestradiol) + progestin combinations

## Mechanism of action
- Suppress ovarian androgen production (LH suppression), raise sex hormone-binding globulin (less free testosterone), reduce sebum
- Progestins with anti-androgenic action preferred: drospirenone, cyproterone, chlormadinone, dienogest; avoid androgenic progestins (levonorgestrel, norgestrel)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne in women (FDA-approved COCs: drospirenone, norgestimate, norethindrone acetate/ferrous fumarate combinations)
- Hirsutism, PCOS, female pattern hair loss, hidradenitis suppurativa
- Contraception during teratogenic therapy (isotretinoin, acitretin, thalidomide, spironolactone)

## Dose & formulations
- One tablet daily (21/7 or 24/4 regimens); acne improves after 3–6 cycles

## Adverse effects
- Venous thromboembolism (higher with drospirenone/cyproterone than levonorgestrel), stroke/MI (smokers >35)
- Nausea, breast tenderness, breakthrough bleeding, mood change, melasma (can worsen), erythema nodosum, photosensitivity, spider angiomas
- Hypertension

## Contraindications
- Thrombosis history or thrombophilia, smokers over 35, migraine with aura, uncontrolled hypertension, liver disease, oestrogen-dependent cancer, breastfeeding <6 weeks

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, griseofulvin, carbamazepine, efavirenz) reduce efficacy
- Tetracyclines: no clinically significant reduction (except rifampicin) per current evidence

## Monitoring
- BP, migraine history, smoking status

## Pregnancy & lactation
Stop if pregnant.

## Viva points
- Choose anti-androgenic progestins for acne
- Melasma and erythema nodosum can be caused by COCs
- Rifampicin and griseofulvin reduce efficacy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34; Khopkar (Antiandrogens — oral contraceptives). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Contact sensitisers: DPCP, DNCB, SADBE
posts.summary: Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics · Topical immunotherapy with strong contact allergens — diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP), dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB), sq
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics_

**Class:** Topical immunotherapy with strong contact allergens — diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP), dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB), squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE)

## Mechanism of action
- Induce allergic contact dermatitis (type IV) at the site → 'antigenic competition': recruits suppressor T cells and cytokines that disrupt the autoimmune attack on hair follicles or the immune evasion of HPV
- DNCB is mutagenic (Ames test) — largely abandoned; DPCP and SADBE are preferred

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Extensive or chronic alopecia areata (DPCP — the most studied; response 30–60%)
- Recalcitrant viral warts, multiple warts in children (SADBE/DPCP)

## Dose & formulations
- Sensitise with 2% DPCP to a small area (arm/scalp patch); after 2 weeks apply weekly starting at 0.001%, increasing concentration until a mild eczematous reaction (itch and erythema lasting 24–36 h) is achieved; leave 48 h, shield from light (DPCP is light-degraded)
- Regrowth after 8–12 weeks; continue for at least 6 months before calling failure
- Wear gloves; store in amber bottles

## Adverse effects
- Severe eczema, blistering, regional lymphadenopathy
- Pigmentary changes — dyschromia in confetti pattern, vitiligo (especially dark skin)
- Urticaria, erythema multiforme-like reactions; sensitisation of staff (gloves)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and women planning pregnancy; DNCB (mutagenic) — not recommended

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (DPCP not studied; DNCB mutagenic).

## Viva points
- Antigenic competition mechanism
- DNCB mutagenic → DPCP preferred
- Shield DPCP from light; titrate to mild dermatitis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.23 (DNCB, DPCP, SADBE); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Copper
posts.summary: Vitamins & trace elements · Trace element (oral copper salts; copper peptides topically)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements_

**Class:** Trace element (oral copper salts; copper peptides topically)

## Mechanism of action
- Cofactor of tyrosinase (melanin), lysyl oxidase (collagen and elastin cross-linking), cytochrome oxidase, superoxide dismutase

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Copper deficiency (malnutrition, high-dose zinc, bariatric surgery): hypopigmentation of skin and hair, anaemia, neutropenia, neuropathy
- Menkes kinky hair disease (copper histidinate injections — early)
- Topical copper peptides (GHK-Cu): wound healing, cosmeceuticals

## Dose & formulations
- Oral copper 2–4 mg/day elemental for deficiency (specialist guidance)

## Adverse effects
- Excess: GI upset, hepatic toxicity; Wilson disease (copper accumulation — Kayser–Fleischer rings, azure lunulae)

## Contraindications
- Wilson disease

## Drug interactions
- Zinc reduces copper absorption (used therapeutically in Wilson disease)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Dietary amounts safe.

## Viva points
- Menkes disease — pili torti, hypopigmentation; Wilson disease — azure lunulae
- Long-term zinc causes copper deficiency

_Sources: Khopkar (Trace elements — copper; copper peptides). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Crisaborole 2% ointment
posts.summary: IX Immunomodulators · Topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (boron-containing benzoxaborole)
posts.body:
_Topicals · IX Immunomodulators_

**Class:** Topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (boron-containing benzoxaborole)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits PDE4 → increases intracellular cAMP → reduces TNF-α, IL-12, IL-23 and other cytokines
- Small molecule with boron atom → good skin penetration; rapidly metabolised to inactive forms when absorbed

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Mild–moderate atopic dermatitis in patients aged 3 months and older (approved)
- Off-label: seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis (intertriginous), vitiligo (limited)

## Dose & formulations
- Thin layer twice daily to affected areas

## Adverse effects
- Application-site burning or stinging (about 4%)
- Contact urticaria (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; limited data.

## Viva points
- Non-steroidal, PDE4 → ↑cAMP
- Approved from 3 months of age
- Burning at application is the main complaint

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.18 (PDE4 inhibitors — crisaborole); Khopkar edition predates it. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Crotamiton (10%)
posts.summary: Scabicides & pediculicides · Scabicide with antipruritic action
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Scabicides & pediculicides_

**Class:** Scabicide with antipruritic action

## Mechanism of action
- Mechanism unclear; weakly scabicidal; antipruritic (blocks TRPV4 itch channel)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Scabies (second-line, less effective), post-scabetic itch, pruritus of other causes

## Dose & formulations
- Scabies: apply neck down for 2–5 consecutive nights, wash off 48 h after last application

## Adverse effects
- Irritation, contact dermatitis; low efficacy (frequent failure)

## Contraindications
- Raw/weeping skin, mucosa

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; permethrin preferred.

## Viva points
- Weak scabicide but good antipruritic — post-scabetic itch

_Sources: Khopkar ch.21 (Crotamiton); Wolverton 4e ch.44. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cyclophosphamide injection
posts.summary: V Immunosuppressants · Nitrogen mustard alkylating agent (prodrug)
posts.body:
_Injectables · V Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Nitrogen mustard alkylating agent (prodrug)

## Mechanism of action
- Activated in the liver (CYP2B6, 2C19) to phosphoramide mustard, which cross-links DNA strands (guanine N7) → cell death; cell-cycle non-specific
- Strongly suppresses B cells (antibody production) and T cells
- By-product acrolein causes bladder toxicity

## Pharmacokinetics
- Oral and IV; metabolites excreted in urine — reduce dose in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pemphigus: DCP pulse (dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide; third line in the Derma Desk ladder); also refractory pemphigoid and mucous membrane pemphigoid (ocular)
- Systemic vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, polyarteritis nodosa), lupus nephritis, dermatomyositis with lung disease, systemic sclerosis lung
- Lymphoma/mycosis fungoides (oncology), pyoderma gangrenosum (refractory)

## Dose & formulations
- DCP: 500 mg IV on day 1 of each monthly dexamethasone pulse, plus 50 mg orally daily between pulses
- Vasculitis/lupus (IV pulse): 500–1000 mg/m² (or 15 mg/kg) monthly
- Oral: 1–2 mg/kg/day
- Give in the morning with plenty of fluid (2–3 L/day), frequent voiding; mesna with high IV doses

## Adverse effects
- Bone marrow suppression (nadir 8–14 days)
- Haemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein) and bladder cancer (long-term, cumulative) — prevent with hydration and mesna
- Infertility: premature ovarian failure, azoospermia (consider sperm/oocyte preservation)
- Nausea, vomiting, alopecia (anagen effluvium), nail and skin hyperpigmentation
- Infections (including PJP — consider co-trimoxazole prophylaxis), secondary malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma, skin cancer)
- SIADH, pulmonary fibrosis, cardiotoxicity (high doses)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding; active serious infection; bone marrow failure
- Urinary outflow obstruction

## Drug interactions
- Allopurinol: increases marrow toxicity
- Enzyme inducers (phenobarbital, rifampicin) increase toxic metabolites
- Succinylcholine: prolonged apnoea (cyclophosphamide inhibits pseudocholinesterase)

## Monitoring
- CBC weekly to 2-weekly during therapy; urine for blood monthly and then for life (bladder cancer risk)
- Renal function, LFT; pregnancy test; fertility counselling

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D) — teratogenic. Effective contraception during and for some months after treatment.

## Viva points
- Prodrug activated in the liver; acrolein → haemorrhagic cystitis; mesna is the antidote for the bladder
- Lifelong urine checks for bladder cancer
- DCP regimen for pemphigus (Pasricha)
- Fertility counselling before starting

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.19 (Cytotoxic agents); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs; DCP pulse). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cyclosporine
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclic peptide from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclic peptide from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds cyclophilin inside T cells; the complex inhibits calcineurin
- Calcineurin cannot dephosphorylate NFAT, so NFAT does not enter the nucleus → less IL-2 and other cytokines → T-cell activation blocked
- Also inhibits mast-cell and keratinocyte activation

## Pharmacokinetics
- Microemulsion form (Neoral and generics) has more reliable absorption than the old form (Sandimmune) — do not switch between brands casually
- Metabolised by CYP3A4; excreted in bile
- Grapefruit juice raises levels

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Severe psoriasis — rapid control ('crisis' drug), erythrodermic and generalised pustular psoriasis
- Severe atopic dermatitis (approved in Europe)
- Chronic urticaria (refractory to antihistamines)
- SJS/TEN (early use may reduce mortality; first line in the Derma Desk SJS ladder)
- Pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet disease, lichen planus, chronic actinic dermatitis, prurigo nodularis, immunobullous diseases (adjunct)

## Dose & formulations
- Psoriasis/atopic dermatitis: 2.5–5 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (Wolverton favours starting at the higher end for rapid control, then tapering)
- Taper by 0.5–1 mg/kg every 2–4 weeks once controlled
- Short courses (intermittent therapy, 12–16 weeks) are preferred; continuous use generally limited to 1–2 years
- Capsules 25, 50, 100 mg; oral solution 100 mg/mL

## Adverse effects
- Nephrotoxicity — the most important; dose- and duration-dependent; early functional (vasoconstriction) then irreversible interstitial fibrosis
- Hypertension (about a quarter of psoriasis patients)
- Hypertrichosis, gingival hyperplasia, sebaceous hyperplasia, follicular keratosis
- Tremor, headache, paraesthesia; hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia
- Increased skin cancer (especially after previous PUVA) and lymphoma; infections

## Contraindications
- Uncontrolled hypertension, abnormal renal function
- Malignancy (except non-melanoma skin cancer, with caution); high cumulative PUVA (above about 200 treatments)
- Concurrent phototherapy; active serious infection; live vaccines

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels (nephrotoxicity): azoles (ketoconazole, itraconazole), macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), diltiazem, verapamil, grapefruit
- CYP3A4 inducers lower levels (rejection/flare): rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort
- Additive nephrotoxicity: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides
- Statins (myopathy), potassium-sparing diuretics (hyperkalaemia)

## Monitoring
- Blood pressure and serum creatinine twice at baseline, then every 2 weeks for 1–2 months, then monthly
- If creatinine rises more than 25–30% above baseline (on two readings), reduce dose by 25–50%; stop if it stays high
- Also: K⁺, Mg²⁺, uric acid, lipids, LFT, CBC, urine
- Trough levels are not needed routinely in dermatology

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not teratogenic in humans (old FDA category C); has been used in transplant pregnancies, but prematurity and low birth weight are reported. Avoid breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Calcineurin–NFAT–IL-2 pathway
- Most important side effects: nephrotoxicity and hypertension
- Creatinine rule: more than 25–30% above baseline → reduce dose
- Microemulsion form has better absorption
- Avoid with PUVA history and with phototherapy (skin cancer)

## Note on sources
Wolverton notes that recent guidelines use a 25% creatinine threshold while the traditional dermatology threshold is 30% — both are mentioned.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.17 (Cyclosporine); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cyproheptadine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · First-generation H1 antihistamine — piperidine; also serotonin (5-HT2) antagonist
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** First-generation H1 antihistamine — piperidine; also serotonin (5-HT2) antagonist

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks H1 and 5-HT2 receptors; anticholinergic; appetite stimulant

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cold urticaria (drug of choice among older agents), chronic urticaria, pruritus
- Serotonin syndrome (antidote), appetite stimulation, migraine prophylaxis in children

## Dose & formulations
- 4 mg three times daily (max 32 mg/day); children 0.25 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, increased appetite and weight gain, anticholinergic effects

## Contraindications
- Glaucoma, urinary retention, neonates, elderly debilitated

## Drug interactions
- Reduces effect of SSRIs; CNS depressants

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in late pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Antiserotonergic — cold urticaria and serotonin syndrome; causes weight gain

_Sources: Khopkar (First generation H1 antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cyproterone acetate (± ethinylestradiol)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Progestogen with strong anti-androgenic activity (androgen receptor blocker)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Progestogen with strong anti-androgenic activity (androgen receptor blocker)

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks androgen receptors; as a progestogen suppresses LH → lower ovarian androgen production
- With ethinylestradiol (2 mg + 35 µg) acts as a combined oral contraceptive

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne in women (moderate–severe, not responding to other therapy), hirsutism, PCOS, female pattern hair loss
- High-dose: prostate cancer, paraphilias (men)

## Dose & formulations
- CPA 2 mg + ethinylestradiol 35 µg daily for 21 days, 7-day break
- Severe hirsutism: add CPA 25–100 mg on days 1–10 of cycle (reverse sequential regimen)

## Adverse effects
- Venous thromboembolism (higher than some other COCs)
- Meningioma with long-term high doses (EMA restriction 2020 — use lowest dose, MRI if symptoms)
- Hepatotoxicity at high doses, mood change, weight gain, breast tenderness, loss of libido

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, thrombosis history, liver disease, meningioma, smokers over 35, migraine with aura

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine) reduce efficacy

## Monitoring
- BP, weight; LFT at high doses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (feminises male fetus).

## Viva points
- Anti-androgen + contraceptive in one pill
- Meningioma risk with long-term high doses
- Stop 3 cycles after acne clears (VTE risk)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34; Khopkar (Antiandrogens). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dapsone (oral + topical gel)
posts.summary: Antileprosy drugs · Sulfone (4,4'-diaminodiphenyl sulfone); antibacterial and anti-inflammatory
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** Sulfone (4,4'-diaminodiphenyl sulfone); antibacterial and anti-inflammatory

## Mechanism of action
- Antibacterial: like sulfonamides, competes with PABA and inhibits dihydropteroate synthase → no folate synthesis in M. leprae (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits neutrophil myeloperoxidase and the halide–peroxide system → less oxidative tissue damage
- Also inhibits neutrophil adherence (integrin-mediated) and chemotaxis, and eosinophil peroxidase
- Hence its value in neutrophil-predominant dermatoses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; half-life about 24–30 h (once daily)
- Metabolised by N-acetylation (fast/slow acetylators) and N-hydroxylation (CYP2C9, 3A4) → hydroxylamine metabolite causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia
- Enterohepatic circulation; excreted in urine

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Leprosy (part of MDT)
- Dermatitis herpetiformis (drug of choice — itch improves within 48–72 h)
- Linear IgA disease, bullous SLE, subcorneal pustular dermatosis, erythema elevatum diutinum, mucous membrane pemphigoid, bullous pemphigoid (adjunct), IgA pemphigus
- Neutrophilic and vasculitic: urticarial vasculitis, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, Sweet syndrome, pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet disease
- Others: chronic urticaria (refractory), granuloma faciale, actinomycetoma (Welsh regimen with co-trimoxazole), loxoscelism, relapsing polychondritis, acne (topical)

## Dose & formulations
- Leprosy: 100 mg daily (adults), 1–2 mg/kg in children
- Dermatoses: start 25–50 mg/day, increase by 25–50 mg weekly to 100–200 mg/day (max usually 300 mg); taper to the lowest effective dose
- Check G6PD before starting
- Tablets 25, 50, 100 mg

## Adverse effects
- Dose-related haemolysis (in everyone; Hb falls 1–2 g/dL) — severe in G6PD deficiency
- Methaemoglobinaemia (dose-related): grey-blue lips, breathlessness, headache; usually tolerated below 10–12%; cimetidine or vitamin E may reduce it; methylene blue for severe cases (not in G6PD deficiency)
- Agranulocytosis (idiosyncratic, usually in the first 3 months) — sore throat, fever
- Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS-like): 2–8 weeks after starting — fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis; linked to HLA-B*13:01 (common in Asians); can be fatal
- Hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice; peripheral motor neuropathy (distal weakness); psychosis
- Exfoliative dermatitis, TEN, fixed drug eruption

## Contraindications
- Severe G6PD deficiency; previous dapsone hypersensitivity
- Caution: anaemia, cardiopulmonary disease (cannot tolerate methaemoglobinaemia), sulfonamide allergy (cross-reactivity uncommon)

## Drug interactions
- Trimethoprim raises dapsone levels (and vice versa) → more methaemoglobinaemia
- Rifampicin lowers dapsone levels (about 7–10 times) — not clinically important in MDT
- Probenecid raises levels; other oxidant drugs (primaquine, nitrates, EMLA/prilocaine) add to methaemoglobinaemia
- Cimetidine reduces hydroxylamine formation (used to lower methaemoglobin)

## Monitoring
- Baseline: G6PD, CBC, LFT, renal function, urine; HLA-B*13:01 where available
- CBC weekly for 4 weeks, every 2 weeks until 12 weeks, then every 3–4 months; LFT periodically; methaemoglobin if symptomatic
- Ask about fever, rash, sore throat and weakness at each visit

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy for leprosy (WHO); risk of neonatal haemolysis and hyperbilirubinaemia near term. Excreted in milk — watch for haemolysis in G6PD-deficient infants.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis
- Haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia are dose-related; agranulocytosis and hypersensitivity syndrome are idiosyncratic
- Check G6PD first; HLA-B*13:01 for dapsone hypersensitivity
- Mechanism in skin: inhibits neutrophil myeloperoxidase

## Topical form: Dapsone gel (5%, 7.5%)
_Topical sulfone in a gel vehicle_

**Mechanism**
- Anti-inflammatory (neutrophil myeloperoxidase inhibition) and antibacterial against C. acnes

**Indications**
- Acne vulgaris (inflammatory, especially in adult women); rosacea (off-label)

**Dose & how to apply**
- 5% gel twice daily or 7.5% gel once daily

**Adverse effects**
- Dryness, redness; temporary orange-brown discolouration if used with benzoyl peroxide
- Blood levels are about 100 times lower than with oral dapsone — no routine G6PD test needed

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity

**Pregnancy:** Limited data; minimal absorption.

**Viva points**
- Topical dapsone + BPO → orange skin staining

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.20 (Dapsone); Khopkar ch.6 (Antileprosy drugs); Wolverton 4e ch.20 and ch.46 (topical dapsone). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Decapeptide lotion (e.g. Melbild/Melgain)
posts.summary: VIII Pigmentary / depigmenting · Synthetic decapeptide (repigmenting agent) — a bFGF-related peptide
posts.body:
_Topicals · VIII Pigmentary / depigmenting_

**Class:** Synthetic decapeptide (repigmenting agent) — a bFGF-related peptide

## Mechanism of action
- Mimics a part of basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), a natural mitogen for melanocytes
- Stimulates melanocyte proliferation and migration, and melanogenesis
- Used to support repigmentation (not depigmentation)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Stable vitiligo (localised and generalised) — adjunct to phototherapy, topical steroids or tacrolimus
- Children and face (steroid-sparing)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply once daily to patches; many protocols advise sun exposure (morning) or NB-UVB after application
- Response takes 3–6 months

## Adverse effects
- Mild itching, burning, redness; generally very well tolerated

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Insufficient data; low absorption.

## Viva points
- A repigmenting peptide, not a depigmenting agent — classified here with pigmentary agents
- bFGF-mimicking decapeptide → melanocyte proliferation
- Evidence is modest (Indian studies)

_Sources: Khopkar (Topical immunomodulators — basic fibroblast growth factor decapeptide). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Deflazacort
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting oxazoline derivative of prednisolone (prodrug)
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting oxazoline derivative of prednisolone (prodrug)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to its active metabolite (21-desacetyl-deflazacort), which acts on the glucocorticoid receptor like prednisolone

## Pharmacokinetics
- Rapidly absorbed and activated; half-life of the active metabolite about 1–2 h but biological effect 12–36 h
- Equivalence: 6 mg deflazacort ≈ 5 mg prednisolone (ratio about 1.2 : 1)
- Little mineralocorticoid effect

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Same indications as prednisolone — used in India as an alternative in children and patients with diabetes or bone loss concerns
- Approved in the USA for Duchenne muscular dystrophy

## Dose & formulations
- Usual 0.5–1.2 mg/kg/day as a single morning dose (6 mg replaces 5 mg prednisolone)
- Tablets 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 mg

## Adverse effects
- Same class side effects as prednisolone
- It is claimed (in Khopkar and product data) to have fewer effects on bone, glucose and weight, but this advantage is modest and inconsistent
- Weight gain and Cushingoid features are still seen

## Contraindications
- Same as other systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inducers lower levels; CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels

## Monitoring
- Same as prednisolone

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; prednisolone is preferred in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- 6 mg deflazacort = 5 mg prednisolone
- Claimed bone- and glucose-sparing, but it still causes the full range of steroid side effects and is more expensive (Khopkar)

## Note on sources
Deflazacort is not covered in Wolverton; Khopkar and product data were used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (Oral and injectable steroids); not covered in Wolverton 4e. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Denileukin diftitox
posts.summary: Biologicals · Fusion protein of interleukin-2 and diphtheria toxin
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Biologicals_

**Class:** Fusion protein of interleukin-2 and diphtheria toxin

## Mechanism of action
- The IL-2 part binds CD25 (IL-2 receptor) on malignant and activated T cells; the diphtheria toxin part enters the cell and stops protein synthesis → cell death

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Persistent or recurrent CD25-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (originally approved 1999, withdrawn 2014; a new formulation was re-approved in the USA in 2024)

## Dose & formulations
- IV infusion daily for 5 days every 21 days (dose per product label)

## Adverse effects
- Capillary leak syndrome (oedema, hypoalbuminaemia, hypotension) — boxed warning
- Infusion reactions, visual loss (rare), hepatotoxicity, infections

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; low albumin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- IL-2–diphtheria toxin fusion targeting CD25 in CTCL; capillary leak syndrome

_Sources: Khopkar (Immunobiologicals — denileukin diftitox); Wolverton 4e ch.37. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dermal fillers (hyaluronic acid and others)
posts.summary: Chemical agents, peels & baths · Injectable soft-tissue fillers — temporary (hyaluronic acid, collagen), semi-permanent/biostimulatory (calcium hydroxylapatite,
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths_

**Class:** Injectable soft-tissue fillers — temporary (hyaluronic acid, collagen), semi-permanent/biostimulatory (calcium hydroxylapatite, poly-L-lactic acid), permanent (PMMA, silicone)

## Mechanism of action
- Hyaluronic acid (cross-linked, non-animal stabilised): fills volume and binds water; reversible with hyaluronidase
- Biostimulators (PLLA, CaHA): stimulate neocollagenesis over months

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Nasolabial folds, lips, cheeks/midface volume loss, tear trough, chin and jawline contouring, acne scars (rolling), HIV facial lipoatrophy (PLLA — approved)

## Dose & formulations
- Volume per region (0.5–2 mL typical); duration: HA 6–18 months, CaHA 12–18 months, PLLA ~2 years

## Adverse effects
- Bruising, swelling, lumps/nodules, Tyndall effect (blue hue — superficial HA), infection, biofilm, delayed hypersensitivity nodules
- Vascular occlusion (most serious): skin necrosis (glabella, nasal tip) and blindness (retinal artery embolism) — emergency high-dose hyaluronidase

## Contraindications
- Active infection at site, autoimmune flare, pregnancy, allergy to components (lidocaine), unrealistic expectations

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Hyaluronidase dissolves HA fillers — key in vascular occlusion
- Danger zones: glabella, nose, nasolabial (angular artery)
- Tyndall effect = superficial HA

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.59 (Injectable dermal and subcutaneous fillers); Khopkar ch.34 (Dermal fillers). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Desloratadine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · Second-generation H1 antihistamine — active metabolite of loratadine
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine — active metabolite of loratadine

## Mechanism of action
- Highly potent selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist; some anti-inflammatory effect

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria, allergic rhinitis

## Dose & formulations
- 5 mg once daily (updosing up to 20 mg in urticaria); children 6–11 years 2.5 mg

## Adverse effects
- Headache, fatigue; non-sedating at standard dose

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to loratadine

## Drug interactions
- Minimal; erythromycin/ketoconazole raise levels without QT change

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; loratadine preferred.

## Viva points
- Active metabolite of loratadine; long half-life (~27 h)

_Sources: Khopkar (Second generation H1 antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Desonide 0.05% cream/lotion
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Low-potency non-fluorinated topical steroid (US class 6)
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Low-potency non-fluorinated topical steroid (US class 6)

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist; low atrophy risk

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Atopic dermatitis and seborrhoeic dermatitis of face and flexures, children (approved from 3 months)
- Mild eczema in sensitive areas

## Dose & formulations
- Thin layer twice daily; usually up to 4 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Burning, mild atrophy with long use; perioral dermatitis

## Contraindications
- Untreated infections, rosacea, perioral dermatitis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Acceptable (low potency).

## Viva points
- Low potency, non-fluorinated — suitable for face and children
- Belongs to the acetonide group (class B contact allergy)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dexamethasone sodium phosphate injection
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Potent glucocorticoid receptor agonist (about 25–30 times hydrocortisone) with no mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble phosphate ester — IV, IM, intralesional
- Equivalence: 0.75 mg dexamethasone = 5 mg prednisolone
- Crosses the placenta (not inactivated by 11β-HSD2)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP) and dexamethasone pulse (DP) for pemphigus (Pasricha regimen; third line in the Derma Desk pemphigus ladder)
- Anaphylaxis/angioedema adjunct; acute severe allergic reactions
- SJS/TEN, DRESS (short courses, some centres)
- Cerebral oedema, fetal lung maturation (obstetrics)
- Intralesional/IM use in some Indian practice (less preferred than triamcinolone)

## Dose & formulations
- DCP pulse: dexamethasone 100 mg in 500 mL 5% dextrose over 1–2 h on 3 consecutive days + cyclophosphamide 500 mg IV on day 1; repeated every 4 weeks; oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg daily between pulses
- Phases of DCP: I (pulses until complete remission), II (pulses continue for 9 months with daily oral cyclophosphamide), III (oral cyclophosphamide alone for 9 months), IV (off treatment, follow-up)
- Anaphylaxis adjunct: 4–8 mg IV
- Ampoules 4 mg/mL (2 mL); 8 mg/2 mL

## Adverse effects
- As for pulse steroids: hyperglycaemia, hypertension, hypokalaemia, arrhythmia, psychosis, infection
- Perineal burning/itching with rapid IV injection
- Long-acting — more HPA suppression if given daily

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids; active serious infection, systemic fungal infection

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inducer itself (may lower levels of some drugs); enzyme inducers lower its levels

## Monitoring
- As for methylprednisolone pulse: ECG, electrolytes, glucose, BP before and during pulse

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta — used deliberately for fetal lung maturity; avoid for skin disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- 0.75 mg dexamethasone = 5 mg prednisolone
- DCP regimen: phases I–IV (Pasricha)
- No mineralocorticoid action

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (injectable steroids, DCP/DAP pulse); Wolverton 4e ch.13. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dexpanthenol (provitamin B5)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous topicals & wound care · Pantothenic acid precursor (topical)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Pantothenic acid precursor (topical)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to pantothenic acid (part of coenzyme A) → supports epidermal regeneration and barrier lipid synthesis; humectant and anti-inflammatory

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Minor wounds, post-laser/peel care, radiation dermatitis, nipple fissures, napkin dermatitis, dry skin, cheilitis with isotretinoin

## Dose & formulations
- 5% cream/ointment once or several times daily

## Adverse effects
- Allergic contact dermatitis (occasional)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Wound-healing moisturiser; occasional contact allergen

_Sources: Khopkar ch.28 (Topical pantothenic acid). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Piperazine derivative; antifilarial
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Piperazine derivative; antifilarial

## Mechanism of action
- Makes microfilariae more susceptible to host immune attack (alters arachidonic acid metabolism and surface membranes); some macrofilaricidal effect on adult worms

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi) — individual treatment and mass drug administration (MDA with albendazole ± ivermectin in India's elimination programme)
- Loiasis (Loa loa) — drug of choice (with caution)
- Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia; toxocariasis (alternative)
- Not for onchocerciasis (severe Mazzotti reaction, eye damage)

## Dose & formulations
- Treatment: 6 mg/kg/day for 12 days (tropical pulmonary eosinophilia: 21 days)
- MDA: 6 mg/kg single annual dose (with albendazole 400 mg)
- Loiasis: start low and increase (to avoid encephalopathy), with steroids/antihistamines

## Adverse effects
- Mazzotti-like reaction from dying microfilariae: fever, headache, itch, rash, lymphadenitis, hypotension — worse with heavy infection
- Encephalopathy and death in heavy Loa loa microfilaraemia
- GI upset, dizziness

## Contraindications
- Onchocerciasis (eye damage); heavy Loa loa microfilaraemia (>2500/mL without pre-treatment); pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Few significant interactions

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (excluded from MDA).

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for lymphatic filariasis and loiasis
- Contraindicated in onchocerciasis
- Mazzotti reaction

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5 (Diethylcarbamazine); Wolverton 4e ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Diphenhydramine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · First-generation H1 antihistamine — ethanolamine
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** First-generation H1 antihistamine — ethanolamine

## Mechanism of action
- H1 inverse agonist; strongly sedative and anticholinergic; local anaesthetic effect

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acute allergic reactions, urticaria, night-time itch, anaphylaxis adjunct
- 1% injection as local anaesthetic in patients allergic to amides and esters

## Dose & formulations
- 25–50 mg every 4–6 h (max 300 mg/day); injection 10–50 mg IV/IM

## Adverse effects
- Marked sedation, impaired performance, anticholinergic delirium in elderly
- Topical diphenhydramine: frequent contact sensitiser and photosensitiser

## Contraindications
- Neonates, breastfeeding; caution in elderly (Beers list)

## Drug interactions
- CNS depressants; CYP2D6 inhibitor (raises metoprolol, TCAs)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Has been used; avoid near term.

## Viva points
- Can be used as an alternative local anaesthetic (1%) in 'caine' allergy
- Avoid topical antihistamines — sensitisation

_Sources: Khopkar (First generation H1 antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32 and ch.58. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dithranol (anthralin)
posts.summary: Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics · Synthetic anthrone (derived from chrysarobin of Goa powder)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics_

**Class:** Synthetic anthrone (derived from chrysarobin of Goa powder)

## Mechanism of action
- Generates free radicals (oxidation) → inhibits keratinocyte proliferation and mitochondrial function; also reduces neutrophil and T-cell activity

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic plaque psoriasis (thick, stable plaques; especially in children or when steroids should be avoided) — inpatient Ingram regimen (with tar baths and UVB) or outpatient short-contact therapy
- Alopecia areata (irritant therapy — off-label)

## Dose & formulations
- Short-contact therapy: start 0.1–0.5% for 10–30 min daily, increase to 1–3% as tolerated, then wash off
- Ingram regimen: tar bath → UVB → dithranol in Lassar's paste (with salicylic acid to stabilise) overnight
- Apply to plaques only; protect surrounding skin with petroleum jelly

## Adverse effects
- Irritation and burning of surrounding normal skin ('dithranol burn')
- Purple-brown staining of skin, nails, hair, clothes, bathtubs (oxidation products) — skin staining fades in 1–2 weeks
- Perilesional pigmentation as a sign of clearing

## Contraindications
- Acute, erythrodermic, pustular or unstable psoriasis; face, flexures, genitals

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe (not mutagenic in humans).

## Viva points
- Short-contact therapy reduces staining and irritation
- Ingram regimen
- Salicylic acid stabilises dithranol (prevents oxidation)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.28 (Anthralin — dithranol, dithranol pomade); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dolutegravir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), second generation
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), second generation

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the HIV integrase active site and blocks the strand-transfer step
- So viral DNA cannot integrate into the host chromosome
- High genetic barrier to resistance

## Pharmacokinetics
- Taken once daily with or without food; half-life about 14 h
- Metabolised by UGT1A1 (and CYP3A4 to a lesser extent)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Part of the preferred first-line ART regimen in India (TLD: tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg once daily) for adults, adolescents and pregnant women
- Children: with abacavir + lamivudine (weight-band dosing)
- Second-line regimens and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)

## Dose & formulations
- 50 mg once daily (usually within the TLD tablet)
- 50 mg twice daily if taken with rifampicin or when INSTI resistance is suspected

## Adverse effects
- Insomnia, headache, abnormal dreams, depression (uncommon)
- Weight gain
- Small rise in serum creatinine (blocks tubular creatinine secretion; true kidney function is not reduced)
- Hypersensitivity reactions and hepatotoxicity (rare)
- Early concern about neural tube defects with use at conception; later data show the risk is very small — it is now recommended in pregnancy

## Contraindications
- Dofetilide (raised levels)
- Previous hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Polyvalent cations (antacids with Mg/Al, calcium, iron, zinc supplements) chelate it — take dolutegravir 2 h before or 6 h after
- Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin lower levels (double the dose with rifampicin; avoid the others)
- Raises metformin levels — limit the metformin dose (about 1 g/day) and monitor

## Monitoring
