- CD4 and viral load per programme
- Weight, mood, renal function (expect a small, stable creatinine rise)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Recommended in pregnancy as part of TLD; give folic acid. Compatible with national breastfeeding guidance for women on ART.

## Viva points
- INSTI — blocks integration of viral DNA
- TLD is the preferred first-line regimen in India
- Separate from zinc, iron, calcium or antacids — relevant when we prescribe zinc
- Creatinine rise without real kidney damage

## Note on sources
Khopkar's edition predates dolutegravir, and Wolverton only lists it, so this post follows current NACO/WHO guidance. Please check.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (older edition, before dolutegravir); Wolverton 4e ch.11 (lists the drug); current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Doxepin (oral + topical)
posts.summary: Antihistamines · Tricyclic antidepressant with very potent H1 and H2 receptor blocking activity
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** Tricyclic antidepressant with very potent H1 and H2 receptor blocking activity

## Mechanism of action
- H1 affinity about 800 times diphenhydramine and 50 times hydroxyzine; also H2 blockade, anticholinergic, sedative and antidepressant (noradrenaline/serotonin reuptake inhibition)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria (especially with anxiety/depression, nocturnal itch), cold urticaria, dermographism
- Neuropathic itch and pain, psychogenic excoriation, lichen simplex chronicus
- Topical 5% cream: itch of atopic dermatitis and lichen simplex (short courses)

## Dose & formulations
- Oral: 10–25 mg at bedtime (up to 75 mg/day); elderly 10 mg
- Topical 5% cream: four times daily for up to 8 days, maximum 10% body surface

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, dry mouth, constipation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension
- Cardiac arrhythmia (QT prolongation), lethal in overdose
- Topical: drowsiness from absorption (about 20%), allergic contact dermatitis (common), burning

## Contraindications
- Recent MI, heart block, narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, MAO inhibitors within 14 days, mania

## Drug interactions
- CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, terbinafine) raise levels; alcohol; other serotonergic drugs

## Monitoring
- ECG in older patients or cardiac history

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (neonatal withdrawal, limited data).

## Viva points
- Most potent H1 blocker available
- Topical doxepin: absorbed enough to cause drowsiness; frequent contact allergy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32 and ch.35; Khopkar (Antihistamines; topical doxepin). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Doxycycline
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines · Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline (lipophilic)
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines_

**Class:** Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline (lipophilic)

## Mechanism of action
- Antibacterial: binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment → stops protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory (independent of antibacterial action): inhibits matrix metalloproteinases, neutrophil chemotaxis, and pro-inflammatory cytokines
- This anti-inflammatory action is the basis of sub-antimicrobial dosing in rosacea

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed (about 95%); food reduces absorption only slightly, but iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc and bismuth chelate it
- Half-life 18–22 h → once- or twice-daily dosing
- Excreted mainly through the gut, so it is the safest tetracycline in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (moderate–severe inflammatory) — always with topical benzoyl peroxide or retinoid; limit to 3–4 months
- Rosacea (papulopustular), perioral dermatitis
- Bullous pemphigoid (anti-inflammatory, often with nicotinamide)
- STIs: chlamydia/NGU, LGV, donovanosis, early and late syphilis when penicillin cannot be used
- Community MRSA skin infections, Lyme disease, rickettsial infections, Mycobacterium marinum
- Hidradenitis suppurativa; filariasis (kills Wolbachia); confluent and reticulated papillomatosis

## Dose & formulations
- Acne/rosacea: 50–100 mg once or twice daily
- Sub-antimicrobial: 40 mg modified-release once daily, or 20 mg twice daily (rosacea)
- Chlamydia/NGU: 100 mg twice daily × 7 days; LGV: 100 mg twice daily × 21 days
- Early syphilis (penicillin allergy): 100 mg twice daily × 14 days; late latent: × 28 days
- Donovanosis: 100 mg twice daily for at least 3 weeks and until lesions heal
- Take with a full glass of water, sitting upright, not at bedtime

## Adverse effects
- GI upset; pill oesophagitis (take upright with water)
- Phototoxicity, including photo-onycholysis — the most phototoxic of the commonly used tetracyclines
- Tooth staining and enamel hypoplasia in children under 8 years (less than older tetracyclines)
- Pseudotumor cerebri; vaginal candidiasis
- Rare: hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (after about 15 weeks) and breastfeeding (long courses)
- Children under 8 years (except short courses for serious infections such as rickettsial disease)
- Concurrent isotretinoin or acitretin; known hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, magnesium, bismuth, milk: reduce absorption — separate by 2–3 h
- Isotretinoin/acitretin: pseudotumor cerebri
- Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates: lower doxycycline levels
- Warfarin: effect may increase

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests for courses used in acne
- Counsel about sun protection and correct swallowing

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D): tooth discolouration and bone effects after about 15 weeks. Short courses in breastfeeding are generally acceptable; avoid long courses.

## Viva points
- Safest tetracycline in renal failure (gut excretion)
- Most phototoxic of the common tetracyclines; photo-onycholysis
- Sub-antimicrobial 40 mg MR works by anti-inflammatory action and does not select resistance
- Never combine with isotretinoin

## Note on sources
Khopkar says doxycycline lacks the anti-inflammatory effect of tetracycline. Wolverton describes clear anti-inflammatory actions (the basis of sub-antimicrobial dosing). We follow Wolverton.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9 (Systemic antibacterial agents); Khopkar ch.1. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dutasteride
posts.summary: VIII Antiandrogen · Dual 5α-reductase inhibitor (types I and II)
posts.body:
_Oral · VIII Antiandrogen_

**Class:** Dual 5α-reductase inhibitor (types I and II)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits both type I (sebaceous glands, skin) and type II (hair follicle, prostate) 5α-reductase
- Lowers serum DHT by more than 90% — more than finasteride

## Pharmacokinetics
- Very long half-life (about 5 weeks); effect persists for months after stopping
- Metabolised by CYP3A4

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Male androgenetic alopecia (approved in Korea/Japan at 0.5 mg; off-label elsewhere) — slightly more effective than finasteride
- Female pattern hair loss in post-menopausal women (off-label)
- Mesotherapy (intradermal dutasteride) for AGA
- Benign prostatic hyperplasia

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5 mg once daily (some use 0.5 mg 2–3 times a week); soft capsules should not be opened

## Adverse effects
- Sexual side effects (similar to or slightly more than finasteride)
- Gynaecomastia, breast tenderness
- PSA lowered by about 50%

## Contraindications
- Women of childbearing potential and pregnancy; children
- Men should not donate blood for 6 months after the last dose (long half-life)

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole) raise levels

## Monitoring
- Baseline PSA in older men

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category X). Pregnant women should not handle leaking capsules.

## Viva points
- Blocks both isoenzymes — more DHT suppression than finasteride
- Very long half-life — no blood donation for 6 months after stopping

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34; Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ebastine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · Second-generation H1 antihistamine — piperidine (prodrug of carebastine)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine — piperidine (prodrug of carebastine)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted in liver (CYP3A4) to carebastine — selective H1 inverse agonist

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria, allergic rhinitis

## Dose & formulations
- 10–20 mg once daily

## Adverse effects
- Headache, dry mouth; QT prolongation possible at high doses or with CYP3A4 inhibitors

## Contraindications
- Severe liver impairment; long QT

## Drug interactions
- Ketoconazole/erythromycin raise levels (QT caution)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data — avoid.

## Viva points
- Prodrug activated by CYP3A4; QT caution with azoles/macrolides

_Sources: Khopkar (Second generation H1 antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Efalizumab & alefacept (withdrawn T-cell biologics)
posts.summary: Biologicals · T-cell targeted biologics for psoriasis — efalizumab (anti-CD11a monoclonal) and alefacept (LFA-3/IgG1 fusion protein)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Biologicals_

**Class:** T-cell targeted biologics for psoriasis — efalizumab (anti-CD11a monoclonal) and alefacept (LFA-3/IgG1 fusion protein)

## Mechanism of action
- Efalizumab: blocks CD11a (LFA-1) → prevents T-cell activation and migration into skin
- Alefacept: binds CD2 on memory T cells → blocks LFA-3/CD2 co-stimulation and causes NK-mediated apoptosis of CD45RO+ memory T cells

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Formerly: moderate–severe chronic plaque psoriasis
- Efalizumab withdrawn in 2009 (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy); alefacept withdrawn in 2011 (commercial reasons/low efficacy)

## Dose & formulations
- Historic: efalizumab 1 mg/kg SC weekly; alefacept 15 mg IM weekly × 12 weeks (needed CD4 count monitoring)

## Adverse effects
- Efalizumab: PML (JC virus), rebound/flare of psoriasis on stopping, thrombocytopenia, aseptic meningitis
- Alefacept: CD4 lymphopenia, infections, malignancy concerns

## Contraindications
- No longer marketed

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not applicable (withdrawn).

## Viva points
- Efalizumab withdrawn due to PML
- Alefacept — first biologic approved for psoriasis (2003); depletes memory T cells; CD4 monitoring

_Sources: Khopkar (Immunobiologicals — efalizumab, alefacept); Wolverton 4e ch.8 (Drugs taken off the market). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Efavirenz
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)

## Mechanism of action
- Non-competitive inhibitor binding the allosteric pocket of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase; inactive against HIV-2

## Pharmacokinetics
- Long half-life (40–55 h); take at bedtime on an empty stomach (food raises levels and CNS effects); CYP2B6 metabolism (slow-metaboliser genotype → high levels); CYP3A4 inducer

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Formerly the preferred NNRTI in first-line ART (TLE — tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz); now alternative to dolutegravir (TLD)
- Women who cannot take dolutegravir, or with rifampicin-based TB treatment

## Dose & formulations
- 600 mg once daily at bedtime (400 mg in some regimens)

## Adverse effects
- CNS: vivid dreams, insomnia, dizziness, poor concentration, depression, psychosis — usually settle in 2–4 weeks
- Rash in about 15–25% (usually mild, in first 2 weeks; SJS rare) — less severe than nevirapine
- Hyperlipidaemia, gynaecomastia, raised LFT, false-positive cannabinoid tests

## Contraindications
- Significant psychiatric illness (relative); hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inducer: lowers levels of voriconazole (avoid standard doses), itraconazole, protease inhibitors, oral contraceptives (use additional method), methadone, artemether-lumefantrine
- Rifampicin: can be used together (dose unchanged in most guidelines)

## Monitoring
- LFT, lipids; mood and sleep

## Pregnancy & lactation
Earlier concern about neural tube defects is not confirmed; can be used, though dolutegravir regimens are preferred.

## Viva points
- Bedtime dosing because of CNS effects
- Rash milder and less frequent than nevirapine
- Gynaecomastia and dyslipidaemia

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Efavirenz); Wolverton 4e ch.11 and ch.66; current NACO ART guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Eflornithine 13.9% cream
posts.summary: Miscellaneous topicals & wound care · Ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Ornithine decarboxylase inhibitor

## Mechanism of action
- Irreversibly inhibits ornithine decarboxylase in hair follicle cells → slows hair growth (does not remove hair)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Facial hirsutism in women (with laser or other hair removal)
- Systemic eflornithine: African trypanosomiasis

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily (at least 8 h apart); effect in 6–8 weeks; hair regrows within 8 weeks of stopping

## Adverse effects
- Acne, pseudofolliculitis, burning, stinging

## Contraindications
- Under 12 years

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data — avoid.

## Viva points
- ODC inhibitor; slows facial hair growth; combine with laser

_Sources: Khopkar ch.28 (Eflornithine); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Enfuvirtide
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · HIV fusion inhibitor (36-amino-acid synthetic peptide)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** HIV fusion inhibitor (36-amino-acid synthetic peptide)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the HR1 region of HIV gp41 → prevents the conformational change needed for fusion of virus and cell membranes → virus cannot enter CD4 cells

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Salvage therapy in heavily treatment-experienced patients with multidrug-resistant HIV (rarely used now)

## Dose & formulations
- 90 mg subcutaneously twice daily

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site reactions in almost all patients: painful erythematous nodules, induration, cysts (dermatology viva point)
- Increased bacterial pneumonia; hypersensitivity (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data.

## Viva points
- The only injectable fusion inhibitor — injection-site nodules in ~98%

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Enfuvirtide); Wolverton 4e ch.11. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Erythromycin (oral + topical)
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Macrolide antibiotic (14-membered lactone ring; prototype macrolide)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Macrolide antibiotic (14-membered lactone ring; prototype macrolide)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit → blocks translocation → bacteriostatic (bactericidal at high concentration)
- Anti-inflammatory effects (reduces neutrophil chemotaxis) — used in some inflammatory dermatoses
- Motilin receptor agonist → GI cramps

## Pharmacokinetics
- Destroyed by gastric acid — given as enteric-coated base, stearate or estolate (estolate best absorbed)
- Metabolised by CYP3A4 (and inhibits it strongly); poor CSF penetration

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Penicillin-allergic patients: streptococcal and staphylococcal skin infections, erysipelas
- STIs in pregnancy or penicillin/tetracycline allergy: chlamydia, chancroid, LGV, donovanosis
- Erythrasma, pitted keratolysis, acne in pregnancy and children under 8
- Bullous pemphigoid (with nicotinamide), pityriasis rosea (controversial, early use)
- Topical 2% gel/solution: acne (always with BPO — resistance very high), erythrasma

## Dose & formulations
- 500 mg four times daily (30–50 mg/kg/day in children)
- Chlamydia: 500 mg four times daily × 7 days; chancroid: 500 mg three times daily × 7 days; LGV: 500 mg four times daily × 21 days
- Topical 2–4% once or twice daily with BPO

## Adverse effects
- GI cramps, nausea, diarrhoea (motilin effect) — the main problem
- Cholestatic hepatitis (mainly estolate; more in pregnancy)
- QT prolongation, transient hearing loss with high IV doses
- Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis when given to young infants
- Topical: dryness; resistant C. acnes and staphylococci

## Contraindications
- Liver disease (estolate); long QT
- Concurrent CYP3A4 substrates with serious toxicity: simvastatin/lovastatin, pimozide, ergotamine, terfenadine/astemizole

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor: raises cyclosporine, tacrolimus, carbamazepine, warfarin, theophylline, statins, colchicine, benzodiazepines
- Topical erythromycin and clindamycin antagonise each other (same 50S site)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Base and stearate are safe in pregnancy; avoid estolate (hepatotoxicity). Note: erythromycin does not adequately treat fetal syphilis.

## Viva points
- Estolate → cholestatic hepatitis
- CYP3A4 inhibitor — cyclosporine and statin interactions
- Safe acne antibiotic in pregnancy/children (oral)
- Topical erythromycin — high resistance; always add BPO

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Macrolides — erythromycin; Table 1.6) and ch.18; Wolverton 4e ch.9 and ch.41. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Etanercept
posts.summary: Biologicals · TNF-α inhibitor — fusion protein of TNF receptor 2 (p75) with the Fc portion of IgG1
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Biologicals_

**Class:** TNF-α inhibitor — fusion protein of TNF receptor 2 (p75) with the Fc portion of IgG1

## Mechanism of action
- Acts as a soluble decoy receptor binding TNF-α (and lymphotoxin-α), preventing it from activating cell receptors
- Does not lyse TNF-bearing cells (unlike monoclonal antibodies) — less granulomatous infection risk

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Moderate–severe plaque psoriasis (adults and children ≥4 years), psoriatic arthritis
- Off-label: hidradenitis (weak), pyoderma gangrenosum, SJS/TEN (single dose in trials), sarcoidosis (ineffective)

## Dose & formulations
- Psoriasis: 50 mg SC twice weekly for 12 weeks, then 50 mg once weekly; children 0.8 mg/kg weekly

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site reactions (common), upper respiratory infections
- Serious infections; TB reactivation (lower than monoclonals but still screen); hepatitis B reactivation
- Demyelinating disease, drug-induced lupus, worsening heart failure
- Paradoxical psoriasis (palmoplantar pustular), lymphoma risk (small)

## Contraindications
- Active serious infection, untreated latent TB, multiple sclerosis/demyelination, NYHA III–IV heart failure, live vaccines

## Drug interactions
- Do not combine with other biologics or anakinra/abatacept (serious infections)

## Monitoring
- TB screening (IGRA) before and yearly; hepatitis B/C, HIV; CBC/LFT periodically

## Pregnancy & lactation
Low placental transfer (Fc fusion protein) — can be used if needed; avoid live vaccines in infants for 6 months if exposed late.

## Viva points
- Receptor fusion protein — decoy for TNF
- TNF inhibitors: screen for TB, avoid in demyelination and severe heart failure
- Paradoxical psoriasis with TNF inhibitors

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.26 (TNF inhibitors); Khopkar (Immunobiologicals). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ethambutol (E)
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Ethylenediamine derivative; first-line antituberculous drug
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Ethylenediamine derivative; first-line antituberculous drug

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits arabinosyl transferase → blocks arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall (bacteriostatic)
- Mainly prevents resistance to other drugs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- TB (intensive and continuation phases in India's daily regimen), cutaneous TB
- Atypical mycobacteria (M. marinum with clarithromycin; MAC)

## Dose & formulations
- 15 mg/kg/day (range 15–25) in fixed-dose combinations
- Reduce dose/interval in renal impairment

## Adverse effects
- Optic (retrobulbar) neuritis: reduced visual acuity and red–green colour blindness (dose-related, usually reversible if stopped early)
- Hyperuricaemia, peripheral neuropathy, rash (rare)

## Contraindications
- Pre-existing optic neuritis; young children who cannot report visual symptoms (relative)

## Drug interactions
- Aluminium antacids reduce absorption

## Monitoring
- Visual acuity and colour vision (Ishihara) at baseline and monthly

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Optic neuritis — red–green colour vision test
- Used with clarithromycin for M. marinum

_Sources: Khopkar ch.7; Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Etretinate
posts.summary: Retinoids · Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid — ethyl ester prodrug of acitretin (withdrawn)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Retinoids_

**Class:** Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid — ethyl ester prodrug of acitretin (withdrawn)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to acitretin; acts on RAR/RXR like other retinoids

## Pharmacokinetics
- Highly lipophilic, stored in fat; terminal half-life 80–160 days; detected in blood up to 2–3 years after stopping

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Formerly: psoriasis, disorders of keratinisation — replaced by acitretin (withdrawn from the US market in 1998)

## Dose & formulations
- Historic: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- As for acitretin (mucocutaneous, lipids, liver, bone, teratogenicity) — prolonged teratogenic risk

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy for years after stopping

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated; prolonged teratogenicity.

## Viva points
- Acitretin + alcohol → etretinate (re-esterification) — the reason for 3-year contraception with acitretin

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22; Khopkar (Etretinate and acitretin). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Famciclovir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes · Diacetyl ester prodrug of penciclovir (guanosine analogue)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes_

**Class:** Diacetyl ester prodrug of penciclovir (guanosine analogue)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to penciclovir in the gut wall and liver
- Penciclovir is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then by host kinases, to penciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase
- Not an obligate chain terminator (unlike acyclovir), but stays inside infected cells much longer (intracellular half-life 7–20 h)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 77%
- Plasma half-life about 2 h, but long intracellular half-life → less frequent dosing
- Renal excretion — reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Herpes zoster (start within 72 h)
- Genital herpes: first episode, recurrences, suppression
- Herpes labialis (single dose)
- Recurrent HSV in HIV

## Dose & formulations
- Herpes zoster: 500 mg three times daily × 7 days
- First-episode genital herpes: 250 mg three times daily × 7–10 days
- Recurrent genital herpes: 1 g twice daily for 1 day (or 125 mg twice daily × 5 days)
- Suppression: 250 mg twice daily
- Herpes labialis: 1500 mg single dose
- HIV, recurrent HSV: 500 mg twice daily × 7 days

## Adverse effects
- Headache, nausea, diarrhoea
- Confusion in the elderly (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to famciclovir or penciclovir

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid may raise penciclovir levels
- Few clinically important interactions

## Monitoring
- Renal function for dose adjustment

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category B; limited human data — acyclovir and valacyclovir are preferred in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Prodrug of penciclovir; long intracellular half-life
- Cross-resistance with acyclovir (both need viral thymidine kinase)
- Single-day treatment options for herpes labialis and recurrent genital herpes

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.11; Khopkar ch.3. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fexofenadine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (active metabolite of terfenadine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (active metabolite of terfenadine)

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist; a P-glycoprotein substrate, so it is pumped out of the brain — truly non-sedating

## Pharmacokinetics
- Onset 1–2 h; half-life about 14 h
- Excreted mostly unchanged in faeces and urine; little liver metabolism, so no QT problems (unlike its parent terfenadine)
- Fruit juices (grapefruit, orange, apple) reduce absorption via OATP — take with water

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria, allergic rhinitis
- Preferred in pilots, drivers and people needing no sedation

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 120–180 mg once daily; urticaria may be updosed up to 360–720 mg/day (Wolverton mentions 180–360 mg)
- Children 6–11 years: 30 mg twice daily

## Adverse effects
- Headache; generally very well tolerated
- No significant sedation even at high doses

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antacids with aluminium/magnesium and fruit juices reduce absorption
- Erythromycin and ketoconazole raise levels (not clinically important)

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Less data than cetirizine or loratadine; use those first in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Least sedating antihistamine (P-gp efflux)
- Metabolite of terfenadine, but without its QT toxicity
- Avoid fruit juice at the time of dosing

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32; Khopkar (Antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Finasteride
posts.summary: VIII Antiandrogen · 5α-reductase inhibitor (type II isoenzyme selective)
posts.body:
_Oral · VIII Antiandrogen_

**Class:** 5α-reductase inhibitor (type II isoenzyme selective)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits type II 5α-reductase (found in hair follicles, prostate), blocking conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
- Lowers serum DHT by about 70% and scalp DHT by about 60%
- Reverses miniaturisation of androgen-sensitive scalp follicles

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4); half-life 5–6 h, but enzyme inhibition lasts longer

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Male androgenetic alopecia (vertex and mid-scalp) — approved at 1 mg
- Female pattern hair loss in post-menopausal women (off-label, higher doses 2.5–5 mg)
- Hirsutism (off-label, with contraception), frontal fibrosing alopecia (off-label)
- Benign prostatic hyperplasia (5 mg)

## Dose & formulations
- Male AGA: 1 mg once daily; results take 3–6 months, assess at 12 months
- Must be continued — benefit is lost within about 12 months of stopping
- Topical finasteride 0.25% solution is available

## Adverse effects
- Sexual: decreased libido, erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction (about 1–2%; usually reversible)
- Gynaecomastia, breast tenderness
- Depression; 'post-finasteride syndrome' (persistent symptoms after stopping) is reported but unproven
- Lowers PSA by about 50% — double the measured PSA when screening for prostate cancer

## Contraindications
- Women of childbearing potential (unless strict contraception) and pregnancy — risk of feminising a male fetus
- Pregnant women should not handle crushed or broken tablets
- Children

## Drug interactions
- No important interactions

## Monitoring
- None routinely; record baseline PSA in men over 40–50

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated in pregnancy (old FDA category X) — causes hypospadias/ambiguous genitalia in male fetuses. Men on finasteride need no contraception (semen levels are negligible).

## Viva points
- Type II 5α-reductase inhibitor; dutasteride blocks types I and II
- 1 mg for hair; 5 mg for prostate
- PSA is halved — double it
- Pregnant women should not handle broken tablets

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34 (Antiandrogens and androgen inhibitors); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fluconazole
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Triazole antifungal (first generation)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Triazole antifungal (first generation)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis
- Fungistatic; membrane damage from accumulated toxic methylated sterols

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble; about 90% bioavailable; absorption not affected by food or gastric acid
- Low protein binding; excellent CSF, eye and urine penetration
- Half-life about 30 h → weekly dosing possible
- Excreted unchanged in urine — reduce dose in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Vulvovaginal, oropharyngeal and oesophageal candidiasis; candidal intertrigo and paronychia
- Pityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis
- Dermatophytosis and onychomycosis (alternative)
- Cryptococcosis (including meningitis, with amphotericin B first), coccidioidomycosis
- Prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients

## Dose & formulations
- Vulvovaginal candidiasis: 150 mg single dose; recurrent: 150 mg every 72 h × 3 doses, then weekly for 6 months
- Oropharyngeal candidiasis: 100–200 mg/day × 7–14 days
- Tinea corporis: 150–300 mg once weekly × 2–4 weeks
- Pityriasis versicolor: 300 mg weekly × 2 weeks (or 400 mg single dose)
- Onychomycosis: 150–450 mg once weekly for 6–12 months
- Children: 3–6 mg/kg/day (tinea capitis 6 mg/kg/day)

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache
- Hepatotoxicity (usually mild)
- QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
- Alopecia with prolonged high doses
- Rash; fixed drug eruption (common in Indian practice); rarely SJS/TEN

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to azoles
- With QT-prolonging drugs metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g. cisapride, pimozide, quinidine, erythromycin)
- Pregnancy (high-dose or prolonged use)

## Drug interactions
- Inhibits CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and (moderately) CYP3A4
- Raises levels of warfarin, phenytoin, sulfonylureas, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, some statins, benzodiazepines
- Rifampicin lowers fluconazole levels

## Monitoring
- LFT for courses longer than a few weeks; ECG if other QT risks; renal function for dosing

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid. High-dose or prolonged use in the first trimester is linked to birth defects (old FDA category D); a single 150 mg dose was category C. Compatible with breastfeeding in usual doses.

## Viva points
- Water-soluble azole — best CSF penetration, renal excretion
- Absorption is not acid-dependent (unlike itraconazole)
- Main enzyme inhibited for interactions: CYP2C9 (warfarin, phenytoin)
- Weekly dosing is possible because of the long half-life

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Flucytosine (5-FC)
posts.summary: Other antifungals · Fluorinated pyrimidine antifungal
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antifungals_

**Class:** Fluorinated pyrimidine antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Taken up by fungal cytosine permease and converted by cytosine deaminase (absent in human cells) to 5-fluorouracil
- 5-FU inhibits thymidylate synthase and is incorporated into fungal RNA
- Rapid resistance when used alone — always combined

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; excellent CSF penetration; renal excretion (adjust dose)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cryptococcal meningitis (induction with amphotericin B or fluconazole)
- Chromoblastomycosis (with itraconazole/amphotericin B)
- Severe candidiasis (with amphotericin B)

## Dose & formulations
- 100 mg/kg/day orally in 4 divided doses (adjust to renal function and serum levels)

## Adverse effects
- Bone marrow suppression (leucopenia, thrombocytopenia), especially with renal failure
- Hepatotoxicity, GI upset (enterocolitis)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy; severe marrow suppression

## Drug interactions
- Amphotericin B reduces its renal clearance (synergy but toxicity); cytosine arabinoside antagonises

## Monitoring
- CBC, LFT, renal function; drug levels where available

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (teratogenic in animals; converted to 5-FU).

## Viva points
- Prodrug converted to 5-FU only in fungi (cytosine deaminase)
- Never used alone — resistance
- Chromoblastomycosis and cryptococcal meningitis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.2; Wolverton 4e ch.10. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, sparfloxacin, norfloxacin)
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Synthetic fluorinated quinolone antibiotics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Synthetic fluorinated quinolone antibiotics

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II — main target in Gram-negatives) and topoisomerase IV (Gram-positives) → DNA breaks → bactericidal
- Concentration-dependent killing

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed but chelated by antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, dairy
- Good tissue and intracellular penetration; ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin/ofloxacin renally excreted; moxifloxacin hepatic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Gram-negative skin and soft-tissue infections (Pseudomonas — ciprofloxacin), diabetic foot, osteomyelitis
- Chancroid (ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily × 3 days), donovanosis (ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily ≥3 weeks)
- Gonorrhoea — no longer recommended (high resistance)
- Leprosy (ofloxacin, moxifloxacin — second-line), TB (MDR regimens), rapid-growing NTM (sensitivity-guided)
- Typhoid, anthrax, rickettsial infections (alternative)

## Dose & formulations
- Ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg twice daily; ofloxacin 200–400 mg twice daily; levofloxacin 500–750 mg once daily; moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily

## Adverse effects
- Tendinopathy and tendon rupture (Achilles; risk higher with age >60, steroids, renal transplant) — FDA boxed warning, also peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, myasthenia exacerbation
- QT prolongation, dysglycaemia, aortic aneurysm/dissection
- Phototoxicity (sparfloxacin highest — withdrawn in many countries; ofloxacin least); photo-onycholysis
- Fixed drug eruption, SJS/TEN, vasculitis
- Arthropathy in growing animals → avoided in children and pregnancy (relative)
- C. difficile diarrhoea, seizures (especially with NSAIDs)

## Contraindications
- Children and adolescents (relative), pregnancy and breastfeeding (relative)
- History of tendon disorder with fluoroquinolones; myasthenia gravis; long QT

## Drug interactions
- Antacids/iron/calcium/zinc: separate by 2–6 h
- Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 → theophylline, caffeine, tizanidine toxicity
- Warfarin (INR rises), NSAIDs (seizures), steroids (tendon rupture), QT drugs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (use only when no alternative).

## Viva points
- DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV
- Tendon rupture — boxed warning; worse with steroids
- Sparfloxacin most phototoxic, ofloxacin least
- Ciprofloxacin–theophylline interaction

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Fluoroquinolones, Table 1.8); Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Flutamide
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Non-steroidal pure anti-androgen (androgen receptor antagonist)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Non-steroidal pure anti-androgen (androgen receptor antagonist)

## Mechanism of action
- Competitively blocks androgen receptors in target tissues (hair follicle, sebaceous gland, prostate)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Prostate cancer (approved)
- Off-label in women: hirsutism, acne, female pattern hair loss — limited by liver toxicity (bicalutamide is now preferred)

## Dose & formulations
- Women (off-label): 62.5–250 mg/day with contraception

## Adverse effects
- Hepatotoxicity — may be fatal (boxed warning); dose-related
- Dry skin, GI upset, green-brown urine, photosensitivity

## Contraindications
- Liver disease; pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Warfarin (INR rises)

## Monitoring
- LFT monthly for 4 months, then periodically

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (feminisation of male fetus).

## Viva points
- Pure anti-androgen; fatal hepatotoxicity limits use in women

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34; Khopkar (Antiandrogens). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fluticasone propionate + Mupirocin cream
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Combination: medium-potency fluorinated steroid (fluticasone 0.05%, US class 5) + mupirocin 2%
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Combination: medium-potency fluorinated steroid (fluticasone 0.05%, US class 5) + mupirocin 2%

## Mechanism of action
- Fluticasone: potent glucocorticoid receptor agonist with rapid hepatic inactivation (low systemic effect)
- Mupirocin: isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase inhibitor — kills S. aureus and Streptococcus that colonise and worsen eczema

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Secondarily infected (impetiginised) eczema and dermatitis — short term
- Infected insect bite reactions, infected lichen simplex

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily for 7–10 days, then switch to plain steroid

## Adverse effects
- Steroid side effects with misuse; mupirocin resistance with long use; burning

## Contraindications
- Primary bacterial, fungal or viral infections without dermatitis; rosacea, acne
- Not for long-term use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Acceptable on limited areas.

## Viva points
- Rational combination only for short-term infected eczema
- Fluticasone is safe in children (approved from 3 months) as plain cream

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45 and ch.41; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Formalin & glutaraldehyde
posts.summary: Wart & antiviral agents · Aldehyde antiseptics/fixatives — formaldehyde (formalin 3–10% soaks) and glutaraldehyde (10–20%)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents_

**Class:** Aldehyde antiseptics/fixatives — formaldehyde (formalin 3–10% soaks) and glutaraldehyde (10–20%)

## Mechanism of action
- Cross-link proteins → kill virus-infected keratinocytes and dry the skin (anhidrotic and antiviral effects)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Plantar and mosaic warts (soaks/paints)
- Plantar hyperhidrosis and bromhidrosis (soaks)
- Instrument disinfection (glutaraldehyde 2%)

## Dose & formulations
- Formalin 3–5% foot soak for 10–15 min daily; glutaraldehyde 10% paint twice daily to warts

## Adverse effects
- Allergic contact dermatitis (formaldehyde is a major allergen), irritation, brown staining (glutaraldehyde), hardening of skin

## Contraindications
- Formaldehyde allergy; broken skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Formaldehyde — common contact allergen (cosmetics, textiles)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.20 and ch.30. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Foscarnet
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Pyrophosphate (phosphonoformic acid) analogue
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Pyrophosphate (phosphonoformic acid) analogue

## Mechanism of action
- Directly blocks the pyrophosphate-binding site of viral DNA polymerase — does not need activation by viral thymidine kinase
- So it works against acyclovir-resistant (TK-deficient) HSV and VZV and ganciclovir-resistant CMV

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acyclovir-resistant mucocutaneous HSV and VZV in immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant)
- Ganciclovir-resistant CMV

## Dose & formulations
- 40 mg/kg IV every 8 h (or 60 mg/kg every 12 h) for HSV/VZV; with pre-hydration; adjust to creatinine clearance

## Adverse effects
- Nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)
- Electrolyte disturbances: hypocalcaemia (ionised — chelation), hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, hypo/hyperphosphataemia → paraesthesia, seizures, arrhythmia
- Painful genital (penile/vulval) ulcers from high drug concentration in urine — good hygiene after voiding
- Anaemia, nausea

## Contraindications
- Severe renal impairment (relative); hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Other nephrotoxic drugs; pentamidine IV (severe hypocalcaemia); QT drugs

## Monitoring
- Creatinine, Ca²⁺ (ionised), Mg²⁺, K⁺, PO₄ 2–3 times weekly; ECG

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid unless life-threatening.

## Viva points
- TK-independent — used for acyclovir-resistant HSV
- Genital ulceration from urinary excretion
- Electrolyte chaos — especially low ionised calcium

_Sources: Khopkar ch.3 (Foscarnet); Wolverton 4e ch.11. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Framycetin sulphate 1% cream
posts.summary: II Antibacterials · Aminoglycoside antibiotic (closely related to neomycin; neomycin B)
posts.body:
_Topicals · II Antibacterials_

**Class:** Aminoglycoside antibiotic (closely related to neomycin; neomycin B)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of mRNA → bactericidal
- Active against staphylococci and many Gram-negative bacilli; weak against streptococci

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Superficial bacterial skin infections, infected wounds, burns, ulcers (also as impregnated gauze — tulle dressings)
- Commonly used in India; limited by sensitisation

## Dose & formulations
- Apply 2–3 times daily for up to 7 days; gauze dressings changed daily

## Adverse effects
- Allergic contact dermatitis (common; cross-reacts with neomycin, gentamicin)
- Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity if absorbed from large raw areas, especially in renal impairment

## Contraindications
- Large raw areas/burns in renal impairment; perforated ear drum (ototoxic)
- Known aminoglycoside allergy

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid on large areas (fetal ototoxicity in theory).

## Viva points
- Aminoglycoside — contact sensitiser (neomycin group) and ototoxic if absorbed
- Suspect allergy if a wound worsens on framycetin tulle

_Sources: Khopkar ch.18; Wolverton 4e ch.41 (neomycin/aminoglycosides) and ch.56 (Irritants and allergens). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fusidic acid 2% cream
posts.summary: II Antibacterials · Fusidane (steroid-like) antibiotic
posts.body:
_Topicals · II Antibacterials_

**Class:** Fusidane (steroid-like) antibiotic

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits elongation factor G → stops bacterial protein synthesis
- Excellent penetration through intact skin and crusts; active against S. aureus (including many MRSA) and streptococci

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Impetigo, folliculitis, infected eczema, erythrasma, paronychia
- Combinations with steroid (fusidic acid + betamethasone/hydrocortisone) for infected eczema

## Dose & formulations
- Apply 3 times daily for up to 7–10 days (short courses limit resistance)

## Adverse effects
- Local irritation; rare contact dermatitis
- Rapid emergence of resistance with prolonged or widespread use

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- EF-G inhibitor; steroid-like structure
- Resistance is a major problem — keep courses short
- Good penetration through crusts

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.41; Khopkar ch.18. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Gamma benzene hexachloride (lindane, 1%)
posts.summary: Scabicides & pediculicides · Organochlorine insecticide
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Scabicides & pediculicides_

**Class:** Organochlorine insecticide

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks GABA-gated chloride channels in mite/louse nervous system → hyperexcitation, death; partly ovicidal

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Formerly scabies and lice — now second-line only (banned in many countries; withdrawn in India for human use in 2013)

## Dose & formulations
- Historic: thin layer neck down, wash off after 8 h; single application

## Adverse effects
- Neurotoxicity: seizures, death (especially infants, elderly, malnourished, broken skin, repeated use); aplastic anaemia (rare); resistance

## Contraindications
- Infants, children under 50 kg, elderly, pregnancy, breastfeeding, seizure disorders, crusted scabies, broken skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated.

## Viva points
- Neurotoxic — seizures; banned/withdrawn in many countries

_Sources: Khopkar ch.21 (Gamma benzene hexachloride); Wolverton 4e ch.44. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ganciclovir & valganciclovir
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Guanosine analogue (ganciclovir) and its oral L-valyl ester prodrug (valganciclovir)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Guanosine analogue (ganciclovir) and its oral L-valyl ester prodrug (valganciclovir)

## Mechanism of action
- In CMV-infected cells, phosphorylated by the viral UL97 kinase, then by host kinases → triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase
- Much more active against CMV than acyclovir

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- CMV infections in immunocompromised patients (retinitis, colitis, pneumonitis, CMV cutaneous ulcers in HIV/transplant)
- Prevention of CMV in transplant recipients
- HHV-6/CMV reactivation in severe DRESS (selected cases)

## Dose & formulations
- Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 h (induction), then 5 mg/kg daily
- Valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily (induction), then 900 mg daily; adjust for renal function

## Adverse effects
- Bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) — dose-limiting
- Renal impairment, CNS effects, fever, rash
- Carcinogenic, teratogenic and aspermatogenic in animals

## Contraindications
- Severe neutropenia (<500/mm³) or thrombocytopenia; pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Zidovudine, MMF, other marrow suppressants: more myelosuppression; imipenem (seizures)

## Monitoring
- CBC 2–3 times a week during induction; renal function

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (teratogenic); contraception during and after treatment (men 90 days).

## Viva points
- Activated by CMV UL97 kinase
- Neutropenia is dose-limiting
- Valganciclovir is the oral prodrug

_Sources: Khopkar ch.3; Wolverton 4e ch.11. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Gentian violet (crystal violet) 0.5–1%
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Triphenylmethane (aniline) dye; antiseptic
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Triphenylmethane (aniline) dye; antiseptic

## Mechanism of action
- Binds microbial DNA and disrupts cell walls → active against Gram-positive bacteria (including MRSA) and Candida; also anti-angiogenic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intertrigo, candidiasis (oral thrush — 0.5%), weeping eczema, chronic paronychia, MRSA colonised wounds, tinea pedis maceration

## Dose & formulations
- Paint once or twice daily for a few days (0.5–1% aqueous)

## Adverse effects
- Purple staining of skin and clothes; irritation, ulceration on mucosa with strong solutions; contact dermatitis
- Tattooing if applied to granulation tissue; possible carcinogenicity in animals (restricted in some countries)

## Contraindications
- Ulcerated or granulating areas; mucosa with high concentrations

## Pregnancy & lactation
Small areas acceptable.

## Viva points
- Antiseptic dye — Gram-positive and Candida; stains purple

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Eusol/Gentian violet). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Glycolic acid (cream, lotion, peel)
posts.summary: VI Keratolytics & emollients · α-hydroxy acid (AHA) — smallest AHA (from sugar cane)
posts.body:
_Topicals · VI Keratolytics & emollients_

**Class:** α-hydroxy acid (AHA) — smallest AHA (from sugar cane)

## Mechanism of action
- Reduces corneocyte cohesion (loosens the stratum corneum) → exfoliation
- At higher concentrations: dermal effects — increases collagen and glycosaminoglycan production
- Disperses melanin and speeds removal of pigmented keratinocytes

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Creams/lotions 6–12% (home use): xerosis, ichthyosis, keratosis pilaris, photoageing, acne (comedonal), melasma and PIH (adjunct), dull skin
- Chemical peels 20–70% (superficial peels, office use): acne, melasma, PIH, photoageing, superficial scars
- Also in the anti-acne list (glycolic acid cream)

## Dose & formulations
- Creams: once daily at night, starting with lower strength; sunscreen during the day
- Peels: start 20–35% for 2–3 min, increase strength and time every 2–4 weeks; neutralise with sodium bicarbonate solution or water

## Adverse effects
- Stinging, redness, dryness, peeling
- Photosensitivity — use sunscreen
- Peels: frosting/burns if left too long, PIH (dark skin), herpes reactivation

## Contraindications
- Active infection, open wounds, inflamed eczema/rosacea; recent isotretinoin (peels — relative)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Low-strength creams and superficial peels are considered safe.

## Viva points
- Smallest AHA — penetrates best
- Glycolic acid peels are time-dependent — must be neutralised
- Increases sun sensitivity

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.52 (α-Hydroxy acids) and ch.53 (Chemical peels); Khopkar ch.31. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Glycopyrrolate & propantheline (oral + topical glycopyrronium)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Quaternary ammonium antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) — poor CNS penetration
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Quaternary ammonium antimuscarinics (anticholinergics) — poor CNS penetration

## Mechanism of action
- Block muscarinic (M3) receptors on eccrine sweat glands (sympathetic cholinergic innervation) → reduced sweating

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Hyperhidrosis (generalised, craniofacial, compensatory, palmoplantar) — oral glycopyrrolate or propantheline
- Topical glycopyrronium tosylate 2.4% cloth (axillary hyperhidrosis, approved USA), 1% cream (Europe), iontophoresis with glycopyrrolate solution for refractory palmar hyperhidrosis
- Drooling (sialorrhoea), anaesthetic premedication

## Dose & formulations
- Glycopyrrolate 1–2 mg once or twice daily (titrate); propantheline 15 mg three times daily
- Topical cloth once daily to both axillae

## Adverse effects
- Dry mouth (most common), blurred vision (mydriasis), constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, heat intolerance (risk of heat stroke)
- Topical: local irritation, transient mydriasis if touched to eyes

## Contraindications
- Glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, obstructive uropathy, paralytic ileus, severe ulcerative colitis, tachyarrhythmia

## Drug interactions
- Other anticholinergics (TCAs, antihistamines); potassium chloride tablets (GI lesions)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data — avoid.

## Viva points
- Quaternary amine — fewer CNS effects than atropine
- Hyperhidrosis treatment ladder: topical aluminium chloride → iontophoresis → botulinum toxin → oral anticholinergics → sympathectomy

_Sources: Khopkar (Glycopyrrolate and propantheline bromide); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Griseofulvin
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Benzofuran fungistatic antibiotic (from Penicillium griseofulvum)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Benzofuran fungistatic antibiotic (from Penicillium griseofulvum)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds microtubule proteins (tubulin) and disrupts the mitotic spindle → arrests fungal cell division in metaphase
- Deposited in keratin precursor cells, so new keratin resists infection
- Active only against dermatophytes; no effect on Candida, Malassezia or deep fungi

## Pharmacokinetics
- Poorly water-soluble; absorption improves with a fatty meal and with smaller particle size
- Microsize and ultramicrosize forms are not interchangeable mg-for-mg (ultramicrosize is better absorbed)
- Half-life 9–24 h; reaches the stratum corneum through sweat; washes out quickly after stopping
- Metabolised in the liver; a CYP inducer

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea capitis — especially Microsporum infections (first choice), and children
- Extensive tinea corporis/cruris when other drugs are unavailable
- Not suitable for onychomycosis (needs 12–18 months, poor cure)
- Rarely used for anti-inflammatory purposes (lichen planus, etc.)

## Dose & formulations
- Children (tinea capitis): microsize 20–25 mg/kg/day, or ultramicrosize 10–15 mg/kg/day, with fatty food, for at least 6–8 weeks
- Adults: microsize 500 mg–1 g/day (ultramicrosize 375–750 mg/day)
- Tinea corporis: 2–4 weeks; tinea pedis: 4–8 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Headache (most common; often settles)
- GI upset, taste disturbance
- Photosensitivity; can precipitate or worsen lupus erythematosus and acute porphyria
- Urticaria, morbilliform rash, fixed drug eruption, rarely SJS/TEN
- Hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, proteinuria (rare)
- Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy; men should not father children during treatment and for 6 months after
- Porphyria, hepatic failure, systemic lupus

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducer: reduces efficacy of oral contraceptives, warfarin, cyclosporine
- Phenobarbital reduces griseofulvin absorption
- Alcohol: disulfiram-like reaction

## Monitoring
- CBC and LFT only for prolonged courses
- Advise extra contraception

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category X) — teratogenic and embryotoxic.

## Viva points
- Fungistatic; acts on the mitotic spindle
- Drug of choice for Microsporum tinea capitis; terbinafine is better for Trichophyton tonsurans
- Give with a fatty meal (e.g. milk)
- Ineffective against Candida and Malassezia
- Enzyme inducer — reduces oral contraceptive efficacy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10 (Systemic antifungal agents), Table 10.5; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Growth factors (becaplermin, EGF)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous topicals & wound care · Recombinant growth factors for wound healing — becaplermin (PDGF-BB) gel 0.01%, epidermal growth factor (rhEGF)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous topicals & wound care_

**Class:** Recombinant growth factors for wound healing — becaplermin (PDGF-BB) gel 0.01%, epidermal growth factor (rhEGF)

## Mechanism of action
- Stimulate chemotaxis and proliferation of fibroblasts, endothelial cells and keratinocytes → granulation tissue and re-epithelialisation

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Diabetic neuropathic foot ulcers (becaplermin — approved), pressure ulcers, chronic non-healing wounds (rhEGF — available in India)

## Dose & formulations
- Becaplermin: amount calculated by ulcer size, once daily, covered with moist saline dressing; continue with offloading and debridement

## Adverse effects
- Local rash; possible increased cancer mortality with ≥3 tubes of becaplermin (boxed warning later removed)

## Contraindications
- Malignancy at the application site; infected or ischaemic wounds

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- PDGF-BB gel for diabetic foot ulcers — only with good wound care and offloading

_Sources: Khopkar ch.32 (Growth factor preparations); Wolverton 4e ch.54. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: H2 antihistamines (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine)
posts.summary: Antihistamines · H2 receptor antagonists
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** H2 receptor antagonists

## Mechanism of action
- Block H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells and on skin blood vessels (part of wheal and flare)
- Cimetidine also has immunomodulatory (blocks suppressor T-cell H2 receptors) and anti-androgenic effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Add-on to H1 antihistamines in chronic urticaria (small extra benefit), anaphylaxis adjunct, mastocytosis
- Cimetidine: warts in children (immunomodulatory — evidence weak), hirsutism (anti-androgen), reduces dapsone methaemoglobinaemia

## Dose & formulations
- Famotidine 20–40 mg twice daily; cimetidine 400 mg twice daily (warts 30–40 mg/kg/day)

## Adverse effects
- Generally safe; cimetidine — gynaecomastia, impotence, confusion in elderly, CYP inhibition
- Ranitidine withdrawn worldwide in 2020 (NDMA carcinogen contamination)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Cimetidine inhibits CYP1A2, 2D6, 3A4 → raises warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin, lignocaine, doxepin levels

## Pregnancy & lactation
Famotidine considered safe.

## Viva points
- H1 + H2 combination in refractory urticaria
- Cimetidine: interactions, gynaecomastia, warts (immunomodulation)
- Ranitidine withdrawn — NDMA

_Sources: Khopkar (Antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Halobetasol propionate (0.05% / 0.01% lotion)
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Super-potent fluorinated steroid (US class 1); 0.01% lotion in a newer vehicle remains high/super-high potency
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Super-potent fluorinated steroid (US class 1); 0.01% lotion in a newer vehicle remains high/super-high potency

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist with very high potency (similar to clobetasol)
- The 0.01% lotion (polymeric emulsion) delivers drug efficiently, allowing a lower concentration with less HPA suppression and longer use (up to 8 weeks)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Plaque psoriasis (adults)
- Other steroid-responsive thick dermatoses (lichen simplex, hypertrophic lichen planus)

## Dose & formulations
- 0.05% cream/ointment: once or twice daily, max 50 g/week, up to 2 weeks
- 0.01% lotion: once daily for up to 8 weeks, max 50 g/week
- Halobetasol 0.01% + tazarotene 0.045% lotion is also available for psoriasis

## Adverse effects
- As for super-potent steroids: atrophy, striae, folliculitis, HPA suppression

## Contraindications
- Face, flexures, groin; children under 12–18 (label); untreated infection, rosacea

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid large areas.

## Viva points
- Class 1 steroid; 0.01% lotion allows 8-week use
- Fixed combination with tazarotene reduces retinoid irritation and steroid atrophy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45; product information for 0.01% lotion (Bryhali). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Halobetasol + Salicylic acid
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Combination: super-potent steroid + keratolytic
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Combination: super-potent steroid + keratolytic

## Mechanism of action
- Salicylic acid (usually 3%) dissolves the cement between corneocytes (desmolytic) → removes scale
- This increases penetration of the steroid into thick plaques

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Thick, scaly plaque psoriasis, hyperkeratotic eczema, lichen simplex chronicus, palmoplantar psoriasis/eczema

## Dose & formulations
- Once or twice daily for up to 2 weeks (max 50 g/week), then taper

## Adverse effects
- Steroid side effects; irritation and stinging from salicylic acid
- Salicylism if used over large areas (especially with renal impairment, children)

## Contraindications
- Face, flexures, children; large body areas; aspirin allergy (relative); untreated infection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid large areas.

## Viva points
- Salicylic acid improves steroid penetration in thick plaques
- Salicylate toxicity if large areas are treated

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45 and ch.55 (Agents for hyperkeratosis); Khopkar ch.22 and ch.27. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Histoglobulin (Histoglob PFS)
posts.summary: IV Immunotherapy · Human normal immunoglobulin + histamine dihydrochloride combination (non-specific immunotherapy / 'histaminopexy')
posts.body:
_Injectables · IV Immunotherapy_

**Class:** Human normal immunoglobulin + histamine dihydrochloride combination (non-specific immunotherapy / 'histaminopexy')

## Mechanism of action
- The histamine–immunoglobulin complex is thought to stimulate antibodies that bind histamine
- This raises the blood's capacity to bind and neutralise free histamine (histaminopexy) and lowers responsiveness to histamine
- May also reduce IgE levels and eosinophil counts and dampen mast-cell activation
- Exact mechanism is not fully established

## Pharmacokinetics
- Given by subcutaneous injection; effect builds over the induction course

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic spontaneous urticaria not controlled with antihistamines (adjunct)
- Allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma (adjunct)
- Atopic dermatitis (limited evidence)

## Dose & formulations
- One prefilled syringe (PFS) subcutaneously per dose
- Induction: 6 injections at 4-day intervals (days 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 as in the manufacturer's calendar); more injections may be given depending on response
- Maintenance: booster doses at 1, 3 and 6 months
- Continue the patient's antihistamine and taper it according to response

## Adverse effects
- Pain, redness or swelling at the injection site
- Fever, headache, transient flare of itch or urticaria
- Rare: hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (contains human immunoglobulin) — observe after injection
- Blood-product precautions: very small theoretical risk of transmissible infection

## Contraindications
- Known hypersensitivity to human immunoglobulin or histamine
- IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
- Acute febrile illness or infection (postpone), uncontrolled asthma attack
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding (insufficient data)

## Drug interactions
- Systemic corticosteroids may blunt the response (some prescribing information advises against simultaneous use)
- Live vaccines: immunoglobulin may reduce response — space as per immunoglobulin guidance

## Monitoring
- Urticaria activity score (UAS7) at baseline and follow-up
- Observe 15–30 min after each injection

## Pregnancy & lactation
No adequate data — avoid.

## Viva points
- Histamine + human immunoglobulin → histaminopexy
- Schedule: 6 SC injections every 4 days, then boosters at 1, 3 and 6 months
- Evidence is limited (small studies); guideline step-up for chronic urticaria is antihistamine updosing → omalizumab → cyclosporine

## Note on sources
Histoglobulin is in neither book. The dosing follows the Histoglob PFS card you shared (6 injections 4 days apart, then boosters at 1, 3 and 6 months).

_Sources: Not covered in Wolverton or Khopkar; Histoglob PFS prescribing information (Bharat Serums and Vaccines) and dosing card shared by the user. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) & prevention of parent-to-child transmission (PPTCT)
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Antiretroviral prophylaxis regimens (current NACO guidance)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Antiretroviral prophylaxis regimens (current NACO guidance)

## Mechanism of action
- ART given soon after exposure prevents establishment of infection in local dendritic cells and lymph nodes
- In pregnancy, maternal viral suppression plus infant prophylaxis prevents transmission

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Occupational PEP (needle-stick in dermatology procedures, splash on mucosa) and non-occupational PEP (sexual exposure, sexual assault)
- Risk assessment: exposure type (percutaneous, mucous membrane, broken skin) and source status
- PPTCT: all HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women start lifelong ART irrespective of CD4 count

## Dose & formulations
- PEP: start as early as possible (ideally within 2 h, not beyond 72 h); preferred regimen TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) once daily for 28 days
- Baseline HIV test of exposed person; follow-up HIV tests at 6 weeks, 3 months (and 6 months as per programme)
- Immediate care: wash wound with soap and water, do not squeeze or use bleach; flush mucous membranes with water
- PPTCT: mother on TLD lifelong; infant prophylaxis with nevirapine syrup for 6 weeks (low risk), or zidovudine + nevirapine (dual prophylaxis) if high risk — mother not on ART, no viral load or viral load ≥1000 copies/ml after 32 weeks, or diagnosed within 6 weeks of delivery (NACO 2021); dual prophylaxis for 6 weeks, extended to 12 weeks if the baby is breastfed, with early infant diagnosis (DNA-PCR at 6 weeks)
- Hepatitis B: check vaccination status after needle-stick; give vaccine ± HBIG

## Adverse effects
- See component drugs; PEP side effects are usually mild with TLD

## Contraindications
- PEP not indicated if the exposed person is already HIV-positive or exposure is beyond 72 h

## Monitoring
- HIV test at baseline and follow-up; LFT/renal function if indicated; counsel safe sex/blood donation avoidance until follow-up negative

## Pregnancy & lactation
TLD is used in pregnancy for PEP and PPTCT.

## Viva points
- PEP within 72 h (ideally 2 h) for 28 days — TLD
- Infant prophylaxis: NVP 6 weeks or AZT+NVP 12 weeks (high risk)
- Lifelong ART for all pregnant women with HIV

## Note on sources
Khopkar's PEP and perinatal regimens (zidovudine-based, single-dose nevirapine) are outdated; only current NACO regimens are given here. Please confirm with the latest NACO technical guidelines.

_Sources: NACO National Guidelines for HIV Care and Treatment 2021 (PEP sec. 2.10, PPTCT sec. 2.5); Khopkar ch.4 (Postexposure prophylaxis, perinatal transmission regimens — older regimens superseded). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: HPV vaccine (quadrivalent)
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Recombinant non-infectious virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Recombinant non-infectious virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18

## Mechanism of action
- L1 capsid protein self-assembles into VLPs (no viral DNA) → strong neutralising antibody response
- Types 6 and 11 cause about 90% of anogenital warts; types 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers
- Prophylactic — does not clear established infection (therapeutic use in warts is off-label)

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.5 mL IM in the deltoid

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Prevention of cervical, vulvar, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal cancers and anogenital warts in girls and boys
- Best given before sexual debut (9–14 years)
- Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis prevention
- Off-label: recalcitrant cutaneous and anogenital warts (case series; Wolverton notes some reports of benefit)
- India: indigenous qHPV vaccine (Cervavac) and introduction into the national programme for girls

## Dose & formulations
- 9–14 years: 2 doses (0 and 6–12 months)
- 15–26 years: 3 doses (0, 2 and 6 months) — WHO now also accepts 1–2 doses in younger groups
- Immunocompromised (including HIV): 3 doses
- 9-valent vaccine (Gardasil 9) adds types 31, 33, 45, 52, 58

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain, swelling
- Syncope (observe seated for 15 min), headache, fever
- Anaphylaxis very rare (yeast protein)

## Contraindications
- Severe allergy to a previous dose or to yeast
- Pregnancy (defer remaining doses until after delivery; inadvertent dosing is not harmful)

## Drug interactions
- Immunosuppressants may reduce response

## Monitoring
- Observe 15 min for syncope

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not recommended in pregnancy (precaution); safe in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- VLP vaccine — no DNA, cannot cause infection
- 6 and 11 → warts; 16 and 18 → cancer
- 2 doses if started before 15; 3 doses after 15 or if immunocompromised
- Prevents anogenital warts — relevant for STI clinic counselling

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (HPV vaccine in warts); WHO HPV position paper 2022. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydrocortisone (injection + topical)
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Short-acting natural glucocorticoid (cortisol) with mineralocorticoid action
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Short-acting natural glucocorticoid (cortisol) with mineralocorticoid action

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist — anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive
- Significant mineralocorticoid effect (salt and water retention) — the right steroid for adrenal insufficiency

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble succinate ester — rapid onset IV (within 1 h)
- Biological half-life 8–12 h (short-acting)
- Equivalence: 20 mg hydrocortisone = 5 mg prednisolone

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Anaphylaxis — adjunct after adrenaline (prevents late/biphasic reaction; not a first-line drug)
- Acute severe angioedema, severe acute urticaria, acute drug reactions
- Adrenal crisis and stress-dose cover in patients on long-term steroids (surgery, illness)
- Status asthmaticus

## Dose & formulations
- Anaphylaxis: 200 mg IV or IM (adults); children 6–12 years 100 mg, 6 months–6 years 50 mg, under 6 months 25 mg
- Adrenal crisis: 100 mg IV bolus, then 50 mg every 6 h (or 200 mg/24 h infusion)
- Vials 100 mg (reconstitute with sterile water)

## Adverse effects
- Short courses: hyperglycaemia, fluid retention, hypokalaemia, hypertension, mood change
- Rapid IV bolus of large doses: hypotension, arrhythmia (rare)
- Long use: full range of steroid side effects

## Contraindications
- No absolute contraindication in emergencies
- Caution: systemic fungal infection, uncontrolled diabetes, active peptic ulcer

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducers lower effect; diuretics add to hypokalaemia; NSAIDs increase GI risk

## Monitoring
- BP, glucose, potassium with repeated doses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe for emergency use; mostly inactivated by the placenta.

## Viva points
- Only injectable steroid with significant mineralocorticoid effect — drug of choice in adrenal crisis
- In anaphylaxis, steroids are adjuncts — adrenaline is the life-saving drug
- 20 mg hydrocortisone = 5 mg prednisolone

## Topical form: Hydrocortisone acetate 1% lotion/cream
_Least potent topical steroid (US class 7; UK 'mild'); non-fluorinated_

**Mechanism**
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist — mild anti-inflammatory action with very little atrophy

**Indications**
- Face, eyelids, flexures, genitals and nappy area
- Infants and children: mild eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis, intertrigo
- Maintenance after stronger steroids

**Dose & how to apply**
- Apply thinly once or twice daily; can be used for longer periods than potent steroids

**Adverse effects**
- Very low risk; prolonged use on the face can still cause perioral dermatitis/rosacea
- Contact allergy (tixocortol pivalate group — class A)

**Contraindications**
- Untreated infection, rosacea, perioral dermatitis

**Pregnancy:** Safe.

**Viva points**
- Safest steroid for face and infants
- Hydrocortisone is the marker of class A (Coopman) contact allergy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13; Khopkar ch.8 (Table 8.4, injectable steroids); Wolverton 4e ch.45; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydrogen peroxide (1.5–6%)
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Oxidising antiseptic
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Oxidising antiseptic

## Mechanism of action
- Releases oxygen on contact with tissue catalase → effervescence loosens debris; weak antibacterial (especially anaerobes)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cleansing of dirty wounds and crusts, ear wax; 40% solution for seborrhoeic keratoses (approved USA); cream 1% for impetigo (Europe)

## Dose & formulations
- 3% for cleansing (diluted); short contact

## Adverse effects
- Delays healing (toxic to fibroblasts) with repeated use; gas embolism if used in closed cavities under pressure; bleaching of hair and skin (transient white blanching)

## Contraindications
- Closed body cavities, deep wounds under pressure

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Effervescence from catalase; harmful to granulation tissue with repeated use

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Hydrogen peroxide). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydroquinone 2% (and 4%)
posts.summary: VIII Pigmentary / depigmenting · Phenolic tyrosinase inhibitor (hydroxyphenol); gold-standard depigmenting agent
posts.body:
_Topicals · VIII Pigmentary / depigmenting_

**Class:** Phenolic tyrosinase inhibitor (hydroxyphenol); gold-standard depigmenting agent

## Mechanism of action
- Competitive substrate inhibitor of tyrosinase → less melanin
- Also generates reactive oxygen species that damage melanosomes and melanocytes (cytotoxic)
- Unstable — oxidises to brown (do not use if the cream turns brown)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Melasma (first-line, alone 2–4% or in triple combination), PIH, solar lentigines, ephelides
- Monobenzone (monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone) is different — causes permanent depigmentation (used for universal vitiligo)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply at night to pigmented areas only; with strict daytime broad-spectrum sunscreen
- Use for 3–4 months, then take a break (cycling) or switch to non-hydroquinone maintenance (azelaic acid, kojic acid, niacinamide)
- 2% available OTC in some countries; 4% prescription

## Adverse effects
- Irritant and allergic contact dermatitis
- Transient hypopigmentation, 'halo' effect around treated areas, confetti-like depigmentation
- Exogenous ochronosis (blue-black pigmentation, caviar-like papules) — especially with long-term use, high concentrations and in dark skin (common in Africa with unregulated products)
- Nail discolouration

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding (avoid; significant absorption 35–45%)
- Hypersensitivity; sunburnt or inflamed skin

## Drug interactions
- Benzoyl peroxide and hydrogen peroxide: transient dark staining

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in pregnancy (old FDA category C; high absorption).

## Viva points
- Tyrosinase inhibitor + melanocytotoxic
- Exogenous ochronosis with prolonged use
- Monobenzone (not hydroquinone) for permanent depigmentation
- Banned in cosmetics in the EU; prescription-only in many countries

_Sources: Khopkar ch.26 (Demelanizing agents); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide)
posts.summary: Immunomodulators · Antimetabolite; ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Immunomodulators_

**Class:** Antimetabolite; ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase → no deoxyribonucleotides → blocks DNA synthesis (S-phase)
- Antiproliferative for keratinocytes; raises fetal haemoglobin (sickle cell)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis (refractory; older alternative to methotrexate), HIV (historical with didanosine)
- Hypereosinophilic syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders (polycythaemia vera, CML, essential thrombocythaemia), sickle cell disease

## Dose & formulations
- Psoriasis: 500 mg–1.5 g/day (1–2 g in divided doses), adjusted to blood counts

## Adverse effects
- Bone marrow suppression (megaloblastic anaemia, leucopenia); macrocytosis is expected
- Skin: painful leg ulcers (malleolar), dermatomyositis-like eruption (hands — 'hydroxyurea dermopathy'), xerosis, hyperpigmentation (skin, nails — longitudinal melanonychia), lichenoid eruptions, alopecia
- Squamous cell carcinoma and actinic keratoses with long-term use (photo-exposed sites)
- GI upset, fever, hepatitis

## Contraindications
- Marked marrow suppression, pregnancy, breastfeeding

## Drug interactions
- Other myelosuppressants; didanosine/stavudine (pancreatitis, neuropathy)

## Monitoring
- CBC every 1–2 weeks initially, then monthly; LFT, renal function; skin examination

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (teratogenic).

## Viva points
- Ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor
- Leg ulcers and dermatomyositis-like eruption
- Melanonychia and SCC with long-term use

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.19 (Cytotoxic agents); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydroxyzine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; piperazine class
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; piperazine class

## Mechanism of action
- Inverse agonist at H1 receptors (stabilises the inactive form)
- Crosses the blood–brain barrier → sedation and anxiolysis
- Also anticholinergic, antiserotonergic and mild antiemetic effects

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; onset 15–30 min; metabolised in the liver to cetirizine (active metabolite)
- Half-life about 20 h in adults (shorter in children, longer in elderly)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pruritus of atopic dermatitis and other itchy dermatoses — night-time sedation helps
- Urticaria (usually as a night-time add-on to a non-sedating antihistamine)
- Anxiety; pre-procedure sedation

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10–25 mg at night, up to 25 mg three to four times daily (max 100 mg/day; lower in elderly)
- Children: about 1–2 mg/kg/day in divided doses (syrup 10 mg/5 mL)

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, impaired driving and school performance, next-day hangover
- Anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, confusion in elderly
- QT prolongation at high doses (caution)
- Paradoxical excitation in children

## Contraindications
- Prolonged QT; early pregnancy
- Caution: glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, elderly, hepatic impairment, porphyria

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol and CNS depressants (additive sedation)
- Other QT-prolonging drugs; other anticholinergics

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in early pregnancy (EMA advice); cetirizine/loratadine preferred. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- First-generation, crosses BBB
- Its metabolite is cetirizine
- Useful at night for itch-related sleep loss, but sedation lowers daytime performance
