- Guidelines recommend second-generation antihistamines as first line for urticaria

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32 (Antihistamines); Khopkar (Antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hypochlorite solutions: EUSOL & Dakin's solution
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Chlorine-releasing antiseptics (EUSOL = Edinburgh University Solution of Lime: chlorinated lime + boric acid; Dakin's = s
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Chlorine-releasing antiseptics (EUSOL = Edinburgh University Solution of Lime: chlorinated lime + boric acid; Dakin's = sodium hypochlorite 0.25–0.5%)

## Mechanism of action
- Release hypochlorous acid → oxidises proteins → kills bacteria, fungi, viruses; dissolves necrotic tissue (chemical debridement)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Sloughy, infected, malodorous ulcers and wounds (short courses)
- Dilute bleach baths (0.005%) for atopic dermatitis with recurrent staphylococcal infection

## Dose & formulations
- Soaked gauze changed once or twice daily for a few days; bleach bath: ½ cup 6% bleach in a full tub, 10 min, twice weekly

## Adverse effects
- Toxic to fibroblasts and granulation tissue — delays healing with prolonged use; irritation, pain

## Contraindications
- Clean granulating wounds

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Chemical debridement of sloughy ulcers; stop once clean
- Dilute bleach baths in atopic dermatitis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (EUSOL, 1% sodium hypochlorite — Dakin's solution) and ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Idoxuridine
posts.summary: Wart & antiviral agents · Iodinated thymidine analogue (first antiviral drug)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents_

**Class:** Iodinated thymidine analogue (first antiviral drug)

## Mechanism of action
- Incorporated into viral (and host) DNA instead of thymidine → faulty DNA → inhibits replication of HSV and VZV; toxic systemically

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Historic: herpes simplex keratitis (eye drops), herpes labialis and zoster (5–40% in DMSO) — replaced by acyclovir

## Dose & formulations
- Historic topical application several times daily

## Adverse effects
- Irritation, contact dermatitis; systemic toxicity (marrow) — topical only

## Contraindications
- Systemic use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- First antiviral (1962) — now obsolete

_Sources: Khopkar ch.20 (Idoxuridine). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Imiquimod 5% cream
posts.summary: IX Immunomodulators · Imidazoquinoline immune response modifier; Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonist
posts.body:
_Topicals · IX Immunomodulators_

**Class:** Imidazoquinoline immune response modifier; Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonist

## Mechanism of action
- Activates TLR7 (and TLR8) on dendritic cells and macrophages → release of IFN-α, TNF-α, IL-12
- Boosts innate and Th1 cell-mediated immunity → clears virus-infected and tumour cells; also directly pro-apoptotic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Approved: external anogenital warts, actinic keratosis, superficial basal cell carcinoma
- Off-label: molluscum (not effective in trials in children), common warts, Bowen disease, lentigo maligna, extramammary Paget disease, keloid (post-excision), cutaneous metastases

## Dose & formulations
- Anogenital warts: 3 times a week at bedtime (e.g. Mon/Wed/Fri), wash off after 6–10 h, up to 16 weeks
- Superficial BCC: 5 times a week for 6 weeks
- Actinic keratosis: twice a week for 16 weeks (5%); 3.75% daily for two 2-week cycles
- Sachets — use one sachet per application; wash hands

## Adverse effects
- Local inflammation (erythema, erosion, crusting, oedema) — often needed for efficacy; rest days if severe
- Flu-like symptoms (fever, myalgia, fatigue) with large areas
- Hypo- or hyperpigmentation; induction or worsening of psoriasis, vitiligo-like depigmentation
- Weakens condoms and diaphragms

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; internal (urethral, intravaginal, cervical, rectal) warts
- Caution: autoimmune disease, psoriasis, immunosuppression, broken skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data — avoid in pregnancy (old FDA category C); use cryotherapy for warts in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- TLR7 agonist → IFN-α
- Warts: 3 times weekly; sBCC: 5 times weekly × 6 weeks
- Inflammation = sign it is working
- Damages latex condoms

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (Topical antivirals — imiquimod) and ch.47; Khopkar ch.23. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Infliximab
posts.summary: Biologicals · TNF-α inhibitor — chimeric (mouse–human) IgG1 monoclonal antibody
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Biologicals_

**Class:** TNF-α inhibitor — chimeric (mouse–human) IgG1 monoclonal antibody

## Mechanism of action
- Binds soluble and membrane-bound TNF-α with high affinity; lyses TNF-expressing cells (complement and antibody-dependent cytotoxicity)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Severe plaque psoriasis (fastest onset of TNF inhibitors), erythrodermic and generalised pustular psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis
- Pyoderma gangrenosum (especially with IBD), hidradenitis suppurativa (off-label), Behçet disease, sarcoidosis, SJS/TEN (case reports)
- Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis

## Dose & formulations
- 5 mg/kg IV infusion at weeks 0, 2 and 6, then every 8 weeks (over 2 h)

## Adverse effects
- Infusion reactions (acute — fever, urticaria, hypotension; delayed serum-sickness-like)
- Antibodies against the drug (chimeric) → loss of response; methotrexate reduces this
- TB reactivation (highest risk among TNF inhibitors — often extrapulmonary/disseminated), opportunistic infections, hepatitis B reactivation
- Hepatotoxicity, demyelination, lupus-like syndrome, heart failure, hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (young men with azathioprine)
- Paradoxical psoriasis

## Contraindications
- As for TNF inhibitors; murine protein hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Other biologics; live vaccines

## Monitoring
- TB, hepatitis, HIV screening; LFT; infusion monitoring

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses placenta in late pregnancy (IgG1) — stop by about 16–24 weeks if possible; avoid live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus) in exposed infants for 6–12 months.

## Viva points
- Chimeric antibody — infusion reactions and antidrug antibodies
- Highest TB risk among anti-TNFs
- Fastest-acting TNF blocker in psoriasis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.26; Khopkar (Immunobiologicals). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Interferons (systemic, intralesional, topical)
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Cytokine immunomodulators — IFN-α (2a, 2b, pegylated), IFN-β, IFN-γ (1b); recombinant proteins
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Cytokine immunomodulators — IFN-α (2a, 2b, pegylated), IFN-β, IFN-γ (1b); recombinant proteins

## Mechanism of action
- Bind interferon receptors → JAK-STAT signalling → hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes
- Antiviral: inhibit viral replication (2',5'-oligoadenylate synthetase, protein kinase R)
- Antiproliferative and immunomodulatory: activate NK cells, cytotoxic T cells and macrophages, increase MHC expression; IFN-γ activates macrophage killing

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intralesional IFN-α2b: condylomata acuminata (refractory), keloids (after excision), BCC and SCC (selected), keratoacanthoma, common warts
- Systemic IFN-α: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides, Sézary — often with PUVA/retinoids), Kaposi sarcoma, melanoma (adjuvant — historical), Behçet disease, chronic hepatitis B/C (historical), life-threatening infantile haemangioma (historical — spastic diplegia risk)
- IFN-γ-1b: chronic granulomatous disease (reduces infections — approved), severe atopic dermatitis (limited), osteopetrosis
- Topical IFN gel/cream: genital warts, herpes (limited)

## Dose & formulations
- Intralesional IFN-α2b for genital warts: 1 million IU into each wart (up to 5 warts) three times a week for 3 weeks
- Systemic IFN-α for CTCL: 3–9 million IU SC three times weekly
- IFN-γ-1b (CGD): 50 µg/m² SC three times weekly

## Adverse effects
- Flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, myalgia, headache) — premedicate with paracetamol; tachyphylaxis over weeks
- Fatigue, depression and suicidal ideation, cognitive changes
- Cytopenias, raised LFT, thyroid dysfunction (hypo/hyper), autoimmunity
- Skin: injection-site reactions/necrosis, alopecia, induction or flare of psoriasis, sarcoidosis, lichen planus, vitiligo, lupus

## Contraindications
- Severe depression or suicidal history; autoimmune hepatitis; decompensated liver disease; uncontrolled thyroid disease; pregnancy (relative)

## Drug interactions
- Theophylline levels rise; additive marrow suppression with zidovudine and other myelosuppressives

## Monitoring
- CBC, LFT, TSH, mood assessment during systemic use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (abortifacient in animals at high doses).

## Viva points
- IL IFN-α2b for genital warts — 1 MIU per wart thrice weekly × 3 weeks
- IFN-γ for chronic granulomatous disease
- IFN therapy can induce psoriasis and sarcoidosis
- Flu-like illness and depression are the key side effects

_Sources: Khopkar ch.3, ch.13 (Immunobiologicals — interferons) and ch.20 (topical/intralesional IFN); Wolverton 4e ch.43 and ch.37. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Intralesional vinblastine
posts.summary: Wart & antiviral agents · Vinca alkaloid (antimitotic)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents_

**Class:** Vinca alkaloid (antimitotic)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds tubulin → blocks microtubule assembly → mitotic arrest

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Kaposi sarcoma (localised lesions) — intralesional; warts (rarely)
- Systemic: lymphomas, Langerhans cell histiocytosis

## Dose & formulations
- Intralesional 0.1–0.5 mg/mL (0.1 mL per 0.5 cm² lesion) every 2–3 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Pain at injection site, hyperpigmentation, ulceration; systemic: neuropathy, marrow suppression; extravasation necrosis

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy; IV only for systemic use (intrathecal fatal)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated.

## Viva points
- Intralesional vinblastine for Kaposi sarcoma

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.47; Khopkar (intralesional agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)
posts.summary: Biologicals · Pooled polyclonal IgG from thousands of healthy donors
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Biologicals_

**Class:** Pooled polyclonal IgG from thousands of healthy donors

## Mechanism of action
- Saturates the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) → faster breakdown of pathogenic autoantibodies (key in pemphigus)
- Blocks Fas–FasL interaction → stops keratinocyte apoptosis (proposed in TEN)
- Neutralises autoantibodies (anti-idiotypes), blocks Fc receptors on macrophages, inhibits complement, modulates cytokines, expands regulatory T cells

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Kawasaki disease (with aspirin — prevents coronary aneurysms)
- Dermatomyositis (refractory; approved in USA), pemphigus vulgaris/foliaceus (refractory — 3rd line in the Derma Desk ladder), bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid, EBA
- SJS/TEN (controversial benefit), scleromyxoedema (first line), pyoderma gangrenosum, chronic urticaria (refractory), vasculitis, primary immunodeficiency, ITP

## Dose & formulations
- Immunomodulatory dose: 2 g/kg per cycle divided over 2–5 days, repeated every 4 weeks
- TEN: 1 g/kg/day for 3 days (total 3 g/kg) in studies
- Infuse slowly (start 0.5 mL/kg/h and increase)

## Adverse effects
- Infusion reactions (headache, chills, flushing, back pain) — slow rate, premedicate
- Aseptic meningitis, thrombosis (stroke, MI — hyperviscosity), acute kidney injury (sucrose-containing products), haemolysis (anti-A/B antibodies)
- Anaphylaxis in IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies
- Eczematous/pompholyx-like eruptions after infusion

## Contraindications
- IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (use IgA-depleted product); caution in renal failure, thrombosis risk, heart failure

## Drug interactions
- Live vaccines: response reduced (delay for months)

## Monitoring
- Baseline IgA level, renal function, CBC; BP and vitals during infusion; hydration

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- FcRn saturation increases IgG catabolism
- Check IgA levels before first infusion
- 2 g/kg per cycle for autoimmune disease
- Scleromyxoedema — IVIG is first-line

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.36 (Intravenous immunoglobulin); Khopkar (Intravenous immunoglobulins). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Iron
posts.summary: Vitamins & trace elements · Mineral supplement (ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate; IV iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements_

**Class:** Mineral supplement (ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate; IV iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose)

## Mechanism of action
- Restores haemoglobin and tissue iron; iron is a cofactor for ribonucleotide reductase in rapidly dividing hair matrix cells

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Iron deficiency in telogen effluvium and female pattern hair loss (many experts aim for ferritin >40–70 ng/mL)
- Koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis, pruritus of iron deficiency, Plummer–Vinson syndrome
- Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss (e.g. dermatitis herpetiformis/coeliac, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia)

## Dose & formulations
- Oral elemental iron 60–120 mg once daily or on alternate days (better absorption), with vitamin C, away from tea/calcium; continue 3 months after Hb normalises
- IV iron for intolerance or malabsorption

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, constipation, black stools; IV — hypersensitivity, skin staining at infusion site (brown pigmentation from extravasation)

## Contraindications
- Haemochromatosis, haemosiderosis, haemolytic anaemia without iron deficiency

## Drug interactions
- Reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine, dolutegravir, mycophenolate; PPIs/antacids reduce iron absorption

## Monitoring
- Hb, ferritin, transferrin saturation

## Pregnancy & lactation
Recommended in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Check ferritin in diffuse hair loss
- Separate iron from tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones

_Sources: Khopkar (Trace elements — iron); Wolverton 4e ch.40. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Isoniazid (INH)
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Isonicotinic acid hydrazide; first-line antituberculous drug
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Isonicotinic acid hydrazide; first-line antituberculous drug

## Mechanism of action
- Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG)
- Inhibits InhA (enoyl-ACP reductase) → blocks mycolic acid synthesis in the cell wall
- Bactericidal for rapidly dividing bacilli; bacteriostatic for resting ones

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; penetrates all tissues and caseous material
- Metabolised by N-acetylation (NAT2) — slow acetylators (about half of Indians) have more neuropathy; fast acetylators more hepatitis (debated)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- All forms of TB including cutaneous TB (lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma, TBVC, tuberculids)
- Latent TB infection before biologics/JAK inhibitors (6–9 months alone, or with rifapentine/rifampicin in short regimens)

## Dose & formulations
- 5 mg/kg/day (max 300 mg) in fixed-dose combinations (India NTEP weight bands)
- Pyridoxine 10–25 mg/day to prevent neuropathy (higher in HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, pregnancy, alcoholism)

## Adverse effects
- Hepatitis (age-related; higher with rifampicin, alcohol)
- Peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine deficiency) — prevented by pyridoxine
- Pellagra (niacin deficiency) — photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia
- Drug-induced lupus (ANA, antihistone antibodies)
- Acneiform eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, DRESS; optic neuritis, seizures, psychosis (rare)

## Contraindications
- Previous INH-induced hepatitis; acute liver disease

## Drug interactions
- Inhibits CYP2C19/3A4 → raises phenytoin and carbamazepine levels
- Antacids reduce absorption; alcohol adds hepatotoxicity

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline and if symptoms (routine in high-risk); ask about neuropathy

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy with pyridoxine.

## Viva points
- Give pyridoxine with INH
- Cutaneous side effects: pellagra, acneiform eruption, drug-induced lupus
- Slow acetylators → neuropathy

_Sources: Khopkar ch.7 (Antituberculous agents); Wolverton 4e ch.9 and ch.26 (TB screening before biologics). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Isotretinoin
posts.summary: I Retinoids · First-generation (non-aromatic) retinoid; 13-cis-retinoic acid
posts.body:
_Oral · I Retinoids_

**Class:** First-generation (non-aromatic) retinoid; 13-cis-retinoic acid

## Mechanism of action
- Acts mainly through its metabolites on nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR) to change gene transcription
- Shrinks sebaceous glands and cuts sebum output by up to ~90%; this is the only acne drug that does this
- Normalises follicular keratinisation, so fewer microcomedones
- Indirectly reduces C. acnes because the follicle becomes less favourable for it; also anti-inflammatory

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 25%; roughly doubles when taken with a fatty meal (a lidose form, Absorica, is less food-dependent)
- 99% bound to albumin; half-life 10–20 h; main metabolite 4-oxo-isotretinoin
- Metabolised in the liver, excreted in bile and urine; not stored in fat, so it clears in about 1 month

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Severe nodulocystic acne (approved use)
- Moderate acne that fails oral antibiotics, scarring acne, or acne causing marked distress
- Rosacea (papulopustular, phymatous; low dose), Gram-negative folliculitis
- Hidradenitis suppurativa and dissecting cellulitis (limited benefit)
- Sebaceous hyperplasia; chemoprevention of skin cancer in xeroderma pigmentosum (high dose)
- Disorders of keratinisation such as Darier disease and PRP (acitretin usually preferred)

## Dose & formulations
- Acne: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day in 1–2 doses with food
- Aim for a total (cumulative) dose of 120–150 mg/kg; relapse is higher below 120 mg/kg
- Start low (e.g. 0.25–0.5 mg/kg) in severe or nodular acne to avoid an early flare
- Low-dose regimens (≈0.25–0.4 mg/kg/day) are used for moderate acne and rosacea
- Capsules 10, 20, 40 mg

## Adverse effects
- Mucocutaneous (almost universal): cheilitis — the earliest and most constant sign, often used as a marker of adherence; dry skin, dry nose with epistaxis, dry eyes and conjunctivitis, retinoid dermatitis
- Initial flare of acne; excess granulation tissue (pyogenic-granuloma-like) in nail folds or acne lesions
- Hair thinning, paronychia, photosensitivity
- Lipids: raised triglycerides (common); a rapid rise above 800–1000 mg/dL can cause pancreatitis
- Raised transaminases (usually mild and reversible)
- Musculoskeletal: myalgia and back pain; hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure with long, high-dose courses
- CNS: headache; pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension), especially with tetracyclines
- Mood change and depression or suicide have been reported; a causal link is not proven, but screen and ask at each visit
- Inflammatory bowel disease: reported, but no causal link shown
- Night blindness (reduced dark adaptation)
- Teratogenic: retinoid embryopathy (CNS, craniofacial, cardiac and thymic defects)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (absolute) and breastfeeding
- Women unable to follow reliable contraception
- Hypersensitivity, including to soy or paraben in some capsule fillers
- Relative: marked hyperlipidaemia, significant liver disease, hypervitaminosis A, concurrent tetracycline

## Drug interactions
- Tetracyclines raise the risk of pseudotumor cerebri — avoid together
- Vitamin A supplements: additive toxicity
- Methotrexate and alcohol: added liver toxicity
- Progestin-only 'mini-pill' is not reliable contraception during therapy
- Carbamazepine levels may fall

## Monitoring
- Women: 2 negative pregnancy tests before starting, then monthly, and 1 month after stopping
- Fasting lipids and LFTs at baseline and after about 1–2 months on the target dose; repeat only if abnormal or the dose rises
- CBC is not routinely needed
- At every visit: mood, headache or visual change, back pain

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Two methods of contraception from 1 month before, throughout, and for 1 month after stopping. No blood donation during treatment or for 1 month after. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Isotretinoin is the only acne drug that hits all four pathogenic factors: sebum, keratinisation, C. acnes and inflammation
- Cheilitis is the most common side effect; its absence suggests poor adherence
- Do not combine with tetracyclines (pseudotumor cerebri)
- Cumulative dose of 120–150 mg/kg reduces relapse
- Traditional advice was to delay waxing, dermabrasion and laser for 6 months; newer consensus says superficial procedures are probably acceptable — mention both

## Topical form: Isotretinoin topical (0.05%)
_Topical 13-cis-retinoic acid (gel 0.05%, combined with erythromycin in some products)_

**Mechanism**
- Comedolytic and anti-inflammatory; no effect on sebum when applied topically

**Indications**
- Mild–moderate comedonal and inflammatory acne (available in India/Europe, not USA)

**Dose & how to apply**
- Thin layer once or twice daily at night

**Adverse effects**
- Irritation, dryness, photosensitivity

**Contraindications**
- Pregnancy (precaution); eczema

**Pregnancy:** Avoid (precaution).

**Viva points**
- Topical isotretinoin does not reduce sebum — only oral isotretinoin does

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22 (Systemic retinoids); Khopkar (Oral retinoids); Khopkar (Topical retinoids); Wolverton 4e ch.46. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Itraconazole
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Triazole antifungal (first generation; lipophilic)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Triazole antifungal (first generation; lipophilic)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase → ergosterol depletion
- Fungistatic; broad spectrum: dermatophytes, Candida, Malassezia, Aspergillus and dimorphic fungi

## Pharmacokinetics
- Capsules need gastric acid and food — take with a full meal; avoid antacids and PPIs (or take with a cola drink)
- Oral solution is better absorbed on an empty stomach; super-bioavailable (SUBA) forms are less food-dependent
- Highly lipophilic and keratophilic; reaches skin via sebum and sweat and stays in nails for 6–9 months after stopping
- Half-life 24–42 h; metabolised by CYP3A4 (active metabolite hydroxy-itraconazole)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Dermatophytosis (tinea corporis, cruris, pedis), onychomycosis (pulse therapy)
- Pityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Candidiasis (mucocutaneous, candida onychomycosis)
- Sporotrichosis (drug of choice for cutaneous forms), chromoblastomycosis, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis
- Aspergillosis (alternative)

## Dose & formulations
- Tinea corporis/cruris: 100–200 mg/day × 2–4 weeks (longer courses at 200 mg/day are often needed in India)
- Onychomycosis pulse: 200 mg twice daily for 1 week each month — 2 pulses for fingernails, 3 for toenails
- Onychomycosis continuous: 200 mg/day × 12 weeks (toenails)
- Pityriasis versicolor: 200 mg/day × 5–7 days
- Sporotrichosis: 100–200 mg/day for 3–6 months
- Children: about 5 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache, rash
- Hepatotoxicity (rare but can be severe)
- Negative inotropic effect: can cause or worsen congestive heart failure (boxed warning)
- Hypokalaemia, hypertension, oedema (mineralocorticoid-like effect at high doses)
- QT prolongation; peripheral neuropathy (rare)

## Contraindications
- Congestive heart failure or ventricular dysfunction (for nail infections)
- Pregnancy
- Concurrent CYP3A4 substrates with dangerous toxicity: simvastatin, lovastatin, midazolam/triazolam, cisapride, pimozide, quinidine, dofetilide, ergot alkaloids

## Drug interactions
- Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor (and P-glycoprotein inhibitor)
- Raises cyclosporine, tacrolimus, digoxin, warfarin, calcium-channel blockers, some benzodiazepines, colchicine
- Rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine lower itraconazole levels; PPIs/H2 blockers/antacids reduce capsule absorption

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline and monthly if continuous therapy beyond 1 month
- Ask about heart failure symptoms

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category C); women should use contraception during treatment and for 2 months after. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Capsule absorption needs acid and food; solution on an empty stomach
- Pulse therapy works because the drug persists in the nail for months
- Contraindicated in congestive heart failure
- Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor — statin interaction (rhabdomyolysis)
- Drug of choice for cutaneous sporotrichosis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ivermectin (oral + topical)
posts.summary: V Antiparasitic · Macrocyclic lactone (semisynthetic avermectin from Streptomyces avermitilis)
posts.body:
_Oral · V Antiparasitic_

**Class:** Macrocyclic lactone (semisynthetic avermectin from Streptomyces avermitilis)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells (also GABA-gated channels)
- Increases chloride entry → hyperpolarisation → paralysis and death of the parasite
- In mammals these channels are only in the CNS, and P-glycoprotein at the blood–brain barrier keeps ivermectin out — hence its safety

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorption increases with a fatty meal (often given with food for scabies; the label advises water on an empty stomach)
- Highly lipophilic, widely distributed; half-life about 18 h
- Metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4); excreted in faeces
- Kills mites and lice but not eggs — so a second dose is needed

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Scabies — classic (alternative to permethrin, and for mass treatment, institutions, poor compliance) and crusted (Norwegian) scabies with topical therapy
- Head lice resistant to topical treatment
- Strongyloidiasis (drug of choice), cutaneous larva migrans, larva currens
- Onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis (mass drug administration with albendazole/DEC)
- Demodicosis and rosacea (topical 1% cream mainly)

## Dose & formulations
- Usual dose: 200 µg/kg as a single dose; tablets 3, 6 and 12 mg
- Scabies: 200 µg/kg, repeated after 7–14 days
- Crusted scabies: 200 µg/kg on days 1, 2, 8, 9 and 15 (plus days 22 and 29 in severe cases), with topical permethrin
- Head lice: 400 µg/kg on days 1 and 8 (some use 200 µg/kg)
- Strongyloidiasis: 200 µg/kg for 1–2 days; cutaneous larva migrans: 200 µg/kg for 1–2 days
- Onchocerciasis: 150 µg/kg once (repeat every 6–12 months)

## Adverse effects
- Generally very well tolerated: dizziness, nausea, transient worsening of itch
- Mazzotti reaction in onchocerciasis (fever, itch, lymphadenopathy, hypotension from dying microfilariae)
- Severe encephalopathy in people with very high Loa loa microfilaraemia
- Neurotoxicity in people with P-glycoprotein defects or with P-gp inhibitors

## Contraindications
- Children under 15 kg
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding (avoid, though accidental exposure has not shown clear harm)
- High Loa loa microfilaraemia (endemic areas); conditions with a damaged blood–brain barrier (e.g. meningitis)

## Drug interactions
- Warfarin: INR may rise
- P-gp/CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, cyclosporine, verapamil) may raise CNS exposure

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not recommended in pregnancy (old FDA category C) or breastfeeding; use permethrin instead.

## Viva points
- Acts on glutamate-gated chloride channels; P-glycoprotein keeps it out of the human brain
- Not ovicidal — repeat the dose after 7–14 days
- Drug of choice for crusted scabies (with topical) and strongyloidiasis
- Avoid in children under 15 kg and in pregnancy

## Topical form: Ivermectin 1% cream (and 0.5% lotion)
_Macrocyclic lactone (avermectin) — topical_

**Mechanism**
- Binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrates → paralysis of Demodex mites and lice
- Anti-inflammatory effects (reduces neutrophil activity and cytokines)

**Indications**
- 1% cream: papulopustular rosacea (more effective than metronidazole gel), demodicosis
- 0.5% lotion: head lice (age 6 months and older) — single 10-min application, no nit combing needed
- Scabies (off-label, compounded 1% lotion/cream)

**Dose & how to apply**
- Rosacea: 1% cream once daily for up to 16 weeks, then maintenance
- Head lice: 0.5% lotion to dry hair and scalp, leave 10 min, rinse — single use

**Adverse effects**
- Burning, irritation, dry skin; transient rosacea flare at start

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity

**Pregnancy:** Minimal absorption; limited data — avoid unless needed.

**Viva points**
- Targets Demodex in rosacea
- Single-application head lice treatment

## Note on sources
Wolverton says to repeat the scabies dose in 1 week to 10 days; other guides say 7–14 days. Both fit — 7–14 days is used here.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.12 (Systemic antiparasitic agents); Khopkar ch.5; Wolverton 4e ch.44; Khopkar ch.21. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Jessner's solution
posts.summary: Chemical agents, peels & baths · Combination superficial peeling agent: resorcinol 14% + salicylic acid 14% + lactic acid 14% in ethanol
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths_

**Class:** Combination superficial peeling agent: resorcinol 14% + salicylic acid 14% + lactic acid 14% in ethanol

## Mechanism of action
- Keratolytic action of all three components → superficial exfoliation; resorcinol also weakens hydrogen bonds of keratin

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Superficial peel for acne, comedones, PIH, melasma, mild photoageing
- As a primer before 35% TCA (Monheit medium-depth peel)

## Dose & formulations
- 1–3 coats, depending on response (erythema → patchy frosting); no neutralisation needed

## Adverse effects
- Burning, erythema, peeling; salicylism (large areas); resorcinol — contact allergy, thyroid effects, ochronosis (rare)

## Contraindications
- Resorcinol/salicylate allergy, pregnancy (salicylate), active infection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (salicylate).

## Viva points
- Composition: resorcinol + salicylic + lactic acid 14% each
- Jessner + TCA 35% = Monheit peel

_Sources: Khopkar ch.31 (Combination peeling agents); Wolverton 4e ch.53. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ketoconazole + Clobetasone butyrate cream
posts.summary: V Steroid combinations · Combination: imidazole antifungal (ketoconazole 2%) + moderate-potency steroid (clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, UK 'moderate')
posts.body:
_Topicals · V Steroid combinations_

**Class:** Combination: imidazole antifungal (ketoconazole 2%) + moderate-potency steroid (clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, UK 'moderate')

## Mechanism of action
- Ketoconazole: anti-Malassezia, anti-dermatophyte, mild anti-inflammatory
- Clobetasone butyrate: moderate steroid (much weaker than clobetasol — do not confuse the names)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Short-term for inflamed seborrhoeic dermatitis (face, flexures) and inflamed intertrigo
- Not recommended for tinea

## Dose & formulations
- Once or twice daily for up to 1–2 weeks, then plain ketoconazole for maintenance

## Adverse effects
- Steroid side effects with prolonged use: perioral dermatitis, rosacea, atrophy; tinea incognito

## Contraindications
- Tinea, rosacea, acne, perioral dermatitis; long-term use on face

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid prolonged use.

## Viva points
- Clobetasone (moderate) ≠ clobetasol (super-potent) — classic confusion
- Rationale is seborrhoeic dermatitis, not tinea

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ketoconazole (topical + oral)
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Azoles · Imidazole antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51) → ergosterol deficiency and toxic sterol build-up → fungistatic
- Strong activity against Malassezia; also mild anti-inflammatory and anti-androgenic effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis (face, scalp), dandruff
- Pityriasis versicolor (shampoo as a body wash), Malassezia folliculitis
- Tinea corporis/cruris/pedis, cutaneous candidiasis
- Androgenetic alopecia (adjunct shampoo)

## Dose & formulations
- Cream 2%: once or twice daily for 2–4 weeks (tinea), longer for seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Shampoo 2%: seborrhoeic dermatitis/dandruff — lather, leave 3–5 min, rinse; twice weekly for 2–4 weeks, then weekly to prevent relapse
- Pityriasis versicolor: shampoo on affected skin for 5 min daily for 1–3 days (single-application regimens also used)
- Lotion 2% for scalp/hairy areas

## Adverse effects
- Local irritation, burning, dryness of hair; rare contact dermatitis
- Shampoo may change hair texture or colour (permanent-waved/grey hair)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity (including sulfite allergy for some formulations)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Topical use is safe (negligible absorption).

## Viva points
- Drug of choice topically for seborrhoeic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor
- Oral ketoconazole is no longer used for skin infections (hepatotoxicity, adrenal suppression) — topical is safe
- Shampoo needs contact time of 3–5 min

## Oral form: Ketoconazole oral
_Imidazole antifungal (oral)_

**Mechanism**
- Inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase; also inhibits human steroid-synthesising CYP enzymes (17,20-lyase, 11β-hydroxylase) → lowers cortisol and testosterone

**Pharmacokinetics**
- Needs gastric acid for absorption; potent CYP3A4 inhibitor

**Indications**
- Formerly used for dermatophytosis, PV, candidiasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- No longer recommended for skin and nail infections — withdrawn/restricted in Europe and the USA (2013) because of serious liver injury and adrenal suppression
- Still used by endocrinologists for Cushing syndrome (anti-steroidogenic)

**Dose & how to apply**
- 200–400 mg/day (historic dermatology dose)

**Adverse effects**
- Serious hepatotoxicity (including fulminant hepatitis, deaths)
- Adrenal insufficiency; gynaecomastia, reduced libido, oligospermia (anti-androgenic)
- QT prolongation

**Contraindications**
- Liver disease; with CYP3A4 substrates (simvastatin, cisapride, midazolam, ergot)

**Interactions**
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (cyclosporine, statins, warfarin); antacids/PPIs reduce absorption

**Pregnancy:** Avoid.

**Viva points**
- Oral ketoconazole is obsolete for skin infections — hepatotoxicity and adrenal suppression
- Topical ketoconazole remains safe and useful

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42 (Topical antifungals) and ch.51 (Therapeutic shampoos); Khopkar ch.19; Khopkar ch.2; Wolverton 4e ch.10. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ketotifen
posts.summary: Antihistamines · H1 antihistamine with mast cell–stabilising properties (benzocycloheptathiophene)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** H1 antihistamine with mast cell–stabilising properties (benzocycloheptathiophene)

## Mechanism of action
- Stabilises mast cells (inhibits calcium influx and mediator release), blocks H1 receptors, inhibits eosinophil accumulation

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria (adjunct), cholinergic and cold urticaria, physical urticarias
- Mastocytosis (symptom control), allergic conjunctivitis (eye drops), neurofibromatosis-associated itch (trials)

## Dose & formulations
- 1 mg twice daily (start 1 mg at night); children 0.5 mg twice daily (age >3)

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, weight gain (appetite), dry mouth; full effect takes 6–12 weeks

## Contraindications
- Epilepsy (lowers seizure threshold — caution)

## Drug interactions
- Oral hypoglycaemics (reversible thrombocytopenia reported), CNS depressants

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data — avoid.

## Viva points
- Mast cell stabiliser + antihistamine; slow onset; weight gain

_Sources: Khopkar (Mast cell stabilizers/ketotifen); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Khellin (oral + topical, KUVA)
posts.summary: Photoprotective agents · Furochromone (from the plant Ammi visnaga); photosensitiser
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Photoprotective agents_

**Class:** Furochromone (from the plant Ammi visnaga); photosensitiser

## Mechanism of action
- Similar to psoralens but forms only monoadducts with DNA after UVA → stimulates melanocytes with minimal phototoxicity

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Vitiligo (KUVA — khellin + UVA/sunlight); topical khellin with UVA/NB-UVB or excimer

## Dose & formulations
- Oral: 50–100 mg 2.5 h before UVA (historic); topical 2–5% gel/cream before UVA

## Adverse effects
- Oral: raised liver enzymes (hepatotoxicity limits oral use), nausea, orthostatic hypotension
- Topical: minimal phototoxicity

## Contraindications
- Liver disease (oral); pregnancy

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Low phototoxicity vs psoralens; oral use limited by hepatotoxicity

_Sources: Khopkar (Systemic photoprotective agents / PUVA); Wolverton 4e ch.23. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Kojic acid + Arbutin + Glycolic acid cream
posts.summary: VIII Pigmentary / depigmenting · Non-hydroquinone combination depigmenting cream (cosmeceutical)
posts.body:
_Topicals · VIII Pigmentary / depigmenting_

**Class:** Non-hydroquinone combination depigmenting cream (cosmeceutical)

## Mechanism of action
- Kojic acid (fungal metabolite, 1–4%): chelates copper at the tyrosinase active site → inhibits tyrosinase; antioxidant
- Arbutin (glycosylated hydroquinone from bearberry, 1–3%): competitive tyrosinase inhibitor with less melanocytotoxicity than hydroquinone
- Glycolic acid: exfoliates pigmented keratinocytes and enhances penetration

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Melasma (maintenance or hydroquinone-intolerant patients), PIH, mild lentigines
- Maintenance after triple combination cream

## Dose & formulations
- Once daily at night (or twice daily) with daytime sunscreen; results over 8–12 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Irritation, contact dermatitis (kojic acid is a sensitiser)
- Photosensitivity (glycolic acid)
- Kojic acid is unstable — oxidises in air and light

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; inflamed skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; generally considered low risk (arbutin releases small amounts of hydroquinone — use caution).

## Viva points
- Kojic acid chelates copper of tyrosinase
- Arbutin = natural hydroquinone glycoside
- Useful hydroquinone-free maintenance

_Sources: Khopkar ch.26 and ch.29 (Cosmeceuticals); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lamivudine + Nevirapine + Zidovudine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Fixed-dose triple combination: 2 NRTIs (lamivudine, zidovudine) + 1 NNRTI (nevirapine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Fixed-dose triple combination: 2 NRTIs (lamivudine, zidovudine) + 1 NNRTI (nevirapine)

## Mechanism of action
- NRTIs: chain-terminating nucleoside analogues of HIV reverse transcriptase
- Nevirapine: non-competitive inhibitor that binds a pocket near the reverse transcriptase active site

## Pharmacokinetics
- Nevirapine induces its own metabolism (CYP3A4 and 2B6 autoinduction) over the first 2 weeks
- So the full triple combination is used only after a 2-week lead-in with once-daily nevirapine

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Former first-line ART regimen (the 'ZLN' regimen), now largely replaced by dolutegravir-based TLD
- May still be met in patients started long ago

## Dose & formulations
- Lead-in (14 days): lamivudine 150 mg + zidovudine 300 mg twice daily, with nevirapine 200 mg once daily only
- Then: fixed-dose lamivudine 150 mg + nevirapine 200 mg + zidovudine 300 mg twice daily
- If rash appears during lead-in: do not increase the dose until it resolves; do not extend lead-in beyond 28 days

## Adverse effects
- Nevirapine rash (about 15–20%), mostly in the first 6 weeks; SJS/TEN and DRESS
- Nevirapine hepatotoxicity — higher in women with CD4 above 250 and men with CD4 above 400
- Zidovudine anaemia and neutropenia; melanonychia
- Lamivudine: hepatitis B flare on stopping

## Contraindications
- Previous severe nevirapine rash or hepatitis
- Moderate–severe liver disease
- Severe anaemia (zidovudine)

## Drug interactions
- Nevirapine induces CYP3A4: lowers oral contraceptives, ketoconazole, methadone, protease inhibitors
- Rifampicin lowers nevirapine — avoid together
- Zidovudine: other marrow suppressants

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline, 2, 4, 8 and 12 weeks (nevirapine)
- Hb/CBC (zidovudine)
- Check skin and mucosa at each visit in the first 6–8 weeks

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used widely in the past; nevirapine-related liver toxicity is higher in women with higher CD4 counts. TLD is now preferred.

## Viva points
- Why the lead-in? Autoinduction — the 2-week once-daily dose lowers the risk of rash and hepatitis
- Nevirapine is one of the commonest causes of SJS/TEN in Indian studies
- Stop permanently if rash comes with fever, blisters, mucosal involvement or hepatitis

## Note on sources
Wolverton gives little detail on ART; Khopkar and NACO used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Table 4.2); Wolverton 4e ch.3 and ch.67; check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lamivudine + Zidovudine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs

## Mechanism of action
- Zidovudine (AZT) is a thymidine analogue; lamivudine (3TC) is a cytidine analogue
- Both are phosphorylated to triphosphates that inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase and terminate viral DNA chains

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed with or without food
- Zidovudine is glucuronidated in the liver (short half-life, twice-daily dosing); lamivudine is excreted by the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Alternative NRTI backbone in ART when tenofovir or abacavir cannot be used
- Older first-line regimens (with nevirapine or efavirenz)
- Zidovudine alone: infant prophylaxis in PMTCT (prevention of mother-to-child transmission) programmes

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: lamivudine 150 mg + zidovudine 300 mg twice daily
- Children: weight-band dosing as per NACO tables

## Adverse effects
- Zidovudine: bone marrow suppression — macrocytic anaemia and neutropenia (avoid if Hb below about 8 g/dL)
- Zidovudine: nausea, headache, myopathy, lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis, lipoatrophy
- Skin and mucosal signs of zidovudine: longitudinal melanonychia, nail and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation
- Lamivudine: generally well tolerated; hepatitis B flare on stopping

## Contraindications
- Severe anaemia (Hb under about 7–8 g/dL) or neutropenia
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Other bone marrow suppressants raise anaemia risk: ganciclovir, co-trimoxazole (high dose), pyrimethamine, interferon, chemotherapy
- Stavudine is antagonistic — never combine with zidovudine
- Probenecid and fluconazole raise zidovudine levels

## Monitoring
- Hb and CBC at baseline, then monthly for the first 3 months, then periodically
- CD4 and viral load per programme; LFT

## Pregnancy & lactation
Zidovudine has the longest safety record in pregnancy; currently TLD is preferred, with zidovudine kept for infant prophylaxis and special cases.

## Viva points
- Zidovudine → anaemia (macrocytic) and neutropenia
- Zidovudine causes longitudinal melanonychia — a common viva photo
- Never combine zidovudine with stavudine (antagonism)

## Note on sources
Wolverton gives little detail on ART; Khopkar and NACO used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4; Wolverton 4e ch.11; check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Leflunomide
posts.summary: Immunomodulators · Pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor (isoxazole immunomodulator, prodrug of teriflunomide)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Immunomodulators_

**Class:** Pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor (isoxazole immunomodulator, prodrug of teriflunomide)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase → blocks de novo pyrimidine synthesis → activated lymphocytes arrested in G1 phase

## Pharmacokinetics
- Active metabolite teriflunomide has a very long half-life (about 2 weeks) and enterohepatic recirculation — persists for up to 2 years without washout

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis (approved)
- Off-label: cutaneous/systemic lupus, Sjögren, dermatomyositis, vasculitis, sarcoidosis, BK/CMV infections in transplant

## Dose & formulations
- 10–20 mg/day (loading doses no longer routinely used)
- Washout: cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days (or activated charcoal) — before planned pregnancy or for toxicity

## Adverse effects
- Hepatotoxicity (boxed warning), diarrhoea, hypertension, weight loss, alopecia
- Cytopenias, infections, interstitial lung disease, peripheral neuropathy
- Skin: rash, SCLE induction, SJS/TEN, DRESS, cutaneous vasculitis

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (boxed warning — teratogenic) and women not using contraception; liver disease; severe immunodeficiency

## Drug interactions
- Methotrexate (more liver toxicity), rifampicin (raises teriflunomide), cholestyramine (lowers levels), warfarin

## Monitoring
- LFT, CBC monthly for 6 months, then every 6–8 weeks; BP

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated; after stopping, washout and confirm plasma teriflunomide <0.02 mg/L on two tests before conception.

## Viva points
- DHODH inhibitor
- Cholestyramine washout because of very long half-life

_Sources: Khopkar (Leflunomide); Wolverton 4e ch.40 (Miscellaneous systemic drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Leucovorin calcium (folinic acid) injection
posts.summary: V Immunosuppressants · Reduced folate (5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate); antidote
posts.body:
_Injectables · V Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Reduced folate (5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate); antidote

## Mechanism of action
- Already in reduced form, so it bypasses the dihydrofolate reductase step blocked by methotrexate
- Restores purine and thymidine synthesis in normal cells ('leucovorin rescue')
- Also enhances 5-FU effect (stabilises thymidylate synthase binding) in oncology

## Pharmacokinetics
- IV, IM or oral; rapidly converted to active folates

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Methotrexate toxicity/overdose (pancytopenia, mucositis, accidental daily dosing) — the antidote
- Planned rescue after high-dose methotrexate (oncology)
- Folate deficiency megaloblastic anaemia when oral folic acid cannot be used
- With 5-FU in colorectal cancer; pyrimethamine/trimethoprim toxicity

## Dose & formulations
- MTX toxicity: give as early as possible (ideally within 24 h; effectiveness falls after 24–48 h)
- Typical: 10–15 mg/m² (or 15–25 mg) IV/IM/orally every 6 h until counts recover and MTX level is below safe threshold; larger doses for high levels
- Ampoules 15 mg/2 mL, 50 mg vials; tablets 15 mg
- Folic acid cannot replace leucovorin in acute toxicity (needs DHFR for activation)

## Adverse effects
- Rare: allergic reactions, fever
- Do not give intrathecally; do not give faster than 160 mg/min IV (calcium content)

## Contraindications
- Pernicious anaemia/B12 deficiency (may correct anaemia while neurological damage progresses)

## Drug interactions
- Reduces efficacy of methotrexate (intended) and of co-trimoxazole for PJP
- Increases 5-FU toxicity
- Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, phenobarbital): levels may fall

## Monitoring
- CBC daily in MTX toxicity; renal function; MTX level where available
- Supportive care: hydration, urine alkalinisation, mouth care, G-CSF if needed

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe when needed.

## Viva points
- Bypasses DHFR → antidote for methotrexate toxicity
- Give within 24 h
- Folic acid prevents side effects of low-dose MTX; leucovorin treats acute toxicity

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.14 (Methotrexate — overdose management); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Levocetirizine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · Second-generation H1 antihistamine — active R-enantiomer of cetirizine
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine — active R-enantiomer of cetirizine

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist; twice the receptor affinity of cetirizine

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria, allergic rhinitis, pruritus

## Dose & formulations
- 5 mg once daily in the evening (updosing up to 20 mg in urticaria); children 6–11 years 2.5 mg; 2–6 years 1.25 mg twice daily
- Halve or space doses in renal impairment

## Adverse effects
- Mild sedation (similar to cetirizine), dry mouth, fatigue

## Contraindications
- End-stage renal disease; children under 6 months

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol, CNS depressants

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data — cetirizine/loratadine preferred.

## Viva points
- 5 mg levocetirizine = 10 mg cetirizine; renal dose adjustment

_Sources: Khopkar (Second generation H1 antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

Topical acceptable.

posts.title: Lignocaine (lidocaine) 2% injection
posts.summary: I Local anaesthetics · Amide local anaesthetic (intermediate duration)
posts.body:
_Injectables · I Local anaesthetics_

**Class:** Amide local anaesthetic (intermediate duration)

## Mechanism of action
- The unionised form crosses the nerve membrane; inside, the ionised form blocks voltage-gated sodium channels from within
- No sodium influx → no depolarisation → no nerve conduction
- Small, unmyelinated fibres (pain, temperature, autonomic) are blocked first, then touch, pressure and motor

## Pharmacokinetics
- pKa 7.9 — fast onset (1–2 min by infiltration); works poorly in acidic, infected tissue
- Duration about 30–120 min alone; 2–6 h with adrenaline (vasoconstriction slows absorption)
- Metabolised in the liver (CYP1A2, 3A4); reduce total dose in liver disease and heart failure
- 2% = 20 mg/mL; 1% = 10 mg/mL

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Infiltration anaesthesia for biopsy, excision, electrosurgery, cryo, lasers, IL injections
- Nerve blocks (digital, ring, supraorbital, mental, etc.), field blocks
- Tumescent anaesthesia (very dilute, 0.05–0.1%) for liposuction and large procedures
- Topical forms (gel, EMLA with prilocaine — topicals slot)
- Antiarrhythmic (IV, ventricular arrhythmias)

## Dose & formulations
- Maximum (Wolverton): plain 4.5 mg/kg (up to 300 mg); with adrenaline 7 mg/kg (up to 500 mg)
- Example: 300 mg = 15 mL of 2% plain lignocaine
- Formula: maximum volume (mL) = max dose (mg/kg) × weight (kg) ÷ 10 ÷ % concentration
- Tumescent: up to 35–55 mg/kg because of very slow absorption from fat
- Children: same mg/kg limits; dilute to 0.5–1% to give enough volume

## Adverse effects
- Pain and burning on injection (reduce by buffering with sodium bicarbonate 1 mL 8.4% per 10 mL, warming, slow injection, small needle)
- Systemic toxicity (overdose or intravascular injection) — CNS first: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, light-headedness, slurred speech → muscle twitching → seizures → coma
- Then cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest
- Vasovagal reaction (the commonest 'reaction' in practice)
- Adrenaline effects: palpitations, tremor, anxiety, tachycardia
- True allergy to amides is rare (preservative methylparaben may be the cause); esters (procaine, benzocaine — PABA) are more allergenic

## Contraindications
- Known allergy to amide anaesthetics
- Caution: complete heart block, severe liver disease, heart failure
- With adrenaline — caution: uncontrolled hypertension, severe cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, narrow-angle glaucoma; patients on non-selective β-blockers, MAOIs or tricyclics
- Adrenaline in digits/penis: traditionally avoided; Wolverton notes dilute adrenaline is now considered safe in healthy digits (avoid in vascular disease)

## Drug interactions
- β-blockers (propranolol) with adrenaline: unopposed α effect → hypertension and reflex bradycardia
- Cimetidine, propranolol, amiodarone reduce lignocaine clearance
- Other anti-arrhythmics: additive cardiac effects

## Monitoring
- Calculate the maximum dose before starting; aspirate before injecting
- Watch for early CNS symptoms; have resuscitation equipment and 20% lipid emulsion available
- Treatment of toxicity: stop injecting, airway and oxygen, benzodiazepine for seizures, 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B) and breastfeeding; defer elective procedures to the second trimester; adrenaline in small doses acceptable.

## Viva points
- Amide vs ester: amides have two 'i's in the name (lIdocaIne); esters are metabolised by plasma cholinesterase and cause more allergy (PABA)
- Max dose: 4.5 mg/kg plain, 7 mg/kg with adrenaline
- Signs of toxicity progress from CNS to CVS
- Buffering with bicarbonate reduces pain
- Lipid emulsion is the antidote for systemic toxicity

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (Local anesthetics); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents / Appendix). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lignocaine + Prilocaine (EMLA cream/gel)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics (lidocaine 2.5% + prilocaine 2.5%)
posts.body:
_Topicals · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics (lidocaine 2.5% + prilocaine 2.5%)

## Mechanism of action
- The two amides mixed in equal amounts have a melting point below room temperature (eutectic) → a liquid oil that penetrates intact skin
- Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in dermal nerve endings → surface anaesthesia

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Topical anaesthesia before venepuncture, IV cannulation, laser treatments, curettage of molluscum, wart removal, superficial biopsies, split-skin grafts, microneedling, leg ulcer debridement
- Genital mucosa (shorter application time: 5–10 min)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply a thick layer (1–2 g per 10 cm²) under occlusion (film dressing) for 60 min (depth about 3 mm); 120 min for deeper anaesthesia (about 5 mm)
- Infant limits: 0–3 months — max 1 g over 10 cm² for 1 h; 3–12 months — max 2 g over 20 cm²; larger limits in older children by weight
- Wipe off before the procedure

## Adverse effects
- Blanching then redness at application site (vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation)
- Methaemoglobinaemia — the most serious adverse effect (prilocaine metabolite o-toluidine oxidises haemoglobin); risk in infants under 3 months, large areas, G6PD deficiency, with other oxidising drugs
- Purpura, contact urticaria, irritant reactions
- Eye injury if applied near eyes (corneal abrasion)

## Contraindications
- Congenital or idiopathic methaemoglobinaemia
- Infants under 12 months on methaemoglobin-inducing drugs; premature infants (under 37 weeks)
- Amide anaesthetic allergy; open wounds (except leg ulcers per protocol); near eyes or middle ear

## Drug interactions
- Methaemoglobin-inducing drugs: dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrates (nitroglycerin), paracetamol (high dose), phenytoin, antimalarials (primaquine, chloroquine)
- Class I antiarrhythmics: additive toxicity

## Monitoring
- In infants or large areas: watch for cyanosis (grey-blue colour with normal oxygen); treat methaemoglobinaemia with methylene blue (avoid in G6PD deficiency)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B).

## Viva points
- Eutectic = mixture melts below room temperature → penetrates intact skin
- 60 min under occlusion
- Methaemoglobinaemia due to prilocaine (worse with dapsone)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (Local anesthetics — EMLA, methemoglobinemia); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Loratadine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (tricyclic, piperidine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (tricyclic, piperidine)

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist; poor CNS penetration

## Pharmacokinetics
- Prodrug; metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4, 2D6) to desloratadine (active, longer acting)
- Half-life (with metabolite) about 27 h; once daily

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Urticaria, allergic rhinitis, itch

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10 mg once daily (updosing to 40 mg in urticaria)
- Children 2–12 years: 5 mg daily (under 30 kg), 10 mg (over 30 kg)
- Liver impairment: 10 mg on alternate days

## Adverse effects
- Headache, fatigue, dry mouth; minimal sedation at standard dose

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in severe liver disease

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, cimetidine) raise levels without important QT effects

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Preferred antihistamine in pregnancy (with cetirizine); compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Prodrug of desloratadine
- Safe in pregnancy (most data)
- Non-sedating at standard dose

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32; Khopkar (Antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Low molecular weight dextran
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Plasma expander (dextran 40) with rheological (anti-sludging) effects
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Plasma expander (dextran 40) with rheological (anti-sludging) effects

## Mechanism of action
- Reduces blood viscosity and red-cell aggregation, coats platelets and endothelium → improves microcirculation

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Historically in livedoid vasculopathy, Raynaud phenomenon/digital ischaemia, frostbite, necrotic ulcers due to microvascular occlusion, pyoderma gangrenosum (adjunct)

## Dose & formulations
- 500 mL of 10% dextran 40 IV infusion daily for a few days (historic regimens)

## Adverse effects
- Anaphylactoid reactions (dextran-reactive antibodies), fluid overload, renal failure, bleeding tendency (platelet coating)

## Contraindications
- Heart failure, renal failure, bleeding disorders, dextran allergy

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid unless essential.

## Viva points
- Improves microcirculation — historical use in livedoid vasculopathy and digital ischaemia

_Sources: Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents — low molecular weight dextran). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Luliconazole 1% cream
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Azoles · Imidazole (ketene dithioacetal structure) — newest topical azole
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole (ketene dithioacetal structure) — newest topical azole

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits 14-α-demethylase; very low MICs against dermatophytes (among the most potent topical azoles)
- High stratum corneum retention → short, once-daily courses

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea corporis, cruris and pedis (approved)
- Cutaneous candidiasis, pityriasis versicolor
- Onychomycosis (10% solution in Japan)

## Dose & formulations
- Once daily: tinea corporis/cruris for 1 week, interdigital tinea pedis for 2 weeks (FDA label)
- In Indian practice with chronic/recurrent tinea, courses of 2–4 weeks are common

## Adverse effects
- Application-site irritation, contact dermatitis (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; animal data reassuring; use if needed.

## Viva points
- Most potent topical azole against dermatophytes
- Once daily, short course
- Widely used in India — rising resistance concerns with misuse

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42 (luliconazole); Khopkar edition predates it. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Malathion (0.5%)
posts.summary: Scabicides & pediculicides · Organophosphate (cholinesterase inhibitor) pediculicide
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Scabicides & pediculicides_

**Class:** Organophosphate (cholinesterase inhibitor) pediculicide

## Mechanism of action
- Irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase in lice → paralysis; ovicidal; residual activity on hair

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Head lice resistant to permethrin (age ≥6 years); pubic lice; scabies (aqueous lotion, some countries)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply 0.5% lotion to dry hair, leave 8–12 h, then wash; repeat after 7–9 days if lice still present

## Adverse effects
- Scalp irritation; alcohol-based lotion is flammable (no hairdryers/smoking); ingestion → cholinergic toxicity

## Contraindications
- Children under 6 (USA label), neonates; flammable

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data.

## Viva points
- Organophosphate — ovicidal; flammable lotion

_Sources: Khopkar ch.21 (Topical ivermectin/malathion); Wolverton 4e ch.44. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mebendazole
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Benzimidazole anthelmintic
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Benzimidazole anthelmintic

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits parasite microtubule (β-tubulin) polymerisation → impaired glucose uptake → worm death

## Pharmacokinetics
- Very poorly absorbed (<10%) — mainly acts in the gut lumen

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intestinal worms (pinworm, roundworm, hookworm, whipworm)
- Cutaneous larva migrans (less effective than albendazole — poor absorption)
- Trichinosis (with steroids), hydatid disease (high doses, historical)

## Dose & formulations
- 100 mg twice daily × 3 days, or 500 mg single dose; pinworm 100 mg single, repeat after 2 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Abdominal pain, diarrhoea; with high doses — neutropenia, hepatitis, alopecia
- SJS/TEN reported when combined with metronidazole

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (first trimester); children under 1 year

## Drug interactions
- Metronidazole: SJS/TEN reports; cimetidine raises levels; carbamazepine lowers them

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in the first trimester.

## Viva points
- Poorly absorbed — luminal worms; albendazole preferred for tissue parasites like CLM

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5; Wolverton 4e ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Menadione (vitamin K3) injection
posts.summary: IX Miscellaneous · Synthetic water-soluble vitamin K analogue (provitamin; menadione sodium bisulfite)
posts.body:
_Injectables · IX Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Synthetic water-soluble vitamin K analogue (provitamin; menadione sodium bisulfite)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted in the liver to active vitamin K2 (menaquinone-4)
- Vitamin K is a cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S)
- Corrects bleeding from vitamin K deficiency, but acts slowly and weakly compared with vitamin K1

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble — does not need bile for absorption (useful in obstructive jaundice)
- Onset slower than phytomenadione (vitamin K1); not reliable for reversing warfarin

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Hypoprothrombinaemia due to vitamin K deficiency: obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics, prolonged parenteral nutrition
- Used as a haemostatic in some Indian practice
- Not the drug of choice for warfarin reversal or haemorrhagic disease of the newborn — phytomenadione (vitamin K1) is preferred

## Dose & formulations
- Typically 10 mg IM/IV (menadione sodium bisulfite) as directed by the product
- Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) for comparison: newborn prophylaxis 1 mg IM at birth; warfarin reversal 1–10 mg slow IV (no faster than 1 mg/min)

## Adverse effects
- Haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency
- Neonates: haemolysis, hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus — contraindicated
- Vitamin K injection-site skin reactions (mostly with vitamin K1): itchy eczematous plaques at the injection site (early), and later sclerodermoid plaques with a 'cowboy belt' distribution on the buttocks and thighs (Texier disease)
- Rapid IV vitamin K1: anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, collapse)

## Contraindications
- Neonates and infants; late pregnancy (risk to the newborn)
- G6PD deficiency
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antagonises warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists
- Long-term antibiotics (cephalosporins) and cholestyramine increase vitamin K needs

## Monitoring
- Prothrombin time/INR

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid menadione in late pregnancy (neonatal haemolysis and jaundice); vitamin K1 is safe.

## Viva points
- Menadione (K3) vs phytomenadione (K1): K1 is preferred in neonates and for warfarin reversal
- Menadione causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and kernicterus in newborns
- Skin reactions to vitamin K injections: eczematous plaques; Texier disease (pseudo-scleroderma, cowboy-belt pattern)

## Note on sources
Menadione is not covered in Wolverton. Khopkar and standard pharmacology texts were used; please check whether your examiners mean menadione (K3) or phytomenadione (K1).

_Sources: Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements); pharmacology references; Wolverton 4e (drug eruption sections). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methotrexate
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Folic acid antagonist (antimetabolite); immunomodulator
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Folic acid antagonist (antimetabolite); immunomodulator

## Mechanism of action
- Competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → less tetrahydrofolate → less purine and thymidine synthesis → inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells (S-phase specific)
- At low weekly doses the main effect is anti-inflammatory: polyglutamated MTX inhibits AICAR transformylase → adenosine builds up and acts as an anti-inflammatory signal
- Reduces T-cell activation and keratinocyte proliferation

## Pharmacokinetics
- Oral absorption is variable and saturable at higher doses; subcutaneous route gives more reliable levels (useful above 15–20 mg/week)
- About 50% protein bound (displaced by NSAIDs, sulfonamides, salicylates)
- Stored in cells as polyglutamates; excreted mainly unchanged by the kidneys — reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis (plaque, erythrodermic, pustular, psoriatic arthritis) — approved
- Atopic dermatitis, chronic urticaria (refractory), alopecia areata
- Immunobullous disease (bullous pemphigoid, pemphigus as steroid-sparing)
- Connective tissue disease: dermatomyositis, morphoea and systemic sclerosis skin, cutaneous lupus
- Sarcoidosis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, pityriasis lichenoides, lymphomatoid papulosis, Mycosis fungoides (early), vasculitis, pyoderma gangrenosum

## Dose & formulations
- Once weekly — never daily (daily dosing errors cause fatal toxicity)
- Psoriasis: start 7.5–15 mg/week (test dose of 2.5–5 mg optional, especially in elderly or renal impairment), increase by 2.5–5 mg to 15–25 mg/week; maximum usually 25–30 mg/week
- Children: 0.2–0.7 mg/kg/week
- Folic acid 1–5 mg daily (except MTX day) or 5 mg weekly reduces GI and liver side effects and cytopenias
- Weekly oral, subcutaneous or IM routes; tablets 2.5, 7.5, 10 mg

## Adverse effects
- GI: nausea, anorexia, stomatitis, oral ulcers
- Bone marrow suppression — pancytopenia is the main cause of death (risk: renal failure, elderly, interacting drugs, no folate, dosing errors)
- Hepatotoxicity: raised enzymes, fibrosis and cirrhosis with long-term use (risk: alcohol, obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, hepatitis B/C)
- Pulmonary: acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis (idiosyncratic) and chronic fibrosis
- Skin: alopecia, ulceration of psoriatic plaques (early sign of overdose), photo-recall, epidermal necrosis
- Teratogenic and abortifacient; reversible oligospermia
- Infections; lymphoma (EBV-related, may regress on stopping)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: pregnancy and breastfeeding; significant liver disease or alcoholism; severe renal impairment; bone marrow failure; active serious infection
- Relative: hepatitis B/C, obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, unreliable patient, immunodeficiency, recent live vaccine

## Drug interactions
- Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole): additive antifolate → severe pancytopenia (most important)
- NSAIDs, salicylates, penicillins, probenecid, PPIs: reduce renal clearance or displace MTX
- Dapsone and other antifolates; retinoids and alcohol (liver); leflunomide
- Phenytoin, sulfonylureas, tetracyclines displace MTX from albumin

## Monitoring
- Baseline: CBC, LFT, renal function, hepatitis B/C, HIV, chest X-ray, pregnancy test, TB screening (IGRA) where relevant
- CBC and LFT weekly–2-weekly for the first month, then every 1–3 months; renal function every 3–6 months
- Liver fibrosis: non-invasive tests (e.g. transient elastography/FibroScan, procollagen III peptide) — liver biopsy only if these suggest fibrosis
- Traditionally biopsy was considered after a cumulative dose of 3.5–4 g in high-risk-free patients (Wolverton reviews this older approach)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Stop 3 months before conception (women; also commonly advised for men). Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Weekly dosing — check the patient is not taking it daily
- Co-trimoxazole is the most dangerous interaction
- Antidote for overdose: leucovorin (folinic acid) — bypasses DHFR; give as early as possible (covered in slot 3)
- Painful ulceration of psoriatic plaques can be the first sign of toxicity
- Liver monitoring has moved from routine biopsy to non-invasive tests

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.14 (Methotrexate); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methoxsalen (8-MOP) — oral and topical PUVA
posts.summary: X Photochemotherapy · Psoralen (furocoumarin) photosensitiser; used with UVA (PUVA)
posts.body:
_Oral · X Photochemotherapy_

**Class:** Psoralen (furocoumarin) photosensitiser; used with UVA (PUVA)

## Mechanism of action
- Intercalates between DNA base pairs; after UVA exposure it forms monofunctional adducts and then cross-links between DNA strands
- Result: inhibits DNA synthesis and keratinocyte proliferation; apoptosis of activated T cells; immunosuppression
- In vitiligo: stimulates melanocyte proliferation and migration and melanogenesis

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorption variable; peak photosensitivity at about 1–2 h (liquid capsules about 1 h, crystalline about 2 h); lasts about 8 h
- Large first-pass metabolism; food slows absorption

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis (plaque, palmoplantar, erythrodermic in selected cases)
- Vitiligo (generalised), mycosis fungoides (early stage), chronic hand eczema, atopic dermatitis
- Lichen planus, polymorphous light eruption (prophylactic hardening), urticaria pigmentosa, generalised granuloma annulare, morphoea

## Dose & formulations
- 0.4–0.6 mg/kg orally, 1–2 h before UVA exposure (10 mg tablets/capsules)
- Treatments 2–3 times a week, never on consecutive days (phototoxic reaction peaks at 48–72 h)
- UVA dose started by skin type or minimal phototoxic dose (MPD), increased gradually
- 5-MOP (bergapten) 1.2 mg/kg is an alternative with less nausea and phototoxicity

## Adverse effects
- Nausea (most common), dizziness, headache
- Phototoxic reaction (erythema, blistering, pain); PUVA itch; PUVA lentigines
- Long-term: photoageing, non-melanoma skin cancer (especially SCC, dose-dependent, highest in genitals of men — shield them), melanoma (late)
- Cataract — eye protection with UVA-blocking glasses for 12–24 h after the dose
- Hepatotoxicity (rare)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: pregnancy (relative in many texts), lupus erythematosus, xeroderma pigmentosum, porphyria and other photosensitive disorders, melanoma history, children under 10–12 years
- Relative: previous arsenic or ionising radiation, non-melanoma skin cancer, cataract, liver disease, immunosuppression (cyclosporine), heavy sun damage

## Drug interactions
- Other photosensitising drugs (tetracyclines, thiazides, fluoroquinolones, phenothiazines) increase phototoxicity
- Cyclosporine: much higher skin cancer risk
- Phenytoin and other enzyme inducers lower psoralen levels

## Monitoring
- Baseline eye exam, ANA, LFT (if indicated); yearly eye and skin examination
- Record cumulative UVA dose and number of treatments (risk of SCC rises above about 200 treatments)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category C); no clear teratogenicity seen, but use NB-UVB instead.

## Viva points
- DNA cross-linking after UVA activation
- Dose 0.6 mg/kg, 2 h before UVA
- Never on consecutive days — phototoxicity peaks at 48–72 h
- Eye protection for 24 h; shield male genitalia
- Main long-term risk: SCC

## Topical form: Methoxsalen topical solution (topical PUVA)
_Psoralen (8-methoxypsoralen) for topical photochemotherapy_

**Mechanism**
- Applied psoralen is activated by UVA/sunlight → DNA cross-linking, T-cell apoptosis
- In vitiligo: stimulates melanocyte proliferation, migration from hair follicle reservoirs, and melanogenesis

**Indications**
- Localised vitiligo (under 20% BSA), including children over about 5 years (oral PUVA not suitable)
- Localised palmoplantar psoriasis and hand/foot eczema (soak or paint PUVA)
- Alopecia areata (limited)

**Dose & how to apply**
- Commercial 1% lotion must be diluted (usually to 0.1% or lower, e.g. 1:10 with alcohol/acetone; Wolverton uses even lower 0.001–0.005% for bath/soak)
- Apply to patches only, 15–30 min before exposure to UVA or morning sunlight
- Start with 1–2 min of sun/low UVA, increase gradually; 2–3 times a week, never on consecutive days
- Wash the area after exposure and protect from further sun for the day

**Adverse effects**
- Phototoxic reaction: severe erythema, blistering (common if undiluted or overexposed)
- Hyperpigmentation of surrounding skin (perilesional 'halo' or patchy darkening)
- Contact dermatitis
- Less systemic risk than oral PUVA (no nausea, eye protection less critical, but avoid getting it near eyes)

**Contraindications**
- Photosensitive disorders (lupus, porphyria, XP), children under 5
- Pregnancy (relative)

**Pregnancy:** Avoid.

**Viva points**
- Always dilute — the 1% lotion causes blistering
- Suitable for limited vitiligo and children
- Never treat on consecutive days

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.23 (PUVA photochemotherapy); Khopkar (Psoralens, PUVA and phototherapy); Wolverton 4e ch.23 (PUVA — topical psoralen); Khopkar (Psoralens, PUVA and phototherapy). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methylprednisolone (IV pulse)
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid; methylprednisolone sodium succinate for IV use
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid; methylprednisolone sodium succinate for IV use

## Mechanism of action
- At pulse doses, genomic effects are saturated and rapid non-genomic effects on cell membranes add to immunosuppression
- Rapid lymphocyte depletion and suppression of inflammation — gives quick disease control with fewer long-term side effects than prolonged high oral doses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 4 mg methylprednisolone = 5 mg prednisolone
- Minimal mineralocorticoid effect, so preferred for pulse therapy
- Methylprednisolone acetate (depot) is a different, long-acting IM/IL suspension — never give it IV

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pemphigus vulgaris/foliaceus (severe, not responding), bullous pemphigoid (severe)
- SJS/TEN (early, short course — controversial), DRESS (severe), severe erythema multiforme
- Pyoderma gangrenosum, dermatomyositis (severe/with lung involvement), vasculitis, SLE
- Rapidly progressive alopecia areata (selected), severe type 1 lepra reaction or ENL with neuritis

## Dose & formulations
- Pulse: 500 mg–1 g (about 10–15 mg/kg/day) in 250–500 mL of 5% dextrose or normal saline over 1–3 h, daily for 3 (to 5) consecutive days
- Never as a rapid IV bolus (risk of arrhythmia and sudden death)
- Follow with oral steroid or steroid-sparing drug
- Vials 40, 125, 500 mg, 1 g

## Adverse effects
- Acute: flushing, metallic taste, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, insomnia, mood change, psychosis
- Electrolyte shifts (hypokalaemia), fluid retention
- Cardiac arrhythmia and sudden death (especially with diuretics, low potassium, heart disease, fast infusion)
- Anaphylaxis (rare), seizures, infections; avascular necrosis with repeated pulses

## Contraindications
- Active uncontrolled infection, systemic fungal infection
- Caution: heart disease, renal failure, electrolyte imbalance, uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension, psychiatric disease

## Drug interactions
- Diuretics and amphotericin B (hypokalaemia → arrhythmia)
- Enzyme inducers reduce effect; CYP3A4 inhibitors increase it

## Monitoring
- Before each pulse: BP, pulse, ECG, electrolytes (K⁺), blood glucose, renal function, infection screen, pregnancy test
- During infusion: BP and cardiac monitoring; repeat glucose and K⁺ after

## Pregnancy & lactation
Partly inactivated by the placenta; use only for life-threatening disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Pulse = 500 mg–1 g over at least 1 h on 3 consecutive days
- Check K⁺ and ECG before each pulse
- Succinate (IV, soluble) vs acetate (depot, never IV)
