_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13 (pulse definition); Khopkar ch.8. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methylprednisolone (oral)
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h)
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist; slightly more potent than prednisolone
- Minimal mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 4 mg methylprednisolone ≈ 5 mg prednisolone
- Metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Oral alternative to prednisolone (when less fluid retention is desired)
- Oral step-down after IV methylprednisolone pulses
- IV pulse use (pemphigus, SJS/TEN, pyoderma gangrenosum) — covered in the injectables slot

## Dose & formulations
- Oral: 4–48 mg/day depending on condition (e.g. 0.8 mg/kg/day ≈ 1 mg/kg prednisolone)
- Tablets 4, 8, 16, 32 mg

## Adverse effects
- Same as systemic steroids; less fluid retention than prednisolone

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, macrolides) raise levels; inducers lower them

## Monitoring
- As for prednisolone

## Pregnancy & lactation
Partly inactivated by the placenta; prednisolone is usually preferred.

## Viva points
- 4 mg methylprednisolone = 5 mg prednisolone
- Less mineralocorticoid effect than prednisolone
- Used for IV pulse therapy (slot 3)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13; Khopkar ch.8. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Metronidazole (oral + topical)
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — c) Nitroimidazole · 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial and antiprotozoal
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — c) Nitroimidazole_

**Class:** 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial and antiprotozoal

## Mechanism of action
- Prodrug: its nitro group is reduced inside anaerobic bacteria and protozoa
- The reduced reactive intermediates damage DNA → cell death (bactericidal)
- Active against anaerobes, Trichomonas, Giardia and Entamoeba; inactive against aerobes

## Pharmacokinetics
- Nearly 100% oral bioavailability; wide distribution including CSF, abscesses, vaginal secretions
- Half-life about 8 h; metabolised in the liver; excreted in urine (can turn urine dark)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Trichomoniasis (patient and partner)
- Bacterial vaginosis; part of PID regimens; vaginal discharge syndrome kits
- Amoebiasis (including cutaneous amoebiasis), giardiasis
- Anaerobic skin infections, infected ulcers, fungating tumours (also topical for odour)
- Rosacea (mainly topical gel); perianal Crohn's disease; dracunculiasis

## Dose & formulations
- Trichomoniasis: 2 g single dose (men); 500 mg twice daily × 7 days (women, preferred)
- Bacterial vaginosis: 500 mg twice daily × 7 days
- Amoebiasis: 750 mg three times daily × 7–10 days
- Anaerobic infections: 400–500 mg three times daily

## Adverse effects
- Metallic taste, nausea, anorexia, dry mouth
- Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (flushing, vomiting, headache, palpitations)
- Dark urine
- Peripheral neuropathy and seizures with high doses or long courses; aseptic meningitis; encephalopathy
- Fixed drug eruption; reversible neutropenia

## Contraindications
- Alcohol during treatment and for 72 h after (some sources say 48 h)
- Recent disulfiram use (within 2 weeks): risk of psychosis
- First trimester: high-dose single-dose regimen best avoided; active neurological disease

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol: disulfiram-like reaction
- Warfarin: markedly increased INR
- Lithium, phenytoin, busulfan, 5-FU: levels may rise
- Phenobarbital, rifampicin: lower metronidazole levels

## Monitoring
- CBC and neurological review if courses exceed 10 days

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category B; current guidelines allow use in all trimesters for trichomoniasis and BV. For the 2 g single dose in breastfeeding, pause breastfeeding for 12–24 h.

## Viva points
- Prodrug activated only in anaerobes — hence selective toxicity
- Avoid alcohol for 72 h (disulfiram-like reaction)
- Trichomoniasis: always treat the partner
- Commonly causes fixed drug eruption

## Topical form: Metronidazole gel/cream (0.75–1%)
_Topical nitroimidazole_

**Mechanism**
- Anti-inflammatory (reduces reactive oxygen species from neutrophils) and antimicrobial — benefit in rosacea is mainly anti-inflammatory

**Indications**
- Papulopustular rosacea (first-line topical), perioral dermatitis
- Malodorous fungating wounds and ulcers (reduces anaerobic odour)
- Vaginal gel 0.75%: bacterial vaginosis

**Dose & how to apply**
- 0.75% twice daily or 1% once daily; maintenance after oral therapy in rosacea

**Adverse effects**
- Mild irritation, dryness; no disulfiram reaction (negligible absorption)

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity

**Pregnancy:** Safe.

**Viva points**
- Topical metronidazole for rosacea; ivermectin cream is more effective

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1 and ch.5; Khopkar ch.18; Wolverton 4e ch.41 and ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Miconazole 2% cream
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Azoles · Imidazole antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits 14-α-demethylase; at higher concentrations directly damages membranes
- Also active against Gram-positive bacteria

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous and mucosal candidiasis (cream, oral gel, vaginal)
- Tinea corporis/cruris/pedis, pityriasis versicolor, angular cheilitis (Candida/staph)
- Napkin candidiasis

## Dose & formulations
- Cream 2%: twice daily, continue 10–14 days after lesions clear
- Oral gel: 4 times daily after food (oral thrush)

## Adverse effects
- Local irritation, contact dermatitis

## Contraindications
- Oral gel in infants under 4–6 months (choking risk)
- Oral gel with warfarin (see interactions)

## Drug interactions
- Miconazole oral gel (and even vaginal/topical use in large amounts) is absorbed and inhibits CYP2C9 → markedly raised INR with warfarin; also raises sulfonylurea and phenytoin levels

## Pregnancy & lactation
Topical use safe.

## Viva points
- Miconazole oral gel + warfarin → bleeding (classic interaction)
- Useful in angular cheilitis (antifungal + antibacterial)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42 and ch.66 (Drug interactions); Khopkar ch.19. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Minocycline (oral + topical foam)
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines · Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline — the most lipophilic
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines_

**Class:** Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline — the most lipophilic

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 30S ribosome and blocks protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits MMPs, neutrophil chemotaxis and lymphocyte activity
- High lipophilicity → good penetration into the pilosebaceous unit, CNS and skin

## Pharmacokinetics
- Almost completely absorbed; food has little effect; still chelated by metal ions
- Half-life 11–22 h; metabolised mainly in the liver

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (second choice after doxycycline because of its safety profile)
- Leprosy: part of the ROM regimen (rifampicin, ofloxacin, minocycline) and an alternative drug
- Atypical mycobacteria (especially M. marinum), Nocardia, community MRSA
- Rosacea; anti-inflammatory use in bullous pemphigoid, sarcoidosis, CARP

## Dose & formulations
- Acne: 50–100 mg twice daily, or extended-release 1 mg/kg once daily
- Leprosy: 100 mg daily (alternative regimens); ROM monthly: 100 mg as part of the single monthly dose

## Adverse effects
- Vestibular toxicity (dizziness, vertigo, ataxia) — commoner in women
- Hyperpigmentation — Type I: blue-black in scars and inflamed sites (iron/haemosiderin stains); Type II: blue-grey on normal skin of shins and forearms (iron and melanin); Type III: muddy-brown diffuse in sun-exposed skin (melanin)
- Pigmentation can also affect teeth (even adult teeth), nails, sclera, oral mucosa, thyroid ('black thyroid') and bone
- Autoimmune: drug-induced lupus (often p-ANCA positive), autoimmune hepatitis, serum-sickness-like reaction, polyarteritis-like vasculitis
- Hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS) in the first weeks, pneumonitis
- Less phototoxic than doxycycline; pseudotumor cerebri

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 8 years
- Lupus or autoimmune hepatitis history; concurrent oral retinoids

## Drug interactions
- Metal ions and antacids reduce absorption
- Isotretinoin/acitretin: pseudotumor cerebri
- Warfarin effect may increase

## Monitoring
- No routine tests for short courses
- For courses beyond a few months: watch for pigmentation, joint pain, rash, and check LFT/ANA if symptoms

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D). Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Most lipophilic tetracycline → vestibular side effects and best CNS penetration
- Three types of pigmentation — be able to describe them
- Autoimmune side effects: drug-induced lupus and autoimmune hepatitis
- Least phototoxic of the commonly used tetracyclines
- Used in leprosy (ROM)

## Topical form: Minocycline 4% topical foam
_Tetracycline antibiotic in a hydrophobic foam base (topical minocycline foam)_

**Mechanism**
- Binds the 30S ribosome; anti-inflammatory (MMP inhibition, neutrophil effects)
- Topical delivery gives high follicular levels with negligible blood levels — avoids systemic minocycline side effects

**Indications**
- Moderate–severe inflammatory acne (4% foam, age 9 and over)
- Papulopustular rosacea (1.5% foam)

**Dose & how to apply**
- Apply once daily at about the same time, at least 1 h before bathing/sleep; avoid fire (flammable)

**Adverse effects**
- Mild irritation; possible hyperpigmentation (rare)
- Theoretically tooth discolouration in children under 8 — not used in that age group

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity to tetracyclines; children under 9

**Pregnancy:** Avoid in pregnancy (tetracycline class).

**Viva points**
- Topical tetracycline that avoids vestibular and autoimmune side effects of oral minocycline
- Foam is flammable

_Note: The exam list says 4% gel; the approved product is minocycline 4% foam (acne) and 1.5% foam (rosacea), so it is listed as a foam. Topical minocycline is not described in Wolverton 4e or Khopkar; added at your request._

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1; Not covered in Wolverton 4e or Khopkar (newer product); product information (Amzeeq/Zilxi). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Minoxidil 5% solution
posts.summary: X Hair & scalp agents · Piperidinopyrimidine derivative; potassium-channel opener (originally an oral antihypertensive)
posts.body:
_Topicals · X Hair & scalp agents_

**Class:** Piperidinopyrimidine derivative; potassium-channel opener (originally an oral antihypertensive)

## Mechanism of action
- Prodrug — converted in the hair follicle by sulfotransferase (SULT1A1) to minoxidil sulfate (active)
- Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels → vasodilation and increased follicle blood flow
- Prolongs anagen, shortens telogen, enlarges miniaturised follicles; stimulates VEGF and dermal papilla cells
- Low follicular sulfotransferase activity predicts poor response

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Androgenetic alopecia — men (5%) and women (2% solution or 5% foam once daily)
- Alopecia areata (adjunct), chemotherapy-induced alopecia (to shorten duration), eyebrow/beard hypotrichosis (off-label)
- Oral low-dose minoxidil (0.25–5 mg/day) — in the Derma Desk 2nd-line ladder

## Dose & formulations
- Men: 1 mL of 5% solution twice daily to dry scalp (affected area), leave at least 4 h; or 5% foam twice daily
- Women: 2% solution 1 mL twice daily or 5% foam once daily
- Shedding in the first 2–8 weeks is expected (telogen release); judge at 6–12 months; must continue — benefit lost in 3–4 months after stopping

## Adverse effects
- Scalp irritation, itching, scaling, contact dermatitis (often due to propylene glycol — foam is PG-free)
- Hypertrichosis of the face/forehead (especially women; from drips or hand transfer)
- Initial shedding; rarely headache, dizziness, palpitations, hypotension (systemic absorption)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; broken or inflamed scalp
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding; caution in cardiovascular disease

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in pregnancy (fetal hypertrichosis/malformations reported with systemic exposure) and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Prodrug activated by follicular sulfotransferase
- Initial shedding is a sign of response, not failure
- Must be used indefinitely
- Propylene glycol causes most contact dermatitis — switch to foam

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.57 (Miscellaneous topical agents — minoxidil); Khopkar ch.28. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mizolastine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · Second-generation H1 antihistamine — benzimidazole derivative with anti-inflammatory activity
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine — benzimidazole derivative with anti-inflammatory activity

## Mechanism of action
- Selective H1 antagonist; also inhibits 5-lipoxygenase (leukotriene) production

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria, allergic rhinitis

## Dose & formulations
- 10 mg once daily

## Adverse effects
- Drowsiness, dry mouth, weight gain; QT prolongation (cardiac caution)

## Contraindications
- Long QT, significant heart disease, hypokalaemia; with macrolides or azoles

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) — contraindicated together

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Antihistamine + anti-leukotriene action; QT warning

_Sources: Khopkar (Second generation H1 antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: MMR vaccine
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Live attenuated viral vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella)
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Live attenuated viral vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella)

## Mechanism of action
- Attenuated viruses replicate briefly and induce long-lasting humoral and cell-mediated immunity
- Intralesional use in warts: the antigen triggers a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Th1) response with cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF) that also clears distant, untreated warts

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.5 mL subcutaneous (or IM); seroconversion over 2–3 weeks

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Prevention of measles, mumps and rubella (national schedule: MR at 9–12 months and 16–24 months; MMR in private schedule at 9 months, 15 months, 4–6 years)
- Rubella-susceptible women before pregnancy
- Dermatology: intralesional immunotherapy for multiple or recalcitrant warts (common, plantar, anogenital)

## Dose & formulations
- Prophylaxis: 0.5 mL SC
- Warts: 0.3–0.5 mL injected into the largest (mother) wart, every 2–3 weeks, up to 3–5 sessions (pre-sensitisation not needed)

## Adverse effects
- Pain, swelling, fever, flu-like symptoms
- Transient measles-like rash, parotid swelling, arthralgia (rubella component, adult women)
- Febrile seizures (rare), thrombocytopenia (rare), anaphylaxis (gelatin/neomycin)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination)
- Immunosuppression (high-dose steroids, chemotherapy, biologics, advanced HIV)
- Severe allergy to neomycin or gelatin; recent immunoglobulin or blood products (defer 3–11 months)
- Acute febrile illness

## Drug interactions
- Can temporarily suppress tuberculin skin test — do Mantoux on the same day or 4–6 weeks after
- Immunoglobulin products reduce response
- Give other live vaccines the same day or 4 weeks apart

## Monitoring
- Observe 15–30 min after injection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (live vaccine); inadvertent vaccination is not a reason for termination.

## Viva points
- Live vaccine — avoid in pregnancy and immunosuppression
- Immunotherapy for warts: induces Th1 response, clears distant warts
- Interferes with Mantoux reading

## Note on sources
Wolverton discusses Candida antigen and HPV vaccine more than MMR; MMR wart protocol is from published Indian studies and IADVL practice.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (Topical and intralesional antiviral agents — IL immunotherapy for warts); national immunisation schedule. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Moisturisers & emollients (Aquasoft, Physiogel-type, ceramide creams)
posts.summary: VI Keratolytics & emollients · Barrier repair agents: occlusives, humectants, emollients and physiological lipids
posts.body:
_Topicals · VI Keratolytics & emollients_

**Class:** Barrier repair agents: occlusives, humectants, emollients and physiological lipids

## Mechanism of action
- Occlusives (petrolatum, mineral oil, dimethicone, lanolin) form a film that reduces transepidermal water loss (TEWL); petrolatum is the most effective
- Humectants (glycerin, urea, lactic acid, hyaluronic acid, propylene glycol) draw water into the stratum corneum
- Emollients (fatty esters, plant oils, ceramides) fill gaps between corneocytes → smooth, soft skin
- Physiological lipid mixtures (ceramides : cholesterol : free fatty acids in about 3:1:1 ratio) repair the lamellar barrier in atopic skin (low ceramides)
- Physiogel AI-type creams add palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) — an anti-inflammatory/antipruritic lipid
- Aquasoft (glycerin–paraffin based cream) is a humectant–occlusive moisturiser commonly used in India

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Atopic dermatitis (cornerstone of treatment; proactive use reduces flares and steroid need)
- Ichthyoses, xerosis, asteatotic eczema in the elderly, hand eczema, psoriasis (adjunct)
- Barrier recovery with retinoid/isotretinoin therapy, after procedures
- Infant skin care (early emollient use may lower AD risk in high-risk infants — conflicting data)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply liberally and often (at least twice daily), within 3 min after bathing ('soak and seal')
- Adults may need 250–500 g per week for widespread disease; children 150–250 g per week
- Apply in the direction of hair growth (avoid folliculitis); apply 15–30 min apart from topical steroid

## Adverse effects
- Folliculitis (occlusive ointments), acneiform eruption on face
- Stinging (urea, lactic acid, propylene glycol)
- Contact allergy to fragrance, lanolin, preservatives (parabens, methylisothiazolinone)
- Fire risk: paraffin-soaked clothing/dressings near flames

## Contraindications
- Known allergy to an ingredient

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Occlusive vs humectant vs emollient — give examples
- Ceramide : cholesterol : FFA = 3:1:1
- Soak-and-seal within 3 min of bathing
- Paraffin-based emollients are a fire hazard

## Note on sources
Aquasoft and Physiogel are brand names; the post explains the ingredient types they represent.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.57 (Miscellaneous topical agents — moisturisers); Khopkar ch.27 (Moisturizers). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mometasone furoate 0.1% (cream, ointment, lotion)
posts.summary: IV Topical corticosteroids · Medium (cream, US class 4) to high (ointment, class 2) potency non-fluorinated (chlorinated) steroid; 'soft steroid'
posts.body:
_Topicals · IV Topical corticosteroids_

**Class:** Medium (cream, US class 4) to high (ointment, class 2) potency non-fluorinated (chlorinated) steroid; 'soft steroid'

## Mechanism of action
- Potent glucocorticoid receptor agonist with high skin activity but low systemic bioavailability (rapid hepatic breakdown)
- Favourable ratio of benefit to atrophy

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Atopic dermatitis, psoriasis (including scalp — lotion), lichen planus, discoid lupus, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Children over 2 years (short courses), and limited face use under supervision
- Proactive twice-weekly maintenance in atopic dermatitis

## Dose & formulations
- Once daily (its long skin activity allows single daily application)
- Children: avoid long courses, large areas and occlusion

## Adverse effects
- Atrophy, striae, perioral dermatitis with misuse (lower than other potent steroids)
- Widely misused in India in fairness/combination creams

## Contraindications
- As for topical steroids; avoid in nappy area under occlusion

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use on limited areas for short periods.

## Viva points
- Once-daily 'soft' steroid with low systemic absorption
- Cream class 4 vs ointment class 2 — vehicle changes potency

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45; Khopkar ch.22. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Monobenzone (monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, 20%)
posts.summary: Pigmentary & cosmeceutical agents · Melanocytotoxic depigmenting agent
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Pigmentary & cosmeceutical agents
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Pigmentary & cosmeceutical agents_

**Class:** Melanocytotoxic depigmenting agent

## Mechanism of action
- Converted by tyrosinase to reactive quinones → haptens that trigger an immune (melanocyte-specific) response → permanent destruction of melanocytes, even at distant sites

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Permanent depigmentation of remaining normal skin in extensive (universal) vitiligo (>50–80% body surface)
- Never for melasma or cosmetic lightening

## Dose & formulations
- 20% cream once or twice daily to remaining pigmented areas; depigmentation over 4–12 months

## Adverse effects
- Irritant/allergic dermatitis, distant depigmentation (unintended), repigmentation in sun-exposed areas, permanent sun sensitivity
- Psychological impact — counsel carefully (irreversible)

## Contraindications
- Melasma, freckles, PIH (causes irreversible confetti depigmentation), children

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Only for universal vitiligo — permanent
- Different from hydroquinone (which is reversible)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.26 (Monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone); Wolverton 4e ch.57. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Multidrug therapy (MDT) for leprosy
posts.summary: Antileprosy drugs · NLEP 3-drug multidrug therapy (rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone) for both PB and MB leprosy — revised regimen in force from 1 April 2025
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** NLEP 3-drug multidrug therapy (rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone) for both PB and MB leprosy — revised regimen in force from 1 April 2025

## Mechanism of action
- Combining a bactericidal drug (rifampicin) with bacteriostatic drugs (dapsone, clofazimine) prevents resistance and kills persisters
- Monthly supervised doses ensure the key drug (rifampicin) is taken
- Since 1 April 2025 India uses the same three drugs for PB and MB (WHO 2018 recommendation); only the duration differs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Revised NLEP classification:
- Paucibacillary (PB): 1–5 skin lesions AND no nerve involvement AND slit-skin smear negative
- Multibacillary (MB): more than 5 skin lesions, OR involvement of one or more nerves, OR slit-skin smear positive
- (Change from the old classification: any nerve involvement now makes the case MB)
- Adult (PB and MB): rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) + clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + clofazimine 50 mg daily + dapsone 100 mg daily
- Duration: PB 6 months; MB 12 months
- Child 10–14 years (PB 6 months / MB 12 months): rifampicin 450 mg monthly + clofazimine 150 mg monthly + clofazimine 50 mg on alternate days + dapsone 50 mg daily
- Child under 10 years (or 20–40 kg): rifampicin 10 mg/kg monthly + clofazimine 100 mg monthly + clofazimine 50 mg twice weekly + dapsone 2 mg/kg daily; separate single-drug formulations are used under 40 kg where packs are not suitable
- Patients already on treatment on 31 March 2025 complete their old regimen (PB 2-drug MDT; MB MDT) until release from treatment
- Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): single-dose rifampicin (SDR-PEP) to eligible contacts of an index case (NLEP, since 2017)
- Rifampicin-resistant leprosy (WHO 2018): clofazimine + two of ofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin
- Terms from Khopkar often asked in viva: U-MDT (uniform MDT trial — one regimen for all), A-MDT (accompanied MDT — full course handed over at diagnosis), ROM (rifampicin 600 mg + ofloxacin 400 mg + minocycline 100 mg)

## Dose & formulations
- Blister packs: adult and child packs supplied free under NLEP (WHO supply of revised packs from April 2025)
- Instructions to patients: take the monthly dose in front of the health worker; urine may turn red; skin darkens with clofazimine and fades after treatment; report reactions, nerve pain or weakness at once; treatment is free

## Adverse effects
- See individual drugs
- Leprosy reactions may occur during or after treatment and are treated without stopping MDT: type 1 (reversal) — prednisolone 40 mg/day tapered over about 12–20 weeks; type 2 (ENL) — prednisolone, thalidomide, clofazimine

## Contraindications
- Rifampicin hypersensitivity/resistance → clofazimine-based alternative regimens
- Dapsone allergy → omit dapsone, continue rifampicin + clofazimine

## Monitoring
- Monthly review: compliance, reactions, nerve function (voluntary muscle testing and sensory testing), drug side effects
- Notification is mandatory from all sectors (government, private, NGO, medical colleges) — Nikusth portal
- Release from treatment after the fixed duration; follow up for relapse and reactions

## Pregnancy & lactation
MDT is safe and should be continued in pregnancy and breastfeeding; reactions may flare after delivery.

## Viva points
- Revised classification (2025): any nerve involvement = MB
- 3 drugs for both PB (6 months) and MB (12 months) since 1 April 2025
- Adult and child doses — clofazimine 50 mg daily (adult), alternate days (10–14 y), twice weekly (<10 y)
- SDR-PEP for contacts; leprosy is notifiable from all sectors

## Note on sources
Updated to the NLEP regimen in force from 1 April 2025 (MoHFW/DGHS NLEP page and DO letter). The older 2-drug PB regimen is no longer used for new patients.

_Sources: NLEP / MoHFW revised classification and treatment regimen (DGHS letter Z-14020/80/2023-Lep, 17 Jan 2024; implemented from 1 Apr 2025, DO letter 6 Mar 2025); WHO Guidelines for leprosy 2018; Khopkar ch.6 (U-MDT, A-MDT, ROM). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mupirocin 2% cream/ointment
posts.summary: II Antibacterials · Monoxycarbolic acid antibiotic (pseudomonic acid A, from Pseudomonas fluorescens)
posts.body:
_Topicals · II Antibacterials_

**Class:** Monoxycarbolic acid antibiotic (pseudomonic acid A, from Pseudomonas fluorescens)

## Mechanism of action
- Reversibly binds bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase → stops protein synthesis
- Unique target — no cross-resistance with other antibiotics
- Bacteriostatic at low concentration, bactericidal at the high concentrations reached on skin
- Active against Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Impetigo (localised), secondarily infected eczema, folliculitis, small infected wounds
- Nasal decolonisation of S. aureus/MRSA carriers (recurrent furunculosis, before surgery)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply 2–3 times daily for 5–10 days
- Nasal ointment: twice daily into both nostrils for 5 days (with chlorhexidine body washes for recurrent boils)

## Adverse effects
- Burning, itching
- Polyethylene glycol (ointment base) can be absorbed from large wounds → nephrotoxicity (avoid in renal impairment on extensive raw areas)
- Resistance with prolonged or repeated use (low-level and high-level mupA-mediated)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; large burns or open wounds in renal impairment (PEG base)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Target: isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase
- Nasal decolonisation for recurrent furunculosis
- Limit course to under 10 days to prevent resistance

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.41; Khopkar ch.18. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mycobacterium w vaccine (Mw / Immuvac / MIP)
posts.summary: Biologicals · Heat-killed Mycobacterium indicus pranii (formerly Mycobacterium w) — Indian immunomodulatory vaccine
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Biologicals_

**Class:** Heat-killed Mycobacterium indicus pranii (formerly Mycobacterium w) — Indian immunomodulatory vaccine

## Mechanism of action
- Shares antigens with M. leprae; boosts Th1 cell-mediated immunity and modulates cytokines
- Used as a non-specific immunostimulant

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Leprosy: adjunct to MDT in multibacillary leprosy (faster bacterial clearance, fewer reactions), immunoprophylaxis of contacts (trials)
- Off-label: recalcitrant warts (intralesional/intradermal), anogenital warts, molluscum, psoriasis, alopecia areata, vitiligo (limited data)
- Approved in India for gram-negative sepsis (adjunct)

## Dose & formulations
- Intradermal 0.1 mL (first dose may be 0.2 mL split at two sites), repeated every 2–4 weeks for warts; leprosy schedules per protocol

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site papule, ulcer, abscess and scar; fever, flu-like symptoms; lymphadenopathy

## Contraindications
- Immunosuppression; acute febrile illness; pregnancy (insufficient data)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Indian immunomodulator from M. indicus pranii — adjunct in MB leprosy and in warts

## Note on sources
Mw vaccine is described in Khopkar; Wolverton does not cover it.

_Sources: Khopkar (Immunobiologicals — Immuvac / Mw vaccine). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) inhibitor; prodrug of mycophenolic acid
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) inhibitor; prodrug of mycophenolic acid

## Mechanism of action
- Mycophenolic acid reversibly inhibits IMPDH → blocks de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis
- Lymphocytes depend on the de novo pathway (other cells can use the salvage pathway), so the effect is fairly selective for T and B cells
- Also reduces antibody production and adhesion molecule expression

## Pharmacokinetics
- Rapidly converted to mycophenolic acid; glucuronidated in the liver; enterohepatic recirculation
- Enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium (720 mg ≈ 1 g MMF) has fewer GI effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Immunobullous diseases: pemphigus vulgaris (second line with rituximab in the Derma Desk ladder), bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid
- Dermatomyositis, cutaneous lupus, systemic sclerosis (skin and lung), vasculitis
- Atopic dermatitis, psoriasis (modest), pyoderma gangrenosum, lichen planus

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 1–1.5 g twice daily (2–3 g/day); start at 500 mg twice daily and increase over 2–4 weeks
- Children: about 600 mg/m² twice daily
- Tablets 250 and 500 mg; mycophenolate sodium 180 and 360 mg

## Adverse effects
- GI (the commonest): nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps
- Myelosuppression (leucopenia, anaemia), opportunistic infections (CMV, herpes zoster)
- Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (rare); lymphoma and skin cancer risk
- Teratogenic

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy; hypersensitivity
- Active serious infection; caution in peptic ulcer disease and HGPRT deficiency (Lesch–Nyhan, Kelley–Seegmiller)

## Drug interactions
- Antacids, cholestyramine, PPIs, iron: reduce absorption
- Acyclovir/valacyclovir: both levels rise (compete for tubular secretion)
- Azathioprine: do not combine (double myelosuppression)
- Lowers oral contraceptive levels; rifampicin lowers MMF

## Monitoring
- CBC weekly for the first month, every 2 weeks for 2 months, then monthly
- LFT and renal function periodically; pregnancy tests

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D; embryopathy including ear, facial and limb defects). Women need two forms of contraception during treatment and for 6 weeks after; men should use condoms during and for 90 days after.

## Viva points
- IMPDH inhibitor — lymphocyte-selective because of dependence on de novo purine synthesis
- GI side effects commonest; enteric-coated sodium salt helps
- Steroid-sparing agent in pemphigus

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.16 (Mycophenolates); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Nadifloxacin 1% cream
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Topical fluoroquinolone
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Topical fluoroquinolone

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → bactericidal against C. acnes, S. aureus (including MRSA) and S. epidermidis; also anti-inflammatory (reduces cytokines)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Inflammatory acne (with BPO), impetigo, folliculitis, infected dermatoses

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily; acne up to 8–12 weeks with BPO

## Adverse effects
- Itching, irritation, contact dermatitis (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to quinolones

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (limited data).

## Viva points
- Topical quinolone for acne in India/Japan; combine with BPO to prevent resistance

_Sources: Khopkar ch.18; Wolverton 4e ch.41. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Neomycin, bacitracin & polymyxin B
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Topical antibiotics often combined: neomycin (aminoglycoside), bacitracin (polypeptide), polymyxin B (cationic cyclic dec
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Topical antibiotics often combined: neomycin (aminoglycoside), bacitracin (polypeptide), polymyxin B (cationic cyclic decapeptide)

## Mechanism of action
- Neomycin: 30S ribosome — Gram-negatives and staphylococci
- Bacitracin: blocks cell-wall synthesis (bactoprenol dephosphorylation) — Gram-positives
- Polymyxin B: disrupts Gram-negative outer membrane phospholipids (detergent-like); Pseudomonas

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Minor wounds, abrasions, superficial infections (triple antibiotic ointments)
- Not first choice for impetigo (mupirocin, fusidic acid, ozenoxacin better)

## Dose & formulations
- 1–3 times daily for up to 7 days

## Adverse effects
- Allergic contact dermatitis — neomycin is one of the commonest contact allergens (patch-test series); cross-reacts with framycetin, gentamicin
- Bacitracin: contact allergy and rare anaphylaxis/contact urticaria
- Ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity if absorbed from large wounds

## Contraindications
- Known allergy; large raw areas; perforated ear drum (neomycin)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Small areas acceptable.

## Viva points
- Neomycin — top contact allergen; avoid on stasis eczema/leg ulcers
- Bacitracin — contact allergy and anaphylaxis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.18 (Bacitracin, Polymyxin B); Wolverton 4e ch.41 and ch.56. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Nevirapine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds directly to a hydrophobic pocket close to the active site of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase
- Non-competitive inhibition of the enzyme; no phosphorylation needed
- Not active against HIV-2

## Pharmacokinetics
- Over 90% absorbed; crosses the placenta and enters breast milk
- Metabolised by CYP3A4 and 2B6 and induces these enzymes (autoinduction), so the half-life falls from about 45 h to 25–30 h after 2–4 weeks

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Former first-line ART (with zidovudine + lamivudine), now replaced by dolutegravir-based regimens
- Infant prophylaxis in PMTCT (nevirapine syrup) under national programmes

## Dose & formulations
- 200 mg once daily for 14 days (lead-in), then 200 mg twice daily
- Infant prophylaxis: weight-based syrup for 6–12 weeks as per NACO

## Adverse effects
- Rash in about 15–20%, mostly in the first 6 weeks; SJS/TEN and DRESS (hypersensitivity syndrome)
- Hepatotoxicity: can be fulminant; risk higher in women with CD4 above 250 and men with CD4 above 400
- Fever, myalgia, nausea

## Contraindications
- Women with CD4 above 250 and men with CD4 above 400 (when starting)
- Moderate or severe liver disease (Child–Pugh B/C)
- Previous severe rash or hepatitis with nevirapine — never restart

## Drug interactions
- Lowers levels of oral contraceptives, ketoconazole, methadone, protease inhibitors
- Rifampicin lowers nevirapine levels — avoid
- Fluconazole raises nevirapine levels

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline, 2, 4, 8 and 12 weeks, then periodically
- Skin examination in the first 6–8 weeks; stop if rash with fever, blisters, mucosal involvement, or hepatitis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Has been used in pregnancy, but liver toxicity is higher in women with high CD4 counts. Dolutegravir-based regimens are now preferred.

## Viva points
- Lead-in dosing because of autoinduction
- Rash in the first 6 weeks; one of the commonest causes of SJS/TEN in India
- CD4 thresholds for hepatotoxicity: women above 250, men above 400
- HLA associations with nevirapine hypersensitivity are described (Wolverton ch.3)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4; Wolverton 4e ch.3, ch.11 and ch.67; check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Newer antileprosy drugs (ofloxacin, moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin, rifapentine, ethionamide)
posts.summary: Antileprosy drugs · Second-line bactericidal drugs used for resistance, intolerance and alternative regimens
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** Second-line bactericidal drugs used for resistance, intolerance and alternative regimens

## Mechanism of action
- Fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin, moxifloxacin): inhibit DNA gyrase — strongly bactericidal against M. leprae (moxifloxacin is the most potent)
- Minocycline: 30S ribosome inhibitor; the only tetracycline with significant activity against M. leprae
- Clarithromycin: 50S ribosome inhibitor; bactericidal against M. leprae
- Rifapentine: long-acting rifamycin, more potent than rifampicin in mice
- Ethionamide/prothionamide: inhibit mycolic acid synthesis; hepatotoxic — rarely used now

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Rifampicin-resistant leprosy (with clofazimine)
- Patients intolerant of standard MDT drugs
- ROM regimens and trial regimens (e.g. rifapentine–moxifloxacin–minocycline, PEP studies)

## Dose & formulations
- Ofloxacin 400 mg daily; moxifloxacin 400 mg daily; minocycline 100 mg daily; clarithromycin 500 mg daily
- Rifapentine 900 mg monthly (in trial regimens)

## Adverse effects
- Fluoroquinolones: GI upset, tendinopathy, QT prolongation, CNS effects, photosensitivity (sparfloxacin)
- Minocycline: vestibular effects, pigmentation, autoimmune reactions
- Clarithromycin: GI upset, taste change, CYP3A4 interactions
- Ethionamide: severe hepatotoxicity, GI upset

## Contraindications
- Fluoroquinolones in pregnancy and children (cartilage effects — relative)
- Minocycline in pregnancy and children under 8

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid fluoroquinolones and minocycline in pregnancy; clarithromycin with caution.

## Viva points
- Most bactericidal second-line drugs: moxifloxacin, rifapentine
- ROM = rifampicin + ofloxacin + minocycline
- Rifampicin-resistant leprosy = clofazimine + 2 of (FQ, minocycline, clarithromycin)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.6 (Newer drugs in leprosy); Wolverton 4e ch.9; WHO 2018 leprosy guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Nicotinamide (oral + topical)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Amide form of vitamin B3
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Amide form of vitamin B3

## Mechanism of action
- Precursor of NAD⁺ — restores cellular energy after UV damage, improving DNA repair
- Prevents UV-induced immunosuppression
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis, mast-cell degranulation and PARP; reduces sebum

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; does not cause flushing (unlike nicotinic acid/niacin)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chemoprevention of non-melanoma skin cancer in high-risk patients (ONTRAC trial: 23% fewer new cancers)
- Bullous pemphigoid (with tetracycline/doxycycline)
- Acne and rosacea (oral and topical), pellagra
- Other neutrophilic or inflammatory dermatoses: linear IgA, dermatitis herpetiformis (adjunct), granuloma annulare, necrobiosis lipoidica

## Dose & formulations
- Skin cancer chemoprevention: 500 mg twice daily
- Bullous pemphigoid: 500 mg three times daily (up to 2 g/day) with doxycycline/tetracycline
- Pellagra: 100 mg every 6 h until symptoms resolve, then maintenance

## Adverse effects
- Generally very safe: mild GI upset, headache
- At very high doses (above 3 g/day): hepatotoxicity

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in liver disease at high doses

## Drug interactions
- Carbamazepine and primidone levels may rise

## Monitoring
- None at usual doses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe at dietary/standard supplement doses.

## Viva points
- Nicotinamide does not cause flushing — nicotinic acid does
- ONTRAC trial: 500 mg twice daily reduces new skin cancers
- Nicotinamide + tetracycline for bullous pemphigoid

## Topical form: Topical niacinamide (2–5%)
_Topical vitamin B3 (cosmeceutical/therapeutic)_

**Mechanism**
- Inhibits melanosome transfer, improves barrier (ceramide synthesis), reduces sebum and inflammation

**Indications**
- Acne (4% gel), rosacea, melasma/PIH (adjunct), atopic dermatitis barrier, photoageing

**Dose & how to apply**
- Once or twice daily

**Adverse effects**
- Mild irritation (rare)

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity

**Pregnancy:** Safe.

**Viva points**
- Blocks melanosome transfer (not tyrosinase)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40 (Miscellaneous systemic drugs); Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements); Khopkar ch.28 (Topical vitamin B3 — niacinamide). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Nystatin
posts.summary: Topical antifungals · Polyene antifungal (from Streptomyces noursei)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antifungals_

**Class:** Polyene antifungal (from Streptomyces noursei)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds ergosterol → membrane pores → leakage (fungicidal); not absorbed from gut or skin

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Candidiasis only: oral thrush (suspension), intertrigo, napkin candidiasis, candidal paronychia, vaginal candidiasis
- Combined with steroids/antibiotics in some creams

## Dose & formulations
- Cream/ointment 100,000 U/g two to three times daily; oral suspension 100,000 U/mL, 1–4 mL four times daily (swish and swallow)

## Adverse effects
- Very safe; irritation, GI upset with large oral doses

## Contraindications
- Dermatophyte infections (ineffective)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe (not absorbed).

## Viva points
- Polyene — Candida only, not dermatophytes; not absorbed orally

_Sources: Khopkar ch.19; Wolverton 4e ch.42. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Oral cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefadroxil, cefuroxime, cefixime, cefpodoxime)
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · β-lactam antibiotics — 1st (cephalexin, cefadroxil), 2nd (cefuroxime) and 3rd generation (cefixime, cefpodoxime) oral cephalosporins
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** β-lactam antibiotics — 1st (cephalexin, cefadroxil), 2nd (cefuroxime) and 3rd generation (cefixime, cefpodoxime) oral cephalosporins

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibit cell-wall synthesis (PBP binding) → bactericidal
- Moving from 1st to 3rd generation: less Gram-positive (staph) activity, more Gram-negative activity and β-lactamase stability

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- 1st generation (cephalexin, cefadroxil): staphylococcal and streptococcal skin infections — impetigo, cellulitis, furunculosis, infected eczema, wound infection
- 2nd generation (cefuroxime axetil): early Lyme disease (alternative to doxycycline), skin infections
- 3rd generation: cefixime 400 mg single dose (NACO grey and yellow kits — gonorrhoea/cervicitis, PID); cefpodoxime for skin and soft-tissue infections
- Injectable 3rd generation (ceftriaxone): see exam-list post

## Dose & formulations
- Cephalexin 500 mg four times daily (25–50 mg/kg/day in children)
- Cefadroxil 500 mg–1 g twice daily
- Cefuroxime axetil 500 mg twice daily (Lyme 14–21 days)
- Cefixime 400 mg single dose (gonorrhoea, as per NACO kit); 200 mg twice daily for other infections
- Cefpodoxime 200 mg twice daily

## Adverse effects
- Diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis
- Hypersensitivity — cross-reactivity with penicillin is low (about 1–2%), mainly with similar side chains (cephalexin/cefadroxil share amoxicillin's side chain)
- Serum-sickness-like reaction (classically cefaclor in children)
- Positive Coombs test, rarely haemolytic anaemia

## Contraindications
- Previous anaphylaxis to a cephalosporin; caution in immediate penicillin allergy

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid raises levels; alcohol (some injectables with MTT side chain — disulfiram-like)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Generations and their spectrum shift
- Cefixime is the oral drug in NACO kits
- Low cross-reactivity with penicillin — related to side chains

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Cephalosporins); Wolverton 4e ch.9; NACO STI guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Other protease inhibitors (lopinavir, atazanavir, indinavir, nelfinavir, saquinavir)
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · HIV protease inhibitors (PIs), usually boosted with ritonavir
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** HIV protease inhibitors (PIs), usually boosted with ritonavir

## Mechanism of action
- Block HIV protease → gag-pol polyproteins not cleaved → immature non-infectious virions

## Pharmacokinetics
- CYP3A4 substrates; ritonavir boosting raises levels (see ritonavir post)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Second-line ART in India: lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) with 2 NRTIs (and dolutegravir in some regimens)
- Children: LPV/r formulations (older guidance)
- Indinavir, nelfinavir, saquinavir: historical, now rarely used

## Dose & formulations
- LPV/r 400/100 mg twice daily; ATV/r 300/100 mg once daily with food

## Adverse effects
- Class: lipodystrophy (central fat accumulation, buffalo hump), dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance, GI upset
- Atazanavir: unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice, yellow eyes — benign, UGT1A1 inhibition), nephrolithiasis
- Indinavir: retinoid-like effects — paronychia, ingrown toenails, pyogenic granulomas, xerosis, cheilitis, alopecia; nephrolithiasis (drink plenty)
- Lopinavir: diarrhoea, PR/QT prolongation; nelfinavir: diarrhoea

## Contraindications
- With rifampicin (use rifabutin), simvastatin/lovastatin, ergot, oral midazolam, pimozide; PPIs with atazanavir

## Drug interactions
- As for ritonavir: inhaled/injected corticosteroids → Cushing syndrome; colchicine, cyclosporine, azoles

## Monitoring
- Lipids, glucose, LFT, bilirubin (atazanavir), renal function

## Pregnancy & lactation
LPV/r and ATV/r can be used in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Indinavir → retinoid-like nail fold changes and pyogenic granuloma
- Atazanavir → benign jaundice
- PI lipodystrophy

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Protease inhibitors); Wolverton 4e ch.11 and ch.67; current NACO ART guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Other psoralens: trioxsalen & 5-methoxypsoralen (5-MOP)
posts.summary: Photoprotective agents · Furocoumarin photosensitisers used with UVA (PUVA)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Photoprotective agents_

**Class:** Furocoumarin photosensitisers used with UVA (PUVA)

## Mechanism of action
- Intercalate DNA; with UVA form monoadducts (and cross-links with 8-MOP/5-MOP) → antiproliferative, immunosuppressive and melanogenic effects
- Trioxsalen (4,5',8-trimethylpsoralen): more melanogenic, less phototoxic orally; very phototoxic topically and in bath PUVA
- 5-MOP (bergapten): less nausea and less phototoxicity than 8-MOP; needs higher dose

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Vitiligo (trioxsalen orally with sunlight — PUVAsol; trioxsalen bath PUVA)
- Psoriasis and other PUVA indications (5-MOP — used in Europe)

## Dose & formulations
- Trioxsalen 0.6 mg/kg orally 2 h before sunlight/UVA (Indian practice; tablets 5 mg)
- 5-MOP 1.2–1.8 mg/kg orally 2 h before UVA
- Bath PUVA: trioxsalen or 8-MOP dissolved in bath water (e.g. 0.5–1 mg/L), UVA immediately after 15 min soak

## Adverse effects
- Phototoxic burns, PUVA itch, nausea (less with 5-MOP and trioxsalen)
- Long-term PUVA risks: SCC, lentigines, photoageing, cataract

## Contraindications
- As for methoxsalen: photosensitive disorders, pregnancy, children <10–12, melanoma/skin cancer history

## Drug interactions
- Other photosensitisers

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- 5-MOP — less nausea, needs 1.2 mg/kg
- Trioxsalen — popular in India for vitiligo (PUVAsol)
- Bath PUVA avoids systemic side effects

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.23; Khopkar (Psoralens, PUVA and phototherapy). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Other topical azoles: econazole, sulconazole, bifonazole
posts.summary: Topical antifungals · Imidazole antifungals (topical)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antifungals_

**Class:** Imidazole antifungals (topical)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibit 14-α-demethylase → ergosterol depletion; econazole and sulconazole also antibacterial (Gram-positives)
- Bifonazole also inhibits HMG-CoA reductase — stays in skin long enough for once-daily use

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea corporis, cruris, pedis; cutaneous candidiasis; pityriasis versicolor; erythrasma (econazole)
- Bifonazole 1% with 40% urea: onychomycosis (nail avulsion kit)

## Dose & formulations
- Econazole 1% once or twice daily; sulconazole 1% once or twice daily; bifonazole 1% once daily — 2–4 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Burning, itching, contact dermatitis (imidazoles cross-react)

## Contraindications
- Imidazole allergy

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; acceptable.

## Viva points
- Bifonazole — once daily, long skin retention
- Econazole — also antibacterial (useful in infected toe webs)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.19; Wolverton 4e ch.42. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Oxiconazole nitrate 1% cream
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Azoles · Imidazole antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits ergosterol synthesis; good stratum corneum retention allows once-daily use

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea pedis, corporis, cruris
- Pityriasis versicolor

## Dose & formulations
- Once or twice daily: 2 weeks (corporis/cruris, versicolor), 4 weeks (pedis)

## Adverse effects
- Itching, burning, irritation (uncommon)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; minimal absorption.

## Viva points
- Once-daily imidazole for dermatophytosis and PV

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42; Khopkar ch.19. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ozenoxacin 1% cream
posts.summary: II Antibacterials · Non-fluorinated quinolone (topical only)
posts.body:
_Topicals · II Antibacterials_

**Class:** Non-fluorinated quinolone (topical only)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits both bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → bactericidal
- Dual-target binding means a lower chance of resistance; active against MRSA and quinolone-resistant strains, and Streptococcus pyogenes

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Impetigo (non-bullous and bullous, localised) in adults and children 2 months and older

## Dose & formulations
- Thin layer twice daily for 5 days (up to 100 cm² in adults; 2% BSA in children)

## Adverse effects
- Rare: application-site itching, rosacea flare, seborrhoeic dermatitis

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; not for eyes, mouth or mucosa

## Pregnancy & lactation
Negligible absorption — acceptable.

## Viva points
- Newer impetigo treatment; works against MRSA and mupirocin-resistant staph
- 5-day course, twice daily

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.41 (Topical antibacterial agents — ozenoxacin). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Penciclovir 1% cream
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Topical guanosine analogue (active metabolite of famciclovir)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Topical guanosine analogue (active metabolite of famciclovir)

## Mechanism of action
- Phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase → inhibits viral DNA polymerase; long intracellular half-life

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Recurrent herpes labialis in adults and children over 12 (slightly better than topical acyclovir)

## Dose & formulations
- Every 2 h while awake for 4 days, starting at the first sign

## Adverse effects
- Local irritation, numbness

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; mucous membranes

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption — acceptable.

## Viva points
- Topical form of famciclovir's active drug; frequent application needed

_Sources: Khopkar ch.20 (Penciclovir); Wolverton 4e ch.43. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Penicillins (penicillin G, amoxicillin, ampicillin, cloxacillin)
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · β-lactam antibiotics — natural penicillins, aminopenicillins and penicillinase-resistant penicillins
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** β-lactam antibiotics — natural penicillins, aminopenicillins and penicillinase-resistant penicillins

## Mechanism of action
- Bind penicillin-binding proteins → block transpeptidation (cross-linking) of the peptidoglycan cell wall → lysis of dividing bacteria (bactericidal)
- Natural penicillin G: streptococci, Treponema, Neisseria (sensitive strains)
- Aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin): add some Gram-negatives; destroyed by β-lactamase — clavulanic acid protects them
- Cloxacillin/flucloxacillin: resist staphylococcal penicillinase → anti-staphylococcal (not MRSA)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Amoxicillin is better absorbed than ampicillin and unaffected by food; cloxacillin best on an empty stomach
- Renal excretion (probenecid prolongs levels)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Aqueous crystalline penicillin G: neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis — 18–24 million U/day IV (3–4 MU every 4 h) for 10–14 days
- Procaine penicillin 2.4 MU IM daily + probenecid 500 mg four times daily × 10–14 days: alternative for neurosyphilis
- Benzathine penicillin: see exam-list post
- Amoxicillin (± clavulanate): impetigo/cellulitis (step-down), infected eczema, bites (co-amoxiclav), early Lyme disease in children, actinomycosis
- Cloxacillin/flucloxacillin: staphylococcal impetigo, furunculosis, cellulitis, SSSS (with IV forms)
- Erysipelas/streptococcal cellulitis: penicillin V or amoxicillin

## Dose & formulations
- Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily (co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily)
- Cloxacillin 500 mg four times daily, 1 h before food
- Children: amoxicillin 25–45 mg/kg/day; cloxacillin 50–100 mg/kg/day in divided doses

## Adverse effects
- Hypersensitivity: urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis (1–4 per 10,000 courses)
- Ampicillin/amoxicillin maculopapular rash in infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — up to 80–100%, not true allergy
- Serum-sickness-like reaction (amoxicillin, children), AGEP, SJS/TEN, DRESS (rare)
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction in syphilis; Hoigné syndrome (procaine penicillin: acute anxiety, hallucinations from procaine embolism)
- Diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis; cholestatic hepatitis (co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin)

## Contraindications
- Penicillin allergy (immediate type) — avoid; desensitise when penicillin is essential (syphilis in pregnancy, neurosyphilis)
- Amoxicillin in suspected infectious mononucleosis

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid raises levels; allopurinol increases ampicillin rash
- Methotrexate: reduced renal clearance → toxicity
- Warfarin: INR may rise

## Monitoring
- Watch for allergy; LFT on long co-amoxiclav/flucloxacillin courses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding (old FDA category B).

## Viva points
- Neurosyphilis needs aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV — benzathine does not reach CSF
- Ampicillin rash in EBV infection
- Cloxacillin = penicillinase-resistant, for staph (not MRSA)
- Hoigné syndrome vs anaphylaxis vs Jarisch–Herxheimer

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Penicillins); Wolverton 4e ch.9 (β-lactams). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pentamidine
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Aromatic diamidine; antiprotozoal and anti-Pneumocystis
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Aromatic diamidine; antiprotozoal and anti-Pneumocystis

## Mechanism of action
- Interferes with parasite DNA, RNA, phospholipid and protein synthesis (binds kinetoplast DNA)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous leishmaniasis due to L. guyanensis (New World) — drug of choice
- Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (treatment and aerosolised prophylaxis when co-trimoxazole cannot be used)
- Early-stage African trypanosomiasis (T. b. gambiense); visceral leishmaniasis (second-line, historical)

## Dose & formulations
- Leishmaniasis: 4 mg/kg IM/IV on alternate days for 3–4 doses (L. guyanensis) or longer courses
- PCP: 4 mg/kg IV daily for 21 days; prophylaxis 300 mg nebulised monthly

## Adverse effects
- Hypoglycaemia (pancreatic β-cell toxicity — early), followed later by diabetes mellitus
- Hypotension (especially with rapid IV infusion — give slowly lying down), arrhythmias (QT prolongation)
- Nephrotoxicity, pancreatitis, leucopenia; sterile abscess at IM sites

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in diabetes, heart disease, renal impairment

## Drug interactions
- Foscarnet (severe hypocalcaemia), nephrotoxic and QT drugs

## Monitoring
- Blood glucose, BP during and after infusion, ECG, renal function, CBC

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use only when essential.

## Viva points
- Hypoglycaemia then diabetes
- Drug of choice for L. guyanensis cutaneous leishmaniasis

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5 (Pentamidine); Wolverton 4e ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pentavalent antimonials (sodium stibogluconate, meglumine antimoniate)
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Pentavalent antimony (SbV) compounds; antileishmanial
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Pentavalent antimony (SbV) compounds; antileishmanial

## Mechanism of action
- Prodrug: SbV reduced to trivalent SbIII inside macrophages and amastigotes
- Inhibits trypanothione reductase and parasite glycolysis/fatty acid oxidation → amastigote death; also enhances macrophage killing

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Cutaneous leishmaniasis: intralesional for small, few lesions (Old World — L. tropica, L. major); systemic for multiple, large, facial/joint lesions, lymphatic spread, mucosal or New World species
- Mucocutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis (visceral: largely replaced in India by liposomal amphotericin B/miltefosine because of resistance in Bihar)
- Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (older regimens; miltefosine now preferred)

## Dose & formulations
- Systemic: 20 mg SbV/kg/day IV or IM for 20 days (cutaneous) or 28 days (mucosal/visceral)
- Intralesional: 0.2–1 mL (100 mg SbV/mL) infiltrated until the lesion blanches, weekly or every 2 weeks for 3–8 sessions (often combined with cryotherapy)
- Sodium stibogluconate 100 mg SbV/mL; meglumine antimoniate 85 mg SbV/mL

## Adverse effects
- Cardiotoxicity: QT prolongation, T-wave changes, arrhythmia — dose and duration related
- Pancreatitis (raised amylase/lipase), hepatitis, nephrotoxicity
- Myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, headache; cytopenias
- IL: pain, swelling, local reactions

## Contraindications
- Heart disease (prolonged QT), significant renal/hepatic disease, pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics)

## Monitoring
- ECG twice weekly (stop if QTc >500 ms), amylase/lipase, LFT, renal function, CBC weekly

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (systemic); prefer local measures or liposomal amphotericin B.

## Viva points
- SbV prodrug → SbIII
- 20 mg SbV/kg/day × 20 days (cutaneous)
- ECG monitoring — QT prolongation
- Resistance in Bihar → replaced for kala-azar

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5 (Antileishmanial agents — sodium stibogluconate); Wolverton 4e ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Permethrin (5% cream, 1% creme rinse)
posts.summary: III Antiparasitics · Synthetic pyrethroid
posts.body:
_Topicals · III Antiparasitics_

**Class:** Synthetic pyrethroid

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks sodium channels in the parasite's nerve membranes (delays repolarisation) → paralysis and death of mites and lice
- Poorly absorbed (under 2%) and rapidly inactivated by esterases in humans → very safe
- Partly ovicidal

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- 5% cream: scabies (first line), including children over 2 months and pregnant/breastfeeding women
- 1% creme rinse: head lice (pediculosis capitis) and pubic lice
- Crusted scabies (with oral ivermectin)

## Dose & formulations
- Scabies: apply 5% cream to the whole body from the neck down (include scalp, face and ears in infants, elderly and immunocompromised), especially between fingers, wrists, genitals and under nails; wash off after 8–14 h; repeat after 7 days
- Treat all close contacts at the same time; wash clothes and bedding in hot water or store in a sealed bag for 72 h
- Head lice: apply 1% rinse to washed, towel-dried hair for 10 min, rinse; repeat on day 9–10; wet-comb to remove nits

## Adverse effects
- Burning, stinging, itch (post-scabetic itch may last 2–4 weeks — not treatment failure)
- Contact dermatitis (rare; cross-reaction with chrysanthemum/ragweed)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to pyrethrins/chrysanthemums; infants under 2 months (5% cream)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe — first choice in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for scabies
- Apply neck down (whole body in infants and elderly), 8–14 h, repeat after 1 week
- Treat contacts simultaneously
- Itch persisting 2–4 weeks is expected

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.44 (Topical antiparasitic agents); Khopkar ch.21. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pheniramine maleate injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; alkylamine group
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; alkylamine group

## Mechanism of action
- H1 receptor inverse agonist — blocks histamine-mediated itch, wheal, flare and vascular leak
- Anticholinergic and sedative effects

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM or slow IV; onset within 15–30 min; duration 4–6 h

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Adjunct in anaphylaxis (after adrenaline) — relieves itch and urticaria; does not treat airway or shock
- Acute urticaria, angioedema (non-airway), allergic drug reactions, insect bite reactions
- Pre-medication before contrast media or blood products in sensitised patients

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 22.75–45.5 mg (1–2 mL of 22.75 mg/mL) IM or slow IV; repeat up to 2–3 times a day if needed
- Children: about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day in divided doses (avoid in infants)
- Ampoule 22.75 mg/mL (2 mL)

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, dizziness; hypotension with fast IV injection
- Anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision
- Paradoxical excitation in children, convulsions in overdose

## Contraindications
- Neonates and premature infants; breastfeeding
- Caution: glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, epilepsy, elderly

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol, sedatives, opioids: additive CNS depression
- MAO inhibitors, other anticholinergics

## Monitoring
- Watch BP and level of consciousness after IV use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use only if needed; prefer second-generation oral antihistamines for routine use.

## Viva points
- Commonly used injectable antihistamine in Indian practice (brand Avil)
- Second-line drug in anaphylaxis — never a substitute for adrenaline
- Inject IV slowly (hypotension)

_Sources: Khopkar (Antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers); Wolverton 4e ch.32 (H1 antihistamines — class). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Phenol (carbolic acid)
posts.summary: Chemical agents, peels & baths · Aromatic alcohol — antiseptic, anaesthetic, keratocoagulant
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths_

**Class:** Aromatic alcohol — antiseptic, anaesthetic, keratocoagulant

## Mechanism of action
- Low concentration: antiseptic and topical anaesthetic (antipruritic in calamine with phenol)
- 88% phenol: keratocoagulation — denatures proteins instantly (paradoxically less penetration than 50%)
- Baker–Gordon formula (phenol + croton oil + septisol + water): deep peel

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chemical matricectomy for ingrown toenails (88% phenol, 3 × 30 s)
- Deep chemical peels for severe photoageing and wrinkles (Baker–Gordon — rarely now)
- Antipruritic in lotions (0.5–1%); cautery of small lesions

## Dose & formulations
- Matricectomy: tourniquet, apply 88% phenol to matrix with cotton tip for 3 × 30 s, then irrigate with alcohol

## Adverse effects
- Systemic absorption (deep peels): cardiac arrhythmias — ECG monitoring, IV hydration, treat in segments over 60–90 min; renal and hepatic toxicity
- Permanent hypopigmentation ('alabaster' skin) after deep peels, scarring, laryngeal oedema

## Contraindications
- Deep peels: cardiac, renal, hepatic disease; dark skin types

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid.

## Viva points
- Deep phenol peel → arrhythmia (ECG monitoring)
- 88% phenol for ingrown nail matricectomy

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Phenol — carbolic acid) and ch.31 (Phenol peels); Wolverton 4e ch.53. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pimecrolimus 1% cream
posts.summary: Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics · Topical calcineurin inhibitor (ascomycin macrolactam)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical immunomodulators & antipsoriatics_

**Class:** Topical calcineurin inhibitor (ascomycin macrolactam)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds macrophilin-12 (FKBP-12); complex inhibits calcineurin → blocks NFAT → reduces T-cell cytokines and mast cell mediator release
- More lipophilic and lower systemic absorption than tacrolimus; weaker effect (similar to low-potency steroid)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Mild–moderate atopic dermatitis (≥2 years; approved) — face, eyelids, flexures
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis, vitiligo (face), intertriginous psoriasis, perioral dermatitis, steroid rosacea

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily; maintenance twice weekly

## Adverse effects
- Application-site burning/warmth (less than tacrolimus), skin infections (herpes, molluscum), alcohol flushing
- FDA boxed warning (theoretical malignancy) as for tacrolimus

## Contraindications
- Under 2 years (label), immunosuppression, Netherton syndrome, active infection at site

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; limited areas acceptable.

## Viva points
- Cream (pimecrolimus) vs ointment (tacrolimus); pimecrolimus is weaker and for mild disease

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.48; Khopkar ch.23. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Placental extract (injection + topical gel)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Aqueous extract of human placenta (biogenic stimulator; e.g. Placentrex)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Aqueous extract of human placenta (biogenic stimulator; e.g. Placentrex)

## Mechanism of action
- Contains nucleotides, peptides, enzymes and growth factors claimed to stimulate wound healing, melanogenesis and tissue regeneration (mechanism not well established)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Indian practice: chronic non-healing ulcers, burns, post-procedure healing (gel); vitiligo (older topical preparations — weak evidence); periodontitis, pelvic inflammatory disease (injection — historic)

## Dose & formulations
- Injection 2 mL IM daily or alternate days (as per product); gel applied once or twice daily to wounds

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain, allergic reactions; theoretical risk of transmissible infection (human-derived)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (insufficient data).

## Viva points
- Indian biogenic product; evidence is weak — mention as an adjunct only

_Sources: Khopkar (Placental extract). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23)
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Inactivated polysaccharide vaccine — 23 serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Inactivated polysaccharide vaccine — 23 serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae

## Mechanism of action
- Capsular polysaccharides induce antibodies by a T-cell-independent pathway
- Gives no immunological memory, no booster effect, and is poorly immunogenic in children under 2 years
- Conjugate vaccines (PCV13/15/20) link the polysaccharide to a protein → T-cell-dependent, better memory

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.5 mL IM or SC; antibodies within 2–3 weeks; wane after about 5 years

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Adults 65 years and over
- People at high risk aged 2–64: asplenia, chronic heart/lung/liver/kidney disease, diabetes, HIV
- Dermatology: before or early in immunosuppressive therapy — rituximab, long-term systemic steroids, methotrexate, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide, JAK inhibitors, biologics
- Give at least 2 weeks before rituximab (rituximab blunts antibody response for 6+ months)

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5 mL IM or SC
- Usual sequence: conjugate vaccine (PCV) first, then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later; one revaccination with PPSV23 after 5 years in high-risk patients
- If PCV20 or PCV21 is used, PPSV23 is usually not needed (current CDC advice)

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain and swelling (more after revaccination)
- Low-grade fever, myalgia
- Severe reactions rare

## Contraindications
- Severe allergy to a previous dose or component
- Defer during acute illness

## Drug interactions
- Immunosuppressants and rituximab reduce response — vaccinate before starting where possible

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not routinely given; may be given to high-risk women if needed (inactivated).

## Viva points
- Polysaccharide = T-independent = no memory, poor in under-2s
- Vaccinate before rituximab and other immunosuppressants
- PCV first, then PPSV23 ≥8 weeks later

## Note on sources
Adult pneumococcal recommendations changed recently (PCV20/PCV21). Please confirm the current schedule.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.30 (Rituximab — vaccination before therapy); CDC/ACIP adult schedule. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Podophyllin & podophyllotoxin
posts.summary: Wart & antiviral agents · Antimitotic plant resins — podophyllin (crude 10–25% resin in tincture of benzoin) and podophyllotoxin (purified active lignan, 0.5% s
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Wart & antiviral agents_

**Class:** Antimitotic plant resins — podophyllin (crude 10–25% resin in tincture of benzoin) and podophyllotoxin (purified active lignan, 0.5% solution / 0.15% cream)

## Mechanism of action
- Bind tubulin → arrest mitosis in metaphase → necrosis of wart tissue

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- External anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata) — podophyllotoxin is the patient-applied form; podophyllin is clinic-applied

## Dose & formulations
- Podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution/0.15% cream: twice daily for 3 days, then 4 days off; up to 4 cycles (patient-applied, ≤10 cm², ≤0.5 mL/day)
- Podophyllin 20–25%: applied by clinician to warts (≤10 cm², ≤0.5 mL), protect surrounding skin with petroleum jelly, wash off after 1–4 h; weekly

## Adverse effects
- Local burning, erosion, ulceration
- Podophyllin systemic toxicity if large amounts are applied or absorbed: nausea, vomiting, neuropathy, bone marrow suppression, coma, death
- Podophyllin causes histological changes that mimic dysplasia (podophyllin effect)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (teratogenic, fetal death); mucosal (urethral, vaginal, cervical, anal canal) warts; bleeding or large wart areas

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated — use cryotherapy or TCA instead.

## Viva points
- Contraindicated in pregnancy
- Podophyllotoxin is safer, patient-applied (3 days on, 4 off)
- Wash off podophyllin after 1–4 h

_Sources: Khopkar ch.20 (Podophyllin); Wolverton 4e ch.43. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄) 1:10,000
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Oxidising agent; antiseptic and astringent
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Oxidising agent; antiseptic and astringent

## Mechanism of action
- Releases oxygen → oxidises organic matter; antibacterial and antifungal; astringent (dries weeping lesions)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Wet compresses and soaks for weeping/oozing dermatoses: acute eczema, pemphigus erosions, infected eczema, tinea pedis maceration, leg ulcers, bullous disorders
- Potassium permanganate baths

## Dose & formulations
- 1:10,000 solution (pale pink) — dissolve crystals fully; soak or compress for 10–15 min, once or twice daily for a few days

## Adverse effects
- Brown staining of skin and nails; burns and corrosive injury with concentrated solution or undissolved crystals; dryness
- Ingestion is toxic

## Contraindications
- Concentrated solutions; mucosa

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- 1:10,000 pale pink solution — astringent for weeping lesions
- Undissolved crystals cause burns

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 and ch.33 (Potassium permanganate bath). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Povidone-iodine (5–10%)
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Iodophor (iodine complexed with polyvinylpyrrolidone)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Iodophor (iodine complexed with polyvinylpyrrolidone)

## Mechanism of action
- Slowly releases free iodine → oxidises microbial proteins and nucleic acids → broad-spectrum killing of bacteria, fungi, viruses, spores

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Skin antisepsis before procedures, wound cleansing, infected ulcers, mouth gargle, vaginal antisepsis

## Dose & formulations
- 10% solution/5% scrub; allow 2 min contact and to dry; ointment once or twice daily on wounds

## Adverse effects
- Irritant dermatitis (especially under occlusion), allergic contact dermatitis (rare), skin staining
- Systemic iodine absorption from large wounds/neonates → hypothyroidism, metabolic acidosis, renal toxicity

## Contraindications
- Iodine allergy; thyroid disease (large areas); neonates and pregnancy (prolonged/large-area use)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid prolonged or large-area use (fetal/neonatal hypothyroidism).

## Viva points
- Needs contact time and drying; caution in neonates (hypothyroidism)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Povidone iodine); Wolverton 4e ch.54. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Praziquantel
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Pyrazinoisoquinoline anthelmintic (anti-trematode, anti-cestode)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Pyrazinoisoquinoline anthelmintic (anti-trematode, anti-cestode)

## Mechanism of action
- Increases calcium permeability of the worm's tegument → spastic paralysis and tegument damage → exposure to host immunity

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Schistosomiasis (including cercarial dermatitis sequelae and cutaneous schistosomiasis)
- Cysticercosis (cysticercosis cutis, neurocysticercosis — with or after albendazole), taeniasis
- Liver and lung flukes (clonorchiasis, paragonimiasis)

## Dose & formulations
- Schistosomiasis: 40 mg/kg single dose or 20 mg/kg twice in one day
- Taeniasis: 5–10 mg/kg single dose
- Neurocysticercosis: 50 mg/kg/day in 3 doses for 15 days (with steroids)
- Cysticercosis cutis (Khopkar): single or short courses; excision is often curative

## Adverse effects
- Headache, dizziness, abdominal pain, malaise; inflammatory reactions from dying cysts (seizures in neurocysticercosis)

## Contraindications
- Ocular cysticercosis (inflammation can destroy the eye — remove surgically)
- With strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin)

## Drug interactions
- Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, dexamethasone lower levels; cimetidine raises them

## Pregnancy & lactation
May be used for schistosomiasis in pregnancy (WHO).

## Viva points
- Calcium influx → spastic paralysis of worms
- Never treat ocular cysticercosis medically first

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5 (Table 5.1); Wolverton 4e ch.12. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Precipitated sulphur (5–10%)
posts.summary: Scabicides & pediculicides · Elemental sulphur in petrolatum (scabicide); also keratolytic and antimicrobial
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Scabicides & pediculicides_

**Class:** Elemental sulphur in petrolatum (scabicide); also keratolytic and antimicrobial
