## Mechanism of action
- Converted to hydrogen sulphide/pentathionic acid on skin → toxic to mites, fungi and bacteria; keratolytic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Scabies in infants under 2 months and pregnancy (safe, cheap)
- Acne, rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis, pityriasis versicolor (with salicylic acid)

## Dose & formulations
- Scabies: 5–10% ointment nightly for 3 nights (wash off before next application), repeat after a week

## Adverse effects
- Messy, malodorous, staining; irritant dermatitis with prolonged use

## Contraindications
- Sulphur sensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe — option in pregnancy and infancy.

## Viva points
- Safest scabicide in infants and pregnancy (but messy)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.21 (Precipitated sulfur); Wolverton 4e ch.44. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Prednisolone
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h); reference steroid for oral dosing
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h); reference steroid for oral dosing

## Mechanism of action
- Enters cells and binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor; the complex enters the nucleus
- Genomic effects: switches on anti-inflammatory genes (lipocortin/annexin-1, IκB) and switches off pro-inflammatory genes (NF-κB and AP-1 targets: IL-1, IL-2, TNF-α, COX-2)
- Result: fewer circulating lymphocytes, eosinophils and monocytes; less vascular permeability; reduced antibody production with high doses
- Non-genomic (rapid) effects with high pulse doses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Prednisolone is active itself (prednisone needs conversion in the liver to prednisolone)
- Well absorbed; bound to transcortin and albumin; metabolised in the liver (enzyme inducers raise clearance)
- Equivalence: 5 mg prednisolone = 20 mg hydrocortisone = 4 mg methylprednisolone = 6 mg deflazacort = 0.75 mg dexamethasone = 0.6 mg betamethasone
- Glucocorticoid potency 4 (hydrocortisone = 1); mineralocorticoid effect 0.8

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Immunobullous diseases: pemphigus vulgaris (1–1.5 mg/kg/day initially), bullous pemphigoid (0.5–0.75 mg/kg/day if topical not possible)
- Connective tissue disease: dermatomyositis (1 mg/kg/day), SLE
- Vasculitis, neutrophilic dermatoses (Sweet syndrome, pyoderma gangrenosum)
- Short courses: acute severe allergic contact dermatitis, severe urticaria/angioedema (short), DRESS, erythema nodosum leprosum and type 1 lepra reaction
- Lichen planus (extensive), sarcoidosis, alopecia areata (selected)

## Dose & formulations
- Short courses: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 1–3 weeks, then taper
- Give as a single morning dose (mimics normal cortisol rhythm, less HPA suppression); divided doses for severe disease
- Alternate-day dosing for maintenance reduces HPA suppression and side effects
- Taper slowly once disease is controlled; below physiological dose (about 5–7.5 mg/day) taper more slowly
- Courses under 2–3 weeks can usually be stopped without taper

## Adverse effects
- Metabolic: hyperglycaemia/steroid diabetes, weight gain, Cushingoid features, hyperlipidaemia, hypokalaemia
- Bone: osteoporosis and fractures, avascular necrosis of femoral head, growth retardation in children
- Eye: posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma
- GI: peptic ulcer (mainly with NSAIDs), pancreatitis
- CNS: insomnia, mood change, psychosis
- Infections (TB reactivation, strongyloides hyperinfection, opportunistic); poor wound healing
- HPA axis suppression and adrenal crisis on sudden withdrawal
- Skin: striae, atrophy, purpura, steroid acne, hirsutism, delayed healing
- Hypertension, fluid retention; myopathy (proximal)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: systemic fungal infection, herpes simplex keratitis, hypersensitivity
- Relative: active TB, uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension, peptic ulcer, osteoporosis, psychosis, recent live vaccines, pregnancy (prefer lowest dose)

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) lower steroid levels — dose may need doubling
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) raise levels
- NSAIDs: GI ulcer risk
- Diuretics/amphotericin B: hypokalaemia
- Live vaccines: avoid with immunosuppressive doses

## Monitoring
- Baseline: weight, BP, glucose, lipids, electrolytes, eye exam, TB screen, bone density (if long-term), stool for strongyloides in endemic areas
- Follow-up: BP, weight, glucose, electrolytes regularly; eye exam every 6–12 months; bone density annually if long-term
- Prevention: calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonate if long-term (≥3 months, ≥7.5 mg/day), PPI if ulcer risk, deworming (albendazole) in endemic areas

## Pregnancy & lactation
Prednisolone is mostly inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2, so it is the preferred steroid in pregnancy; slight risk of cleft palate with first-trimester use and growth restriction with high doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Know the equivalence table
- Morning single dose; alternate-day dosing to spare the HPA axis
- Prophylaxis for long-term use: calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate, PPI if needed, deworming
- Prednisone is a prodrug; prednisolone is active (use in liver disease)
- Placenta inactivates prednisolone — preferred in pregnancy (dexamethasone and betamethasone cross)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13 (Systemic corticosteroids); Khopkar ch.8 (Oral and injectable steroids), Table 8.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pregabalin + Nortriptyline
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Fixed-dose combination: gabapentinoid (pregabalin) + tricyclic antidepressant (nortriptyline)
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Fixed-dose combination: gabapentinoid (pregabalin) + tricyclic antidepressant (nortriptyline)

## Mechanism of action
- Pregabalin binds the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in nerve endings → less release of glutamate, substance P and noradrenaline → reduces neuropathic pain and neuropathic itch
- Nortriptyline (secondary-amine TCA, metabolite of amitriptyline) blocks reuptake of noradrenaline (and serotonin) → strengthens descending pain-inhibiting pathways; fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline
- The two act at different points, so lower doses of each can be used

## Pharmacokinetics
- Pregabalin: well absorbed, not metabolised, excreted by kidneys — reduce in renal impairment; no CYP interactions
- Nortriptyline: metabolised by CYP2D6; long half-life (about 30 h)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN)
- Neuropathic itch: brachioradial pruritus, notalgia paraesthetica, post-zoster itch, scalp dysaesthesia
- Leprosy neuritis-related neuropathic pain, diabetic neuropathy
- Pregabalin alone: uraemic pruritus, chronic prurigo, burning mouth (adjunct)

## Dose & formulations
- Common Indian FDC: pregabalin 75 mg + nortriptyline 10 mg, one tablet at bedtime; may increase to twice daily
- Pregabalin alone: start 75 mg twice daily (or 75 mg at night), up to 150–300 mg/day (max 600 mg/day); halve in renal impairment
- Start low and go slow in the elderly; taper slowly when stopping

## Adverse effects
- Pregabalin: dizziness, drowsiness, weight gain, peripheral oedema, blurred vision; misuse and dependence potential; withdrawal on abrupt stop
- Nortriptyline: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, postural hypotension, sedation
- Nortriptyline: arrhythmias and QT prolongation; overdose is dangerous (cardiotoxic)
- Suicidal thoughts (antidepressant class warning)

## Contraindications
- Recent myocardial infarction, heart block or arrhythmia (TCA)
- Use of MAO inhibitors within 14 days
- Narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, severe liver disease
- Caution: elderly (falls), renal impairment, history of substance misuse, suicidal risk

## Drug interactions
- Other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines): more sedation and respiratory depression
- SSRIs, tramadol, linezolid with TCA: serotonin syndrome
- CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, terbinafine) raise nortriptyline levels
- Other QT-prolonging and anticholinergic drugs

## Monitoring
- ECG before starting in patients over 40–50 or with cardiac history
- Renal function for pregabalin dosing; mood and suicidal ideation; weight

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in pregnancy unless clearly needed (possible malformation signal with pregabalin; TCA neonatal withdrawal). Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Pregabalin: α2δ calcium-channel ligand
- Nortriptyline: fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline
- Terbinafine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) raises nortriptyline levels
- Used for PHN and neuropathic itch

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.35 (Psychotropic agents) and ch.39 (Drugs for the skinternist; pregabalin); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Promethazine
posts.summary: Antihistamines · First-generation H1 antihistamine — phenothiazine
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antihistamines_

**Class:** First-generation H1 antihistamine — phenothiazine

## Mechanism of action
- H1 inverse agonist with strong anticholinergic, sedative, antiemetic and anti-dopaminergic effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Night-time itch and sedation, allergic reactions, motion sickness, nausea, pre-medication

## Dose & formulations
- Adults 10–25 mg at night (up to 25 mg three times daily); injection 25 mg deep IM

## Adverse effects
- Marked sedation; respiratory depression in children under 2 (boxed warning — contraindicated)
- Photosensitivity and photoallergy (phenothiazine), contact dermatitis with topical use
- Extrapyramidal reactions, QT prolongation; severe tissue injury/gangrene with intra-arterial or perivascular injection

## Contraindications
- Children under 2 years; intra-arterial or SC injection

## Drug interactions
- CNS depressants, other anticholinergics, QT drugs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Has been used; avoid near term (neonatal effects).

## Viva points
- Phenothiazine antihistamine — photosensitivity; contraindicated under 2 years

_Sources: Khopkar (First generation H1 antihistamines); Wolverton 4e ch.32. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Propranolol
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Non-selective β-adrenergic blocker
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Non-selective β-adrenergic blocker

## Mechanism of action
- In infantile haemangioma: early vasoconstriction (lighter colour, softer within days), then inhibition of angiogenic signals (VEGF, bFGF) and induction of apoptosis of endothelial cells
- Also blocks the renin–angiotensin system in haemangioma tissue

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; large first-pass metabolism; lipophilic (crosses BBB); half-life 3–6 h
- Hypoglycaemia risk: blocks glycogenolysis and masks its warning signs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Infantile haemangioma — first-line systemic therapy: ulcerated, function-threatening (eye, airway, ear), disfiguring (face, nose, lip), segmental (PHACE), or multiple with liver involvement
- Best started early (proliferative phase, ideally before 5 months of age)
- Off-label: performance anxiety, rosacea flushing, essential tremor

## Dose & formulations
- Infantile haemangioma: start 0.5–1 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses, increase over 1–2 weeks to 2–3 mg/kg/day (Wolverton: 1–3 mg/kg/day divided twice or three times daily)
- Give with or just after feeds (avoid hypoglycaemia); stop during illness or poor feeding
- Continue for at least 6 months (often until 12 months of age), then taper
- Oral solution 20 mg/5 mL or 40 mg/5 mL; in India often prepared from tablets

## Adverse effects
- Hypoglycaemia (especially with poor feeding or vomiting) — the most important in infants
- Bradycardia, hypotension
- Bronchospasm/wheeze
- Sleep disturbance, cold hands and feet, GI upset
- Rebound growth of haemangioma after stopping

## Contraindications
- Cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia, heart block above first degree, heart failure
- Bronchial asthma or bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia tendency
- Premature infants under 5 weeks corrected age, weight under 2 kg (caution)
- PHACE syndrome with significant brain vessel abnormalities — careful assessment before starting (stroke risk)

## Drug interactions
- Other antihypertensives and calcium-channel blockers (verapamil — bradycardia)
- Insulin and oral hypoglycaemics (masking of hypoglycaemia)
- CYP2D6 inhibitors raise levels

## Monitoring
- Baseline: history and examination of heart and lungs, heart rate and BP; ECG if bradycardia or family history of arrhythmia
- Heart rate and BP 1–2 h after the first dose and after each dose increase
- Counsel parents on hypoglycaemia signs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy for maternal indications (may cause fetal growth restriction and neonatal bradycardia/hypoglycaemia). Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- First-line systemic treatment for problematic infantile haemangioma
- Give with feeds — hypoglycaemia is the main risk
- Check heart rate and BP after starting and after dose increases
- Screen for PHACE syndrome in large segmental facial haemangiomas

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.70 (Dermatologic drug therapy in children), ; Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pyrazinamide (PZA)
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Nicotinamide analogue; first-line antituberculous drug
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Nicotinamide analogue; first-line antituberculous drug

## Mechanism of action
- Prodrug converted by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase to pyrazinoic acid, which is active in acidic environments (inside macrophages and caseous lesions)
- Disrupts membrane energy and trans-translation → kills semi-dormant bacilli — key to the 6-month short-course regimen

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intensive phase of TB treatment (first 2 months), including cutaneous TB
- Not effective against M. bovis (naturally resistant) — relevant for BCG complications

## Dose & formulations
- 25 mg/kg/day (range 20–30) in fixed-dose combinations

## Adverse effects
- Hepatotoxicity (dose-related) — the most hepatotoxic first-line drug at high doses
- Hyperuricaemia and gout (inhibits urate excretion); arthralgia
- Photosensitivity, rash, pruritus; GI upset

## Contraindications
- Severe liver disease; acute gout

## Drug interactions
- Antagonises probenecid and allopurinol (raises uric acid)

## Monitoring
- LFT; uric acid if joint symptoms

## Pregnancy & lactation
WHO recommends its use in pregnancy (US guidance more cautious).

## Viva points
- Works in acid pH — kills intracellular, semi-dormant bacilli
- Hyperuricaemia; M. bovis/BCG is naturally resistant

_Sources: Khopkar ch.7; Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Regimens for atypical (non-tuberculous) mycobacterial infections
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Treatment of cutaneous infections by non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Treatment of cutaneous infections by non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM)

## Mechanism of action
- NTM are naturally resistant to many first-line TB drugs; therapy is based on species and, for rapid growers, on sensitivity testing

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- M. marinum (fish tank/swimming pool granuloma): clarithromycin + ethambutol (or rifampicin), or minocycline/doxycycline or co-trimoxazole alone for limited disease — continue 1–2 months after lesions resolve (usually 3–4 months total)
- Rapid growers (M. fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. abscessus — post-injection/post-procedure abscesses): clarithromycin plus another drug by sensitivity (amikacin, ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin, linezolid, cefoxitin, imipenem) for 4–6 months; surgical debridement
- M. ulcerans (Buruli ulcer): rifampicin + clarithromycin for 8 weeks (WHO), surgery/grafting as needed
- M. avium complex: clarithromycin/azithromycin + ethambutol + rifampicin
- M. kansasii: rifampicin + ethambutol + isoniazid/macrolide

## Dose & formulations
- Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily; ethambutol 15 mg/kg/day; rifampicin 10 mg/kg/day; minocycline/doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily

## Adverse effects
- See component drugs; long courses need monitoring of liver, blood counts, vision (ethambutol), hearing (amikacin)

## Contraindications
- See component drugs

## Monitoring
- Culture and sensitivity for rapid growers; clinical response; drug toxicity monitoring

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid tetracyclines and aminoglycosides; macrolides with care.

## Viva points
- M. marinum — sporotrichoid spread on the hand; clarithromycin + ethambutol
- Rapid growers after injections/cosmetic procedures — clarithromycin-based combination by sensitivity
- Buruli ulcer — rifampicin + clarithromycin 8 weeks

_Sources: Khopkar ch.7 (Table 7.2, regimens for atypical mycobacterial infections); Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Resorcinol
posts.summary: Chemical agents, peels & baths · Phenolic keratolytic, antiseptic and peeling agent
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths_

**Class:** Phenolic keratolytic, antiseptic and peeling agent

## Mechanism of action
- Keratolytic (breaks keratin hydrogen bonds), antibacterial and antifungal

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne (2% with sulphur), seborrhoeic dermatitis, component of Jessner's solution and Castellani's paint, Unna's paste (resorcinol paste peel)

## Dose & formulations
- 1–2% creams/lotions; 14% in Jessner's

## Adverse effects
- Contact dermatitis, brown-black discolouration of light hair, exogenous ochronosis; myxoedema with chronic large-area use (antithyroid), methaemoglobinaemia in infants

## Contraindications
- Infants, large areas, broken skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid large areas.

## Viva points
- Antithyroid effect with chronic absorption; component of Jessner's solution

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Resorcinol). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Rifampicin
posts.summary: Antileprosy drugs · Rifamycin (semisynthetic antibiotic); antileprosy and antituberculous
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** Rifamycin (semisynthetic antibiotic); antileprosy and antituberculous

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (β-subunit, rpoB gene) → no RNA synthesis → bactericidal
- Most potent bactericidal drug against M. leprae — a single 600 mg dose kills over 99.9% of viable bacilli
- Resistance from rpoB mutations — never used as monotherapy

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed on an empty stomach; widely distributed (CSF, tissues, secretions)
- Metabolised in the liver; excreted in bile (enterohepatic circulation)
- Potent inducer of CYP3A4, 2C9, 2C19 and P-gp — induces its own metabolism

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Leprosy: part of MDT (monthly supervised dose); single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts
- Tuberculosis including cutaneous TB (HRZE regimen)
- Atypical mycobacteria (M. marinum, M. ulcerans), rhinoscleroma, cutaneous leishmaniasis (limited)
- Hidradenitis suppurativa: clindamycin 300 mg + rifampicin 300 mg twice daily for 10–12 weeks
- Recurrent staphylococcal furunculosis (decolonisation, with another antibiotic)
- Pruritus of cholestasis (pregnancy excluded), brucellosis

## Dose & formulations
- Leprosy MDT: 600 mg once a month (supervised); children 10–14 years 450 mg; under 10 years 10 mg/kg
- TB: 10 mg/kg/day (max 600 mg) in fixed-dose combinations
- Take on an empty stomach (1 h before or 2 h after food)

## Adverse effects
- Orange-red discolouration of urine, sweat, tears (stains soft contact lenses)
- Hepatotoxicity (more with isoniazid and in alcoholics)
- Intermittent dosing: 'flu-like syndrome', thrombocytopenia, haemolytic anaemia, acute renal failure (immune-mediated)
- Rash, pruritus, flushing; rarely SJS/TEN, DRESS

## Contraindications
- Jaundice; hypersensitivity
- Concurrent protease inhibitors (except with rifabutin substitution) and some other ART

## Drug interactions
- Powerful enzyme inducer — reduces levels of: oral contraceptives (use another method), corticosteroids (double steroid dose in lepra reactions/ENL), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azoles (itraconazole, voriconazole), warfarin, sulfonylureas, methadone, digoxin, dapsone, PIs, nevirapine, dolutegravir (needs 50 mg twice daily)
- Hepatotoxicity increased with isoniazid, pyrazinamide, alcohol

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline and if symptoms; CBC on intermittent dosing
- Review all co-prescribed drugs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy for leprosy and TB; vitamin K to the newborn (risk of haemorrhagic disease) when given in late pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Single monthly dose kills >99.9% of M. leprae
- Enzyme inducer — OCP failure and need to double steroid dose
- Orange-red body fluids
- Flu-like syndrome with intermittent dosing

_Sources: Khopkar ch.6 and ch.7; Wolverton 4e ch.9 (rifamycins) and ch.66 (Drug interactions). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ritonavir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · HIV protease inhibitor (PI); used today mainly as a pharmacokinetic booster
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** HIV protease inhibitor (PI); used today mainly as a pharmacokinetic booster

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits HIV protease, which cleaves the gag-pol polyprotein → immature, non-infectious virus particles
- At low dose (100 mg) it strongly inhibits CYP3A4 (and P-gp), so it is used to 'boost' levels of other PIs (lopinavir, atazanavir, darunavir)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Take with food; metabolised by CYP3A4 (and also induces some enzymes such as glucuronidation, CYP1A2, 2C9 and 2C19)
- Highly protein bound

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Booster in second-line ART: lopinavir/ritonavir 400/100 mg twice daily, atazanavir/ritonavir 300/100 mg once daily, darunavir/ritonavir
- Full-dose ritonavir as the only PI is no longer used because of poor tolerance

## Dose & formulations
- Booster dose: 100 mg once or twice daily with the partner PI
- Heat-stable tablet formulations; take with food

## Adverse effects
- GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; altered taste; perioral and peripheral paraesthesia
- Metabolic: hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, insulin resistance
- Lipodystrophy: central fat gain (buffalo hump, increased abdominal fat) with peripheral lipoatrophy
- Hepatitis, pancreatitis; PR/QT prolongation

## Contraindications
- Co-administration with CYP3A4 substrates that are dangerous at high levels: simvastatin, lovastatin, midazolam (oral), pimozide, ergot alkaloids, amiodarone, sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension, colchicine in renal/liver impairment

## Drug interactions
- Dermatology-relevant: inhaled, intranasal or injected corticosteroids (fluticasone, budesonide, intralesional or intra-articular triamcinolone) → iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and adrenal suppression
- Raises cyclosporine, tacrolimus, colchicine (fatal toxicity reported), itraconazole and some antihistamines
- Lowers oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol) levels and voriconazole levels
- Rifampicin lowers PI levels — avoid

## Monitoring
- Lipids and glucose; LFT
- Review all co-prescribed drugs, including steroid injections and creams over large areas

## Pregnancy & lactation
Boosted PIs (e.g. atazanavir/ritonavir, lopinavir/ritonavir) are used in pregnancy when needed.

## Viva points
- Ritonavir is mostly a 'booster' through CYP3A4 inhibition
- Triamcinolone injection or inhaled fluticasone with ritonavir → Cushing syndrome
- PI-related lipodystrophy and dyslipidaemia

## Note on sources
Wolverton gives little detail on ART; Khopkar and NACO used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4; Wolverton 4e ch.11 and ch.66 (Drug interactions); check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Roxithromycin
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Semisynthetic 14-membered macrolide
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Semisynthetic 14-membered macrolide

## Mechanism of action
- 50S ribosomal inhibitor (like erythromycin); acid-stable

## Pharmacokinetics
- Better absorbed and longer acting than erythromycin (half-life about 12 h); less CYP3A4 inhibition

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Skin and soft-tissue infections, impetigo, folliculitis in penicillin allergy
- Acne (alternative), NGU/chlamydia (older regimens)

## Dose & formulations
- 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg once daily before food; children 5–8 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- GI upset (less than erythromycin), rash, raised LFT, QT prolongation (rare)

## Contraindications
- Macrolide allergy; with ergot alkaloids

## Drug interactions
- Weaker CYP3A4 inhibition than erythromycin; caution with QT drugs, theophylline, warfarin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; erythromycin or azithromycin preferred.

## Viva points
- Acid-stable erythromycin analogue with twice-daily dosing and fewer GI effects

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Roxithromycin, Table 1.7); Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Salicylic acid (6% ointment, paint)
posts.summary: VI Keratolytics & emollients · β-hydroxy acid; keratolytic (desmolytic) agent
posts.body:
_Topicals · VI Keratolytics & emollients_

**Class:** β-hydroxy acid; keratolytic (desmolytic) agent

## Mechanism of action
- Dissolves the intercellular cement (desmosomes) between corneocytes, so scale sheds — 'desmolytic' rather than true keratolytic
- Lipophilic — penetrates the pilosebaceous unit (comedolytic)
- Mild antibacterial/antifungal; enhances penetration of other topicals

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- 3–6%: psoriasis plaques and scalp, ichthyosis, palmoplantar keratoderma, seborrhoeic dermatitis (shampoo), hyperkeratotic eczema
- 0.5–2%: acne washes and gels (comedolytic)
- Salicylic acid paint/collodion (10–20% with lactic acid): common and plantar warts, corns, calluses
- 40% plaster: corns, plantar warts
- 20–30% peels: acne, PIH (see chemical peels)

## Dose & formulations
- 6% ointment/cream: once or twice daily to thick scaly areas
- Wart paint: soak wart, pare, apply daily to the wart only (protect surrounding skin with petroleum jelly), for up to 12 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Irritation, peeling, stinging
- Salicylism (salicylate toxicity) with use over large areas, high concentrations, broken skin, children, renal impairment: nausea, tinnitus, hyperventilation, confusion, metabolic acidosis
- Ulceration of normal skin around warts

## Contraindications
- Children under 2 years; large areas (over about 20% BSA) in children
- Diabetics and peripheral vascular disease (wart paints on feet — ulceration risk)
- Aspirin allergy (relative); renal impairment

## Drug interactions
- Methotrexate, sulfonylureas, warfarin — absorbed salicylate can increase their effects

## Pregnancy & lactation
Small areas acceptable; avoid large-area or high-concentration use.

## Viva points
- Desmolytic — dissolves the cement between cells
- Salicylism in children treated over large areas
- Avoid wart paints on diabetic feet

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.55 (Agents used for hyperkeratosis); Khopkar ch.27 (Moisturizers and keratolytic agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Second-line & newer antituberculous agents
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Drugs for drug-resistant TB and intolerance (ethionamide, cycloserine, PAS, injectable agents, fluoroquinolones, thiacetazone, newer dru
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Drugs for drug-resistant TB and intolerance (ethionamide, cycloserine, PAS, injectable agents, fluoroquinolones, thiacetazone, newer drugs)

## Mechanism of action
- Ethionamide/prothionamide: inhibit InhA (mycolic acid synthesis)
- Cycloserine: inhibits cell-wall peptidoglycan synthesis (D-alanine analogue)
- Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS): folate antagonist
- Injectables (kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin): protein synthesis inhibitors
- Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): DNA gyrase inhibitors — backbone of MDR regimens
- Thiacetazone: older cheap drug, now abandoned
- Newer drugs (bedaquiline, delamanid, pretomanid, linezolid) now replace injectables in MDR-TB

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- MDR/RR-TB and XDR-TB (including cutaneous forms) under the national programme
- Atypical mycobacterial infections (amikacin, clarithromycin, fluoroquinolones)

## Dose & formulations
- As per NTEP drug-resistant TB guidelines (e.g. bedaquiline-pretomanid-linezolid-moxifloxacin, BPaLM, 6 months)

## Adverse effects
- Ethionamide: GI upset, hepatitis, hypothyroidism, gynaecomastia, alopecia, acne
- Cycloserine: psychosis, depression, seizures
- PAS: GI upset, hypothyroidism, lichenoid rash
- Injectables: ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity
- Thiacetazone: severe SJS/TEN, especially in HIV — the reason it was abandoned
- Bedaquiline/clofazimine/fluoroquinolones: QT prolongation; linezolid: myelosuppression, neuropathy

## Contraindications
- Thiacetazone in HIV (never use)

## Monitoring
- ECG (QT), CBC, LFT, thyroid, audiometry (injectables), psychiatric review (cycloserine)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Specialist decision; avoid injectables (ototoxic).

## Viva points
- Thiacetazone → SJS/TEN in HIV
- Ethionamide → hypothyroidism, gynaecomastia
- MDR-TB now treated with all-oral bedaquiline-based regimens

_Sources: Khopkar ch.7 (Second-line and newer antituberculous agents); NTEP/WHO drug-resistant TB guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Selenium (oral)
posts.summary: Vitamins & trace elements · Trace element (antioxidant; component of glutathione peroxidase)
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Vitamins & trace elements_

**Class:** Trace element (antioxidant; component of glutathione peroxidase)

## Mechanism of action
- Part of selenoproteins (glutathione peroxidase, thioredoxin reductase) that protect against oxidative/UV damage

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Selenium deficiency (long-term parenteral nutrition, Keshan disease): leuconychia, hair and skin hypopigmentation, cardiomyopathy
- Adjunct antioxidant in vitiligo, psoriasis, polymorphous light eruption (limited evidence)
- Thyroid eye disease (mild — selenium 100 µg twice daily)

## Dose & formulations
- 50–200 µg/day (do not exceed 400 µg/day)

## Adverse effects
- Selenosis (excess): garlic breath, brittle nails and hair loss, skin rash, neuropathy; possible higher diabetes and skin cancer risk with long-term supplements

## Contraindications
- Excess intake

## Pregnancy & lactation
Dietary amounts safe.

## Viva points
- Selenosis — garlic breath, nail and hair loss
- Do not confuse with selenium sulfide shampoo

_Sources: Khopkar (Trace elements — selenium). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Selenium sulfide shampoo (1–2.5%)
posts.summary: X Hair & scalp agents · Inorganic sulfide; cytostatic and antifungal
posts.body:
_Topicals · X Hair & scalp agents_

**Class:** Inorganic sulfide; cytostatic and antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Cytostatic — reduces epidermal (keratinocyte) turnover, so less scale
- Antifungal against Malassezia (sporicidal)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pityriasis versicolor (2.5% as a body lotion/shampoo)
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff
- Tinea capitis (adjunct, 2.5% twice weekly — reduces spore shedding and transmission)

## Dose & formulations
- Pityriasis versicolor: apply 2.5% to affected skin for 10 min daily for 7 days (or overnight once weekly), then monthly for prevention
- Scalp: leave 2–3 min, rinse; twice weekly for 2 weeks, then weekly

## Adverse effects
- Irritation (avoid broken skin, genitals), unpleasant smell
- Oily scalp, hair discolouration (orange tinge on grey/dyed hair), hair loss (rare)
- Absorption from broken skin can be toxic

## Contraindications
- Broken or inflamed skin; genital area

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid large-area use in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Cytostatic + antifungal
- Used in tinea capitis to reduce spore shedding (adjunct to oral therapy)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.51; Khopkar ch.19 and ch.28. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Sertaconazole 2% (cream, lotion)
posts.summary: I Antifungals — Azoles · Imidazole with a benzothiophene ring
posts.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole with a benzothiophene ring

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits 14-α-demethylase (fungistatic)
- The benzothiophene ring mimics tryptophan and is inserted into the fungal membrane, making pores → direct fungicidal effect
- Also antibacterial (Gram-positive), anti-inflammatory and antipruritic (inhibits cytokines, activates p38–COX-2–PGE2 pathway)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea pedis (interdigital) — approved in the USA; tinea corporis/cruris
- Cutaneous candidiasis, pityriasis versicolor, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Lotion for hairy areas, scalp and large areas

## Dose & formulations
- Twice daily for 4 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Contact dermatitis, burning, dryness (uncommon)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to imidazoles

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; use if needed.

## Viva points
- Fungistatic + fungicidal (benzothiophene ring)
- Antipruritic and anti-inflammatory — useful in itchy tinea

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42 (azoles — sertaconazole); Khopkar ch.19. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Silver nitrate (0.5% compress; 75% caustic stick)
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Silver salt — antiseptic, astringent, caustic
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Silver salt — antiseptic, astringent, caustic

## Mechanism of action
- Silver ions precipitate proteins → antiseptic and astringent at low concentration, caustic (chemical cautery) at high concentration

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Stick: haemostasis after shave/punch biopsy, excess granulation tissue (hypergranulation), pyogenic granuloma (small), umbilical granuloma, warts (adjunct)
- 0.5% solution: wet dressings for burns and weeping lesions; ophthalmia neonatorum prophylaxis (historic, 1%)

## Dose & formulations
- Touch the moistened stick to the area for a few seconds; protect surrounding skin

## Adverse effects
- Black/brown staining of skin (silver deposition), local pain, argyria with chronic use; hyponatraemia with large-area wet dressings

## Contraindications
- Large areas; eyes (stick)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Chemical haemostasis and hypergranulation; black staining

_Sources: Khopkar ch.30 (Silver nitrate) and ch.13 (Topical haemostatic agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Silver sulfadiazine 1% cream
posts.summary: Topical antibacterials & antiseptics · Silver salt of a sulfonamide
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Topical antibacterials & antiseptics_

**Class:** Silver salt of a sulfonamide

## Mechanism of action
- Silver ions bind bacterial DNA and cell membranes; sulfadiazine adds antibacterial action — broad spectrum including Pseudomonas and Candida

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Burns (partial-thickness) — prevents infection
- Infected leg ulcers and wounds (short term)

## Dose & formulations
- Apply 1–3 mm layer once or twice daily with sterile technique

## Adverse effects
- Transient leucopenia (in burns), argyria with prolonged large-area use, pseudoeschar, skin staining
- Sulfonamide hypersensitivity; haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; kernicterus (neonates)

## Contraindications
- Sulfonamide allergy; pregnancy at term, newborns under 2 months; G6PD deficiency (large areas)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid near term.

## Viva points
- Burn wound antimicrobial; leucopenia; avoid in newborns and late pregnancy

_Sources: Khopkar ch.18 and ch.32 (Wound care products); Wolverton 4e ch.54. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Sodium bicarbonate injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · Alkalinising agent (systemic buffer)
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** Alkalinising agent (systemic buffer)

## Mechanism of action
- Bicarbonate combines with hydrogen ions → carbonic acid → CO₂ (breathed out) and water → raises blood pH
- Alkalinises urine; shifts potassium into cells
- In local anaesthesia: raises solution pH so more drug is unionised → faster onset and much less injection pain

## Pharmacokinetics
- Available as 7.5% (≈0.9 mEq/mL) and 8.4% (1 mEq/mL) solutions; hypertonic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Buffering lignocaine before injection (dermatology use): 1 mL 8.4% NaHCO₃ to 10 mL lignocaine (with or without adrenaline)
- Severe metabolic acidosis (e.g. pH below 7.1), hyperkalaemia (adjunct), tricyclic antidepressant overdose (QRS widening)
- Urinary alkalinisation in methotrexate toxicity and salicylate poisoning
- Not given routinely in cardiac arrest

## Dose & formulations
- Buffering: 1 : 10 with lignocaine — use within about a week (adrenaline breaks down faster in alkaline solution); prepare fresh where possible
- Metabolic acidosis: 1 mEq/kg slow IV, then guided by blood gases
- Hyperkalaemia/TCA overdose: 50–100 mEq IV slowly

## Adverse effects
- Metabolic alkalosis, hypernatraemia, fluid overload
- Hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia (tetany)
- Severe tissue necrosis if extravasated (hypertonic)
- Paradoxical CSF acidosis (CO₂ crosses BBB)

## Contraindications
- Metabolic or respiratory alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, chloride loss from vomiting
- Caution: heart failure, renal failure, hypernatraemia

## Drug interactions
- Incompatible with calcium salts and catecholamines in the same line (precipitates/inactivates)
- Alkaline urine increases excretion of salicylates and methotrexate, decreases excretion of amphetamines

## Monitoring
- Arterial blood gas, sodium, potassium, calcium during IV use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use when indicated.

## Viva points
- Buffered lignocaine (1:10) — less pain, faster onset
- Urine alkalinisation in MTX toxicity
- Not routine in CPR

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (buffering local anaesthetics) and ch.14 (MTX toxicity). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Spectinomycin
posts.summary: Other antibacterials · Aminocyclitol antibiotic (related to aminoglycosides)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antibacterials_

**Class:** Aminocyclitol antibiotic (related to aminoglycosides)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds 30S ribosomal subunit → inhibits protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Gonorrhoea (urogenital/anorectal) in patients allergic to cephalosporins or in pregnancy — not effective for pharyngeal gonorrhoea
- Disseminated gonococcal infection (older regimens)

## Dose & formulations
- 2 g IM single dose; DGI 2 g IM daily (older regimens)

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain, urticaria, fever, nausea (uncommon)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe (old FDA category B).

## Viva points
- Gonorrhoea alternative — poor pharyngeal activity; largely unavailable now

_Sources: Khopkar ch.1 (Spectinomycin). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Spinosad 0.9% lotion
posts.summary: III Antiparasitics · Spinosyn insecticide (from fermentation of the soil bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa)
posts.body:
_Topicals · III Antiparasitics_

**Class:** Spinosyn insecticide (from fermentation of the soil bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa)

## Mechanism of action
- Activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the insect nervous system → hyperexcitation, paralysis and death
- Pediculicidal and ovicidal (contains benzyl alcohol) — often one application is enough

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Head lice in patients 6 months and older (FDA)
- Scabies (approved in the USA for age 4 years and older)

## Dose & formulations
- Head lice: cover dry scalp and hair, leave 10 min, rinse; repeat after 7 days only if live lice are seen
- Scabies: apply to the whole body, leave 10 min (label) — check current label

## Adverse effects
- Redness and irritation of scalp and eyes

## Contraindications
- Infants under 6 months (benzyl alcohol — gasping syndrome)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; considered acceptable.

## Viva points
- Ovicidal — nit combing not mandatory
- Benzyl alcohol content — avoid under 6 months

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.44 (spinosad, head lice); not in Khopkar. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Spironolactone
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Aldosterone antagonist (potassium-sparing diuretic) with anti-androgenic activity
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Aldosterone antagonist (potassium-sparing diuretic) with anti-androgenic activity

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks androgen receptors in sebaceous glands and hair follicles; reduces ovarian/adrenal androgen synthesis (inhibits 17α-hydroxylase); increases SHBG

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne in adult women (especially jawline/hormonal, PCOS) — 'off-label first-line hormonal therapy'
- Hirsutism, female pattern hair loss, hidradenitis suppurativa in women

## Dose & formulations
- Acne: 50–100 mg/day (25–200 mg range); hirsutism/FPHL: 100–200 mg/day; results in 3 months
- Often combined with combined oral contraceptives (prevents menstrual irregularity, provides contraception)

## Adverse effects
- Menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, diuresis, dizziness, postural hypotension
- Hyperkalaemia — rare in young healthy women (routine K⁺ checks not needed per recent guidance); check in renal disease, older patients, ACE inhibitor/ARB users
- Gynaecomastia in men (not used for men's acne)
- Animal tumour data (high doses) — not seen in humans

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (feminisation of male fetus), hyperkalaemia, renal failure, Addison disease; men (gynaecomastia)

## Drug interactions
- ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, trimethoprim, NSAIDs (hyperkalaemia); digoxin levels rise

## Monitoring
- Potassium only if risk factors; BP

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated in pregnancy — use with contraception.

## Viva points
- Anti-androgen for female acne and hirsutism
- Routine potassium monitoring not needed in healthy young women
- Pregnancy — feminisation risk

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34 (Antiandrogens); Khopkar (Antiandrogens). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Stanozolol & danazol (attenuated androgens)
posts.summary: Miscellaneous systemic drugs · Synthetic anabolic steroids with fibrinolytic activity
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Miscellaneous systemic drugs_

**Class:** Synthetic anabolic steroids with fibrinolytic activity

## Mechanism of action
- Increase hepatic synthesis of C1-esterase inhibitor (hereditary angioedema prophylaxis)
- Enhance fibrinolysis (stanozolol) — used in lipodermatosclerosis and cryofibrinogenaemia

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Hereditary angioedema long-term prophylaxis (older choice; now C1-INH, lanadelumab, berotralstat preferred)
- Lipodermatosclerosis, livedoid vasculopathy, cryofibrinogenaemia (stanozolol — off-label; withdrawn in many countries)
- Raynaud, chronic urticaria (danazol — limited)

## Dose & formulations
- Stanozolol 2–5 mg twice daily (historic); danazol 200 mg/day (HAE, reduce to lowest effective)

## Adverse effects
- Virilisation in women (hirsutism, acne, voice change), menstrual irregularity
- Hepatotoxicity, peliosis hepatis, hepatic adenoma; dyslipidaemia; fluid retention, hypertension

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, children, liver disease, prostate/breast cancer

## Drug interactions
- Warfarin (INR rises), cyclosporine levels rise

## Monitoring
- LFT, lipids, liver ultrasound (long-term)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated.

## Viva points
- Androgens raise C1-INH levels in hereditary angioedema
- Stanozolol in lipodermatosclerosis (fibrinolytic)

_Sources: Khopkar (Stanozolol); Wolverton 4e ch.40. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Stavudine & didanosine (older NRTIs)
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors — stavudine (d4T, thymidine analogue) and didanosine (ddI, adenosine analogue)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors — stavudine (d4T, thymidine analogue) and didanosine (ddI, adenosine analogue)

## Mechanism of action
- Phosphorylated to triphosphates that terminate HIV DNA chains (mitochondrial DNA polymerase-γ inhibition explains toxicity)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Historical: stavudine-based first-line regimens (D4T/3TC/NVP, D4T/3TC/EFV) were widely used in India; phased out by WHO/NACO because of toxicity
- Important for exams because of their adverse effects

## Dose & formulations
- Stavudine 30 mg twice daily (historic); didanosine 400 mg once daily on an empty stomach (historic)

## Adverse effects
- Stavudine: lipoatrophy (facial and limb fat loss — the classic cause), painful peripheral neuropathy, lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis, pancreatitis
- Didanosine: pancreatitis (can be fatal), peripheral neuropathy, lactic acidosis, non-cirrhotic portal hypertension
- Stavudine + didanosine together: fatal lactic acidosis in pregnancy — never combined

## Contraindications
- Never combine stavudine with zidovudine (antagonism) or with didanosine (toxicity)

## Drug interactions
- Hydroxyurea, ribavirin increase didanosine toxicity; tenofovir raises didanosine levels

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not used now.

## Viva points
- Stavudine → lipoatrophy (facial wasting) and neuropathy — reason for its withdrawal
- Mitochondrial toxicity of 'd-drugs' (d4T, ddI, ddC)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Stavudine, Didanosine; D4T/3TC/NVP regimens); Wolverton 4e ch.11. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: STI kits (NACO colour-coded kits)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Pre-packed syndromic treatment kits supplied free under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACO) — 7 colour-coded kits
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Pre-packed syndromic treatment kits supplied free under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACO) — 7 colour-coded kits

## Mechanism of action
- Syndromic case management: treats all the common organisms that cause a given syndrome at the first visit, without waiting for lab tests
- Each kit is a single complete course, which improves adherence; partners get the same kit

## Pharmacokinetics
- See each component drug (azithromycin, cefixime, secnidazole, fluconazole, benzathine penicillin, doxycycline, acyclovir, metronidazole)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Kit 1 — Grey: urethral discharge, anorectal discharge, cervicitis → azithromycin 1 g single dose + cefixime 400 mg single dose
- Kit 2 — Green: vaginal discharge (vaginitis: trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis, candida) → secnidazole 2 g single dose + fluconazole 150 mg single dose
- Kit 3 — White: genital ulcer disease, non-herpetic (syphilis, chancroid) → benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose (with sterile water and syringe) + azithromycin 1 g single dose
- Kit 4 — Blue: genital ulcer disease, non-herpetic, for penicillin allergy → doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 15 days + azithromycin 1 g single dose
- Kit 5 — Red: genital ulcer disease, herpetic → acyclovir 400 mg three times daily × 7 days
- Kit 6 — Yellow: lower abdominal pain (PID) → cefixime 400 mg single dose + metronidazole 400 mg twice daily × 14 days + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 14 days
- Kit 7 — Black: inguinal bubo (LGV, chancroid) → doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 21 days + azithromycin 1 g single dose

## Dose & formulations
- Given as the full kit to the patient, with an identical kit (or appropriate treatment) for each partner
- Pregnancy: avoid doxycycline kits (blue, black, yellow) — use erythromycin/azithromycin alternatives as per NACO; secnidazole avoided in the first trimester

## Adverse effects
- As for the individual drugs: GI upset (azithromycin, metronidazole, doxycycline), disulfiram-like reaction (metronidazole/secnidazole with alcohol), Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction and anaphylaxis risk (benzathine penicillin), photosensitivity (doxycycline)

## Contraindications
- Kit 3 (white): penicillin allergy → use kit 4 (blue)
- Doxycycline kits in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children under 8
- Avoid alcohol with kits containing metronidazole or secnidazole

## Drug interactions
- See component drugs

## Monitoring
- Follow-up at 7 days (14 days for ulcers and PID) to check response
- Offer HIV and syphilis testing, condoms, partner notification and counselling (the '4 Cs': compliance, counselling, condoms, contact tracing)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Adjust in pregnancy (no doxycycline); syphilis in pregnancy → benzathine penicillin (desensitise if allergic).

## Viva points
- Know each colour and its contents — a favourite viva question
- Grey = urethral discharge; Green = vaginal discharge; White = non-herpetic ulcer; Blue = non-herpetic ulcer with penicillin allergy; Red = herpetic ulcer; Yellow = lower abdominal pain; Black = bubo
- Syndromic approach — treat the patient and partner at the first visit
- 4 Cs of STI management

## Note on sources
The kit contents follow NACO's standard 7-kit scheme. The exam list names 5 colours (white, green, blue, yellow, black), but all 7 are included because grey and red are commonly asked too. Please check against the latest NACO technical guidelines in case your hospital supply differs.

_Sources: NACO National Guidelines on Prevention, Management and Control of RTI including STI (colour-coded kits); not covered in Wolverton or Khopkar. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Streptomycin
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Aminoglycoside antibiotic (first aminoglycoside); injectable antituberculous drug
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Aminoglycoside antibiotic (first aminoglycoside); injectable antituberculous drug

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of mRNA → bactericidal for extracellular bacilli

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- TB (now rarely; previously in retreatment regimens)
- Plague, tularaemia, brucellosis (with doxycycline)
- Donovanosis and mycetoma (historical/alternative regimens)

## Dose & formulations
- 15 mg/kg IM daily (max 1 g; 0.75 g in older patients)

## Adverse effects
- Ototoxicity — mainly vestibular (vertigo, ataxia), also hearing loss
- Nephrotoxicity (less than other aminoglycosides), neuromuscular blockade
- Hypersensitivity rashes, contact dermatitis in health workers handling it

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (fetal deafness), myasthenia gravis, pre-existing hearing/vestibular disease

## Drug interactions
- Other ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs (loop diuretics, vancomycin, amphotericin B)

## Monitoring
- Hearing, balance, renal function

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D — congenital deafness).

## Viva points
- Vestibular toxicity — the classic streptomycin side effect
- Contraindicated in pregnancy

_Sources: Khopkar ch.7; Wolverton 4e ch.9 (aminoglycosides). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Sunscreens (avobenzone, oxybenzone, tinted sunscreens)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Ultraviolet filters: organic (chemical) absorbers and inorganic (physical/mineral) blockers
posts.body:
_Topicals · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Ultraviolet filters: organic (chemical) absorbers and inorganic (physical/mineral) blockers

## Mechanism of action
- Organic filters absorb UV energy and release it as heat
- Avobenzone (butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane): the main UVA1 filter (320–400 nm, peak 357 nm); photo-unstable — needs stabilisers (octocrylene, bemotrizinol)
- Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3): absorbs UVB and UVA2 (broad, up to about 350 nm); the most common photoallergen; concerns about hormone effects and coral reefs
- Inorganic filters (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide) reflect, scatter and absorb UVB and UVA; zinc oxide covers UVA1 better
- Tinted sunscreens contain iron oxides → block visible light (blue light), which worsens melasma and PIH in skin types IV–VI

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Prevention of sunburn, photoageing, actinic keratoses, SCC (proven), melanoma and BCC (supportive data)
- Photodermatoses (PLE, lupus, porphyrias, chronic actinic dermatitis, XP)
- Melasma, PIH, vitiligo (prevent burning and contrast), patients on photosensitising drugs or after procedures

## Dose & formulations
- Broad spectrum, SPF 30 or more (SPF 50+ for photosensitive), UVA rating PA+++ or higher; tinted for melasma
- Amount: 2 mg/cm² (about ½ teaspoon for face and neck; ~30 mL — a 'shot glass' — for the whole adult body); most people apply only a quarter to half of this
- Apply 15–30 min before going out; reapply every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating
- SPF = ratio of MED with sunscreen to MED without (UVB); SPF 15 blocks ~93%, SPF 30 ~97%, SPF 50 ~98% of UVB
- UVA protection measures: PPD/PA rating, critical wavelength ≥370 nm

## Adverse effects
- Irritant dermatitis (stinging, especially around eyes)
- Allergic and photoallergic contact dermatitis (oxybenzone, octocrylene, PABA)
- Acne/comedones with oily formulations; white cast with inorganic filters
- Possible lower vitamin D synthesis (rarely clinically significant)

## Contraindications
- Known allergy to a filter; infants under 6 months — prefer shade and clothing; mineral sunscreen on small areas if needed

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe; mineral sunscreens preferred by some in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Avobenzone = UVA1 filter but photo-unstable
- Oxybenzone = commonest photoallergen
- Iron oxide (tinted) protects against visible light — melasma
- SPF measures UVB; PA/PPD measures UVA; 2 mg/cm²

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.50 (Sunscreens); Khopkar ch.25. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.summary: IX Immunomodulators · Topical calcineurin inhibitor (TCI); macrolide from Streptomyces tsukubaensis
posts.body:
_Topicals · IX Immunomodulators_

**Class:** Topical calcineurin inhibitor (TCI); macrolide from Streptomyces tsukubaensis

## Mechanism of action
- Binds FKBP-12 inside T cells; the complex inhibits calcineurin → NFAT not dephosphorylated → less IL-2, IL-4 and other cytokines
- Also reduces mast-cell and basophil mediator release, and Langerhans cell function
- Does not cause skin atrophy (no effect on collagen synthesis)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Atopic dermatitis (moderate–severe; approved) — face, eyelids, flexures; proactive twice-weekly maintenance
- Vitiligo (face and neck — good response), seborrhoeic dermatitis, intertriginous/facial psoriasis
- Oral and genital lichen planus, cutaneous lupus (facial), steroid-induced rosacea/perioral dermatitis (steroid withdrawal)
- Lichen sclerosus (second line), morphoea, chronic actinic dermatitis

## Dose & formulations
- 0.03%: children 2–15 years (and adults); 0.1%: adults (16 years and older)
- Twice daily until clear, then twice weekly as maintenance
- Off-label use under 2 years is common with 0.03%

## Adverse effects
- Burning, stinging, warmth at application site in the first week (most common; improves)
- Alcohol intolerance (facial flushing after drinking)
- Skin infections: folliculitis, herpes simplex/eczema herpeticum, molluscum, warts
- Boxed warning (FDA 2006) about theoretical malignancy (lymphoma, skin cancer) — long-term studies have not shown a clear increase

## Contraindications
- Immunosuppressed patients, Netherton syndrome (high absorption), active infection at site, malignant/pre-malignant skin lesions
- Children under 2 (label)

## Drug interactions
- Systemic CYP3A4 inhibitors — minimal relevance (low absorption) except with large areas or barrier defects

## Pregnancy & lactation
Minimal absorption; may be used on limited areas if needed.

## Viva points
- Calcineurin inhibitor — no atrophy, so ideal for face and eyelids
- 0.03% for 2–15 years, 0.1% for adults
- Burning sensation and alcohol flushing
- Boxed warning — theoretical malignancy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.48 (Topical calcineurin inhibitors); Khopkar ch.23 (Topical immunomodulators). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Tazarotene 0.1% (gel, cream)
posts.summary: VII Anti-acne — Retinoids · Third-generation acetylenic retinoid (prodrug of tazarotenic acid)
posts.body:
_Topicals · VII Anti-acne — Retinoids_

**Class:** Third-generation acetylenic retinoid (prodrug of tazarotenic acid)

## Mechanism of action
- Tazarotenic acid binds RAR-β and RAR-γ
- Normalises keratinocyte differentiation and proliferation, reduces inflammatory markers (psoriasis); induces tazarotene-induced genes (TIG1–3)
- Comedolytic in acne

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Plaque psoriasis (0.05%/0.1%) — often with a topical steroid to reduce irritation
- Acne vulgaris (0.1%; foam 0.1%; 0.045% lotion)
- Photoageing, nail psoriasis (off-label), congenital ichthyoses, keratosis pilaris

## Dose & formulations
- Thin layer once daily in the evening to lesions only (avoid surrounding skin in psoriasis)
- Short-contact therapy (wash off after 2–5 min, increasing) reduces irritation

## Adverse effects
- Irritation (most irritating topical retinoid): burning, redness, peeling
- Photosensitivity

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (contraindicated — old FDA category X); women must have a negative pregnancy test and use contraception
- Eczematous or sunburnt skin

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated in pregnancy (old FDA category X).

## Viva points
- Only topical retinoid that is pregnancy category X
- Used for both psoriasis and acne
- Most irritating — combine with a steroid or use short contact

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.46; Khopkar ch.24. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: TB regimens for cutaneous tuberculosis
posts.summary: Antituberculous drugs · Standard short-course antituberculous chemotherapy (India NTEP)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antituberculous drugs_

**Class:** Standard short-course antituberculous chemotherapy (India NTEP)

## Mechanism of action
- Combination of bactericidal (H, R, Z) and resistance-preventing (E) drugs
- Intensive phase kills the bulk of bacilli; continuation phase kills persisters

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- All forms of cutaneous TB: lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma, tuberculosis verrucosa cutis, orificial TB, metastatic tuberculous abscess, miliary TB of skin
- Tuberculids (papulonecrotic tuberculid, lichen scrofulosorum, erythema induratum) — when an active TB focus is found or empirically
- Therapeutic trial in suspected cutaneous TB (response in 4–6 weeks supports the diagnosis)

## Dose & formulations
- India NTEP (daily regimen, new patients): intensive phase 2 months HRZE, continuation phase 4 months HRE (ethambutol continued) — total 6 months, fixed-dose combinations by weight band
- Extend continuation phase for extensive/scrofuloderma or slow responders (total 9–12 months, by physician decision)
- Drug-resistant TB: per NTEP drug-resistant guidelines (rapid molecular testing, bedaquiline-based regimens)

## Adverse effects
- Hepatotoxicity (H, R, Z) — commonest reason to interrupt
- Cutaneous drug reactions to ATT are common: morbilliform rash, lichenoid eruptions, DRESS, SJS/TEN — reintroduce drugs one by one after recovery

## Contraindications
- See individual drugs

## Monitoring
- Monthly clinical review; LFT if symptoms or risk; notification to NTEP (Nikshay); HIV test

## Pregnancy & lactation
First-line drugs (HRZE) are used in pregnancy; avoid streptomycin.

## Viva points
- 2HRZE + 4HRE daily (NTEP)
- Therapeutic trial — response by 4–6 weeks
- Reintroduction of ATT after cutaneous reactions

_Sources: India NTEP Technical & Operational Guidelines (daily FDC regimen); Khopkar ch.7; Wolverton 4e ch.9. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Tenofovir & emtricitabine (NRTIs)
posts.summary: Antivirals & ART · Tenofovir: nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (TDF / TAF); emtricitabine: cytidine NRTI (like lamivudine)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antivirals & ART_

**Class:** Tenofovir: nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (TDF / TAF); emtricitabine: cytidine NRTI (like lamivudine)

## Mechanism of action
- Tenofovir (adenosine nucleotide analogue) needs only two phosphorylation steps → tenofovir diphosphate terminates HIV DNA chains; also active against hepatitis B
- Emtricitabine (FTC) is a fluorinated lamivudine analogue — interchangeable with lamivudine in regimens (never together)

## Pharmacokinetics
- TDF (disoproxil fumarate) gives high plasma tenofovir; TAF (alafenamide) concentrates inside cells → lower plasma levels, less kidney and bone toxicity
- Renal excretion

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Backbone of preferred first-line ART in India: TLD = tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg once daily
- Post-exposure prophylaxis (TLD for 28 days)
- Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP): TDF + FTC (or TDF + 3TC) daily for people at high risk
- Chronic hepatitis B (TDF/TAF), including HIV–HBV co-infection

## Dose & formulations
- TDF 300 mg once daily (in FDC); TAF 25 mg; emtricitabine 200 mg once daily

## Adverse effects
- TDF: nephrotoxicity (proximal tubulopathy — Fanconi syndrome, falling GFR), reduced bone mineral density
- GI upset, headache; lactic acidosis (class, rare)
- Hepatitis B flare on stopping
- Emtricitabine: palmoplantar hyperpigmentation (especially in dark skin)

## Contraindications
- TDF: creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min (avoid/adjust) — use abacavir or TAF

## Drug interactions
- Other nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cidofovir, high-dose NSAIDs)
- Didanosine levels rise (avoid)

## Monitoring
- Creatinine/eGFR, urine dipstick (protein, glucose) at baseline and periodically; HBsAg before starting

## Pregnancy & lactation
TDF-based TLD is the recommended regimen in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- TLD = preferred first-line in India
- TDF → kidney and bone; TAF is safer
- Emtricitabine → palmoplantar hyperpigmentation
- Also treats hepatitis B — stopping can cause a flare

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Tenofovir, Emtricitabine); Wolverton 4e ch.11; current NACO ART guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Terbinafine (oral + topical)
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Allylamine antifungal
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Allylamine antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits squalene epoxidase, an early step in ergosterol synthesis
- Toxic build-up of squalene inside the cell → fungicidal against dermatophytes
- Ergosterol deficiency adds a fungistatic effect (mainly against yeasts)

## Pharmacokinetics
- 70–80% absorbed; food does not matter
- Highly lipophilic and keratophilic; reaches the stratum corneum via sebum and the nail via the matrix
- Persists in nails for weeks to months after stopping; long terminal half-life
- Metabolised in the liver; inhibits CYP2D6

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Dermatophytosis: tinea corporis, cruris, pedis and manuum
- Onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes (drug of choice)
- Tinea capitis — especially Trichophyton tonsurans (less effective for Microsporum)
- Some activity in sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis; poor against Candida and Malassezia orally

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 250 mg once daily
- Tinea corporis/cruris: 2–4 weeks (often longer in India due to resistance — follow current national consensus)
- Onychomycosis: fingernails 6 weeks, toenails 12 weeks
- Tinea capitis (children): 10–20 kg 62.5 mg; 21–40 kg 125 mg; over 40 kg 250 mg daily, for 2–6 weeks (T. tonsurans)

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache
- Taste disturbance (can last weeks), loss of smell
- Rash, urticaria; rarely SJS/TEN, AGEP, DRESS
- Induction or worsening of subacute cutaneous lupus; worsening of psoriasis
- Hepatotoxicity — rare but can be severe (cholestatic or hepatitic; liver failure reported)
- Neutropenia, depression (rare)

## Contraindications
- Chronic or active liver disease
- Severe renal impairment (clearance under 50 mL/min — avoid or reduce dose)
- Lupus erythematosus (relative)

## Drug interactions
- CYP2D6 inhibition: raises levels of tricyclic antidepressants, some SSRIs, beta-blockers (metoprolol), codeine activation reduced
- Rifampicin lowers terbinafine levels; cimetidine raises them

## Monitoring
- Baseline LFT (as advised by the label); repeat if courses exceed 6 weeks or symptoms of liver injury
- CBC if course exceeds 6 weeks

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category B, but because it is not urgent, treatment of onychomycosis is postponed until after pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- The only commonly used oral antifungal that is fungicidal
- Squalene epoxidase inhibition — not CYP450 dependent
- Inhibits CYP2D6, not CYP3A4 (unlike azoles)
- Squalene epoxidase gene mutations explain terbinafine resistance in T. indotineae seen in India

## Topical form: Terbinafine 1% cream
_Allylamine (topical)_

**Mechanism**
- Squalene epoxidase inhibitor — fungicidal against dermatophytes; persists in stratum corneum

**Indications**
- Tinea corporis, cruris, pedis (including interdigital), pityriasis versicolor (solution/spray)
- Less effective for cutaneous candidiasis than azoles

**Dose & how to apply**
- Once or twice daily for 1–2 weeks (tinea pedis 1 week interdigital; continue 1–2 weeks after clearing in recurrent disease)

**Adverse effects**
- Burning, itching, irritation; rare contact dermatitis

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity

**Pregnancy:** Safe (minimal absorption).

**Viva points**
- Fungicidal topical — shorter courses than azoles for dermatophytes

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10, Table 10.5; Khopkar ch.2; Khopkar ch.19; Wolverton 4e ch.42. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Thalidomide
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Glutamic acid derivative; immunomodulatory drug (IMiD)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Glutamic acid derivative; immunomodulatory drug (IMiD)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds cereblon (part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase), changing which proteins are degraded
- Reduces TNF-α production (by speeding TNF mRNA breakdown); shifts Th1 responses
- Anti-angiogenic (explains teratogenicity — limb defects) and sedative

## Pharmacokinetics
- Slowly absorbed; half-life about 5–7 h
- Broken down mainly by non-enzymatic hydrolysis — few CYP interactions

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) — drug of choice for severe/recurrent ENL
- Cutaneous lupus (refractory discoid/subacute), Behçet disease and aphthous ulcers (especially HIV)
- Prurigo nodularis, actinic prurigo, Jessner lymphocytic infiltrate, sarcoidosis, graft-versus-host disease
- Multiple myeloma (oncology)

## Dose & formulations
- ENL: 100–400 mg/day at bedtime (start 100 mg; higher doses split), taper to the lowest effective dose (e.g. 50–100 mg) once controlled
- Lupus, prurigo, aphthae: 50–100 mg/day at night
- Capsules 50, 100 mg

## Adverse effects
- Teratogenic — phocomelia and other limb, ear, heart, GI defects even after a single dose in early pregnancy (days 20–36 after conception)
- Peripheral neuropathy (sensory, often irreversible; dose- and duration-related)
- Sedation, dizziness, constipation, oedema
- Venous thromboembolism (especially with steroids or chemotherapy)
- Rash, bradycardia, neutropenia, hypothyroidism

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and women unable to use reliable contraception
- Existing peripheral neuropathy; breastfeeding

## Drug interactions
- CNS depressants (alcohol, sedatives): more sedation
- Drugs causing neuropathy (dapsone, metronidazole, isoniazid): more neuropathy
- Drugs raising clot risk (oral contraceptives, steroids)

## Monitoring
- Pregnancy tests before, weekly in the first month, then monthly
- Baseline and periodic nerve conduction studies or clinical sensory examination
- Watch for signs of thrombosis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Women: two contraceptive methods from 4 weeks before until 4 weeks after. Men must use condoms (drug is present in semen) during treatment and for 4 weeks after. Restricted-distribution programme in many countries.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for severe ENL
- Teratogenicity — phocomelia; sensitive period days 20–36 after conception
- Peripheral neuropathy — monitor
- Mechanism: cereblon binding, TNF-α reduction, anti-angiogenesis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40 (Miscellaneous systemic drugs); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Therapeutic baths (oatmeal, oil, KMnO₄, bleach, tar, PUVA)
posts.summary: Chemical agents, peels & baths · Bath additives used as adjunct therapy
posts.category: More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Chemical agents, peels & baths_

**Class:** Bath additives used as adjunct therapy

## Mechanism of action
- Hydrate and soften scale, remove crusts and exudate, reduce bacterial load, soothe itch; allow treatment of large body surfaces

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Colloidal oatmeal bath: itch of atopic dermatitis, varicella, urticaria (anti-inflammatory avenanthramides)
- Oil baths (emollient bath oils): xerosis, ichthyosis, atopic dermatitis (slippery — fall risk)
- Potassium permanganate bath (1:10,000): weeping/infected eczema, pemphigus, bullous disorders
- Dilute bleach baths: atopic dermatitis with recurrent staphylococcal infections
- Tar baths (Ingram regimen), bath PUVA (trioxsalen/8-MOP), salt (Dead Sea) baths for psoriasis
- Cleansing baths for erosive and blistering diseases; wax bath (paraffin) for joint stiffness in scleroderma hands

## Dose & formulations
- 10–15 min, lukewarm water, followed by emollient within 3 min (soak and seal)

## Adverse effects
- Over-drying with prolonged hot baths; KMnO₄ staining/burns; slipping in oil baths

## Contraindications
- Hot baths in rosacea/urticaria flares (heat aggravates)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe.

## Viva points
- Soak-and-seal; KMnO₄ 1:10,000; bleach bath in AD; Ingram regimen tar baths

_Sources: Khopkar ch.33 (Baths — cleansing, oatmeal, oil, potassium permanganate, wax bath). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Thiabendazole (oral + topical)
posts.summary: Other antiparasitics · Benzimidazole anthelmintic (first of its class)
posts.body:
_More from Khopkar · Other antiparasitics_

**Class:** Benzimidazole anthelmintic (first of its class)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits helminth fumarate reductase and microtubule function; also anti-inflammatory and antipyretic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Topical 10–15% (suspension/cream, compounded, or crushed tablets in petrolatum): cutaneous larva migrans — applied to the track and 2 cm beyond
- Oral: strongyloidiasis, CLM, visceral larva migrans (now replaced by ivermectin/albendazole; oral form withdrawn in many countries)

## Dose & formulations
- Topical: 10–15% three times daily for 5 days (or until track stops progressing)
- Oral (historic): 25 mg/kg twice daily for 2–5 days (max 3 g/day)

## Adverse effects
- Oral: frequent nausea, vomiting, dizziness, foul-smelling urine, hepatotoxicity, SJS/TEN, hallucinations
- Topical: minimal irritation

## Contraindications
- Oral: liver disease, pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Oral: raises theophylline levels

## Pregnancy & lactation
Topical acceptable; avoid oral.

## Viva points
- Topical thiabendazole for localised CLM (useful in children and pregnancy)
- Oral form largely abandoned because of side effects

_Sources: Khopkar ch.5 and ch.21; Wolverton 4e ch.12 and ch.44. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Tofacitinib (oral + 2% ointment)
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor — mainly JAK1 and JAK3 (pan-JAK at higher doses)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor — mainly JAK1 and JAK3 (pan-JAK at higher doses)

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks JAK enzymes that pass on signals from cytokine receptors
- So STAT proteins are not activated, and responses to IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-15, IL-21 and interferons are reduced
- Dampens T-cell, B-cell and NK-cell function

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; half-life about 3 h (twice daily or once-daily extended release)
- Metabolised by CYP3A4 (70%) and kidneys (30%)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Approved: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis
- Off-label in dermatology: alopecia areata, vitiligo (with phototherapy), refractory dermatomyositis, atopic dermatitis, sarcoidosis, lichen planopilaris, psoriasis
- In the Derma Desk ladders it is a later-line option (e.g. alopecia areata, vitiligo)

## Dose & formulations
- 5 mg twice daily (or 11 mg extended release once daily); 10 mg twice daily used in some trials and off-label for alopecia areata
- Reduce to 5 mg once daily with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or moderate–severe renal/hepatic impairment

## Adverse effects
- Infections: upper respiratory, herpes zoster (notable risk), TB reactivation, opportunistic infections
- Boxed warnings (ORAL Surveillance study, patients over 50 with cardiovascular risk): major cardiac events, thrombosis (DVT/PE), malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma), and death
- Raised lipids, LFT and creatine kinase; cytopenias (lymphopenia, neutropenia, anaemia)
- Acne, headache, GI perforation (rare)

## Contraindications
- Active serious infection including TB; severe hepatic impairment
- Lymphocytes under 500/mm³, neutrophils under 1000/mm³, Hb under 9 g/dL
- Pregnancy; caution if over 50 with cardiovascular risk factors or smokers, history of thrombosis or cancer

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole) → reduce dose; inducers (rifampicin) → avoid
- Do not combine with biologics or potent immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine or azathioprine
- Live vaccines — avoid; give recombinant zoster vaccine beforehand

## Monitoring
- Baseline: CBC, LFT, lipids, renal function, TB screen (IGRA), hepatitis B/C, HIV
- CBC and LFT at 4–8 weeks, then every 3 months; lipids at 4–8 weeks
- Skin check; cardiovascular risk review

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (limited data; animal teratogenicity). Stop at least 4 weeks before planned conception. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- JAK-STAT pathway — 'cytokine signal blocker'
- Herpes zoster risk — consider the recombinant zoster vaccine
- Boxed warning from ORAL Surveillance: MACE, thrombosis, malignancy, death
- Oral JAK inhibitor; topical 2% ointment is in the topicals slot

## Topical form: Tofacitinib 2% ointment
_Topical Janus kinase (JAK1/3) inhibitor_

**Mechanism**
- Blocks JAK-STAT signalling of cytokines (IL-2, IL-4, IL-13, IL-15, IFN-γ) in skin
- In vitiligo: reduces IFN-γ–CXCL10 signalling that recruits cytotoxic T cells; in AA: blocks the IFN-γ/IL-15 axis

**Indications**
- Off-label/compounded in India: vitiligo (face), alopecia areata (limited areas), atopic dermatitis, plaque psoriasis (trials)
- Note: ruxolitinib 1.5% cream is the approved topical JAK inhibitor (vitiligo and atopic dermatitis, USA)

**Dose & how to apply**
- Twice daily to limited areas (studies used up to about 10–20% BSA); combine with NB-UVB or sun exposure for vitiligo

**Adverse effects**
- Local irritation, acne, folliculitis
- Theoretical systemic JAK effects with large-area use (labs if used extensively)

**Contraindications**
- Large body areas; active skin infection; pregnancy

**Pregnancy:** Avoid.

**Viva points**
- Topical JAK inhibitors — newer, best results on facial vitiligo
- Ruxolitinib cream is the approved one; tofacitinib topical is mostly compounded/trial use

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.18 (PDE-4 and JAK inhibitors); Khopkar edition predates JAK inhibitors; Wolverton 4e ch.18 (JAK inhibitors — tofacitinib 2% ointment, compounded). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
