posts.title: Radiofrequency vs electrocautery
posts.summary: How RF and cautery differ, modes, pacemaker precautions, steps and plume safety
posts.body:
Both devices remove or coagulate tissue using heat, but they work differently, and choosing the right one matters for safety and cosmesis.

## Principle
- **Radiofrequency (RF)**: high-frequency alternating current (around 4 MHz) passes through the tissue. Cell water heats and vaporises at the electrode tip, giving "cold" cutting with minimal lateral heat damage and less charring.
- **Electrocautery (EC)**: a metal tip is heated by current, and the heat is transferred to tissue by direct contact. No current passes through the patient. It chars more and spreads heat more widely.

## Modes (RF)
- **Cut**: fully filtered current, clean incision with little haemostasis
- **Cut-coag (blend)**: cutting with some haemostasis
- **Coag**: haemostasis, tissue shrinkage
- **Fulguration**: spark gap from the tip held slightly off the skin; superficial destruction

## Indications
- DPN, seborrhoeic keratosis, skin tags, syringoma, small warts
- Shave excision of naevi (benign, for cosmesis) and biopsies
- Haemostasis during minor surgery
- Rhinophyma sculpting, sebaceous hyperplasia, xanthelasma (careful use)

## Contraindications
- Pacemaker or ICD: avoid RF (current can interfere); use EC instead
- Flammable surroundings: alcohol not dried, oxygen in use
- Uncertain diagnosis: biopsy first
- Keloid tendency (relative)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: scab, pigment changes, scar, recurrence
- Ask about pacemaker, implants and metal near the site
- Topical or local anaesthesia
- Let alcohol dry fully; keep oxygen away

## Equipment
- RF unit or EC unit (check your machine's settings — they vary)
- Electrodes: **loop** (shave excision), **ball** (coagulation), **fine needle** (DPN, syringoma)
- Passive (return) plate when required by the manual
- Smoke evacuator and surgical mask
- Saline gauze, antibiotic ointment, sunscreen

## Procedure step by step
1. Consent and mark lesions.
2. Clean with antiseptic and let alcohol dry fully.
3. Give local anaesthetic.
4. Place the passive plate if the machine requires it, close to the site, on dry, hairless skin.
5. Choose the electrode and mode for the lesion.
6. Start at the lowest power; increase until the tissue responds without drag or sparking.
7. Switch on the smoke evacuator; staff and patient wear masks (plume may contain HPV and other particles).
8. Use quick, light strokes; avoid lingering at one spot.
9. Wipe char with saline gauze, then re-check depth.
10. **Endpoint**: lesion removed or flattened, with surrounding skin intact.

## Post-procedure care
- Antibiotic ointment twice daily until healed
- Sunscreen for 4–6 weeks to limit PIH
- Do not pick the scab

## Complications & management
- Burn at plate site: correct plate placement
- PIH or hypopigmentation: sunscreen; lower power
- Scar: avoid deep or repeated passes
- Infection: topical or oral antibiotics
- Fire: never use with wet alcohol or oxygen

## Sessions & follow-up
- Review at 1–2 weeks for healing
- Touch-up at 4–6 weeks as needed

posts.title: Salicylic acid peel
posts.summary: Lipophilic superficial peel for acne, oily skin and PIH; safe in skin types IV–V
posts.body:
Salicylic acid (SA) is a lipophilic beta-hydroxy acid. It dissolves in sebum, so it works well in the follicle and on oily, acne-prone skin. Clinic strength is usually 20–30% in an ethanol base. It is a superficial peel, comedolytic and mildly anti-inflammatory, and among the safest peels for Indian skin.

## Indications
- Comedonal and mild–moderate inflammatory acne
- Post-acne PIH, oily skin, enlarged pores
- Superficial melasma and facial melanoses (adjunct to topical therapy)
- Rough photo-damaged texture, keratosis pilaris (body)

## Contraindications
- Salicylate (aspirin) allergy
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Active infection at the site: herpes labialis, impetigo, warts, open wounds
- Eczema, dermatitis or recent sunburn at the site
- Unrealistic expectations or poor sun-protection compliance
- Large-area peels in renal or hepatic disease (salicylism risk)

## Pre-procedure
- Written consent: expected stinging, dryness, flaking, and possible PIH
- Counsel that 4–6 sessions are needed and results are gradual
- **Priming 2–4 weeks**: broad-spectrum sunscreen + 2–4% hydroquinone or azelaic acid ± tretinoin 0.025% at night
- Stop retinoids and scrubs 3–5 days before; no waxing or threading for 1 week
- Herpes history: start acyclovir/valacyclovir on the day of the peel
- Test patch behind the ear or on the jawline before the first full peel
- Clinical photographs in standard lighting

## Equipment
- SA 20% and 30% solution, gloves, gauze, cotton-tipped applicators
- Cleanser, alcohol or acetone for degreasing
- Petrolatum for the nasal alae, lip commissures and inner canthi
- Hand-held fan, timer, cool water, ice packs

## Procedure step by step
1. Cleanse the face and degrease with alcohol or acetone; let it dry.
2. Protect the eyes; apply petrolatum to the alar creases, commissures and canthi.
3. Apply the first coat quickly and evenly with gauze: forehead, cheeks, nose, chin, then perioral.
4. Expect burning for 1–2 minutes, then a relative numbness from the anaesthetic effect of SA; use the fan.
5. **Endpoint**: an even white crystalline precipitate (pseudofrost) with mild erythema, usually at 3–5 minutes. This is salicylic acid crystallising, not protein coagulation.
6. A second coat can be applied to oily or acne-prone areas in later sessions.
7. Neutralisation is not required (the peel is self-limiting). Wash off with plain water after 3–5 minutes.
8. Apply a bland moisturiser and sunscreen before the patient leaves.

## Post-procedure care
- Gentle cleanser, plain moisturiser, SPF 30+ reapplied every 3 hours outdoors
- Do not pick or peel the flakes; mild flaking lasts 2–4 days
- Restart priming agents after 3–5 days once the skin is calm

## Complications & management
- Excess erythema or burning: cool compresses, mid-potency topical steroid for 2–3 days
- PIH: hydroquinone or azelaic acid, strict photoprotection; space out sessions
- Acneiform flare: usually settles with continued treatment
- Herpes reactivation: treatment-dose antiviral
- Salicylism (tinnitus, nausea, dizziness) with large areas: stop and wash off; avoid body peels over large surfaces

## Sessions & follow-up
- Every 2–3 weeks for 4–6 sessions; start at 20% and step up to 30% if tolerated
- Review the photographs at each visit; continue maintenance topicals between sessions

posts.title: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel
posts.summary: Non-neutralised peel graded by frost; superficial use and TCA CROSS for scars
posts.body:
Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) coagulates epidermal proteins and produces a visible **frost**. Depth depends on concentration, number of coats, how much is applied and how the skin is prepared. It does not need neutralising, and it is not systemically toxic. Concentrations of 10–25% act superficially. At 35% and above it reaches the papillary dermis (medium depth), and in skin types IV–V scarring and PIH become real risks.

## Indications
- Superficial (10–20%): melasma, PIH, lentigines, fine lines, superficial acne scars
- Medium-depth (35%, usually combined with Jessner's or GA): rarely used in Indian skin; consider only after careful selection
- **TCA CROSS** (70–100%, focal): ice-pick and narrow boxcar acne scars
- Focal: xanthelasma, seborrhoeic keratoses (experienced hands only)

## Contraindications
- Active infection or dermatitis at the site, open wounds
- Keloid or hypertrophic scar tendency
- Isotretinoin in the past 6 months (deeper peels)
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Previous radiotherapy at the site, poor wound healing
- Inability to follow sun protection and aftercare

## Pre-procedure
- Written consent: visible peeling for 5–7 days, PIH, scarring and hypopigmentation
- **Priming 2–4 weeks** with tretinoin and hydroquinone; this is essential in skin types IV–V
- Antiviral prophylaxis for perioral and full-face peels
- Test spot with the planned concentration
- Baseline photographs

## Equipment
- Freshly made TCA in the required w/v concentration, in labelled amber bottles
- Cotton-tipped applicators (moist, not dripping), gauze
- For CROSS: wooden toothpick or fine applicator
- Degreaser, petrolatum, cold compresses, fan

## Procedure step by step
1. Cleanse and degrease thoroughly; uneven degreasing gives patchy frost.
2. Protect the eyes; apply petrolatum to the alae, commissures and canthi.
3. Apply TCA one cosmetic unit at a time, with even strokes.
4. Wait 2–3 minutes after each coat; frost develops slowly. Add a further coat only where the frost is short of the target.
5. **Endpoints by frost level**:
- Level I: erythema with scattered speckles of frost (superficial; the usual goal in skin types IV–V)
- Level II: white frost with pink showing through (upper papillary dermis)
- Level III: solid opaque white frost (deeper; avoid in brown skin except focal CROSS)
6. Apply cool compresses for comfort. No neutralisation is needed.
7. **TCA CROSS**: press the sharpened applicator into the base of each pitted scar for a few seconds, until the scar turns white. Do not treat adjacent normal skin.

## Post-procedure care
- Skin darkens and peels on days 3–7; do not pick
- Bland ointment or moisturiser, gentle cleanser, strict photoprotection
- Restart priming agents only after peeling is complete

## Complications & management
- PIH: common in skin types IV–V; hydroquinone, sunscreen, delay further peels
- Persistent erythema beyond 3 weeks: suspect impending scarring and start a potent topical steroid early
- Hypertrophic scarring: intralesional steroid, silicone gel
- Infection (bacterial, candida, herpes): swab and treat promptly
- Hypopigmentation or demarcation lines: feather the edges at the jawline

## Sessions & follow-up
- Superficial TCA every 3–4 weeks for 3–4 sessions
- TCA CROSS every 4–6 weeks for 3–6 sessions
- Review at day 7 after the first peel

posts.title: Whole-body phototherapy (cabin NB-UVB ± PUVA)
posts.summary: Cabin NB-UVB and PUVA: dosing, protection, missed doses, logs, stopping
posts.body:
Whole-body phototherapy treats patients standing in a cabin lined with UV tubes. NB-UVB (311 nm) is first line; PUVA (oral psoralen plus UVA) is reserved for thick or resistant disease. Safe practice depends on careful dosing and record-keeping.

## Indications
- Psoriasis involving more than ~10% body surface area, or resistant to topicals
- Generalised vitiligo (NB-UVB is first line)
- Atopic dermatitis, generalised pruritus, prurigo
- Mycosis fungoides (patch / thin plaque: NB-UVB; thicker plaque: PUVA)
- PLE prophylaxis, lichen planus, pityriasis lichenoides

## Contraindications
- Absolute: XP, photosensitive lupus, porphyria, history of melanoma; PUVA: pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 12 (for oral psoralen)
- Relative: multiple NMSC, photosensitising drugs, immunosuppressants, cataract, liver disease (PUVA), claustrophobia, unable to stand for several minutes
- NB-UVB is acceptable in pregnancy (consider folate supplement)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: long course, 2–3 visits per week; erythema, itching, tanning; skin-cancer and cataract risk with PUVA
- Determine skin type (Fitzpatrick) and, if available, **MED** (NB-UVB) or **MPD** (PUVA)
- Baseline: drug history, ANA if suspicion of lupus, LFT for PUVA, eye check for PUVA
- Photographs, PASI/BSA or VASI

## Equipment
- Calibrated cabin; UV meter; dosimetry software or log book
- UV-blocking goggles for every session
- Genital protection (shields for men), face shield if face not affected
- PUVA: 8-methoxypsoralen tablets; UVA-blocking glasses for after the session

## Procedure step by step
1. **Starting dose (NB-UVB)**: 70% of MED, or by skin type when MED is not done (psoriasis: roughly 0.33 J/cm² for type IV and 0.35 J/cm² for type V). Vitiligo is commonly started at a fixed low dose of about 0.2 J/cm² regardless of type.
2. **Increments**: 10–20% each session if no erythema; hold if mild erythema.
3. **PUVA**: give 8-MOP 0.6 mg/kg orally 1.5–2 hours before exposure with food; start UVA around 1.5–2.5 J/cm² for skin types IV–V (or 70% of MPD); increase by 0.5–1 J/cm² per session; treat twice weekly, not on consecutive days.
4. Patient stands in the centre of the cabin with goggles and genital protection.
5. **Endpoint**: faint, painless erythema the next day (NB-UVB) or at 48–72 h (PUVA, so no dose increase within 72 h of a previous increase).
6. **Missed-dose rules (NB-UVB)**:
- Under 1 week: same dose
- 1–2 weeks: reduce by 25%
- 2–3 weeks: reduce by 50%
- More than 3–4 weeks: restart at the initial dose
7. **Cumulative dose log**: record each session's dose and running total; document the number of treatments.

## Post-procedure care
- PUVA: UVA-blocking glasses for 12–24 hours after psoralen and sun protection on that day
- Emollients; avoid extra sun exposure on treatment days
- Report erythema, blistering or itching

## Complications & management
- Painful erythema: skip until settled; resume at 10–20% lower dose
- Blistering: stop until healed; resume at 50% of the last dose
- Nausea from psoralen: take with food, split dose
- Polymorphic light eruption: reduce dose
- Long-term: photoageing and skin-cancer risk (higher with PUVA, especially beyond about 150–200 treatments)

## Sessions & follow-up
- NB-UVB: 2–3 times weekly; PUVA: twice weekly
- Psoriasis: clearance usually takes 20–30 sessions
- Vitiligo: assess at 3 and 6 months; stop if no repigmentation at 6 months
- Stop at clearance; taper only if relapse risk is high
- Annual skin examination for long courses

posts.title: Wood's lamp examination
posts.summary: 365 nm UVA examination: fluorescence patterns and pigment depth
posts.body:
A Wood's lamp emits long-wave UVA (peak about 365 nm) through a nickel oxide filter. Under it, some organisms and compounds fluoresce, and differences in epidermal pigment become easier to see. It is a quick, painless bedside test.

## Indications
- Vitiligo: diagnosis, extent, and activity in fair or early lesions
- Fungal and bacterial infections: tinea capitis, pityriasis versicolor, erythrasma, Pseudomonas
- Pigmentary disorders: depth of pigment in melasma, ash-leaf macules in tuberous sclerosis, hypopigmented macules
- Porphyria: urine, stool or teeth fluorescence
- Comedones and acne bacteria (orange-red fluorescence)

## Contraindications
- None important
- Do not look directly into the lamp
- Do not use on recently washed or treated skin (topicals and soaps alter or mask fluorescence)

## Pre-procedure
- Explain that the room will be dark and the test is painless
- Ask the patient not to apply topicals or wash the area before the test
- Warm up the lamp for about 1 minute

## Equipment
- Wood's lamp (with magnifier if possible)
- Dark room
- Comparison normal skin

## Procedure step by step
1. Darken the room fully; allow the examiner's eyes to adapt for about 1 minute.
2. Hold the lamp 10–15 cm from the skin.
3. Examine the lesion and compare with normal skin.
4. **Interpret findings**:
- Vitiligo: sharp, bright blue-white (milky) depigmentation
- Hypopigmentation (pityriasis alba, leprosy, post-inflammatory): less contrast, off-white
- Ash-leaf macules: more visible
- Epidermal pigment (e.g. epidermal melasma): accentuated; dermal pigment is not
- Tinea capitis (Microsporum): bright green; T. schoenleinii: dull blue-green; T. tonsurans: none
- Pityriasis versicolor: yellow to coppery-orange
- Erythrasma: coral red
- Pseudomonas: green
- Porphyria: pink-red urine or teeth
5. Record the findings; photograph if possible.

## Post-procedure care
- None needed

## Complications & management
- None significant
- False positives: lint, soap, creams, cosmetics, ink
- False negatives: recent washing, topical antifungals, non-fluorescent species
- In skin types IV–V, epidermal vs dermal melasma differentiation is less reliable; use dermoscopy as well

## Sessions & follow-up
- Repeat at follow-up visits to track vitiligo extent and response
- Recheck tinea capitis fluorescence after treatment

posts.title: Acanthosis nigricans — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acanthosis nigricans** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define acanthosis nigricans (AN).**
- Symmetrical, velvety, hyperpigmented thickening of skin, especially in flexures (neck, axillae, groin, antecubital, submammary, umbilicus, knuckles); a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance or, rarely, internal malignancy

**Q2. Classify AN (Curth/Schwartz).**
- Benign hereditary (autosomal dominant; FGFR3 — childhood onset)
- Obesity-associated (pseudoacanthosis nigricans — commonest)
- Syndromic: insulin resistance syndromes — type A (insulin receptor mutation, HAIR-AN: Hyperandrogenism, Insulin Resistance, AN), type B (anti-insulin receptor antibodies — autoimmune), lipodystrophies, Rabson–Mendenhall, Donohue (leprechaunism), PCOS, Crouzon/FGFR3 syndromes (SADDAN)
- Malignant AN: sudden, extensive, rapidly progressive, with mucosal and palmar involvement — gastric adenocarcinoma (commonest), other GI, lung, ovary
- Drug-induced: systemic corticosteroids, nicotinic acid, insulin injections (local), OCP, protease inhibitors, testosterone
- Acral (acral acanthotic anomaly — dorsa of hands/feet, darker skin), unilateral (naevoid), mixed

**Q3. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Hyperinsulinaemia → insulin binds IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts → proliferation
- Malignant AN: tumour-derived growth factors — TGF-α (EGFR activation), IGF-1, FGF
- Genetic: activating FGFR3 mutations (keratinocyte FGFR signalling)
- Friction and moisture in flexures contribute

**Q4. Clinical features.**
- Grey-brown velvety plaques with accentuated skin markings; later verrucous/papillomatous; skin tags (acrochordons) common in the same areas; mild itch
- Severity graded by Burke's scale (neck 0–4; texture 0–3)
- Malignant AN: older, non-obese, rapid onset, extensive (including unusual sites), oral mucosa (papillomatosis of lips/tongue), palms (tripe palms — rugose velvety thickening of palms), Leser–Trélat sign (eruptive seborrhoeic keratoses), florid cutaneous papillomatosis, weight loss

**Q5. What are tripe palms and the sign of Leser–Trélat?**
- Tripe palms: acquired velvety, thickened palms with pronounced dermatoglyphics — paraneoplastic (lung cancer when isolated; gastric when with AN)
- Leser–Trélat: sudden eruption/increase in size and number of seborrhoeic keratoses — paraneoplastic (GI adenocarcinoma, lymphoma)

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis (finger-like upward projections of dermal papillae) with mild acanthosis and minimal hyperpigmentation — the brown colour is mostly from hyperkeratosis, not melanin

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (trunk; responds to minocycline), Dowling–Degos disease (reticulate flexural pigmentation, comedo-like pits), terra firma-forme dermatosis (dirt — wipes off with alcohol), erythrasma, pellagra (Casal's), Addison's, haemochromatosis, LPP inverse type, seborrhoeic keratosis, epidermal naevus, frictional melanosis

**Q8. Investigations.**
- BMI, waist circumference, BP; fasting glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin (HOMA-IR), lipid profile, liver enzymes (NAFLD)
- Women: menstrual history, hirsutism — testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH, pelvic ultrasound (PCOS)
- Malignant AN suspicion: CBC, upper GI endoscopy, CT abdomen/chest, tumour markers
- Thyroid, cortisol (Cushing's) if indicated

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Treat cause: weight loss, exercise, dietary change, metformin (improves insulin resistance), pioglitazone; PCOS management (OCP, spironolactone); stop offending drug; treat malignancy (AN regresses with tumour removal)
- Topical: retinoids (tretinoin 0.05–0.1%, adapalene), keratolytics (salicylic acid, urea, lactic/glycolic acid), vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), trichloroacetic acid peels, topical metformin
- Systemic: oral retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin), omega-3 fatty acids, octreotide (selected)
- Procedures: long-pulsed alexandrite/Q-switched/fractional CO2 lasers, dermabrasion; remove skin tags

**Q10. Why is AN important?**
- Easily visible marker of insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, prediabetes/type 2 diabetes, PCOS and NAFLD — screening opportunity in children and adolescents; rarely heralds internal malignancy

**Q11. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Brown-grey 'crista cutis' (elevated ridges) and 'sulcus cutis' (furrows) pattern, papillomatous projections, hyperpigmented dots, no vessels — distinguishes from DDD and CARP

**Q12. What is the Burke scale?**
- Neck severity 0–4 (0 absent, 1 visible on close inspection, 2 limited to base of skull, 3 extending laterally, 4 visible anteriorly) + texture 0–3 (smooth to extremely coarse/ raised); also grades axilla, knuckles, elbows, knees — correlates with insulin levels

**Q13. Describe HAIR-AN syndrome.**
- Hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, irregular menses), Insulin Resistance, Acanthosis Nigricans — adolescent girls, variant of PCOS; treat with weight loss, metformin, OCPs/ spironolactone

**Q14. What is the association with obesity in Indian children?**
- Indian children have higher insulin resistance at lower BMI ('thin-fat' phenotype); AN in a child is a marker for prediabetes/ type 2 diabetes — check fasting glucose, insulin, HbA1c, lipids, BP

**Q15. Treatment response expectations.**
- AN improves slowly over months with weight loss and insulin sensitisers; topical therapy gives cosmetic improvement; recurrence if weight regained; malignant AN improves after cancer treatment and reappears with recurrence

**Q16. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Velvety dark neck/axillae in an obese adolescent — AN (insulin resistance)
- Sudden extensive AN + tripe palms + Leser–Trélat — gastric cancer
- HAIR-AN syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Acanthosis nigricans). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Acne excoriée — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acne excoriée** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is acne excoriée?**
- Psychocutaneous disorder in which (usually mild) acne lesions — or even normal skin — are repetitively picked and squeezed, producing excoriations, crusted erosions, scars and post-inflammatory pigmentation out of proportion to the acne; also 'acné excoriée des jeunes filles' (young women)
- Part of skin-picking (excoriation) disorder in DSM-5 (obsessive-compulsive and related disorders)

**Q2. Associated psychological conditions.**
- Anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, borderline personality traits, eating disorders, stress, perfectionism

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Crusted excoriations, erosions, linear scratch marks, atrophic and hypertrophic scars, PIH on face (forehead, cheeks, chin, along hairline), sometimes upper back; few primary acne lesions visible
- Patient often admits picking (unlike dermatitis artefacta)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Dermatitis artefacta (denies self-infliction), neurotic excoriations, acne vulgaris with secondary infection, impetigo, herpes simplex, prurigo, scabies, delusional infestation

**Q5. Management.**
- Empathetic approach; treat the underlying acne effectively (retinoid, BPO, isotretinoin if needed) to remove the 'trigger'
- Behavioural therapy: habit-reversal training, CBT, mindfulness; occlusive dressings/hydrocolloid patches, keeping nails short
- Psychiatric referral; SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline), N-acetylcysteine (glutamate modulator), low-dose antipsychotics in severe cases; treat PIH and scars once picking stops

**Q6. Which scale/tool helps assess skin picking?**
- Skin Picking Scale–Revised, Skin Picking Impact Scale; screen for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), OCD (Y-BOCS) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD questionnaire)

**Q7. What is the role of SSRIs and other drugs?**
- SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine — often higher doses) for underlying OCD/anxiety/depression; N-acetylcysteine 1200–3000 mg/day (glutamate modulator) helps picking behaviour; doxepin/hydroxyzine for itch; low-dose antipsychotics (olanzapine, aripiprazole) in resistant cases

**Q8. What is habit reversal therapy?**
- Behavioural therapy: awareness training (recognising triggers and urges), competing response (e.g. clenching fists, holding an object for 1 min), social support — combined with CBT; often the most effective long-term approach

**Q9. How do you manage the skin itself?**
- Treat even mild acne effectively (topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, oral antibiotics or isotretinoin when indicated — reduces triggers), occlusive hydrocolloid dressings to stop picking, keep nails short, treat secondary infection; later scar and pigment treatment (peels, lasers, microneedling) once picking stops

**Q10. Epidemiology.**
- Mostly young women (late adolescence to 30s); often mild acne with disproportionate excoriations; also in men with obsessive traits; comorbid anxiety, depression, OCD, BDD, eating disorders

**Q11. What is body dysmorphic disorder and its link?**
- Preoccupation with imagined or slight defects in appearance causing distress and repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, skin picking, camouflaging); 'acne dysmorphophobia'; poor satisfaction with cosmetic procedures; treat with SSRIs and CBT

**Q12. Describe the clinical appearance of lesions.**
- Excoriations, crusts, erosions, linear and angulated scars, post-inflammatory hyper/ hypopigmentation, few primary comedones/ papules; within reach — forehead, cheeks, chin; may be denied or admitted

**Q13. How do you communicate with the patient?**
- Non-judgemental, acknowledge distress, explain the cycle of picking and scarring, agree on goals; involve psychiatry/ psychology for CBT/ habit reversal; maintain regular follow-up

**Q14. What is 'picker's nodule'?**
- Chronic nodules from repeated picking (prurigo-like) — treat with intralesional steroid, occlusive dressings, cryotherapy, psychological intervention

**Q15. Prognosis.**
- Chronic and relapsing if underlying psychological issue untreated; with combined dermatology–psychiatry care many improve; scars may need later procedures

## Quick spotter facts
- Excoriations and scars out of proportion to few acne lesions in a young woman — acne excoriée
- Habit-reversal + treat acne + SSRIs/N-acetylcysteine

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Acne; psychocutaneous disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Acne vulgaris — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acne vulgaris** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. Define acne vulgaris.**
- Chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit with comedones, papules, pustules, nodules and cysts on face, chest and back; affects >85% of adolescents; may persist into adulthood (adult female acne)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Four key factors: (1) increased sebum production under androgen control (DHT via 5α-reductase type 1 in sebocytes; IGF-1, insulin); (2) follicular hyperkeratinisation of the infundibulum → microcomedone (IL-1α, altered linoleic acid); (3) Cutibacterium acnes (phylotype IA1 dysbiosis) — activates TLR2, inflammasome (IL-1β), lipases produce free fatty acids, biofilm; (4) inflammation — may precede comedone formation (innate immunity, Th17)
- Exposome: high glycaemic-load diet, dairy (skimmed milk), whey protein, stress, cosmetics, occlusion/friction, smoking, pollution, sleep deprivation

**Q3. Grade acne (Indian/IAA grading).**
- Grade 1: comedones, occasional papules
- Grade 2: papules, comedones, few pustules
- Grade 3: predominant pustules, nodules, abscesses
- Grade 4: mainly cysts, abscesses, widespread scarring (nodulocystic/conglobata)
- Others: Global Acne Grading System (GAGS), Leeds technique, IGA; mild/moderate/severe by lesion counts

**Q4. Discuss the variants of acne (PYQ).**
- Neonatal (maternal androgens; also neonatal cephalic pustulosis — Malassezia) and infantile acne (3–6 months; persistent — check hyperandrogenism)
- Acne conglobata (nodules, abscesses, interconnecting sinuses, double comedones — men, trunk)
- Acne fulminans (sudden severe ulcerative acne with fever, arthralgia, osteolytic bone lesions, leucocytosis — adolescent boys, sometimes triggered by isotretinoin) — treat with oral steroids then low-dose isotretinoin
- Acne excoriée, acne mechanica (friction — helmets, backpacks), acne cosmetica, pomade acne, occupational (oil acne, chloracne), drug-induced/acneiform (steroids, androgens, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, EGFR inhibitors, halogens), tropical acne, acne aestivalis (Mallorca acne), adult female acne (lower face/jawline, hormonal), acne with facial oedema (solid facial oedema/Morbihan), gram-negative folliculitis, SAPHO and PAPA/PASH syndromes

**Q5. Discuss systemic associations of acne (PYQ).**
- Hyperandrogenism: PCOS (acne + hirsutism + irregular cycles + AN), congenital adrenal hyperplasia (late-onset 21-hydroxylase), androgen-secreting tumours (sudden virilisation), Cushing's, HAIR-AN
- Syndromes: SAPHO (Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, Osteitis), PAPA (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum, Acne — PSTPIP1), PASH/PAPASH (with hidradenitis), Apert syndrome (FGFR2 — severe acne), XYY, Behçet's (acneiform)
- Insulin resistance/obesity, eating disorders (bulimia — acne excoriée?), endocrine — acromegaly

**Q6. Which investigations are needed?**
- Usually none
- Hormonal work-up for women with signs of hyperandrogenism (irregular menses, hirsutism, sudden onset/resistant acne, androgenic alopecia): total/free testosterone, DHEAS, LH/FSH ratio, 17-OH progesterone, prolactin, fasting glucose/insulin, pelvic ultrasound — ideally day 2–5 of cycle
- Before isotretinoin: fasting lipids, LFT, CBC, pregnancy test (women)

**Q7. Topical treatment of acne.**
- Retinoids (tretinoin 0.025–0.1%, adapalene 0.1–0.3%, tazarotene, trifarotene 0.005% — RAR-γ selective) — comedolytic, anti-inflammatory; first-line in all grades and for maintenance
- Benzoyl peroxide 2.5–5% — bactericidal, no resistance; combine with antibiotics to prevent resistance
- Topical antibiotics (clindamycin 1%, nadifloxacin, minocycline foam 4%) — never as monotherapy
- Azelaic acid 15–20% (also for PIH), dapsone gel 5–7.5%, clascoterone 1% (topical androgen receptor antagonist), salicylic acid, niacinamide
- Fixed combinations: adapalene–BPO, clindamycin–BPO, clindamycin–tretinoin

**Q8. Discuss the various drugs used for acne (systemic) (PYQ).**
- Oral antibiotics for moderate–severe inflammatory acne: doxycycline 100 mg/day, minocycline 50–100 mg, sarecycline (narrow-spectrum), azithromycin (pulse; pregnancy alternatives erythromycin), — limit to 3–4 months, always with topical retinoid/BPO
- Hormonal (women): combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl oestradiol + drospirenone/cyproterone acetate/desogestrel), spironolactone 50–100 mg/day, cyproterone acetate, flutamide (hepatotoxicity — rarely), metformin for insulin resistance
- Oral isotretinoin: severe nodulocystic acne, scarring, treatment-resistant moderate acne, acne with psychological distress, gram-negative folliculitis; 0.25–0.5 (up to 1) mg/kg/day; cumulative 120–150 mg/kg or low-dose long-term regimens
- Others: oral zinc, dapsone (acne conglobata), oral steroids (acne fulminans, flares with isotretinoin), ibuprofen

**Q9. Isotretinoin: mechanism, side effects and monitoring.**
- Mechanism: 13-cis-retinoic acid — shrinks sebaceous glands (~90% sebum reduction), normalises follicular keratinisation, reduces C. acnes indirectly, anti-inflammatory; only drug affecting all 4 pathogenic factors
- Mucocutaneous: cheilitis (universal — compliance marker), xerosis, xerophthalmia, epistaxis, photosensitivity, retinoid dermatitis, paronychia, pyogenic granulomas, telogen effluvium
- Systemic: hypertriglyceridaemia, raised transaminases, myalgia/raised CK, headache, benign intracranial hypertension (avoid tetracyclines together), night-blindness, mood changes/depression (monitor), IBD (unproven), DISH/premature epiphyseal closure (high dose)
- Teratogenicity: craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, CNS defects — two reliable contraception methods 1 month before, during and 1 month after; monthly pregnancy test (iPLEDGE-style)
- Monitoring: lipids and LFT at baseline and 1–2 months, then as needed; mood assessment

**Q10. Discuss management of acne scars (PYQ).**
- Classification: atrophic — ice-pick (narrow deep <2 mm), boxcar (round/oval sharp walls 1.5–4 mm), rolling (wide undulating); hypertrophic and keloidal scars (chest, back, jawline); Goodman–Baron qualitative grading
- Prevention: early adequate treatment of inflammatory acne
- Atrophic: chemical reconstruction of skin scars (CROSS) with 70–100% TCA for ice-pick; subcision for rolling; punch excision/elevation/grafting for deep boxcar/ice-pick; microneedling ± PRP; fractional ablative (CO2, Er:YAG) and non-ablative (1550 nm) lasers; radiofrequency microneedling; dermal fillers (hyaluronic acid) for rolling; medium-depth peels
- Hypertrophic/keloid: intralesional triamcinolone, silicone, 5-FU, PDL, cryotherapy
- Combination approach and adequate sun protection; wait 6 months after isotretinoin for ablative procedures (traditional caution, evidence weak)

**Q11. Differential diagnosis.**
- Rosacea (no comedones, flushing, telangiectasia), perioral dermatitis, Pityrosporum folliculitis (monomorphic, itchy), drug-induced acneiform eruptions, folliculitis, milia, syringoma, adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas), steroid acne, Favre–Racouchot (comedones in sun-damaged skin of elderly), Demodex folliculitis

**Q12. Write a note on chloracne/oil acne (PYQ).**
- Oil acne: mineral oils/cutting oils in mechanics — comedones, folliculitis on thighs, forearms (where oil-soaked clothes contact)
- Chloracne: halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (dioxins) — straw-coloured cysts and comedones on malar, retroauricular, scrotum; systemic toxicity marker; very resistant

**Q13. What is the role of Cutibacterium acnes?**
- Anaerobic commensal of sebaceous follicles; certain phylotypes (IA1) associated with acne; activates TLR2/4 on keratinocytes and monocytes, inflammasome (NLRP3) → IL-1β, IL-8; forms biofilms; lipases release free fatty acids; target for benzoyl peroxide and antibiotics

**Q14. Explain hormonal influences.**
- Androgens (DHT, DHEA-S, testosterone) enlarge sebaceous glands and increase sebum; IGF-1 (high glycaemic diets, dairy, puberty) enhances androgen effects and lipogenesis via mTORC1; menstrual flares (progesterone), PCOS, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumours, insulin resistance

**Q15. Describe the role of diet in acne.**
- Moderate evidence: high-glycaemic-load diets and skimmed milk/whey protein supplements aggravate acne (insulin/IGF-1–mTORC1); chocolate/ fatty foods — weak evidence; advise low-glycaemic balanced diet, avoid whey protein supplements

**Q16. What is the global acne grading system (GAGS) and other grading?**
- GAGS: six regions with factors (forehead 2, each cheek 2, nose 1, chin 1, chest+upper back 3) × lesion grade (0 none, 1 comedone, 2 papule, 3 pustule, 4 nodule); total 1–18 mild, 19–30 moderate, 31–38 severe, ≥39 very severe
- Indian (IADVL) grading: Grade 1 comedones ± few papules; Grade 2 papules, comedones, few pustules; Grade 3 predominant pustules, nodules, abscesses; Grade 4 mainly cysts, abscesses, widespread scarring

**Q17. Describe acne fulminans and its management.**
- Severe, sudden ulcerative haemorrhagic nodular acne on trunk/face in adolescent boys, often triggered by isotretinoin start or testosterone; systemic — fever, arthralgia, myalgia, osteolytic bone lesions (sternum, clavicles), hepatosplenomegaly, raised ESR/ leucocytosis
- Treatment: prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg for 2–4 weeks then add low-dose isotretinoin (0.1 mg/kg) slowly while tapering steroids; dapsone; avoid starting full-dose isotretinoin

**Q18. What is the SAPHO and PAPA syndromes?**
- SAPHO: Synovitis, Acne (conglobata/fulminans), Pustulosis (palmoplantar), Hyperostosis, Osteitis (anterior chest wall)
- PAPA: Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum, Acne — PSTPIP1 autoinflammatory; PASH (PG, acne, hidradenitis), PAPASH; treat with IL-1/ TNF blockade

**Q19. Antibiotic stewardship in acne.**
- Never use topical or oral antibiotics as monotherapy — combine with benzoyl peroxide (prevents resistance) and a retinoid; limit oral antibiotics to 3–4 months; avoid using different topical and oral antibiotics together; prefer doxycycline/minocycline (sarecycline — narrow spectrum); macrolides only when tetracyclines contraindicated

**Q20. Hormonal therapy in women.**
- Combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl oestradiol with anti-androgenic progestin — cyproterone acetate, drospirenone, desogestrel) — 3–6 months for benefit; contraindications (thrombosis, migraine with aura, smoking >35 y)
- Spironolactone 50–150 mg/day (anti-androgen) — hyperkalaemia rare in healthy women, menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness; avoid in pregnancy (feminisation of male fetus)
- Topical clascoterone 1% (androgen receptor antagonist) for ≥12 y

**Q21. Isotretinoin — dosing strategies and newer evidence.**
- 0.5–1 mg/kg/day to a cumulative dose of 120–150 mg/kg (reduces relapse); low-dose (0.25–0.4 mg/kg or 10–20 mg/day) for moderate acne — similar efficacy with fewer side effects, longer duration
- Monitoring: pregnancy prevention (2 contraceptive methods, tests monthly, avoid pregnancy 1 month after), baseline and 1–2 month lipid profile and LFT; depression/ suicide monitoring (causality unproven), IBD (no causal link), avoid tetracyclines (pseudotumour cerebri), avoid waxing/ laser resurfacing during and 6 months after (old advice now relaxed)

**Q22. Topical retinoids — mechanism and pearls.**
- Bind RAR-γ/β → normalise follicular keratinisation (comedolytic), anti-inflammatory (TLR2 down-regulation), improve post-inflammatory pigmentation; tretinoin 0.025–0.1%, adapalene 0.1–0.3% (most stable, least irritating, OTC), tazarotene 0.1% (pregnancy category X), trifarotene 0.005% (RAR-γ selective — trunk acne)
- Apply thin layer at night to whole affected area, start alternate nights, sunscreen; retinoid dermatitis — irritation, dryness; first-line maintenance therapy

**Q23. Benzoyl peroxide and azelaic acid.**
- BPO 2.5–5%: oxidising agent — bactericidal (no resistance), mildly comedolytic; bleaches fabrics, irritation; combine with clindamycin/ adapalene
- Azelaic acid 15–20%: antibacterial, comedolytic, anti-inflammatory, tyrosinase inhibition — good for PIH-prone darker skin, pregnancy-safe

**Q24. Differentiate acne from rosacea and folliculitis.**
- Acne: comedones (hallmark), adolescents, face/back/chest, nodules/scars
- Rosacea: no comedones, central face, flushing, telangiectasia, adults, sensitive skin
- Folliculitis: monomorphic pustules around hairs, no comedones, may be bacterial/ Malassezia/ Gram-negative

**Q25. What are the types of acne scars and their treatments?**
- Atrophic: ice-pick (narrow deep — TCA CROSS, punch excision), rolling (broad, tethered — subcision, fillers, microneedling), boxcar (sharp edges — punch elevation, fractional lasers, chemical peels)
- Hypertrophic/ keloidal: intralesional steroids, silicone, PDL, cryotherapy
- Combined approach: fractional CO2/ Er:YAG, microneedling ± PRP, radiofrequency microneedling, fillers; treat active acne first

**Q26. What is post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in acne and its management?**
- Common in Indian skin; prevent by early treatment of inflammatory acne and sunscreen; treat with azelaic acid, retinoids, niacinamide, hydroquinone short-term, chemical peels (glycolic/ salicylic), avoid picking

**Q27. Acne in pregnancy — safe treatments.**
- Topical azelaic acid, benzoyl peroxide (limited area), topical clindamycin/ erythromycin; oral erythromycin/ azithromycin if needed; avoid retinoids (topical and oral), tetracyclines, spironolactone, hormonal therapy

**Q28. What is drug-induced acne and acneiform eruption?**
- Monomorphic papulopustules without comedones on trunk: corticosteroids, anabolic steroids/ testosterone, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, halogens (iodide, bromide), vitamin B6/B12, cyclosporine, EGFR inhibitors (papulopustular rash — treat with doxycycline, topical steroids), JAK inhibitors, dupilumab (facial), progesterone-only contraceptives

**Q29. What is acne mechanica and acne cosmetica?**
- Acne mechanica: friction/ occlusion/ pressure (helmets, straps, backpacks, sports gear) — avoid trigger
- Acne cosmetica: comedones from occlusive cosmetics/ hair oils (pomade acne on forehead) — use 'non-comedogenic' oil-free products

**Q30. What investigations are needed in a woman with acne and hirsutism?**
- Menstrual history, BMI, signs of virilisation; early follicular phase total/ free testosterone, DHEA-S, 17-OH progesterone (CAH), LH:FSH, prolactin, TSH, fasting glucose/insulin; pelvic ultrasound (PCOS — Rotterdam criteria 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries)

## Quick spotter facts
- Comedones = acne (rosacea has none)
- Isotretinoin — teratogen; cheilitis universal
- Ice-pick → TCA CROSS; rolling → subcision

posts.title: Acquired melanocytic nevus (mole) — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acquired melanocytic nevus (mole)** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. What is an acquired melanocytic naevus?**
- Benign proliferation of naevus cells (melanocytes) in nests, appearing after 6 months of age, increasing in childhood/young adulthood (peak in 3rd decade) and regressing in old age; number linked to sun exposure in childhood and genetics; fewer in dark skin

**Q2. Classify by histological level (life cycle).**
- Junctional: flat, uniformly brown, nests at dermo-epidermal junction (children)
- Compound: slightly raised brown papule, junctional + dermal nests
- Intradermal: dome-shaped skin-coloured/light-brown papule, often with hairs, dermal nests only with maturation (smaller, neurotised cells deeper) — adults, face
- Special types: blue naevus (dermal dendritic melanocytes — blue due to Tyndall effect), Spitz naevus, halo naevus, dysplastic (atypical/Clark's) naevus, recurrent naevus, acral naevus (parallel furrow pattern), Meyerson naevus (eczematous halo), combined naevus

**Q3. What is a dysplastic (atypical) naevus and the atypical mole syndrome?**
- Clinically atypical naevus: ≥5 mm, irregular/ill-defined border, variegated colour, flat component ('fried-egg'); histology — architectural disorder (bridging, lentiginous growth, shouldering), cytological atypia, lamellar fibroplasia
- Atypical mole syndrome / FAMMM (familial atypical multiple mole melanoma): >50–100 naevi, several atypical, family history of melanoma — CDKN2A (p16) mutations (also pancreatic cancer risk); lifelong surveillance with total body photography and dermoscopy

**Q4. Write a short note on Kamino bodies (PYQ).**
- Eosinophilic, PAS-positive, diastase-resistant, globular hyaline bodies (basement membrane material — collagen IV/laminin) at the dermo-epidermal junction above the nests in Spitz naevus; seen in ~60–80% — favour Spitz over melanoma when numerous and confluent

**Q5. What is a Spitz naevus?**
- Benign melanocytic naevus of spindle and/or epithelioid cells, children and young adults; dome-shaped pink-red or brown papule on face/legs growing quickly then stabilising; dermoscopy — starburst pattern (pigmented Reed naevus) or dotted vessels (pink)
- Histology: symmetric, well-circumscribed, maturation, Kamino bodies, clefts around junctional nests, epidermal hyperplasia
- Atypical Spitz tumours — uncertain potential; excision recommended in adults/atypical lesions

**Q6. Dermoscopy of benign naevi.**
- Reticular (network), globular, homogeneous (blue naevus), starburst (Spitz/Reed), parallel furrow (acral), peripheral rim of globules (growing naevus in children)
- Melanoma-specific structures: atypical network, negative network, irregular streaks, irregular dots/globules, blue-white veil, regression structures, atypical vessels, parallel ridge pattern (acral), shiny white lines

**Q7. What are the ABCDE warning signs?**
- Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variegation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution (change in size/shape/colour, symptoms) — plus 'ugly duckling' sign (lesion different from the patient's other naevi)
- Glasgow 7-point checklist: major — change in size, shape, colour; minor — diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing/bleeding, altered sensation

**Q8. Risk factors for melanoma related to naevi.**
- Number of common naevi (>100), atypical naevi (≥5), large congenital naevi, family history (CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1, MITF), fair skin, sunburns, immunosuppression; in India, acral lentiginous melanoma is commonest (soles, nails — not UV-related)

**Q9. Management.**
- Benign naevi — reassurance; sun protection; monitor with photographs/dermoscopy
- Excision biopsy (narrow 2 mm margins, full thickness) for any suspicious lesion; do not shave/laser suspicious pigmented lesions
- Cosmetic removal: shave excision, punch, radiofrequency (only after confirming benign)
- Teach self-examination; total-body photography for many/atypical naevi

**Q10. What is the 'ugly duckling' sign?**
- A naevus that looks different from the patient's other naevi (signature pattern) is suspicious for melanoma regardless of ABCD — useful in patients with many naevi

**Q11. Explain the 7-point checklist and dermoscopy algorithms.**
- Glasgow 7-point checklist — major: change in size, shape, colour; minor: diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing/ crusting, change in sensation
- Dermoscopy: ABCD rule (TDS score), Menzies method, 7-point checklist (atypical network, blue-white veil, atypical vascular pattern — major; irregular streaks, dots/globules, blotches, regression — minor; score ≥3 suspicious), 3-point checklist (asymmetry, atypical network, blue-white structures)

**Q12. Acral naevi dermoscopy — key patterns.**
- Benign: parallel furrow pattern (pigment in sulci), lattice-like, fibrillar pattern; Melanoma: parallel ridge pattern (pigment on ridges where sweat pores open) — important in Indian patients with acral lesions

**Q13. Longitudinal melanonychia — evaluation.**
- Band of brown-black pigment along the nail: causes — racial (multiple bands in dark skin), drugs (zidovudine, hydroxyurea, minocycline), trauma, naevus, lentigo, Laugier–Hunziker, Addison's, fungal (Trichophyton rubrum nigricans), melanoma
- Red flags (ABCDEF of nail melanoma): Age 50–70, Band >3 mm/ brown-black/ irregular, Change, Digit (thumb, hallux, index), Extension onto nail folds (Hutchinson's sign), Family/ personal history — nail matrix biopsy

**Q14. Blue naevus — features.**
- Dermal melanocytic proliferation — steel-blue papule (Tyndall effect) on dorsa of hands/feet, scalp, buttocks; common blue naevus vs cellular blue naevus (larger, buttocks/ sacrum); dermoscopy — homogeneous steel-blue pigmentation; malignant blue naevus rare

**Q15. Describe melanoma types and Breslow/ Clark levels (often linked question).**
- Types: superficial spreading (commonest in West), nodular, lentigo maligna melanoma, acral lentiginous (commonest in Indians — soles, palms, nails), mucosal, desmoplastic, amelanotic
- Breslow thickness (mm, from granular layer to deepest cell) — main prognostic factor: T1 ≤1 mm, T2 1–2, T3 2–4, T4 >4 mm (a/b by ulceration); Clark levels I–V (anatomical) now largely replaced
- Margins: in situ 0.5–1 cm, ≤1 mm 1 cm, 1–2 mm 1–2 cm, >2 mm 2 cm; sentinel node biopsy for >0.8 mm or ulcerated

## Quick spotter facts
- Ugly duckling — biopsy
- Kamino bodies — Spitz naevus
- Acral lentiginous melanoma — commonest in India

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Melanocytic naevi; melanoma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Acrochordon (skin tag) — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acrochordon (skin tag)** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is an acrochordon?**
- Common benign soft fibroepithelial polyp (skin tag, soft fibroma) — small, soft, skin-coloured or pigmented, pedunculated papules on neck, axillae, groin, eyelids, inframammary; middle age, obese, pregnant women

**Q2. Associations.**
- Obesity, insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, acanthosis nigricans, dyslipidaemia, pregnancy (hormonal), acromegaly, PCOS; Birt–Hogg–Dubé (fibrofolliculomas mistaken for tags), Cowden; association with colonic polyps is debated

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Polypoid lesion with loose fibrovascular stroma (collagen and dilated vessels), thin overlying epidermis (may be acanthotic/papillomatous), no adnexa; fat in larger lesions (fibrolipoma)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Pedunculated seborrhoeic keratosis, intradermal naevus, neurofibroma (button-hole sign), molluscum, filiform wart, fibroepithelioma of Pinkus, pedunculated BCC/melanoma (rare — remove and send if atypical), fibrofolliculomas (BHD)

**Q5. Treatment.**
- Snip excision with sterile scissors (with or without local anaesthetic) and haemostasis, cryotherapy, radiofrequency/electrocautery, ligation for larger ones; send atypical lesions for histopathology
- Screen for diabetes/metabolic syndrome in patients with multiple tags (especially with AN)

**Q6. What is Birt–Hogg–Dubé syndrome?**
- Autosomal dominant FLCN mutation: multiple fibrofolliculomas, trichodiscomas and acrochordons on face/neck, lung cysts with spontaneous pneumothorax, renal tumours (chromophobe/oncocytic) — screen kidneys with MRI

**Q7. Can skin tags be a marker of systemic disease?**
- Multiple skin tags associated with insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes, obesity, metabolic syndrome, acanthosis nigricans, dyslipidaemia, pregnancy (hormonal), and possibly colonic polyps (controversial); check fasting sugar, lipids in multiple tags

**Q8. What causes a skin tag to become painful and dark?**
- Torsion of the stalk with infarction — black, tender, may auto-amputate; differentiate from a thrombosed haemangioma or melanoma (biopsy if doubtful)

**Q9. Dermoscopy of a skin tag.**
- Pedunculated lesion with central or 'comma'/hairpin vessels and skin-coloured/light-brown structureless areas; cerebriform features if seborrhoeic keratosis-like

**Q10. Epidemiology and sites.**
- Very common (≈ 25–50% adults), increase with age, obesity, pregnancy; neck, axillae, groin, eyelids, inframammary folds; single or multiple soft pedunculated skin-coloured/ brown papules

**Q11. What is the treatment technique?**
- Snip excision with fine scissors (small ones without anaesthesia), electrodesiccation/ radiofrequency at base, cryotherapy (forceps dipped in LN2), ligation; haemostasis with aluminium chloride; send atypical/ pigmented ones for histology

**Q12. Explain the principles of cryotherapy (PYQ).**
- Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C): rapid freezing causes intracellular ice crystals, cell dehydration, vascular stasis and ischaemic necrosis; slow thaw maximises damage; techniques — spray, cotton-tipped applicator, cryoprobe; lethal temperature for benign lesions −20 to −30 °C, malignant −50 °C (double freeze–thaw)
- Side effects: pain, blistering, hypo/ hyperpigmentation (avoid in dark skin cosmetic areas), scarring, nerve damage over superficial nerves, alopecia

**Q13. Describe radiofrequency/ electrosurgery modalities used for benign lesions.**
- Electrodesiccation (monoterminal, superficial dehydration), electrofulguration (sparking, no contact), electrocoagulation (biterminal, deeper), electrosection (cutting — radiofrequency 'radiosurgery' 3–4 MHz gives fine cuts with less thermal damage); precautions — pacemakers (use bipolar), alcohol-based prep (fire), smoke plume (HPV), avoid on keloid-prone skin

**Q14. What are fibroepithelial polyps and soft fibromas?**
- Larger pedunculated skin tags (soft fibroma/ fibroma molle, 'bag-like') on trunk/ groin — same lesion spectrum; histology shows loose collagen, vessels and fat in a polypoid stalk covered by thin epidermis

**Q15. Skin tags in pregnancy and hormonal states.**
- Increase in number and size in pregnancy (oestrogen/ progesterone, growth factors) and acromegaly; many regress post-partum

## Quick spotter facts
- Multiple soft pedunculated neck papules with AN — skin tags; check sugar

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Benign fibrous tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AKV)?**
- Rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis (ATP2A2 — SERCA2 calcium pump, allelic with Darier's disease) presenting in childhood with multiple flat-topped, skin-coloured, wart-like papules on the dorsa of hands and feet, knees, elbows; may coexist with Darier's disease

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Small (1–5 mm) polygonal flat warty papules, punctate keratoses and pits on palms/soles, nail changes (thickening, longitudinal ridging, leukonychia); asymptomatic; persists lifelong

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis with circumscribed elevations resembling 'church spires'; no acantholysis or dyskeratosis (vs Darier's) and no koilocytes (vs warts)

**Q4. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Genodermatoses: inherited single-gene (or chromosomal) disorders with skin manifestations
- By inheritance: autosomal dominant (NF1, TSC, Darier's, Hailey–Hailey, AKV), autosomal recessive (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, Netherton, PXE), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Menkes, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (incontinentia pigmenti, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi–Hünermann), mitochondrial, mosaic
- By system/pathway: disorders of keratinisation, blistering (EB), pigmentation, DNA repair (XP, Bloom, Cockayne, Rothmund–Thomson, trichothiodystrophy), connective tissue (PXE, Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan, cutis laxa), vascular, ectodermal dysplasias, tumour syndromes, neurocutaneous (phakomatoses), metabolic (porphyrias)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Plane warts (koilocytes, Koebner), seborrhoeic keratoses (stucco keratosis in elderly), Darier's disease (acral papules + seborrhoeic distribution), epidermodysplasia verruciformis, lichen planus, acrokeratoelastoidosis (marginal papules)

**Q6. Management.**
- Benign; cryotherapy, shave/curettage, CO2/Er:YAG laser, topical retinoids/keratolytics; oral acitretin for extensive lesions; genetic counselling

**Q7. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Plane warts (Koebner, HPV, resolve), epidermodysplasia verruciformis, stucco keratoses (elderly), seborrhoeic keratoses, Darier's disease acral lesions (look for seborrhoeic papules elsewhere), lichen planus, acrokeratoelastoidosis (keratotic papules at palm margins)

**Q8. Management in detail.**
- Usually cosmetic; superficial ablation — cryotherapy, CO2/ Er:YAG laser, curettage, electrodesiccation; topical retinoids/ keratolytics; oral acitretin for extensive disease; recurrence possible

**Q9. What is acrokeratoelastoidosis?**
- Autosomal dominant (or sporadic) small firm translucent/ keratotic papules along the margins of palms and soles (at junction of dorsal and ventral skin); histology — fragmented elastic fibres (elastorrhexis) with hyperkeratosis

**Q10. Why is skin biopsy important in AKV?**
- To differentiate from plane warts (koilocytes, HPV) and from acral lesions of Darier's disease (acantholysis and dyskeratosis); AKV shows only church-spire hyperkeratosis without dyskeratosis — diagnosis affects genetic counselling

**Q11. What does 'genodermatosis with ATP2A2' teach about calcium in the skin?**
- Calcium gradient (low basal, high granular) controls keratinocyte differentiation and desmosome assembly; SERCA2 (Darier/ AKV) and SPCA1 (Hailey–Hailey) pump defects disrupt intracellular calcium stores → acantholysis/ dyskeratosis

**Q12. Onset and course.**
- Appears in early childhood or adolescence, slowly progressive, persists lifelong; asymptomatic

**Q13. What is the genetic basis and relation to Darier's disease?**
- Autosomal dominant ATP2A2 (SERCA2) mutations — same gene as Darier's disease; AKV-like lesions occur in ~30–70% of Darier's patients; isolated AKV is considered an allelic variant

**Q14. What is the histopathological pattern?**
- Hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis with circumscribed epidermal elevations resembling 'church spires'; no dyskeratosis or acantholysis (unlike Darier's)

**Q15. Associated nail and palmar findings.**
- Nail changes (thick, white, longitudinal ridging, subungual hyperkeratosis), punctate keratoses/pits on palms; lesions are flat-topped skin-coloured warty papules on dorsa of hands/feet, knees, elbows

## Quick spotter facts
- Flat wart-like papules on dorsa of hands since childhood, 'church-spire' histology — AKV of Hopf (ATP2A2)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Genodermatoses — ATP2A2 spectrum). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Actinic keratosis — viva
posts.summary: Premalignant & malignant tumours · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Actinic keratosis** (Premalignant & malignant tumours)_

**Q1. Define actinic keratosis (AK).**
- UV-induced intra-epidermal proliferation of atypical keratinocytes on chronically sun-damaged skin (solar keratosis) — regarded as SCC in situ (early) / premalignant; marker of field cancerisation
- Fair-skinned elderly, outdoor workers, immunosuppressed (transplant recipients); uncommon in Indian skin types except albinos and farmers

**Q2. Clinical features and variants.**
- Rough, sandpaper-like, scaly red/skin-coloured macules or papules (better felt than seen) on face, scalp (bald), ears, dorsa of hands, forearms; background photodamage
- Variants: hypertrophic, atrophic, pigmented, lichenoid, bowenoid, cutaneous horn, actinic cheilitis (lower lip — scaling, blurred vermilion border)

**Q3. Risk of progression to SCC.**
- Individual AK: ~0.1–0.6% per year (up to 10% over 10 years); ~60% of SCCs arise from AKs; some regress spontaneously
- Warning signs: induration, inflammation, diameter >1 cm, rapid growth, bleeding, ulceration, pain (IFRBU)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Atypical keratinocytes in the basal layer extending upward, alternating ortho- and parakeratosis ('flag sign' — parakeratosis over atypical epidermis, orthokeratosis over spared adnexal ostia), solar elastosis, budding of basal layer; Olsen grading (AK I–III)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Seborrhoeic keratosis (stuck-on), SCC in situ/Bowen's, superficial BCC, DLE, porokeratosis (DSAP), lichen planus-like keratosis, solar lentigo (pigmented AK), arsenical keratoses (palms/soles), wart

**Q6. Management.**
- Lesion-directed: cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen — most common), curettage and cautery, excision/biopsy for suspicious lesions, CO2 laser
- Field-directed: 5-fluorouracil 0.5–5% cream, imiquimod 3.75–5%, diclofenac 3% gel, tirbanibulin 1% (5-day course — microtubule/Src inhibitor), photodynamic therapy (ALA/MAL + red/blue light or daylight PDT), chemical peels, ablative laser resurfacing
- Prevention: daily sunscreen (reduces new AKs), nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily (reduces new AK/NMSC in high-risk), acitretin chemoprevention in transplant recipients; regular skin checks

**Q7. Describe the clinical variants in detail.**
- Classic (rough, sandpaper-like erythematous scaly papule — felt better than seen), hypertrophic (thick hyperkeratotic — may form cutaneous horn), atrophic, pigmented (mimics lentigo maligna), lichenoid, bowenoid, actinic cheilitis (lower lip — diffuse scaling, blurred vermilion border)

**Q8. What is a cutaneous horn and its significance?**
- Conical hyperkeratotic projection; base may be AK, SK, wart, keratoacanthoma or SCC (in ~20%) — always biopsy the base, especially with induration or in elderly

**Q9. Actinic cheilitis — management.**
- Premalignant (SCC of lip has higher metastasis); sun protection with lip balms (SPF), avoid smoking; treat with 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT, CO2/ Er:YAG laser vermilionectomy; biopsy ulcerated/ indurated areas

**Q10. Histopathology of AK in detail.**
- Atypical keratinocytes in basal layer extending partially (AK I/II) or fully (AK III ≈ Bowen's) through epidermis, alternating parakeratosis over affected epidermis and orthokeratosis over spared adnexal openings ('flag sign' — pink and blue), budding of atypical cells into papillary dermis, solar elastosis

**Q11. Photodynamic therapy — how does it work?**
- Topical photosensitiser (5-aminolaevulinic acid or methyl aminolaevulinate) is taken up preferentially by dysplastic cells and converted to protoporphyrin IX; illumination with red (630 nm), blue light or daylight generates reactive oxygen species → selective cell death; side effects — pain/ burning during illumination, erythema, crusting; excellent cosmesis

**Q12. Prevention of AK.**
- Regular sunscreen use reduces AK incidence (Australian trials), sun avoidance, protective clothing; oral nicotinamide in high-risk; acitretin for transplant recipients; treat AK early to prevent SCC

**Q13. What is field cancerisation and why treat the field?**
- Chronic UV damage produces clinically invisible genetic alterations (p53 mutant clones) over the whole sun-exposed area; treating only visible AKs misses subclinical lesions — field therapies treat the whole area

**Q14. Field therapies and their details.**
- 5-fluorouracil 5% cream twice daily for 2–4 weeks (or 0.5% with salicylic acid); imiquimod 5% 2–3 times/week for 4–16 weeks or 3.75% daily cycles; diclofenac 3% gel 90 days (mild); ingenol mebutate (withdrawn — skin cancer signal); tirbanibulin 1% ointment once daily for 5 days (tubulin/Src inhibitor — newer); PDT with ALA/MAL (conventional or daylight); chemical peels, ablative laser resurfacing
- Calcipotriol + 5-FU combination (short, immune-enhancing); oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily reduces new AKs and NMSC in high-risk patients (ONTRANS/ONTRAC)

**Q15. Grading of AK (Olsen) and clinical clues to SCC.**
- Olsen grade I (more palpable than visible), II (moderately thick, easily seen), III (very thick, hyperkeratotic)
- Red flags for invasive SCC (IDRBEU): Induration/inflammation, Diameter >1 cm, Rapid enlargement, Bleeding, Erythema, Ulceration — biopsy

**Q16. Who are high-risk patients?**
- Organ-transplant recipients (on immunosuppressants — 65–250× SCC risk), CLL, HIV, prior skin cancers, albinism, XP, chronic voriconazole use, long-term PUVA, heavy sun exposure in fair skin — need regular skin surveillance and aggressive field treatment

## Quick spotter facts
- Rough sandpaper scaly papules on bald scalp of an elderly farmer — AK
- Flag sign on histology
- Field therapy: 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT, tirbanibulin

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Premalignant epidermal lesions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define AGEP.**
- Acute severe cutaneous adverse reaction with rapid eruption of numerous small (<5 mm) non-follicular sterile pustules on oedematous erythema, fever and neutrophilia; >90% drug-induced

**Q2. Common culprit drugs.**
- Aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin) and other β-lactams, macrolides, quinolones, pristinamycin, sulphonamides, hydroxychloroquine (long latency), terbinafine, diltiazem, calcium-channel blockers, ketoconazole, carbamazepine
- Non-drug triggers: infections (enterovirus, parvovirus B19, CMV, Mycoplasma), spider bites, mercury

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Onset within 1–2 days of the drug (antibiotics; up to 1–3 weeks for some like HCQ)
- Burning/itchy erythema starting on face or intertriginous areas (axillae, groin) → spreads; hundreds of pinhead pustules; may have purpura, targetoid lesions, facial oedema; mucosal involvement mild in ~20% (only one site)
- Fever >38 °C, neutrophilia (>7×10⁹/L), mild eosinophilia; organ involvement (liver, kidney, lung) in ~20%
- Resolves in 1–2 weeks with collarette/punctate desquamation after stopping drug

**Q4. Pathogenesis.**
- Drug-specific T cells (CD4, CD8) release CXCL8 (IL-8), IL-17, IL-22, GM-CSF → neutrophil recruitment to epidermis — type IVd hypersensitivity
- IL36RN mutations in some patients (link with generalised pustular psoriasis)

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Spongiform subcorneal and/or intra-epidermal pustules, papillary dermal oedema, perivascular infiltrate with neutrophils and eosinophils, necrotic keratinocytes; may have leukocytoclastic vasculitis
- Psoriasis features (regular acanthosis, tortuous vessels) absent

**Q6. Differentiate AGEP from generalised pustular psoriasis (GPP).**
- AGEP: drug history, acute onset (days), no personal/family history of psoriasis, rapid resolution in <15 days after stopping drug, eosinophils and necrotic keratinocytes on histology, positive patch test sometimes
- GPP: history of psoriasis, slower evolution, recurrent, longer duration, arthritis, psoriasiform histology, IL36RN mutations

**Q7. Other differentials of pustular eruption (PYQ: causes of pustular eruption).**
- GPP, subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon–Wilkinson — annular, flexural, chronic), IgA pemphigus, pustular vasculitis, DRESS with pustules, SJS/TEN early (pustular), bacterial folliculitis, candidiasis, pustular drug eruptions (acneiform, halogenoderma), infantile acropustulosis, erythema toxicum neonatorum, transient neonatal pustular melanosis

**Q8. Diagnostic score.**
- EuroSCAR AGEP validation score (morphology, course, histology): ≥8 definite, 5–7 probable, 1–4 possible, ≤0 no AGEP

**Q9. Management.**
- Stop the culprit drug (most important); supportive care — antipyretics, emollients, wet compresses
- Moderate/potent topical steroids for symptoms; systemic steroids (prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg) for severe disease or organ involvement; cyclosporine/infliximab rarely
- Avoid unnecessary antibiotics (pustules are sterile); patch test after recovery (positive in ~50%) — useful to confirm the drug
- Drug card and cross-reactivity counselling

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Excellent; mortality ~1–5% mainly in elderly with comorbidities or organ involvement

**Q11. What is the patch test protocol for AGEP?**
- Patch test with suspected drugs (5–10% in petrolatum) 6 weeks–6 months after recovery on previously affected back; read at 48, 72, 96 h — pustular reaction at site confirms; positivity ~50%; delayed readings important

**Q12. Localised AGEP (ALEP).**
- Acute localised exanthematous pustulosis — pustules confined to face/ neck/ chest after drugs (amoxicillin, clindamycin) — same mechanism, milder

**Q13. Differentiate AGEP from DRESS with pustules.**
- DRESS: latency 2–8 weeks, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, internal organ involvement (liver), prolonged course >2 weeks; AGEP: latency <48 h (antibiotics), resolves in <2 weeks, neutrophilia

**Q14. Classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions by Gell–Coombs (revised).**
- Type I (IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Type II (cytotoxic antibody): drug-induced pemphigus, immune thrombocytopenic purpura
- Type III (immune complex): serum sickness, vasculitis
- Type IV T-cell: IVa (Th1 — contact dermatitis), IVb (Th2/ eosinophils — DRESS, MPE), IVc (cytotoxic — SJS/TEN, FDE, MPE), IVd (neutrophilic — AGEP)
- Non-immune: pseudo-allergy (MRGPRX2), phototoxic, pigmentation, overdose/ side effects

**Q15. Why are antibiotics often wrongly continued in AGEP?**
- Fever with pustules and neutrophilia suggests sepsis, so antibiotics (often the culprit) are escalated — recognise sterile pustules (Gram stain/ culture negative), stop suspected drugs

## Quick spotter facts
- Hundreds of non-follicular pinhead pustules in flexures 1–2 days after amoxicillin — AGEP
- Resolves in <15 days with collarette desquamation

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous adverse drug reactions); EuroSCAR AGEP validation score. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Alopecia areata — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Alopecia areata** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define alopecia areata (AA).**
- Chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated, non-scarring hair loss with well-circumscribed patches of hair loss on scalp or any hair-bearing area, with preserved follicular openings; affects ~2% lifetime; any age, peak 20–40 y

**Q2. Classify alopecias (PYQ).**
- Non-scarring (non-cicatricial): AA, androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction (early), tinea capitis (non-inflammatory), secondary syphilis, hair shaft defects, hypothyroidism, nutritional
- Scarring (cicatricial) — primary: lymphocytic (DLE, LPP, frontal fibrosing alopecia, central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, pseudopelade of Brocq), neutrophilic (folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis), mixed (acne keloidalis, erosive pustular dermatosis); secondary: burns, radiation, trauma, kerion, tumours, morphoea, infections (lupus vulgaris)

**Q3. Describe the hair cycle (PYQ).**
- Anagen (growth): 2–7 years, ~85–90% of scalp hairs, determines length
- Catagen (regression): 2–3 weeks, ~1%
- Telogen (rest): ~3 months, 10–15%; club hair shed in exogen
- Kenogen: empty follicle interval; scalp has ~100,000 hairs, normal shedding 50–100/day; growth ~1 cm/month

**Q4. Pathogenesis of AA.**
- Collapse of immune privilege of anagen hair bulb (reduced MHC I, TGF-β, α-MSH) → autoreactive CD8+NKG2D+ T cells attack follicular autoantigens (melanocyte/keratinocyte), IFN-γ and IL-15 via JAK–STAT signalling → follicle forced into dystrophic anagen/telogen; follicle stem cells spared (non-scarring, reversible)
- Genetic (HLA-DQB1, ULBP, CTLA4, IL2RA), family history 10–20%, stress, viral infections, vaccination triggers
- Associations: atopy, thyroid autoimmunity, vitiligo, Down syndrome, APECED, lupus, diabetes, iron deficiency

**Q5. Clinical patterns and signs.**
- Patchy (commonest), ophiasis (band along occipital and temporal margins — poor prognosis), sisaipho (inverse ophiasis — frontoparietal), diffuse (acute diffuse and total alopecia — mimics TE), alopecia totalis (whole scalp), universalis (all body hair), reticular
- Exclamation-mark hairs (tapering proximal ends) at active edge, positive pull test at margin, regrowth with white (vellus) hairs first, sparing of grey hairs ('sudden whitening overnight')
- Nails (10–60%): fine regular geometric pitting, trachyonychia, Beau's lines, red lunulae, onychomadesis

**Q6. Trichoscopy in AA.**
- Yellow dots (keratin in empty follicles), black dots (cadaverised hairs — active), exclamation-mark hairs, broken hairs, tapered hairs, short vellus/regrowing hairs, Pohl–Pinkus constrictions

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate ('swarm of bees') around anagen bulbs (acute), increased catagen/telogen hairs, miniaturised follicles, fibrous streamers, pigment casts, eosinophils; no scarring

**Q8. Severity assessment.**
- SALT score (Severity of Alopecia Tool): % scalp hair loss — vertex 40%, posterior 24%, each side 18% — S1 <25%, S2 25–49, S3 50–74, S4 75–99, S5 100%; severe AA = SALT ≥50
- Alopecia areata investigator global assessment (AA-IGA)

**Q9. Differential diagnosis.**
- Tinea capitis (scaling, broken hairs, KOH), trichotillomania (bizarre shapes, broken hairs of varying length, no exclamation-mark hairs, trichoscopy — flame hairs, tulip hairs, V-sign), telogen effluvium (diffuse, positive pull test everywhere), secondary syphilis (moth-eaten), androgenetic alopecia (diffuse AA), early scarring alopecia, traction alopecia, loose anagen syndrome, temporal triangular alopecia (congenital)

**Q10. Investigations.**
- Clinical/trichoscopy; thyroid function and antibodies, CBC, ferritin, vitamin D, blood sugar; VDRL if moth-eaten; KOH; biopsy if doubtful

**Q11. Treatment.**
- Limited patchy (<50%): intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 2.5–10 mg/ml (5 mg/ml commonly) every 4–6 weeks (first line in adults), super-potent topical steroids (children), minoxidil 5% adjunct, topical immunotherapy for chronic (DPCP, SADBE — induce allergic contact dermatitis), anthralin short contact (children)
- Extensive/rapidly progressive: oral mini-pulse betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg twice weekly, pulse methylprednisolone, short oral prednisolone; methotrexate (± low-dose steroid), azathioprine, cyclosporine, oral minoxidil
- JAK inhibitors for severe AA (SALT ≥50): baricitinib 4 mg (FDA 2022, adults; approved in India), ritlecitinib 50 mg (≥12 y), deuruxolitinib; tofacitinib off-label — monitor CBC, lipids, LFT, infections (TB/HZV screening)
- Supportive: wigs, hair pieces, eyebrow tattooing/microblading, counselling, support groups

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- ~50% of limited patchy AA regrow within a year without treatment; poor prognostic factors — onset in childhood, extensive (totalis/universalis), ophiasis, long duration (>1 y), nail changes, atopy, family history, associated autoimmunity, Down syndrome

**Q13. What is immune privilege of the hair follicle and its collapse?**
- Anagen bulb normally has low MHC class I, local immunosuppressants (TGF-β, α-MSH, IL-10, CGRP) — protecting follicle autoantigens
- In AA, IFN-γ (and stressors/ viral triggers) upregulates MHC class I/II, NKG2D ligands (MICA, ULBP3) → CD8+ NKG2D+ T cells attack the bulb → dystrophic anagen/ catagen; IFN-γ–JAK1/2 and IL-15–JAK1/3 signalling (rationale for JAK inhibitors)

**Q14. Describe the exclamation-mark hair and other signs.**
- Exclamation-mark hair: short broken hair, thicker distally and tapering proximally with depigmented root — sign of active disease (at the edge of patches)
- Positive hair-pull test at margin (active), Coudability sign (hairs bend at the base), cadaver hairs/ black dots, regrowth of white (vellus) hairs first
- Sudden whitening ('turning white overnight') — selective loss of pigmented hairs

**Q15. Describe the clinical patterns.**
- Patchy (commonest), multifocal, reticular, ophiasis (band along occipital and temporal margins — poor prognosis), sisaipho (ophiasis inversus — frontoparietal), diffuse AA (mimics TE), alopecia totalis (whole scalp), universalis (all body hair), AA incognita (diffuse thinning with yellow dots), beard/ eyebrow/ eyelash AA

**Q16. Associated conditions.**
- Atopy (eczema, asthma — poorer prognosis), thyroid autoimmunity, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, lupus, Down syndrome (higher prevalence), autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APECED), psychiatric stress, iron/ vitamin D deficiency

**Q17. Nail changes in AA.**
- Fine regular geometric pitting ('Scotch plaid'), trachyonychia, longitudinal ridging, red/ mottled lunulae, onychomadesis — more common in severe AA (marker of poor prognosis)

**Q18. How is SALT score calculated?**
- Severity of Alopecia Tool: scalp divided — vertex 40%, right side 18%, left side 18%, posterior 24%; % hair loss in each area × its weight summed (0–100); S1 25–49%, S2 25–49 ... (S0 no loss, S1 <25%, S2 25–49%, S3 50–74%, S4a 75–95%, S4b 96–99%, S5 100%); SALT ≤20 used as response target in trials

**Q19. Intralesional steroid therapy — practical points.**
- Triamcinolone acetonide 2.5–10 mg/ml (5 mg/ml commonly on scalp, 2.5 mg/ml on face/eyebrows), 0.05–0.1 ml per injection point 1 cm apart into deep dermis, every 4–6 weeks; maximum ~20 mg per session; side effects — atrophy (reversible), hypopigmentation, telangiectasia; best for limited patchy AA (<50% scalp) in adults

**Q20. Topical immunotherapy — mechanism and protocol.**
- Induces allergic contact dermatitis with diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP) or squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE) — antigenic competition shifts the immune response away from the follicle ('perifollicular CD4/CD8 ratio change')
- Sensitise with 2% on a small area, then weekly applications starting 0.001% and increasing until mild eczema persists 24–36 h; continue 12–24 weeks; response ~50–60% in extensive AA; side effects — severe eczema, lymphadenopathy, pigment changes (vitiligo/ dyschromia in confetti), urticaria

**Q21. Systemic steroids in AA — regimens.**
- Oral mini-pulse: betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg on two consecutive days weekly for 3–6 months
- Monthly pulses (prednisolone 300 mg or methylprednisolone 500 mg × 3 days), short courses of prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg tapering — relapse common on stopping; use for rapidly progressive disease

**Q22. JAK inhibitors in AA — details.**
- Baricitinib (JAK1/2) 2–4 mg/day — approved for severe AA (≥50% SALT) in adults; ritlecitinib (JAK3/ TEC) 50 mg/day — approved ≥12 y; deuruxolitinib (JAK1/2) approved in US; tofacitinib off-label (cheaper — widely used in India)
- Response: SALT ≤20 in ~35–40% at 36 weeks, better with longer duration; eyebrow/eyelash regrowth; relapse after stopping
- Monitoring: TB, hepatitis, CBC, lipids, LFT, CK; risks — infections, acne, VTE, MACE in older smokers

**Q23. Other treatments.**
- Topical minoxidil 5% (adjunct), anthralin short-contact (irritant therapy), topical steroids (children), methotrexate (± steroids), cyclosporine, azathioprine, simvastatin/ezetimibe (weak), excimer laser, PRP, low-level laser; hairpieces/ wigs, eyebrow tattooing/ microblading, psychological support
- Children: topical steroids, minoxidil, anthralin, DPCP (older children), mini-pulse steroids for extensive progressive disease

**Q24. Poor prognostic factors in AA.**
- Onset in childhood, long duration (>1 year), extensive loss (totalis/universalis), ophiasis pattern, nail involvement, atopy, family history, associated autoimmunity, Down syndrome, multiple relapses

**Q25. Differentiate AA from tinea capitis and trichotillomania.**
- Tinea capitis: scaling, inflammation, broken hairs, black dots, comma/corkscrew hairs on trichoscopy, KOH positive
