- Trichotillomania: irregular patches with hairs of varying lengths, no exclamation-mark hairs, broken hairs with trichoptilosis, V-sign, flame hairs on trichoscopy, behavioural history
- AA: smooth patch, exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots, regrowing vellus hairs

**Q26. What psychiatric issues are linked and how to address?**
- Anxiety, depression, social phobia, low self-esteem; validated QoL tools (AA-QLI, Skindex); offer counselling, support groups, camouflage; screen children for bullying

**Q27. What is the role of vitamin D and iron in AA?**
- Low serum vitamin D and ferritin are frequently reported in AA; correct deficiencies (not proven as primary treatment); topical calcipotriol has modest benefit in patchy AA

**Q28. Histopathology of AA by stage.**
- Acute: peribulbar 'swarm of bees' lymphocytic infiltrate around anagen bulbs, eosinophils, pigment incontinence
- Subacute: increased catagen/telogen hairs
- Chronic: miniaturised follicles, fibrous streamers, reduced terminal:vellus ratio, minimal inflammation; no scarring — follicles preserved

**Q29. Differential diagnosis of diffuse AA.**
- Telogen effluvium (normal trichoscopy, club hairs), androgenetic alopecia (miniaturisation pattern, no exclamation hairs), anagen effluvium (chemotherapy), syphilitic alopecia (moth-eaten), SLE alopecia, loose anagen syndrome (children — ruffled cuticle, painless pluckable hairs)

**Q30. Prognosis in patchy AA.**
- Most limited patchy AA regrow within 1 year (spontaneous regrowth in ~50%); relapses common (~85% have more than one episode); ~5–10% progress to totalis/universalis

## Quick spotter facts
- Smooth round patch with exclamation-mark hairs — AA
- Yellow dots, black dots on trichoscopy
- Severe AA — baricitinib/ritlecitinib

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Alopecia areata); SALT score; JAK inhibitor approvals. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Androgenetic alopecia — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 29 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Androgenetic alopecia** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define androgenetic alopecia (AGA).**
- Common, genetically determined, androgen-dependent, progressive non-scarring hair loss characterised by follicular miniaturisation in a patterned distribution; male pattern hair loss (MPHL) and female pattern hair loss (FPHL)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Genetic susceptibility (polygenic — androgen receptor gene on X chromosome, chromosome 20p11) + androgens: testosterone converted by 5α-reductase type 2 (outer root sheath/dermal papilla) to DHT → binds androgen receptors in dermal papilla of susceptible follicles → shortening of anagen and progressive miniaturisation (terminal → vellus-like), increased telogen; perifollicular micro-inflammation and fibrosis
- Occipital follicles are androgen-insensitive — basis for hair transplantation (donor dominance)
- FPHL: less clearly androgen-dependent; hyperandrogenism in some (PCOS)

**Q3. Discuss classifications (PYQ: AGA with a note on…).**
- Men: Hamilton–Norwood (I–VII; frontotemporal recession and vertex thinning; type A variant), BASP classification
- Women: Ludwig (I–III diffuse thinning of crown with preserved frontal hairline), Olsen ('Christmas tree' pattern — frontal accentuation), Sinclair (1–5) visual scale; Savin scale

**Q4. Clinical features.**
- MPHL: onset after puberty; bitemporal recession and vertex thinning progressing to bald crown with retained occipital/parietal fringe
- FPHL: diffuse thinning over crown and widening of central parting with intact frontal hairline; may begin at puberty or menopause
- Signs of hyperandrogenism in women: hirsutism, acne, irregular menses, AN (SAHA syndrome — Seborrhoea, Acne, Hirsutism, Alopecia)

**Q5. Trichoscopy.**
- Hair shaft diameter diversity >20% (key sign), increased vellus hairs, perifollicular brown halo (peripilar sign), yellow dots (few), single-hair follicular units, frontal > occipital difference (useful in FPHL)

**Q6. Discuss evaluation of hair loss (PYQ).**
- History: onset, duration, pattern, shedding vs thinning, family history, diet, drugs, illness/surgery 2–3 months before, menstrual/obstetric history, hair care practices
- Examination: pattern, scalp (scarring, scaling, erythema), hair pull test (>6 hairs/10% = active shedding), hair density, trichoscopy, signs of hyperandrogenism, nails, body hair
- Investigations: CBC, ferritin (aim >40–70 ng/ml), TSH, vitamin D, B12, zinc; women with hyperandrogenism — total/free testosterone, DHEAS, prolactin, 17-OH progesterone, pelvic USG; trichogram, biopsy (horizontal sections — terminal:vellus ratio <4:1 in AGA vs 7:1 normal) when doubtful

**Q7. Discuss drugs used in AGA including anti-androgens (PYQ).**
- Topical minoxidil 5% (men), 2–5% (women) twice daily or foam — prolongs anagen, increases follicle size (potassium channel opener, vasodilator); initial shedding at 2–8 weeks; results at 4–6 months; must continue
- Oral finasteride 1 mg/day (men) — 5α-reductase type 2 inhibitor, reduces scalp DHT ~60%; side effects — sexual dysfunction (low libido, erectile dysfunction ~1–2%), gynaecomastia, depression (post-finasteride syndrome debated), lowers PSA by ~50%; teratogenic to male fetus (women of child-bearing age must not take/handle broken tablets)
- Dutasteride 0.5 mg (types 1 and 2 inhibitor; more potent) — oral or mesotherapy
- Topical finasteride 0.25% spray (lower systemic exposure)
- Low-dose oral minoxidil 0.25–5 mg/day (men and women) — side effects hypertrichosis, pedal oedema, tachycardia, postural hypotension
- Women: spironolactone 50–200 mg/day, cyproterone acetate (with ethinyl oestradiol), flutamide/bicalutamide (hepatotoxicity monitoring), OCP with anti-androgenic progestins; finasteride/dutasteride only in post-menopausal women
- Adjuncts: PRP injections, microneedling (with minoxidil), low-level laser therapy (LLLT), ketoconazole 2% shampoo, nutritional correction (iron, vitamin D)
- Hair transplantation: follicular unit transplantation (strip/FUT) or follicular unit extraction (FUE) — for stable disease, adequate donor area; continue medical therapy
- Camouflage: scalp micropigmentation, fibres, wigs

**Q8. Discuss the effects of drugs on hair (PYQ).**
- Drug-induced hair loss: anagen effluvium (chemotherapy — cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, taxanes; within 1–4 weeks), telogen effluvium (retinoids, anticoagulants — heparin, warfarin; β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, antithyroids, anticonvulsants — valproate, lithium, OCP withdrawal, interferons, statins)
- Drug-induced hypertrichosis/hirsutism: minoxidil, cyclosporine, phenytoin, diazoxide, streptomycin, steroids, danazol, testosterone, latanoprost (eyelashes), EGFR inhibitors (trichomegaly)
- Hair colour change: chloroquine (bleaching), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib — depigmentation; or darkening), PD-1 inhibitors; curling with retinoids/EGFR inhibitors

**Q9. Prognosis.**
- Progressive without treatment; early treatment preserves rather than fully restores; effect lost within months of stopping

**Q10. Describe the Hamilton–Norwood classification.**
- Male pattern: I — minimal frontotemporal recession; II — symmetrical triangular frontotemporal recession; III — deep recession (III vertex — vertex thinning with stage II recession); IV — further recession + vertex balding separated by band; V — band narrower; VI — bridge lost, confluent; VII — only horseshoe band at sides and back; type A variants — anterior-to-posterior progression without vertex

**Q11. Describe the Ludwig and Sinclair scales for female pattern hair loss.**
- Ludwig: grade I — mild crown thinning with preserved frontal hairline; II — marked; III — near-total crown baldness
- Sinclair: 1–5 based on widening of the central part (stage 1 normal → 5 advanced); Olsen 'Christmas tree' pattern — frontal accentuation of part widening

**Q12. Explain the pathogenesis in detail.**
- Genetic (polygenic — androgen receptor gene on X chromosome, EDA2R, 20p11) + androgens: testosterone converted to DHT by 5α-reductase type 2 (and 1) in dermal papilla → DHT binds AR → shortening of anagen, progressive follicular miniaturisation (terminal → vellus-like), increased telogen
- Other factors: perifollicular micro-inflammation and fibrosis, Wnt/β-catenin down-regulation, PGD2 (inhibits hair growth) increase, ageing, oxidative stress

**Q13. Trichoscopy features.**
- Hair shaft thickness variability >20% (anisotrichosis), increased vellus hairs, yellow dots (few), perifollicular brown halo (peripilar sign), single-hair follicular units, scalp pigmentation honeycomb; frontal more than occipital differences

**Q14. Minoxidil — mechanism, use and side effects.**
- Potassium-channel opener → vasodilation, prolongs anagen, enlarges miniaturised follicles, VEGF up-regulation; topical 5% (men; 2–5% women) twice daily or foam; effect after 3–6 months, maintained only while used
- Low-dose oral minoxidil 0.25–5 mg/day — increasingly used (better adherence); side effects — hypertrichosis, pedal oedema, tachycardia, postural hypotension; topical — irritant/allergic dermatitis (propylene glycol), initial shedding, facial hypertrichosis
- Sulfotransferase activity in follicle predicts response

**Q15. Finasteride and dutasteride.**
- Finasteride 1 mg/day (type 2 5α-reductase inhibitor — reduces scalp DHT ~60%); dutasteride 0.5 mg (types 1 and 2, more potent); effect after 6–12 months; side effects — reduced libido, erectile dysfunction (~1–2%), gynaecomastia, depression ('post-finasteride syndrome' debated); lowers PSA by ~50% (double the value for screening); teratogenic — women of child-bearing potential shouldn't handle crushed tablets
- Topical finasteride 0.25% spray — lower systemic levels

**Q16. Treatment of female pattern hair loss.**
- Topical minoxidil 2–5%, low-dose oral minoxidil, anti-androgens (spironolactone 50–200 mg/day, cyproterone acetate with OCP, flutamide/ bicalutamide), finasteride/ dutasteride in post-menopausal women (contraception if pre-menopausal), correct iron/ thyroid, PRP, LLLT, camouflage, hair transplant

**Q17. Platelet-rich plasma and other procedures.**
- PRP: autologous platelet concentrate (growth factors — PDGF, VEGF, EGF) injected into scalp monthly × 3 then every 3–6 months; modest evidence
- Microneedling (with minoxidil), low-level laser therapy (650–900 nm) devices, botulinum toxin (limited), mesotherapy; hair transplant — follicular unit transplantation (strip) or follicular unit extraction (FUE); need stable donor area and medical therapy to maintain native hair

**Q18. Evaluation of a woman with hair loss — what history and tests?**
- Duration, pattern (diffuse vs patterned), shedding vs thinning, menstrual history, hirsutism/ acne, pregnancy, diet/ weight loss, drugs, illness, family history; examine part width, hair pull, trichoscopy
- Tests: CBC, ferritin (aim >40–70 ng/ml), TSH, vitamin D, B12, zinc; androgen profile if signs of hyperandrogenism; scalp biopsy (horizontal sections) when diagnosis unclear

**Q19. Histopathology of AGA on horizontal sections.**
- Increased vellus-like (miniaturised) hairs with terminal:vellus ratio <4:1 (normal ~7:1), increased telogen, fibrous streamers beneath miniaturised follicles, mild perifollicular lymphocytic inflammation, normal total follicle number (non-scarring)

**Q20. Drugs causing hair loss (PYQ: effects of drugs on hair).**
- Anagen effluvium: chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, taxanes), colchicine, thallium, radiation
- Telogen effluvium: anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin), antithyroid drugs, β-blockers, retinoids (acitretin, isotretinoin), lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, oral contraceptive withdrawal, ACE inhibitors, statins, interferon, antidepressants
- Hypertrichosis/hirsutism: minoxidil, cyclosporine, phenytoin, androgens, steroids, diazoxide, latanoprost (eyelashes), PUVA
- Hair colour changes: chloroquine (lightening), tyrosine kinase inhibitors, cyclosporine/ EGFR inhibitors (curly hair)

**Q21. What is frontal fibrosing alopecia and why differentiate?**
- Scarring alopecia (LPP variant) in post-menopausal women — band-like recession of frontal/ temporal hairline with perifollicular erythema/ scale, loss of eyebrows, lonely hairs, facial papules; association with sunscreen/ leave-on cosmetics debated
- Differs from AGA (non-scarring, preserved follicular openings); treat with 5-α-reductase inhibitors, HCQ, intralesional steroids, low-dose isotretinoin

**Q22. AGA and systemic associations.**
- Early-onset AGA in men associated with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, coronary heart disease, benign prostatic hyperplasia, hypertension; early 'male PCOS' phenotype; screen cardiovascular risk factors in young men with severe early AGA

**Q23. Counselling points in AGA treatment.**
- Medical therapy aims to stop progression and partial regrowth; initial shedding with minoxidil in first 2–8 weeks; assessment at 6 and 12 months with standardised photographs; must continue indefinitely; combination therapy better; realistic expectations and camouflage options (fibres, tinted sprays, wigs, scalp micropigmentation)

**Q24. Differential diagnosis of patterned hair loss.**
- Telogen effluvium, diffuse AA, frontal fibrosing alopecia, LPP, traction alopecia (frontotemporal in tight hairstyles), trichotillomania, hypothyroidism, iron deficiency, secondary syphilis, SLE

**Q25. What is the 'senescent alopecia'?**
- Age-related diffuse thinning after 60 years without miniaturisation pattern or androgen dependency — uniform reduction of follicles and diameter; may overlap with AGA

**Q26. What newer drugs are in development for AGA?**
- Topical clascoterone solution (androgen receptor antagonist), pyrilutamide, KX-826, JAK inhibitors (topical — studied), Wnt activators, botulinum toxin, exosomes and stem-cell-derived products (unproven) — check status before quoting

**Q27. What are the side effects of hair transplant?**
- Folliculitis, cysts, scalp numbness, shock loss of native hair, 'pluggy' appearance (older techniques), donor-site scarring (strip), unnatural hairline, infection, bleeding

**Q28. What scales measure hair growth in trials?**
- Global photographic assessment, phototrichogram/ trichoscan (hair count and density in a target area — 1 cm²), hair weight, patient self-assessment questionnaires

**Q29. Why does the occiput not bald in AGA?**
- Occipital follicles have fewer androgen receptors and less 5α-reductase activity — 'donor dominance' (transplanted occipital follicles maintain resistance at recipient site)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bitemporal recession + vertex thinning, hair diameter diversity >20% — AGA
- Finasteride 1 mg + minoxidil 5% — men; spironolactone/minoxidil — women

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Androgenetic alopecia); Hamilton–Norwood and Ludwig classifications. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Anogenital warts — viva
posts.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 18 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Anogenital warts** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. What are anogenital warts? Which HPV types?**
- Commonest viral STI — benign epithelial proliferations of anogenital skin and mucosa
- ~90% due to low-risk HPV 6 and 11; co-infection with high-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33) possible
- Incubation 3 weeks to 8 months (average 2–3 months); many infections subclinical

**Q2. Describe the clinical types.**
- Condyloma acuminata: soft, pink, filiform/cauliflower-like papillomas on moist areas (prepuce, frenulum, coronal sulcus, vulva, introitus, perianal)
- Papular (dome-shaped, keratinised — shaft, pubis), flat/macular (cervix — seen with acetic acid), keratotic (dry skin)
- Giant condyloma (Buschke–Löwenstein tumour)
- Intra-meatal, vaginal, cervical, anal canal (anoscopy in receptive anal sex)

**Q3. What is the acetowhite test?**
- 5% acetic acid for 3–5 min turns HPV-infected epithelium white — helps find subclinical lesions; not specific (any inflamed/traumatised skin)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Normal variants: pearly penile papules (rows on corona), vestibular papillae (symmetrical, separate bases), Fordyce spots, sebaceous hyperplasia
- Condyloma lata (secondary syphilis — flat, moist, grey; VDRL positive), molluscum, seborrhoeic keratosis, skin tags, lichen planus, bowenoid papulosis, verrucous carcinoma/SCC, Buschke–Löwenstein tumour

**Q5. When do you biopsy?**
- Atypical (pigmented, indurated, fixed, ulcerated) lesions, immunocompromised patient, no response or worsening on therapy, older patient

**Q6. Discuss treatment options.**
- Patient-applied: podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution/0.15% cream twice daily 3 days per week, up to 4 weeks; imiquimod 5% cream 3 times/week overnight up to 16 weeks; sinecatechins 15% (green-tea extract)
- Provider-applied/ablative: cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) weekly; TCA 80–90%; podophyllin 10–25% in tincture benzoin (wash off after 1–4 h; max 0.5 ml/10 cm² per session); electrocautery, radiofrequency, CO2 laser, scissor excision
- Choice depends on number, size, site, keratinisation, cost, pregnancy

**Q7. Write a short note on podophyllin (PYQ).**
- Resin from Podophyllum emodi (Indian) or P. peltatum; active podophyllotoxin binds tubulin → arrests mitosis in metaphase → necrosis of wart
- Podophyllin is non-standardised and contains mutagenic flavonoids; podophyllotoxin is purified and safer for self-use
- Toxicity: local erosion; systemic absorption from large areas/mucosa → peripheral neuropathy, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, coma
- Contraindicated in pregnancy, on cervix/urethra/anal canal, bleeding lesions

**Q8. Management in pregnancy.**
- Warts enlarge and become friable; avoid podophyllin, podophyllotoxin, (imiquimod — limited data)
- Cryotherapy, TCA, excision/electrocautery
- Caesarean only if warts obstruct the birth canal or would bleed heavily; risk of juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis in baby is low

**Q9. What about warts in children?**
- Consider sexual abuse but also vertical transmission (up to 2–3 years), autoinoculation from hand warts, non-sexual household spread; careful history and examination, involve paediatric team

**Q10. What other evaluation and counselling is needed?**
- Screen for other STIs (HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B), examine partner, Pap smear/HPV test for women (cervical screening), anoscopy if anal warts
- Explain recurrence (~30% within 3 months), condoms reduce but don't eliminate transmission, HPV vaccination

**Q11. Discuss cervical intraepithelial neoplasia link (PYQ).**
- High-risk HPV (16, 18) E6 binds p53, E7 binds Rb → cell-cycle dysregulation → CIN 1–3 → invasive cancer
- Screening: Pap smear (cytology), HPV DNA test, VIA/VILI (visual inspection in low-resource settings)
- Prevention: HPV vaccine before sexual debut

**Q12. What is the role of HPV vaccines in genital warts?**
- Quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines (contain 6, 11) prevent ~90% of genital warts — reduction seen in vaccinated populations (Australia); not therapeutic for existing warts

**Q13. Describe the histopathology of condyloma acuminatum.**
- Papillomatosis, acanthosis with broad rete, parakeratosis, koilocytes (perinuclear halo, raisinoid nuclei) in upper layers — may be sparse in old/treated lesions; podophyllin-treated warts show bizarre mitoses (pseudo-dysplasia)

**Q14. Which HPV detection methods are used?**
- PCR/ hybrid capture for HPV DNA typing (not routinely needed for warts), p16 immunostaining (high-risk HPV surrogate in intraepithelial neoplasia), cytology (Pap smear) for cervix

**Q15. What is imiquimod's mechanism?**
- TLR7 agonist → local IFN-α, TNF-α, IL-12 production → Th1 cell-mediated antiviral response; 5% cream 3 nights/week, wash after 6–10 h, up to 16 weeks; erythema, erosions, flu-like symptoms; lower recurrence than ablation

**Q16. What is the role of cryotherapy for genital warts?**
- Liquid nitrogen spray/ cotton bud, 10–20 s freeze, 2 freeze–thaw cycles, weekly; safe in pregnancy; side effects — pain, blistering, hypopigmentation; less effective for large keratinised warts

**Q17. Anal warts — special points.**
- Seen with receptive anal sex but also perianal spread; examine anal canal (proctoscopy); high-risk HPV → anal intraepithelial neoplasia/ cancer (MSM with HIV — screening with anal cytology/ high-resolution anoscopy); avoid podophyllotoxin inside anal canal

**Q18. Why are warts more extensive in HIV?**
- Impaired cell-mediated immunity → larger, numerous, recalcitrant warts, higher dysplasia and malignancy (anal, cervical); may worsen as IRIS after ART; need biopsy of atypical lesions and long follow-up

## Quick spotter facts
- Acetowhitening — subclinical HPV
- HPV 6/11 — 90% of genital warts
- Pearly penile papules are normal — don't treat

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (HPV, genital warts); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Asteatotic eczema — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Asteatotic eczema** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What is asteatotic eczema? Synonyms?**
- Eczema arising on very dry (xerotic) skin with fine cracks — eczema craquelé, winter itch, xerotic eczema
- Commonest in elderly on shins, also arms, trunk

**Q2. Classify eczemas (PYQ).**
- Endogenous: atopic, seborrhoeic, discoid (nummular), asteatotic, pompholyx, lichen simplex chronicus, venous (stasis), juvenile plantar dermatosis, pityriasis alba
- Exogenous: irritant contact, allergic contact, photoallergic/phototoxic, infective (infectious eczematoid), dermatophytide/id reactions
- Morphological stage: acute (vesicles, oozing), subacute (scaling, crusts), chronic (lichenification)

**Q3. Why does the skin crack?**
- Reduced stratum corneum lipids (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids) and natural moisturising factor with age → loss of water, shrinkage of corneocytes → fissures in a 'crazy-paving'/dried river bed pattern; irritant inflammation follows

**Q4. Predisposing factors.**
- Ageing, low humidity (winter, air-conditioning, heating), frequent hot baths and soaps, diuretics, hypothyroidism, malnutrition (zinc, essential fatty acids), hospitalisation
- Drugs: statins, retinoids, cimetidine, EGFR inhibitors
- Widespread sudden asteatotic eczema in elderly may be paraneoplastic (lymphoma) or with hypothyroidism

**Q5. Clinical features.**
- Dry, scaly, itchy skin with superficial polygonal fissures and red edges (crazy-paving); later erythematous plaques, excoriations, secondary infection
- Worse in winter, improves in summer

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Ichthyosis vulgaris (since childhood, family history), stasis dermatitis (varicose veins, haemosiderin), nummular eczema, allergic contact dermatitis to topical medicaments, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, xerosis from renal failure, scabies in elderly

**Q7. Management.**
- Reduce bathing frequency, lukewarm water, soap substitutes, pat dry
- Liberal emollients immediately after bath (soak-and-seal); urea 5–10%, lactic acid 12% (avoid on fissured inflamed skin — sting)
- Mild–moderate potency topical steroid ointment for 1–2 weeks for inflamed areas; humidifier, cotton clothing
- Treat associated hypothyroidism, review drugs

**Q8. What is the role of essential fatty acids? (PYQ)**
- Linoleic acid is needed for ceramide synthesis and barrier function; deficiency (TPN, malabsorption) gives dry scaly eczematous skin, alopecia, poor wound healing — corrected by EFA supplementation/topical oils

**Q9. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q10. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q11. What emollients are best and why?**
- Ointments (petrolatum — occlusive) most effective; humectants (glycerol, urea 5–10%, lactic acid) attract water; physiological lipid mixtures (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA 3:1:1) repair barrier; apply within 3 minutes after bathing; 'soak and smear'

**Q12. Drug causes of xerosis/ asteatosis.**
- Diuretics, statins/ lipid-lowering agents, retinoids, cimetidine, EGFR inhibitors, BRAF inhibitors, clofazimine, nicotinic acid, protease inhibitors

**Q13. What is 'winter itch' and pruritus of the elderly?**
- Generalised itch without primary lesions in elderly during winter — xerosis-related; exclude systemic causes (renal, hepatic, thyroid, iron deficiency, haematological malignancy, drugs, neuropathic); treat with emollients, cooling agents, avoid hot baths, sedating antihistamines cautiously (falls)

**Q14. How does ageing affect the skin barrier?**
- Reduced epidermal lipid synthesis (ceramides, cholesterol), reduced filaggrin/NMF, slower barrier recovery, reduced sebum and sweat, higher pH — dry, itchy, easily irritated skin (xerosis of ageing)

**Q15. Why should widespread asteatotic eczema in elderly be investigated?**
- Can be a sign of hypothyroidism, malnutrition (zinc, essential fatty acid deficiency), renal failure, liver disease, drugs (diuretics, statins), lymphoma/ internal malignancy (acquired ichthyosis), HIV — check thyroid, renal/liver function, CBC

## Quick spotter facts
- Crazy-paving fissured shins in elderly in winter — eczema craquelé

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Eczemas). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Atopic dermatitis — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 37 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Atopic dermatitis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define atopy and atopic dermatitis.**
- Atopy: genetic tendency to produce IgE against common environmental allergens, with asthma, allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, AD, food allergy
- Atopic dermatitis: chronic relapsing intensely itchy inflammatory skin disease with typical age-related distribution, often first sign of the 'atopic march'

**Q2. Epidemiology?**
- 15–20% of children and 2–5% of adults worldwide (lower but rising in India); 60% begin in first year, 85% by 5 years
- Many improve by adolescence; adult-onset or persistent forms recognised

**Q3. Explain the pathogenesis (outside-in and inside-out).**
- Barrier defect: filaggrin (FLG) loss-of-function mutations (strongest genetic risk), reduced ceramides, increased TEWL, alkaline pH, kallikrein (KLK5/7) overactivity (SPINK5) → allergen and microbe entry
- Immune dysregulation: acute Th2 (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31), Th22 (IL-22) and in chronic phase Th1/Th17; keratinocyte alarmins TSLP, IL-33, IL-25; IgE sensitisation
- Microbiome: reduced diversity, S. aureus colonisation (superantigens, δ-toxin); Malassezia (head-neck)
- Itch: IL-31, IL-4/13 act on sensory neurons, histamine-independent — itch-scratch cycle

**Q4. Write a short note on filaggrin (PYQ).**
- 'Filament aggregating protein' — derived from profilaggrin in keratohyaline granules; aggregates keratin filaments in the stratum corneum and is broken down into natural moisturising factor (urocanic acid, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid) that hydrates and acidifies skin
- FLG mutations (R501X, 2282del4) cause ichthyosis vulgaris and increase risk of AD, asthma (with AD), peanut allergy and contact sensitisation; Indian mutations differ

**Q5. What are the Hanifin and Rajka criteria?**
- Major (need ≥3 of 4): pruritus; typical morphology and distribution (flexural lichenification in adults, facial and extensor in infants); chronic or chronically relapsing dermatitis; personal or family history of atopy
- Minor (need ≥3 of 23): xerosis, ichthyosis/palmar hyperlinearity/keratosis pilaris, immediate skin-test reactivity, raised IgE, early age of onset, tendency to skin infections, non-specific hand/foot dermatitis, nipple eczema, cheilitis, recurrent conjunctivitis, Dennie–Morgan fold, keratoconus, anterior subcapsular cataract, orbital darkening, facial pallor/erythema, pityriasis alba, anterior neck folds, itch when sweating, wool/lipid-solvent intolerance, perifollicular accentuation, food intolerance, course influenced by environment/emotions, white dermographism/delayed blanch

**Q6. What are the UK Working Party criteria?**
- Must have itchy skin (or parental report of scratching) in last 12 months, plus ≥3 of: history of flexural involvement (cheeks in <10 y), personal history of asthma/hay fever (or first-degree relative in <4 y), generally dry skin in last year, visible flexural eczema (cheeks/forehead/outer limbs in <4 y), onset before 2 years (not used if <4 y)
- Simpler, validated for epidemiology

**Q7. Describe the phases of AD.**
- Infantile (2 months–2 years): face (cheeks, sparing nose — 'headlight sign'), scalp, extensors; oozing, crusting; napkin area often spared
- Childhood (2–12 years): flexures (antecubital, popliteal), wrists, ankles, neck; lichenification, excoriation
- Adolescent/adult: flexures, face and neck ('head-and-neck dermatitis'), hands, eyelids, nipples; prurigo-like and lichenified
- Variants: nummular, follicular (common in darker skin), prurigo form, erythrodermic, juvenile plantar dermatosis, pityriasis alba

**Q8. What are the stigmata of atopy?**
- Dennie–Morgan infraorbital fold, Hertoghe's sign (thinning of lateral eyebrows), periorbital darkening, palmar hyperlinearity, keratosis pilaris, white dermographism, pityriasis alba, anterior neck folds, Hertoghe's, keratoconus and cataract

**Q9. Complications of AD.**
- Bacterial: impetiginisation (S. aureus), cellulitis
- Viral: eczema herpeticum (emergency), eczema molluscatum, eczema vaccinatum, eczema coxsackium
- Fungal: Malassezia head-neck dermatitis
- Erythroderma, growth retardation, sleep loss, psychosocial impact, ocular (keratoconus, cataract, conjunctivitis — also with dupilumab), contact allergy to topical agents, steroid side effects

**Q10. How do you assess severity?**
- SCORAD (extent by rule of nines, intensity of 6 signs 0–3, subjective itch and sleep 0–10 each; >50 severe), EASI (0–72; area × intensity in 4 regions), IGA, POEM (patient-oriented), DLQI/CDLQI for quality of life

**Q11. Investigations — are they needed?**
- Diagnosis is clinical
- Total IgE and eosinophils (raised in extrinsic AD), specific IgE/skin prick tests only if history suggests food allergy (avoid indiscriminate elimination diets)
- Swab for culture in infected eczema; Tzanck/PCR for suspected eczema herpeticum
- Patch test for suspected contact allergy (topical medicaments, emollients)
- Biopsy if diagnosis doubtful (CTCL in adult-onset)

**Q12. Differential diagnosis in infants and adults.**
- Infants: seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy, folds, non-itchy, early), scabies, Netherton syndrome, Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, hyper-IgE syndrome, SCID/Omenn, zinc deficiency, LCH, phenylketonuria
- Adults: contact dermatitis, psoriasis, CTCL (mycosis fungoides, Sézary), drug eruption, dermatitis herpetiformis, scabies, seborrhoeic dermatitis, photodermatoses

**Q13. Write a short note on Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (PYQ).**
- X-linked recessive WAS gene mutation: triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets (bleeding, petechiae) and recurrent infections (pyogenic, opportunistic); risk of lymphoma and autoimmunity; cure by haematopoietic stem cell transplant / gene therapy

**Q14. Management principles — stepwise.**
- Education, written action plan, avoid triggers (soaps, wool, sweat, heat, stress, dust mites), nails short
- Emollients liberally (≥250–500 g/week in adults), bath oils, soap substitutes; ceramide-dominant moisturisers
- Topical corticosteroids: right potency for site/age, fingertip-unit dosing, once daily; proactive twice-weekly application to healed areas to prevent flares
- Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.03%/0.1%, pimecrolimus 1%) — face, eyelids, flexures, steroid-sparing; burning at start
- Topical PDE4 inhibitor (crisaborole), topical JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib cream), tapinarof
- Wet wraps for severe flares; dilute bleach baths for recurrent infections
- Phototherapy: narrow-band UVB, UVA1
- Systemic: cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day (fast, short-term), methotrexate 7.5–25 mg weekly, azathioprine (check TPMT), mycophenolate; systemic steroids only short bridging
- Biologics: dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα), tralokinumab and lebrikizumab (anti-IL-13), nemolizumab (anti-IL-31RA)
- Oral JAK inhibitors: baricitinib, upadacitinib, abrocitinib (monitor lipids, blood counts, infections, thrombosis)
- Antihistamines: sedating ones at night only for sleep; non-sedating have little effect on AD itch

**Q15. What is the role of diet and allergy testing?**
- Food allergy relevant mainly in infants with moderate–severe AD (egg, milk, peanut, wheat, soy); confirm by history + specific IgE/prick test ± oral food challenge
- Unnecessary elimination diets cause malnutrition; early introduction of peanut/egg reduces allergy (LEAP study)

**Q16. What is the atopic march?**
- Sequence: AD in infancy → food allergy → asthma → allergic rhinitis; barrier dysfunction allows epicutaneous sensitisation
- Early emollient use for prevention showed inconsistent results

**Q17. What is eczema herpeticum and how do you treat it?**
- Disseminated HSV on eczematous skin — monomorphic punched-out erosions, crusts, fever; urgent oral/IV acyclovir, stop topical steroid briefly/treat secondary infection, eye check

**Q18. Fingertip unit (FTU) concept.**
- Amount of cream from a 5 mm tube squeezed from the tip to the first crease of the index finger ≈ 0.5 g — covers two adult palms (2% BSA)
- Adult: face/neck 2.5 FTU, one arm 3, hand 1, one leg 6, foot 2, front trunk 7, back 7

**Q19. Side effects of topical steroids.**
- Atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, purpura, steroid rosacea/perioral dermatitis, acneiform eruption, hypertrichosis, tinea incognito, contact allergy, tachyphylaxis, glaucoma/cataract (eyelids), HPA suppression and growth retardation (children, potent and extensive use)
- Topical steroid addiction/withdrawal (red skin syndrome) on face/genitals with prolonged misuse

**Q20. How does dupilumab work and what are its side effects?**
- Monoclonal antibody against IL-4 receptor α — blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling
- Adults and children ≥6 months; 600 mg loading then 300 mg every 2 weeks SC (adults)
- Side effects: conjunctivitis/keratitis, injection-site reactions, facial erythema (head-neck dermatitis), eosinophilia, arthralgia; no lab monitoring needed

**Q21. Prognosis?**
- Most childhood AD improves; poor prognostic factors: early onset severe disease, FLG mutations, associated asthma/rhinitis, family history, female sex, adult persistence, hand eczema in adulthood (wet work)

**Q22. What is the role of S. aureus and how do you reduce it?**
- Colonises 70–90% of lesions (vs 5% healthy skin); superantigens (SEA, SEB, TSST-1) activate T cells and IgE production; δ-toxin degranulates mast cells; biofilms block sweat ducts
- Reduce: treat inflammation (steroids/ TCIs reduce colonisation), dilute bleach baths (0.005%) twice weekly, antiseptic washes (chlorhexidine), short courses of systemic antibiotics for clinically infected eczema; avoid long-term topical antibiotics (resistance)

**Q23. What are wet wrap therapy and its indications?**
- After bath and emollient (± diluted topical steroid), apply a wet tubular bandage layer then a dry layer, for several hours/ overnight for 3–7 days — cools, reduces itch, enhances absorption; for severe flares/ children; watch for infection and steroid absorption

**Q24. Describe topical calcineurin inhibitors in detail.**
- Tacrolimus ointment 0.03% (≥2 y) and 0.1% (adults); pimecrolimus 1% cream (≥3 months in some countries) — inhibit calcineurin → block T-cell IL-2 transcription
- No atrophy — ideal for face, eyelids, flexures, genitals; proactive twice weekly use reduces flares
- Side effects: burning/ stinging (first week), alcohol flushing, local infections; 'black box' lymphoma warning not substantiated by long-term data

**Q25. Oral JAK inhibitors in AD — details.**
- Upadacitinib (15–30 mg/day, JAK1), abrocitinib (100–200 mg/day, JAK1), baricitinib (2–4 mg/day, JAK1/2) — rapid itch relief within days, high EASI-75 rates
- Screen: TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV, CBC, lipids, LFT, CK, pregnancy; risks — infections (herpes zoster), acne, raised CPK and lipids, cytopenias, VTE, MACE and malignancy (boxed warning in older smokers)

**Q26. Systemic cyclosporine in AD — practical points.**
- 3–5 mg/kg/day in two doses for short-term (3–6 months, up to 1–2 years) — rapid response; monitor BP and creatinine (reduce dose if >25–30% rise), potassium, magnesium, lipids; drug interactions (CYP3A4); taper to avoid rebound; suitable for children with severe disease

**Q27. Methotrexate and azathioprine in AD.**
- Methotrexate 7.5–25 mg/week (0.3–0.5 mg/kg/week in children) with folic acid — slower onset (8–12 weeks), good long-term option, cheap
- Azathioprine 1–3 mg/kg/day, dose by TPMT activity (and NUDT15 in Asians); side effects — marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, nausea, infection, skin cancer risk with UV

**Q28. Phototherapy for AD.**
- NB-UVB 2–3 times weekly for chronic moderate disease (adults, older children); UVA1 (medium dose) for acute flares; PUVA rarely; avoid in photosensitive AD/ XP; maintain emollients

**Q29. Explain 'proactive therapy'.**
- After clearing a flare, continue twice-weekly topical steroid (mid-potency) or tacrolimus on previously affected sites plus daily emollients — significantly reduces flare frequency compared with reactive use

**Q30. Adult-onset AD — what to consider?**
- Exclude contact dermatitis (patch test), scabies, drug eruption, CTCL (biopsy), HIV, dermatitis herpetiformis; head-and-neck dermatitis (Malassezia-driven — antifungals), hand eczema (occupational); more often IgE-normal (intrinsic)

**Q31. Intrinsic vs extrinsic AD.**
- Extrinsic (~80%): high total IgE, specific IgE to aeroallergens/foods, personal/family atopy, FLG mutations more
- Intrinsic (~20%): normal IgE, no specific sensitisation, female, later onset, milder, nickel/metal allergy more common

**Q32. Ocular complications of AD and dupilumab.**
- Atopic keratoconjunctivitis, vernal keratoconjunctivitis, keratoconus (eye rubbing), anterior/posterior subcapsular cataract (disease + steroids), retinal detachment; dupilumab-associated conjunctivitis (goblet-cell loss; treat with lubricants, tacrolimus eye ointment, steroid drops) — ophthalmology referral

**Q33. Psychosocial burden and sleep in AD.**
- Itch–scratch-related sleep loss (child and parents), ADHD association, depression/anxiety, school/work absenteeism, family stress; measure with POEM, CDLQI/DLQI, sleep scores; sedating antihistamines short-term at night, behavioural therapy, education programmes ('eczema school')

**Q34. What is the role of probiotics, vitamin D and dietary supplements?**
- Evidence is weak/inconsistent: probiotics in pregnancy/infancy may modestly reduce AD risk; vitamin D supplementation may help winter-related flares in deficient children; evening primrose oil, fish oil — not recommended

**Q35. What is follicular (papular) eczema?**
- Pattern common in darker skin (African, Indian): tiny skin-coloured follicular papules on trunk/extensors giving 'goosebump' appearance; part of AD; responds to emollients and mild steroids

**Q36. Prevention of AD in high-risk infants — current evidence.**
- Daily emollients from birth — large trials (BEEP, PreventADALL) showed no prevention; exclusive breastfeeding for 4–6 months is encouraged for other benefits; early introduction of allergenic foods (peanut/egg from 4–6 months) reduces food allergy

**Q37. Differentiate AD from scabies in an infant.**
- Scabies: burrows, palms/soles and axillary nodules, other family members itching, acropustules, rapid onset
- AD: chronic relapsing, cheeks/extensors, family history of atopy, xerosis; both can coexist — scrape suspicious lesions

## Quick spotter facts
- Infant cheeks + scalp, nose spared — infantile AD
- Dennie–Morgan fold, Hertoghe's sign — atopic stigmata
- FLG mutation — ichthyosis vulgaris and AD

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Atopic dermatitis); Hanifin & Rajka and UK Working Party criteria; Indian consensus on AD. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Basal cell carcinoma — viva
posts.summary: Premalignant & malignant tumours · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Basal cell carcinoma** (Premalignant & malignant tumours)_

**Q1. Define BCC.**
- Commonest skin (and human) cancer — slow-growing, locally invasive malignant tumour arising from basaloid cells of the epidermis/follicular stem cells; rarely metastasises (<0.1%) but can destroy local tissues ('rodent ulcer')
- In India: commoner than SCC on face; pigmented BCC is the predominant type in Indian skin

**Q2. Discuss risk factors (PYQ).**
- UV radiation (intermittent intense exposure, childhood sunburns), fair skin/Fitzpatrick I–II, light eyes, freckling, older age, male
- Ionising radiation, arsenic (wells, Fowler's solution — multiple trunk BCCs), immunosuppression (transplant), PUVA, previous BCC
- Genetic: basal cell naevus syndrome (Gorlin — PTCH1), xeroderma pigmentosum, Bazex–Dupré–Christol, Rombo syndrome, albinism, nevus sebaceous (trichoblastoma more often)
- Molecular: Hedgehog pathway activation — PTCH1 loss or SMO activation (>90%), p53 mutations (UV signature)

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Nodular (commonest ~50%): pearly translucent papule/nodule with rolled border, arborising telangiectasia, central ulceration ('rodent ulcer') — face (inner canthus, nasolabial fold, nose)
- Pigmented nodular (common in Indians — brown-black, mimics melanoma)
- Superficial (trunk — red scaly plaque with thread-like pearly border, multicentric)
- Morphoeic/infiltrative/sclerosing (ivory scar-like plaque, ill-defined, aggressive, high recurrence)
- Micronodular, basosquamous (metatypical — more aggressive, can metastasise), cystic, fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (pink pedunculated lower back)
- Write a short note on multicentric (superficial) BCC (PYQ): multiple foci within one lesion; on trunk; suitable for topical/cryotherapy/PDT

**Q4. Discuss the HPE of BCC (PYQ).**
- Nests and islands of basaloid cells with scanty cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, peripheral palisading, retraction artefact (clefts between tumour and mucinous stroma), mitoses and apoptotic cells, myxoid stroma; connection to epidermis
- Variants: nodular (large nests), superficial (buds from the epidermis), micronodular, infiltrative/morphoeic (thin cords in sclerotic stroma), keratotic, adenoid, pigmented, basosquamous
- Immunohistochemistry: BerEP4 positive (vs SCC negative), Bcl-2 diffuse, CK5/6

**Q5. Dermoscopy.**
- Arborising (tree-like branching) vessels, blue-grey ovoid nests and globules, leaf-like structures, spoke-wheel areas, ulceration, shiny white structures; absence of pigment network

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Nodular: intradermal naevus, sebaceous hyperplasia, molluscum, keratoacanthoma/SCC, amelanotic melanoma, adnexal tumours (trichoepithelioma)
- Pigmented: melanoma, seborrhoeic keratosis, blue naevus
- Superficial: Bowen's, psoriasis, eczema, AK, tinea
- Morphoeic: scar, morphoea
- Ulcerated: SCC, chronic infections (lupus vulgaris, leishmaniasis)

**Q7. Discuss the management of BCC (PYQ).**
- Risk stratification (NCCN): high-risk — location (H-zone of face: central face, eyelids, eyebrows, nose, lips, chin, ear, temple; hands, feet, genitals), size ≥2 cm on trunk/limbs, ill-defined border, recurrent, immunosuppression, prior radiotherapy, aggressive histology (morphoeic, infiltrative, micronodular, basosquamous), perineural invasion
- Surgery (gold standard): standard excision with 4 mm margins (low-risk) / wider for high-risk; Mohs micrographic surgery — highest cure (~99% primary) for high-risk and facial/recurrent BCC (tissue sparing with complete margin control)
- Destructive (low-risk, superficial/small nodular): curettage and electrodesiccation, cryosurgery, photodynamic therapy, CO2 laser
- Topical (superficial BCC): imiquimod 5% (5 times/week for 6 weeks), 5-FU 5% (twice daily for 3–6 weeks)
- Radiotherapy: elderly/inoperable, as adjuvant after incomplete excision; avoid in Gorlin syndrome (induces new BCCs)
- Advanced/metastatic: Hedgehog pathway inhibitors — vismodegib, sonidegib (SMO inhibitors; side effects — muscle cramps, dysgeusia, alopecia, weight loss, teratogenicity); cemiplimab (anti-PD-1) after HHI failure
- Follow-up yearly (≥5 years) — 40% develop another BCC; sun protection

**Q8. Describe the role of cryosurgery for BCC (PYQ).**
- For low-risk, well-defined superficial or small nodular BCC on trunk/limbs, elderly or poor surgical candidates
- Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C) open spray with 3–5 mm margin, double freeze–thaw cycle (tissue temperature ≤ −50 °C), thaw time ≥60–90 s; cure rates ~90–95% in selected tumours
- Advantages: quick, cheap, office procedure, safe in pacemaker/anticoagulated patients; disadvantages: no histological margin control, hypopigmentation, scarring, oedema, delayed healing; avoid for morphoeic, recurrent, H-zone deep tumours

**Q9. What is Mohs micrographic surgery?**
- Staged excision with horizontal frozen sections examining 100% of the peripheral and deep margin, mapped and re-excised only where tumour remains — maximal cure with maximal tissue preservation; indications — high-risk BCC/SCC, recurrent tumours, facial sites, ill-defined/aggressive histology, DFSP, extramammary Paget's, lentigo maligna (modified)

**Q10. Write short notes on nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin) (PYQ).**
- Autosomal dominant PTCH1 (also PTCH2, SUFU) — Hedgehog pathway
- Multiple BCCs from childhood/adolescence (also non-sun-exposed), odontogenic keratocysts of jaw, palmar/plantar pits, calcification of falx cerebri, bifid/fused/splayed ribs, frontal bossing, macrocephaly, hypertelorism, medulloblastoma (SUFU — childhood), ovarian/cardiac fibromas, milia, epidermoid cysts
- Management: avoid radiation (including CT where possible), sun protection, regular skin checks, early treatment of BCCs (Mohs, PDT, topical), vismodegib for multiple; dental panoramic X-rays for jaw cysts; genetic counselling

**Q11. Write short notes on fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (PYQ — epithelioma).**
- Variant of BCC: sessile/pedunculated pink fleshy plaque on lower back resembling fibroma/skin tag; histology — thin anastomosing strands of basaloid cells in fibrous stroma (fenestrated pattern); excision curative

**Q12. Explain the molecular pathogenesis.**
- Constitutive activation of Hedgehog signalling: loss-of-function PTCH1 (≈ 70–90%) or activating SMO mutations → GLI transcription factors → cell proliferation; UV-signature TP53 mutations; basis for Hedgehog-pathway inhibitors (vismodegib, sonidegib)

**Q13. Describe nodular BCC clinically.**
- Commonest (60%): pearly, translucent, dome-shaped papule/nodule with rolled edges and arborising telangiectasia, central ulceration (rodent ulcer) with crust, bleeds on minor trauma; head and neck (nose, inner canthus, nasolabial folds)

**Q14. Describe superficial, morphoeic and pigmented BCC.**
- Superficial: pink scaly plaque with thread-like raised pearly border on trunk; mimics eczema/ psoriasis/ Bowen's — treatable topically
- Morphoeic (sclerosing/infiltrative): ill-defined, scar-like, ivory/white indurated plaque — aggressive subclinical spread, high recurrence; Mohs preferred
- Pigmented BCC: common in Indian/ Asian skin — brown-black pearly papules with blue-grey globules — mimics melanoma/ seborrhoeic keratosis

**Q15. What are high-risk features of BCC (NCCN)?**
- Location: H-zone of face (central face, eyelids, eyebrows, nose, lips, chin, ears, temples) any size; ≥20 mm on trunk/ extremities; poorly defined borders; recurrent; immunosuppression; prior radiotherapy site; aggressive histology (morphoeic, infiltrative, micronodular, basosquamous, perineural invasion)

**Q16. Topical and non-surgical treatments.**
- Imiquimod 5% (5 days/week for 6 weeks) and 5-FU 5% (twice daily 3–6 weeks) — superficial BCC; photodynamic therapy (MAL/ALA) — superficial and thin nodular; cryotherapy (−50 °C double freeze–thaw) — well-defined low-risk lesions; curettage and electrodesiccation (3 cycles) for small low-risk lesions on non-hair-bearing sites; radiotherapy — elderly, inoperable

**Q17. Surgical margins for BCC.**
- Standard excision with 4 mm clinical margin for well-defined low-risk BCC <2 cm (≈ 95% clearance); larger (5–15 mm) for high-risk or Mohs micrographic surgery (best cure ~99% primary, ~94% recurrent)

**Q18. Hedgehog inhibitors — indications and side effects.**
- Vismodegib 150 mg/day, sonidegib 200 mg/day — locally advanced BCC not amenable to surgery/RT, metastatic BCC, Gorlin syndrome
- Side effects: muscle spasms, alopecia, dysgeusia (taste loss), weight loss, fatigue, raised CK, teratogenicity; resistance (SMO mutations); cemiplimab (PD-1) for those failing Hh inhibitors

**Q19. Gorlin syndrome — diagnostic criteria.**
- Major: >2 BCCs or 1 under age 20, odontogenic keratocysts of jaw, ≥3 palmar/plantar pits, bilamellar calcification of falx cerebri, bifid/fused/splayed ribs, first-degree relative with NBCCS, PTCH1/SUFU mutation
- Minor: macrocephaly, frontal bossing, cleft lip/palate, hypertelorism, medulloblastoma (desmoplastic — SUFU), ovarian/cardiac fibromas, lymphomesenteric cysts, polydactyly, Sprengel deformity, vertebral anomalies
- Diagnosis: 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor; avoid radiotherapy (induces many BCCs)

**Q20. Prognosis and follow-up.**
- Metastasis very rare (<0.1%); local destruction if neglected (rodent ulcer — invasion of bone, orbit, CNS); ~30–50% develop another BCC within 5 years — annual skin examination, sun protection, nicotinamide in high-risk

**Q21. Why is BCC less common in Indians, and what presentation is typical?**
- Melanin protection against UV; still seen in fair-skinned Indians, elderly, outdoor workers, arsenic exposure, xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism; typically pigmented nodular BCC on face (nose, cheek, eyelid) — often confused with naevus or seborrhoeic keratosis

**Q22. What is basosquamous carcinoma?**
- Aggressive BCC variant with squamous differentiation — higher local recurrence and metastatic potential (behaves like SCC); treat with Mohs/ wide excision, sentinel node in selected cases

**Q23. Dermoscopic criteria in more detail.**
- Absence of pigment network plus ≥1 of: arborising vessels, leaf-like areas, large blue-grey ovoid nests, multiple blue-grey globules, spoke-wheel areas, ulceration; superficial BCC — short fine telangiectasia, shiny white-red structureless areas, multiple small erosions

**Q24. Risk of arsenic-related skin cancer — features.**
- Chronic arsenic (groundwater — West Bengal, Bangladesh; old Fowler's solution): raindrop hyper/ hypopigmentation, punctate palmoplantar keratoses, multiple Bowen's disease on trunk, multiple superficial BCCs and SCCs; internal cancers (lung, bladder)

**Q25. Reconstruction after BCC excision — principles.**
- Primary closure along relaxed skin tension lines, local flaps (advancement, rotation, transposition — e.g. bilobed for nose), full-thickness skin graft (nasal tip, eyelids), healing by secondary intention for concave areas (inner canthus); ensure clear margins before complex flaps (or delayed reconstruction)

**Q26. What is fibroepithelioma of Pinkus histology?**
- Thin anastomosing strands of basaloid cells extending from the epidermis into a fibrovascular stroma — fenestrated pattern ('lace-like'); clinically a pink sessile papule on lower back — considered a BCC variant (or trichoblastoma variant)

**Q27. What is the role of nicotinamide?**
- Oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily reduced new non-melanoma skin cancers by ~23% and AKs in high-risk patients (ONTRAC trial) — replenishes cellular ATP for DNA repair, reduces UV immunosuppression; benefit lost on stopping

**Q28. Differential diagnosis of a pearly nodule on the face.**
- Intradermal naevus, sebaceous hyperplasia, trichoepithelioma (no ulceration, smooth, bluish), adnexal tumours, amelanotic melanoma, keratoacanthoma, Merkel cell carcinoma (violaceous fast-growing), molluscum (umbilicated), cylindroma

**Q29. Radiotherapy in BCC — indications and contraindications.**
- Indications: elderly patients unfit for surgery, large lesions in difficult sites (eyelid, nose), adjuvant for perineural invasion/ positive margins
- Contraindications: Gorlin syndrome, XP, young patients (late radiation damage, secondary cancers), connective tissue disease (scleroderma), recurrent after RT

**Q30. What is the histological classification and prognostic relevance?**
- Low-risk: nodular, superficial, pigmented, infundibulocystic, fibroepithelial
- High-risk: micronodular, infiltrative, sclerosing/morphoeic, basosquamous, BCC with sarcomatoid differentiation — need wider margins/ Mohs

## Quick spotter facts
- Pearly nodule with rolled edge and arborising vessels at inner canthus — BCC
- Peripheral palisading + retraction clefts
- Pigmented BCC common in Indians; Mohs for H-zone

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Basal cell carcinoma); NCCN risk stratification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Becker's nevus — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Becker's nevus** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Write a short note on Becker's naevus (PYQ).**
- Acquired-appearing (often congenital but noticed around adolescence) unilateral, large, irregular, light- to dark-brown patch with geographic border on shoulder, upper chest, scapula, upper arm, with hypertrichosis (coarse dark hair) appearing later; men 4–6× more (androgen-dependent — increased androgen receptors)
- A smooth-muscle hamartoma component (Becker's naevus = hamartoma of epidermis, melanocytes, smooth muscle, hair)
- Postzygotic ACTB (β-actin) mutations

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Patch becomes darker and thicker after sun exposure/puberty; acneiform lesions within, pseudo-Darier's sign (smooth muscle — transient elevation/piloerection on rubbing); usually single; may be multiple or bilateral

**Q3. What is Becker's naevus syndrome?**
- Becker's naevus with ipsilateral hypoplasia of breast/areola (most common), pectoralis major, limb shortening, scoliosis, spina bifida, supernumerary nipples, lipoatrophy — included in the epidermal naevus syndromes

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Mild acanthosis with elongated flat-bottomed pigmented rete ridges (basal hyperpigmentation), increased melanin with normal or slightly increased melanocytes, increased smooth muscle bundles in the dermis (smooth muscle hamartoma overlap), prominent hair follicles

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Café-au-lait macule (no hair, earlier onset), congenital melanocytic naevus (raised, darker, nested), smooth muscle hamartoma (congenital, pseudo-Darier's), nevus spilus, plexiform neurofibroma, McCune–Albright CALM, PIH, segmental pigmentation

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign; no malignant potential
- Cosmetic: Q-switched/picosecond lasers (pigment — variable, recurrence), fractional lasers, long-pulsed alexandrite/diode laser hair removal (addresses hypertrichosis and can lighten pigment); camouflage
- Topical flutamide (anti-androgen) for breast hypoplasia reported; spironolactone for associated hypoplasia (reports)

**Q7. Describe the clinical features in detail.**
- Unilateral, irregular, large (often >10 cm) light-to-dark brown patch with 'geographic' map-like border on shoulder, upper chest or back of adolescent males; hypertrichosis (coarse hair) develops after pigmentation; acne localised to patch; may show perifollicular papules (smooth muscle)

**Q8. Histopathology in detail.**
- Acanthosis with elongated, flat-bottomed rete ridges, basal hyperpigmentation (melanocytes slightly increased), increased hair follicles, and bundles of smooth muscle (smooth-muscle hamartoma overlap) in dermis

**Q9. What is the association with smooth muscle hamartoma?**
- Becker's naevus and congenital smooth muscle hamartoma lie on a spectrum — both show smooth muscle bundles and hypertrichosis; pseudo-Darier sign (transient piloerection/ elevation on rubbing) can occur

**Q10. Explain Becker's naevus syndrome features.**
- Ipsilateral breast hypoplasia (or nipple/ areolar hypoplasia), pectoralis major hypoplasia, supernumerary nipples, limb shortening, scoliosis, spina bifida, lipoatrophy — examine chest wall and spine

**Q11. Is there a malignancy risk?**
- No significant malignant potential; rare reports of melanoma within (coincidental); counsel benign nature

**Q12. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Café-au-lait macule (no hair, from birth, uniform), congenital melanocytic naevus (present at birth, darker, raised, hairy), nevus spilus (speckles), plexiform neurofibroma (soft mass), McCune–Albright CALM, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, tinea versicolor

**Q13. What is the genetic basis?**
- Post-zygotic activating mutations in ACTB (β-actin) in a mosaic patch — explaining hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis and smooth-muscle hamartoma features (androgen-sensitive)

**Q14. Why is it more visible after puberty?**
- Increased androgen receptor expression in the lesion — hair and pigmentation become prominent under pubertal androgens; men more affected; acne may be localised to the lesion

**Q15. Lasers in Becker's naevus.**
- Long-pulsed alexandrite/diode/Nd:YAG lasers for hair; Q-switched/picosecond Nd:YAG or ruby for pigment (frequent recurrence), fractional 1550 nm; patch test spot first; topical flutamide (anti-androgen) reported

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral brown patch with coarse hair on the shoulder of a young man — Becker's naevus
- Ipsilateral breast hypoplasia — Becker's naevus syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Becker's naevus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Café-au-lait macules — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Café-au-lait macules** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What are café-au-lait macules (CALMs)?**
- Well-defined, uniformly light- to dark-brown ('coffee with milk') macules/patches with smooth or irregular borders, present at birth or appearing in early childhood; increase in number and size with age in childhood
- 1–3 CALMs are common in normal population (10–25%)

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Increased melanin in basal keratinocytes and melanocytes with normal or slightly increased melanocyte number; giant pigment granules (macromelanosomes) in some, especially NF1 (not specific)

**Q3. When are CALMs significant? Name associated syndromes.**
- ≥6 CALMs >5 mm prepubertal or >15 mm postpubertal suggest NF1
- NF1, NF2 (fewer CALMs), Legius syndrome (SPRED1 — CALMs + axillary freckling without neurofibromas), McCune–Albright syndrome (large unilateral jagged 'coast of Maine' CALMs following midline, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty — GNAS mosaic), constitutional mismatch repair deficiency, Noonan with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD), Fanconi anaemia, ataxia-telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, Watson syndrome, Silver–Russell, ring chromosome syndromes
- Shape: smooth 'coast of California' border in NF1 vs jagged 'coast of Maine' in McCune–Albright

**Q4. Give the NIH diagnostic criteria for NF1 (revised 2021).**
- Two or more of: ≥6 CALMs (>5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal); freckling in axillary or inguinal region (Crowe's sign); ≥2 neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform neurofibroma; optic pathway glioma; ≥2 iris Lisch nodules or ≥2 choroidal abnormalities (on OCT/NIR imaging); distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, anterolateral tibial bowing/pseudarthrosis); heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant
- In a child of an affected parent, one criterion is enough

**Q5. Write a short note on neurocutaneous syndromes (PYQ).**
- Phakomatoses — disorders of neuroectoderm with skin and CNS involvement: NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis complex, Sturge–Weber syndrome, von Hippel–Lindau, ataxia-telangiectasia, incontinentia pigmenti, hypomelanosis of Ito, neurocutaneous melanosis, PHACE, linear nevus sebaceous syndrome (Schimmelpenning)

**Q6. Differential diagnosis of CALMs.**
- Congenital melanocytic naevus (raised, hair, darker), nevus spilus (CALM-like background with dark speckles), Becker's naevus (shoulder, hair, after puberty), lentigines (smaller, darker), freckles (sun-dependent), post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, mastocytoma (Darier's sign), segmental pigmentation disorder

**Q7. Management.**
- Isolated CALMs — reassurance
- Multiple — full skin exam (freckling, neurofibromas), eye exam (Lisch nodules), BP, growth, development, family history; genetic testing; follow-up yearly for children at risk of NF1
- Cosmetic: Q-switched (Nd:YAG 532, ruby, alexandrite) or picosecond lasers — variable response, recurrence common; camouflage

**Q8. How many CALMs are normal?**
- 1–2 CALMs in ~25% of normal children; ≥3 in <1%; ≥6 typical CALMs raise strong suspicion of NF1 (≈ 80% of children with ≥6 develop NF1 if no family history after genetic testing — including Legius)

**Q9. What are 'typical' vs 'atypical' CALMs?**
- Typical (NF1): uniformly pigmented, oval, smooth borders, ≥0.5 cm
- Atypical: irregular jagged borders, variable pigmentation, segmental — suggests other syndromes (McCune–Albright, constitutional mismatch repair deficiency, ring chromosome) or isolated

**Q10. What is constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome (CMMRD)?**
- Biallelic MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 mutations: CALMs (atypical), early childhood brain tumours, haematological malignancies, colorectal cancers; consanguinity; differentiate from NF1 by genetic testing and tumour risk

**Q11. What is the role of lasers and expected outcomes?**
- Q-switched 532/755/694 nm and picosecond lasers: variable clearance (~50%), recurrence common (up to 50% within months), irregular-bordered CALMs respond better; test patch first; risk of hyper/hypopigmentation

**Q12. Describe Watson syndrome and ring chromosome syndromes.**
- Watson: NF1 allelic — CALMs, pulmonary stenosis, short stature, intellectual disability
- Ring chromosome syndromes (ring 7, 11, 12, 15, 17): multiple CALMs with growth retardation and developmental delay

**Q13. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q14. Describe the other cutaneous features of NF1.**
- Axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign — appears 3–5 y), cutaneous neurofibromas (soft, 'button-hole' invagination, puberty onwards), plexiform neurofibromas ('bag of worms'; risk of MPNST), juvenile xanthogranulomas, naevus anaemicus, hypopigmented macules
- Treatment of symptomatic plexiform neurofibroma: selumetinib (MEK inhibitor)

**Q15. What are Lisch nodules?**
- Pigmented hamartomas of the iris (melanocytic) — dome-shaped yellow-brown elevations on slit-lamp; appear in childhood, present in >90% of adults with NF1; asymptomatic

**Q16. Describe McCune–Albright syndrome briefly.**
- Post-zygotic activating GNAS mutation: large segmental CALMs with jagged 'coast of Maine' border respecting midline, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (fractures, deformity), endocrine hyperfunction — precocious puberty (girls), hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, Cushing's, phosphate wasting

## Quick spotter facts
- ≥6 CALMs + axillary freckles — NF1
- Coast of California (NF1) vs coast of Maine (McCune–Albright)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hyperpigmentation; neurocutaneous syndromes); NIH 2021 revised NF1 criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Callus (callosity) — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Callus (callosity)** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is a callus?**
- Diffuse, plaque-like, yellowish thickening of the stratum corneum (hyperkeratosis) at sites of repeated friction or intermittent pressure, without a central core; protective response
- Occupational calluses ('occupational stigmata'): tailor's (fingers), guitarist's fingertips, prayer callus (forehead/knees — 'prayer nodules'), tennis player's palm, writer's callus, cobbler's, farmer's palms; Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting in bulimia)

**Q2. Pathogenesis.**
- Repeated friction/pressure → increased keratinocyte proliferation and retention hyperkeratosis to protect underlying tissue
- Predisposing: ill-fitting footwear, high heels, foot deformities (hallux valgus, flat/high-arched feet), abnormal gait, obesity, peripheral neuropathy (diabetes, leprosy — calluses precede neuropathic ulcers), barefoot walking

**Q3. Differentiate callus, corn and plantar wart.**
- Callus: broad diffuse thickening over pressure/friction areas, skin lines preserved, little pain, no core
- Corn: circumscribed with central translucent conical core pointing inwards, painful on direct pressure, skin lines pass through
- Wart: interrupts skin lines, black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on paring, painful on lateral squeeze

**Q4. Why are calluses important in diabetes and leprosy?**
- In insensate feet, callus acts like a foreign body increasing plantar pressure → haemorrhage beneath callus → neuropathic ulcer; regular callus debridement and offloading footwear (MCR) prevent ulceration

**Q5. Management.**
- Remove cause: proper well-fitting footwear, padding, insoles/orthotics, correct foot deformity, offloading
- Paring with a scalpel or pumice stone after soaking
- Keratolytics: salicylic acid 10–40% (plasters/ointments), urea 20–40%, lactic acid; emollients
- Avoid aggressive self-treatment in diabetics; podiatry referral

**Q6. Histopathology of a callus.**
- Compact orthohyperkeratosis without parakeratosis plug, thickened granular layer may be thin, mild acanthosis; no viral cytopathic changes (vs wart); dermis may show fibrosis

**Q7. What occupational calluses are known?**
- Occupational marks: guitar/violin players' fingertips, tailor's/cobbler's calluses, prayer nodules (knees, forehead — 'prayer mark' in Muslims), 'surfer's knots', writer's callus on middle finger, sitting calluses (ischial — Indian squatting), Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting — bulimia)

**Q8. How do you assess the foot biomechanics?**
- Examine footwear and gait, pressure points, foot deformities (hallux valgus, hammer toes, pes cavus), podoscope/pedobarography; refer to podiatrist/orthotist for offloading insoles

**Q9. Complications in insensate feet.**
- Callus acts like a stone in the shoe — haemorrhage beneath the callus (pre-ulcerative sign) → neuropathic (mal perforans) ulcer, infection, osteomyelitis; routine paring and protective MCR footwear are preventive

**Q10. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q11. What keratolytics are used and how do they work?**
- Salicylic acid 10–40% (plasters/ ointment — dissolves intercellular cement), urea 20–40% (humectant and keratolytic at high strength), lactic acid 12%, propylene glycol; caution in diabetics/ neuropathy (chemical burns)

**Q12. What is the paring technique and safety?**
- Soften by soaking 10 min, pare with scalpel blade (no. 15) parallel to skin until pink skin appears, avoid drawing blood; in diabetics and leprosy patients refer to trained podiatry; pumice stone home maintenance

**Q13. Callus vs plantar wart vs corn on dermoscopy.**
- Callus: homogeneous yellowish structureless keratin with preserved dermatoglyphics
- Wart: interrupted dermatoglyphics, red-black dots (thrombosed capillaries)
- Corn: central translucent keratin core with surrounding callus, dermatoglyphics preserved around

**Q14. Callus in leprosy patients — prevention programme.**
- Daily self-care: soak feet 20 min, scrape with pumice, apply oil/ petroleum jelly, inspect for cracks, protective footwear (MCR/ microcellular rubber insoles), regular follow-up at disability prevention clinics

**Q15. What is the 'pre-ulcerative callus'?**
- Callus with underlying haemorrhage (dark discolouration) or blister — signals high pressure and impending ulcer in neuropathic feet; urgent offloading and debridement

## Quick spotter facts
- Diffuse yellow plaque over pressure point without core — callus
- Calluses in insensate foot precede neuropathic ulcers

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Mechanical and physical injuries; keratoderma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Chancroid — viva
posts.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Chancroid** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. What is chancroid? Organism?**
- Acute STI with painful genital ulcers and suppurative inguinal lymphadenitis caused by Haemophilus ducreyi — small Gram-negative coccobacillus
- Now rare in India (declined with syndromic management); also causes non-sexual chronic leg ulcers in the tropics/Pacific (yaws-like settings)

**Q2. Pathogenic factors of H. ducreyi (PYQ).**
- Entry through micro-abrasions; cytolethal distending toxin (cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis), haemolysin, outer-membrane proteins (DsrA serum resistance, LspA anti-phagocytic), pili; incubation 3–7 days

**Q3. Describe the ulcer.**
- Starts as tender papule → pustule → ulcer in 1–2 days
- Ulcer: painful, soft (not indurated — 'soft sore'), ragged undermined edges, purulent grey-yellow necrotic base that bleeds easily, surrounding erythema; often multiple ('kissing ulcers' by autoinoculation)
- Sites: men — prepuce, frenulum, coronal sulcus; women — fourchette, labia (women may be asymptomatic carriers)

**Q4. Describe the bubo of chancroid.**
- Painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenitis in ~50%, 1–2 weeks after ulcer; matted, fluctuant, may rupture forming a single sinus/ulcer ('bubonulus')
- Overlying skin red; rupture can produce large inguinal ulcers

**Q5. Clinical variants.**
- Giant chancroid, serpiginous chancroid, phagedenic chancroid (destructive with secondary anaerobes), follicular, dwarf (small superficial), transient (heals then bubo — mimics LGV), papular (mimics donovanosis/condyloma lata)
- Mixed chancre — chancroid + syphilis together (rolled induration appearing later)

**Q6. Complications of chancroid (PYQ).**
- Phimosis/paraphimosis, phagedena (tissue destruction), fistula, urethral stricture, bubo rupture and large ulcer
- Increased HIV acquisition and transmission (ulcer breaches mucosa), mixed infection with syphilis

**Q7. Diagnostic tests (PYQ).**
- Gram stain of ulcer edge/bubo pus: Gram-negative coccobacilli in parallel chains — 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' (low sensitivity)
- Culture on enriched selective media (Nairobi/Mueller–Hinton chocolate agar with vancomycin, 33 °C, CO2) — sensitivity <80%
- Multiplex PCR (H. ducreyi, T. pallidum, HSV) — test of choice
- Exclude syphilis (dark-field, serology at baseline and 3 months) and herpes; HIV test
- CDC probable diagnosis: painful ulcer(s), no T. pallidum evidence, typical lymphadenopathy, HSV test negative

**Q8. Differentiate chancroid from syphilitic chancre.**
- Chancroid: incubation 3–7 days, multiple, painful, soft, ragged undermined edge, dirty bleeding base, painful suppurating unilateral bubo
- Chancre: 9–90 days, usually single, painless, indurated (button-like), clean base with serous exudate, rubbery painless bilateral non-suppurating nodes

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Azithromycin 1 g single oral dose OR ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose OR ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days OR erythromycin base 500 mg thrice daily for 7 days
- NACO syndromic: white kit (benzathine penicillin + azithromycin) for non-herpetic ulcer, blue kit if penicillin allergy; black kit for bubo
- Fluctuant bubo: needle aspiration through healthy skin or incision and drainage — do not excise
- Treat partners in last 10 days; review at 3–7 days (ulcers improve symptomatically in 3 days, heal in ~7–14 days)

**Q10. Why is chancroid less common now?**
- Syndromic management, condom promotion, antibiotics for GUD, sex-worker programmes — WHO considers it nearly eliminated in many regions

**Q11. Describe the histopathology of a chancroid ulcer.**
- Three zones: superficial ulcer base with neutrophils, fibrin, necrotic tissue and RBCs; middle zone of oedematous new vessels with endothelial proliferation (thrombosis); deep zone of dense lymphocytes and plasma cells

**Q12. What is the 'mixed chancre'?**
- Simultaneous infection with T. pallidum and H. ducreyi — initially soft painful ulcer of chancroid that later becomes indurated as syphilis develops (incubation longer); test syphilis serology at baseline and 3 months

**Q13. Management of a fluctuant bubo.**
- Needle aspiration with wide-bore needle through adjacent healthy skin (repeat as needed) or small incision and drainage with packing — prevents spontaneous rupture and sinus formation; antibiotics as for chancroid

**Q14. What is the treatment in pregnancy and HIV?**
- Pregnancy: azithromycin 1 g single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM (avoid ciprofloxacin)
- HIV: may need longer courses (erythromycin 7 days preferred over single-dose), close follow-up; slower healing

**Q15. What is the partner management and follow-up?**
- Treat all partners within 10 days before symptom onset even if asymptomatic; re-examine at 3–7 days — ulcers should be less painful and improving; if not, consider misdiagnosis, co-infection (syphilis, HSV, HIV), non-compliance or resistance

## Quick spotter facts
- Painful soft ragged ulcer with dirty base + suppurating bubo — chancroid
- School-of-fish on Gram stain
- Treat with azithromycin 1 g single dose

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Chancroid); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Chickenpox (varicella) — viva
posts.summary: Viral infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Chickenpox (varicella)** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What is chickenpox? Agent and transmission?**
- Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (HHV-3, alpha-herpesvirus)
- Spread by respiratory droplets/aerosols and direct contact with vesicle fluid; highly contagious (secondary attack rate ~90% in susceptible household contacts)
- Incubation 10–21 days (average 14–16); infectious from 1–2 days before rash until all lesions are crusted (~5–7 days)

**Q2. Describe the pathogenesis.**
- Inhalation → replication in the respiratory tract and regional nodes → primary viraemia → liver/spleen → secondary viraemia → skin (in waves → crops)
- Virus then remains latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia → may reactivate later as herpes zoster

**Q3. Describe the rash.**
- Mild prodrome (fever, malaise) in adults, often none in children
- Itchy rash starts on the scalp/face and trunk (centripetal distribution) and spreads to limbs; mucosae may have erosions
- Evolution: macule → papule → vesicle ('dewdrop on a rose petal') → pustule → crust within 24 h; lesions in all stages at the same time (pleomorphism) due to crops over 3–5 days
- Heals in 1–2 weeks; may leave scars (especially if scratched/infected)

**Q4. Differentiate chickenpox from smallpox.**
- Chickenpox: centripetal, superficial thin-walled vesicles, lesions in different stages, mild fever, palms/soles spared, no prodromal severe toxaemia
- Smallpox: centrifugal (face and extremities incl. palms/soles), deep-seated firm vesicles/pustules, all lesions at same stage, severe prodrome; now eradicated (1980)

**Q5. Other differentials?**
- Disseminated herpes simplex or zoster, eczema herpeticum, hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackie — palms, soles, mouth), insect bite reactions/papular urticaria, PLEVA, impetigo, scabies with pyoderma, drug eruptions (AGEP), rickettsial pox, mpox

**Q6. What are the complications?**
- Commonest in children: secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus, group A strep — cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, toxic shock)
- Pneumonia (commonest serious complication in adults, smokers and pregnant women)
- CNS: acute cerebellar ataxia (children), encephalitis, Reye's syndrome (with aspirin — avoid aspirin), Guillain–Barré
- Haemorrhagic varicella (purpura fulminans), hepatitis, myocarditis, nephritis, arthritis, thrombocytopenia
- Immunocompromised: progressive disseminated varicella with high mortality

**Q7. Discuss varicella in pregnancy.**
- Mother: higher risk of severe varicella pneumonia
- Congenital (fetal) varicella syndrome — infection in the first 20 weeks (risk ~1–2%): cicatricial skin scars in dermatomal distribution, limb hypoplasia, eye defects (chorioretinitis, cataract), microcephaly, low birth weight
- Neonatal varicella: mother develops rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → severe disease in baby (no maternal antibodies) — give VZIG to the baby and acyclovir if disease develops
