- Exposure of non-immune pregnant woman: VZIG within 10 days; acyclovir if rash develops

**Q8. How will you investigate?**
- Clinical diagnosis usually
- Tzanck smear (multinucleated giant cells — not specific)
- PCR of vesicle fluid (best), DFA; serology IgM/IgG (immunity status)
- CBC, LFT, chest X-ray if pneumonia suspected

**Q9. Treatment of chickenpox.**
- Healthy children: symptomatic — calamine lotion, oral antihistamines, paracetamol (no aspirin — Reye's), trimmed nails, hygiene
- Oral acyclovir 20 mg/kg (max 800 mg) four times daily for 5 days if started within 24 h — for adolescents >12 y, adults, chronic skin/lung disease, on steroids, secondary household cases
- Adults: acyclovir 800 mg five times a day for 7 days or valacyclovir 1 g thrice daily for 7 days
- IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h for immunocompromised, pneumonia, encephalitis, pregnancy with complications

**Q10. What is the varicella vaccine?**
- Live attenuated Oka strain
- IAP schedule (India): 2 doses — 15 months and 4–6 years (catch-up: 2 doses ≥3 months apart in children <13 y, 4 weeks apart ≥13 y); not in the national (UIP) schedule
- Contraindicated in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression; avoid pregnancy for 1 month after
- Post-exposure: vaccine within 3–5 days; VZIG (within 10 days) for immunocompromised, pregnant non-immune, neonates

**Q11. What is breakthrough varicella?**
- Varicella >42 days after vaccination — mild, few lesions (often <50), mostly papular rather than vesicular, low fever — still contagious

**Q12. Discuss the isolation advice.**
- Exclude from school/work until all lesions crust (about 5–7 days after onset)
- Hospital: airborne and contact precautions; non-immune health workers exposed should avoid patient contact from day 8 to day 21 after exposure

**Q13. Why are adults sicker than children?**
- More vigorous immune (cell-mediated) response and more pneumonia; smoking and pregnancy increase risk

**Q14. What is the link between varicella and zoster?**
- Same virus — chickenpox is primary infection; zoster is reactivation of latent VZV in a sensory ganglion when cell-mediated immunity falls (age, HIV, malignancy)
- Zoster lesions can transmit chickenpox (not zoster) to non-immune contacts

**Q15. What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome? (often linked question)**
- Zoster of the geniculate ganglion — ipsilateral facial palsy + ear pain + vesicles in the ear canal/pinna ± anterior-tongue taste loss, tinnitus, vertigo
- Treat with antivirals and steroids early

## Quick spotter facts
- Lesions in all stages at once, centripetal — chickenpox
- 'Dewdrop on a rose petal' vesicle
- Avoid aspirin — Reye's syndrome

## Note
Vaccine schedule follows IAP recommendations; confirm the current IAP schedule before use.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections); national immunisation guidance (IAP). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Chromoblastomycosis — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Chromoblastomycosis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is chromoblastomycosis?**
- Chronic, slowly progressive implantation mycosis of skin and subcutis caused by dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi, producing verrucous plaques and nodules; tissue shows muriform cells

**Q2. Name the causative agents.**
- Fonsecaea pedrosoi (~90% worldwide; F. compacta now considered the same species), Cladophialophora carrionii (arid areas), Phialophora verrucosa, Rhinocladiella aquaspersa, Exophiala species
- India: Fonsecaea pedrosoi commonest — Western Ghats, Kerala, Karnataka, Sub-Himalayan region

**Q3. Who gets it?**
- Barefoot agricultural workers, men 30–60 years; implantation via wood splinters, thorns
- Lower limbs (foot, leg) commonest, then hands, buttocks

**Q4. Clinical types (Carrión classification).**
- Nodular, tumorous (cauliflower-like), verrucous (commonest), plaque (scaly, slightly raised), cicatricial (atrophic centre, spreading edge)
- Black dots on the surface (transepidermal elimination of fungus) — the best sites to sample
- Satellite lesions by autoinoculation and lymphatic spread

**Q5. What are muriform cells?**
- Thick-walled, dark-brown, round cells (4–12 µm) with septa in two planes — 'medlar bodies', 'sclerotic bodies', 'copper pennies'; the diagnostic tissue form
- Seen in KOH mount of black dots/crusts and in histology (even with H&E — pigmented)

**Q6. Histopathology?**
- Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with intraepidermal microabscesses, transepidermal elimination
- Mixed suppurative and tuberculoid granulomas with giant cells containing muriform cells

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- TBVC, lupus vulgaris (verrucous), sporotrichosis, mycetoma (no sinuses/grains here), blastomycosis, leishmaniasis, verrucous SCC, psoriasis, lichen planus hypertrophicus, podoconiosis/elephantiasis nostras, leprosy

**Q8. Complications?**
- Lymphoedema and elephantiasis of the limb, secondary bacterial infection, malodour, ankylosis, SCC in long-standing lesions; rarely haematogenous spread (brain — Cladophialophora bantiana)

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Small lesions: wide surgical excision, cryotherapy, heat, CO2 laser — combined with antifungal
- Itraconazole 200–400 mg/day for 6–12 months or longer (drug of choice); terbinafine 250–500 mg/day alternative; combinations (itraconazole + terbinafine, + flucytosine); posaconazole
- Cryotherapy to reduce lesions while on itraconazole; imiquimod as immune adjunct
- Cure criteria: clinical healing + negative mycology + histology

**Q10. Why is response poor?**
- Thick-walled muriform cells resist drugs, poor drug penetration in fibrotic tissue, chronic lesions are large at presentation

**Q11. Describe the sources of infection and incubation.**
- Dematiaceous fungi live in soil, decaying wood, plant thorns; implantation via minor trauma (thorns, splinters) in barefoot agricultural workers; incubation weeks to months; slow progression over years

**Q12. What investigations are used?**
- KOH (10–20%) of crust/ black dots — muriform cells (copper pennies); culture on SDA — slow-growing dark olive/ black velvety colonies, species by conidiation pattern (Fonsecaea — Rhinocladiella/ Cladosporium-type) or ITS sequencing; biopsy with H&E/ PAS

**Q13. Physical treatments in detail.**
- Local heat therapy (pocket warmers — fungi intolerant of >40 °C), cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) — for small lesions and to debulk, CO2 laser vaporisation, electrodesiccation, Mohs/ surgical excision with margins (avoid spreading — lymphatic seeding)

**Q14. Combination antifungal therapy.**
- Itraconazole 200–400 mg/day + terbinafine 250–500 mg/day (synergistic); itraconazole pulse therapy; posaconazole for refractory; continue 6–12 months beyond clinical cure; imiquimod as immunomodulator adjunct

**Q15. Classify antifungal drugs (PYQ).**
- Polyenes: amphotericin B (systemic, deep mycoses), nystatin (topical/ oral Candida)
- Azoles — imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole) and triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) — inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis)
- Allylamines: terbinafine, naftifine (squalene epoxidase inhibitors); benzylamine — butenafine
- Echinocandins: caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin (β-1,3-glucan synthase)
- Others: griseofulvin (microtubule — mitotic inhibitor), flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis), ciclopirox (chelator), amorolfine (morpholine — Δ14 reductase/ Δ7-Δ8 isomerase), tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), potassium iodide, efinaconazole, tavaborole

## Quick spotter facts
- Verrucous plaque on foot with black dots — chromoblastomycosis
- Muriform / copper-penny bodies
- Fonsecaea pedrosoi

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 19A (Chromoblastomycosis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Congenital melanocytic nevus — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Congenital melanocytic nevus** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Define congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN).**
- Benign melanocytic proliferation present at birth or appearing within the first 6 months ('tardive' up to 2 years); ~1% of newborns; NRAS mutations (Q61) in most large CMN, BRAF in small

**Q2. Classify by projected adult size.**
- Small <1.5 cm, medium 1.5–20 cm (M1 1.5–10, M2 >10–20), large 20–40 cm, giant >40 cm (projected adult size — head ×1.7, trunk/limbs ×3 growth from infancy)
- Satellite naevi counted (≤20, 20–50, >50) — more satellites → higher risk of neurocutaneous melanosis

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Brown to black, often raised, mammillated or verrucous surface, hypertrichosis, may have nodules (proliferative nodules — usually benign), variegated colour; large CMN in 'bathing trunk' or 'garment' distribution with satellites
- Large/giant CMN may cause pruritus, xerosis, erosions; colour may lighten with time

**Q4. Risks associated with large CMN.**
- Melanoma: lifetime ~2–5% for large/giant (higher in giant >40 cm with many satellites); can arise in deep dermis/subcutis or CNS, often in first 5 years; small/medium — <1% lifetime, mainly after puberty at the dermo-epidermal junction
- Neurocutaneous melanosis: melanocytes in leptomeninges — hydrocephalus, seizures, developmental delay, CNS melanoma; screen with MRI brain and spine (ideally before 6 months of age) in large CMN or >20 satellite naevi

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Naevus cells extending deep into reticular dermis and subcutis, around/within adnexa (hair follicles, eccrine ducts), nerves and vessels, splaying between collagen bundles in single-file arrangement — distinguishes from acquired naevi

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Café-au-lait macule, Becker's naevus, nevus spilus, epidermal naevus, Mongolian spot, plexiform neurofibroma, smooth muscle hamartoma, mastocytoma, nevus sebaceous

**Q7. Management.**
- Individualised: clinical photographs and regular examination (palpation for nodules), dermoscopy; biopsy any new nodule, ulcer or rapid change
- Small/medium: observation or elective excision for cosmetic reasons or difficult-to-monitor sites (scalp)
- Large/giant: staged excision with tissue expanders, flaps, grafts (does not eliminate melanoma risk completely); curettage in neonatal period, dermabrasion, lasers (cosmetic; may hamper monitoring)
- MRI CNS screening as above; psychosocial support; trametinib (MEK inhibitor) under study

**Q8. Describe the clinical evolution of CMN.**
- At birth often lighter, flat; over time becomes thicker, darker, mammillated/ verrucous, develops coarse terminal hairs; some lighten with age; satellite naevi appear in first years in large CMN; proliferative nodules may arise

**Q9. What are satellite naevi and their significance?**
- Smaller CMN scattered away from the main lesion; number (>20) predicts neurocutaneous melanosis risk more than size of the main CMN

**Q10. Melanoma risk by size.**
- Small/ medium CMN (<20 cm projected adult size): lifetime melanoma risk ~1% (mostly after puberty, at dermo-epidermal junction)
- Large/ giant (>20/ >40 cm): ~2–5% (higher in giant with many satellites), half in first 5 years, may arise deep or in CNS

**Q11. Surgical options for large CMN.**
- Serial excision, tissue expansion with flap reconstruction, skin grafting, curettage/ dermabrasion in neonatal period (first weeks — easier cleavage plane), laser for cosmetic lightening (doesn't remove deep cells); surgery doesn't eliminate melanoma risk entirely (deep/ CNS)

**Q12. Psychosocial issues and counselling.**
- Visible large naevi impact self-esteem and family; counsel about realistic risk, signs of change, sun protection, photographic follow-up, support groups (e.g. Caring Matters Now), avoid unnecessary disfiguring surgery

**Q13. Describe melanoma types and Breslow/ Clark levels (often linked question).**
- Types: superficial spreading (commonest in West), nodular, lentigo maligna melanoma, acral lentiginous (commonest in Indians — soles, palms, nails), mucosal, desmoplastic, amelanotic
- Breslow thickness (mm, from granular layer to deepest cell) — main prognostic factor: T1 ≤1 mm, T2 1–2, T3 2–4, T4 >4 mm (a/b by ulceration); Clark levels I–V (anatomical) now largely replaced
- Margins: in situ 0.5–1 cm, ≤1 mm 1 cm, 1–2 mm 1–2 cm, >2 mm 2 cm; sentinel node biopsy for >0.8 mm or ulcerated

**Q14. What is neurocutaneous melanosis?**
- Proliferation of melanocytes in leptomeninges/brain parenchyma with large/giant CMN (especially posterior axial location with multiple satellite naevi >20) — hydrocephalus, seizures, developmental delay, leptomeningeal melanoma; MRI brain with contrast in the first 6 months of life (before myelination masks it)

**Q15. What is the molecular basis?**
- Post-zygotic NRAS (Q61) mutations in ~70–80% of large CMN; BRAF in small/medium; explains multiple satellite naevi from a single clone

**Q16. What should prompt biopsy in CMN follow-up?**
- New nodule (proliferative nodules are common and usually benign but need histology), ulceration, rapid colour/size change, pain, bleeding; melanoma in large CMN often arises deep (dermal/subcutaneous) in the first 5 years

## Quick spotter facts
- Large hairy pigmented naevus with satellites — giant CMN; MRI for neurocutaneous melanosis
- Projected adult size >20 cm = large

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Congenital melanocytic naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Contact dermatitis — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 31 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Contact dermatitis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define contact dermatitis and its types.**
- Inflammatory skin reaction to external substances
- Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD, ~80%): non-immunological direct damage
- Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD): type IV delayed hypersensitivity to a hapten in a sensitised person
- Others: photoallergic, phototoxic, contact urticaria (immediate), protein contact dermatitis, systemic contact dermatitis (ingested allergen), airborne contact dermatitis

**Q2. Explain the pathomechanism of allergic contact dermatitis (PYQ).**
- Sensitisation (induction) phase — 10–15 days: hapten (<500 Da) penetrates, binds skin proteins (haptenation), taken up by Langerhans/dermal dendritic cells → migrate to lymph nodes → present to naive T cells → clonal expansion of hapten-specific memory T cells (Th1/Tc1, Th17)
- Elicitation phase — 24–72 h after re-exposure: memory T cells recognise the hapten-protein → release IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-17 → keratinocyte apoptosis, spongiosis, eczema
- Innate 'danger signals' (TLR, inflammasome) needed — explains why irritated skin sensitises more easily

**Q3. Differentiate irritant and allergic contact dermatitis (PYQ).**
- ICD: anyone exposed (dose-dependent), first exposure can react, onset minutes–hours, burning/stinging > itch, sharply limited to contact area, glazed/ fissured, patch test negative (or irritant), common on hands (wet work)
- ACD: only sensitised (minority), needs prior sensitisation, onset 24–72 h after exposure, itch, spreads beyond contact site/ id reactions, vesicular, patch test positive
- Histology overlaps; ICD more necrotic keratinocytes, ACD more spongiosis and eosinophils

**Q4. Discuss variants of irritant dermatitis (PYQ).**
- Acute irritant (chemical burn-like — acids, alkalis), acute delayed (benzalkonium, podophyllin, anthralin — 8–24 h later), irritant reaction (in wet workers), cumulative/chronic (commonest — repeated mild irritants: soaps, detergents, water), traumatic, pustular/acneiform (oils, metals), asteatotic, frictional, airborne irritant (dust, fibreglass)
- Subjective irritation (stinging without signs — lactic acid sting test)

**Q5. Name common contact allergens and sources (PYQ: list five common sensitisers).**
- Nickel (jewellery, belt buckles, jeans buttons, mobiles) — commonest in women
- Potassium dichromate/chromate (cement — construction workers; leather tanning) — commonest in Indian men
- Paraphenylenediamine (PPD — hair dye, black henna tattoos)
- Fragrances (fragrance mix I and II, balsam of Peru), preservatives (methylisothiazolinone, formaldehyde releasers, parabens)
- Rubber chemicals (thiuram mix, mercaptobenzothiazole, carba mix — gloves, footwear)
- Parthenium hysterophorus (sesquiterpene lactones — airborne contact dermatitis in India), Compositae, Primula, Toxicodendron (poison ivy)
- Topical medicaments (neomycin, benzocaine, ethylenediamine, corticosteroids such as budesonide, tixocortol pivalate), epoxy resin, colophony, cobalt, lanolin, kumkum (Sudan dyes, brilliant lake red)

**Q6. What is parthenium dermatitis? (important in India)**
- Airborne allergic contact dermatitis to sesquiterpene lactones of the weed Parthenium hysterophorus ('congress grass') in farmers; men > women
- Patterns: classical airborne (face, eyelids, V of neck, flexures, retro-auricular and sub-mental — not spared unlike photodermatitis), photosensitive lichenoid, chronic actinic dermatitis-like, mixed, exfoliative, prurigo nodularis-like
- Treatment: avoidance (difficult), topical/systemic steroids, azathioprine (weekly 300 mg pulse used in our protocol or daily), cyclosporine, methotrexate

**Q7. Differentiate airborne contact dermatitis from photodermatitis.**
- Airborne: upper eyelids, behind ears, submental area, nasolabial folds involved (allergen settles there)
- Photo: these shaded areas spared (Wilkinson's triangle behind the ear, submental, upper eyelids)

**Q8. Describe the patch test procedure.**
- Indications: suspected ACD, chronic/recurrent eczema of hands/face/feet, worsening on topical therapy, occupational dermatitis
- Allergens in standard concentration in petrolatum/water (Indian standard series ~20–25 allergens; plus cosmetic, vegetable, footwear, patient's own products) in Finn chambers on upper back
- Remove at 48 h (D2), read 30–60 min later and at D3/D4 (and D7 for late reactors — neomycin, corticosteroids, metals)
- Avoid: potent topical steroid on back for 1 week, oral prednisolone >20 mg/day, immunosuppressants, recent UV exposure, active eczema

**Q9. How do you grade patch test readings (ICDRG)?**
- – negative; ?+ doubtful (faint erythema); + weak (erythema, infiltration, possibly papules); ++ strong (erythema, infiltration, papules, vesicles); +++ extreme (spreading, bullous/ulcerative); IR irritant (patchy, glazed, follicular, pustular, sharply limited, decrescendo)
- Assess relevance: current, past, unknown, cross-reaction

**Q10. What are false positive and false negative patch tests?**
- False positive: irritant concentration, excited skin ('angry back' syndrome — multiple positive reactions when one strong reaction is present), pressure effect, impurities
- False negative: low concentration, poor occlusion, early reading only, steroid/UV, vehicle not releasing allergen, need for photo-patch or open/repeat open application test (ROAT)

**Q11. What are photo-patch tests?**
- Duplicate allergen sets applied; one irradiated with UVA 5 J/cm² at 24–48 h; reaction only at irradiated site = photoallergy (sunscreens, NSAIDs like ketoprofen, fragrances, chlorpromazine)

**Q12. What is systemic contact dermatitis?**
- Flare of previous ACD sites or generalised eczema after oral/IV exposure to the allergen — e.g. nickel in diet, balsam of Peru in spices, drugs (aminoglycosides after neomycin), baboon syndrome (SDRIFE — buttock/flexural symmetrical eruption)

**Q13. Write a note on contact urticaria (PYQ).**
- Wheal-and-flare at contact site within 30–60 min
- Non-immunological (commonest — benzoic/sorbic acid, cinnamal, nettles, cobalt), immunological (IgE — latex, foods; risk of anaphylaxis), unknown mechanism (ammonium persulphate)
- Tests: open test, prick test, RAST; protein contact dermatitis in food handlers (chronic hand eczema with urticarial flares)

**Q14. Classify occupational dermatoses (PYQ).**
- Contact dermatitis (commonest ~90%) — irritant > allergic; contact urticaria
- Infections (milker's nodules, orf, erysipeloid, swimming-pool granuloma), oil acne/chloracne, pigmentary (vitiligo from phenols/hydroquinone monobenzyl ether — occupational leucoderma), skin cancers (arsenic, tar, UV), mechanical (callosities, occupational marks), sclerodermatous (vinyl chloride, silica), nail disorders
- Mathias criteria for causation (7 questions — consistent clinical, exposure, timing, distribution, non-occupational causes excluded, improvement away from work, patch/provocation test)

**Q15. What is chloracne? (PYQ)**
- Acneiform eruption from halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (dioxins, PCBs, PCNs) — many comedones and straw-coloured cysts on malar/retro-auricular areas, axillae, scrotum; marker of systemic toxicity; very persistent

**Q16. Management of contact dermatitis.**
- Identify and avoid allergen/irritant; substitutes (nickel-free, PPD-free dyes, vinyl/nitrile gloves for rubber allergy); patient information leaflet with names and sources
- Acute: wet compresses (Burow's solution), potent topical steroid, oral antihistamine; severe/widespread: short oral prednisolone
- Chronic: emollients, barrier creams (limited value), protective gloves with cotton liners, workplace modification; tacrolimus; phototherapy; azathioprine/methotrexate/cyclosporine for chronic airborne; alitretinoin for chronic hand eczema
- Nickel: dimethylglyoxime test to detect nickel release; EU Nickel Directive

**Q17. What is the dimethylglyoxime test?**
- 1% dimethylglyoxime + 10% ammonia rubbed on a metal object — pink colour means nickel release >0.5 µg/cm²/week

**Q18. What is chronic actinic dermatitis? (PYQ)**
- Persistent photosensitive eczema of sun-exposed skin in elderly men (often with parthenium/ Compositae or fragrance allergy), lichenified plaques, sparing of shaded sites; reduced MED to UVB ± UVA/visible; may mimic lymphoma (actinic reticuloid)
- Treatment: strict photoprotection, allergen avoidance, topical steroids/tacrolimus, azathioprine, cyclosporine, low-dose PUVA/NB-UVB (hardening)

**Q19. What is the Indian standard series and how is it different from the European?**
- Indian Standard Series (Contact and Occupational Dermatoses Forum of India) — ~20–25 allergens chosen for local exposures: parthenium, PPD, nickel, chromate, cobalt, fragrance mix, colophony, neomycin, nitrofurazone, gentian violet, mercaptobenzothiazole, thiuram, black rubber mix, epoxy resin, formaldehyde, parabens, benzocaine, etc.
- European Baseline Series (~30) includes newer preservatives (methylisothiazolinone), budesonide/ tixocortol, textile dye mix, propolis, sesquiterpene lactone mix; supplementary Indian series exist (cosmetic, vegetable, footwear, hair-dye)

**Q20. What is the repeated open application test (ROAT)?**
- Patient applies the suspected product (cosmetic/ medicament) twice daily to the antecubital fossa for 7–14 days; a reaction confirms clinical relevance of a weak or doubtful patch test; useful for leave-on cosmetics

**Q21. What is the 'use test' and 'semi-open test'?**
- Use test: applying the product as normally used to a limited area
- Semi-open test: for irritant products (shampoos, paints) — small amount applied, allowed to dry, then covered, to avoid irritant reactions

**Q22. Pathogenesis of irritant contact dermatitis.**
- Direct damage to stratum corneum lipids and keratinocytes (surfactants, solvents, alkalis) → barrier disruption, TEWL, release of IL-1α, TNF-α, IL-8 from keratinocytes (innate inflammation, no memory); factors — concentration, duration, occlusion, frequency, atopy (barrier), age, site (thin skin), climate

**Q23. Hand dermatitis in health workers — approach.**
- Wet work and frequent handwashing (ICD), rubber glove allergy (thiurams, carbamates), latex contact urticaria (type I — anaphylaxis risk), chlorhexidine/ fragrance; prefer alcohol hand rubs, cotton-lined synthetic (nitrile) gloves, emollients after washing; patch and prick test

**Q24. Rubber allergy — types and alternatives.**
- Type IV to rubber accelerators — thiuram (gloves), carbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole (footwear), black rubber mix (PPD derivatives — tyres, rubber handles) — use vinyl/ nitrile gloves labelled accelerator-free
- Type I latex allergy — natural rubber latex proteins (Hev b); cross-reacts with banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut (latex–fruit syndrome); use non-latex gloves

**Q25. Footwear dermatitis — features.**
- Symmetrical dermatitis on dorsa of feet and toes sparing web spaces (vs tinea), may involve soles in rubber sole allergy; allergens — rubber accelerators (MBT), chromate (leather), adhesives (p-tertiary butylphenol formaldehyde resin — PTBP, also causes leucoderma), dyes; change to vegetable-tanned/ PVC/ cloth footwear

**Q26. Cosmetic allergy — common culprits.**
- Fragrances (fragrance mix I/II, balsam of Peru, cinnamal, isoeugenol), preservatives (methylisothiazolinone — 'epidemic' in Europe, formaldehyde releasers — quaternium-15, DMDM hydantoin; parabens rarely), PPD in hair dyes, kumkum (Sudan I, brilliant lake red R), sunscreen filters, lanolin, propolis, nail acrylates (methacrylates — fingertip dermatitis, gel nails)

**Q27. Medicament allergy — what to suspect?**
- Worsening of a dermatitis despite treatment, or leg ulcer/ stasis dermatitis/ otitis externa/ perianal dermatitis spreading — neomycin, framycetin, gentamicin, benzocaine, lignocaine, nitrofurazone, povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine, steroids (budesonide/tixocortol — groups A, B, D), lanolin, emulsifiers

**Q28. What is pigmented contact dermatitis (Riehl's melanosis)?**
- Minimal eczema with grey-brown facial pigmentation in darker skin due to repeated low-grade allergy to fragrances, cosmetic dyes (brilliant lake red), kumkum, hair dyes; histology — interface damage and pigment incontinence; patch test to identify allergen; strict avoidance, photoprotection

**Q29. Discuss airborne contact dermatitis causes besides parthenium.**
- Other Compositae (chrysanthemum, sunflower, Xanthium), Lantana, Ageratum, wood dust, pollen, epoxy resin vapours, fragrance sprays, insecticides, cement/ fibreglass dust (irritant), Primula, Toxicodendron smoke; clue — involvement of eyelids, behind ears, submental, V-neck, flexures

**Q30. What are the newer treatments for chronic hand eczema?**
- Delgocitinib 2% cream (topical pan-JAK inhibitor, approved for moderate–severe chronic hand eczema), alitretinoin 30 mg/day (chronic hyperkeratotic), dupilumab (atopic hand eczema), oral JAK inhibitors under study; PUVA soaks

**Q31. Prognosis of occupational contact dermatitis.**
- Poor — only 25–30% clear completely; many continue despite job change (persistent post-occupational dermatitis); better with early diagnosis, education, allergen avoidance; chromate allergy has worst prognosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Cement + men + hand eczema — chromate ACD
- Hair-dye — PPD
- Eyelids, behind ears, submental involved — airborne (parthenium) not photodermatitis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Contact dermatitis, occupational dermatoses); Indian standard patch test series. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Corn (clavus) — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Corn (clavus)** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is a corn?**
- Sharply circumscribed, painful hyperkeratotic lesion with a central translucent, conical keratin core (radix) that presses on underlying dermal nerves; due to localised repeated pressure over bony prominences

**Q2. Types.**
- Hard corn (heloma durum): dorsolateral fifth toe, tops of interphalangeal joints (claw/hammer toes), sole over metatarsal heads
- Soft corn (heloma molle): macerated white lesion in the interdigital space (commonly 4th web) from opposing bony prominences — may be mistaken for tinea pedis
- Seed corns (heloma miliare): multiple tiny corns on weight-bearing sole
- Vascular and neurofibrous corns (painful, bleeding on paring)

**Q3. Differential diagnosis.**
- Plantar wart (black dots, interrupted skin lines, pain on lateral pressure), callus, punctate keratoderma, porokeratosis plantaris discreta, foreign body, eccrine poroma, tinea pedis/soft corn

**Q4. Paring test.**
- Paring a corn reveals a central translucent core with intact skin lines; paring a wart shows pinpoint bleeding black dots and interrupted dermatoglyphics

**Q5. Management.**
- Relieve pressure: wide-toed shoes, corn pads/doughnut cushions, toe separators (soft corn), orthotics, correct toe deformities (surgery for persistent cases — exostectomy, arthroplasty)
- Paring/enucleation of the core with a scalpel — immediate relief
- Keratolytic plasters (salicylic acid 40%), urea creams; avoid caustic corn caps in diabetics/peripheral vascular disease
- Recurrence common unless mechanical cause corrected

**Q6. Histopathology of a corn.**
- Cup-shaped depression of the epidermis filled with a dense central column of parakeratotic keratin (the core) pressing into the dermis; surrounding hyperkeratosis; thinned granular layer beneath the core

**Q7. Why are corns painful?**
- The central keratin core (inverted cone) presses on dermal nerve endings and bursa over a bony prominence; soft corns can macerate and become infected

**Q8. Where do soft corns occur and why?**
- Between toes (usually 4th web space) where a bony prominence (condyle of proximal phalanx) presses on the adjacent toe; moisture keeps them soft and white (macerated); may mimic interdigital tinea

**Q9. What surgical or orthopaedic options exist for recurrent corns?**
- Correct underlying deformity — exostectomy, condylectomy, hammer-toe correction; silicone toe separators and padding; avoid tight pointed footwear

**Q10. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q11. Describe the types in detail.**
- Hard corn (heloma durum): dorsolateral aspect of toes (5th toe), over bony prominences in tight shoes
- Soft corn (heloma molle): interdigital (4th web), macerated white
- Seed corns: tiny multiple corns on weight-bearing sole (dry skin)
- Vascular/ neurovascular corns: painful with capillaries/ nerves in core, bleed on paring

**Q12. What padding and footwear advice?**
- Wide toe-box footwear, low heels, silicone toe sleeves/ separators, metatarsal pads, foam corn pads (avoid medicated corn plasters with salicylic acid in diabetics/ PVD), orthotics for biomechanical faults

**Q13. Why should medicated corn plasters be avoided in diabetics?**
- Salicylic acid can macerate and ulcerate neuropathic/ ischaemic skin without pain warning → infection, gangrene

**Q14. Corn vs wart — paring test details.**
- Paring a corn reveals a translucent central keratin core with intact skin lines; a wart shows black dots (thrombosed capillaries) and pinpoint bleeding with interrupted dermatoglyphics; lateral squeeze painful in wart, direct pressure painful in corn

**Q15. What is porokeratosis plantaris discreta?**
- Painful, discrete, hard keratotic plug on the plantar surface (often under metatarsal heads) in middle-aged women — central cornoid-like plug (eccrine duct obstruction); mimics corn/ wart; treat with paring, cryotherapy, excision

## Quick spotter facts
- Painful circumscribed lesion with central translucent core over bony prominence — corn
- Soft corn in 4th toe web

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Mechanical injuries). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Cutaneous candidiasis / intertrigo — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Cutaneous candidiasis / intertrigo** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is candidiasis? Main species?**
- Infection by Candida (yeast; commensal of gut, mouth, vagina) when local or systemic defences fail — C. albicans (commonest); non-albicans: C. glabrata, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei (fluconazole resistant), Candida auris (multidrug-resistant, hospital outbreaks)
- Dimorphic: yeast, pseudohyphae and true hyphae (in tissue)

**Q2. Predisposing factors.**
- Local: moisture, occlusion, obesity, maceration, friction, dentures, wet work, diapers
- Systemic: diabetes, pregnancy, infancy/old age, antibiotics, steroids, OCP, HIV, immunosuppression, iron deficiency, endocrinopathies (hypoparathyroidism, hypothyroidism, Addison's)

**Q3. Clinical forms of mucocutaneous candidiasis.**
- Oral: pseudomembranous (thrush, removable white plaques), erythematous (atrophic — antibiotic/denture), hyperplastic (leukoplakia-like), angular cheilitis, median rhomboid glossitis
- Genital: vulvovaginitis (curdy discharge, itching), balanoposthitis (diabetics, uncircumcised)
- Skin: intertrigo (flexures), napkin candidiasis, interdigital (erosio interdigitalis blastomycetica — 3rd web space of hand in wet workers), chronic paronychia, onychomycosis
- Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC); congenital and neonatal candidiasis; disseminated candidiasis (nodules in neutropenic patients)

**Q4. Describe candidal intertrigo.**
- Bright beefy-red moist glazed patches in folds (groin, submammary, axillae, abdominal folds) with fissure at the base, peripheral scaling (collarette) and satellite papulopustules
- Burning/itching; scrotum often involved (unlike tinea cruris)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis of intertrigo.**
- Tinea cruris (active edge, scrotum spared), erythrasma (brown, coral-red fluorescence), inverse psoriasis (well-defined, no satellites), seborrhoeic dermatitis, irritant/allergic contact dermatitis, Hailey–Hailey disease, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (infants), extramammary Paget's (elderly, persistent)

**Q6. What is chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC)?**
- Group of disorders with persistent/recurrent Candida infections of skin, nails and mucosa due to defective Th17 immunity
- Causes: STAT1 gain-of-function, IL-17RA/IL-17F, CARD9 deficiency, AIRE mutation (APECED/APS-1 — with hypoparathyroidism, Addison's), hyper-IgE (STAT3); thymoma
- Treatment: long-term azoles, treat endocrinopathy

**Q7. Investigations.**
- KOH/Gram stain: budding yeasts with pseudohyphae (pseudohyphae suggest invasion)
- Culture on SDA (creamy colonies); germ tube test (C. albicans positive), CHROMagar for species, antifungal susceptibility for recurrent/non-albicans
- Blood sugar, HIV; in CMC — immunology and endocrine work-up

**Q8. Treatment of cutaneous candidiasis.**
- Keep area dry, separate folds with cotton cloth, weight loss, control diabetes, treat source (oral/gut)
- Topical azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole), nystatin, ciclopirox; short mild steroid combination only if very inflamed
- Oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly/50–100 mg daily for 1–2 weeks for extensive or recurrent; itraconazole alternative

**Q9. Treatment of vulvovaginal candidiasis.**
- Clotrimazole 500 mg vaginal pessary single dose or 100 mg for 6 nights, or fluconazole 150 mg oral single dose (avoid oral in pregnancy — use topical 7 days)
- Recurrent (≥4/year): fluconazole 150 mg every 72 h × 3 doses, then weekly for 6 months; C. glabrata — boric acid vaginal capsules

**Q10. What is chronic paronychia and its management?**
- Inflammation of proximal nail fold >6 weeks in wet workers; loss of cuticle, bolstered red fold, nail dystrophy; now considered mainly an irritant/eczematous process with Candida as secondary
- Keep hands dry, gloves, topical steroid + azole, treat Candida, avoid cuticle trimming

**Q11. What is Candida auris and why important?**
- Emerging multidrug-resistant yeast, hospital outbreaks, colonises skin, often misidentified by routine methods; needs echinocandin and strict infection control

**Q12. Oral candidiasis — treatment.**
- Topical nystatin suspension 1 ml four times daily, clotrimazole troches, miconazole oral gel (interaction with warfarin); fluconazole 100–200 mg/day for 7–14 days for moderate–severe; treat denture stomatitis (denture hygiene); HIV — fluconazole, itraconazole for resistant

**Q13. Candida virulence factors.**
- Adhesins (Als proteins), hyphal/ pseudohyphal transformation, phenotypic switching, secreted aspartyl proteases, phospholipases, biofilm formation, candidalysin (cytolytic peptide toxin), thigmotropism

**Q14. Congenital and neonatal candidiasis.**
- Congenital: within first day — widespread erythematous papulovesicles/ pustules including palms/ soles (ascending infection); neonatal: after 1 week — oral thrush, diaper candidiasis; premature infants — systemic candidiasis (fluconazole/ amphotericin)

**Q15. Classify antifungal drugs (PYQ).**
- Polyenes: amphotericin B (systemic, deep mycoses), nystatin (topical/ oral Candida)
- Azoles — imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole) and triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) — inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis)
- Allylamines: terbinafine, naftifine (squalene epoxidase inhibitors); benzylamine — butenafine
- Echinocandins: caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin (β-1,3-glucan synthase)
- Others: griseofulvin (microtubule — mitotic inhibitor), flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis), ciclopirox (chelator), amorolfine (morpholine — Δ14 reductase/ Δ7-Δ8 isomerase), tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), potassium iodide, efinaconazole, tavaborole

## Quick spotter facts
- Beefy-red fold with satellite pustules and scrotal involvement — candidal intertrigo
- Erosio interdigitalis blastomycetica — 3rd finger web
- Pseudohyphae on KOH

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Candidiasis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Cutaneous tuberculosis — viva
posts.summary: Leprosy & mycobacterial · 31 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Cutaneous tuberculosis** (Leprosy & mycobacterial)_

**Q1. What is cutaneous tuberculosis? How common is it?**
- Infection of skin by M. tuberculosis (rarely M. bovis, BCG) — about 0.1–1% of dermatology patients in India; ~1–2% of extrapulmonary TB
- Commonest Indian forms: lupus vulgaris (adults) and scrofuloderma (children)

**Q2. Classify cutaneous TB (asked very often).**
- True (bacilli in skin): primary — tuberculous chancre (inoculation in a non-immune person); secondary (prior immunity) — lupus vulgaris (haematogenous/lymphatic or exogenous), tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (exogenous re-inoculation), scrofuloderma (contiguous spread), orificial TB (autoinoculation), tuberculous gumma/metastatic abscess (haematogenous), acute miliary TB
- Tuberculids (no bacilli; hypersensitivity): lichen scrofulosorum, papulonecrotic tuberculid, erythema induratum of Bazin (nodular), ± erythema nodosum/nodular tuberculid
- Also classified by bacillary load: multibacillary (chancre, scrofuloderma, orificial, miliary, gumma) vs paucibacillary (LV, TBVC)

**Q3. How does host immunity decide the clinical form?**
- High immunity: TBVC, LV, tuberculids (few bacilli, strong tuberculin)
- Low immunity: miliary, orificial, gumma in malnourished/immunosuppressed; scrofuloderma intermediate
- Th1/Th17 polarisation → localised disease; Th2/Treg → disseminated

**Q4. Describe lupus vulgaris.**
- Chronic progressive paucibacillary form in previously sensitised person; in India mostly on buttocks, trunk, limbs (face in the West)
- Soft reddish-brown plaques that spread at one edge and scar at the other; apple-jelly nodules on diascopy
- Types: plaque (commonest), ulcerative, vegetating, hypertrophic/tumid, papulonodular, sporotrichoid
- Complications: scarring, contractures, mutilation (nose, ear), squamous cell carcinoma in old scars (lupus carcinoma)

**Q5. What is diascopy and its significance?**
- Pressing a glass slide on the lesion blanches erythema to show the yellow-brown 'apple-jelly' colour of granulomas
- Seen in lupus vulgaris, sarcoidosis, granulomatous rosacea, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, leishmaniasis, tuberculoid leprosy

**Q6. Describe tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (TBVC).**
- Exogenous re-infection in an immune host — 'prosector's wart', 'butcher's wart'; on hands, knees, ankles, buttocks of barefoot walkers and those who sit on the ground
- Warty plaque with irregular edge, fissures that may ooze pus on pressure; slow peripheral spread, central healing with atrophic scar
- Histology: pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis, abscesses in upper dermis, tuberculoid granulomas deeper

**Q7. Describe scrofuloderma.**
- Direct extension from an underlying tuberculous focus — cervical lymph node (commonest), bone, joint, epididymis
- Firm painless subcutaneous swelling → cold abscess → breaks to form undermined ulcers and sinuses discharging cheesy material; bridged (cord-like) scars
- Children and young adults; tuberculin strongly positive; bacilli may be found in pus

**Q8. Differential diagnosis of scrofuloderma.**
- Atypical mycobacterial lymphadenitis, actinomycosis (sulphur granules), mycetoma, sporotrichosis, hidradenitis suppurativa (axilla/groin), lymphogranuloma venereum (inguinal), syphilitic gumma, deep fungal infection, pyogenic abscess, branchial cyst sinus

**Q9. Differential diagnosis of lupus vulgaris.**
- Tuberculoid leprosy (anaesthesia, nerve), sarcoidosis, discoid lupus (follicular plugs, atrophy), chromoblastomycosis, leishmaniasis, psoriasis (plaque LV), tertiary syphilis (serpiginous, gumma), deep fungal infection, Bowen's disease, granuloma annulare, tinea (KOH)

**Q10. What is tuberculous chancre?**
- Primary inoculation in a non-immune person (child) after trauma — injection, circumcision, ear piercing, tattooing
- Painless papulonodule → firm shallow ulcer with granular base after 2–3 weeks + marked regional lymphadenopathy (tuberculous primary complex of skin)
- Tuberculin negative at first, converts later; bacilli plentiful; differential: sporotrichosis, cat-scratch disease, primary syphilis, atypical mycobacteria

**Q11. What is orificial tuberculosis?**
- Painful shallow ulcers at mouth, anus, genitals — autoinoculation from advanced internal TB (lung, intestine, urinary) in a poorly immune host; bacilli many; poor prognosis

**Q12. What is a tuberculous gumma (metastatic tuberculous abscess)?**
- Haematogenous spread in immunosuppressed/malnourished children → firm subcutaneous nodules on trunk/limbs which break down into ulcers and sinuses

**Q13. Define tuberculids and list the criteria.**
- Skin eruptions associated with TB elsewhere, thought to be hypersensitivity to bacilli or antigens
- Criteria: typical clinical and histological picture; no bacilli by stain/culture (PCR may be positive); strongly positive Mantoux/IGRA; evidence of present or past TB; response to ATT

**Q14. Describe lichen scrofulosorum.**
- Grouped asymptomatic tiny follicular/perifollicular yellow-brown lichenoid papules on the trunk of children/young adults, often with tuberculous lymph nodes or bone
- Histology: superficial non-caseating granulomas around follicles and sweat ducts
- Differential: lichen nitidus, keratosis pilaris, lichenoid sarcoid, frictional lichenoid eruption

**Q15. Describe papulonecrotic tuberculid.**
- Symmetrical crops of dusky red papules with central necrosis/crust on extensor limbs, knees, elbows, ears, buttocks; heal with varioliform scars
- Histology: wedge-shaped dermal necrosis with vasculitis (leukocytoclastic or granulomatous)
- Differential: PLEVA, lymphomatoid papulosis, perforating disorders, secondary syphilis, prurigo

**Q16. Describe erythema induratum of Bazin.**
- Recurrent tender deep nodules on the backs of calves of young/middle-aged women; may ulcerate and scar
- Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis, caseation and granulomas
- Nodular vasculitis = non-TB counterpart; differential: erythema nodosum (shins, no ulceration, septal panniculitis), polyarteritis nodosa

**Q17. How will you investigate cutaneous TB?**
- Histopathology (tuberculoid granulomas ± caseation) and tissue culture — ideally two biopsies: one for HPE, one for culture/CBNAAT
- Ziehl–Neelsen stain (low yield in paucibacillary forms); culture — LJ medium (4–8 weeks) or liquid MGIT (faster, more sensitive), with drug-susceptibility testing
- CBNAAT/GeneXpert MTB/RIF (rifampicin resistance in ~2 h) and TrueNat — recommended by NTEP; PCR (IS6110) helpful in paucibacillary forms
- Mantoux test (strongly positive in LV, TBVC, tuberculids) and IGRA (QuantiFERON) — support, not diagnose
- Look for systemic focus: chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, FNAC of nodes, sputum; HIV test, blood sugar

**Q18. How do you read a Mantoux test?**
- 0.1 ml (5 TU PPD-S or 2 TU PPD RT23) intradermally on volar forearm, read at 48–72 h as transverse diameter of induration
- ≥10 mm positive in general population; ≥5 mm in HIV/immunosuppressed; very strong (≥15 mm or vesiculation) in tuberculids/LV
- False negative: anergy, HIV, malnutrition, miliary TB, measles, steroids; false positive: BCG, NTM

**Q19. What is a therapeutic trial and when is it justified?**
- When clinical suspicion is strong but bacteriology and histology are inconclusive
- Full four-drug daily regimen for 5–6 weeks; definite improvement supports TB — no response should prompt re-evaluation for other causes
- Use judiciously because of drug toxicity and risk of resistance

**Q20. What is the treatment of cutaneous TB (NTEP)?**
- Same as extra-pulmonary TB — daily fixed-dose combination by weight band
- Intensive phase 2 months: isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (HRZE); continuation phase 4 months: HRE (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol) — total 6 months; may be extended (e.g. to 9–12 months) by the clinician for slow response or associated bone/CNS disease
- Drug-resistant TB (rifampicin resistance on CBNAAT): refer for NTEP DR-TB regimens (e.g. BPaLM — bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin — 6 months)
- Pyridoxine with INH; check LFT; Nikshay registration and Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana nutrition support; surgical excision for small LV, plastic repair later

**Q21. Major side effects of first-line ATT?**
- Isoniazid: hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (prevent with pyridoxine), pellagra, lupus-like syndrome, acneiform rash
- Rifampicin: hepatitis, orange discolouration of secretions, flu-like illness, thrombocytopenia, drug interactions
- Pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia/gout, photosensitivity
- Ethambutol: optic neuritis (red–green colour vision), hypersensitivity
- Cutaneous drug reactions: commonest culprit — first-line drugs cause maculopapular rash, DRESS, SJS/TEN, lichenoid eruption, FDE

**Q22. How do you assess response to treatment?**
- Clinical: lesions flatten and stop spreading in 4–6 weeks; ulcers heal; sinus discharge stops
- Most heal by the end of 6 months; residual scarring is common

**Q23. What is BCG-related skin disease?**
- Normal: papule → ulcer → scar in 6–12 weeks
- Complications: local abscess, regional lymphadenitis (suppurative), lupus vulgaris at site, keloid, disseminated BCG-osis in immunodeficiency (SCID, HIV)
- BCG reactivation at injection site in Kawasaki disease

**Q24. What is the difference between atypical mycobacterial infection and TB of skin?**
- NTM (M. marinum — fish-tank granuloma, sporotrichoid nodules on hand; M. ulcerans — Buruli ulcer; M. fortuitum/chelonae/abscessus — post-procedure abscesses after injections, liposuction, pedicure)
- NTM: from environment, not person-to-person; often resistant to standard ATT — needs clarithromycin, doxycycline, rifampicin/ethambutol, amikacin by species

**Q25. Histopathology of lupus vulgaris?**
- Tuberculoid granulomas (epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes) in upper and mid dermis, usually with little or no caseation
- Epidermis may be atrophic, ulcerated or hyperplastic; AFB rarely seen

**Q26. Why is scrofuloderma classed as multibacillary but tuberculids as having no bacilli?**
- Scrofuloderma: direct spread from a bacilli-rich deep focus with intermediate immunity
- Tuberculids: strong immunity clears organisms, leaving immune-mediated inflammation (antigen/DNA may be detected by PCR)

**Q27. How do you differentiate lupus vulgaris from sarcoidosis clinically and on histology?**
- Clinical: LV is unilateral, slowly spreading, with scarring and ulceration; sarcoid is often symmetrical, non-ulcerating, with systemic features
- Histology: LV has tuberculoid granulomas with dense lymphocytes, sometimes caseation; sarcoid has 'naked' granulomas with sparse lymphocytes, no caseation
- Mantoux: LV strongly positive; sarcoid often negative (anergy)

**Q28. Prognosis?**
- Excellent with full ATT; complications only from delay — scarring, deformities, SCC in long-standing lupus vulgaris

**Q29. What is the role of IGRA versus Mantoux in skin TB?**
- IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, T-SPOT.TB) measures IFN-γ release to ESAT-6/CFP-10 — not affected by BCG or most NTM, single visit, but cannot distinguish latent vs active and costly; both support diagnosis in paucibacillary forms and tuberculids when combined with clinical and histological evidence

**Q30. What are the newer Indian molecular diagnostics?**
- CBNAAT/GeneXpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra, TrueNat MTB/RIF (Indian chip-based, battery-operated) — rapid detection with rifampicin resistance; Line Probe Assay (first- and second-line drugs: INH, FQ, aminoglycosides); MGIT liquid culture for DST — recommended by NTEP for extrapulmonary samples

**Q31. What is TB-HIV coinfection's effect on skin TB?**
- More multibacillary forms (miliary, gummas, orificial, scrofuloderma), atypical lesions, negative tuberculin, IRIS after ART (paradoxical worsening); give ATT first, start ART within 2–8 weeks depending on CD4; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis

## Quick spotter facts
- Apple-jelly nodules on diascopy — lupus vulgaris (also sarcoid)
- Sinus + undermined ulcer + bridge scars over neck nodes — scrofuloderma
- Warty plaque on the knee of barefoot worker — TBVC

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 16 (Cutaneous tuberculosis); NTEP (India) treatment guidance. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Darier's disease — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Darier's disease** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is Darier's disease (keratosis follicularis)?**
- Autosomal dominant genodermatosis due to ATP2A2 mutations (SERCA2 — sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase) → impaired desmosome assembly → acantholysis and dyskeratosis; onset around puberty (10–20 y)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Greasy, warty, red-brown keratotic papules in a seborrhoeic distribution — scalp margin, forehead, nasolabial folds, ears, central chest/back, flexures (may become vegetating and malodorous); itchy, worse with heat, sweat, UV and friction
- Acral: palmar pits/punctate keratoses, AKV-like papules on dorsa of hands
- Nails (diagnostic): longitudinal alternating red and white bands, V-shaped notching at the free edge, subungual hyperkeratosis
- Oral: cobblestone white papules on palate
- Neuropsychiatric associations: depression, bipolar disorder, epilepsy, intellectual disability; salivary gland obstruction
- Variants: segmental/linear (mosaic), haemorrhagic acral, comedonal, bullous

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Suprabasal acantholysis forming clefts (lacunae) with villi, dyskeratotic cells — corps ronds (large round cells with pyknotic nucleus and clear halo, in spinous/granular layers) and grains (small elongated dark cells in stratum corneum), column of parakeratosis over the clefts
- DIF negative (vs pemphigus)

**Q4. Complications.**
- Secondary bacterial infection, Kaposi's varicelliform eruption (HSV), dermatophyte infections, malodour, social stigma

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis, Hailey–Hailey (flexural, erosions, no nail bands), Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis — older men, trunk, transient), acanthosis nigricans, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, AKV of Hopf, pemphigus vegetans, warts

**Q6. Management.**
- Avoid triggers: heat, sweating, sun (sunscreen), friction; cool cotton clothing; antiseptic washes
- Topical: retinoids (tazarotene, adapalene), steroids (short courses), 5-FU, calcineurin inhibitors, antibiotics/antifungals for infections
- Systemic: acitretin 10–25 mg/day or isotretinoin (most effective); doxycycline for flares; antivirals for HSV; oral magnesium chloride (case reports)
- Procedures: CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, dermabrasion, PDT, excision for localised hypertrophic areas; botulinum toxin for flexural sweat-induced flares

**Q7. Clinical features in more detail.**
- Onset in adolescence: greasy, yellow-brown keratotic papules in seborrhoeic distribution (scalp margin, forehead, nasolabial folds, chest, back, flexures), coalescing into crusted malodorous warty plaques; palmar pits/ punctate keratoses, acral AKV-like papules, nail changes, oral cobblestone papules

**Q8. Histopathology in detail.**
- Suprabasal acantholysis forming clefts (lacunae) with villi (dermal papillae lined by single layer of basal cells), dyskeratotic cells — corps ronds (round with perinuclear halo, in granular layer) and grains (flattened elongated in stratum corneum), overlying parakeratosis

**Q9. Clinical variants.**
- Segmental (type 1 — unilateral along Blaschko lines; type 2 — superimposed severe segment), hypertrophic, vesiculobullous, haemorrhagic acral (blistering), cornifying, comedonal, hypopigmented guttate macules (dark skin)

**Q10. Neuropsychiatric associations.**
- Higher rates of depression, bipolar disorder, suicidal ideation, epilepsy, intellectual disability (ATP2A2 expressed in brain) — screen mood; lithium (for bipolar) may worsen Darier's

**Q11. What is Kaposi's varicelliform eruption in Darier's?**
- Disseminated HSV infection on Darier lesions — sudden painful monomorphic erosions, fever — treat with acyclovir promptly; also prone to S. aureus, poxvirus infections

**Q12. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q13. What is the genetic and molecular basis?**
- Autosomal dominant ATP2A2 mutation → defective SERCA2 (sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase pump) → abnormal calcium signalling and impaired desmosome assembly → acantholysis and dyskeratosis

**Q14. Describe the nail changes and oral changes.**
- Nails: red and white longitudinal streaks (alternating), V-shaped notching at free edge, subungual hyperkeratosis, fragility — very characteristic
- Oral: white cobblestone papules on palate and gums; salivary gland obstruction

**Q15. Why does Darier's disease worsen in summer?**
- Heat, sweating, UVB (provocation of lesions), friction, lithium, menstruation and infections (S. aureus, HSV — Kaposi's varicelliform eruption) aggravate

**Q16. Treatment details.**
- Avoid heat, sweat, sun; cool cotton clothing; sunscreens; antiseptic washes
- Topical: retinoids (tazarotene, adapalene, tretinoin), 5-FU, steroids/ tacrolimus for inflamed areas
- Systemic: acitretin 10–25 mg/day or isotretinoin (most effective; teratogenicity), doxycycline for secondary infection; oral magnesium, naltrexone (low dose) reported
- Localised resistant: CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, dermabrasion, excision, PDT, botulinum toxin (flexural sweating)

## Quick spotter facts
- Greasy warty papules in seborrhoeic distribution + red/white nail bands with V-nicks — Darier's (ATP2A2)
- Corps ronds and grains

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Darier's disease). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Dermatitis artefacta — viva
posts.summary: Psychocutaneous disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dermatitis artefacta** (Psychocutaneous disorders)_

**Q1. Classify psychocutaneous disorders (PYQ).**
- Psychophysiological disorders — skin disease worsened by stress (psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, urticaria, acne, alopecia areata, hyperhidrosis)
- Primary psychiatric disorders with skin manifestations — dermatitis artefacta (factitious disorder), delusional infestation (delusional parasitosis), body dysmorphic disorder, trichotillomania, skin picking (excoriation) disorder, neurotic excoriations, acne excoriée, onychophagia, dysmorphophobia, Dhat syndrome
- Secondary psychiatric disorders due to skin disease — depression, anxiety, social phobia (vitiligo, psoriasis, acne, alopecia)
- Cutaneous sensory disorders — glossodynia, vulvodynia, scalp dysaesthesia, chronic pruritus without cause
- Skin side-effects of psychotropic drugs (lithium acne/psoriasis, anticonvulsant SJS, antipsychotic pigmentation)

**Q2. Define dermatitis artefacta (PYQ).**
- Self-inflicted skin lesions produced consciously but with motivation that is unconscious (need for care, attention, escape from stress) — the patient denies self-infliction; a factitious disorder (not malingering, where there is conscious external gain)
- Commonest in adolescent girls and young women; often with borderline personality traits, past trauma/abuse, stress, health-care workers

**Q3. Clinical clues.**
- 'Hollow history' — lesions appear fully formed overnight, vague account, patient unconcerned (la belle indifférence) while family anxious
- Bizarre geometric shapes, straight lines, sharp angulated margins, normal surrounding skin, within reach of the dominant hand (spares the hand used, mid-back spared), unilateral, symmetrical patterns
- Lesion types: excoriations, burns (cigarette, chemical — drip marks), ulcers, purpura (suction, ligature), blisters, panniculitis (injection of foreign material — milk, faeces, oil), dermatitis from caustics, hair pulling, eyelid/lip lesions
- Failure to heal with standard therapy; healing under occlusive dressing (e.g. plaster cast) — diagnostic

**Q4. How do you differentiate dermatitis artefacta, malingering and neurotic excoriations?**
- Artefacta: unconscious motive, denies self-infliction
- Malingering: conscious production for external gain (compensation, avoid work/prison)
- Neurotic excoriations/skin picking: patient admits picking (compulsion), lesions in reachable areas, repeated picking of normal skin or minor bumps

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Vasculitis, pyoderma gangrenosum (pathergy — surgery worsens), contact dermatitis, porphyria, bullous diseases, infections (ecthyma, atypical mycobacteria), panniculitis, Munchausen syndrome by proxy (child), child abuse/non-accidental injury

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Mainly clinical and to exclude organic disease: biopsy (foreign-body granuloma, polarisable material), cultures, patch test; occlusion test (healing under sealed dressing)
- Psychological assessment

**Q7. Management.**
- Non-confrontational, empathetic, long-term relationship with the patient — avoid accusing directly; acknowledge distress
- Symptomatic wound care, occlusive dressings, treat infection
- Joint dermatology–psychiatry (psychodermatology) care: psychotherapy (CBT, dialectical behaviour therapy), treat underlying depression/anxiety/personality disorder — SSRIs, low-dose antipsychotics
- Avoid unnecessary investigations/surgeries; involve family carefully; safeguarding in children

**Q8. Write short notes on delusional infestation (PYQ).**
- Fixed false belief of being infested by parasites/organisms despite no evidence; middle-aged/elderly women; 'matchbox sign' (bringing specimens — lint, skin debris)
- Primary (monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis) or secondary (schizophrenia, depression, dementia, drugs — cocaine, amphetamines, dopamine agonists; organic — B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, renal failure)
- Treatment: build trust, exclude real infestation and organic causes, antipsychotics — risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole, (pimozide — older, QT prolongation)

**Q9. Describe dermatitis simulata and dermatitis passivata.**
- Dermatitis simulata: mimicking skin disease without damaging skin (applying dyes, make-up to simulate lesions)
- Dermatitis passivata: self-induced but passive (e.g. allowing a wound to become infected by not treating it)

**Q10. Factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen by proxy).**
- Carer (usually mother) fabricates or induces illness in a child — repeated unexplained lesions, symptoms only in carer's presence, failure to respond to treatment, improvement when separated; child protection referral mandatory

**Q11. Body-focused repetitive behaviours (BFRBs).**
- Trichotillomania, excoriation (skin-picking) disorder, onychophagia (nail biting), onychotillomania, lip/ cheek biting — DSM-5 OCD-related disorders; treat with habit reversal, CBT, NAC, SSRIs

**Q12. Signs on histology suggesting self-infliction.**
- Foreign material (polarisable particles — talc, starch, fibres), epidermal necrosis with sharp cut-off, burns pattern (flattened elongated keratinocytes), haemorrhage without vasculitis, injected substances in fat (oil — lipogranulomas)

**Q13. Prognosis of dermatitis artefacta.**
- Chronic relapsing course (years) especially with personality disorders; better outcome in adolescents with acute stress triggers and early psychological support

**Q14. What psychiatric conditions are associated?**
- Borderline personality disorder, depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, eating disorders, history of abuse; health-care workers over-represented; adolescents under academic/family stress

**Q15. What are the ethical issues and how to communicate?**
- Avoid confrontation and accusation (may break rapport, increase self-harm); acknowledge distress, offer support and joint psychiatric care; document findings carefully; in children consider safeguarding (Munchausen by proxy/ abuse)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bizarre geometric lesions within reach of the dominant hand, 'hollow history' — dermatitis artefacta
- Heals under occlusion

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Psychocutaneous disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Dermatofibroma — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dermatofibroma** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. Write short notes on dermatofibroma (PYQ).**
- Common benign fibrohistiocytic tumour (benign fibrous histiocytoma) — firm, button-like, slightly raised, pink-brown papule/nodule usually on legs of young women; often after minor trauma (insect bite, folliculitis, shaving) — reactive vs clonal debated
- Dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign: lateral compression produces central dimpling because the lesion is tethered to the overlying epidermis

**Q2. Dermoscopy.**
- Central white scar-like patch with delicate peripheral pigment network (light-brown); dotted vessels; ring-like globules

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Ill-defined dermal proliferation of spindle fibroblasts and histiocytes (foam cells, haemosiderin-laden siderophages, Touton giant cells) with collagen trapping at the periphery ('collagen balls'), sparing of a grenz zone
- Overlying epidermis hyperplastic with flat-bottomed elongated pigmented rete ridges ('dirty fingers') and induction of follicular/sebaceous structures (basaloid induction mimicking BCC)
- Factor XIIIa positive, CD34 negative (vs DFSP: CD34 positive, factor XIIIa negative)

**Q4. Variants.**
- Aneurysmal (haemosiderotic — rapid growth, bluish), cellular (higher recurrence), atypical (pseudosarcomatous), epithelioid, lipidised (ankle), multiple eruptive dermatofibromas (SLE, HIV, immunosuppression)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP — larger, growing, multinodular plaque on trunk, CD34+, COL1A1–PDGFB fusion; treat with Mohs/wide excision, imatinib for advanced)
- Melanocytic naevus, melanoma (pigmented DF), keloid/hypertrophic scar, BCC, Kaposi sarcoma, prurigo nodule, epidermoid cyst, Spitz naevus, xanthoma

**Q6. Enumerate painful skin tumours (PYQ).**
- Mnemonic BLENDAN-GG: Blue rubber bleb naevus, Leiomyoma, Eccrine spiradenoma, Neuroma, Dermatofibroma (sometimes), Angiolipoma, Neurilemmoma (schwannoma), Glomus tumour, Granular cell tumour; also chondrodermatitis nodularis helicis, keloid, endometrioma, calcinosis cutis, MPNST

**Q7. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign, often persists; excision if symptomatic, enlarging, cosmetically troublesome or diagnostic doubt (scar may be worse than lesion)
- Cryotherapy, intralesional steroids, lasers (flatten/lighten) — partial results

**Q8. Describe the clinical presentation in detail.**
- Firm, slightly elevated button-like papule/ nodule 0.5–1 cm, brown to pink, adherent to overlying skin, mostly legs of women; often after minor trauma/ insect bite; asymptomatic or itchy; dimple sign positive

**Q9. Histopathology in more detail.**
- Ill-defined dermal proliferation of spindle fibroblasts and histiocytes with collagen trapping at the periphery ('collagen balls'), overlying epidermal hyperplasia with basal hyperpigmentation ('dirty feet'), induction of follicular/ sebaceous structures (can mimic BCC); factor XIIIa positive, CD34 negative

**Q10. Dermoscopy pattern.**
- Central white scar-like patch surrounded by delicate peripheral pigment network — most typical; also ring-like globules, vascular dots in central area

**Q11. Describe radiofrequency/ electrosurgery modalities used for benign lesions.**
- Electrodesiccation (monoterminal, superficial dehydration), electrofulguration (sparking, no contact), electrocoagulation (biterminal, deeper), electrosection (cutting — radiofrequency 'radiosurgery' 3–4 MHz gives fine cuts with less thermal damage); precautions — pacemakers (use bipolar), alcohol-based prep (fire), smoke plume (HPV), avoid on keloid-prone skin

**Q12. Multiple eruptive dermatofibromas — significance.**
- ≥15 DFs or ≥5–8 appearing within 4 months — associated with immunosuppression (SLE, HIV, immunosuppressants, haematological malignancy), pregnancy — investigate

**Q13. Is dermatofibroma a reactive lesion or a neoplasm?**
- Debated — traditionally a reactive fibrohistiocytic proliferation after minor trauma (insect bite, folliculitis, shaving), but clonality (PRKCB/PRKCD gene fusions) suggests a benign neoplasm; multiple eruptive dermatofibromas occur in SLE, HIV, immunosuppression, pregnancy

**Q14. What is the dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign?**
- Lateral compression of the lesion causes it to dimple downward (central depression) because of tethering to the overlying epidermis — characteristic of dermatofibroma

**Q15. Differentiate dermatofibroma from dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP).**
- DFSP: larger, enlarging, multinodular indurated plaque on trunk, slow but locally aggressive; CD34+ (DF is CD34−, factor XIIIa+); storiform spindle cells infiltrating fat in honeycomb pattern; t(17;22) COL1A1–PDGFB fusion; treat with Mohs surgery, imatinib for unresectable

## Quick spotter facts
- Firm leg papule with positive dimple sign — dermatofibroma
- Factor XIIIa+ / CD34− (DFSP is CD34+)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Fibrohistiocytic tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Dermatomyositis — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dermatomyositis** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Define dermatomyositis (DM).**
- Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin lesions and proximal symmetrical muscle weakness; part of the IIM group (with polymyositis, inclusion body myositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, antisynthetase syndrome)
- Bimodal: juvenile (5–15 y) and adult (40–60 y), women 2:1

**Q2. Classify dermatomyositis (Bohan & Peter / Sontheimer).**
- Classic adult DM, juvenile DM, cancer-associated DM, DM overlapping with other CTD
- Clinically amyopathic DM (CADM): skin signs ≥6 months without weakness — amyopathic (normal muscle tests) and hypomyopathic (subclinical abnormal tests)
- Polymyositis (no skin), inclusion body myositis

**Q3. Describe the pathognomonic and characteristic skin signs (Gottron's — PYQ).**
- Pathognomonic: Gottron's papules (violaceous flat-topped papules over knuckles — MCP, PIP, DIP joints) and Gottron's sign (violaceous macules/patches over extensor surfaces of joints — elbows, knees, knuckles, malleoli)
- Characteristic: heliotrope rash (violet-purple erythema ± oedema of upper eyelids), periungual telangiectasia with cuticular overgrowth and haemorrhages (ragged cuticles — Samitz sign), poikiloderma of photo-exposed areas — V-sign (anterior neck/chest), shawl sign (back and shoulders), holster sign (lateral thighs)
- Others: scalp erythema with scaling and non-scarring alopecia, mechanic's hands (hyperkeratotic fissured lateral fingers — antisynthetase syndrome), calcinosis cutis (juvenile), flagellate erythema, Raynaud's, ulcers (MDA5), panniculitis, vasculitis, pruritus (more than in lupus — helps differentiate)

**Q4. Describe the muscle involvement.**
- Proximal symmetrical weakness of shoulder and hip girdles (difficulty combing hair, rising from squatting, climbing stairs), neck flexors, pharyngeal muscles (dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, aspiration), respiratory muscles; myalgia; distal and facial muscles spared

**Q5. Myositis-specific autoantibodies and their associations.**
- Anti-Mi-2: classic DM, prominent skin, good response, low cancer risk
- Anti-TIF1γ (p155/140): strong association with malignancy in adults; severe skin, 'red on white' lesions, palmar hyperkeratotic papules
- Anti-NXP2: calcinosis in juvenile DM, adult malignancy, oedema
- Anti-MDA5 (CADM-140): clinically amyopathic DM, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (high mortality — especially in Asians), palmar papules (inverse Gottron's), skin ulcers, arthritis
- Anti-SAE: skin first then muscle, dysphagia
- Antisynthetase (anti-Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ): myositis, ILD, mechanic's hands, arthritis, Raynaud's, fever

**Q6. How do you investigate DM?**
- Muscle enzymes: CK (most sensitive), aldolase, LDH, AST/ALT; may be normal in CADM
- EMG (myopathic pattern: short polyphasic potentials, fibrillation), MRI of thighs (oedema on STIR — guides biopsy), muscle biopsy (perifascicular atrophy, perivascular inflammation, MxA expression)
- Skin biopsy: interface dermatitis with dermal mucin (similar to lupus); DIF usually negative (unlike lupus)
- ANA, myositis-specific/associated antibody panel
- ILD screen: HRCT chest, PFTs (DLCO); ECG/echo for cardiac; barium swallow/manometry for dysphagia
- Cancer screening in adults (especially first 3 years): CBC, CT chest–abdomen–pelvis, ovarian (CA-125, pelvic USG), breast, colorectal, nasopharyngeal (in Asians), PSA; repeat annually for 3 years

**Q7. Which malignancies are associated with DM?**
- 15–25% of adult DM; ovarian, lung, breast, stomach, colorectal, pancreatic, nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Southeast Asia/China), lymphoma
- Risk factors: age >45–50, male, TIF1γ/NXP2 antibodies, rapid onset, cutaneous necrosis/ulcers, dysphagia, normal CK, poor treatment response

**Q8. Juvenile DM — differences from adult.**
- More vasculopathy (ulceration, lipodystrophy, GI vasculitis), calcinosis (up to 40%), no malignancy association, better prognosis; treat aggressively early (methotrexate + steroids) to prevent calcinosis

**Q9. Differentiate DM from SLE skin disease.**
- DM: violaceous, itchy, over knuckles (Gottron's), heliotrope, scalp involvement, shawl/V sign poikiloderma, periungual changes, muscle weakness, raised CK
- SLE: pink-red, less itchy, between knuckles (spares joints), malar rash spares nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, ANA/anti-dsDNA, DIF lupus band positive

**Q10. Management of DM.**
- Photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreen), physiotherapy, speech therapy for dysphagia
- Systemic corticosteroids prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (or IV methylprednisolone pulse for severe) tapered over months
- Steroid-sparing from the start: methotrexate 15–25 mg/week, azathioprine, mycophenolate (also for ILD)
- Skin: topical steroids/tacrolimus, hydroxychloroquine (watch drug rash — common in DM), methotrexate, dapsone, IVIG (very effective for skin and muscle — approved for DM), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib — refractory skin and MDA5-ILD)
- Refractory: IVIG, rituximab, cyclophosphamide/tacrolimus (ILD), cyclosporine
- Calcinosis: diltiazem, bisphosphonates, probenecid, sodium thiosulphate (topical/intralesional/IV), surgical excision
- Treat underlying malignancy (DM may remit)

**Q11. Prognosis.**
- 5-year survival ~70–90%; worse with malignancy, ILD (MDA5), dysphagia/aspiration, cardiac involvement, older age, delayed treatment

**Q12. Describe the less common skin signs of DM.**
- Mechanic's hands (antisynthetase), palmar papules and ulcers over joint creases (MDA5 — 'inverse Gottron's'), flagellate erythema (scratch-like linear erythema on back), 'V-neck', shawl, holster signs, scalp dermatomyositis (scaly itchy, mimics psoriasis/seb derm), poikiloderma, calcinosis, panniculitis, erythroderma, vesiculobullous DM (malignancy), ovoid palatal patch (TIF1γ), 'red on white' lesions, Wong-type DM (PRP-like follicular hyperkeratosis)

**Q13. What is the mechanism of photosensitivity and itch in DM?**
- UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis increases autoantigen exposure (Mi-2, TIF1γ) and type I IFN production; itch is prominent (IL-31, IFN) — helps differentiate from lupus; photoprotection is essential

**Q14. Muscle biopsy findings.**
- Perifascicular atrophy (pathognomonic), perivascular and perimysial inflammation (CD4 T, B cells, plasmacytoid DCs), MxA overexpression in perifascicular fibres (type I IFN), capillary dropout with complement (MAC) deposition in capillaries
- Polymyositis — endomysial CD8 T-cell invasion; IMNM — necrotic fibres with little inflammation (anti-SRP, anti-HMGCR — statins)

**Q15. What is the antisynthetase syndrome?**
- Anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetase antibodies (Jo-1 commonest, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ, KS): myositis + ILD + non-erosive arthritis + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's + fever; ILD determines prognosis — treat with steroids + MMF/tacrolimus/ rituximab

**Q16. Clinically amyopathic DM — what is important?**
- Skin-predominant (≥6 months) with normal or subclinical muscle tests; still needs malignancy screening and ILD screening — especially anti-MDA5 (rapidly progressive ILD, high mortality in Asians: treat early with steroids + calcineurin inhibitor + cyclophosphamide/ JAK inhibitor; ferritin and KL-6 track severity)

**Q17. Calcinosis in juvenile DM — types and treatment.**
- Superficial plaques/ nodules, deep tumoral masses, intermuscular fascial plane calcification, exoskeleton-like (severe); can ulcerate and extrude chalky material
- Prevention: early aggressive immunosuppression (MTX + steroids, IVIG); treatment: diltiazem, bisphosphonates, sodium thiosulphate (IV/intralesional/topical), probenecid, colchicine, surgery for symptomatic deposits, JAK inhibitors (case series)

**Q18. How is DM disease activity measured?**
- CDASI (Cutaneous Dermatomyositis Disease Area and Severity Index — activity and damage), MMT-8 (manual muscle testing of 8 muscle groups), CK, HAQ, IMACS core set measures, total improvement score (ACR/EULAR 2016)

**Q19. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation role.**
- Early supervised exercise is safe and improves strength and function (even in active disease); prevents contractures; swallowing therapy for dysphagia; dietary advice, aspiration precautions

**Q20. Differential diagnosis of proximal weakness with rash.**
- SLE/MCTD overlap, hypothyroid myopathy, steroid myopathy, statin myopathy (anti-HMGCR), trichinosis, sarcoid myopathy, HIV myositis, muscular dystrophies (no rash), inclusion body myositis (distal/ quadriceps, finger flexors, older men, no rash)

**Q21. Describe heliotrope rash and its differentials.**
- Violaceous erythema ± oedema of upper eyelids (sometimes lower), may extend to periorbital skin; differentials — allergic contact dermatitis (eyelids), angioedema, SLE, trichinosis, nephrotic oedema, rosacea, atopic eyelid dermatitis, myxoedema

**Q22. What drugs can induce DM-like eruptions?**
- Hydroxyurea (DM-like on knuckles without myositis), statins, penicillamine, TNF inhibitors, checkpoint inhibitors, BCG vaccine, interferons, NSAIDs

**Q23. Discuss IVIG in DM.**
- 2 g/kg over 2–5 days monthly — proven (ProDERM trial) for skin and muscle; also refractory dysphagia, calcinosis prevention in JDM; side effects — headache, aseptic meningitis, thrombosis, renal failure (sucrose-containing), anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency; costly

**Q24. How do you monitor for malignancy over time?**
- Screen at diagnosis and annually for 3 years (risk highest in first 3 years); repeat CT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± PET-CT in high-risk (TIF1γ, NXP2, older age, dysphagia, cutaneous necrosis); gender-specific (mammography, Pap/ CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound, PSA), colonoscopy, nasopharyngoscopy in Southeast Asians

**Q25. What is the role of hydroxychloroquine in DM skin and its risk?**
- Useful for photosensitive skin lesions with sunscreen; but drug eruptions (morbilliform) occur much more often in DM than lupus (~30%, especially anti-SAE positive); quinacrine or methotrexate alternatives; monitor eyes

**Q26. Prognostic factors in DM.**
- Poor: malignancy, ILD (MDA5, antisynthetase), cardiac involvement, dysphagia/ aspiration pneumonia, older age, male sex, delayed treatment, high CK in adults with severe weakness; juvenile DM has good survival but calcinosis morbidity

**Q27. What are the overlap myositis antibodies?**
