- Anti-PM/Scl (SSc–myositis overlap, mechanic's hands, calcinosis, ILD), anti-Ku (SLE/ SSc overlap), anti-U1RNP (MCTD), anti-Ro52 (with antisynthetase/ ILD — severe), anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR (necrotising myopathy)

**Q28. Pregnancy and DM.**
- Disease activity at conception predicts outcome; risks of fetal loss and prematurity with active disease; prednisolone, azathioprine, IVIG, HCQ, tacrolimus can be used; stop methotrexate/ MMF/ cyclophosphamide before conception

**Q29. Why is anti-TIF1γ important in children vs adults?**
- In juvenile DM it is the commonest antibody and is NOT linked to cancer (associated with severe skin disease, lipodystrophy and chronic course); in adults it strongly predicts malignancy (≈ 20–65%)

**Q30. Treatment of refractory skin disease in DM.**
- Methotrexate, MMF, IVIG, dapsone, JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, ruxolitinib — strong efficacy on skin and MDA5-ILD), apremilast, lenalidomide/ thalidomide, rituximab (better for muscle), anifrolumab under trial; antihistamines/ gabapentin for itch

## Quick spotter facts
- Gottron's papules over knuckles + heliotrope eyelids — dermatomyositis
- Anti-MDA5 — rapidly progressive ILD; anti-TIF1γ — cancer
- Screen for malignancy in adults

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermatomyositis); 2017 EULAR/ACR idiopathic inflammatory myopathy criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Diaper (napkin) dermatitis — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Diaper (napkin) dermatitis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define diaper dermatitis.**
- Inflammatory eruption in the area covered by a diaper; most commonly irritant contact dermatitis in infants (peak 9–12 months); also in incontinent adults

**Q2. Pathogenesis of irritant napkin dermatitis.**
- Occlusion and over-hydration of skin → friction damage
- Urine urea broken down by faecal urease → ammonia raises pH → activates faecal lipases and proteases that damage the barrier
- Diarrhoea, antibiotics, infrequent changing worsen it; Candida commonly colonises after 72 h

**Q3. Classify diaper dermatoses / differentials (PYQ).**
- Irritant (convex surfaces affected, folds spared — 'W' pattern)
- Candidal (folds involved, beefy red with satellite pustules)
- Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (folds, salmon-coloured, greasy scale, scalp involved)
- Psoriasis (napkin psoriasis — sharply demarcated, may spread to trunk)
- Jacquet's erosive dermatitis (punched-out erosions — severe irritant)
- Granuloma gluteale infantum (purple nodules after potent steroids)
- Allergic contact dermatitis (dyes, rubber, fragrance — waistband/ thighs)
- Others: bullous impetigo, perianal streptococcal dermatitis, acrodermatitis enteropathica (zinc deficiency — periorificial erosions, diarrhoea, alopecia), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (petechial, eroded, in folds — biopsy), congenital syphilis, scabies, herpes, Kawasaki (perineal desquamation)

**Q4. Distinguish irritant from candidal napkin dermatitis.**
- Irritant: convexities (buttocks, genitals, thighs) affected; flexures spared; shiny glazed erythema
- Candidal: flexures involved, bright red with satellite papules/pustules and peripheral scale; KOH positive

**Q5. Management.**
- ABCDE: Air (diaper-free time), Barrier (zinc oxide, petrolatum, dimethicone at each change), Cleansing (gentle water, avoid wipes with fragrance/alcohol), Diapers (super-absorbent disposable, frequent changes — every 2–3 h, immediately after stools), Education
- Mild steroid (1% hydrocortisone) for 3–5 days if inflamed — never potent steroids under the diaper (occlusion → atrophy, granuloma gluteale)
- Candidal: topical clotrimazole/miconazole/nystatin; treat oral thrush
- Bacterial: topical mupirocin/oral antibiotics

**Q6. What is granuloma gluteale infantum?**
- Purplish-red oval nodules on buttocks/groin in infants with napkin dermatitis treated with potent topical steroids (or Candida); benign, resolves over months after stopping steroid

**Q7. What is Jacquet's erosive dermatitis?**
- Severe irritant form with punched-out erosions or ulcers with raised edges, papules in the napkin area; also in adults with incontinence/urostomy

**Q8. Why test zinc in persistent diaper rash?**
- Acrodermatitis enteropathica (SLC39A4 mutation or acquired — premature/breastfed by low-zinc mothers) presents with perioral and perianal eroded, crusted dermatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia, irritability; low serum zinc/alkaline phosphatase; rapid response to zinc 1–3 mg/kg/day

**Q9. When should you biopsy?**
- Non-response to standard care, petechiae, erosions, papules in folds with hepatosplenomegaly (LCH), nodules — to exclude LCH, psoriasis, granuloma gluteale

**Q10. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q11. Describe napkin psoriasis.**
- Well-demarcated bright red glazed plaques in napkin area including folds, often with psoriasiform lesions elsewhere (scalp, umbilicus, trunk); family history; may herald childhood psoriasis; treat with mild steroids, calcipotriol, tacrolimus

**Q12. Langerhans cell histiocytosis in the napkin area — clues.**
- Persistent erosive/ petechial papules in folds (unlike irritant), scalp seborrhoeic-like scaling, purpura, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone lesions, diabetes insipidus; biopsy — CD1a+, CD207 (langerin)+ histiocytes; refer oncology

**Q13. Allergic contact dermatitis in diaper area.**
- Less common; allergens — disperse dyes in diapers (blue/ pink), rubber additives (elastic bands — 'lucky Luke' pattern on outer buttocks/ thighs), fragrances in wipes (methylisothiazolinone), sorbitan sesquioleate; patch test in persistent cases; switch to dye-free diapers

**Q14. Perianal streptococcal dermatitis.**
- Bright red, well-demarcated perianal erythema with pain on defecation, fissures, blood-streaked stools in children 6 months–10 years (group A strep); rapid strep test/ swab; treat with oral penicillin/ amoxicillin 10 days + topical mupirocin

**Q15. Barrier products — composition and mechanism.**
- Zinc oxide (protective, mildly antiseptic), petrolatum (occlusive), dimethicone (silicone barrier), lanolin, titanium dioxide; apply thick layer at each change; avoid talc (inhalation risk) and boric acid

**Q16. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

## Quick spotter facts
- Folds spared — irritant; folds involved + satellites — Candida
- Potent steroid under nappy → granuloma gluteale infantum

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Neonatal and paediatric dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Discoid lupus erythematosus — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Discoid lupus erythematosus** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What is discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)?**
- Commonest form of chronic cutaneous lupus — scarring, photosensitive plaques with adherent scale, follicular plugging, atrophy and dyspigmentation, mostly on head and neck; women 20–40 y; ~5–10% (more if widespread) develop SLE

**Q2. Describe the lesion.**
- Well-defined red-violaceous plaques with adherent scale extending into dilated follicles; on lifting, scale shows keratotic spikes on its undersurface — carpet-tack (tin-tack) sign
- Evolution: centre becomes atrophic, scarred, depigmented with hyperpigmented active border (in dark skin), telangiectasia
- Sites: face (malar, nose, ears — concha and external ear canal very typical), scalp (scarring alopecia), lips, V of neck, arms; localised (above the neck) vs generalised (above and below the neck — higher SLE risk)

**Q3. Name the variants of chronic cutaneous lupus.**
- Hypertrophic/verrucous DLE (extensor arms — mimics SCC/keratoacanthoma), mucosal DLE (lips, oral — risk of SCC), lupus profundus/panniculitis (deep nodules → lipoatrophy; face, upper arms, buttocks), chilblain lupus (acral purple papules in cold), lupus tumidus (urticarial plaques without epidermal change, very photosensitive), LP–LE overlap, childhood DLE

**Q4. Differentiate DLE from LP (PYQ).**
- See LP case — key points: DLE has adherent scale with follicular plugging, atrophy, scarring, depigmentation, photodistribution, ears and scalp; LP has purple flat papules with Wickham's striae, flexures, no atrophy (except atrophic/LPP), hyperpigmentation; histology and DIF differ (lupus band vs fibrinogen/cytoid bodies)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Face: psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea, polymorphic light eruption, sarcoidosis (lupus pernio), lupus vulgaris (apple-jelly, no follicular plugs), tinea faciei, tuberculoid leprosy, actinic keratosis/SCC (hypertrophic), Jessner's lymphocytic infiltrate, lymphocytoma cutis
- Scalp: lichen planopilaris, folliculitis decalvans, morphoea (en coup de sabre), tinea capitis (kerion), pseudopelade of Brocq, alopecia areata

**Q6. Histopathology of DLE.**
- Hyperkeratosis with follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, vacuolar interface dermatitis with Civatte bodies, thickened PAS-positive basement membrane, superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate (patchy, dense), dermal mucin, pigment incontinence; scarring alopecia with loss of sebaceous glands
- DIF: granular IgG/IgM/C3 at DEJ (lupus band) in ~70–90% of lesions >6 weeks old

**Q7. Investigations.**
- Biopsy + DIF; CBC, ESR, urinalysis (proteinuria/haematuria), renal function, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Ro, C3/C4 to screen for SLE; repeat yearly in generalised DLE

**Q8. Management.**
- Strict photoprotection: broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF ≥30 (UVA+UVB) daily, hats, clothing; stop smoking (reduces HCQ efficacy)
- Topical: potent/super-potent steroids (clobetasol) on body/scalp, mid-potency on face; tacrolimus 0.1% ointment (face); intralesional triamcinolone 2.5–10 mg/ml for thick or scalp lesions
- Systemic first-line: hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg/day (≤5 mg/kg) — response in 2–3 months; chloroquine (more retinal risk) or add quinacrine (no retinopathy) if poor response
- Second-line: methotrexate, mycophenolate, dapsone (bullous/profundus), acitretin/isotretinoin (hypertrophic), thalidomide/lenalidomide (refractory — neuropathy, teratogenicity), anifrolumab (newer), JAK inhibitors (experimental)
- Camouflage, scar revision when inactive; lip lesions — monitor for SCC

**Q9. What is antimalarial retinopathy and its screening?**
- Bull's-eye maculopathy from cumulative dose; risk factors: dose >5 mg/kg/day real weight (HCQ), >5 years use, kidney disease, tamoxifen, pre-existing maculopathy
- Baseline eye exam then annual screening after 5 years (earlier if risk factors) — SD-OCT and automated visual fields (10-2)

**Q10. Complications of DLE.**
- Permanent scarring, scarring alopecia, depigmentation (cosmetic disfigurement), SCC in long-standing scars (lips, ears, scalp), progression to SLE (~5–10%)

**Q11. Pathogenesis of DLE.**
- UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis releases nuclear antigens → plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I IFN → CXCL9/10 recruit CXCR3+ cytotoxic T cells → interface dermatitis, follicular destruction, scarring; genetic factors (HLA), smoking worsens disease and reduces antimalarial response

**Q12. Dermoscopy of DLE.**
- Active: perifollicular whitish halo, follicular keratotic plugs (yellow-red dots), arborising/ linear vessels, white scales
- Late: white structureless scarring areas, loss of follicular openings, pigmentation (speckled brown/ blue-grey dots)
- Scalp DLE: large yellow dots with thin arborising vessels (red spider in yellow dot)

**Q13. Scalp DLE — features and management.**
- Scarring alopecia with erythematous scaly patches, follicular plugging, depigmentation; hair-pull positive at active edge; treat aggressively (intralesional triamcinolone, super-potent topical steroid, antimalarials) to save follicles

**Q14. What is hypertrophic (verrucous) DLE?**
- Thick hyperkeratotic warty plaques on extensor arms/ face — resembles SCC, keratoacanthoma, hypertrophic LP; histology shows interface changes with marked hyperkeratosis; responds to acitretin/ isotretinoin, intralesional steroids, thalidomide

**Q15. Antimalarial dosing and combination.**
- HCQ ≤5 mg/kg real body weight/day; chloroquine ≤2.3 mg/kg/day; never combine HCQ and chloroquine (retinal toxicity); add quinacrine 100 mg/day to either for refractory disease (quinacrine causes yellow skin, rarely aplastic anaemia, no retinopathy); response takes 6–12 weeks

**Q16. What is the prognosis for DLE progressing to SLE?**
- ~5% of localised DLE and ~15–20% of generalised DLE progress to SLE, usually mild; risk factors — generalised lesions, high ANA titre, leucopenia, anaemia, raised ESR, arthralgia, nail fold changes, anti-dsDNA

## Quick spotter facts
- Carpet-tack (tin-tack) sign — DLE
- Concha of ear involvement — classic DLE
- Lupus band on lesional DIF

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous lupus erythematosus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Dowling–Degos disease — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dowling–Degos disease** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is Dowling–Degos disease (DDD)?**
- Rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis ('reticulate pigmented anomaly of the flexures') with progressive reticulate hyperpigmentation of flexures; genes — KRT5 (keratin 5), POFUT1, POGLUT1, PSENEN
- Onset usually 3rd–4th decade, slowly progressive

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Reticulate brown-black macules coalescing in axillae, groin, neck, inframammary, antecubital and intergluteal folds
- Comedo-like dark follicular papules on back and neck, pitted perioral acneiform scars; occasionally epidermoid cysts, hidradenitis suppurativa association, seborrhoeic keratosis-like papules

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Filiform (finger-like/antler-like) downward elongation of thin pigmented rete ridges from epidermis and follicular infundibula ('antler-like'), with pigment at the tips, horn cysts; no increase in melanocyte number
- Galli–Galli disease: same + suprabasal acantholysis

**Q4. Enumerate reticulate pigmentary disorders (PYQ: genetically determined pigmentary disorders).**
- Dowling–Degos disease (flexural reticulate pigmentation, comedo-like pits — KRT5, POFUT1, POGLUT1)
- Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (dorsa of hands/feet, palmar pits — ADAM10)
- Galli–Galli disease (DDD with acantholysis)
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (Dohi — acral mottled hypo/hyper — ADAR1) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria
- Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn syndrome and dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (KRT14 — absent dermatoglyphics)
- Dyskeratosis congenita (reticulate pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia — telomere genes)
- Incontinentia pigmenti stage 3, X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder, Haber syndrome, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (acquired)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acanthosis nigricans (velvety, no comedones), RAPK (acral), Galli–Galli, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, Haber syndrome (rosacea-like face + flexural DDD-like), frictional melanosis, Addison's
- Histology distinguishes from adenoid seborrhoeic keratosis (similar pattern)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Difficult; cosmetic concern: topical retinoids (adapalene/tretinoin), hydroquinone, azelaic acid, Er:YAG/ CO2 or Q-switched lasers, IPL (variable)
- Genetic counselling

**Q7. Describe Galli–Galli disease.**
- Acantholytic variant of DDD (KRT5 mutations) — clinically same reticulate pigmentation with itchy papules; histology shows suprabasal acantholysis without dyskeratosis — differentiate from Hailey–Hailey and Darier

**Q8. Describe the generalised DDD variant.**
- Reticulate pigmentation extends beyond flexures to trunk and limbs, with hypopigmented macules in some — overlaps with dyschromatosis universalis

**Q9. What genetic counselling applies?**
- Autosomal dominant with variable expressivity — 50% transmission; examine relatives (often undiagnosed mild cases)

**Q10. Laser and procedure options with evidence.**
- Er:YAG and CO2 ablative lasers — best reported improvement; Q-switched Nd:YAG and IPL — variable; recurrence common; topical adapalene/ tretinoin and azelaic acid modest; avoid friction and heat

**Q11. Explain why it may be misdiagnosed as AN.**
- Both cause flexural pigmentation in adults; DDD shows reticulate (net-like) small macules, comedo-like papules, pitted scars and family history, no velvety thickening, no insulin resistance; biopsy shows antler-like rete in DDD vs papillomatosis in AN

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. What is the relationship between DDD and hidradenitis suppurativa?**
- PSENEN (γ-secretase) and NCSTN mutations cause familial HS; PSENEN mutations can present with both DDD and HS — impaired Notch signalling links follicular occlusion and pigmentation abnormalities

**Q14. What is Haber syndrome?**
- Rosacea-like facial eruption (early onset) with keratotic papules and DDD-like reticulate flexural pigmentation — considered a variant of DDD

**Q15. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Irregular brown reticular network with dark-brown dots/ globules and comedo-like openings

## Quick spotter facts
- Flexural reticulate pigmentation + comedo-like papules + perioral pits — Dowling–Degos
- Antler-like rete ridges

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Reticulate pigmentary disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Ecthyma — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Ecthyma** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define ecthyma.**
- Deep (ulcerative) form of impetigo extending through the epidermis into the dermis, caused by Streptococcus pyogenes ± S. aureus; heals with a scar

**Q2. Who gets it and where?**
- Children and elderly with poor hygiene, malnutrition, diabetes; neglected insect bites, scabies, minor trauma
- Mostly legs and buttocks; soldiers, travellers in hot humid climates, IV drug users, homeless people

**Q3. Describe the lesion.**
- Starts as a vesicopustule on a red base → thick adherent greenish-brown/black crust → removal shows a punched-out shallow ulcer with raised, violaceous, indurated margin
- Usually few lesions; heals slowly over weeks with a scar and pigmentation

**Q4. Differentiate ecthyma from ecthyma gangrenosum.**
- Ecthyma gangrenosum: Pseudomonas aeruginosa septicaemia (rarely local) in neutropenic/immunocompromised patients
- Haemorrhagic vesicle/pustule → painless necrotic ulcer with black eschar and red halo; anogenital and axillary areas
- Histology: bacteria invading vessel walls (necrotising vasculitis without much inflammation) — needs urgent IV antipseudomonal antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam/ceftazidime + aminoglycoside)

**Q5. What is contagious ecthyma (orf)?**
- Not bacterial — a parapoxvirus from sheep and goats; target-like nodule on fingers of handlers; self-limiting in ~6 weeks; may trigger erythema multiforme

**Q6. Give the differential diagnosis.**
- Ecthyma gangrenosum, cutaneous diphtheria (punched-out ulcer with grey membrane), anthrax (painless black eschar with oedema)
- Pyoderma gangrenosum, vasculitic ulcer, sporotrichosis, leishmaniasis, insect bite, PLEVA (multiple crusted lesions), venous ulcer

**Q7. Investigations?**
- Gram stain and culture from under the crust
- Blood sugar; in immunocompromised — blood culture (ecthyma gangrenosum)

**Q8. Treatment?**
- Remove crusts with soaks; topical antiseptic/mupirocin
- Systemic antibiotics for 10 days: cloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate; macrolide if allergic
- Treat the underlying cause (scabies, insect bites); good nutrition and hygiene

**Q9. Complications?**
- Scarring, lymphangitis, cellulitis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

**Q10. What is cutaneous diphtheria?**
- Corynebacterium diphtheriae; chronic punched-out ulcer with grey-yellow slough/membrane and rolled edge; may cause myocarditis and neuritis via toxin
- Treat: erythromycin/penicillin + antitoxin if toxigenic; notify; immunise contacts

**Q11. Describe Staphylococcus aureus virulence factors.**
- Surface: protein A (binds IgG Fc), clumping factor, fibronectin-binding proteins, capsule
- Toxins: exfoliative toxins A/B (SSSS, bullous impetigo), superantigens (TSST-1, enterotoxins — toxic shock syndrome, AD flares), PVL (necrotising infections), haemolysins, leukocidins
- Enzymes: coagulase, catalase, hyaluronidase, lipase, staphylokinase, β-lactamase; MRSA — mecA gene (PBP2a)

**Q12. Describe Streptococcus pyogenes virulence factors.**
- M protein (anti-phagocytic; nephritogenic/ rheumatogenic types), hyaluronic acid capsule, streptolysin O and S, streptokinase, DNases, hyaluronidase, pyrogenic exotoxins (SpeA/B/C — scarlet fever, toxic shock-like syndrome), C5a peptidase

**Q13. What is ecthyma gangrenosum workup?**
- Blood cultures, biopsy for histology and tissue culture (Pseudomonas, also Aeromonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, fungi — Aspergillus, Mucor, Fusarium in neutropenia), absolute neutrophil count, HIV; start empirical anti-pseudomonal therapy immediately

**Q14. Ecthyma in India — common settings.**
- Children with scabies/ insect bites and poor hygiene, rural barefoot workers with minor trauma, diabetics, IV drug users; often secondary to pediculosis or scabies — treat the underlying infestation

**Q15. Prevention advice.**
- Treat insect bites and scabies promptly, keep nails short, hygiene, avoid scratching, protective footwear, nutritional support

**Q16. What is pseudomonal hot-foot syndrome?**
- Painful red plantar nodules in children after wading in contaminated pool water (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) — self-limiting; analgesics; antibiotics in severe cases

## Quick spotter facts
- Punched-out ulcer under a thick crust on the leg — ecthyma (heals with scar, unlike impetigo)
- Neutropenic patient + black eschar with red halo — ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Epidermal nevus / ILVEN — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Epidermal nevus / ILVEN** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. What is an epidermal naevus?**
- Hamartoma of the epidermis and/or adnexal structures due to postzygotic (mosaic) mutation, following Blaschko's lines; present at birth or early childhood (~1 in 1000)
- Types: keratinocytic (verrucous epidermal naevus — FGFR3, PIK3CA, HRAS; epidermolytic — KRT1/10), organoid (nevus sebaceous — HRAS/KRAS, nevus comedonicus — NEK9, Becker's naevus, porokeratotic eccrine naevus), ILVEN (inflammatory)

**Q2. Describe verrucous epidermal naevus.**
- Linear, skin-coloured to brown, velvety then warty papules coalescing into plaques along Blaschko's lines, usually unilateral on trunk/limbs; localised or systematised (ichthyosis hystrix — bilateral extensive)

**Q3. What is ILVEN?**
- Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus: persistent, intensely itchy, erythematous, scaly, psoriasiform papules and plaques in a linear Blaschkoid pattern, usually on the lower limb/buttock, onset in early childhood (girls), very resistant to therapy
- Histology: psoriasiform hyperplasia with alternating orthokeratosis over hypergranulosis and parakeratosis over agranulosis; dermal lymphocytes
- Differential: linear psoriasis (responds to antipsoriatics, other psoriasis features, Munro microabscesses), lichen striatus (self-limiting, not itchy), linear LP, linear porokeratosis, linear DLE

**Q4. What is epidermal naevus syndrome?**
- Epidermal naevus with extracutaneous anomalies of CNS (seizures, intellectual disability, hemimegalencephaly), eye (colobomas, lipodermoids), skeleton (hemihypertrophy, kyphoscoliosis, vitamin D-resistant rickets — FGF23 hypophosphataemia), urogenital and cardiovascular systems
- Includes Schimmelpenning (nevus sebaceous), Proteus, CHILD, phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica, Becker's naevus syndrome, nevus comedonicus syndrome

**Q5. Discuss principles of mosaicism (PYQ).**
- Mosaicism = two or more genetically distinct cell populations derived from one zygote (postzygotic mutation)
- Patterns of cutaneous mosaicism (Happle): Blaschko's lines (narrow and broad bands), checkerboard, phylloid (leaf-like — trisomy 13), patchy without midline separation (large CMN), lateralisation (CHILD)
- Type 1 segmental (heterozygous postzygotic mutation in a dominant disorder — segmental NF1) vs type 2 segmental (loss of heterozygosity — severe segment superimposed on generalised disease); gonadal mosaicism → transmission of generalised disease to offspring (e.g. epidermolytic naevus → epidermolytic ichthyosis child)
- Lethal autosomal dominant mutations survive only in mosaic state (Proteus — AKT1, McCune–Albright — GNAS, Schimmelpenning — HRAS)

**Q6. Management.**
- Topical keratolytics, retinoids, calcipotriol, steroids (ILVEN — potent steroids/occlusion, tacrolimus, dithranol) — usually poor response
- Destructive: full-thickness surgical excision (definitive; deep enough to avoid recurrence), CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, dermabrasion, cryotherapy (recurrence common if superficial)
- Oral acitretin for extensive systematised naevi; examine for associated anomalies

**Q7. Describe the clinical types of epidermal naevi.**
- Keratinocytic: soft (velvety) and hard (verrucous) epidermal naevi, ILVEN, epidermolytic
- Organoid: nevus sebaceous, nevus comedonicus, Becker's naevus, eccrine/ apocrine naevi, porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct naevus (PEODDN)

**Q8. Clinical features of ILVEN in detail.**
- Onset in infancy/ early childhood, usually lower limb, unilateral, linear along Blaschko lines; erythematous scaly psoriasiform papules coalescing into plaques; intense itch; persistent; female predominance; resistant to therapy (topical steroids, calcipotriol, dithranol, laser)

**Q9. What are the components of epidermal naevus syndrome?**
- Epidermal naevus with CNS (seizures, intellectual disability, hemimegalencephaly), eye (colobomas, lipodermoids), skeletal (bone cysts, hemihypertrophy, kyphoscoliosis), urogenital anomalies; subtypes — Schimmelpenning, nevus comedonicus syndrome, CHILD, Proteus, phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica, Becker's naevus syndrome; hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23)

**Q10. Differential diagnosis.**
- Linear psoriasis (responds to therapy, later onset), lichen striatus (sudden, self-limiting), linear LP, linear porokeratosis, linear Darier's, incontinentia pigmenti (verrucous stage — girls), seborrhoeic keratosis, warts

**Q11. Malignant potential.**
- Low; BCC, SCC, keratoacanthoma rarely arise in adult epidermal naevi; epidermolytic naevi carry genetic risk for offspring (gonadal mosaicism)

**Q12. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q13. Which genes are involved in epidermal naevi?**
- Keratinocytic (verrucous) epidermal naevus — FGFR3, PIK3CA, HRAS/KRAS/NRAS mosaicism; epidermolytic epidermal naevus — KRT1/KRT10 (gonadal mosaicism → offspring may get epidermolytic ichthyosis)
- ILVEN — GJA1, CARD14 (some)

**Q14. Histopathology of epidermal naevus.**
- Hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges (seborrhoeic keratosis-like); epidermolytic variant shows granular degeneration (epidermolytic hyperkeratosis); ILVEN shows alternating orthokeratosis over hypogranulosis and parakeratosis over agranulosis (psoriasiform)

**Q15. Treatment options.**
- Surgical excision (small), CO2/ Er:YAG laser ablation, dermabrasion, cryotherapy, electrodesiccation — recurrence common if superficial; topical retinoids, calcipotriol, 5-FU, steroids (ILVEN itch), PDT; topical PI3K inhibitors (experimental)

## Quick spotter facts
- Linear warty plaque along Blaschko's lines from birth — verrucous epidermal naevus
- Itchy psoriasiform linear plaque on leg of a young girl — ILVEN

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Epidermal naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Erysipelas and cellulitis — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erysipelas and cellulitis** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define erysipelas and cellulitis; how do they differ?**
- Erysipelas: infection of the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics — bright red, raised, shiny plaque with a sharp, palpable advancing edge
- Cellulitis: infection of deeper dermis and subcutaneous fat — poorly demarcated, not raised, warm tender swelling
- Erysipelas is mostly Streptococcus pyogenes (group A; also B, C, G); cellulitis is streptococcal and S. aureus; both may coexist

**Q2. Common sites and portals of entry?**
- Legs now commonest (previously face); face erysipelas often butterfly-like, may follow nasal/ear lesion
- Portals: toe-web tinea/intertrigo (most important), leg ulcers, eczema, trauma, insect bites, surgical wounds, venepuncture
- Predisposing: lymphoedema (post-mastectomy, filariasis), venous insufficiency, obesity, diabetes, alcoholism, previous episode, saphenous vein harvest

**Q3. Clinical features?**
- Prodrome of fever, chills, malaise (often precedes rash by hours)
- Red, hot, tender, oedematous area; may have blisters, haemorrhage, lymphangitic streaks, tender regional nodes
- Erysipelas: 'peau d'orange' surface, sharp edge; ear involvement (no deep dermis there) favours erysipelas — Milian's ear sign

**Q4. What is Milian's ear sign?**
- Ear involvement in facial erysipelas; it helps differentiate erysipelas from deep cellulitis since the ear has no subcutaneous fat

**Q5. Discuss the differential diagnosis.**
- Bilateral red legs are rarely cellulitis — think venous (stasis) dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, contact dermatitis
- DVT, acute gout, erythema nodosum, early necrotising fasciitis, herpes zoster (prodrome), fixed drug eruption, insect bite reaction, eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells), erythema migrans, lupus (malar), angioedema

**Q6. What are the red flags for necrotising fasciitis? (short note topic)**
- Pain out of proportion to the visible signs; rapid spread; woody hardness of subcutis beyond the erythema; dusky/grey discoloration, haemorrhagic bullae; anaesthesia of skin; crepitus; systemic toxicity, shock
- Type I polymicrobial (diabetics, perineum — Fournier's gangrene), type II group A strep ± S. aureus, type III Vibrio/clostridial
- LRINEC score helps; diagnosis is surgical (finger test — no resistance, dishwater pus); needs urgent debridement + broad IV antibiotics (including clindamycin to switch off toxin)

**Q7. Investigations?**
- Mainly clinical; CBC, CRP, blood sugar, renal function
- Blood culture if systemic toxicity; swab only if open wound/blister
- ASO/anti-DNase B retrospectively; Doppler to exclude DVT; X-ray/MRI if osteomyelitis or gas suspected; creatine kinase high in necrotising infection

**Q8. How do you treat?**
- Mild: oral penicillin V / amoxicillin, or cloxacillin/cephalexin (covers staph) for 5–10 days; clindamycin or macrolide if penicillin allergy
- Moderate–severe: IV benzylpenicillin + cloxacillin, or cefazolin/ceftriaxone; vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA
- Leg elevation, rest, analgesia; treat toe-web tinea and other portals; mark the edge to monitor

**Q9. How do you prevent recurrence?**
- Treat interdigital tinea, control oedema (compression), weight loss, skin care, treat venous disease
- For ≥2 episodes/year: prophylactic penicillin V 250 mg twice daily (PATCH trial) or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU every 3–4 weeks
- Erythromycin for allergic patients

**Q10. Complications?**
- Recurrence (in about 1/3) leading to lymphoedema — elephantiasis nostras verrucosa
- Abscess, necrotising fasciitis, septicaemia, toxic shock, glomerulonephritis, thrombophlebitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis (facial)

**Q11. Name special forms of cellulitis.**
- Perianal streptococcal dermatitis (children; bright red perianal rash, painful defecation)
- Blistering distal dactylitis (group A strep, fingertip pulp blister)
- Haemophilus influenzae facial cellulitis (bluish-purple, unvaccinated children)
- Animal bites: Pasteurella multocida (rapid onset within 24 h) — amoxicillin-clavulanate
- Water exposure: Aeromonas (freshwater), Vibrio vulnificus (seawater, liver disease)
- Orbital/periorbital cellulitis — emergency

**Q12. What is eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells syndrome)?**
- Recurrent cellulitis-like red indurated plaques, not infective, with dermal eosinophils and 'flame figures'; triggers — insect bites, drugs, infections; responds to steroids, not antibiotics

**Q13. What is erysipeloid?**
- Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae from handling fish, meat, poultry — violaceous, well-defined plaque on the hand/finger with central clearing, sparing terminal phalanx; penicillin

**Q14. What is scarlet fever? (short note)**
- Group A strep producing erythrogenic (pyrogenic) toxin, usually from tonsillitis in children
- Fine sandpaper-like punctate erythema starting on neck/upper trunk, Pastia's lines in flexures, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue (white then red), later desquamation of palms/soles
- Penicillin 10 days; complications: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

**Q15. What is toxic shock syndrome?**
- Superantigen-mediated (TSST-1/ enterotoxins of S. aureus; streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins) — fever ≥38.9 °C, hypotension, diffuse macular erythroderma ('sunburn'), desquamation of palms/soles 1–2 weeks later, multiorgan involvement (GI, muscle, mucosal hyperaemia, renal, hepatic, CNS); tampon, wound, post-surgical, nasal packing
- Treat: remove source, fluids/ ICU, anti-staphylococcal β-lactam/ vancomycin + clindamycin (switches off toxin), IVIG in severe

## Quick spotter facts
- Sharp raised edge + ear involved = erysipelas
- Pain out of proportion + anaesthetic skin + crepitus = necrotising fasciitis — surgical emergency

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Erythema multiforme — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythema multiforme** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define erythema multiforme (EM).**
- Acute, self-limited, often recurrent immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction characterised by typical target lesions in an acral distribution, usually triggered by infection (most often HSV)
- EM minor (no or one mucosa mildly) and EM major (≥1 mucosa severely, more systemic upset); now considered separate from SJS/TEN

**Q2. Causes.**
- Infections (~90%): herpes simplex (commonest — HSV-1 > HSV-2, appears 3–14 days after herpes), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (children; mucosa-dominant — MIRM), others (hepatitis C, EBV, orf, histoplasmosis, COVID-19)
- Drugs (<10%): NSAIDs, sulphonamides, antiepileptics, antibiotics
- Others: vaccines, radiotherapy, IBD, idiopathic

**Q3. Describe a typical target lesion.**
- Round <3 cm with three distinct concentric zones and a well-defined border: central dusky/blistered or crusted disc, middle paler oedematous ring, outer erythematous ring
- Atypical raised target: only two zones, palpable, poorly defined edge (EM major)
- Atypical flat targets/purpuric macules with blisters = SJS/TEN pattern, not EM

**Q4. Distribution and mucosal features.**
- Symmetrical, acral — backs of hands, palms, forearms, feet, elbows, knees, face; spreads centripetally; Koebner phenomenon; lesions appear in crops over 3–5 days and are fixed for ≥7 days (unlike urticaria)
- Mucosa: lips (haemorrhagic crusts), buccal mucosa erosions; eyes and genitals in major

**Q5. Pathogenesis of HSV-associated EM.**
- HSV DNA fragments (polymerase gene, Pol) carried by CD34+ circulating cells to skin → expressed in keratinocytes → HSV-specific CD4 Th1 response with IFN-γ → cytotoxic damage
- HLA-DQ3 association in recurrent EM

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Interface dermatitis with vacuolar change, scattered necrotic keratinocytes (more than in other interface dermatoses), lymphocyte exocytosis, papillary oedema; sub-epidermal bulla in severe lesions; normal basket-weave stratum corneum (acute process)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Urticaria (transient wheals <24 h, no dusky centre — urticarial multiforme in children), SJS/TEN, fixed drug eruption (multiple), bullous pemphigoid (urticarial phase), Rowell syndrome (lupus + EM-like lesions with ANA, anti-Ro), Sweet syndrome, vasculitis, Kawasaki disease, serum sickness-like reaction, annular erythemas, polymorphic light eruption

**Q8. What is Rowell's syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Lupus erythematosus (usually SCLE/DLE) with EM-like lesions, speckled ANA, anti-Ro/La, positive rheumatoid factor, chilblains — criteria by Zeitouni

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Treat/remove trigger; symptomatic: antihistamines, topical steroids, oral antiseptic/anaesthetic mouthwashes and steroid gels for mucosa
- Severe mucosal: short course systemic steroids (controversial), ophthalmology care
- Recurrent HSV-associated EM: continuous suppressive acyclovir 400 mg twice daily (or valacyclovir 500 mg BD) for 6–12 months even if herpes not evident
- Refractory: dapsone, azathioprine, mycophenolate, thalidomide, apremilast, JAK inhibitors
- Mycoplasma: macrolide/doxycycline

**Q10. Classify annular/figurate erythemas (PYQ: list annular erythemas).**
- Erythema annulare centrifugum (trailing scale), erythema marginatum (rheumatic fever), erythema migrans (Lyme), erythema gyratum repens (wood-grain; malignancy), EM, urticaria, SCLE, granuloma annulare, tinea, sarcoid, Hansen's, necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma — 'migratory erythema')

**Q11. What is MIRM?**
- Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis — children/young adults; prominent mucositis (oral, ocular, genital) with few or no skin lesions; good prognosis with macrolides and supportive care

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- Self-limiting in 2–4 weeks without scarring; recurrences common in HSV-related EM; ocular sequelae rarely in major

**Q13. Recurrent and persistent EM.**
- Recurrent EM: ≥6 episodes/year, usually HSV — continuous suppressive antivirals for ≥6–12 months; persistent EM (continuous lesions without remission) — associated with occult HSV, EBV, IBD, malignancy; dapsone, thalidomide, azathioprine, MMF, JAK inhibitors

**Q14. Oral EM — features and management.**
- Painful erosions/ haemorrhagic crusts of lips, buccal mucosa, tongue (may occur without skin); topical steroid gels, anaesthetic/ antiseptic mouthwashes, soft diet, oral acyclovir if HSV-triggered

**Q15. Classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions by Gell–Coombs (revised).**
- Type I (IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Type II (cytotoxic antibody): drug-induced pemphigus, immune thrombocytopenic purpura
- Type III (immune complex): serum sickness, vasculitis
- Type IV T-cell: IVa (Th1 — contact dermatitis), IVb (Th2/ eosinophils — DRESS, MPE), IVc (cytotoxic — SJS/TEN, FDE, MPE), IVd (neutrophilic — AGEP)
- Non-immune: pseudo-allergy (MRGPRX2), phototoxic, pigmentation, overdose/ side effects

## Quick spotter facts
- Typical three-zone acral targets after herpes labialis — EM minor
- Recurrent EM — suppressive acyclovir

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Erythema multiforme). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Erythema nodosum — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythema nodosum** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define erythema nodosum (EN).**
- Commonest panniculitis — acute, tender, red, warm subcutaneous nodules mainly on shins, a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to various antigens; resolves without ulceration or scarring

**Q2. Causes (mnemonic: NODOSUM).**
- Idiopathic (30–50%)
- Infections: streptococcal pharyngitis (commonest in children), tuberculosis (important in India), Yersinia, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, hepatitis B/C, EBV, leprosy (ENL is different), COVID-19
- Drugs: oral contraceptives/oestrogens, sulphonamides, penicillin, bromides, isotretinoin, vemurafenib/BRAF inhibitors
- Systemic disease: sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome), inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's > UC), Behçet's
- Pregnancy, malignancy (lymphoma, leukaemia)

**Q3. Describe the clinical features.**
- Young women 20–40 y (F:M ~5:1); prodrome of fever, malaise, arthralgia
- Bilateral, symmetrical, tender, bright red, poorly defined nodules 1–5 cm on anterior shins, also knees, ankles, thighs, forearms
- Evolve like a bruise (contusiform): red → purple → yellow-green (erythema contusiformis) over 2 weeks; never ulcerate; crops for 3–6 weeks

**Q4. What is Löfgren syndrome?**
- Acute sarcoidosis: EN + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + fever + migratory polyarthritis/periarticular ankle inflammation ± anterior uveitis; HLA-DRB1*03; excellent prognosis (spontaneous remission)

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Septal panniculitis without vasculitis — thickened oedematous septa with lymphocytes, neutrophils (early), histiocytes
- Miescher's radial granulomas (small histiocytes around a central stellate cleft) — hallmark
- Deep incisional biopsy needed (punch may miss fat)

**Q6. Investigations to find the cause.**
- CBC, ESR/CRP, throat swab, ASO/anti-DNase B, Mantoux/IGRA, chest X-ray (TB, sarcoid hilar nodes), stool culture if diarrhoea, pregnancy test, serum ACE, IBD work-up (faecal calprotectin) if bowel symptoms, HBV/HCV

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Erythema induratum/nodular vasculitis (calves, ulcerate, lobular panniculitis with vasculitis)
- ENL in leprosy (anywhere, evanescent, systemic signs, smear positive)
- Cellulitis (unilateral), superficial thrombophlebitis, cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (livedo, nodules along vessels), lupus panniculitis, pancreatic panniculitis (ulcerate, oily discharge), α1-antitrypsin panniculitis, Sweet syndrome, subcutaneous lymphoma, insect bites

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Treat the underlying cause; stop OCP/drug
- Bed rest, leg elevation, compression, NSAIDs (indomethacin, naproxen, ibuprofen)
- Potassium iodide 300–900 mg/day (SSKI) for 3–4 weeks — useful in persistent cases (avoid in pregnancy/thyroid disease)
- Colchicine, hydroxychloroquine, dapsone; systemic steroids only after excluding infection (TB) and when severe
- EN in IBD — treat the bowel disease

**Q9. Differentiate septal from lobular panniculitis with examples.**
- Septal without vasculitis: EN, necrobiosis lipoidica, morphoea/scleroderma; septal with vasculitis: superficial thrombophlebitis, cutaneous PAN
- Lobular without vasculitis: lupus panniculitis, pancreatic, α1-antitrypsin, cold, factitial, sclerema/subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn, lipodermatosclerosis; lobular with vasculitis: erythema induratum (nodular vasculitis), ENL

**Q10. Prognosis?**
- Self-limited in 3–6 weeks; may recur (with recurrent streptococcal infection or persistent cause); chronic/migratory variants rare

**Q11. Erythema nodosum leprosum vs EN.**
- ENL: in BL/LL leprosy, crops of evanescent tender nodules anywhere (face, arms, trunk), may ulcerate (necrotic ENL), systemic symptoms (fever, neuritis, iritis, orchitis), smear positive; histology — neutrophilic vasculitis with foamy macrophages and AFB
- EN: shins, does not ulcerate, septal panniculitis without vasculitis or bacilli

**Q12. EN in pregnancy and OCP use.**
- Oestrogen-related EN in first/ second trimester or with OCPs — supportive care, stop OCP; NSAIDs avoided in third trimester (ductus closure) — use rest, compression, short steroid if needed

**Q13. Chronic/ migratory EN variants.**
- Erythema nodosum migrans (subacute nodular migratory panniculitis of Vilanova — unilateral migratory plaques with central clearing on legs of women; responds to potassium iodide)

**Q14. EN and TB in India.**
- Strongly positive Mantoux/ IGRA with EN — look for primary TB (hilar lymphadenopathy, pulmonary focus) especially in children; treat TB if confirmed; EN usually resolves

**Q15. EN in IBD — features.**
- More with Crohn's (5–15%) than UC; parallels bowel activity; treat the bowel disease (steroids, anti-TNF); differentiate from pyoderma gangrenosum (ulcerates, independent of activity)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bilateral tender bruise-like shin nodules in a young woman — EN (never ulcerates)
- Miescher's radial granulomas
- EN + hilar nodes + arthritis — Löfgren syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Panniculitis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Erythrasma — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythrasma** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define erythrasma.**
- Chronic superficial infection of the stratum corneum by Corynebacterium minutissimum (Gram-positive diphtheroid) in body folds

**Q2. Clinical types?**
- Interdigital (commonest — 4th toe web; maceration, scaling, fissuring)
- Intertriginous/flexural (groin, axillae, submammary, intergluteal) — sharply marginated reddish-brown, finely scaling, slightly wrinkled patches; mild or no itch
- Generalised/disciform (rare; trunk, in diabetics)

**Q3. Predisposing factors?**
- Diabetes, obesity, hyperhidrosis, warm humid climate, poor hygiene, advanced age, immunosuppression

**Q4. What is the key bedside test?**
- Wood's lamp: coral-red fluorescence from porphyrins (coproporphyrin III) produced by the organism
- Recent washing removes porphyrins → false negative; ask patient not to wash for a day

**Q5. Differentiate erythrasma from tinea cruris.**
- Tinea: active raised scaly border with central clearing, itchy, KOH shows hyphae, no coral-red fluorescence
- Erythrasma: uniform brown patch without active edge, not very itchy, coral-red fluorescence, KOH negative, Gram stain shows rods/filaments
- Both may coexist (interdigital 'complex' with Candida)

**Q6. Other differentials?**
- Candidal intertrigo (satellite pustules), inverse psoriasis (glazed red, no scale), seborrhoeic dermatitis, pityriasis versicolor, Hailey–Hailey disease, acanthosis nigricans

**Q7. Treatment?**
- Topical: fusidic acid, clindamycin, erythromycin, mupirocin, or azoles (miconazole, clotrimazole — also cover fungi and Candida), benzoyl peroxide wash
- Oral: erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 14 days or clarithromycin 1 g single dose for widespread disease
- Prevent: keep folds dry, loose cotton clothes, weight loss, antibacterial soap, control diabetes

**Q8. Which other diseases show fluorescence under Wood's lamp?**
- Tinea capitis — Microsporum: bright green; favus (T. schoenleinii): dull green
- Pityriasis versicolor: yellow-green/golden
- Pseudomonas: green; pitted keratolysis/trichomycosis: coral red/none
- Porphyria cutanea tarda: pink-red urine fluorescence; vitiligo: chalk-white accentuation
- Erythrasma: coral-red

**Q9. What is trichomycosis axillaris?**
- Corynebacterium (C. tenuis) concretions on axillary/pubic hairs — yellow, red or black nodules on the hair shaft; sweat may be coloured; shave and topical antibiotics/benzoyl peroxide

**Q10. Describe the organism and its fluorescence.**
- Corynebacterium minutissimum — Gram-positive, non-spore-forming diphtheroid rod (lipophilic); produces coproporphyrin III which fluoresces coral-red under Wood's lamp (washed off by bathing)

**Q11. Interdigital erythrasma — features and complex.**
- Commonest form — macerated white scaling and fissuring in 3rd/4th toe webs, often with dermatophytes, Candida and Gram-negative bacteria ('dermatophytosis complex'); treat with topical azoles (cover all organisms) and keep webs dry

**Q12. Histopathology/ Gram stain findings.**
- Gram stain of scrapings: Gram-positive rods/ filaments in stratum corneum; histology rarely needed — organisms in upper stratum corneum on PAS/ Gram stain, minimal inflammation

**Q13. Erythrasma and diabetes — significance.**
- Disciform/ generalised erythrasma is commoner in diabetics and obese — screen blood sugar in extensive or recurrent disease

**Q14. Systemic treatment doses.**
- Erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 14 days, or single-dose clarithromycin 1 g; tetracyclines alternative; topical fusidic acid/ clindamycin/ erythromycin/ azoles for localised

**Q15. Prevention of recurrence.**
- Keep folds dry, loose cotton clothing, antibacterial soap washes, absorbent powders, weight loss, control diabetes, treat hyperhidrosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Coral-red fluorescence in the groin — erythrasma
- Most common site: 4th toe web

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Erythroderma — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythroderma** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define erythroderma.**
- Generalised erythema and scaling involving ≥90% of body surface area (synonym: exfoliative dermatitis); a dermatological emergency because of systemic complications

**Q2. What are the causes? (common PYQ)**
- Pre-existing dermatoses (~50–60%): psoriasis (commonest in India), eczemas (atopic, airborne contact — parthenium, seborrhoeic, chronic actinic dermatitis), pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen planus, pemphigus foliaceus, ichthyoses, crusted scabies, dermatophytosis
- Drugs (~15–20%): antiepileptics (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone), allopurinol, sulphonamides, dapsone, β-lactams, anti-TB drugs, gold, NSAIDs, also topical medicaments
- Malignancy (~10%): cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome, erythrodermic MF), leukaemia, Hodgkin's, paraneoplastic (solid tumours)
- Idiopathic (~10–30%) — 'red man syndrome' in elderly men; some later declare CTCL
- Neonates/infants: ichthyoses (CIE, Netherton), SSSS, immunodeficiency (Omenn), seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis

**Q3. Clues to the underlying cause on examination.**
- Psoriasis: silvery scales on scalp, nail pits/oil-drop, history; may lose typical features
- PRP: islands of sparing, orange-red waxy palmoplantar keratoderma, follicular papules on knuckles
- Atopic/eczema: lichenification, intense itch, raised IgE
- Airborne contact: worse on exposed sites, seasonal flares
- Drug: recent drug, morbilliform onset, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy (DRESS)
- CTCL: intense itch, lymphadenopathy, leonine facies, palmoplantar keratoderma, ectropion, alopecia, nail dystrophy, circulating Sézary cells
- Pemphigus foliaceus: crusted erosions, cornflake scales, Nikolsky positive
- Crusted scabies: hyperkeratosis on hands, nails, contacts itching

**Q4. Describe the clinical features.**
- Onset acute (drugs, eczema) or insidious (CTCL, idiopathic); redness then scaling (fine bran-like in eczema, large sheets in drug), pruritus, oedema, lichenification
- Hair: telogen effluvium/alopecia; nails: Beau's lines, shiny nails, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis; ectropion, epiphora
- Systemic: chills (loss of thermoregulation), lymphadenopathy (dermatopathic), hepatomegaly, pedal oedema, tachycardia
- Palmoplantar keratoderma — PRP, CTCL, psoriasis

**Q5. Describe the pathophysiological consequences / complications.**
- Thermoregulation failure — hypothermia or hyperthermia
- Increased transepidermal water loss → dehydration, electrolyte imbalance; loss of protein in scales (up to 20–30 g/day) → hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, negative nitrogen balance
- Increased cutaneous blood flow → high-output cardiac failure in elderly
- Secondary infection (S. aureus), sepsis, pneumonia
- Gynaecomastia, anaemia (iron, folate loss), dermatopathic lymphadenopathy
- Dermatogenic enteropathy (malabsorption) — PYQ

**Q6. What is dermatogenic enteropathy? (PYQ)**
- Reversible malabsorption (steatorrhoea, reduced D-xylose absorption) and protein-losing enteropathy in patients with extensive skin disease like erythroderma/psoriasis; improves when skin improves

**Q7. How do you investigate erythroderma?**
- CBC (eosinophilia — drug, atopic, CTCL; anaemia), ESR, total protein/albumin, electrolytes, renal and liver function, blood sugar
- Peripheral smear for Sézary cells; flow cytometry (CD4:CD8 >10, CD7/CD26 loss), TCR gene rearrangement
- Multiple skin biopsies (repeat if non-diagnostic — 50% give the cause), lymph node biopsy if suspicious
- KOH and skin scraping for scabies/tinea; IgE; DIF if pemphigus foliaceus suspected
- Chest X-ray, ultrasound abdomen, HIV, cultures if febrile; age-appropriate malignancy screening

**Q8. Histopathology.**
- Often non-specific: hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis, perivascular infiltrate
- Specific features in ~50%: psoriasis (regular acanthosis, Munro microabscesses), PRP (alternating ortho/parakeratosis — chequerboard), CTCL (epidermotropism, Pautrier microabscesses, atypical cerebriform lymphocytes), drug (eosinophils, necrotic keratinocytes), PF (subcorneal acantholysis)

**Q9. Management — general.**
- Admit severe cases; warm room, monitor temperature, fluids, input–output, weight
- Bland emollients (white soft paraffin, liquid paraffin) frequently; wet wraps; oatmeal baths; low/mid-potency topical steroids (avoid extensive potent use); sedating antihistamines
- High-protein diet, correct electrolytes, albumin; treat infection; manage cardiac failure
- Stop all non-essential drugs

**Q10. Specific treatment according to cause.**
- Psoriasis: methotrexate, cyclosporine (fast), acitretin, biologics (infliximab, IL-17/23 inhibitors); avoid systemic steroids (rebound pustular flare); avoid phototherapy in acute phase
- Eczema/airborne: systemic steroids short course, azathioprine, cyclosporine, methotrexate, dupilumab (atopic)
- Drug-induced: withdraw, steroids for DRESS
- PRP: retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin), methotrexate, biologics (IL-17, TNF)
- CTCL: refer — ECP, bexarotene, interferon, mogamulizumab, chemotherapy
- Idiopathic: symptomatic + long-term follow-up for evolving CTCL

**Q11. Prognosis.**
- Depends on cause — drug-induced resolves fastest (weeks); psoriasis/eczema relapse; idiopathic chronic; mortality 20–40% historically in elderly due to sepsis, cardiac failure; CTCL poor prognosis

**Q12. Differentiate erythroderma due to Sézary syndrome from benign causes.**
- Sézary: triad of erythroderma, generalised lymphadenopathy, circulating clonal atypical T cells (≥1000/µL Sézary cells, CD4:CD8 ≥10, loss of CD7 ≥40% or CD26 ≥30%), intense itch, keratoderma, leonine facies, alopecia; poor response to steroids

**Q13. How do you approach an erythroderma patient in the ward (step-by-step)?**
- Stabilise: vitals, temperature, hydration, urine output, sepsis screen, cardiac status
- History: prior dermatosis, drugs (last 8 weeks), atopy, photosensitivity, systemic symptoms (weight loss, nodes, itch severity), family history
- Examine for clues: scalp, nails, palms/soles, islands of sparing, mucosa, lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly
- Investigate: bloods, multiple biopsies, Sézary screen, KOH/scrapings, IgE, imaging
- Treat: supportive + cause-specific; avoid starting many new drugs

**Q14. Drug-induced erythroderma — which drugs and features?**
- Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, allopurinol, dapsone, sulfonamides, β-lactams, vancomycin, anti-TB drugs, gold, lithium, calcium channel blockers, NSAIDs; often part of DRESS (fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hepatitis) — RegiSCAR scoring; onset 2–8 weeks after drug; fastest resolution after withdrawal

**Q15. Describe erythrodermic psoriasis triggers and management.**
- Triggers: abrupt withdrawal of systemic steroids/ potent topicals, phototherapy burn, infection, HIV, stress, lithium/antimalarials, alcohol
- Management: admit; bland emollients; cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg (rapid) or infliximab/ IL-17/IL-23 inhibitors; methotrexate or acitretin for maintenance; avoid steroids; fluids and temperature control

**Q16. What is the 'red man syndrome' (idiopathic erythroderma of elderly)?**
- Chronic idiopathic erythroderma in elderly men with marked itch, lichenification, palmoplantar keratoderma, dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, raised IgE; evolves to CTCL in some — repeated biopsies and T-cell clonality/flow cytometry every 6–12 months

**Q17. Neonatal and infantile erythroderma — causes and approach.**
- Ichthyoses (collodion baby, congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, Netherton — bamboo hair, hypernatraemic dehydration), SSSS, seborrhoeic/atopic dermatitis, immunodeficiency (Omenn, SCID, Wiskott–Aldrich, hyper-IgE), diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis, metabolic (biotinidase, multiple carboxylase, zinc, essential fatty acid deficiency), maternal GVHD, psoriasis
- Investigate: hair microscopy, immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets, zinc/biotin, skin biopsy; manage dehydration, hypernatraemia, temperature, sepsis

**Q18. Why should systemic steroids be avoided in psoriatic erythroderma but may be used in others?**
- Steroid withdrawal precipitates generalised pustular psoriasis/ rebound erythroderma; in drug-induced (DRESS), eczematous/airborne contact, pemphigus foliaceus and some idiopathic cases steroids are useful with careful tapering

**Q19. Fluid and nutrition care in erythroderma.**
- Daily weight, input–output charts; extra fluids for insensible losses (≈ 2–4 l/day extra), correct electrolytes (Na, K), monitor albumin; high-protein (1.5–2 g/kg) and high-calorie diet, vitamin/ iron/ folate supplements; avoid hypothermia (warm room 30–32 °C, blankets)

**Q20. Cardiac complications and why.**
- Generalised cutaneous vasodilation increases blood flow (up to 10–20% of cardiac output) → high-output cardiac failure, tachycardia, especially in elderly with heart disease; monitor ECG, avoid fluid overload

**Q21. Lymphadenopathy in erythroderma — dermatopathic vs lymphoma.**
- Dermatopathic lymphadenitis: reactive, soft, mobile, paracortical expansion with melanin- and lipid-laden macrophages and Langerhans cells
- Lymphoma: hard, rapidly enlarging, matted; atypical cells, clonal TCR — biopsy suspicious nodes (excisional)

**Q22. Nail and hair changes in erythroderma.**
- Nails: Beau's lines, onycholysis, shiny polished nails (rubbing), subungual hyperkeratosis (psoriasis/PRP/crusted scabies), onychomadesis
- Hair: telogen effluvium, diffuse alopecia (CTCL may have alopecia with 'leonine facies'), madarosis

**Q23. Erythroderma in HIV.**
- Causes: psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, drug reactions (nevirapine, cotrimoxazole), crusted scabies, PRP type VI, CTCL, chronic actinic dermatitis; check CD4 and viral load; treat cause and optimise ART

**Q24. What is pityriasis rubra pilaris erythroderma's characteristic picture?**
- Orange-red erythroderma with sharply demarcated islands of sparing ('nappes claires'), follicular papules on knuckles, waxy orange keratoderma (sandal), fine bran-like scales; responds to retinoids/ methotrexate/ IL-17 inhibitors

**Q25. Pemphigus foliaceus erythroderma — clues.**
- Crusted, scaly, oozing erosions with 'cornflake' scales on seborrhoeic areas, positive Nikolsky, no mucosal involvement, smell; biopsy (subcorneal acantholysis), DIF intercellular IgG, anti-Dsg1 ELISA

**Q26. Crusted scabies presenting as erythroderma — clues.**
- Thick crusts over hands, feet, extensors, scalp and nails, sometimes little itch, immunocompromised/elderly/ institutionalised, outbreak among staff and contacts; mineral oil scraping shows abundant mites — isolate and treat with ivermectin + topical scabicide

**Q27. What follow-up is needed after recovery?**
- Treat underlying disease, review drugs (drug card), monitor for relapse, repeat biopsies in idiopathic cases for CTCL every 6–12 months, maintain skin care with emollients

**Q28. Describe the Sézary cell.**
- Atypical T lymphocyte with hyperchromatic convoluted ('cerebriform') nucleus, scant cytoplasm (CD4+, CD7−, CD26− typically); >1000/µl in blood (B2 blood involvement) defines Sézary syndrome with clonal TCR

**Q29. Prognosis by cause in erythroderma.**
- Best: drug-induced (resolves in weeks after withdrawal), eczema
- Intermediate: psoriasis, PRP (relapses)
- Worst: Sézary syndrome/CTCL (median survival ~2–5 years), idiopathic in elderly (chronic, may evolve)

**Q30. Exfoliative dermatitis in children due to SSSS — management.**
- Admit, IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (cloxacillin/ cefazolin; clindamycin to reduce toxin), fluids, temperature control, gentle skin care with emollients, analgesia; no steroids; heals without scarring in 1–2 weeks

## Quick spotter facts
- ≥90% BSA red and scaly — erythroderma
- Islands of sparing + orange keratoderma — PRP
- Erythroderma + nodes + Sézary cells — Sézary syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Erythroderma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Fixed drug eruption — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Fixed drug eruption** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. What is a fixed drug eruption (FDE)?**
- Drug eruption that recurs at exactly the same site(s) each time the drug is taken, often adding new sites — usually 30 min to 8 h after re-exposure (first exposure: 1–2 weeks)

**Q2. Common culprit drugs (India).**
- Cotrimoxazole and sulphonamides, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin), NSAIDs (paracetamol, ibuprofen, oxicams, metamizole), tetracyclines, metronidazole/tinidazole, fluconazole, dapsone, barbiturates, phenolphthalein laxatives, carbamazepine
- Food and colours can cause it (fixed food eruption)

**Q3. Describe the lesion.**
- One or a few sharply demarcated round/oval dusky red to violaceous plaques, may blister centrally; burning/itching
- Heals with persistent slate-grey/brown hyperpigmentation (more marked in dark skin) which darkens and enlarges with each episode
- Sites: lips, genitals (glans penis — commonest site in men), hands, feet, face, oral mucosa
- Variants: generalised bullous FDE (GBFDE — mimics SJS/TEN, elderly, can be fatal), non-pigmenting FDE (pseudoephedrine), linear, eczematous, urticarial, wandering

**Q4. Pathogenesis — why does it recur at the same site?**
- Intra-epidermal resident memory CD8+ T cells (effector memory) persist at the healed site; on re-exposure they release IFN-γ, granzyme, perforin → keratinocyte death; regulatory T cells limit spread
- Explains the 'fixed' nature and rapid onset

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Interface dermatitis with many necrotic keratinocytes, mixed infiltrate including eosinophils and neutrophils, deep and superficial perivascular infiltrate, prominent pigment incontinence (melanophages) in dermis even in active lesions

**Q6. How do you confirm the culprit drug?**
- Detailed drug history and timeline; drug causality assessment (Naranjo scale, WHO-UMC)
- Patch test on the previously affected site (lesional patch test) — positive in ~40%; safe
- Oral provocation test with small dose under supervision (not for GBFDE); avoid if severe

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Genital: herpes simplex (recurrent vesicles, Tzanck/PCR), syphilitic chancre, Behçet's, traumatic ulcer
- Skin: EM (targets, acral), bullous insect bite, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, lichen planus pigmentosus, ashy dermatosis, mastocytoma, morphoea (early)
- GBFDE vs SJS/TEN: GBFDE has larger well-demarcated patches with intervening normal skin, less mucosal involvement, rapid onset, past history of similar episodes, better prognosis

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Identify and stop the drug; give the patient a written list of culprit and cross-reacting drugs (drug card)
- Topical potent steroid for non-erosive lesions; antiseptic/wet dressings for erosions; antihistamines
- GBFDE: manage like SJS/TEN in a burn-unit setting (cyclosporine/supportive)
- Pigmentation fades slowly; avoid re-exposure

**Q9. Why is cross-reactivity relevant?**
- Structurally related drugs (e.g. among fluoroquinolones, oxicam NSAIDs) may trigger the same lesions — test or avoid the whole class

**Q10. Generalised bullous FDE (GBFDE) in detail.**
- Multiple large dusky patches with blisters involving >10% BSA, few mucosal sites, elderly with comorbidities; mortality ~20% (similar to SJS/TEN); history of previous FDE at same sites; manage in burns unit, cyclosporine, avoid culprit

**Q11. Non-pigmenting FDE — features.**
- Large symmetrical erythematous plaques without residual pigmentation, often on hips, limbs; classically pseudoephedrine; also NSAIDs, piroxicam

**Q12. Oral provocation test — protocol and contraindications.**
- Start with 1/10–1/4 therapeutic dose under observation, increase stepwise; reaction within 30 min–8 h confirms; contraindicated in GBFDE, extensive mucosal involvement, pregnancy; informed consent

**Q13. Fixed food eruption — examples.**
- Cashew, peanut, lentils, strawberries, tonic water (quinine), food colours (tartrazine), aspartame; diagnosis by elimination and challenge

**Q14. Classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions by Gell–Coombs (revised).**
- Type I (IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Type II (cytotoxic antibody): drug-induced pemphigus, immune thrombocytopenic purpura
- Type III (immune complex): serum sickness, vasculitis
- Type IV T-cell: IVa (Th1 — contact dermatitis), IVb (Th2/ eosinophils — DRESS, MPE), IVc (cytotoxic — SJS/TEN, FDE, MPE), IVd (neutrophilic — AGEP)
- Non-immune: pseudo-allergy (MRGPRX2), phototoxic, pigmentation, overdose/ side effects

**Q15. Why does FDE heal with pigmentation more in Indians?**
- Basal keratinocyte damage leads to pigment incontinence — melanophages in dermis; darker skin with more melanin gives more prominent and prolonged slate-grey pigmentation

## Quick spotter facts
- Recurrent dusky plaque on glans at same site after drug — FDE
- Heals with slate-grey pigmentation
- Lesional patch test

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous adverse drug reactions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Folliculitis — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Folliculitis** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define folliculitis and classify it.**
- Inflammation of the hair follicle (infective or non-infective)
- By depth: superficial (ostial — Bockhart's) vs deep (sycosis, furuncle, carbuncle)
- By cause: bacterial (S. aureus, Pseudomonas 'hot-tub', Gram-negative in acne on long antibiotics), fungal (Pityrosporum/Malassezia, dermatophytic Majocchi's granuloma, Candida), viral (herpetic, molluscum), parasitic (Demodex), non-infective (eosinophilic, pseudofolliculitis barbae, perforating, actinic, drug-induced — EGFR inhibitors, steroids)

**Q2. Describe Bockhart's (superficial) folliculitis.**
- Small dome-shaped pustules pierced by a hair, on scalp, beard, limbs, buttocks; heal without scars
- Predisposed by shaving, occlusion, sweating, oils, topical steroids

**Q3. What is sycosis barbae? How does it differ from tinea barbae?**
- Chronic deep follicular staphylococcal infection of the beard area in men; perifollicular papules/pustules that recur, with crusting; hair pulls out with difficulty
- Tinea barbae: zoophilic dermatophyte, usually unilateral, kerion-like boggy plaques, hairs loose and easily pulled out, KOH positive; upper lip usually spared in tinea and involved in sycosis

**Q4. What is lupoid sycosis?**
- Chronic scarring form of sycosis with central atrophic scar and peripheral pustules — resembles lupus vulgaris

**Q5. Differentiate pseudofolliculitis barbae from sycosis.**
- Pseudofolliculitis is a foreign-body reaction to curved hairs re-entering skin after close shaving — common in tightly curled hair; papules with embedded hair, sterile
- Treatment: stop close shaving, laser hair removal, topical retinoid, mild steroid

**Q6. What is hot-tub folliculitis?**
- Pseudomonas aeruginosa from poorly chlorinated pools/tubs; itchy follicular papulopustules on areas covered by swimwear, 1–2 days after exposure
- Self-limiting in 7–10 days; ciprofloxacin if severe

**Q7. Describe Pityrosporum (Malassezia) folliculitis.**
- Itchy monomorphic follicular papules and pustules on upper back, chest, shoulders in young adults; after antibiotics, steroids, humidity, diabetes
- KOH: round budding yeasts in follicles (no hyphae); responds to azoles (topical ketoconazole, oral itraconazole/fluconazole), not to antibiotics
- Differential: acne vulgaris (comedones, polymorphous)

**Q8. What is Gram-negative folliculitis?**
- Complication of long-term tetracycline in acne: Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus — pustules around nose and chin, or deep nodules
- Treat with isotretinoin (best) or culture-directed antibiotic

**Q9. What is eosinophilic pustular folliculitis? Name its types.**
- Ofuji type (classic, Japanese adults; annular plaques of sterile follicular pustules on face/trunk)
- HIV-associated (very itchy; CD4 <250; improves with ART)
- Infantile (scalp)
- Treatment: indomethacin (Ofuji responds dramatically), phototherapy, antihistamines, topical steroids

**Q10. What is folliculitis decalvans?**
- Chronic neutrophilic scarring alopecia of vertex/occiput with tufted hairs (polytrichia), pustules and crusts; S. aureus has a role
- Treatment: rifampicin + clindamycin (10 weeks), doxycycline, dapsone, isotretinoin, intralesional steroid

**Q11. What is Majocchi's granuloma?**
- Dermatophyte invading follicles and the dermis — often after topical steroid on tinea; legs of women who shave
- Needs oral antifungal

**Q12. Name the drugs that cause acneiform or folliculitis-like eruptions.**
- Corticosteroids, androgens, lithium, isoniazid, phenytoin, halogens (iodides, bromides), EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, erlotinib, gefitinib), MEK inhibitors, vitamin B12, cyclosporine
- Monomorphic; usually no comedones

**Q13. How do you manage recurrent staphylococcal folliculitis?**
- Swab nares, axillae, perineum for carriage; treat diabetes, obesity, iron deficiency, immunodeficiency
- Decolonisation: nasal mupirocin twice daily 5 days monthly, chlorhexidine or dilute bleach baths, wash linen in hot water
- Topical clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide; oral cloxacillin/cephalexin; for recurrent: clindamycin, or rifampicin combined with another drug (never alone)
- Avoid shaving against grain, occlusive clothing

**Q14. How do you investigate folliculitis?**
- Gram stain and culture of pus; KOH for fungi; Demodex mount (standardised skin surface biopsy)
- Biopsy in non-responders (eosinophilic, perforating)
- Blood sugar, HIV if indicated

**Q15. What is Demodex folliculitis?**
- Rosacea-like facial papulopustules with heavy Demodex load (>5 mites/cm²); immunosuppressed and topical steroid users
- Treatment: ivermectin 1% cream, permethrin, metronidazole, oral ivermectin

## Quick spotter facts
- Upper lip involved — sycosis; spared — tinea barbae
- Monomorphic itchy back pustules, no comedones — think Pityrosporum folliculitis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Fox–Fordyce disease — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Fox–Fordyce disease** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is Fox–Fordyce disease?**
- Chronic, intensely itchy papular eruption of apocrine gland-bearing areas ('apocrine miliaria') due to keratin plugging of the apocrine duct in the follicular infundibulum with duct rupture; women 13–35 years; worsened by heat, sweating, stress, menstruation; improves in pregnancy and with OCPs/after menopause

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Dome-shaped skin-coloured to slightly yellow/hyperpigmented follicular papules in axillae (commonest), areolae, pubic and perineal areas, periumbilical
- Intense itch, decreased apocrine sweating, sparse axillary hair
- Reported after laser hair removal

**Q3. Discuss apocrine and eccrine glands (PYQ).**
- Eccrine: distributed all over (palms/soles most), open directly on skin, cholinergic sympathetic innervation, merocrine secretion of watery hypotonic sweat — thermoregulation
- Apocrine: axillae, anogenital, areola, ear canal (ceruminous), eyelids (Moll's glands); open into hair follicle above sebaceous duct; adrenergic innervation; functional after puberty; viscous secretion — odour after bacterial action (bromhidrosis)
- Apoeccrine glands: axillae in adults, mixed features — hyperhidrosis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Infundibular hyperkeratosis plugging the apocrine duct, spongiosis of the follicular infundibulum, perifollicular xanthomatous (foamy) macrophages (characteristic), lymphocytic infiltrate, dilated apocrine glands

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Lichen nitidus, lichen planus, folliculitis, syringomas, miliaria, Darier's disease, lichen amyloidosis, acanthosis nigricans, hidradenitis suppurativa (early), periductal mastitis (areola)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Avoid heat/sweating; loose clothing
- Topical: steroids, clindamycin, tretinoin/adapalene, calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus/tacrolimus), aluminium chloride (limited)
- Systemic: combined OCPs, isotretinoin, botulinum toxin injections, oral antihistamines; procedures — electrocoagulation, fractional laser, liposuction-curettage, surgical excision for severe localised disease

**Q7. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Perifollicular translucency, keratin plugs in follicles, loss of hair shafts, yellowish background — helps support diagnosis

**Q8. Fox–Fordyce after laser hair removal — mechanism.**
- Thermal damage to the follicular infundibulum leads to keratin plugging of apocrine ducts — reported weeks to months after laser hair removal of axillae

**Q9. Topical and procedural treatments in detail.**
- Topical: clindamycin, tretinoin/ adapalene (unplug ducts), steroids (mid-potency), tacrolimus/ pimecrolimus, benzoyl peroxide; botulinum toxin (reduces apocrine secretion — good results); microwave/ liposuction curettage, electrocautery, fractional CO2 laser, surgical excision in refractory cases
- Systemic: OCPs, isotretinoin (case reports)

**Q10. Compare eccrine and apocrine glands (PYQ).**
- Eccrine: everywhere (palms/soles most), open directly onto skin, merocrine, watery sweat for thermoregulation, cholinergic sympathetic innervation, present from birth
- Apocrine: axillae, anogenital, areolae, eyelids (Moll), ear canal (ceruminous); open into hair follicle above sebaceous duct; decapitation secretion; viscous odourless secretion (odour from bacteria); active after puberty; adrenergic innervation

**Q11. What is chromhidrosis?**
- Coloured sweat (yellow, green, blue, black) — apocrine (lipofuscin) on face/ axillae; eccrine (dyes/ drugs — clofazimine, rifampicin); pseudochromhidrosis (bacterial/ chromogenic); treat with capsaicin, botulinum toxin

**Q12. Hyperhidrosis — classification and grading (linked question).**
- Primary focal (palms, soles, axillae, face — onset young, bilateral symmetric, family history, absent during sleep) vs secondary generalised (fever, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, phaeochromocytoma, menopause, lymphoma, drugs — SSRIs)
- HDSS (Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale) 1–4; gravimetry, starch-iodine (Minor) test
- Treatment: aluminium chloride 20%, iontophoresis, botulinum toxin A, oral glycopyrrolate/ oxybutynin, microwave thermolysis, endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy (compensatory sweating)

**Q13. Pathogenesis.**
- Keratin plugging of the intra-infundibular part of apocrine ducts → rupture → apocrine sweat retention and inflammation; hormonal (begins after puberty, improves in pregnancy and after menopause); can follow laser hair removal of axillae

**Q14. Describe the clinical presentation in detail.**
- Young women (13–35 y): intensely itchy, dome-shaped, skin-coloured to yellowish follicular papules in apocrine areas — axillae (commonest), areolae, pubic/ labial region, periumbilical; worse with heat, emotion, exercise; reduced axillary sweating and sparse hair

**Q15. Enumerate apocrine gland disorders.**
- Fox–Fordyce disease, hidradenitis suppurativa (now considered follicular), apocrine bromhidrosis (malodour — bacterial breakdown), chromhidrosis (coloured sweat — lipofuscin), apocrine hidrocystoma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum, extramammary Paget's disease, apocrine carcinoma

## Quick spotter facts
- Itchy follicular axillary papules in a young woman, worse with sweating — Fox–Fordyce
- Perifollicular foamy macrophages
