_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of apocrine glands). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Freckles (ephelides) — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Freckles (ephelides)** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What are freckles?**
- Small (1–5 mm) light-brown/red-brown macules on sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned (Fitzpatrick I–II) individuals; appear in early childhood (~age 3), darken in summer and fade in winter
- Strongly associated with red hair/ MC1R variants (red hair colour alleles) — markers of UV sensitivity and melanoma risk

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Increased melanin in basal keratinocytes with normal number of melanocytes (which are larger and more active); no elongation of rete ridges — unlike lentigo

**Q3. Differentiate freckles from lentigines.**
- Freckles: childhood onset, sun-dependent (fade in winter), sun-exposed sites only, lighter colour, normal melanocyte number, no rete elongation
- Lentigines: any age, not sun-dependent, can be on any site including mucosa, darker, increased melanocytes along basal layer, elongated rete ridges

**Q4. Associations.**
- Axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign — NF1), xeroderma pigmentosum (freckling in first years of life with marked photosensitivity), Peutz–Jeghers (perioral lentigines — not true freckles), LEOPARD/Noonan with multiple lentigines

**Q5. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign; photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreen, clothing) — also reduces skin cancer risk; counsel skin self-examination in fair, freckled individuals
- Cosmetic: hydroquinone/azelaic acid, chemical peels, cryotherapy, Q-switched/picosecond lasers, IPL — recurrence with sun exposure

**Q6. Why do freckles darken in summer? Explain at cell level.**
- UV upregulates POMC/α-MSH and MC1R signalling → more tyrosinase activity and larger, more numerous eumelanin/pheomelanin melanosomes transferred to keratinocytes; melanocyte number is not increased, so pigment fades when UV stimulus falls in winter

**Q7. What is the role of MC1R?**
- Melanocortin-1 receptor on melanocytes; α-MSH binding raises cAMP → eumelanin synthesis
- Loss-of-function variants (R151C, R160W, D294H — 'red hair colour' alleles) give red hair, fair skin, freckling, poor tanning and higher melanoma and NMSC risk independent of UV

**Q8. Dermoscopy of a freckle?**
- Light-brown homogeneous or faint reticular pattern with sharp moth-eaten border; no globules or dots — helps distinguish from naevi

**Q9. What is the significance of freckling in xeroderma pigmentosum?**
- Freckle-like pigmentation in the first 1–2 years of life with severe sunburn on minimal exposure; followed by poikiloderma, actinic keratoses and skin cancers in the first decade — DNA repair (NER) defect; needs strict photoprotection

**Q10. Freckles and skin cancer risk — counselling.**
- Freckling (especially with red hair, blue eyes, poor tanning) is an independent risk factor for melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer — counsel sunscreen, shade, clothing, avoid sunburn and tanning beds, regular skin self-examination

**Q11. What is the Fitzpatrick skin type classification?**
- I always burns never tans; II usually burns tans minimally; III sometimes burns tans gradually; IV burns minimally tans well (most North Indians); V rarely burns tans profusely (South Indians); VI never burns deeply pigmented — guides phototherapy dosing and laser settings

**Q12. What is the UV index and photoprotection advice?**
- UV index ≥3 — protection needed; avoid 10 am–4 pm sun, seek shade, protective clothing (UPF ≥30), wide-brimmed hat, broad-spectrum SPF ≥30 sunscreen 2 mg/cm² reapplied every 2 h, sunglasses

**Q13. Classify sunscreens (PYQ: classify sunscreens).**
- Organic (chemical) UV absorbers: UVB — PABA derivatives, cinnamates (octinoxate), salicylates, octocrylene; UVA — benzophenones (oxybenzone), avobenzone, ecamsule, newer broad-spectrum (bemotrizinol/ Tinosorb S, bisoctrizole/ Tinosorb M)
- Inorganic (physical) blockers: zinc oxide, titanium dioxide (micronised/ nano); iron oxides for visible light
- Ideal sunscreen: broad spectrum UVA+UVB, photostable, water-resistant, cosmetically acceptable, non-irritant, non-comedogenic

**Q14. What is SPF and PA?**
- SPF = MED with sunscreen / MED without (UVB protection) at 2 mg/cm² application; SPF 30 blocks ~97% UVB
- PA (+ to ++++) grading by persistent pigment darkening (UVA protection factor); UVA-PF ≥1/3 of SPF for 'broad spectrum' (EU)

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Sun-exposed tiny brown macules darkening in summer in fair child — freckles
- Axillary freckling — NF1

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypermelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Furuncle and carbuncle — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Furuncle and carbuncle** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define furuncle and carbuncle.**
- Furuncle (boil): acute deep necrotising infection of a single hair follicle and its surrounding tissue, usually by S. aureus, forming a tender red nodule that suppurates and discharges a core
- Carbuncle: a cluster of interconnecting furuncles extending into subcutaneous fat, with multiple openings (sieve-like) — usually back of neck, back, thighs

**Q2. What are the predisposing factors? (frequently asked)**
- Nasal/perineal carriage of S. aureus (most important for recurrence)
- Diabetes mellitus, obesity, malnutrition, iron deficiency anaemia
- Immune defects: HIV, chronic granulomatous disease, hyper-IgE (Job's) syndrome, neutrophil dysfunction, chemotherapy, steroids
- Friction, sweating, poor hygiene, occlusive clothing, crowding (hostels, prisons, sports teams)
- Atopic dermatitis; PVL-producing community MRSA

**Q3. Where do furuncles not occur and why?**
- Palms and soles — no hair follicles

**Q4. What is the danger area of the face?**
- Triangle from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose — venous drainage via angular and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus; squeezing a boil here can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis

**Q5. What is Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL)?**
- Pore-forming S. aureus toxin that destroys neutrophils; linked to recurrent boils, abscesses in families/close contacts, and necrotising pneumonia
- Suspect when boils recur in several family members

**Q6. Differential diagnosis of a furuncle?**
- Hidradenitis suppurativa (flexural, recurrent, sinus tracts, double comedones)
- Inflamed epidermal/pilar cyst, acne conglobata nodule
- Myiasis (furuncular), deep fungal infection, kerion (scalp)
- Anthrax (black eschar, painless) for carbuncle
- Erythema nodosum (no fluctuation)

**Q7. Complications?**
- Cellulitis, lymphangitis, bacteraemia, septicaemia; osteomyelitis, endocarditis, septic arthritis
- Cavernous sinus thrombosis (face); scarring; glomerulonephritis is not a feature of staphylococcal infection
- Carbuncle in diabetics: extensive necrosis, ketoacidosis

**Q8. Management of a furuncle.**
- Moist warm compresses to bring to a point
- Incision and drainage once fluctuant — the single most important step for a large lesion; send pus for culture
- Systemic antibiotics if >1 cm with cellulitis, face, multiple lesions, systemic features, immunosuppression: cloxacillin/cephalexin; MRSA — doxycycline, clindamycin, cotrimoxazole, linezolid
- Do not squeeze lesions on the face

**Q9. Management of a carbuncle.**
- Admit if large, diabetic or toxic; control blood sugar
- Parenteral antibiotics (cloxacillin/cefazolin, vancomycin for MRSA)
- Surgical drainage / cruciate incision and debridement of necrotic tissue; dressings; skin graft for large defects

**Q10. Approach to recurrent furunculosis.**
- Exclude diabetes, anaemia, HIV; check neutrophil function/IgE if childhood onset
- Culture swabs of nose, axilla, groin (patient and family)
- Decolonisation: mupirocin to nares twice daily for 5 days (repeat monthly), chlorhexidine 4% body wash or dilute bleach bath twice weekly, treat whole family
- Long-term low-dose clindamycin 150 mg daily for 3 months has evidence; rifampicin 600 mg with cloxacillin/doxycycline for 10 days for carriers
- Hygiene: separate towels, hot wash of bed linen, nails short

**Q11. Histopathology of furuncle?**
- Perifollicular neutrophilic abscess with necrosis of the follicle extending into dermis and subcutis; Gram-positive cocci

**Q12. What is a stye (hordeolum)?**
- Furuncle of an eyelash follicle / gland of Zeis; internal hordeolum = Meibomian gland infection

**Q13. What is botryomycosis (asked as a short note)?**
- Chronic granulomatous bacterial infection (usually S. aureus, also Pseudomonas) producing nodules, sinuses and grains — mimics mycetoma
- Grains show Gram-positive cocci with Splendore–Hoeppli material; treat with prolonged culture-guided antibiotics ± excision

**Q14. Describe Staphylococcus aureus virulence factors.**
- Surface: protein A (binds IgG Fc), clumping factor, fibronectin-binding proteins, capsule
- Toxins: exfoliative toxins A/B (SSSS, bullous impetigo), superantigens (TSST-1, enterotoxins — toxic shock syndrome, AD flares), PVL (necrotising infections), haemolysins, leukocidins
- Enzymes: coagulase, catalase, hyaluronidase, lipase, staphylokinase, β-lactamase; MRSA — mecA gene (PBP2a)

**Q15. What is community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) and its treatment?**
- MRSA strains (e.g. USA300, SCCmec IV) causing skin infections in healthy people (athletes, prisoners, military), often PVL-positive — recurrent boils/ abscesses; treat by incision and drainage + oral cotrimoxazole, doxycycline, clindamycin or linezolid; decolonisation for recurrence

## Quick spotter facts
- Danger triangle of face — cavernous sinus thrombosis
- Recurrent boils in a family — think PVL-positive S. aureus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Genital ulcer disease — viva
posts.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 19 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Genital ulcer disease** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. Give the causes of genital ulcers — infective and non-infective (PYQ: differential diagnosis of genital ulcers).**
- STI: herpes genitalis (commonest in India now), primary syphilis, chancroid, donovanosis (granuloma inguinale), LGV
- Other infective: candidal balanitis erosions, scabies, secondary bacterial infection, tuberculosis, amoebiasis, CMV/HIV ulcers
- Non-infective: trauma (zipper, bites, sexual), fixed drug eruption, Behçet's/aphthae, erosive lichen planus, pemphigus vulgaris, SJS, lichen sclerosus erosions, Crohn's disease, pyoderma gangrenosum, Lipschütz ulcer (acute vulvar ulcer, EBV), SCC, Zoon's balanitis, dermatitis artefacta

**Q2. How do you approach a patient with genital ulcer?**
- History: incubation, number, pain, recurrence, bubo, sexual exposure/partners, drug intake (FDE), systemic symptoms (Behçet's)
- Examination: number, size, edge, base, induration, bleeding on touch, regional lymph nodes (character, uni/bilateral), other mucocutaneous signs
- Investigations: dark-field microscopy, Tzanck/PCR for HSV, Gram stain, Giemsa crush smear (Donovan bodies), serology (VDRL/RPR, TPHA), HIV, biopsy for chronic or atypical
- Treat syndromically if lab not available (NACO kits) and review

**Q3. Compare the main ulcers in a table-like way.**
- Syphilis: painless, single, indurated, clean base, rubbery bilateral nodes, incubation ~3 weeks
- Herpes: painful, multiple grouped vesicles/small erosions, recurrent, tender bilateral nodes, incubation 2–7 days
- Chancroid: painful, multiple, soft, ragged undermined, dirty base, suppurative unilateral bubo, 3–7 days
- Donovanosis: painless, beefy-red, friable, bleeds on touch, extends by continuity, pseudobubo (subcutaneous granulation, no true node), 8–80 days
- LGV: small transient painless ulcer often missed; later painful bubo with groove sign, 3–30 days

**Q4. What is donovanosis? (PYQ: granuloma inguinale)**
- Chronic progressive ulcerative STI by Klebsiella granulomatis (Calymmatobacterium); endemic in Papua New Guinea, South Africa, India (rare now)
- Types: ulcerogranulomatous (commonest, beefy red), hypertrophic/verrucous, necrotic, sclerotic/cicatricial
- Complications: pseudoelephantiasis, stenosis, SCC, haematogenous spread to bone/liver
- Treatment: azithromycin 1 g weekly (or 500 mg daily) for at least 3 weeks until healed; doxycycline 100 mg BD alternative

**Q5. What are Donovan bodies? (PYQ)**
- Intracytoplasmic bipolar-staining ('safety-pin') encapsulated rod-shaped organisms inside large mononuclear cells (macrophages), seen on Giemsa/Leishman-stained crush/tissue smear from ulcer edge — diagnostic of donovanosis

**Q6. How do you do dark-field microscopy?**
- Clean ulcer with saline, squeeze/abrade to get serous exudate (avoid blood), place on slide with coverslip, examine within 20 min under dark-field condenser
- T. pallidum: thin, tightly coiled, corkscrew motility with flexion at the middle (angulation)
- Not for oral lesions (commensal treponemes); negative after topical/systemic antibiotics — repeat thrice

**Q7. Serological tests for syphilis — classify.**
- Non-treponemal (cardiolipin): VDRL, RPR — quantitative, used for activity and treatment response (4-fold fall); false positives (biological false positive — pregnancy, SLE, APLA, leprosy, malaria, IV drug use); prozone phenomenon
- Treponemal: TPHA/TPPA, FTA-ABS, EIA/CLIA, rapid immunochromatographic tests — remain positive for life
- Reverse algorithm (treponemal first, then non-treponemal) used in many labs

**Q8. Treatment of early syphilis.**
- Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose (after test dose as per local protocol)
- Penicillin allergy (non-pregnant): doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days (azithromycin 2 g single dose — resistance reported)
- Pregnancy: penicillin only (desensitise if allergic)
- Watch for Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (fever, myalgia within 24 h); follow VDRL at 3, 6, 12 months

**Q9. What is syndromic management? Advantages and limitations (PYQ).**
- Treatment based on a clinical syndrome (discharge, ulcer, bubo, lower abdominal pain, scrotal swelling, neonatal conjunctivitis) using flowcharts to cover the common organisms at the first visit
- Advantages: simple, quick, treats at first visit without lab, cost-effective, high cure, wide coverage, partner treatment
- Limitations: overtreatment and overdiagnosis, misses asymptomatic infections, poor for cervical infection in women, encourages resistance, no second-line pathway, no aetiological data

**Q10. Name the NACO colour-coded kits.**
- Kit 1 Grey — urethral/anorectal discharge, cervicitis: azithromycin 1 g + cefixime 400 mg stat
- Kit 2 Green — vaginal discharge: secnidazole 2 g + fluconazole 150 mg stat
- Kit 3 White — non-herpetic genital ulcer: benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM + azithromycin 1 g
- Kit 4 Blue — non-herpetic ulcer, penicillin allergy: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 15 days + azithromycin 1 g
- Kit 5 Red — herpetic ulcer: acyclovir 400 mg TDS × 7 days
- Kit 6 Yellow — lower abdominal pain: cefixime 400 mg stat + metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days
- Kit 7 Black — inguinal bubo: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days + azithromycin 1 g stat

**Q11. What are the '4 Cs' and '5 Cs' of STI management?**
- Compliance, Counselling, Condoms, Contact (partner) tracing — plus Case detection/confidentiality as the 5th
- Also offer HIV and syphilis testing (and hepatitis B)

**Q12. Why is genital ulcer disease important for HIV?**
- Breach of mucosa and recruitment of CD4 cells increase HIV acquisition 2–5 fold and increase shedding; treating GUD is part of HIV prevention

**Q13. Describe the primary chancre in detail.**
- After incubation 9–90 days (average 21): single painless indurated ('button-like') ulcer with clean red base, serous exudate, regular raised border; bilateral painless rubbery non-suppurating inguinal nodes ('satellite bubo'); heals in 3–6 weeks without treatment
- Extragenital chancres: lips, tongue, tonsils, fingers, nipples, anus (may be painful)

**Q14. Describe secondary syphilis skin features.**
- 6–12 weeks after chancre: non-itchy symmetrical macular (roseola)/ papular/ papulosquamous eruption including palms and soles (copper-coloured, collarette — 'Biett's collarette'), condylomata lata (moist flat papules in anogenital area — highly infectious), mucous patches/ snail-track ulcers, split papules at angles of mouth, moth-eaten alopecia, annular lesions on face (dark skin), lues maligna (ulceronodular in HIV); generalised lymphadenopathy, malaise

**Q15. Tertiary and congenital syphilis — skin features.**
- Tertiary: gummas (punched-out ulcers with wash-leather slough, heal with tissue-paper scars), nodular/ noduloulcerative syphilides (arciform), cardiovascular (aortitis), neurosyphilis
- Congenital early: snuffles, vesiculobullous palms/soles (syphilitic pemphigus), condylomata, hepatosplenomegaly, pseudoparalysis (Parrot); late: Hutchinson's teeth, interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness (Hutchinson's triad), saddle nose, rhagades, sabre tibia, frontal bossing, Clutton's joints

**Q16. Interpretation of serology results (VDRL/TPHA combinations).**
- VDRL+ TPHA+: current or recently treated syphilis (use VDRL titre)
- VDRL− TPHA+: treated past syphilis, very early primary (VDRL not yet positive), late latent/ tertiary
- VDRL+ TPHA−: biological false positive (repeat; check APLA, SLE, pregnancy)
- Both negative: no syphilis or incubation/ very early primary (repeat at 2–4 weeks); prozone in secondary — dilute serum

**Q17. What is the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction?**
- Acute febrile reaction within 2–24 h of first antibiotic dose (penicillin) for spirochaetal infection — fever, chills, myalgia, headache, worsening rash, hypotension — due to release of treponemal lipoproteins/ cytokines; common in secondary syphilis; treat with antipyretics, reassurance; in pregnancy may cause preterm labour/ fetal distress (monitor); not an allergy — continue treatment

**Q18. Treatment of late latent syphilis and neurosyphilis.**
- Late latent/ unknown duration/ tertiary (non-neuro): benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3 doses
- Neurosyphilis/ ocular/ otic: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 MU/day IV (3–4 MU every 4 h) for 10–14 days; procaine penicillin + probenecid alternative; CSF follow-up

**Q19. Syphilis in pregnancy — screening and treatment.**
- Universal antenatal screening (VDRL/ RPR or rapid test) at first visit (and third trimester in high-risk); treat with benzathine penicillin as per stage — only penicillin prevents congenital syphilis (desensitise if allergic); treat partner; evaluate newborn (titres, exam); India's goal — elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV and syphilis

## Quick spotter facts
- Painless indurated clean ulcer — syphilis
- Beefy red friable ulcer, pseudobubo — donovanosis (safety-pin Donovan bodies)
- White kit = non-herpetic GUD

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Approach to genital ulcer); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Gonorrhoea / urethral discharge — viva
posts.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 17 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Gonorrhoea / urethral discharge** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. What is gonorrhoea? Organism?**
- STI caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — Gram-negative intracellular kidney-shaped diplococcus; infects columnar/cuboidal epithelium (urethra, endocervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva)
- Virulence: pili (attachment, antigenic variation), Opa proteins, porin, IgA1 protease, LOS (endotoxin)

**Q2. Clinical features in men and women.**
- Men: incubation 2–5 days; dysuria and profuse purulent urethral discharge; meatal oedema; ~10% asymptomatic
- Women: >50% asymptomatic; mucopurulent cervicitis, dysuria, vaginal discharge, intermenstrual bleeding
- Extragenital: rectal (receptive anal sex; proctitis), pharyngeal (mostly silent), ophthalmia

**Q3. Complications — local and metastatic (PYQ).**
- Men: epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, periurethral abscess, Littre's gland and Tyson's gland infections, urethral stricture, infertility
- Women: Bartholin abscess, PID (salpingitis → infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain), Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis
- Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI, ~1%): arthritis–dermatitis syndrome — fever, tenosynovitis, migratory polyarthralgia, few acral haemorrhagic pustules on a red base; or septic monoarthritis; rarely endocarditis, meningitis (complement C5–C9 deficiency predisposes)
- Ophthalmia neonatorum (2–5 days after birth)

**Q4. Ophthalmia neonatorum (PYQ).**
- Conjunctivitis in first 4 weeks of life: gonococcal (2–5 days, hyperacute purulent, corneal perforation risk), chlamydial (5–14 days, milder), chemical (silver nitrate, first day)
- Gonococcal treatment: ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IM single dose (max 125 mg) + saline eye irrigation; treat mother and partner
- Prophylaxis: erythromycin/tetracycline eye ointment or povidone-iodine at birth

**Q5. Approach to a case of urethral discharge (PYQ).**
- History: duration, incubation, nature of discharge, dysuria, sexual exposure and partners, previous episodes, antibiotic use
- Examine: milk the urethra, look at meatus, check epididymis, nodes, other STIs
- Gram stain of urethral smear: >2 (≥2–5) polymorphs per oil-immersion field = urethritis; Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = gonococcal (sensitivity >95% in symptomatic men)
- If no diplococci — non-gonococcal urethritis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma, Trichomonas, HSV, adenovirus)
- First-void urine NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia (most sensitive); culture on Thayer–Martin/modified New York City medium for drug susceptibility
- Syndromic: NACO grey kit (azithromycin 1 g + cefixime 400 mg) to patient and partner

**Q6. Treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhoea.**
- Ceftriaxone single dose IM (500 mg current CDC/WHO; older guidelines 250 mg) plus treat chlamydia (doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days, or azithromycin 1 g) unless chlamydia excluded
- Alternative: cefixime 400–800 mg orally single dose; gentamicin 240 mg IM + azithromycin 2 g
- Abstain until 7 days after treatment and partner treated; test of cure for pharyngeal infection

**Q7. Discuss drug resistance in gonorrhoea (PYQ).**
- Sequentially lost penicillin (PPNG — plasmid β-lactamase), tetracycline (TRNG), fluoroquinolones (gyrA, parC), and now reduced susceptibility to cephalosporins (penA mosaic alleles) and azithromycin (23S rRNA, mtr efflux)
- Extensively drug-resistant strains reported (ceftriaxone-resistant FC428 clone); WHO priority pathogen
- Responses: higher ceftriaxone dose, culture and susceptibility surveillance (GASP), new oral drugs zoliflodacin and gepotidacin (recently approved in some countries — confirm current status)

**Q8. Discuss non-gonococcal urethritis (PYQ).**
- Commonest STI syndrome in men in many places; Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D–K (~30–50%), Mycoplasma genitalium (10–25%), Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas, HSV, adenovirus
- Incubation 1–3 weeks; mild mucoid discharge, dysuria; often asymptomatic
- Complications: epididymitis, reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis — HLA-B27), PID/infertility in women
- Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days (preferred), azithromycin 1 g; M. genitalium — doxycycline then moxifloxacin (resistance-guided)

**Q9. What is Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Perihepatitis complicating PID (Chlamydia > gonorrhoea) — right upper quadrant pain, pleuritic, 'violin-string' adhesions between liver capsule and abdominal wall on laparoscopy; LFT often normal

**Q10. How do you take a cervical sample?**
- Speculum examination, wipe ectocervix, insert swab 1–2 cm into endocervix, rotate 10–15 seconds; Gram stain less sensitive in women (50%) — prefer NAAT/culture

**Q11. Differentiate gonococcal and non-gonococcal urethritis clinically.**
- Gonococcal: shorter incubation (2–5 days), abrupt, profuse purulent yellow-green discharge, marked dysuria
- NGU: longer incubation (1–3 weeks), gradual, scanty mucoid/ watery discharge, mild dysuria, often early-morning 'glue' at meatus

**Q12. What is the Gram stain criterion for urethritis?**
- ≥2 polymorphonuclear leucocytes per oil-immersion field (×1000) in urethral smear (some use ≥5), or ≥10 PMN/hpf in first-void urine sediment, or positive leucocyte esterase

**Q13. What is the treatment of disseminated gonococcal infection?**
- Hospitalise; ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM daily (24–48 h after improvement then oral cefixime to complete 7 days); arthrocentesis for septic joint; endocarditis/ meningitis — high-dose ceftriaxone 1–2 g every 12–24 h for 2–4 weeks; test for complement deficiency if recurrent

**Q14. Gonorrhoea in pregnancy and neonates.**
- Pregnancy: ceftriaxone (avoid quinolones, tetracyclines); risk of chorioamnionitis, preterm birth, PROM, ophthalmia neonatorum; test of cure
- Neonate of infected mother: ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IM single dose prophylactic; treat ophthalmia as emergency

**Q15. What are the culture media for N. gonorrhoeae?**
- Selective media: Thayer–Martin (vancomycin, colistin, nystatin, trimethoprim), modified New York City medium, Martin–Lewis; incubate at 35–37 °C in 5–10% CO2 (candle jar); oxidase-positive, ferments only glucose; transport in Stuart/ Amies medium quickly

**Q16. Discuss Chlamydia trachomatis infections beyond NGU.**
- Serovars A–C: trachoma; D–K: urethritis, cervicitis, PID, epididymitis, proctitis, neonatal conjunctivitis/ pneumonia, reactive arthritis; L1–L3: LGV
- Diagnosis by NAAT; treatment doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days (azithromycin 1 g in pregnancy)

**Q17. Trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis — brief features (vaginal discharge syndrome).**
- Trichomoniasis: frothy yellow-green malodorous discharge, strawberry cervix, pH >4.5, motile flagellates on wet mount — metronidazole 2 g single dose or 500 mg BD × 7 days, treat partner
- Bacterial vaginosis: thin grey homogeneous fishy-smelling discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test (KOH), clue cells — Amsel criteria (3 of 4)/ Nugent score; metronidazole 400–500 mg BD × 7 days
- Candidiasis: curdy white discharge, itching, pH normal (<4.5), pseudohyphae on KOH — fluconazole 150 mg; NACO green kit (secnidazole + fluconazole) covers all three

## Quick spotter facts
- Gram-negative intracellular diplococci in pus cells — gonorrhoea
- Acral haemorrhagic pustules + tenosynovitis — DGI
- Grey kit — urethral discharge

## Note
Ceftriaxone dose: newer guidelines use 500 mg (older 250 mg) — this is one of the open questions for the department.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Gonorrhoea, non-gonococcal urethritis); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits); WHO 2024 STI guidelines. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Granuloma annulare — viva
posts.summary: Granulomatous disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Granuloma annulare** (Granulomatous disorders)_

**Q1. What is granuloma annulare (GA)?**
- Benign, usually self-limiting, non-infectious granulomatous dermatosis with annular arrangement of smooth papules; children and young adults (localised), middle-aged women (generalised)

**Q2. Clinical variants.**
- Localised (commonest — dorsa of hands/feet, fingers, ankles; skin-coloured to pink beaded papules in a ring without scale; central skin normal or slightly violaceous)
- Generalised/disseminated (≥10 lesions on trunk and limbs; adults; associations — diabetes, dyslipidaemia, thyroid disease, HIV, malignancy (lymphoma) in some; chronic)
- Subcutaneous (deep nodules on shins, scalp, hands of children — 'pseudo-rheumatoid nodules')
- Perforating (umbilicated papules with central crust — hands)
- Patch/macular (erythematous patches — 'interstitial GA'), micropapular, actinic (photo-exposed — annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma), drug-induced (TNF inhibitors, allopurinol, ACE inhibitors)

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Unknown — delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to an unknown antigen with collagen degeneration (necrobiosis) and mucin; triggers: insect bites, trauma, tuberculin test, vaccines, sun, viral infections, drugs; Th1 cells, TNF-α, JAK-STAT signalling (basis for JAK inhibitors)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Palisading granuloma: central zone of altered (necrobiotic) collagen with abundant mucin surrounded by palisading histiocytes and lymphocytes in upper/mid dermis
- Interstitial pattern: histiocytes scattered between collagen bundles with mucin ('busy dermis')
- Mucin (Alcian blue/colloidal iron) differentiates from necrobiosis lipoidica (little mucin, layered 'cake' pattern, plasma cells) and rheumatoid nodule (fibrinoid necrosis, deeper)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis of annular plaques.**
- Tinea corporis (scaly active edge, KOH), annular lichen planus (violaceous, Wickham's striae), tuberculoid/borderline-tuberculoid leprosy (anaesthesia, nerve), sarcoidosis (annular), necrobiosis lipoidica (shins, yellow atrophic), erythema annulare centrifugum (trailing scale), SCLE, secondary syphilis (annular), mycosis fungoides, actinic GA, porokeratosis (keratotic ridge)

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Clinical ± biopsy; in generalised GA: blood sugar/HbA1c, lipid profile, thyroid function, HIV, hepatitis; consider malignancy screen if atypical in elderly

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Localised: reassurance (50% resolve within 2 years), potent topical steroid under occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone (2.5–5 mg/ml), cryotherapy, tacrolimus; 'biopsy-induced resolution' is described
- Generalised: phototherapy (PUVA, NB-UVB, UVA1), hydroxychloroquine, dapsone, isotretinoin, doxycycline/minocycline + rifampicin + ofloxacin ('ROM' monthly combination), pentoxifylline, methotrexate, TNF inhibitors (paradoxical GA reported too), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) for refractory
- Treat associated diabetes/dyslipidaemia

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Localised GA resolves spontaneously in ~50% within 2 years without scars but recurs in ~40% (often at same site); generalised GA more chronic and resistant

**Q9. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Pinkish-yellow/ orange structureless areas with dotted/ linear irregular vessels, peripheral white/ pink annular rim; no scale (vs tinea)

**Q10. What is 'interstitial granuloma annulare' vs interstitial granulomatous dermatitis?**
- Interstitial GA: histiocytes between collagen bundles with mucin, patch-type clinical lesions
- Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis: linear cords ('rope sign') on trunk/ flanks with arthritis, associated with RA/ autoimmune disease/ drugs (drug-induced IGDR — ACE inhibitors, statins, TNF inhibitors); differentiate by mucin (less in IGD)

**Q11. Drug-induced GA.**
- TNF inhibitors, allopurinol, amlodipine, gold, diclofenac, PD-1 inhibitors, vaccines (BCG, influenza, hepatitis B) — remove trigger

**Q12. GA and HIV.**
- Generalised/ perforating GA can occur in HIV (often CD4 low) — offer HIV test in generalised or atypical GA

**Q13. Classify cutaneous granulomas (linked question).**
- Infectious: TB, leprosy, NTM, deep fungi, leishmaniasis, syphilis
- Non-infectious: sarcoidal (sarcoidosis), palisading (GA, necrobiosis lipoidica, rheumatoid nodule, necrobiotic xanthogranuloma), foreign body (tattoo, silica, suture, keratin), tuberculoid (rosacea, LMDF), xanthogranulomatous, granulomatous vasculitis, granulomatous mycosis fungoides

**Q14. What is the association of generalised GA with diabetes and lipids?**
- Generalised GA in adults has a higher prevalence of diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia and thyroid disease than controls; screening with HbA1c, lipids and TSH is recommended

**Q15. What is subcutaneous GA and how is it managed?**
- Firm, non-tender deep nodules on shins, scalp, hands of young children; histology — palisaded granulomas with mucin in subcutis (resembles rheumatoid nodule but RF negative); benign, resolves; avoid unnecessary excision (recurs)

## Quick spotter facts
- Ring of smooth skin-coloured beaded papules on dorsa of hands, no scale — GA
- Palisading granuloma with mucin

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Non-infectious granulomas). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Hailey–Hailey disease — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hailey–Hailey disease** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Write short notes on Hailey–Hailey disease (PYQ).**
- Familial benign chronic pemphigus — autosomal dominant ATP2C1 mutation (SPCA1 — Golgi Ca²⁺/Mn²⁺ ATPase) → defective desmosome assembly → suprabasal acantholysis; onset in 3rd–4th decade

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Recurrent flaccid vesicles and erosions on erythematous base in intertriginous areas (neck, axillae, groin, perianal, submammary), with crusting, painful fissures ('cracked/ dried mud' or 'rhagades'), maceration and foul odour; worse with heat, sweat, friction, infection
- Nails: longitudinal white bands (asymptomatic); mucosa rarely involved
- Segmental/linear types (mosaic)

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Suprabasal and full-thickness acantholysis with partially attached keratinocytes giving a 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance, few dyskeratotic cells (fewer than Darier's), DIF negative

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Intertrigo (candidal, bacterial, tinea — KOH/culture), pemphigus vegetans (DIF positive), Darier's disease, inverse psoriasis, erythrasma, contact dermatitis, impetigo, HSV

**Q5. Management.**
- Avoid friction/heat/sweating, weight loss, loose clothing; treat secondary infections (antibiotics, antifungals, antivirals)
- Topical steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, antiseptics, calcitriol
- Oral: doxycycline/minocycline (anti-inflammatory), dapsone, acitretin, low-dose naltrexone (newer evidence), cyclosporine short-term, oral magnesium, glycopyrrolate (sweat)
- Botulinum toxin to reduce sweating in flexures
- Procedures: CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, dermabrasion, PDT, excision with grafting for refractory localised disease

**Q6. Differentiate Darier's and Hailey–Hailey diseases.**
- Darier's: ATP2A2 (SERCA2, ER), seborrhoeic areas + flexures, keratotic papules, nail red-white bands with V-notch, palmar pits, oral papules, neuropsychiatric associations; histology — prominent dyskeratosis (corps ronds, grains)
- Hailey–Hailey: ATP2C1 (SPCA1, Golgi), flexures only, vesicles/erosions/fissures, nails white bands only, no mucosa; histology — dilapidated brick wall, little dyskeratosis

**Q7. Clinical features in detail.**
- Familial benign chronic pemphigus: onset 3rd–4th decade; recurrent flaccid vesicles and erosions in flexures (neck sides, axillae, groin, perianal, submammary) forming macerated, fissured plaques ('cerebriform' rhagades), malodour, pain; longitudinal white lines on fingernails; worse with heat, sweat, friction, infection

**Q8. Histopathology in detail.**
- Widespread suprabasal and intraepidermal acantholysis with partially attached cells — 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance; few dyskeratotic cells (fewer than Darier); DIF negative (vs pemphigus)

**Q9. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Pemphigus vegetans (DIF positive), intertrigo (candidal, bacterial), inverse psoriasis, flexural Darier's, erythrasma, tinea cruris, seborrhoeic dermatitis, extramammary Paget's, contact dermatitis

**Q10. Laser and procedural treatments.**
- CO2 or Er:YAG ablation of affected skin (re-epithelialisation from adnexa with normal cells reduces recurrences), dermabrasion, PDT, excision with grafting; botulinum toxin in axillae/ groin; long remissions reported

**Q11. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- Chronic relapsing course with flares in summer; does not affect life expectancy; may improve with age

**Q13. What is the genetic basis?**
- Autosomal dominant ATP2C1 mutation → defective SPCA1 (Golgi calcium/manganese pump) → impaired desmosome assembly → suprabasal acantholysis ('dilapidated brick wall' appearance)

**Q14. What newer treatments help?**
- Botulinum toxin A (reduces sweating — fewer flares), low-dose naltrexone (1.5–4.5 mg/day — reported benefit), dupilumab/apremilast (case reports), oral magnesium chloride, glycopyrrolate, laser ablation (CO2, Er:YAG), PDT, dermabrasion; topical steroids/ tacrolimus/ antibiotics/ antifungals for flares

**Q15. Why is secondary infection a problem?**
- Macerated flexural erosions get colonised by S. aureus, Candida and HSV — flares; swab and treat; consider HSV if sudden painful worsening (Kaposi's varicelliform eruption)

## Quick spotter facts
- Recurrent flexural erosions with fissures in adults with family history — Hailey–Hailey (ATP2C1)
- Dilapidated brick wall

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hailey–Hailey disease). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Halo nevus — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Halo nevus** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Discuss halo naevus — pathophysiology (PYQ).**
- Melanocytic naevus (usually compound or intradermal) surrounded by a symmetrical round/oval depigmented halo, due to immune-mediated (CD8+ T-cell) destruction of naevus cells and surrounding melanocytes — Sutton's naevus / leucoderma acquisitum centrifugum
- Children and adolescents, trunk (back) commonest; may be multiple

**Q2. Stages.**
- Stage I: pigmented naevus with halo; II: naevus becomes pink/lighter; III: naevus disappears leaving a depigmented macule; IV: repigmentation of the halo (may take years)

**Q3. Associations.**
- Vitiligo (in ~20–50% of patients with halo naevi; multiple halo naevi increase vitiligo risk), autoimmune thyroid disease, Turner syndrome, melanoma (halo around melanoma or distant halo naevi in metastatic melanoma — especially in adults; immunotherapy-associated leucoderma)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Dense lymphocytic infiltrate (CD8 T cells, macrophages) intermingled with naevus cells in the dermis ('naevus being destroyed'), loss of melanocytes in the halo epidermis

**Q5. When should a halo naevus be biopsied?**
- Atypical central naevus (asymmetry, irregular colour, ulceration), eccentric/irregular halo, onset in adulthood (>40 y), history of melanoma, change in the central lesion — to exclude melanoma

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Melanoma with regression/halo, vitiligo around naevus, halo around other lesions (blue naevus, Spitz, seborrhoeic keratosis, molluscum, neurofibroma, BCC), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation

**Q7. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign, spontaneous course; full skin and eye examination; photoprotection of halo
- No treatment needed; excision only if atypical; screen for vitiligo/thyroid

**Q8. Describe the clinical features.**
- Central pigmented naevus (usually compound, <5 mm) surrounded by a symmetrical round/ oval depigmented halo 1–5 mm; back of adolescents; multiple in ~25–50%; central naevus may fade and disappear leaving white macule which later repigments

**Q9. Explain the immunology.**
- CD8+ T cells (and antibodies) against naevus melanocyte antigens cause immune destruction of the naevus and surrounding melanocytes; HLA association; similar mechanism to vitiligo and immunotherapy-related leucoderma

**Q10. What is halo phenomenon around other lesions?**
- Halo around melanoma (primary or metastatic — irregular, asymmetric halo in older adults), blue naevus, Spitz naevus, congenital naevus, seborrhoeic keratosis, dermatofibroma, neurofibroma, BCC, molluscum — atypical halos need assessment

**Q11. Should halo naevi be excised?**
- Usually no — benign self-limiting process; excise if central naevus atypical (asymmetric, irregular colour), halo asymmetric, onset in older age (>40), or patient has history of melanoma

**Q12. What is the Sutton naevus?**
- Synonym for halo naevus (described by Sutton 1916 as 'leukoderma acquisitum centrifugum')

**Q13. Halo naevus and vitiligo surgery/ prognosis.**
- Presence of halo naevi in vitiligo patients associated with earlier onset, family history, more extensive disease, possibly poorer response; leucotrichia within halo signals deeper melanocyte loss

**Q14. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Central naevus with regular globular/ homogeneous pattern surrounded by a symmetrical structureless white halo; atypical features (irregular central pigment, asymmetric halo) should prompt excision

**Q15. Relationship to vitiligo.**
- Halo naevi occur in ~20–30% of vitiligo patients; multiple halo naevi or those with leucotrichia are a risk factor for developing non-segmental vitiligo; mechanism — CD8+ T-cell response cross-reacting with melanocyte antigens

## Quick spotter facts
- Symmetric depigmented ring around a mole on a child's back — halo naevus
- Atypical halo in adult — biopsy (melanoma)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Halo naevus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Hand eczema & pompholyx — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hand eczema & pompholyx** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Why is hand eczema important?**
- Commonest occupational skin disease (prevalence ~10% in general population, much higher in wet workers — health workers, cleaners, hairdressers, cooks, construction); chronic, causes job loss and poor quality of life

**Q2. Classify hand eczema.**
- By cause: irritant contact (commonest), allergic contact, atopic hand eczema, protein contact dermatitis/contact urticaria, combinations
- By morphology: pompholyx (recurrent vesicular), hyperkeratotic (palmar), fingertip (pulpitis), nummular, apron (proximal palm and adjacent fingers), chronic fissured, ring dermatitis, wear-and-tear (dorsa)
- Acute (<3 months) vs chronic (>3 months or ≥2 relapses/year)

**Q3. What is pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema)? (PYQ)**
- Recurrent crops of deep-seated, itchy, tense vesicles ('sago-grain'/tapioca) on sides of fingers and palms ± soles; may form bullae; dry to brown spots and peeling in 2–3 weeks
- Triggers: hot weather, sweating, stress, atopy, nickel/cobalt systemic exposure, dermatophyte id reaction, IVIG, smoking
- Not a disorder of sweat glands despite the name

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of vesicular hand eczema.**
- Tinea manuum/id reaction (look at feet, KOH), palmoplantar pustulosis (pustules, smokers), scabies (burrows), bullous pemphigoid (dyshidrosiform), herpes, hand-foot-mouth disease, dermatitis herpetiformis, EBS
- Hyperkeratotic hand eczema vs palmar psoriasis — psoriasis has sharper edges, other sites, nail pits; histology helps

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Detailed occupational and exposure history, look at feet (tinea), KOH, patch test (standard + occupational series) in every chronic hand eczema, prick test for contact urticaria, biopsy if psoriasis suspected

**Q6. Management of hand eczema.**
- Skin protection programme: avoid wet work >2 h/day, cotton-lined gloves, emollients after each wash, alcohol-based hand rubs preferable to soap
- Topical: potent steroids (clobetasol, mometasone) for short courses then intermittent; tacrolimus; delgocitinib cream (topical pan-JAK inhibitor approved for chronic hand eczema)
- Phototherapy: hand PUVA (topical psoralen) or NB-UVB
- Systemic: alitretinoin 30 mg/day for chronic hyperkeratotic hand eczema (teratogenic), acitretin (hyperkeratotic), short oral steroid for acute flares, cyclosporine, methotrexate, azathioprine, dupilumab (atopic hand eczema)
- Pompholyx: potassium permanganate soaks (1:10,000), potent steroid, drain large bullae, treat id source, botulinum toxin if hyperhidrosis, low-nickel diet if nickel-sensitive

**Q7. What is apron eczema?**
- Eczema on the proximal palm and adjacent volar surfaces of fingers — often allergic (food handlers) or atopic

**Q8. What is fingertip eczema?**
- Dry, fissured, scaly fingertips (pulpitis) — irritant (paper handlers), allergic (garlic — tulipalin/diallyl disulphide in chefs; Alstroemeria tulipalin in florists), atopic

**Q9. Prognosis?**
- Poor in atopics and when wet work continues; ~50% still have it after 15 years; early diagnosis, education and allergen avoidance improve outcome

**Q10. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q11. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q12. What is the 'id reaction' in hand eczema?**
- Autoeczematisation: vesicular eruption on hands (pompholyx-like) triggered by distant inflammatory focus — tinea pedis (dermatophytide), stasis dermatitis, contact dermatitis; resolves after treating the primary site; KOH of feet

**Q13. What is hyperkeratotic hand eczema?**
- Thick, fissured, scaly plaques on palms (central/ proximal) of middle-aged men, not very itchy; differentiate from palmar psoriasis (biopsy, nail/ scalp signs) and tinea manuum; treat with keratolytics, potent steroids under occlusion, acitretin/ alitretinoin, PUVA

**Q14. Patient education — hand care programme.**
- Use lukewarm water, mild soap substitutes, dry hands well (including web spaces), apply emollient after every wash and at night (cotton gloves), gloves for wet work (≤15–20 min stretches with cotton liners), remove rings during wet work, avoid direct contact with irritants (detergents, solvents, raw foods)

**Q15. Prognosis factors for hand eczema.**
- Poor prognosis: atopy (childhood eczema), extensive disease at diagnosis, early onset, contact allergy, continued wet work exposure, delay in diagnosis; better with early patch testing and allergen avoidance

## Quick spotter facts
- Tapioca-like deep vesicles on finger sides — pompholyx
- Chronic hand eczema — always patch test

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hand eczema); ESCD hand eczema guideline. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Hansen's disease (leprosy) — viva
posts.summary: Leprosy & mycobacterial · 37 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hansen's disease (leprosy)** (Leprosy & mycobacterial)_

**Q1. Define leprosy.**
- Chronic granulomatous infection by Mycobacterium leprae (and M. lepromatosis) that mainly affects skin and peripheral nerves, also eyes, nasal mucosa, testes, bones; clinical spectrum decided by host cell-mediated immunity

**Q2. Describe the organism.**
- Acid-fast (weaker than M. tuberculosis — decolorise with 5% sulphuric acid), Gram-positive, obligate intracellular bacillus; prefers Schwann cells and macrophages
- Generation time ~12–14 days (slowest known); optimum 30–33 °C → cooler parts of body affected (ear lobes, nose, testes, superficial nerves)
- Not cultivable in vitro; grows in mouse foot-pad (Shepard) and nine-banded armadillo
- Cell wall: phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL-1, species specific — binds laminin-α2 of Schwann cell basal lamina), lipoarabinomannan; genome shows massive gene decay (only ~half functional genes)

**Q3. Transmission and incubation period?**
- Main route: nasal droplets from untreated multibacillary patients → upper respiratory mucosa; less often broken skin; rarely transplacental, insect, armadillo (zoonosis in USA)
- Incubation: average 2–5 years for PB, 8–12 years for MB (range months to decades)
- Most exposed people never develop disease (high natural resistance); household contacts of MB patients have the highest risk

**Q4. What are the cardinal signs of leprosy (NLEP)?**
- 1) Hypopigmented or erythematous skin patch with definite loss of sensation
- 2) Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of muscles supplied by it
- 3) Acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear
- Any one sign is enough to diagnose leprosy

**Q5. Give the Ridley–Jopling classification and the immunological basis.**
- TT – BT – BB – BL – LL (+ indeterminate outside the spectrum; pure neuritic separately)
- TT pole: strong Th1 (IFN-γ, IL-2), few bacilli, lepromin positive; LL pole: Th2 (IL-4, IL-10), anergy to M. leprae, plenty of bacilli, lepromin negative
- Borderline groups are immunologically unstable → shift (upgrade/downgrade) and type 1 reactions

**Q6. Give the WHO / NLEP operational classification.**
- Paucibacillary (PB): 1–5 skin lesions, no nerve involvement, smear negative
- Multibacillary (MB): ≥6 skin lesions, OR any nerve involvement (NLEP 2025: any nerve involvement = MB), OR positive slit-skin smear irrespective of lesions
- When in doubt classify as MB

**Q7. Compare TT, BT, BB, BL and LL clinically.**
- TT: 1–3 well-defined dry, scaly, anaesthetic plaques with raised edges, hair loss, one thickened nerve near the lesion
- BT: few–many (≤10) asymmetrical lesions with satellite lesions and irregular edges, sensory loss, several nerves asymmetrically thickened
- BB: many 'punched-out', inverted-saucer or Swiss-cheese lesions with sloping outer edge; unstable
- BL: many lesions, roughly symmetrical, some sensation preserved, many nerves, early nodules
- LL: innumerable symmetrical shiny macules/papules/nodules, diffuse infiltration, leonine facies, madarosis, ear lobe thickening, glove-and-stocking anaesthesia, late nerve damage, systemic involvement

**Q8. What is indeterminate leprosy?**
- Earliest form: one or few vague hypopigmented macules with ill-defined edges and doubtful/slight sensory loss, usually in children; smear negative; nerves not thickened
- Histology: perineural/peri-appendageal lymphocytes, rare bacilli in nerve
- May heal spontaneously or progress to any group

**Q9. What is pure neuritic leprosy?**
- Nerve involvement (thickening, sensory/motor loss) without any skin lesion; ~5–10% in India
- Diagnosis: nerve biopsy (sural or radial cutaneous) or FNAC; treat as MB

**Q10. Which nerves do you palpate and where?**
- Supraorbital, great auricular (neck, across sternomastoid on turning head), ulnar (above medial epicondyle), median (wrist, medial to palmaris longus), radial cutaneous (lateral border of radius at wrist), radial (spiral groove), common peroneal (behind fibular head), superficial peroneal (dorsum of foot), sural, posterior tibial (behind medial malleolus)
- Note: thickening, tenderness, consistency, nodules/abscess; compare both sides

**Q11. Describe the deformities in leprosy and classify them.**
- Primary (due to disease): madarosis, leonine facies, nasal collapse (saddle nose), lagophthalmos, claw hand, foot drop, ape thumb
- Secondary (due to anaesthesia/neglect): ulcers, shortening and absorption of digits, contractures, Charcot joints
- Ulnar claw (ring and little finger), median + ulnar = complete claw with ape-thumb (thenar wasting), radial = wrist drop (rare), common peroneal = foot drop, posterior tibial = claw toes and plantar anaesthesia, facial = lagophthalmos, trigeminal = corneal anaesthesia

**Q12. Grade disability (WHO).**
- Hands and feet: Grade 0 — no anaesthesia, no visible deformity; Grade 1 — anaesthesia, no visible deformity; Grade 2 — visible deformity or damage (ulcers, claw, foot drop, resorption)
- Eyes: Grade 0 normal; Grade 1 — eye problems due to leprosy but vision not severely affected (≥6/60); Grade 2 — lagophthalmos, iridocyclitis, corneal opacity, vision <6/60
- EHF score: sum of grades of 2 eyes, 2 hands, 2 feet (0–12) — better for monitoring

**Q13. How do you do and read a slit-skin smear?**
- Sites: both ear lobes, forehead/eyebrow, active edge of lesions (usually 4–6 sites); blanch skin by pinching, 5 mm long 2–3 mm deep slit, scrape dermal fluid, smear, fix, Ziehl–Neelsen with 5% H2SO4
- Bacteriological index (Ridley log scale, 0 to 6+): 1+ = 1–10 bacilli in 100 fields … 6+ = >1000 per field; average of sites
- Morphological index: % of solid (uniformly stained, viable) bacilli — falls quickly with treatment; BI falls ~0.6–1 log per year

**Q14. What is the Fite–Faraco stain?**
- Modified acid-fast stain using peanut oil–xylene to protect the fragile lipid coat of M. leprae in tissue sections — better than ZN for biopsies

**Q15. Describe the histopathology across the spectrum.**
- TT: well-formed epithelioid granulomas reaching up to epidermis, dense lymphocytic mantle, nerves destroyed, no bacilli
- BT: granulomas with a narrow grenz zone sometimes absent, fewer lymphocytes, nerves swollen, AFB rare
- BB: diffuse epithelioid cells, no giant cells, few lymphocytes, moderate bacilli
- BL: macrophage granulomas with some foamy cells, lymphocytes, 'onion-skin' perineurium
- LL: clear grenz zone (Unna band), sheets of foamy Virchow (lepra) cells with globi, very few lymphocytes, many bacilli

**Q16. What is the lepromin test? How is it read and what is its value?**
- Intradermal injection of 0.1 ml heat-killed M. leprae (Mitsuda/Dharmendra antigen)
- Early Fernandez reaction at 48–72 h (delayed hypersensitivity to soluble antigen); late Mitsuda reaction at 21–28 days (nodule ≥5 mm = positive; reflects ability to mount granulomatous CMI)
- Not diagnostic (positive in healthy people); used for classification and prognosis — negative in LL/BL

**Q17. Other diagnostic tests?**
- Sensory testing: monofilaments (Semmes–Weinstein), ball-pen, temperature/pain tests
- Histamine test (incomplete triple response in anaesthetic patch — sensory nerve loss), sweat test with pilocarpine/starch-iodine (anhidrosis)
- Nerve conduction studies, high-resolution ultrasound of nerves
- Serology: anti-PGL-1 IgM (correlates with bacterial load; useful in MB and contact surveillance)
- PCR for M. leprae DNA (RLEP) — pure neuritic, paucibacillary, relapse; rpoB/folP/gyrA for drug resistance

**Q18. What are lepra reactions? Compare type 1 and type 2.**
- Acute inflammatory episodes during otherwise chronic course, before, during or after MDT; main cause of nerve damage
- Type 1 (reversal reaction): delayed-type hypersensitivity (Th1 up), in borderline cases (BT, BB, BL); existing lesions become red, swollen, tender; new lesions; acute neuritis (pain, tenderness, new loss of function); oedema of hands/feet/face; little systemic upset
- Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL): immune-complex (type III) with neutrophils and high TNF-α, in BL/LL with high BI; crops of tender evanescent red nodules on normal skin, fever, malaise, neuritis, iridocyclitis, orchitis, arthritis, lymphadenitis, nephritis, dactylitis; often recurrent/chronic

**Q19. How do you treat type 1 reaction?**
- Continue MDT; rest, splint affected nerves, analgesics
- Prednisolone 40 mg/day (≈1 mg/kg) tapering slowly: e.g. 40 mg ×2 wk, 30, 25, 20, 15, 10, 5 mg in 2–4 weekly steps — about 12 weeks for PB and 20–24 weeks for MB/neuritis
- Severe neuritis not responding: higher dose, then consider nerve decompression

**Q20. How do you treat ENL?**
- Mild: NSAIDs, rest
- Moderate–severe: prednisolone 40–60 mg/day with taper (short course)
- Chronic/recurrent: clofazimine 100 mg three times daily up to 12 weeks then taper (total ≤12 months) — steroid-sparing, slow onset
- Thalidomide 100–400 mg/day (very effective; teratogenic — not in women of child-bearing age without strict contraception; neuropathy, thrombosis); pentoxifylline, methotrexate, minocycline also used

**Q21. What is the Lucio phenomenon?**
- Occurs in untreated diffuse non-nodular lepromatous leprosy (Lucio–Latapi, 'lepra bonita' with smooth shiny skin) — Mexico/Central America
- Necrotising vasculitis by bacilli in endothelium → painful purpuric angular lesions becoming haemorrhagic bullae and ulcers on limbs, without fever
- Treat with MDT + steroids, wound care; may need exchange transfusion in severe cases

**Q22. What is histoid leprosy?**
- Variant of LL (often after dapsone monotherapy or irregular treatment) with soft, shiny skin-coloured to red papules and nodules on apparently normal skin, especially over joints and back
- Histology: spindle-shaped histiocytes in a whorled/storiform pattern with huge numbers of bacilli (high BI) — a source of drug resistance and transmission

**Q23. Name the other clinical variants.**
- Lazarine leprosy (ulcerating lesions in borderline cases without neuritis)
- Lepra bonita / Lucio leprosy, histoid, pure neuritic, conjugal leprosy (between spouses, low rate)
- Childhood leprosy (indicator of active transmission in the community)
- Leprosy in HIV (more type 1 reactions after ART — immune reconstitution)

**Q24. What is the MDT regimen now (NLEP from 1 April 2025)?**
- Same 3 drugs for both PB and MB: rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone; PB for 6 months, MB for 12 months
- Adult (>14 y): monthly supervised rifampicin 600 mg + clofazimine 300 mg; daily self-administered clofazimine 50 mg + dapsone 100 mg
- Child 10–14 y: rifampicin 450 mg + clofazimine 150 mg monthly; clofazimine 50 mg alternate days + dapsone 50 mg daily
- Child <10 y: by weight — rifampicin 10 mg/kg monthly, clofazimine 6 mg/kg monthly + 1 mg/kg alternate days, dapsone 2 mg/kg daily
- Blister packs: adult (red for MB), child (yellow); release from treatment after completing the course (PB in 6 within 9 months, MB in 12 within 18 months)

**Q25. Mechanism of action and important side effects of MDT drugs.**
- Rifampicin: inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB) — kills 99.9% with one dose; red urine, hepatitis, flu-like syndrome/thrombocytopenia with intermittent dosing, enzyme inducer (reduces OCP and steroid efficacy)
- Dapsone: blocks folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase; folP); haemolysis (worse in G6PD deficiency), methaemoglobinaemia, agranulocytosis, dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (~4–6 weeks; fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy; HLA-B*13:01), neuropathy
- Clofazimine: binds mycobacterial DNA, anti-inflammatory; reddish-brown pigmentation and ichthyosis (reversible slowly), GI crystal deposition (abdominal pain), dry skin

**Q26. Newer drugs / alternative regimens?**
- Ofloxacin/levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin — for drug intolerance or resistance
- Rifampicin resistance: 24 months of daily clofazimine with two of ofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin (WHO)
- Rifapentine, bedaquiline under study

**Q27. What is chemoprophylaxis of leprosy?**
- Single-dose rifampicin (SDR-PEP) to contacts of new cases after excluding leprosy and TB — adults 600 mg; children by age/weight (not under 2 years)
- Reduces risk in contacts by about 50–60% in the first 2 years (COLEP)
- Used under NLEP in contact tracing campaigns (LCDC)

**Q28. Vaccines in leprosy?**
- BCG gives variable protection (≈ 26–50%); repeat BCG adds some
- Mycobacterium indicus pranii (MIP, formerly Mw) — immunotherapy with MDT and in contacts (Indian vaccine)
- LepVax (LEP-F1) in trials

**Q29. Define relapse; differentiate it from type 1 reaction.**
- Relapse: re-appearance of disease activity after successful completion of MDT (new lesions, new nerve damage, rise in BI ≥2+ at any site)
- Reaction: sudden onset (days), within ~6 months of stopping MDT, existing lesions inflamed, often tender nerves, rapid response to steroids (2–4 weeks), BI not rising
- Relapse: insidious onset, usually >3 years after RFT, new lesions slowly, no response to steroid trial, BI rises/solid bacilli

**Q30. What are persisters and resisters?**
- Persisters: drug-sensitive but dormant viable bacilli that survive despite therapy (in nerves, smooth muscle, bone marrow) — cause late relapse
- Resisters: genetically drug-resistant bacilli (mutations in rpoB, folP1, gyrA) — primary or secondary (after monotherapy)

**Q31. How is the eye involved?**
- Lagophthalmos (facial nerve, zygomatic branch — in reactions), corneal anaesthesia (trigeminal) → exposure keratitis and ulcer
- Madarosis, iridocyclitis (acute in ENL, chronic in LL), scleritis, iris pearls, cataract, secondary glaucoma
- Vision loss → grade 2 disability; needs eye exercises, goggles, tarsorrhaphy if severe

**Q32. Systemic involvement in lepromatous leprosy?**
- Nose: stuffiness, epistaxis, septal perforation, saddle nose
- Testes: atrophy → infertility, gynaecomastia
- Bones: absorption of phalanges, maxilla (facies leprosa); osteoporosis
- Kidney: amyloidosis, glomerulonephritis (ENL); liver, lymph nodes, larynx (hoarseness)

**Q33. What is the role of reconstructive surgery? (short note)**
- Only after disease and reactions are inactive for ≥6 months
- Tendon transfers: claw hand — Brand's procedures/lasso; foot drop — tibialis posterior transfer; ape thumb — opponensplasty
- Eyebrow reconstruction (hair grafts), nasal reconstruction, tarsorrhaphy for lagophthalmos; nerve decompression for abscess/neuritis

**Q34. Prevention of disability and care of anaesthetic hands/feet?**
- Soak, scrape (oil), oil daily for dry skin; inspect for cracks and wounds; protective footwear (MCR micro-cellular rubber chappals), avoid hot objects
- Self-care groups; splints and physiotherapy for weak muscles; early steroid for neuritis
- Ulcer: rest, cleaning, dressing, offloading; avoid walking on ulcerated foot

**Q35. Differential diagnosis of hypopigmented patches (common short note).**
- Pityriasis alba, pityriasis versicolor, nevus depigmentosus/anaemicus, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, vitiligo (depigmented), indeterminate leprosy, hypopigmented mycosis fungoides, idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, progressive macular hypomelanosis, sarcoidosis, PKDL (post-kala-azar)
- Sensation, nerve thickening and smear help separate leprosy

**Q36. Differential diagnosis of nodular lesions as in LL.**
- PKDL (no sensory loss, LD bodies), neurofibromatosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, sarcoidosis, lymphoma/leukaemia cutis, xanthomas, secondary syphilis, multiple histiocytomas, Kaposi sarcoma, onchocerciasis

**Q37. Leprosy elimination status in India?**
- Elimination as a public health problem (prevalence <1/10,000) achieved nationally in December 2005; some districts still above
- National Strategic Plan aims at interruption of transmission / zero new cases by 2027 (SDG target 2030)
- Indicators: new case detection rate, grade 2 disability per million, child proportion

## Quick spotter facts
- Cardinal signs — anaesthetic patch, thick nerve, positive smear (any one)
- Lucio phenomenon — diffuse LL + necrotic angular ulcers without fever
- Histoid — shiny nodules, spindle cells, very high BI

## Note
Doses and duration follow the NLEP revised regimen (effective 1 April 2025) as already used in Exam drugs; check with the department for local practice.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (leprosy chapters); NLEP revised MDT guidance effective 1 April 2025; WHO disability grading. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) — viva
posts.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Define IgA vasculitis (HSP).**
- Small-vessel vasculitis with IgA1-dominant immune deposits affecting skin, joints, gut and kidneys; commonest systemic vasculitis of childhood (3–15 y, peak 4–6), often after upper respiratory infection (group A streptococcus); adults have more renal disease

**Q2. Classify vasculitis (PYQ) — Chapel Hill 2012.**
- Large vessel: Takayasu arteritis, giant cell arteritis
- Medium vessel: polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease
- Small vessel — ANCA-associated: microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), eosinophilic GPA (Churg–Strauss); immune-complex: anti-GBM disease, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, IgA vasculitis (HSP), hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis (anti-C1q)
- Variable vessel: Behçet's, Cogan's syndrome
- Single-organ: cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis
- Vasculitis associated with systemic disease (lupus, RA, sarcoid) and with probable aetiology (hepatitis B PAN, hepatitis C cryoglobulinaemia, drug-associated, cancer-associated)

**Q3. Give the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES classification criteria.**
- Mandatory: purpura or petechiae with lower-limb predominance (non-thrombocytopenic)
- Plus ≥1 of: diffuse abdominal pain; histopathology showing leukocytoclastic vasculitis or proliferative glomerulonephritis with predominant IgA deposits; arthritis or arthralgia; renal involvement (proteinuria >0.3 g/24 h or haematuria/red cell casts)

**Q4. Describe the clinical features.**
- Skin (100%): palpable purpura — symmetrical on buttocks, extensor lower limbs, ankles (dependent areas); starts as urticarial/erythematous papules; may become bullous, haemorrhagic, necrotic; oedema of scalp, face, hands, scrotum in young children
- Joints (75%): transient arthralgia/arthritis of knees and ankles, non-deforming
- GI (50–75%): colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, GI bleed (melaena), intussusception (ileo-ileal), bowel perforation
- Renal (20–50%): microscopic haematuria, proteinuria, nephritic/nephrotic syndrome — determines long-term prognosis (ESRD in 1–2% children, more in adults)
- Others: orchitis (mimics torsion), CNS vasculitis, pulmonary haemorrhage (rare)

**Q5. Classify purpura (PYQ).**
- Non-palpable (haemorrhage without vessel inflammation): thrombocytopenic (ITP, TTP, marrow failure, DIC), platelet dysfunction, coagulation defects, vascular fragility (senile/actinic purpura, steroid purpura, scurvy — perifollicular haemorrhage with corkscrew hairs, Ehlers–Danlos, amyloidosis — pinch purpura), raised intravascular pressure (cough, vomiting), pigmented purpuric dermatoses
- Palpable (inflammatory — vasculitis): leukocytoclastic vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia, urticarial vasculitis
- Retiform/net-like (occlusion of vessels): APS, cryoglobulinaemia type I, calciphylaxis, purpura fulminans, warfarin/heparin necrosis, septic emboli, cholesterol emboli, levamisole-adulterated cocaine

**Q6. Discuss the evaluation of vasculitis (PYQ).**
- Confirm vasculitis: skin biopsy from a fresh (<24–48 h) lesion for histology + DIF (IgA in vessel walls in HSP — best in lesions <48 h old)
- Assess extent: urine dipstick and microscopy (haematuria, casts), urine protein:creatinine ratio, serum creatinine, BP; stool occult blood, abdominal ultrasound (intussusception) if pain; chest X-ray; nerve conduction if neuropathy
- Find cause: CBC, ESR/CRP, ASO, throat swab, hepatitis B/C, HIV, ANA, anti-dsDNA, RF, C3/C4, cryoglobulins, ANCA (MPO, PR3), serum IgA (raised in 50%), serum protein electrophoresis, drug history, malignancy screen in adults

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of superficial dermal post-capillary venules: fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls, neutrophils with nuclear dust (leukocytoclasia), extravasated RBCs, endothelial swelling
- DIF: granular IgA (± C3) deposits in vessel walls — key differentiating feature
- Kidney: mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis with mesangial IgA (same as IgA nephropathy)

**Q8. Differential diagnosis.**
- Other small-vessel vasculitis (hypersensitivity/drug, cryoglobulinaemia, urticarial vasculitis, ANCA), acute haemorrhagic oedema of infancy (large rosette/cockade purpura on face and limbs of well infant <2 y, self-limiting), ITP (non-palpable), meningococcaemia (sick child, retiform purpura — emergency), child abuse, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, septic emboli

**Q9. Management.**
- Mostly self-limiting (4–6 weeks): rest, leg elevation, compression; NSAIDs/paracetamol for arthralgia (avoid NSAIDs if renal involvement)
- Severe abdominal pain, scrotal involvement, extensive necrotic skin: systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day) — relieve GI/joint symptoms; do not prevent nephritis
- Renal disease (proteinuria, nephrotic, crescentic GN): steroids (pulse methylprednisolone) + azathioprine/mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide; ACE inhibitors for proteinuria; nephrology follow-up
- Skin-only chronic: dapsone, colchicine
- Urine monitoring (dipstick and BP) weekly for the first month, then monthly up to 6–12 months — nephritis can appear late

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Excellent in most children; recurrences in ~1/3 within months; long-term outcome depends on renal involvement — worse in adults, nephrotic range proteinuria, crescents on biopsy

**Q11. Explain the pathogenesis (4-hit hypothesis).**
- Hit 1: increased galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) in serum (genetic); hit 2: IgG/IgA autoantibodies against Gd-IgA1; hit 3: immune complexes form; hit 4: deposition in small vessels/ mesangium → complement (alternative/ lectin pathway) activation and neutrophil-mediated inflammation; triggers — infections (streptococcal, viral), vaccines, drugs

**Q12. Adult IgA vasculitis — how different?**
- Less common but more severe renal involvement (nephritis 50–80%, CKD), more necrotic/ bullous skin lesions, higher association with malignancy (solid tumours — lung, prostate) and IBD, infections (HCV, HIV); requires malignancy screening if no obvious trigger

**Q13. What is hypersensitivity (cutaneous small-vessel) vasculitis?**
- Single-organ cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis — palpable purpura on legs 7–10 days after drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, diuretics, allopurinol) or infections; DIF IgM/C3 rather than IgA; self-limiting after removing trigger; colchicine/ dapsone/ steroids if persistent

**Q14. What are the ANCA-associated vasculitides and their skin signs?**
- GPA (PR3-ANCA): palpable purpura, nodules, ulcers, oral 'strawberry' gingivitis, saddle nose, sinusitis, lung nodules, glomerulonephritis
- MPA (MPO-ANCA): purpura, livedo, renal–pulmonary syndrome
- EGPA (MPO-ANCA ± ): asthma, eosinophilia, purpura, nodules on scalp/ extensors, neuropathy
- Treat with steroids + rituximab/ cyclophosphamide, mepolizumab (EGPA), avacopan

**Q15. Cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis — features.**
- Type I (monoclonal — myeloma/ Waldenström): hyperviscosity, retiform purpura, necrosis, acral ulcers on cold exposure
- Types II/III (mixed — HCV commonest): palpable purpura, arthralgia, weakness (Meltzer triad), neuropathy, glomerulonephritis; low C4, RF positive; treat HCV (DAAs), rituximab

## Quick spotter facts
- Palpable purpura on buttocks/legs + abdominal pain + arthritis + haematuria in a child — IgA vasculitis
- DIF: IgA in vessel walls
- Monitor urine for 6–12 months

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous vasculitis); 2012 Chapel Hill nomenclature; EULAR/PRINTO/PRES 2010 criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Herpes simplex — viva
posts.summary: Viral infections · 17 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Herpes simplex** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What is the causative agent and classification of HSV?**
- Herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2 — human herpesvirus 1 and 2; alpha-herpesviruses (enveloped, double-stranded DNA)
- HSV-1 mainly orolabial (now also many genital first episodes); HSV-2 mainly genital and neonatal; both stay latent in sensory ganglia (trigeminal for HSV-1, sacral for HSV-2)

**Q2. Name the 8 human herpesviruses and their diseases (very common question).**
- HHV-1 (HSV-1): orolabial herpes, keratitis, encephalitis; HHV-2 (HSV-2): genital and neonatal herpes
- HHV-3 (VZV): varicella, zoster
- HHV-4 (EBV): infectious mononucleosis, oral hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Gianotti–Crosti, hydroa vacciniforme-like lymphoma
- HHV-5 (CMV): perianal ulcers in HIV, congenital infection ('blueberry muffin'), mononucleosis
- HHV-6 and 7: roseola infantum (exanthem subitum); HHV-6 reactivation in DRESS; HHV-7 linked to pityriasis rosea
- HHV-8: Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease

**Q3. Describe the pathogenesis and latency.**
- Entry through mucosa/abraded skin → replication in epidermis → retrograde axonal transport to sensory ganglion → latent (latency-associated transcripts) → reactivation with triggers travels back to skin
- Triggers: fever, UV light, menstruation, stress, trauma, immunosuppression
- Asymptomatic shedding is the main source of transmission

**Q4. Describe primary herpetic gingivostomatitis.**
- Usually HSV-1 in children 1–5 years; fever, malaise, painful vesicles that erode on gums, tongue, palate, lips; swollen bleeding gums; drooling; tender cervical nodes
- Resolves in ~2 weeks; oral acyclovir within 72–96 h shortens it

**Q5. Describe recurrent herpes labialis.**
- Prodrome of tingling/burning for hours → grouped vesicles on an erythematous base at vermilion border → pustules, crusts; heals in 7–10 days without scar
- Same site each time

**Q6. Clinical features of genital herpes.**
- First episode primary: multiple painful bilateral vesicles/erosions with fever, inguinal lymphadenopathy, dysuria; lasts 2–3 weeks; may cause aseptic meningitis, urinary retention (sacral radiculopathy)
- Recurrent: fewer, unilateral, shorter (5–10 days), less painful; HSV-2 recurs more than HSV-1
- Atypical: fissures, erythema only, in HIV — chronic deep ulcers

**Q7. What is the Tzanck smear and what does it show?**
- Scraping from the base of a fresh vesicle stained with Giemsa
- Multinucleated giant cells with nuclear moulding, margination of chromatin, and intranuclear (Cowdry A) inclusions; also acantholytic ballooned cells
- Cannot distinguish HSV from VZV; low sensitivity — PCR is now the test of choice

**Q8. Investigations for herpes?**
- PCR of vesicle fluid/swab — most sensitive and specific; typing HSV-1 vs 2
- Viral culture (declining use), direct immunofluorescence
- Type-specific serology (glycoprotein G) to detect past infection or counsel discordant couples — not for diagnosis of an active ulcer
- Screen for other STIs incl. HIV and syphilis in genital herpes

**Q9. Give the differential diagnosis of genital ulcer.**
- Painful: herpes (multiple grouped small), chancroid (ragged undermined purulent ulcer, painful suppurative bubo), traumatic, Behçet's, fixed drug eruption (recurrent same site), aphthae
- Painless: primary syphilis (indurated clean ulcer, rubbery nodes), donovanosis (beefy red, bleeds, pseudobubo), LGV (transient ulcer, then bubo with groove sign)

**Q10. Treatment of first episode genital herpes.**
- Acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 7–10 days (or 200 mg five times daily); valacyclovir 1 g twice daily 7–10 days; famciclovir 250 mg thrice daily
- Saline baths, analgesics, lidocaine gel; abstain from sex during lesions

**Q11. Treatment of recurrences and suppressive therapy.**
- Episodic: start within 24 h of prodrome — acyclovir 800 mg three times daily for 2 days, or 800 mg twice daily 5 days; valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily 3 days or 1 g daily 5 days; famciclovir 1 g twice daily for 1 day
- Suppressive (≥6 recurrences/year, severe, psychological distress, discordant partner): acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or valacyclovir 500 mg–1 g once daily; review yearly

**Q12. What is the mechanism of acyclovir? (short note)**
- Guanosine analogue phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase (so active only in infected cells) then by cellular kinases to the triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates DNA chain
- Poor oral bioavailability (~15–20%); valacyclovir prodrug gives 3–5 times higher levels
- Side effects: nausea, headache; IV — crystalline nephropathy (hydrate well), neurotoxicity in renal failure
- Resistance (thymidine kinase mutation) in immunocompromised — use foscarnet or cidofovir

**Q13. What is eczema herpeticum (Kaposi's varicelliform eruption)?**
- Widespread HSV infection on skin with an existing dermatosis (atopic dermatitis commonest, Darier's disease, pemphigus, burns, Hailey–Hailey, CTCL)
- Clusters of monomorphic punched-out haemorrhagic erosions and vesicles, fever, lymphadenopathy
- Dermatological emergency — oral/IV acyclovir; check eye involvement; risk of viraemia

**Q14. What is herpetic whitlow?**
- HSV infection of the finger — children with gingivostomatitis (thumb-sucking) and health workers; painful deep vesicles on fingertip
- Do not incise (confused with bacterial paronychia/felon)

**Q15. Name other clinical patterns of HSV infection.**
- Herpes gladiatorum (wrestlers), herpetic keratitis/keratoconjunctivitis, herpetic sycosis (beard), lumbosacral herpes
- Neonatal herpes (skin-eye-mouth, CNS, disseminated) — mother with primary genital herpes near delivery; caesarean if lesions at labour
- HSV-associated erythema multiforme (commonest cause of recurrent EM) — suppressive acyclovir prevents it
- HSV encephalitis (temporal lobe); chronic ulcerative herpes in HIV (CD4 <100) — an AIDS-defining illness if >1 month

**Q16. How do you manage herpes in pregnancy?**
- Primary infection in third trimester → highest neonatal risk: acyclovir, and caesarean section
