- Recurrent herpes: suppressive acyclovir from 36 weeks; caesarean only if lesions/prodrome at labour
- Acyclovir is safe in pregnancy

**Q17. Counselling points for genital herpes?**
- Lifelong infection but recurrences become fewer with time
- Transmission can occur without lesions; condoms and suppressive therapy reduce (not eliminate) risk; inform partners
- Genital herpes increases risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV

## Quick spotter facts
- Grouped vesicles on red base, same site each time — recurrent HSV
- Tzanck: multinucleated giant cells with nuclear moulding (HSV/VZV, not distinguishable)
- Punched-out erosions on atopic skin with fever — eczema herpeticum

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections); CDC STI treatment guidelines 2021 for antiviral doses. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Herpes zoster — viva
posts.summary: Viral infections · 18 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Herpes zoster** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. Define herpes zoster. What is its pathogenesis?**
- Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus from a sensory (dorsal root or cranial nerve) ganglion, producing painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption
- Fall in VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity with age (>50 y), HIV, malignancy (lymphoma), chemotherapy, steroids, JAK inhibitors, transplant, stress, trauma
- Virus travels down the sensory nerve to skin; ganglionitis causes pain

**Q2. Which dermatomes are commonly affected?**
- Thoracic (T3–L2) commonest (~50%), then trigeminal (ophthalmic division), cervical, lumbosacral
- Usually one dermatome; may involve adjacent ones; crosses midline only slightly

**Q3. Describe the clinical course.**
- Prodrome 1–5 days: burning, itching, pain (may mimic angina, cholecystitis, renal colic), fever, malaise
- Erythematous papules → grouped vesicles in a band along the dermatome → pustules → crusts by 7–10 days; heals in 2–4 weeks
- Zoster sine herpete: pain without rash
- Few vesicles (<20) outside the dermatome are allowed; more suggests dissemination

**Q4. What is disseminated zoster?**
- More than 20 vesicles outside the primary and adjacent dermatomes, or ≥3 dermatomes involved, or visceral involvement — implies immunosuppression (HIV, malignancy); needs IV acyclovir

**Q5. What is herpes zoster ophthalmicus and Hutchinson's sign?**
- Zoster of the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (V1)
- Hutchinson's sign: vesicles on the tip/side of nose (external nasal branch of nasociliary nerve) — high risk of eye involvement (keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma, retinitis, optic neuritis)
- Needs ophthalmology referral and systemic antivirals

**Q6. What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome?**
- Zoster of geniculate ganglion of facial nerve — ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy, ear pain, vesicles on the ear (concha, external canal), taste loss in anterior 2/3 of tongue, tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss
- Worse recovery than Bell's palsy — antivirals + prednisolone early

**Q7. Name other complications.**
- Post-herpetic neuralgia (commonest)
- Secondary bacterial infection, scarring, pigmentation, Koebner (granulomatous/ lichenoid lesions at healed sites — Wolf's isotopic response)
- Motor palsy (e.g. foot drop, bladder dysfunction in sacral zoster, abdominal wall pseudohernia)
- Meningoencephalitis, myelitis, Guillain–Barré, stroke (VZV vasculopathy — granulomatous arteritis), pneumonitis, hepatitis

**Q8. Define post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) and its risk factors. (short note)**
- Pain persisting ≥90 days (3 months) after rash onset (some use 1 month)
- Risk: older age (>50), severe prodromal pain, severe acute pain, extensive rash, ophthalmic involvement, immunosuppression, diabetes, delayed antiviral therapy
- Pain types: burning, lancinating, allodynia (pain to light touch — very characteristic)

**Q9. Management of PHN.**
- First line: pregabalin (75–300 mg twice daily) or gabapentin (titrate to 1800–3600 mg/day); tricyclics — amitriptyline/nortriptyline 10–75 mg at night
- Topical: lidocaine 5% patch, capsaicin 0.075% cream or 8% patch
- Second line: tramadol, opioids; duloxetine; nerve blocks; TENS
- Prevention: early antiviral, adequate acute pain control, vaccination

**Q10. How do you treat acute zoster?**
- Antivirals ideally within 72 h of rash onset (later if new vesicles still forming, ophthalmic, immunosuppressed): acyclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7 days; valacyclovir 1 g thrice daily × 7 days; famciclovir 500 mg thrice daily × 7 days
- IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly for disseminated/immunocompromised/CNS involvement
- Adjust dose for renal function
- Analgesics (paracetamol/NSAIDs, pregabalin for severe acute pain), calamine, wet compresses, antibiotics for secondary infection
- Systemic steroids do not prevent PHN — only for Ramsay Hunt/ocular inflammation under supervision

**Q11. What is the Tzanck smear and PCR role?**
- Tzanck — multinucleated giant cells; cannot differentiate HSV vs VZV
- PCR of vesicle fluid is the test of choice for atypical or zoster sine herpete (PCR on CSF/blood)

**Q12. Differentiate herpes zoster from zosteriform herpes simplex.**
- HSV: recurrent at the same site, smaller grouped vesicles, less pain, no PHN, younger patients
- Zoster: usually once (recurrence in ~5%), dermatomal band, severe pain, older age, PHN risk
- PCR settles it

**Q13. Differential diagnosis of herpes zoster.**
- Zosteriform HSV, contact dermatitis (linear plant contact), bullous impetigo, insect bites, fixed drug eruption, linear lichen planus/porokeratosis (chronic, no pain)
- Prodrome mimics: myocardial infarction, renal colic, appendicitis, migraine

**Q14. What are zosteriform lesions? (asked in PYQ)**
- Lesions arranged in a band along a dermatome but not due to VZV — zosteriform herpes simplex, zosteriform metastases (breast cancer), zosteriform lichen planus, segmental vitiligo, zosteriform naevi, segmental neurofibromatosis, zosteriform leiomyomas
- Contrast with blaschkoid (follow Blaschko's lines — mosaic genetic disorders)

**Q15. Why should you test for HIV in zoster?**
- Zoster in a young adult (<50 y), multi-dermatomal, recurrent, disseminated, necrotic/chronic verrucous lesions may be the first sign of HIV — offer HIV test

**Q16. Zoster vaccines?**
- Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix — gE glycoprotein + AS01B adjuvant): 2 doses IM 2–6 months apart; ≥50 years and ≥18 years if immunocompromised; ~90% efficacy; non-live, safe in immunocompromised (available in India since 2023)
- Live attenuated zoster vaccine (Zostavax) — discontinued in many countries; contraindicated in immunosuppression
- Reduces zoster and PHN

**Q17. Is zoster contagious?**
- Yes — vesicle fluid can give chickenpox (not zoster) to non-immune people; cover lesions; airborne precautions for disseminated zoster or immunocompromised patients

**Q18. Zoster in pregnancy?**
- Fetal risk is minimal (maternal antibodies present); treat mother with acyclovir if needed

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral dermatomal grouped vesicles with pain — zoster
- Hutchinson's sign — nasal tip vesicles → eye involvement
- PHN = pain ≥90 days; allodynia

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections — VZV). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Hidradenitis suppurativa — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hidradenitis suppurativa** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. Define hidradenitis suppurativa (HS).**
- Chronic, recurrent, inflammatory, debilitating follicular occlusive disease of intertriginous apocrine gland-bearing areas, presenting with painful deep nodules, abscesses, draining tunnels (sinus tracts) and scarring, usually after puberty (acne inversa)
- Diagnosis: typical lesions (nodules, tunnels, scars) + typical sites (axillae, groin, inframammary, perineal, buttocks) + chronicity/recurrence (≥2 episodes in 6 months)

**Q2. Pathogenesis.**
- Primary event is follicular occlusion (infundibular hyperkeratosis) → dilation and rupture of follicle → spillage of keratin/bacteria → intense innate inflammation (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) → abscesses and epithelialised tunnels
- Risk factors: obesity, smoking (strong), mechanical friction, genetic (γ-secretase genes — NCSTN, PSENEN, PSEN1; ~30–40% family history), hormones (premenstrual flares), metabolic syndrome
- Follicular occlusion tetrad: HS, acne conglobata, dissecting cellulitis of scalp, pilonidal sinus

**Q3. Severity staging.**
- Hurley staging: I — single/multiple abscesses without tunnels or scarring; II — recurrent abscesses with tunnels and scarring, widely separated; III — diffuse/near-diffuse involvement with interconnected tunnels and abscesses across an entire area
- Others: IHS4 (nodules ×1 + abscesses ×2 + draining tunnels ×4), Sartorius score, HiSCR (≥50% reduction in abscess + nodule count without increase in abscesses/draining tunnels) — trial outcome

**Q4. Associated conditions.**
- Metabolic syndrome, diabetes, obesity, PCOS, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's), spondyloarthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum (PASH/PAPASH syndromes), depression, anxiety, Down syndrome, Dowling–Degos disease (PSENEN), SCC in chronic gluteal/perineal HS (men, smokers)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Furuncles/carbuncles (acute, not recurrent at same flexural sites, no tunnels), epidermoid/pilonidal cysts, Crohn's disease (perianal fistulae), lymphogranuloma venereum, scrofuloderma, actinomycosis, granuloma inguinale, Bartholin abscess, cutaneous TB, anal fistula

**Q6. Discuss treatment including biologics (PYQ).**
- General: weight loss, smoking cessation, loose clothing, antiseptic washes (chlorhexidine, BPO), pain control, psychological support, warm compresses, dressings
- Hurley I/mild: topical clindamycin 1% twice daily, resorcinol 15% peel, intralesional triamcinolone 10 mg/ml for acute nodules; oral tetracyclines (doxycycline 100 mg BD for 12 weeks)
- Moderate: clindamycin 300 mg BD + rifampicin 300 mg BD for 10–12 weeks; metformin, zinc gluconate, anti-androgens (spironolactone, OCP) in women; acitretin (men), dapsone
- Moderate–severe: biologics — adalimumab (160 mg week 0, 80 mg week 2, then 40 mg weekly or 80 mg alternate weeks — first approved), secukinumab (IL-17A), bimekizumab (IL-17A/F) — approved for HS; infliximab, ustekinumab, anakinra (off-label); JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib) in trials
- Surgery: incision and drainage (acute relief only), deroofing of tunnels (preferred for Hurley II), STEEP, wide excision with healing by secondary intention or flaps/grafts (Hurley III), CO2 laser excision; laser hair removal (Nd:YAG) reduces recurrences

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Follicular plugging and dilatation, ruptured follicles with neutrophilic abscesses, granulomas, epithelialised sinus tracts, fibrosis; apocrine involvement is secondary

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic relapsing; marked impact on quality of life (DLQI often very high); early recognition (average diagnostic delay 7–10 years) and early systemic/biologic therapy prevent tunnels and scarring

**Q9. Diagnostic criteria (Dessau).**
- (1) Typical lesions — deep painful nodules, abscesses, draining tunnels (sinus tracts), bridged scars, double-ended comedones; (2) typical sites — axillae, groin, inframammary, perineum, buttocks; (3) chronicity and recurrence (≥2 recurrences in 6 months) — all three needed

**Q10. Severity scores other than Hurley.**
- Refined Hurley, IHS4 (International HS Severity Score = nodules + 2×abscesses + 4×draining tunnels; ≤3 mild, 4–10 moderate, ≥11 severe), HiSCR (≥50% reduction in abscess + inflammatory nodule count without increase in abscesses/draining tunnels — trial outcome), DLQI, pain NRS

**Q11. Medical treatment ladder.**
- General: weight loss, stop smoking, loose clothing, antiseptic washes, pain control, psychological support
- Mild: topical clindamycin 1%, resorcinol 15% peel, intralesional triamcinolone for acute nodules
- Moderate: doxycycline/tetracyclines 12 weeks; clindamycin + rifampicin (300 mg each twice daily) for 10–12 weeks; metformin (insulin resistance), anti-androgens in women (spironolactone, OCP), zinc gluconate; acitretin (men), dapsone
- Moderate–severe: biologics — adalimumab (160 mg week 0, 80 mg week 2, then 40 mg weekly), secukinumab (IL-17A), bimekizumab (IL-17A/F); infliximab off-label; JAK inhibitors under trial

**Q12. Surgical options.**
- Incision and drainage only for painful abscess relief (high recurrence); deroofing of tunnels (preferred office procedure), local excision, wide excision with secondary intention healing or flaps/ grafts, CO2 laser excision/marsupialisation, laser hair removal (Nd:YAG) to prevent new lesions

**Q13. Complications of long-standing HS.**
- Scarring and contractures, lymphoedema (genital), fistulae (urethral, anal), anaemia of chronic disease, secondary amyloidosis (AA — nephrotic syndrome), SCC in chronic gluteal/perineal disease (aggressive, men, smokers), depression, suicide risk, sexual dysfunction

**Q14. Explain the pathogenesis — follicular occlusion concept.**
- Primary event is infundibular hyperkeratosis and follicular occlusion → dilatation and rupture → release of keratin and bacteria into dermis → intense innate inflammation (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) → abscesses, sinus tracts (epithelialised tunnels), scarring
- Contributors: genetics (γ-secretase genes NCSTN, PSENEN, PSEN1 in familial), obesity, smoking (nicotine stimulates follicular plugging), mechanical friction, hormones (androgens, premenstrual flares), dysbiosis — apocrine glands are secondarily involved

**Q15. Describe Hurley staging.**
- Stage I: single or multiple abscesses without sinus tracts or scarring
- Stage II: recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts and scarring, single or multiple widely separated lesions
- Stage III: diffuse or near-diffuse involvement or multiple interconnected tracts and abscesses across an entire area

**Q16. What is the follicular occlusion tetrad?**
- Hidradenitis suppurativa, acne conglobata, dissecting cellulitis of the scalp (perifolliculitis capitis abscedens et suffodiens), pilonidal sinus — share follicular occlusion pathogenesis

**Q17. What syndromes include HS?**
- PASH (pyoderma gangrenosum, acne, suppurative hidradenitis), PAPASH (with pyogenic arthritis), PsAPASH (psoriatic arthritis), SAPHO; associations — Crohn's disease, spondyloarthritis, Down syndrome, Dowling–Degos disease (PSENEN), metabolic syndrome, PCOS

**Q18. Ultrasound in HS.**
- High-frequency ultrasound detects subclinical lesions, measures abscesses and tunnels (fluid collections, widened follicles, dermal pseudocysts), guides surgery and staging (SOS-HS score); colour Doppler shows activity

**Q19. Why is HS often misdiagnosed and delayed?**
- Mistaken for recurrent boils/ abscesses and treated with repeated short antibiotics and incision–drainage; average diagnostic delay 7–10 years; clue — recurrence at the same flexural sites, double comedones, sterile cultures, tunnels

**Q20. What is the role of antibiotics and their limitations?**
- Anti-inflammatory and anti-biofilm effects: tetracyclines (12 weeks) for mild–moderate, clindamycin–rifampicin combination (10–12 weeks) for moderate–severe, ertapenem IV (6 weeks) rescue for severe; high relapse after stopping; resistance concerns

**Q21. Adalimumab and other biologics — details.**
- Adalimumab: 160 mg week 0, 80 mg week 2, then 40 mg weekly (or 80 mg every other week) from week 4 — HiSCR ~50–60%; evaluate at 12 weeks
- Secukinumab 300 mg every 2–4 weeks; bimekizumab (IL-17A/F) — high responses; infliximab off-label; screen TB/ HBV; combine with surgery for tunnels (biologics don't close fibrotic tracts)

**Q22. What is deroofing and how is it done?**
- Under local anaesthesia, a probe is passed into the sinus tract, the roof is excised with scissors/ electrosurgery, the base (gelatinous granulation) curetted, and the wound left to heal by secondary intention — low recurrence, tissue-sparing, office procedure for Hurley II tunnels

**Q23. Pain management and quality of life in HS.**
- HS has the worst DLQI impact among skin diseases; pain from nodules/ abscesses — NSAIDs, paracetamol, intralesional steroids (triamcinolone 10 mg/ml for acute nodules — quick relief), gabapentin/ pregabalin for neuropathic pain, avoid opioids long term; psychological support, depression/ suicide screening, sexual health

**Q24. Lifestyle advice in HS.**
- Weight loss (bariatric surgery for morbid obesity improves HS), stop smoking, loose clothing, avoid shaving/ friction, antiseptic washes (chlorhexidine, benzoyl peroxide), zinc supplements, dairy/ brewer's yeast avoidance reported to help some

**Q25. Histopathology in more detail.**
- Follicular occlusion with infundibular hyperkeratosis, ruptured follicles with mixed inflammation (neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, foreign-body giant cells), sinus tracts lined by squamous epithelium, dermal fibrosis; apocrine gland involvement secondary

**Q26. HS in women — hormonal treatments.**
- Premenstrual flares, PCOS association; combined OCPs with anti-androgenic progestins, spironolactone 100–150 mg/day, finasteride 5 mg/day (post-menopausal or with contraception), metformin (insulin resistance) — useful adjuncts

**Q27. Differential diagnosis (expanded).**
- Furunculosis/ carbuncles, infected epidermoid/ pilonidal cysts, Bartholin's abscess, Crohn's disease (perianal/ genital fistulae, metastatic Crohn's), scrofuloderma, actinomycosis, LGV, donovanosis, granuloma inguinale, cutaneous TB, deep fungal infection, Fox–Fordyce disease, SCC in chronic HS

**Q28. Disease activity scoring — HS-PGA and Sartorius.**
- Hidradenitis Suppurativa Physician Global Assessment (6 levels: clear to very severe), Modified Sartorius score (counts nodules, fistulas, distance between lesions, Hurley stage per region)

**Q29. Surgery after biologics — timing.**
- Combine biologics to quieten inflammation then excise/ deroof residual tunnels and scars; continue biologic perioperatively (no increase in infection in studies) to reduce recurrence

**Q30. Paediatric HS — features.**
- Onset before puberty suggests premature adrenarche, obesity, endocrine disorders (precocious puberty, CAH); treat with topical clindamycin, antiseptics, weight loss, adalimumab approved ≥12 y; avoid tetracyclines <8 y

## Quick spotter facts
- Recurrent painful nodules + double comedones + tunnels in axillae/groin — HS
- Hurley staging; adalimumab, secukinumab, bimekizumab
- Deroofing for tunnels

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hidradenitis suppurativa); North American/European HS guidelines. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Ichthyosis — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 29 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Ichthyosis** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. Describe the process of keratinisation (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes divide → spinous cells (keratins K1/K10 replace K5/K14, desmosomes) → granular layer (keratohyaline granules with profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies with lipids and enzymes) → stratum corneum: cornified cell envelope (crosslinked by transglutaminase-1) with lipid envelope, extracellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids — 'bricks and mortar'), desquamation by proteases (kallikreins KLK5/7, inhibited by LEKTI) cleaving corneodesmosomes
- Ichthyoses result from defects at any of these steps — increased production (proliferation hyperkeratosis) or decreased shedding (retention hyperkeratosis)

**Q2. Classify ichthyoses (PYQ).**
- Non-syndromic inherited: common — ichthyosis vulgaris (FLG, AD-semidominant), recessive X-linked ichthyosis (STS); autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) — harlequin ichthyosis (ABCA12), lamellar ichthyosis (TGM1), congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma (ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4); keratinopathic — epidermolytic ichthyosis (K1/K10), superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis (K2), ichthyosis with confetti; others — loricrin keratoderma, erythrokeratodermia variabilis, peeling skin syndrome
- Syndromic: Netherton (SPINK5), Sjögren–Larsson (ALDH3A2 — spasticity, intellectual disability, glistening retinal dots), Refsum (phytanic acid), Conradi–Hünermann–Happle (CDPX2 — Blaschkoid, chondrodysplasia punctata), KID syndrome (keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness, GJB2), CHILD (NSDHL — unilateral), trichothiodystrophy (IBIDS), neutral lipid storage disease (Chanarin–Dorfman — lipid vacuoles in leucocytes), Rud syndrome, multiple sulphatase deficiency, ARC, MEDNIK
- Acquired ichthyosis: lymphoma (Hodgkin's), leprosy (LL), HIV, sarcoidosis, malnutrition, hypothyroidism, CKD, drugs (clofazimine, statins, nicotinic acid, kava)

**Q3. Ichthyosis vulgaris — features.**
- Commonest (1:250); onset after 2–3 months of age; fine white/grey scales on extensors (especially shins), flexures spared; palmar hyperlinearity, keratosis pilaris; strongly associated with atopic dermatitis; improves in summer and with age
- Histology: reduced/absent granular layer, compact orthokeratosis

**Q4. Discuss X-linked ichthyosis (PYQ).**
- Recessive X-linked steroid sulphatase (STS) deficiency (deletion Xp22.3) — males; cholesterol sulphate accumulates and impairs desquamation
- Onset at birth/first weeks; large dark-brown polygonal adherent scales on trunk, extensors and flexures, sides of neck ('dirty neck'); palms, soles and face (central) spared; does not improve much with age
- Associations: comma-shaped corneal opacities (asymptomatic, also in carrier mothers), cryptorchidism (testicular cancer risk), ADHD/autism; contiguous gene deletion — Kallmann syndrome (anosmia), chondrodysplasia punctata
- Obstetric: low maternal oestriol (placental sulphatase deficiency) → failure of labour onset/prolonged labour
- Diagnosis: increased serum cholesterol sulphate, rapid lipoprotein electrophoresis (fast-moving LDL), STS enzyme assay, FISH for deletion

**Q5. Describe lamellar ichthyosis and collodion baby.**
- Collodion baby: newborn encased in a shiny, tight, cellophane-like membrane with ectropion, eclabium, flattened ears; sheds in 2–4 weeks; underlying ARCI (lamellar/CIE) most commonly, or self-healing collodion baby (~10%)
- Risks: hypothermia, dehydration/hypernatraemia, infection, poor feeding — nurse in humidified incubator, emollients (white soft paraffin), avoid keratolytics, monitor electrolytes
- Lamellar ichthyosis (TGM1): large plate-like dark scales over whole body including flexures, ectropion, eclabium, scarring alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, heat intolerance (hypohidrosis)

**Q6. What is harlequin ichthyosis?**
- Most severe ARCI (ABCA12 — defective lipid transport into lamellar bodies): thick armour-like plates separated by deep red fissures, severe ectropion, eclabium, rudimentary ears, restricted limb movement; high neonatal mortality — systemic retinoids (acitretin) improve survival

**Q7. Write a short note on Comèl–Netherton syndrome (PYQ).**
- Autosomal recessive SPINK5 mutation (LEKTI deficiency) → uncontrolled kallikrein activity → excess desquamation and Th2 inflammation
- Triad: congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma or ichthyosis linearis circumflexa (migratory polycyclic plaques with double-edged scale), trichorrhexis invaginata ('bamboo hair' — eyebrows best), atopic diathesis (high IgE, food allergy, asthma)
- Complications: hypernatraemic dehydration, failure to thrive, sepsis, high systemic absorption of topical drugs (tacrolimus); treatment — emollients, topical tacrolimus cautiously, IVIG, dupilumab/secukinumab (reports)

**Q8. Write short notes on Refsum's disease (PYQ).**
- Autosomal recessive phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (PHYH) or PEX7 deficiency → phytanic acid accumulation (dietary — dairy, ruminant fat, fish)
- Ichthyosis-like scaling (adult onset, mild), retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness — earliest), peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia, deafness, anosmia, cardiac arrhythmias, short metatarsals
- Lipid vacuoles in basal keratinocytes on histology; high plasma phytanic acid; treatment — phytanic-acid restricted diet, plasmapheresis

**Q9. Describe Rud's syndrome (PYQ).**
- Rare: congenital ichthyosis + hypogonadism + short stature + intellectual disability + epilepsy (± retinitis pigmentosa); some cases overlap with contiguous gene deletion of X-linked ichthyosis/Kallmann

**Q10. Describe epidermolytic ichthyosis.**
- Autosomal dominant K1/K10 mutation (bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma): blistering and erythema at birth, later corrugated, ridged, malodorous warty hyperkeratosis especially in flexures; histology — epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (vacuolisation of granular/spinous cells with clumped keratohyaline)
- Mosaic form = epidermolytic epidermal naevus; gonadal mosaicism → offspring with generalised disease (genetic counselling)

**Q11. Management of ichthyoses.**
- Emollients and humectants (petrolatum, glycerol, urea 5–10%), keratolytics (lactic acid, salicylic acid — caution for salicylism in children/ large areas, propylene glycol), bath oils, soaking and gentle scrubbing
- Topical retinoids (tazarotene) for localised thick scale; calcipotriol (limited areas)
- Systemic retinoids: acitretin 0.3–1 mg/kg/day or isotretinoin for severe ARCI, epidermolytic ichthyosis, harlequin (lifelong monitoring — bone, lipids, LFT, teratogenicity)
- Eye care for ectropion, ear cleaning, heat precautions, vitamin D supplementation, nutrition, physiotherapy; genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis
- Emerging: IL-17/IL-23 biologics and dupilumab in some ichthyoses (Netherton, CIE)

**Q12. Define ichthyosis and the difference between inherited and acquired.**
- Disorders of cornification with generalised scaling (fish-like scale) due to abnormal epidermal differentiation/ barrier function
- Inherited: present at birth or early childhood; acquired: adult onset — associated with lymphoma (Hodgkin), malignancy, HIV, sarcoidosis, leprosy, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, CKD, drugs (nicotinic acid, statins, clofazimine, cimetidine, kava, hydroxyurea)

**Q13. Describe the clinical approach to a child with scaling from birth.**
- Was there a collodion membrane (ARCI)? Blisters at birth (epidermolytic)? Erythroderma? Hair shaft abnormality (Netherton)? Neurological/ eye signs (Sjögren–Larsson, Refsum)? Family history and pattern (X-linked — boys; AR — consanguinity)
- Examine distribution (flexures spared in IV), scale type (fine white vs large dark plate-like), palms/soles (hyperlinearity — IV), ectropion/eclabium, alopecia, nails, sweating

**Q14. Ichthyosis vulgaris — pathogenesis and associations.**
- Semi-dominant FLG loss-of-function mutations → reduced filaggrin → reduced NMF, poor hydration; reduced keratohyaline granules (thin/absent granular layer on histology)
- Associations: atopic dermatitis (up to 50%), keratosis pilaris, palmar hyperlinearity, allergic rhinitis/ asthma

**Q15. X-linked recessive ichthyosis — more details.**
- Steroid sulfatase (STS) deficiency on Xp22.3 (mostly whole-gene deletion) → cholesterol sulfate accumulation in stratum corneum → retention hyperkeratosis
- Boys: large dark-brown 'dirty' adherent scales on neck ('dirty neck'), trunk, extensor limbs, with flexural involvement possible; palms/soles spared; corneal opacities (also in carrier mothers), cryptorchidism, testicular cancer risk, ADHD/ autism; contiguous gene deletion — Kallmann syndrome (anosmia, hypogonadism)
- Mothers: low oestriol in pregnancy, prolonged labour (placental STS deficiency); diagnosis — STS enzyme assay, FISH/ microarray, cholesterol sulfate on lipoprotein electrophoresis (increased β-LDL mobility)

**Q16. Lamellar ichthyosis vs congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma.**
- Both autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) — TGM1 (transglutaminase 1), ALOX12B, ALOXE3, NIPAL4, CYP4F22, ABCA12
- Lamellar: collodion baby, then large, plate-like dark brown scales, minimal erythema, ectropion, eclabium, alopecia, hypohidrosis/ heat intolerance
- CIE: fine white scales with prominent erythroderma; less ectropion
- Self-improving collodion ichthyosis — mild residual phenotype

**Q17. Describe the management of a collodion baby.**
- Neonatal ICU, humidified incubator (high humidity), temperature regulation, fluid and electrolyte monitoring (hypernatraemic dehydration), sepsis watch, bland emollients (white soft paraffin), avoid keratolytics (salicylate toxicity), eye care for ectropion, feeding support; membrane sheds in 2–4 weeks

**Q18. Harlequin ichthyosis — features and management.**
- Most severe ARCI — ABCA12 mutation (lipid transporter in lamellar granules); thick plate-like scales separated by deep red fissures, severe ectropion, eclabium, flattened ears, restricted movement, respiratory/ feeding difficulty, sepsis
- Management: NICU, oral retinoids (acitretin 0.5–1 mg/kg) early improve survival, emollients, ophthalmic care; survival into adulthood now possible with severe erythroderma phenotype

**Q19. Epidermolytic ichthyosis — genetics and features.**
- Autosomal dominant KRT1/KRT10 mutations (keratin 1/10 — suprabasal keratins); at birth erythroderma with blisters and erosions; later corrugated, ridged hyperkeratosis especially flexures (cobblestone), malodour, secondary infection; KRT1 — palmoplantar keratoderma
- Histology: epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (vacuolar degeneration of upper epidermis, coarse keratohyaline granules); mosaic epidermolytic epidermal naevus parent → risk of generalised disease in child

**Q20. Netherton syndrome — features.**
- Autosomal recessive SPINK5 (LEKTI deficiency → unopposed kallikrein activity): ichthyosis linearis circumflexa (migratory polycyclic double-edged scaly plaques) or congenital erythroderma, trichorrhexis invaginata ('bamboo hair' — eyebrows best), atopy (very high IgE, food allergy), failure to thrive, hypernatraemic dehydration, infections
- Caution: high systemic absorption of topical tacrolimus/steroids; IVIG, IL-17/IL-4R biologics (case reports)

**Q21. Sjögren–Larsson syndrome.**
- Autosomal recessive ALDH3A2 (fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase) deficiency: ichthyosis (yellow-brown velvety, flexural), spastic diplegia/ tetraplegia, intellectual disability, glistening white dots in the retina (perifoveal), itching; diagnosis — FALDH assay

**Q22. Refsum disease — features and treatment.**
- Autosomal recessive PHYH (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) — phytanic acid accumulation: adult onset ichthyosis (vulgaris-like), retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness), anosmia, peripheral neuropathy, cerebellar ataxia, deafness, cardiac arrhythmia, short 4th metatarsal
- Treatment: phytanic acid-restricted diet (avoid dairy, ruminant fat, fish), plasmapheresis during crisis

**Q23. What is KID syndrome?**
- Keratitis–Ichthyosis–Deafness — GJB2 (connexin 26) dominant mutation: erythrokeratoderma-like plaques, spiny hyperkeratosis, PPK (leather-like), vascularising keratitis (blindness), sensorineural deafness, infections, SCC risk

**Q24. What is Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome?**
- X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (EBP mutation), girls: ichthyosiform erythroderma at birth along Blaschko's lines → follicular atrophoderma, patchy cicatricial alopecia, cataracts, short limbs, stippled epiphyses on X-ray

**Q25. What is CHILD syndrome?**
- Congenital Hemidysplasia with Ichthyosiform erythroderma and Limb Defects — X-linked dominant NSDHL mutation; unilateral (usually right) inflammatory ichthyosiform naevus with sharp midline demarcation, ipsilateral limb defects; topical statin + cholesterol therapy helps

**Q26. Describe topical therapy in ichthyosis.**
- Emollients and humectants: petrolatum, urea 5–20% (stings in children), lactic acid 5–12%, glycerol, propylene glycol 40–60% under occlusion; keratolytics: salicylic acid (avoid large areas in infants — salicylism), α-hydroxy acids, N-acetylcysteine; topical retinoids (tazarotene) for localised thick scale; bathing with oils/ baking soda, mechanical scale removal (pumice)

**Q27. Systemic retinoids in ichthyosis.**
- Acitretin 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day for ARCI, epidermolytic (lower doses — may increase fragility), harlequin; isotretinoin alternative; side effects — teratogenicity (contraception 3 years after acitretin), mucocutaneous dryness, hyperlipidaemia, hepatotoxicity, skeletal hyperostosis/ premature epiphyseal closure in children (monitor growth, X-rays)

**Q28. What genetic counselling issues arise?**
- X-linked: carrier mothers have 50% risk of affected sons; AR: 25% recurrence; AD (IV, epidermolytic): 50%; prenatal diagnosis by mutation testing/ fetal skin biopsy (historical); consanguinity counselling

**Q29. Complications of severe ichthyosis.**
- Heat intolerance and hypohidrosis (hyperthermia), ectropion/ exposure keratitis, ear canal blockage, hearing loss, growth failure, vitamin D deficiency/ rickets (reduced UV synthesis), infections, contractures, psychosocial impact

## Quick spotter facts
- Fine shin scales + palmar hyperlinearity + atopy — ichthyosis vulgaris (FLG)
- Dark 'dirty neck' scales in a boy + corneal opacities + cryptorchidism — X-linked ichthyosis (STS)
- Collodion baby — humidified incubator, emollients

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Ichthyoses); 2009 Sorèze consensus classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH)?**
- Common acquired benign condition of multiple small (2–5 mm), well-defined porcelain-white guttate macules on chronically sun-exposed extensor forearms and shins; increases with age (>40 years), women noticed earlier
- Considered a sign of photoageing (UV-induced melanocyte senescence), also genetic and HLA-DQ3 association

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Round/angular white macules with sharp borders, no scaling, no inflammation, stable size, do not enlarge or coalesce; asymptomatic
- Shins and forearms (dorsal), occasionally face, trunk; never on palms/soles or mucosa

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Basket-weave hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy with flattened rete ridges, decreased melanin and reduced number of DOPA-positive melanocytes

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Vitiligo (larger, progressive, any site), guttate morphoea/lichen sclerosus (atrophic, shiny), pityriasis versicolor (scale, KOH), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, leucoderma punctata (after PUVA), progressive macular hypomelanosis (trunk, confluent), tuberous sclerosis confetti macules, chemical leucoderma, indeterminate leprosy (sensory)

**Q5. Treatment.**
- Reassurance and sun protection
- Options for cosmetic improvement: superficial cryotherapy (2–5 s), topical tacrolimus/pimecrolimus, topical retinoids, localised dermabrasion, fractional CO2 or excimer laser, 88% phenol spot application, 5-FU with microneedling, suction blister grafts (variable results)

**Q6. What are the proposed causes of IGH?**
- Chronic UV exposure (photoageing — focal melanocyte loss), ageing/somatic mutation of melanocytes, genetic predisposition (familial), HLA-DQ3, local trauma, autoimmunity (debated)

**Q7. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Well-demarcated white areas with amoeboid/petaloid ('cloudy sky' or 'feathery') margins and absent or reduced pigment network; no perifollicular pigmentation

**Q8. How do you differentiate IGH from guttate vitiligo by Wood's lamp?**
- IGH: off-white, less bright, no enhancement of surrounding activity; vitiligo: bright chalk-white fluorescence with sharp border; histology — vitiligo has complete absence of melanocytes

**Q9. Is IGH a marker of any systemic disease?**
- No — it is benign; indicates cumulative sun damage, so counsel sun protection; patients with many IGH lesions often have other photodamage signs (solar lentigines, actinic keratoses)

**Q10. What is the age and sex distribution and prevalence?**
- Increases with age — >80% of people over 70 have some IGH; women present earlier (cosmetic concern); fair skin with heavy sun exposure but also common in Indian skin

**Q11. Explain the 'four types' on dermoscopy (Ankad classification).**
- Amoeboid, feathery, petaloid, nebuloid (cloudy) patterns of white areas with irregular borders — help differentiate from vitiligo and guttate morphoea

**Q12. Why should guttate morphoea and LS be excluded?**
- They also produce small white macules on trunk/limbs but are slightly indurated or atrophic and shiny, with follicular plugs (LS) — need different treatment; IGH is flat, non-indurated, sun-exposed

**Q13. What are the newer procedural treatments?**
- Fractional CO2 laser, 5-FU tattooing/ microneedling, excimer laser, 88% phenol 'spot peel', non-cultured epidermal cell suspension, platelet-rich plasma with microneedling — small series, variable repigmentation

**Q14. What is leucoderma punctata?**
- Multiple small white guttate macules after PUVA or psoralen + sunlight therapy — similar to IGH; also confetti-like depigmentation after imiquimod/ chemical leucoderma

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Multiple tiny porcelain-white macules on sun-exposed shins of middle-aged — IGH

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Impetigo — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Impetigo** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. Define impetigo. Who gets it?**
- Highly contagious superficial bacterial infection confined to the epidermis (subcorneal), leaving no scar
- Mostly children 2–5 years; spreads in crowded, hot-humid settings, poor hygiene, schools/hostels; in adults usually secondary to another dermatosis

**Q2. Classify pyodermas (a common theory question). Where does impetigo fit?**
- By depth: epidermal — impetigo (non-bullous, bullous); follicular — superficial folliculitis (Bockhart's), sycosis, furuncle, carbuncle; dermal/subcutaneous — ecthyma, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis
- By origin: primary (on normal skin) vs secondary (impetiginisation of eczema, scabies, pediculosis, insect bite, varicella)
- Toxin-mediated: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), toxic shock syndrome, scarlet fever

**Q3. Name the two clinical types and their organisms.**
- Non-bullous (impetigo contagiosa, ~70%): S. aureus is now commonest; Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) alone or together
- Bullous: almost always S. aureus phage group II (commonly type 71) making exfoliative toxins A and B

**Q4. Describe the lesion of non-bullous impetigo.**
- Thin-walled vesicle/pustule on a red base → ruptures quickly → golden-yellow ('honey-coloured') crusts of dried serum
- Face (around nose, mouth) and limbs; satellite lesions by autoinoculation; regional lymphadenopathy common; mild or no itch
- Heals without scarring in 2–3 weeks; may leave transient hypo/hyperpigmentation

**Q5. Describe bullous impetigo.**
- Flaccid, clear-to-turbid bullae 1–2 cm with little surrounding erythema; rupture to leave a thin varnish-like crust with a collarette of scale
- Sites: face, trunk, flexures, napkin area; neonates (formerly 'pemphigus neonatorum')
- No lymphadenopathy usually; localised form of the same toxin disease as SSSS

**Q6. Where is the split in bullous impetigo, and what is the mechanism?**
- Subcorneal / granular layer
- Exfoliative toxins are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein 1 — same target antigen as pemphigus foliaceus and SSSS
- Toxin is local in impetigo (organisms present in the blister); in SSSS it circulates (blister sterile)

**Q7. Why does impetigo stay superficial while SSSS spreads?**
- In SSSS the toxin is absorbed and circulates; babies and adults with renal failure clear it poorly → widespread split at the same level
- Antibodies to the toxin (present in most older children/adults) neutralise it

**Q8. What is the histopathology?**
- Subcorneal pustule/bulla containing neutrophils and Gram-positive cocci; occasional acantholytic cells
- Mild spongiosis; upper dermal neutrophilic infiltrate

**Q9. How will you investigate?**
- Usually a clinical diagnosis
- Gram stain of blister fluid/crust (Gram-positive cocci in clusters/chains); culture and sensitivity if extensive, recurrent, not responding, or MRSA suspected
- Nasal swab for carriage in recurrent cases; urine for haematuria/proteinuria if post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is suspected; ASO titre (often low after skin infection) — anti-DNase B is better

**Q10. Give the differential diagnosis.**
- Non-bullous: herpes simplex / eczema herpeticum (punched-out erosions, grouped), impetiginised atopic or seborrhoeic dermatitis, tinea faciei, scabies with secondary infection, pemphigus foliaceus, discoid eczema
- Bullous: bullous insect-bite reaction, chronic bullous disease of childhood, bullous fixed drug eruption, thermal burn, bullous pemphigoid (adult), SSSS, bullous erythema multiforme, epidermolysis bullosa

**Q11. What are the complications?**
- Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (nephritogenic strains; not prevented by antibiotics) — 1–2 weeks to 1 month later
- Rheumatic fever is NOT a recognised sequel of skin streptococcal infection
- Ecthyma, cellulitis, lymphangitis, bacteraemia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis; SSSS from bullous strains; scarlet fever; guttate psoriasis
- Psychosocial: school exclusion

**Q12. Outline management.**
- General: gentle removal of crusts with saline/soap-water soaks, separate towels, nail hygiene, keep child off school until 24–48 h of treatment or crusts dry
- Localised: topical mupirocin 2% or fusidic acid 2% (or retapamulin 1%, ozenoxacin 1%) 2–3 times daily for 5–7 days
- Extensive, bullous, systemic features, or failure: oral antibiotics 7 days — cloxacillin/flucloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate; erythromycin/azithromycin if penicillin allergy; MRSA — doxycycline (>8 y), clindamycin, cotrimoxazole, linezolid
- Treat underlying dermatosis; decolonise recurrent carriers (nasal mupirocin, chlorhexidine washes)

**Q13. Why limit use of topical fusidic acid and mupirocin?**
- Resistance develops quickly with long or repeated use
- Use for short courses only; prefer antiseptics (povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine, hydrogen peroxide cream) for prevention

**Q14. What is 'impetigo of Bockhart'?**
- Not true impetigo — it is superficial follicular pustules (superficial folliculitis) of S. aureus

**Q15. What is common impetigo variant 'circinate impetigo'?**
- Lesions clear centrally and spread at the edge to form rings — may be mistaken for tinea

**Q16. Topical antibiotics in dermatology — classify (asked as a short note).**
- Mupirocin (inhibits isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase), fusidic acid (blocks elongation factor G), retapamulin (pleuromutilin, 50S), ozenoxacin (quinolone), neomycin + bacitracin + polymyxin (high contact-allergy risk with neomycin), gentamicin, nadifloxacin, clindamycin and erythromycin (acne), metronidazole (rosacea), silver sulfadiazine (burns), sodium fusidate

## Quick spotter facts
- Honey-coloured crust = non-bullous impetigo
- Desmoglein 1 split — bullous impetigo, SSSS, pemphigus foliaceus
- Skin strep → glomerulonephritis, not rheumatic fever

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Incontinentia pigmenti — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Incontinentia pigmenti** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is incontinentia pigmenti (IP, Bloch–Sulzberger)?**
- X-linked dominant multisystem genodermatosis due to IKBKG (NEMO) mutations (commonly exon 4–10 deletion) — lethal in males in utero (affected females; rare males with Klinefelter or mosaicism); skewed X-inactivation
- Defective NF-κB activation → keratinocyte apoptosis and inflammation along Blaschko's lines

**Q2. Describe the stages.**
- Stage 1 — vesicular/inflammatory (birth–4 months): linear vesicles and bullae on erythematous base along Blaschko's lines on limbs/trunk, with blood eosinophilia
- Stage 2 — verrucous (2–6 months): linear warty keratotic plaques (limbs)
- Stage 3 — hyperpigmented (6 months–adolescence): swirling/whorled slate-grey to brown pigmentation along Blaschko's lines on trunk (not necessarily at earlier sites)
- Stage 4 — hypopigmented/atrophic (adolescence/adult): pale, hairless, anhidrotic linear streaks on calves
- Stages may overlap or be absent

**Q3. Extracutaneous features.**
- Teeth (most common extracutaneous ~80%): hypodontia/anodontia, conical/peg teeth, delayed eruption
- Hair: vertex scarring alopecia, woolly hair; nails: dystrophy, painful subungual keratotic tumours (later life)
- Eyes (~35%): retinal vasculopathy, retinal detachment, strabismus, microphthalmia — urgent ophthalmology review and serial retinal exams in infancy
- CNS (~30%): seizures, intellectual disability, spastic paresis, microcephaly, stroke-like lesions
- Breast hypoplasia, supernumerary nipples

**Q4. Histopathology by stage.**
- Stage 1: eosinophilic spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles full of eosinophils, dyskeratotic cells
- Stage 2: hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, dyskeratosis (whorls)
- Stage 3: marked pigment incontinence (dermal melanophages) — origin of the name
- Stage 4: atrophic epidermis, absent adnexa

**Q5. Diagnostic criteria (Minić et al. 2014).**
- Major: typical skin lesions at any stage along Blaschko's lines
- Minor: dental, ocular, CNS anomalies, alopecia/woolly hair, nail abnormalities, palate anomalies, breast/nipple anomalies, multiple male miscarriages, typical histology
- With positive IKBKG mutation, any one major or minor criterion suffices

**Q6. Differential diagnosis (stage-wise).**
- Stage 1: bullous impetigo, HSV, varicella, EB, bullous mastocytosis, LCH
- Stage 2: linear epidermal naevus, warts, lichen striatus
- Stage 3: linear and whorled naevoid hypermelanosis (no preceding stages), X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder, Naegeli syndrome
- Stage 4: hypomelanosis of Ito, Goltz syndrome, linear morphoea

**Q7. Management.**
- Skin: supportive, gentle wound care, prevent infection — lesions resolve spontaneously
- Multidisciplinary follow-up: ophthalmology (retinal exam at diagnosis and frequently in first year; laser photocoagulation), neurology (MRI if neurological signs), dental care, developmental assessment
- Genetic counselling: 50% risk to daughters; affected male pregnancies usually miscarry

**Q8. Describe the four stages in detail.**
- Stage 1 (vesicular, birth–4 months): linear vesicles/ pustules on erythematous base along Blaschko lines, eosinophilia
- Stage 2 (verrucous, weeks–months): warty hyperkeratotic linear plaques mostly on limbs
- Stage 3 (hyperpigmented, months–adolescence): swirling grey-brown streaks/ whorls on trunk (not necessarily same sites)
- Stage 4 (atrophic/ hypopigmented, adolescence–adulthood): hairless, anhidrotic pale atrophic streaks on legs
- Stages may overlap or be skipped

**Q9. Histopathology by stage in detail.**
- Stage 1: eosinophilic spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles full of eosinophils
- Stage 2: hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, dyskeratotic cells in whorls
- Stage 3: pigment incontinence — melanophages in dermis
- Stage 4: atrophic epidermis, absent adnexa

**Q10. Differential diagnosis of vesicular stage.**
- Neonatal HSV infection (critical — do Tzanck/ PCR), bullous impetigo, epidermolysis bullosa, varicella, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, transient neonatal pustular melanosis, linear IgA disease

**Q11. Management and follow-up.**
- Wound care for vesicles (avoid infection), skin lesions resolve; genetic testing (IKBKG deletion); urgent ophthalmology screening (retinal vasculopathy — laser), neurological assessment and MRI if symptomatic, dental review (implants), genetic counselling (50% risk to daughters; male pregnancies often miscarry)

**Q12. What is NEMO and its other disorders?**
- NF-κB essential modulator (IKKγ) — required for NF-κB activation (protects cells from TNF-induced apoptosis); hypomorphic IKBKG mutations in males cause anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency (EDA-ID)

**Q13. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q14. Explain the genetics and why it is mostly female.**
- X-linked dominant IKBKG (NEMO) mutation — commonest a recurrent exon 4–10 deletion; usually lethal in hemizygous males (in utero), so mostly girls; affected males survive with Klinefelter (XXY) or somatic mosaicism; extreme skewed X-inactivation in carrier mothers

**Q15. Dental, hair and nail changes.**
- Teeth: hypodontia/anodontia, conical/peg-shaped teeth, delayed eruption (most common extracutaneous feature)
- Hair: vertex scarring alopecia (cicatricial), woolly hair, sparse eyebrows
- Nails: dystrophy, painful subungual keratotic tumours in adolescence/adulthood (may erode bone — mimic SCC)

**Q16. What eye and CNS findings are critical?**
- Retinal vascular abnormalities (peripheral avascularity, neovascularisation) → retinal detachment and blindness — needs ophthalmology screening from birth (monthly early, then periodically) and laser photocoagulation
- CNS: seizures, ischaemic strokes, developmental delay, spastic paralysis — in ~30%; neonatal encephalopathy

## Quick spotter facts
- Female infant with linear vesicles along Blaschko's lines + eosinophilia — IP stage 1 (NEMO)
- Peg teeth, retinal vasculopathy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Incontinentia pigmenti). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Infantile haemangioma & vascular malformations — viva
posts.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 18 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Infantile haemangioma & vascular malformations** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Give the ISSVA classification of vascular anomalies.**
- Vascular tumours (endothelial proliferation): benign — infantile haemangioma, congenital haemangioma (RICH, NICH, PICH), tufted angioma, spindle-cell haemangioma, pyogenic granuloma; locally aggressive/borderline — kaposiform haemangioendothelioma, Kaposi sarcoma; malignant — angiosarcoma
- Vascular malformations (errors of morphogenesis, no proliferation): simple — capillary (CM, port-wine stain), venous (VM), lymphatic (LM — macro/microcystic), arteriovenous (AVM, high flow), AV fistula; combined (CVM, CLVM, CLAVM); of major named vessels; associated with other anomalies (Sturge–Weber, Klippel–Trenaunay, Parkes Weber, Proteus, CLOVES, Maffucci, PROS)

**Q2. Differentiate infantile haemangioma from vascular malformation.**
- Haemangioma: usually absent or a premonitory mark at birth; appears in first weeks; rapid proliferation till 3–5 months (80% of final size), slow involution over years; GLUT-1 positive; female, premature, low birth weight, multiple gestation, placental anomalies
- Malformation: present at birth (may be inapparent), grows proportionately with the child, never involutes, may enlarge with trauma, infection, hormones; GLUT-1 negative; flow characteristics on Doppler (slow vs fast flow)

**Q3. Describe clinical types of infantile haemangioma.**
- Superficial (bright red, lobulated 'strawberry'), deep (bluish subcutaneous swelling), mixed
- Pattern: focal, segmental (plaque in a developmental segment — more complications), indeterminate, multifocal (≥5 lesions — screen for hepatic haemangiomas with ultrasound)
- Abortive/minimal-growth haemangioma (telangiectatic patch, lower body)

**Q4. Which haemangiomas are high-risk and need treatment?**
- Life-threatening: airway ('beard area' segmental — subglottic), liver (high-output cardiac failure, hypothyroidism), large lesions with cardiac failure
- Functional impairment: periocular (amblyopia, astigmatism), lip, nasal tip, ear canal, feeding problems
- Ulceration (commonest complication — lip, anogenital, flexures; painful, scarring)
- Disfigurement: central face, large facial, nose ('Cyrano'), breast in girls
- Associated syndromes: PHACE (Posterior fossa anomalies, Haemangioma (large segmental facial), Arterial anomalies, Cardiac defects/coarctation, Eye anomalies, ± sternal cleft/supraumbilical raphe); LUMBAR/SACRAL/PELVIS (lumbosacral haemangioma with spinal dysraphism, genitourinary, anorectal anomalies — do spine USG/MRI)

**Q5. Treatment of infantile haemangioma.**
- Oral propranolol — first line for high-risk lesions: 1 mg/kg/day increasing to 2–3 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses with feeds, start ideally by 1–2 months of age (before 5 months), continue till ~12 months of age (6 months minimum); baseline examination (heart rate, BP, ± ECG if bradycardia/heart disease), side effects — hypoglycaemia (feed regularly; stop if not feeding), bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension, sleep disturbance, cold extremities; rebound growth on stopping
- Atenolol (fewer CNS effects) and nadolol as alternatives
- Topical timolol 0.5% gel for small superficial lesions
- Systemic/intralesional steroids (second line), vincristine, sirolimus (kaposiform)
- Pulsed-dye laser for ulceration and residual telangiectasia; surgery for fibrofatty residue after involution
- Ulcer care: barrier creams, dressings, topical antibiotics, propranolol

**Q6. Mechanism of propranolol in haemangiomas.**
- Vasoconstriction (early colour change), inhibition of VEGF and bFGF (angiogenesis), induction of apoptosis of endothelial cells, effects on haemangioma stem cells and renin–angiotensin system

**Q7. What is Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon?**
- Profound thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy due to platelet trapping in kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma (NOT infantile haemangioma)
- Rapidly enlarging, firm, purpuric/ecchymotic mass in infancy; treat with sirolimus, vincristine, steroids; avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding

**Q8. Describe port-wine stain and Sturge–Weber syndrome.**
- Port-wine stain (capillary malformation): pink-red macular patch present at birth, persists, darkens and thickens with age (nodularity — 'cobblestoning'), soft-tissue hypertrophy; somatic GNAQ mutation
- Sturge–Weber: facial CM in V1 (forehead/upper eyelid) distribution + ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis (seizures, hemiparesis, intellectual disability, tram-track calcification on imaging) + eye (glaucoma, choroidal haemangioma)
- Treatment of PWS: pulsed-dye laser (585/595 nm) early in infancy — best results; topical rapamycin adjunct; MRI brain and eye check for V1 lesions

**Q9. What is Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Capillary–lymphatic–venous malformation of a limb (usually lower) + soft-tissue and bone overgrowth (limb hypertrophy) + varicosities/persistent embryonic lateral marginal vein (vein of Servelle) — slow flow; PIK3CA mutation (PROS spectrum)
- Complications: DVT/pulmonary embolism, bleeding, lymphatic leaks, cellulitis, limb-length discrepancy, coagulopathy
- Parkes Weber syndrome — similar but with arteriovenous fistulas (fast flow; RASA1) — high-output cardiac failure
- Management: compression, sclerotherapy, sirolimus, alpelisib (PIK3CA inhibitor), orthopaedic correction, anticoagulation when indicated

**Q10. Write a short note on blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome (PYQ).**
- Multifocal venous malformations of skin (soft, compressible blue rubbery nodules that refill after pressure, may be painful/sweat) and GI tract (bleeding → iron-deficiency anaemia); TEK (TIE2) somatic mutations
- Treatment: iron, endoscopic ablation/resection of bleeding lesions, sirolimus

**Q11. Enumerate syndromes associated with vascular anomalies (PYQ).**
- Sturge–Weber, Klippel–Trenaunay, Parkes Weber, Proteus, CLOVES, PHACE, LUMBAR, Maffucci (enchondromas + spindle-cell haemangiomas; risk of chondrosarcoma), blue rubber bleb, Cobb (spinal AVM + cutaneous vascular lesion in dermatome), von Hippel–Lindau, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu — epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasia, AVMs; ENG/ACVRL1), ataxia-telangiectasia, capillary malformation–AVM (RASA1), macrocephaly–capillary malformation (M-CM), Beckwith–Wiedemann (glabellar naevus flammeus)

**Q12. Lasers for vascular lesions (PYQ).**
- Selective photothermolysis targeting oxyhaemoglobin (peaks 418, 542, 577 nm): pulsed-dye laser 585/595 nm (port-wine stain, haemangioma, telangiectasia, rosacea), KTP 532 nm, long-pulsed Nd:YAG 1064 nm (deeper veins, leg veins), IPL, alexandrite 755 nm (hypertrophic PWS)
- Side effects: purpura, dyspigmentation, blistering, scarring

**Q13. Describe congenital haemangiomas (RICH, NICH, PICH).**
- Fully grown at birth, GLUT-1 negative
- RICH (rapidly involuting) — involutes in first 12–14 months, may leave atrophic skin; NICH (non-involuting) — persists, grows with child; PICH (partially involuting)
- GNAQ/GNA11 mutations; may cause transient thrombocytopenia or heart failure (RICH)

**Q14. Describe venous malformations.**
- Soft, compressible, bluish swellings that enlarge with dependency/ Valsalva and empty on pressure; phleboliths on X-ray; pain and localised intravascular coagulopathy (raised D-dimer, low fibrinogen); TEK/PIK3CA mutations
- Treatment: compression, sclerotherapy (polidocanol, bleomycin, ethanol), surgery, sirolimus, LMWH for painful thrombosis

**Q15. Describe lymphatic malformations.**
- Macrocystic (cystic hygroma — neck/ axilla; transilluminates) or microcystic (lymphangioma circumscriptum — 'frog-spawn' clear/ haemorrhagic vesicles on skin, lymph leakage); recurrent infection/ swelling; treat with sclerotherapy (doxycycline, OK-432, bleomycin), sirolimus, CO2 laser/ excision for circumscriptum

**Q16. Arteriovenous malformations — Schöbinger staging.**
- High-flow: I quiescence (warm pink stain), II expansion (pulsation, thrill, bruit, enlargement), III destruction (pain, ulceration, bleeding, necrosis), IV decompensation (high-output cardiac failure)
- Triggers — puberty, pregnancy, trauma, partial treatment; management — embolisation + surgical resection by multidisciplinary team; MEK inhibitors (MAP2K1) under study

**Q17. What investigations are used for vascular anomalies?**
- Doppler ultrasound (flow — first line), MRI with contrast (extent, slow vs fast flow), CT/ angiography for AVM, D-dimer/ fibrinogen (VM), GLUT-1 immunostaining on biopsy, genetic testing on tissue (PIK3CA etc.)

**Q18. Ulcerated haemangioma — management.**
- Pain control (paracetamol, topical lidocaine with care), barrier creams, non-adherent dressings, topical/ oral antibiotics if infected, topical timolol, oral propranolol, pulsed-dye laser; common in lip, anogenital and flexural lesions during proliferation

## Quick spotter facts
- Absent at birth, grows fast, then involutes, GLUT-1+ — infantile haemangioma
- Propranolol 2–3 mg/kg/day
- V1 port-wine stain — look for Sturge–Weber; KMP is with kaposiform HE, not infantile haemangioma

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Vascular anomalies); ISSVA 2018 classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Keloid and hypertrophic scar — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Keloid and hypertrophic scar** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. Define and differentiate keloid and hypertrophic scar.**
- Both are abnormal fibroproliferative wound healing with excess collagen
- Hypertrophic scar: raised scar confined to the original wound, appears within weeks, may regress over 1–2 years, common across tension lines/joints (burns), no racial predilection, lower recurrence after excision
- Keloid: extends beyond original wound margins (claw-like), appears months–years after injury (or spontaneously), does not regress, recurs after excision, more in dark skin (Africans, Asians), familial, sites — sternum, shoulders, upper back, earlobes (piercing), mandible; itchy and painful

**Q2. Pathogenesis.**
- Prolonged inflammation and fibroblast hyperactivity: increased TGF-β1/β2 (decreased TGF-β3), PDGF, VEGF, IL-6; excess type I collagen (keloid) / type III (hypertrophic early); reduced apoptosis, mechanical tension, hypoxia
- Genetic: HLA associations, NEDD4, familial AD forms; hormones (puberty, pregnancy enlarge)

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Keloid: thick, hyalinised, eosinophilic glassy collagen bundles ('keloidal collagen') haphazardly arranged, fewer fibroblasts, mucin, no nodules
- Hypertrophic scar: nodules of fine collagen and myofibroblasts (α-SMA+) arranged parallel to the surface, more vessels

**Q4. Assessment.**
- Vancouver Scar Scale (vascularity, pigmentation, pliability, height), POSAS (Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale)

**Q5. Prevention.**
- Avoid elective surgery/piercing/tattoos in keloid-prone individuals; minimal tension closure along relaxed skin tension lines; early silicone gel/sheets and pressure garments after surgery/burns; prompt treatment of acne

**Q6. Discuss treatment (combination approach).**
- First line: intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 10–40 mg/ml every 3–4 weeks (side effects — atrophy, hypopigmentation, telangiectasia), silicone gel/sheets (12–24 h/day for months), pressure therapy (earlobe pressure earrings, garments 24–30 mmHg)
- Combined: intralesional 5-FU (with steroid), bleomycin, verapamil; cryotherapy (contact or intralesional cryoprobe) before steroid; botulinum toxin A
- Surgery: excision (intramarginal/core excision) ALWAYS followed by adjuvant therapy (steroids, pressure, radiation) — excision alone has 50–100% recurrence
- Radiotherapy: postoperative superficial X-ray or electron beam/brachytherapy within 24–72 h (recurrent/large keloids in adults)
- Lasers: pulsed-dye laser (erythema, itch), fractional CO2 laser with laser-assisted drug delivery
- Others: imiquimod post-excision, topical/oral tranilast, dupilumab (reports), fat grafting/PRP (hypertrophic)

**Q7. Discuss relaxed skin tension lines (PYQ).**
- Lines of minimal tension on relaxed skin, perpendicular to underlying muscle pull (follow wrinkles on face — Borges' lines); incisions parallel to RSTL heal with narrow, less noticeable scars and less hypertrophy, vs Langer's lines (cleavage lines on cadavers)

**Q8. What is the Vancouver scar scale and POSAS?**
- Vancouver Scar Scale: vascularity (0–3), pigmentation (0–2), pliability (0–5), height (0–3) — total 0–13
- POSAS: Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale — includes patient-reported pain, itch, colour, stiffness, thickness, irregularity

**Q9. Explain silicone gel sheeting mechanism and use.**
- Occlusion and hydration of stratum corneum reduces keratinocyte signalling (IL-1, TGF-β) to fibroblasts; static electricity, temperature effects; use ≥12–24 h/day for at least 2–3 months from 2 weeks after wound closure; first-line prevention and treatment of hypertrophic scars

**Q10. Post-excision keloid adjuvant therapy.**
- Simple excision alone has 45–100% recurrence; combine with intralesional steroids (at surgery and monthly), postoperative radiotherapy (electron beam 15–20 Gy within 24–72 h), pressure (earrings, garments 24–30 mmHg), silicone; core excision with keloidal skin flap

**Q11. What is intralesional 5-FU and bleomycin use?**
- 5-FU 50 mg/ml (alone or with triamcinolone 9:1) weekly to monthly — inhibits fibroblast proliferation; side effects pain, ulceration, purpura; avoid in pregnancy
- Bleomycin 1.5 IU/ml by multiple punctures — for resistant keloids; side effects hyperpigmentation, ulceration

**Q12. Explain the principles of cryotherapy (PYQ).**
- Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C): rapid freezing causes intracellular ice crystals, cell dehydration, vascular stasis and ischaemic necrosis; slow thaw maximises damage; techniques — spray, cotton-tipped applicator, cryoprobe; lethal temperature for benign lesions −20 to −30 °C, malignant −50 °C (double freeze–thaw)
- Side effects: pain, blistering, hypo/ hyperpigmentation (avoid in dark skin cosmetic areas), scarring, nerve damage over superficial nerves, alopecia

**Q13. Keloid in the context of genetics and syndromes.**
- Familial keloids (autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance), commoner in African, Asian and Hispanic ancestry; syndromic associations — Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome, Goeminne syndrome; note Ehlers–Danlos gives wide atrophic 'fish-mouth' scars, not keloids

**Q14. Which sites are keloid-prone and why?**
- Presternal, shoulders/deltoid, upper back, ear lobes (piercing), mandibular area — high skin tension and movement (presternal, shoulder) and sebaceous-rich areas; genetics (darker skin, family history, HLA), pregnancy and puberty (hormonal) increase risk

**Q15. Intralesional steroid technique.**
- Triamcinolone acetonide 10–40 mg/ml injected into the upper/mid dermis of the keloid (blanching), using 26–30 G needle or dermojet, every 3–6 weeks; can combine with 5-FU (50 mg/ml, 9:1 or 3:1 ratio), cryotherapy before injection softens lesion; side effects — atrophy, hypopigmentation, telangiectasia, Cushingoid if large doses

**Q16. What are the newer treatments?**
- Intralesional verapamil, bleomycin, botulinum toxin A, PRP; pulsed-dye laser for erythema, fractional CO2 with drug delivery, intralesional cryotherapy (cryoneedle), postoperative radiotherapy (electron beam within 24–48 h), silicone gel/sheet for ≥12 h/day for 3 months, pressure earrings after ear keloid excision, dupilumab (case reports)

## Quick spotter facts
- Scar extending beyond wound margins, not regressing, on the sternum/earlobe — keloid
- Excision only with adjuvant (steroid/radiation/pressure)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Keloids and hypertrophic scars); International scar management recommendations. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Keratolysis exfoliativa — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Keratolysis exfoliativa** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What is keratolysis exfoliativa?**
- Common benign recurrent superficial peeling of palms (and soles) — also called lamellar dyshidrosis/exfoliatio areata manuum
- Young adults; worse in summer, with sweating, friction, wet work, detergents

**Q2. Describe the clinical features.**
- Small air-filled white 'collarettes' or blisters (no fluid) that burst to leave expanding rings of peeling; leaves normal or slightly red, tender skin
- Usually asymptomatic or mild dryness; symmetrical palms > soles; no vesicles with fluid, no significant inflammation

**Q3. What causes it?**
- Premature separation of corneocytes in the stratum corneum — possibly reduced corneodesmosomes/protease imbalance; irritants, hyperhidrosis and seasonal factors aggravate; some link with atopy

**Q4. Classify palmoplantar eczema / differentials (PYQ).**
- Palmar eczema types: irritant, allergic, atopic, pompholyx (dyshidrotic), hyperkeratotic, nummular, fingertip, apron eczema, recurrent focal palmar peeling (= keratolysis exfoliativa)
- Differentials of peeling palms: pompholyx (deep fluid vesicles, itchy), tinea manuum (one hand, KOH +), psoriasis, acral peeling skin syndrome (TGM5 — genetic, from birth, worse with friction), post-scarlet fever/Kawasaki/TSS desquamation, epidermolysis bullosa simplex (localised), juvenile plantar dermatosis, secondary syphilis

**Q5. Investigations?**
- Clinical diagnosis; KOH to exclude tinea; patch test if associated eczema

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Reassurance; avoid soaps, detergents, irritants and wet work; gloves
- Emollients and keratolytic/humectant creams (urea 10–20%, lactic acid 12%, salicylic acid 3–6%); barrier creams
- Topical steroids usually not useful (non-inflammatory) unless eczematous; NB-UVB in extensive recurrent cases; treat hyperhidrosis

**Q7. Differentiate keratolysis exfoliativa from pompholyx.**
- KE: air-filled superficial collarettes, minimal itch, no fluid vesicles, non-inflammatory
- Pompholyx: deep-seated tapioca-like fluid-filled vesicles on sides of fingers, intense itching, inflammatory, responds to steroids

**Q8. Prognosis?**
- Benign, recurrent each summer; tends to resolve on its own in 2–3 weeks per episode

**Q9. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q10. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q11. What is juvenile plantar dermatosis?**
- Glazed, shiny, fissured erythema of weight-bearing forefoot and toe pads (sparing toe webs) in atopic children 3–14 y; worse in summer with synthetic socks/ occlusive shoes; treat with cotton socks, emollients/ barrier creams, change footwear; resolves at puberty

**Q12. Recurrent focal palmar peeling — management advice.**
- Avoid wet work, detergents and solvents; cotton-lined gloves; regular emollients and urea 10% cream; avoid picking/ peeling the collarettes; reassure about benign recurrence

**Q13. Hyperhidrosis link and treatment.**
- Palmar hyperhidrosis can aggravate keratolysis exfoliativa and pompholyx; treat with aluminium chloride hexahydrate 15–20%, tap water iontophoresis, botulinum toxin, oral glycopyrrolate/ oxybutynin, sympathectomy (last resort — compensatory sweating)

**Q14. What is acral peeling skin syndrome?**
- Autosomal recessive TGM5 (transglutaminase 5) or CSTA mutations — painless superficial peeling of hands and feet from infancy, worse with heat, humidity and friction; distinguished from keratolysis exfoliativa by early onset and family history; treat with emollients and avoidance of friction

**Q15. Dermoscopy and histology of keratolysis exfoliativa.**
- Dermoscopy: whitish collarettes of scale with central erythema-free skin; histology: separation within the stratum corneum without inflammation, vesiculation or spongiosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Air-filled collarettes on palms in summer — keratolysis exfoliativa

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Palmoplantar dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Keratosis pilaris — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Keratosis pilaris** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is keratosis pilaris (KP)?**
- Very common, benign, inherited (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance) follicular keratinisation disorder: rough, skin-coloured to red, keratotic follicular papules ('chicken skin') on extensor upper arms, thighs, buttocks, cheeks (children)
- Begins in childhood, peaks in adolescence, improves with age; worse in winter/dry climate

**Q2. Associations.**
- Atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris (FLG mutations), obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, Down syndrome, Noonan/cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes, drugs (BRAF inhibitors — vemurafenib, lithium)

**Q3. Variants.**
- KP rubra (prominent erythema), KP alba
- Keratosis pilaris atrophicans group: ulerythema ophryogenes (lateral eyebrows — atrophy and loss; Noonan, Cornelia de Lange), atrophoderma vermiculatum (honeycomb atrophy on cheeks), keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (X-linked, scarring alopecia of scalp, photophobia)
- Erythromelanosis follicularis faciei et colli (red-brown pigmentation with follicular papules on cheeks/neck)
- Keratosis pilaris rubra faceii

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Keratin plug distending the follicular infundibulum, often with a coiled/twisted hair, mild perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Phrynoderma (nutritional; elbows/knees, larger spiny papules), lichen spinulosus (grouped spiny papules), Darier's disease (greasy seborrhoeic distribution), PRP (follicular knuckle papules), folliculitis (pustules), lichen nitidus, scurvy (perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs), follicular eczema, acne (comedones)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — benign, improves with age
- Emollients and keratolytics: urea 10–20%, lactic acid 12%, salicylic acid 3–6%, glycolic acid; gentle exfoliation
- Topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene); short course of mild topical steroids for red/itchy KP
- Lasers: PDL/KTP for erythema, long-pulsed Nd:YAG/diode laser hair removal, Q-switched Nd:YAG for pigmentation; microdermabrasion

**Q7. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q8. Describe the clinical features in detail.**
- Small (1–2 mm) rough follicular keratotic papules ('chicken skin'/ 'goose bumps'), sometimes with perifollicular erythema, on extensor upper arms, thighs, buttocks, cheeks (children); asymptomatic or mildly itchy; worse in winter; improves after adolescence

**Q9. Treatment in detail.**
- Emollients with keratolytics — urea 10–20%, lactic acid 12%, salicylic acid 2–6%, glycolic acid; topical retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene), mild steroids for inflamed lesions; gentle exfoliation; pulsed-dye laser/ Nd:YAG/ IPL for erythema; microdermabrasion; recurrence on stopping

**Q10. What drugs cause KP-like eruptions?**
- BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib), nilotinib, sorafenib, ciclosporin (also trichodysplasia spinulosa)

**Q11. Ulerythema ophryogenes and Noonan syndrome link.**
- Lateral eyebrow erythema with follicular papules → scarring loss of eyebrows; associated with Noonan syndrome, cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, Cornelia de Lange, Rubinstein–Taybi, woolly hair — examine for dysmorphism

**Q12. Differentiate KP from phrynoderma.**
- KP: atopic/ genetic, upper outer arms/ thighs, fine papules, normal nutrition; phrynoderma: larger spiny papules on elbows/ knees/ buttocks, malnutrition signs (night blindness, Bitot's spots, angular cheilitis), responds to vitamin/ nutritional supplementation

**Q13. What is the pathogenesis?**
- Abnormal follicular keratinisation with keratin plug in the infundibulum, often encircling a coiled hair; associated with filaggrin mutations (ichthyosis vulgaris, atopy); worse in winter (low humidity), improves in summer and with age

**Q14. Describe keratosis pilaris atrophicans variants.**
- Ulerythema ophryogenes (lateral eyebrows — erythema, papules, loss of eyebrows; Noonan syndrome, Cornelia de Lange), atrophoderma vermiculatum (honeycomb pitting of cheeks), keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (X-linked — scarring alopecia, photophobia)

**Q15. What is keratosis pilaris rubra?**
- Variant with prominent erythema extending beyond the follicular papules (face, arms) — pulsed-dye laser helps erythema

## Quick spotter facts
- Rough follicular papules on outer arms of an atopic adolescent — keratosis pilaris
- Ulerythema ophryogenes — lateral eyebrow loss

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Follicular keratoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Leg ulcers — viva
posts.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 27 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Leg ulcers** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Define a chronic leg ulcer.**
- Loss of skin below the knee (leg or foot) that does not heal within 4–6 weeks

**Q2. Classify leg ulcers by cause (PYQ).**
- Vascular: venous (70–80%), arterial (10–15%), mixed arteriovenous, lymphatic, vasculitic (PAN, rheumatoid, cryoglobulinaemia, ANCA), microthrombotic (antiphospholipid, livedoid vasculopathy, calciphylaxis, cholesterol emboli)
- Neuropathic (trophic): diabetes, leprosy, spinal disorders, alcohol, tabes dorsalis
- Infective: tropical ulcer, ecthyma, mycobacterial (TB, Buruli, leprosy), deep fungal (mycetoma, sporotrichosis), leishmaniasis, syphilis (gumma), yaws
- Haematological: sickle-cell disease, thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, polycythaemia, dysproteinaemias
- Neoplastic: SCC (Marjolin's ulcer in chronic scars), BCC, melanoma, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma
- Others: pyoderma gangrenosum, necrobiosis lipoidica, trauma, burns, dermatitis artefacta, drugs (hydroxyurea — malleolar ulcers), radiation, panniculitis

**Q3. Describe the venous drainage of the lower limb (PYQ).**
- Superficial veins: great saphenous (from medial end of dorsal arch, anterior to medial malleolus, along medial leg and thigh to saphenofemoral junction 3–4 cm below and lateral to pubic tubercle) and small saphenous (behind lateral malleolus, up the back of calf to popliteal vein)
