- Deep veins: paired venae comitantes of anterior/posterior tibial and peroneal veins → popliteal → femoral → external iliac
- Perforators connect superficial to deep with valves directing flow inwards (Cockett's medial ankle perforators, Boyd's below knee, Dodd's/Hunter's in thigh)
- Calf muscle pump: contraction compresses deep veins and pushes blood upwards; valves prevent reflux — failure gives ambulatory venous hypertension

**Q4. Explain the pathogenesis of venous ulcers.**
- Valvular incompetence (primary, or post-thrombotic) and calf pump failure → sustained ambulatory venous hypertension → capillary distension and leakage of fibrinogen, RBCs → pericapillary fibrin cuffs (oxygen diffusion barrier hypothesis), leucocyte trapping (white cell trapping hypothesis), growth-factor trapping, MMP activity → tissue hypoxia, inflammation and ulceration

**Q5. Describe the clinical features of a venous ulcer and its associated signs.**
- Site: gaiter area — above the medial malleolus (commonest), shallow, irregular sloping edges, granulation tissue and fibrinous slough, moderate exudate; mild pain relieved by elevation
- Surrounding changes: varicose veins, oedema, haemosiderin pigmentation (brown), stasis (venous) eczema, lipodermatosclerosis (inverted champagne-bottle leg), atrophie blanche (white stellate scars with telangiectasia), corona phlebectatica (ankle flare)
- CEAP classification: C0 none — C1 telangiectasia/reticular — C2 varicose veins — C3 oedema — C4 skin changes (a pigmentation/eczema, b LDS/atrophie blanche, c corona phlebectatica) — C5 healed ulcer — C6 active ulcer

**Q6. Differentiate venous, arterial and neuropathic ulcers.**
- Venous: gaiter area, shallow, irregular, exudative, mild pain eased by elevation, pulses present, warm, oedema, pigmentation
- Arterial: distal pressure points (toes, heel, shin, lateral malleolus), punched-out, deep, dry pale/necrotic base, severe pain worse on elevation and at night, absent pulses, cold shiny hairless skin, intermittent claudication, ABPI <0.8
- Neuropathic: pressure points of sole (metatarsal heads, heel), punched-out painless with callus rim, sensory loss, warm foot with pulses (unless mixed diabetic), deformity (Charcot joint)

**Q7. Discuss the evaluation of a leg ulcer.**
- History: duration, pain, DVT, varicose veins, diabetes, smoking, trauma, drugs, systemic disease
- Examination: site, size (measure/photograph), edge, base, discharge, surrounding skin, pulses, sensation, joints
- Ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI) with hand-held Doppler: 0.9–1.3 normal; <0.8 arterial disease (avoid high compression); <0.5 severe ischaemia; >1.3 calcified vessels (diabetes — use toe pressures)
- Venous duplex ultrasound (reflux, obstruction); arterial duplex/angiography if ABPI low
- Bloods: CBC, sugar/HbA1c, renal function, albumin, ESR/CRP, lipid profile, autoimmune screen (ANA, ANCA, RF, cryoglobulins, APLA) when vasculitic
- Swab culture only if clinically infected; biopsy from edge if atypical, non-healing >3 months (SCC), PG/vasculitis suspected; X-ray/MRI for osteomyelitis

**Q8. Management of venous ulcers.**
- Compression therapy — cornerstone: multilayer bandage systems (4-layer, 2-layer short-stretch) delivering ~40 mmHg at ankle if ABPI ≥0.8; reduced compression if ABPI 0.5–0.8; then compression stockings class II–III lifelong to prevent recurrence
- Leg elevation, walking/calf exercises, weight loss
- Wound bed preparation (TIME — Tissue debridement, Infection/inflammation control, Moisture balance, Edge advancement): sharp/autolytic/enzymatic/larval debridement; appropriate dressings (hydrocolloid, foam, alginate for exudate, hydrogel for dry, silver/iodine for infection)
- Pentoxifylline 400 mg TDS (improves healing), micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF), aspirin (limited evidence)
- Treat stasis eczema with topical steroid (avoid sensitisers — check patch test), treat infection with systemic antibiotics
- Surgery: endovenous ablation of superficial reflux (EVLA, radiofrequency, foam sclerotherapy) — reduces recurrence (EVRA trial); split-thickness skin grafting, pinch grafts, cellular/tissue-based skin substitutes, PRP, NPWT for large ulcers

**Q9. What is Marjolin's ulcer?**
- Aggressive SCC arising in a chronic ulcer or scar (burns, venous ulcers, osteomyelitis sinus, DLE, lupus vulgaris); suspect with raised everted edge, bleeding, rapid growth, failure to heal — biopsy

**Q10. What is the TIME concept?**
- Framework for wound bed preparation: T — non-viable Tissue removal; I — Infection/Inflammation control; M — Moisture balance; E — Edge of wound (non-advancing/undermined) — later extended to TIMERS (Regeneration, Social factors)

**Q11. Write short notes on Milroy disease (PYQ).**
- Primary congenital lymphoedema (type I) — autosomal dominant FLT4 (VEGFR-3) mutation; bilateral lower-limb lymphoedema at or soon after birth, upslanting toenails, prominent veins, papillomatosis, hydrocele; lymphoscintigraphy shows absent uptake; treated with compression, skin care, prevention of cellulitis
- Other primary lymphoedema: Meige disease (lymphoedema praecox, puberty), lymphoedema tarda (>35 y), lymphoedema–distichiasis (FOXC2)

**Q12. Describe the arterial ulcer and peripheral arterial disease assessment.**
- Risk: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, age; claudication → rest pain → tissue loss (Fontaine/ Rutherford stages)
- Ulcer: punched-out, deep, pale/ necrotic base, little granulation, on toes, heel, lateral malleolus, shin; cold, pale, hairless shiny skin, thickened nails, absent pulses, delayed capillary refill, Buerger's test (pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency)
- ABPI <0.9 PAD, <0.5 critical; toe pressure <30 mmHg poor healing; duplex/ CT angiography; refer for revascularisation; no compression if ABPI <0.5

**Q13. Describe the diabetic foot ulcer and its classification.**
- Neuropathic (painless, plantar pressure points, callus), ischaemic, or neuro-ischaemic; infection and Charcot foot complicate
- Wagner grading: 0 at-risk foot, 1 superficial ulcer, 2 deep ulcer to tendon/ capsule, 3 deep with abscess/ osteomyelitis, 4 forefoot gangrene, 5 whole-foot gangrene; also University of Texas classification (grade + stage — infection/ ischaemia)
- Management: offloading (total contact cast), debridement, infection control (probe-to-bone test — osteomyelitis), glycaemic control, revascularisation, footwear education

**Q14. What is the role of compression — types and pressure?**
- Elastic (long-stretch) bandages/ stockings — high resting pressure; inelastic (short-stretch) bandages/ Unna boot — high working pressure, low resting pressure (better tolerated, good with calf pump)
- Multilayer systems (4-layer: orthopaedic wool, crepe, elastic, cohesive) deliver ~40 mmHg at ankle; stockings — class I (14–17 mmHg), II (18–24, UK) / 20–30 (international), III (25–35) / 30–40 mmHg
- Contraindications: ABPI <0.5–0.6, severe heart failure, severe neuropathy (caution), acute DVT (relative), skin infection

**Q15. Discuss dressings for leg ulcers.**
- Choose by exudate and wound bed: hydrogels (dry/ sloughy — autolytic debridement), hydrocolloids (low–moderate exudate), foams (moderate–heavy exudate), alginates/ hydrofibre (heavy exudate, bleeding), antimicrobial — silver, iodine, honey, PHMB (critical colonisation), non-adherent contact layers (paraffin gauze, silicone); change frequency by exudate
- Avoid sensitisers (lanolin, neomycin, fragrance) — ulcer patients have high contact allergy rates

**Q16. Pyoderma gangrenosum as a cause of leg ulcer — clues.**
- Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with violaceous undermined border, purulent base, starts as pustule, pathergy (worsens after debridement/ surgery), cribriform scarring; associations — IBD, arthritis, haematological malignancy (myeloma, leukaemia), PAPA
- Diagnosis of exclusion (PARACELSUS/ Delphi criteria); biopsy edge to exclude infection/ vasculitis/ malignancy; treat with systemic steroids, cyclosporine, TNF inhibitors (infliximab), IVIG, topical tacrolimus/ steroids; avoid surgical debridement

**Q17. Haematological ulcers — which and why?**
- Sickle cell disease (malleolar ulcers — vaso-occlusion, haemolysis), thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, polycythaemia vera, thrombocytosis, cryoglobulinaemia, cryofibrinogenaemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, protein C/S deficiency — painful ulcers, often around ankles; check CBC, peripheral smear, Hb electrophoresis, thrombophilia screen

**Q18. What is Martorell's ulcer?**
- Hypertensive ischaemic leg ulcer — very painful necrotic ulcer on the lateral/ posterolateral distal leg (often over Achilles) in elderly with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension (and diabetes); arteriolosclerosis with medial calcification; pulses present; treat with BP control, debridement, split-skin grafting (best), pain control

**Q19. Calciphylaxis — features.**
- Calcific uraemic arteriolopathy in end-stage renal disease (and non-uraemic — warfarin, hyperparathyroidism): extremely painful violaceous retiform purpura → necrotic ulcers on thighs, abdomen, legs; high mortality (sepsis); biopsy shows vascular calcification and thrombosis; treat with sodium thiosulphate IV, stop warfarin/ calcium/ vitamin D, cinacalcet/ parathyroidectomy, wound care, hyperbaric oxygen

**Q20. Neuropathic ulcer in leprosy — management.**
- Plantar ulcer over metatarsal heads/ heel due to anaesthesia, dryness, autonomic loss, deformity; rest and offloading (no walking on ulcer), cleaning and dressing, treat infection, below-knee plaster cast for non-healing simple ulcers, protective MCR footwear with insoles, self-care (soak, scrape, oil), surgery for complicated ulcers (osteomyelitis — sequestrectomy)

**Q21. What investigations confirm osteomyelitis under an ulcer?**
- Probe-to-bone test (positive predicts osteomyelitis in diabetic foot), plain X-ray (periosteal reaction, bone destruction — late), MRI (most sensitive), ESR/CRP, bone biopsy for culture and histology (gold standard)

**Q22. Newer advanced therapies for chronic ulcers.**
- Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT/ VAC), autologous platelet-rich plasma/fibrin, growth factors (becaplermin — PDGF), bioengineered skin substitutes (Apligraf, Dermagraft), amniotic membrane, epidermal grafting, hyperbaric oxygen (diabetic foot), electrical stimulation, larval (maggot) debridement therapy, ultrasound debridement

**Q23. What lifestyle advice for venous ulcer patients?**
- Lifelong compression stockings, leg elevation above heart level when resting, regular walking and ankle exercises, weight reduction, avoid prolonged standing/ sitting, skin moisturisation, stop smoking, early review if skin changes or injury

**Q24. Differential diagnosis of an ulcer with raised everted edge.**
- SCC (Marjolin's ulcer), BCC (rolled pearly edge), keratoacanthoma, melanoma (amelanotic), lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, deep fungal infection (chromoblastomycosis, sporotrichosis), tuberculosis (verrucous), leishmaniasis — biopsy the edge

**Q25. Vasculitic ulcer — clues.**
- Multiple, painful, punched-out ulcers with surrounding palpable purpura, livedo racemosa, nodules; systemic symptoms; RA/ SLE/ PAN/ cryoglobulinaemia/ ANCA vasculitis; biopsy (deep, edge) + DIF; treat underlying vasculitis with immunosuppression

**Q26. What is the role of systemic drugs in venous ulcer healing?**
- Pentoxifylline 400 mg three times daily (reduces leucocyte activation, improves microcirculation) — improves healing with or without compression; micronised purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF/ diosmin) — adjunct; aspirin — evidence weak; zinc only if deficient; antibiotics only for clinical infection

**Q27. Prognosis and recurrence.**
- ~50–70% of venous ulcers heal by 12–24 weeks with good compression; recurrence 30–70% in 1 year without stockings and venous surgery; poor prognostic factors — large (>10 cm²), long duration (>6 months), ABPI <0.8, immobility, obesity, deep vein reflux/ post-thrombotic syndrome

## Quick spotter facts
- Gaiter-area shallow ulcer + pigmentation + LDS — venous ulcer
- ABPI <0.8 — no high compression
- Non-healing ulcer with rolled edge — biopsy for Marjolin's SCC

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Leg ulcers, venous disease). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lentigo — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lentigo** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define lentigo.**
- Small (usually <5 mm), well-circumscribed, uniformly brown to brown-black macule due to increased number of melanocytes along the basal layer with elongated pigmented rete ridges; does not darken with sun (unlike freckle)

**Q2. Discuss the various types of lentigines (PYQ).**
- Lentigo simplex: childhood onset, any site including mucosa, not sun-related
- Solar (actinic/senile) lentigo — 'age/liver spots': sun-exposed areas of older adults (dorsa of hands, face), larger, irregular; marker of photodamage; may evolve to reticulated seborrhoeic keratosis or lichen planus-like keratosis
- PUVA lentigines: stellate dark lentigines after PUVA — atypical melanocytes
- Ink-spot (reticulated black solar) lentigo: very dark, irregular, fair skin after sunburn
- Mucosal: labial melanotic macule, genital (penile/vulval) lentiginosis, oral
- Lentiginosis syndromes: Peutz–Jeghers (perioral/buccal lentigines + hamartomatous GI polyps — STK11; GI, breast, pancreatic cancer risk), LEOPARD/Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (PTPN11 — Lentigines, ECG conduction defects, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormal genitalia, Retardation of growth, Deafness), Carney complex (LAMB/NAME — PRKAR1A; cardiac myxomas, endocrine tumours), Laugier–Hunziker (acquired oral and nail pigmentation, benign), Cowden/Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba (penile lentigines — PTEN), centrofacial lentiginosis, partial unilateral lentiginosis, xeroderma pigmentosum

**Q3. Histopathology of solar lentigo.**
- Elongated club/bud-shaped rete ridges with basal hyperpigmentation, increased (not nested, non-atypical) melanocytes, solar elastosis

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Freckle, junctional naevus (nests on histology), lentigo maligna (irregular, enlarging, asymmetric follicular pigmentation on dermoscopy — biopsy), pigmented actinic keratosis, flat seborrhoeic keratosis, café-au-lait macule, pigmented BCC

**Q5. What are the warning signs for lentigo maligna?**
- Asymmetry, irregular borders, variegation, enlargement on face of elderly; dermoscopy — asymmetric pigmented follicular openings, rhomboidal structures, annular-granular pattern, grey dots — needs biopsy

**Q6. Management.**
- Photoprotection; topical hydroquinone, tretinoin, triple combination
- Cryotherapy, Q-switched (532 nm Nd:YAG, ruby, alexandrite) and picosecond lasers, IPL, chemical peels
- Evaluate syndromic lentiginosis (cardiac, GI, endocrine) when multiple/mucosal from childhood

**Q7. What is the LEOPARD syndrome in detail?**
- Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (PTPN11, RAF1): Lentigines (hundreds from childhood, face/ neck/ trunk), ECG conduction defects, Ocular hypertelorism, Pulmonary stenosis, Abnormal genitalia, Retardation of growth, Deafness; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — needs echocardiography

**Q8. What is Laugier–Hunziker syndrome?**
- Acquired, benign macular pigmentation of lips, buccal mucosa, palate, fingertips and longitudinal melanonychia in adults; no GI polyps or cancer risk (unlike Peutz–Jeghers); diagnosis of exclusion

**Q9. What is lentigo maligna and its management?**
- Melanoma in situ on chronically sun-damaged skin (face of elderly) — enlarging irregular brown-black macule; risk of progression to lentigo maligna melanoma (invasion)
- Treatment: surgical excision with 5–10 mm margins/ staged excision or Mohs; imiquimod or radiotherapy for elderly/ non-surgical candidates; long-term follow-up

**Q10. What is the ink-spot lentigo?**
- Reticulated black solar lentigo — a very dark, irregular 'ink-spot' macule on sun-exposed skin of fair individuals; benign; dermoscopy — thick black reticulated network; differentiate from melanoma

**Q11. Mucosal melanotic macules — what to look for?**
- Labial melanotic macule (lower lip), genital lentiginosis — usually benign; biopsy if large (>1 cm), irregular, changing, or multifocal to exclude mucosal melanoma

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. What is Peutz–Jeghers syndrome — management?**
- Autosomal dominant STK11/LKB1; perioral, buccal, digital lentigines from infancy (oral lesions persist, lip lesions fade), hamartomatous GI polyps (intussusception, bleeding), cancer risk — colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, breast, ovarian (sex-cord tumours), testicular (Sertoli) — surveillance endoscopy from age 8, breast and pancreatic screening, genetic counselling

**Q14. What is Carney complex?**
- PRKAR1A mutation: lentigines (face, lips, conjunctiva), blue naevi, cardiac/ cutaneous/ breast myxomas (cardiac myxoma — embolic stroke), endocrine tumours (primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease — Cushing's, pituitary adenoma, thyroid, Sertoli cell tumours), psammomatous melanotic schwannoma; old acronyms LAMB and NAME

**Q15. Lentigo vs solar lentigo dermoscopy.**
- Solar lentigo: light-brown homogeneous areas with sharp moth-eaten borders, fingerprint-like structures, faint reticular network; lentigo simplex: regular network

## Quick spotter facts
- Perioral and buccal lentigines + GI polyps — Peutz–Jeghers
- LEOPARD syndrome — PTPN11
- Enlarging irregular facial pigment in elderly — rule out lentigo maligna

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lentigines). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lichen planus pigmentosus — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen planus pigmentosus** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is lichen planus pigmentosus (LPP)?**
- Variant of LP seen mainly in darker skin (India, Middle East, Latin America) with insidious, persistent dark-brown to slate-grey or blue-grey macules on sun-exposed face and neck or flexures, with little or no itch; now grouped under 'acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation' (ADMH) with ashy dermatosis and pigmented contact dermatitis

**Q2. Triggers.**
- Mustard oil, amla (Indian gooseberry) oil and other hair oils, hair dyes (PPD), henna, fragrances, cosmetics, UV light, hepatitis C, nickel; association with frontal fibrosing alopecia, acrochordons, thyroid disease

**Q3. Clinical patterns.**
- Diffuse, reticulate, blotchy, perifollicular macules
- Sites: forehead, temples, preauricular, neck (most common), upper limbs; inverse LPP — axillae, groin, submammary (lighter-skinned Asians)
- Linear/zosteriform/segmental variants; oral mucosa occasionally; classic LP papules in ~20%

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Vacuolar basal degeneration, sparse lichenoid/perivascular infiltrate, prominent pigment incontinence with many dermal melanophages; atrophic epidermis
- Late lesions: only melanophages (similar to ashy dermatosis/PIH)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Ashy dermatosis/erythema dyschromicum perstans (trunk, grey-blue, active red border in early stage, Latin American), Riehl's melanosis (pigmented contact dermatitis — patch test positive), melasma (brown, symmetrical, cheeks, no grey), drug-induced pigmentation, FDE (recurrent, sharp), macular amyloidosis (rippled, back), acanthosis nigricans (velvety, flexures), post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, exogenous ochronosis, nevus of Ota/Hori

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Dermoscopy (blue-grey dots/globules in perifollicular and speckled patterns), biopsy; patch test (cosmetic, hair-oil and dye series); HCV serology; thyroid function

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Avoid triggers (stop mustard/amla oil, PPD dyes, fragrances); strict photoprotection (including visible light)
- Topical tacrolimus 0.1%, short courses of topical steroids, depigmenting agents (azelaic acid, kojic acid, hydroquinone short-term — limited effect on dermal pigment)
- Systemic: oral tranexamic acid, low-dose isotretinoin, oral mini-pulse steroids (active disease), dapsone, hydroxychloroquine (limited evidence)
- Lasers: Q-switched Nd:YAG low-fluence, picosecond — variable; risk of worsening
- Counsel chronicity

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic, slowly progressive or stable for years; spontaneous fading rare; major cosmetic and psychosocial burden

**Q9. What is the 'acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation' concept?**
- Umbrella term (2014 consensus) for LPP, erythema dyschromicum perstans/ ashy dermatosis, idiopathic eruptive macular pigmentation and pigmented contact dermatitis — overlapping clinical and histological features (interface damage → dermal melanophages) in darker skin

**Q10. Linear/ segmental LPP and inverse LPP.**
- Linear/zosteriform LPP along Blaschko's lines (mosaic predisposition); inverse LPP — axillae, groins, inframammary folds, lighter-skinned Asians/ Caucasians; both chronic

**Q11. What is the association with frontal fibrosing alopecia?**
- Facial LPP occurs in a substantial proportion of FFA patients (especially darker skin) — examine hairline and eyebrows in LPP; both may relate to leave-on cosmetics/ sunscreen exposure

**Q12. Tranexamic acid and other systemic options — doses.**
- Oral tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily (contraindications: thrombosis risk, pregnancy, OCP), low-dose isotretinoin 10–20 mg/day (Indian studies), dapsone 50–100 mg/day, oral mini-pulse dexamethasone in active spreading disease; topical tacrolimus 0.1% twice daily

**Q13. Dermoscopy of LPP.**
- Speckled, dotted, globular blue-grey pigment (dermal melanophages) in perifollicular and diffuse patterns, sparing follicular openings; activity indicated by erythema and fine scale

**Q14. What is the role of patch testing?**
- Contact allergy to hair-dye (PPD), fragrance mix, nickel, mustard oil and cosmetic ingredients is frequently found; avoiding positive allergens can halt progression (overlap with pigmented contact dermatitis/ Riehl's melanosis)

**Q15. Differentiate LPP from ashy dermatosis.**
- LPP: face and neck/flexures, brown to slate-grey, follicular/ diffuse, Indians, triggers (oils/ dyes), may itch; ashy dermatosis (erythema dyschromicum perstans): trunk and proximal limbs, ash-grey oval macules with early raised red border, Latin Americans, asymptomatic; histology similar

## Quick spotter facts
- Slate-grey facial and neck pigmentation in a user of mustard/amla oil — LPP
- Pigment incontinence with sparse lichenoid infiltrate

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen planus pigmentosus; acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lichen planus — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen planus** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define lichen planus (LP).**
- Chronic, immune-mediated (T-cell) inflammatory disease of skin, mucous membranes, hair and nails, classically presenting as pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar (flat-topped), plane-surfaced papules and plaques — the '6 Ps' (pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules, plaques)

**Q2. Aetiopathogenesis.**
- Cell-mediated cytotoxicity: CD8+ T cells target an altered basal keratinocyte antigen (presented via MHC class I) → apoptosis via perforin/granzyme, Fas–FasL; IFN-γ, TNF-α, CXCL9/10 (Th1)
- Associations: hepatitis C virus (oral LP, Mediterranean/Japan), drugs, contact allergens (amalgam — oral), vaccines (HBV), stress, autoimmune disease (thyroid, alopecia areata, vitiligo)

**Q3. Describe the clinical features.**
- Flexor wrists, forearms, shins, ankles, lower back, genitals; symmetrical; intense itch; Koebner phenomenon
- Wickham's striae: fine white lacy network on the surface (focal hypergranulosis) — better seen with oil/dermoscopy
- Heals with marked post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in Indian skin
- Mucosa: oral (50–70%) — reticular (commonest, buccal mucosa), erosive, atrophic, plaque, bullous, papular; genital — glans annular lesions; vulvo-vaginal-gingival syndrome

**Q4. Name the clinical variants.**
- Hypertrophic (shins, verrucous — risk of SCC), annular, linear (Blaschko/Koebner), atrophic, actinic (lichen planus actinicus — sun-exposed, Middle East/India), bullous LP and LP pemphigoides (anti-BP180), ulcerative (palmoplantar), follicular (lichen planopilaris), lichen planus pigmentosus, inverse, guttate, LP–lupus overlap, keratosis lichenoides chronica (Nekam's disease)

**Q5. Discuss variants of lichen planopilaris (PYQ).**
- Classic LPP: perifollicular erythema and scaling with scarring alopecia on vertex
- Frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA): band-like recession of frontal/temporal hairline in post-menopausal women, eyebrow loss, facial papules
- Graham-Little–Piccardi–Lassueur syndrome: scarring scalp alopecia + non-scarring axillary/pubic alopecia + follicular spinous papules
- Treatment: potent/intralesional steroids, hydroxychloroquine, doxycycline, mycophenolate, cyclosporine, 5-α-reductase inhibitors (FFA), pioglitazone

**Q6. Nail changes in lichen planus (PYQ).**
- In ~10%; thinning, longitudinal ridging and splitting (onychorrhexis), dorsal pterygium (fusion of proximal nail fold to bed — characteristic, permanent), trachyonychia (twenty-nail dystrophy), anonychia, red lunulae, subungual hyperkeratosis
- Treat early to prevent permanent damage — intralesional triamcinolone, systemic steroids, retinoids

**Q7. Histopathology of LP.**
- Compact orthokeratosis (no parakeratosis), wedge-shaped hypergranulosis (Wickham's striae), irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, basal vacuolar degeneration with Civatte (colloid) bodies, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the dermo-epidermal junction, pigment incontinence; Max-Joseph spaces (artifactual clefts)
- DIF: shaggy fibrinogen at BMZ, IgM-positive cytoid bodies

**Q8. Define lichenoid reaction and cutaneous lichenoid tissue reaction (PYQ).**
- Lichenoid tissue reaction (interface dermatitis): basal keratinocyte damage (vacuolar change, apoptotic cells) with band-like infiltrate
- Lichenoid diseases: LP, lichenoid drug eruption, lichen nitidus, lichen striatus, LP-like keratosis, GVHD, lupus (vacuolar), EM, fixed drug, lichenoid keratosis, PLEVA, poikiloderma

**Q9. Differentiate lichenoid drug eruption from idiopathic LP.**
- Drugs: antimalarials, gold, β-blockers, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, anti-TB (isoniazid, ethambutol), NSAIDs, imatinib, checkpoint inhibitors, sildenafil
- Clinical: photodistributed, generalised, eczematous/psoriasiform, less Wickham's striae, mucosa less involved, latency weeks–months, resolves slowly after withdrawal
- Histology: parakeratosis, eosinophils, deeper perivascular infiltrate, more necrotic keratinocytes

**Q10. Differentiate LP from DLE (PYQ).**
- LP: purple, polygonal, Wickham's striae, flexures, itchy, hyperpigmentation, no follicular plugging, compact orthokeratosis, band-like infiltrate, DIF — fibrinogen and cytoid bodies
- DLE: red scaly plaques with adherent scale and follicular plugs (carpet-tack sign), face/ears/scalp, photosensitive, atrophy and scarring, depigmentation, periadnexal and perivascular superficial and deep infiltrate, mucin, thick BMZ; DIF — granular IgG/IgM/C3 at DEJ (lupus band)

**Q11. What is Nekam's disease? (PYQ)**
- Keratosis lichenoides chronica: rare chronic lichenoid dermatosis with violaceous keratotic papules in linear/reticulate arrangement on limbs and trunk, seborrhoeic-dermatitis-like facial lesions, nail and oral involvement; resistant to therapy (acitretin, PUVA)

**Q12. Oral LP — significance and management.**
- Reticular often asymptomatic; erosive painful; risk of SCC ~1% (erosive/atrophic types) — long-term follow-up and biopsy of suspicious areas
- Exclude amalgam contact allergy (patch test), HCV, drugs; good oral hygiene, avoid spicy food/tobacco
- Topical potent steroid in orabase/gel (clobetasol), tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, intralesional steroid; systemic steroids, retinoids, HCQ, dapsone, mycophenolate for severe

**Q13. Treatment of cutaneous LP.**
- Localised: potent topical steroid, intralesional triamcinolone for hypertrophic lesions, tacrolimus
- Generalised/rapidly spreading: oral prednisolone 30–60 mg tapered over 4–6 weeks, or betamethasone/dexamethasone weekly oral minipulse (OMP — popular in India), acitretin, NB-UVB/PUVA, metronidazole, griseofulvin (older), methotrexate, cyclosporine, azathioprine, mycophenolate, JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib) for refractory
- Sedating antihistamines for itch; counsel about pigmentation

**Q14. What is lichen planus pigmentosus (LPP)?**
- Variant in darker skin (India, Middle East): slate-grey to brown macules on face, neck, flexures (inverse type) — little itch, chronic; triggers: mustard oil, amla oil, hair dye, sun
- Differential: ashy dermatosis (erythema dyschromicum perstans), melasma, Riehl's melanosis, FDE, acanthosis nigricans
- Treatment difficult: photoprotection, tacrolimus, topical steroid short, tranexamic acid, isotretinoin low-dose, Q-switched laser (caution)

**Q15. Prognosis.**
- Cutaneous LP usually remits in 1–2 years (hypertrophic and oral persist longer); recurrence ~20%; residual pigmentation lasts long

**Q16. Describe dermoscopy of LP.**
- Wickham's striae — white reticular/ radial streaks, 'white network' or 'leaf venation'; red dotted/ linear vessels at periphery; grey-blue dots (pigment incontinence) in resolving/pigmented lesions; useful to differentiate LP from psoriasis and lichenoid drug eruption

**Q17. What is hepatitis C association and its relevance in India?**
- Associations vary geographically — strong in Japan and Mediterranean, weak in India; still advisable to test HCV/HBV in erosive oral LP and extensive disease; LP may flare with interferon therapy (older HCV treatment)

**Q18. Describe genital LP and vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome.**
- Men: annular violaceous papules on glans, 'white lacy' lesions; women: erosive vulvar/vaginal LP with scarring, synechiae, introital stenosis, dyspareunia, + desquamative gingivitis (vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome) — chronic, risk of SCC; treat with clobetasol, tacrolimus, vaginal dilators

**Q19. What is lichen planus pemphigoides vs bullous LP?**
- Bullous LP: blisters within LP lesions due to intense interface damage (Max-Joseph spaces) — DIF negative
- LP pemphigoides: LP plus tense blisters on previously normal skin with antibodies to BP180 (NC16A — MCW-4 epitope); DIF linear IgG/C3 at BMZ; treat like BP + LP (steroids, dapsone, tetracyclines)

**Q20. Describe hypertrophic LP and its risks.**
- Thick hyperkeratotic verrucous plaques on shins/ankles, intensely itchy, chronic (years), pigmented; venous stasis association; may mimic or transform into SCC/keratoacanthoma (biopsy non-healing nodules)
- Treatment: intralesional/ occluded super-potent steroids, acitretin, PUVA, cryotherapy, methotrexate

**Q21. Actinic lichen planus — features.**
- Children and young adults in sunny climates (India, Middle East); annular hyperpigmented plaques with hypopigmented halo or melasma-like patches on face, neck, dorsa of hands; little itch; worse in summer; photoprotection, HCQ, topical steroids, acitretin

**Q22. LP of palms and soles — features.**
- Firm yellowish hyperkeratotic papules/ plaques, sometimes ulcerative LP of soles (painful ulcers, toenail loss — may need grafting); can mimic warts, calluses, psoriasis

**Q23. Drug-induced oral lichenoid reactions vs oral LP.**
- Oral lichenoid lesions near amalgam fillings (contact — patch test to mercury; remove amalgam), unilateral, related to drugs (antimalarials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, antihypertensives), GVHD; oral LP is bilateral, symmetrical

**Q24. What is the Koebner phenomenon in LP?**
- Linear LP papules appear along scratch marks or trauma in ~20% of active disease (isomorphic response) — indicates active disease

**Q25. Childhood LP — differences.**
- Less common; more often linear, eruptive/generalised, actinic and hypertrophic types; oral involvement less; LP-like drug eruption and lichen nitidus overlap; treat with topical steroids, NB-UVB, oral minipulse in extensive disease

**Q26. Lichen nitidus — differentiate from LP.**
- Lichen nitidus: tiny (1–2 mm) shiny skin-coloured flat-topped papules in groups on penis, abdomen, forearms, children; Koebner; asymptomatic; histology — 'ball-and-claw' (well-circumscribed granulomatous infiltrate in a dermal papilla clasped by rete ridges); usually resolves spontaneously

**Q27. What is LP–lupus overlap?**
- Patients have features of both LP and LE (atrophic violaceous plaques on extremities, scarring); histology and DIF show mixed features; ANA may be positive; treat with antimalarials and topical steroids

**Q28. Systemic therapy of severe LP — doses.**
- Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks tapering, or betamethasone/dexamethasone OMP 5 mg on 2 consecutive days/week for 3–6 months
- Acitretin 25–35 mg/day for 8 weeks (strongest evidence among retinoids)
- Methotrexate 7.5–15 mg/week, metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 3–4 weeks (Indian studies), sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine (oral LP), azathioprine, MMF, cyclosporine; NB-UVB/PUVA 2–3 times weekly; JAK inhibitors for refractory

**Q29. Prognosis for scarring forms.**
- LPP, FFA and nail LP (dorsal pterygium) cause permanent scarring/ hair or nail loss — need early aggressive treatment; erosive oral and vulvar LP are chronic with malignancy risk

**Q30. What is the differential diagnosis of violaceous papules?**
- Lichen planus, lichenoid drug eruption, lichen nitidus, lichen striatus, guttate psoriasis, papular secondary syphilis, pityriasis rosea (papular), prurigo, LP-like keratosis (solitary), Kaposi sarcoma (HIV), GVHD (lichenoid)

## Quick spotter facts
- 6 Ps + Wickham's striae — LP
- Dorsal pterygium — nail LP
- Saw-tooth rete ridges, Civatte bodies, band-like infiltrate

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen planus and lichenoid disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen sclerosus et atrophicus** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What is lichen sclerosus (LS)?**
- Chronic inflammatory, scarring, lymphocyte-mediated dermatosis with a strong predilection for anogenital skin; bimodal in women (prepubertal girls and post-menopausal women); in men mostly uncircumcised adults (balanitis xerotica obliterans)
- Associated autoimmunity (thyroid, vitiligo, alopecia areata; antibodies to extracellular matrix protein 1 — ECM1), Koebner, occlusion by urine in uncircumcised males

**Q2. Clinical features in women.**
- Itch (often severe, nocturnal), soreness, dyspareunia, dysuria, constipation in girls
- Porcelain-white atrophic shiny plaques with cigarette-paper wrinkling, purpura/ecchymoses, erosions, fissures in a 'figure-of-eight' around vulva and anus
- Scarring: resorption of labia minora, burying of clitoris (phimosis of clitoral hood), narrowing of introitus; vagina is spared (unlike LP)

**Q3. Clinical features in men.**
- Whitish sclerotic ring on prepuce, glans, coronal sulcus; phimosis (commonest cause of acquired phimosis), meatal stenosis, urethral stricture, painful erections; perianal involvement rare in men

**Q4. Extragenital LS.**
- ~15–20%: white polygonal flat papules coalescing into atrophic plaques with follicular plugging (delling) on trunk, neck, upper arms, under breasts; usually not itchy; does not carry SCC risk

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Hyperkeratosis with follicular plugging, epidermal atrophy, basal vacuolar change, broad band of homogenised pale oedematous collagen in the upper dermis (hyalinisation), beneath which a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Vitiligo (no atrophy/scarring), lichen planus (erosive — vagina involved, Wickham's striae), morphoea (LS–morphoea overlap), mucous membrane pemphigoid (scarring), VIN/ differentiated VIN, extramammary Paget's, child sexual abuse (girls — LS purpura misinterpreted as trauma), lichen simplex, candidiasis

**Q7. What is the malignancy risk?**
- Vulval SCC in ~3–5% of untreated anogenital LS (differentiated VIN pathway, HPV-independent); penile SCC risk also raised; reduced by adequate long-term potent topical steroid therapy
- Lifelong follow-up; biopsy persistent ulcers, thickened, hyperkeratotic or non-responding areas

**Q8. Management.**
- Super-potent topical steroid — clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once daily for 4 weeks, alternate days for 4 weeks, twice weekly for 4 weeks, then maintenance 1–2 times weekly long-term (30 g tube lasts ~3 months)
- Emollients/soap substitutes; avoid irritants; topical tacrolimus/pimecrolimus as second line
- Men: circumcision is often curative for penile LS (with steroids); meatal dilatation/urethroplasty for strictures
- Refractory: intralesional steroids, acitretin, PDT, fractional CO2 laser, PRP/fat grafting (experimental)
- Girls: improves around puberty in some but may persist — continue treatment

**Q9. Dermoscopy of lichen sclerosus.**
- White structureless areas, keratotic follicular plugs (comedo-like openings), linear/dotted vessels, purpuric spots, chrysalis structures (white shiny lines on polarised view)

**Q10. How do you follow up anogenital LS?**
- Review at 3 months, then 6-monthly to yearly lifelong; teach self-examination; ensure adequate steroid use (fear of steroids leads to under-treatment); biopsy any persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque or nodule — differentiated VIN/SCC

**Q11. Pathogenesis of LS in more detail.**
- Autoimmune (anti-ECM1 antibodies in ~70% of women, Th1 cytokines, microRNA-155 up-regulation), genetic (HLA-DQ7), hormonal (low androgen/ oestrogen states — prepubertal, postmenopausal), Koebner (scratching, urine occlusion), possible infection (Borrelia — unproven)

**Q12. Why is circumcision curative in many men?**
- The moist, occluded subpreputial environment with chronic urine exposure drives LS (urine-contact Koebner); removing the prepuce eliminates this trigger — LS confined to prepuce is cured; glans/ meatal disease may persist

**Q13. What is LS in children — key points?**
- Girls 3–7 y: itching, soreness, constipation, dysuria, bleeding/ purpura (can be mistaken for sexual abuse — careful but don't dismiss abuse), figure-of-eight pallor; boys: phimosis
- Treatment same (clobetasol), may improve at puberty but often persists — follow-up into adulthood

**Q14. What is genital LS–LP overlap and differentiation?**
- LP: erosive, involves vagina (LS spares vagina), Wickham's striae at margins, oral involvement; LS: porcelain-white atrophy, figure-of-eight, perianal; overlap occurs — biopsy helps; both treated with clobetasol

**Q15. What is the role of surgery in vulvar LS?**
- Only for complications — perineotomy/ Fenton's procedure for introital narrowing, release of clitoral phimosis/ adhesions, excision of VIN/ SCC; surgery does not cure LS (recurs in grafts)

## Quick spotter facts
- Porcelain-white figure-of-eight atrophy around vulva and anus — LS
- Phimosis in adult male — balanitis xerotica obliterans
- Clobetasol ointment, lifelong follow-up for SCC

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen sclerosus). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lichen simplex chronicus — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen simplex chronicus** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define lichen simplex chronicus (LSC).**
- Circumscribed lichenified plaque produced by chronic repeated rubbing and scratching of skin in response to itch (itch–scratch cycle); also called neurodermatitis circumscripta
- Primary (on apparently normal skin) or secondary (lichenification over AD, contact dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea, insect bites — superimposed LSC)

**Q2. Who gets it and where?**
- Adults 30–50 years, women more; associated with anxiety, stress, obsessive-compulsive tendency, atopy, dry skin
- Sites within reach: nape of neck (women), scalp, ankles/shins, extensor forearms, scrotum, vulva, perianal area, upper eyelids

**Q3. Describe the morphology.**
- Single or few, well-defined, thickened, hyperpigmented (in brown skin) or violaceous plaques with exaggerated skin markings (lichenification), scaling and excoriation; three zones: peripheral papular, middle hyperpigmented/excoriated, central lichenified
- Itch paroxysmal, worse at rest, night, stress; patients 'enjoy' scratching (pleasure-like relief)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Compact hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, irregular psoriasiform acanthosis, vertical collagen streaks in elongated dermal papillae, mild perivascular infiltrate; nerve hyperplasia minimal (more in prurigo nodularis)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Lichen planus hypertrophicus (shins, violaceous, Wickham's striae), psoriasis (silvery scale), chronic eczemas (atopic, nummular, contact), lichen amyloidosis (rippled papules, shins), tinea (KOH), mycosis fungoides, prurigo nodularis, LSC of vulva vs lichen sclerosus (white atrophic) and extramammary Paget's

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Clinical; KOH; patch test for anogenital/scalp LSC (medicaments); biopsy if atypical; screen for systemic causes of itch if widespread; psychological assessment

**Q7. Management — break the itch–scratch cycle.**
- Education: explain the cycle, habit reversal therapy, keep nails short, cover lesions at night (occlusive dressings, Unna boot, hydrocolloid), cotton gloves
- Potent/super-potent topical steroid (clobetasol 0.05%) under occlusion for 2–4 weeks then taper; intralesional triamcinolone 5–10 mg/ml for thick plaques
- Tacrolimus for face/genitals; capsaicin, doxepin cream, menthol, salicylic acid for keratolysis
- Sedating antihistamines (hydroxyzine) at night; SSRIs, gabapentin/pregabalin, tricyclics (doxepin) for neuropathic/psychogenic component; cryotherapy, NB-UVB
- Treat underlying anxiety, depression, OCD

**Q8. What is lichenification?**
- Thickening of skin with accentuated skin markings due to chronic rubbing — seen in LSC, chronic AD, chronic contact dermatitis, lichen planus hypertrophicus

**Q9. Why is the nape of neck commonly involved in women?**
- Accessible spot when stressed, tight collars/hair irritation, associated with seborrhoeic/psychological factors — classic 'lichen nuchae'

**Q10. What is the prognosis?**
- Chronic, relapsing; improves only when scratching habit and psychological factors are controlled

**Q11. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q12. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q13. Dermoscopy findings.**
- White structureless areas with white scales, dotted/ glomerular vessels in clustered/ irregular distribution, erosions/ haemorrhagic crusts (excoriations), accentuated skin markings

**Q14. Anogenital lichen simplex — special points.**
- Scrotum, vulva, perianal skin: intense nocturnal itch, thickened leathery skin; exclude LS, tinea, candidiasis, contact allergy (medicaments, fragrances, condoms), psoriasis, extramammary Paget's (biopsy if persistent); treat with potent steroid ointment, avoid irritants, tacrolimus, address anxiety

**Q15. Intralesional triamcinolone technique for LSC.**
- Triamcinolone acetonide 5–10 mg/ml, 0.1 ml per cm² into the dermis of thickened plaques every 3–4 weeks (max ~20–40 mg/session); side effects — atrophy, hypopigmentation, telangiectasia

## Quick spotter facts
- Single lichenified plaque on nape or ankle in an anxious woman — LSC
- Vertical collagen in papillary dermis on histology

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichen simplex, prurigo). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lichen spinulosus — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen spinulosus** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is lichen spinulosus?**
- Uncommon follicular keratotic eruption, mainly in children and adolescents (boys), with grouped skin-coloured follicular papules each bearing a filiform keratin spine, arranged in round/oval plaques 2–6 cm on neck, buttocks, abdomen, extensor limbs, trunk; feels like a nutmeg grater

**Q2. Aetiology / associations.**
- Mostly idiopathic; atopy, vitamin A deficiency (overlap with phrynoderma), seborrhoeic dermatitis; reported in HIV (with PRP type VI), Crohn's disease, alcoholism, drugs (gold, thallium), lymphoma, syphilis, fungal (id)

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Dilated follicular infundibula filled with keratin plugs (spinous projections above the surface), sparse perifollicular lymphocytes

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Keratosis pilaris (diffuse, not grouped plaques), phrynoderma (malnutrition, larger papules on elbows/knees), PRP (follicular papules on knuckles, orange keratoderma), lichen nitidus (shiny, flat, not spiny), lichen scrofulosorum (TB — yellow-brown lichenoid grouped papules; Mantoux positive), trichodysplasia spinulosa (polyomavirus in immunosuppressed — face), multiple minute digitate hyperkeratoses, follicular eczema, Darier's disease

**Q5. Treatment.**
- Often asymptomatic and self-limiting (months to years)
- Keratolytics: urea 10–20%, salicylic acid 3–6%, lactic acid 12%; topical retinoids; mild topical steroids
- Correct nutritional deficiencies (vitamin A); treat underlying cause (HIV etc.)

**Q6. Describe the clinical features.**
- Children/adolescents (boys more): grouped skin-coloured to slightly red follicular papules each topped by a fine horny spine, forming well-defined round plaques 2–6 cm on neck, trunk, extensor limbs, buttocks; feel like a nutmeg grater; asymptomatic or mildly itchy; symmetrical

**Q7. Name the associations.**
- Atopy, seborrhoeic dermatitis; also reported with HIV, Hodgkin lymphoma, alcoholism, Crohn's disease, vitamin A deficiency (phrynoderma-like), drugs (gold, thallium); 'generalised lichen spinulosus' in adults should prompt systemic evaluation

**Q8. Which other disorders produce follicular spiny papules?**
- Keratosis pilaris, phrynoderma, PRP, Darier's disease, lichen planopilaris, follicular eczema, trichodysplasia spinulosa (polyomavirus in immunosuppressed), multiple minute digitate hyperkeratoses, spiny keratoderma, myeloma-associated follicular spicules

**Q9. Prognosis?**
- Self-limiting — often resolves by puberty; recurrences possible; keratolytics speed improvement

**Q10. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q11. Treatment in detail.**
- Keratolytics — salicylic acid 3–6% ointment, urea 10–20%, lactic acid 12%; topical retinoids (tretinoin, tazarotene); mild topical steroids for itch; emollients; vitamin A in deficient children; resistant cases — oral isotretinoin (rare)

**Q12. Histopathology in detail.**
- Dilated follicular infundibula filled with keratin plugs protruding as spines, mild perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate; hair shaft may be absent

**Q13. Differentiate lichen spinulosus from lichen nitidus and keratosis pilaris.**
- Lichen spinulosus: grouped follicular spiny papules in well-defined plaques
- Lichen nitidus: non-follicular tiny shiny flat-topped papules (ball-in-claw histology)
- KP: diffuse discrete follicular papules on outer arms/ thighs, not in grouped plaques

**Q14. What is the role of dermoscopy?**
- Shows follicular keratotic plugs with central hair shaft or spine, perifollicular erythema; helps differentiate from LP (Wickham's striae) and lichen nitidus

**Q15. Generalised lichen spinulosus in adults — significance.**
- May be associated with HIV, Hodgkin lymphoma, Crohn's disease, alcoholism — consider evaluation if widespread adult-onset

## Quick spotter facts
- Grouped spiny follicular papules forming a plaque on the neck of a child — lichen spinulosus
- Differentiate from lichen scrofulosorum (TB)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Follicular keratoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lichen striatus — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lichen striatus** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. What is lichen striatus?**
- Self-limited, acquired linear inflammatory dermatosis along Blaschko's lines, mainly in children 5–15 years (girls more)
- Thought to be a T-cell reaction to a trigger (viral infection, vaccine, trauma) against a mosaic clone of keratinocytes; associated with atopy

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Sudden eruption of small (1–3 mm) pink, skin-coloured or hypopigmented flat-topped papules that coalesce into a continuous or interrupted band, usually unilateral on one limb (or trunk/neck), may be several centimetres long
- Usually asymptomatic or mild itch; nail involvement (longitudinal ridging, splitting, onycholysis) when the band reaches the finger
- Resolves in 6–12 months (up to 2 years) often leaving hypopigmentation (prominent in Indian skin)

**Q3. What are Blaschko's lines?**
- Lines of embryonic migration of epidermal (ectodermal) cells — V-shape on the back, S-shaped whorls on the abdomen, linear on limbs; they don't follow nerves, vessels or lymphatics; mark genetic mosaicism

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of linear lesions (PYQ: differential diagnosis for linear dermatoses).**
- Following Blaschko lines: lichen striatus, linear LP, ILVEN (inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus — itchy, persistent, from early childhood, psoriasiform), epidermal naevus, linear psoriasis, linear porokeratosis, linear DLE/morphoea (en coup de sabre follows Blaschko), incontinentia pigmenti, blaschkitis (adult)
- Not Blaschko: Koebner lesions (LP, psoriasis, vitiligo), linear warts, zoster (dermatomal), sporotrichoid (lymphatic), phytophotodermatitis (streaks), dermatitis artefacta, linear scleroderma

**Q5. How to differentiate lichen striatus from ILVEN and linear LP.**
- Lichen striatus: sudden onset in a child, self-limiting in months, little itch, hypopigmentation
- ILVEN: onset in infancy, persistent, intensely itchy, psoriasiform/verrucous, resistant to therapy
- Linear LP: violaceous papules with Wickham's striae, adults, itchy, histology of LP, hyperpigmentation

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Lichenoid/interface dermatitis with spongiosis and necrotic keratinocytes plus a deep perivascular and peri-eccrine/peri-follicular lymphocytic infiltrate — the peri-eccrine infiltrate is characteristic

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — self-resolving
- Mild-to-moderate topical steroids or tacrolimus 0.03–0.1% for itch and to hasten resolution, emollients
- Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation recovers gradually; avoid aggressive treatment

**Q8. What is blaschkitis?**
- Adult counterpart with multiple linear bands along Blaschko's lines on the trunk, recurrent, more spongiotic histology — debated whether distinct from lichen striatus

**Q9. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Grey-white structureless areas, white scales, dotted/ glomerular vessels at the periphery of papules — non-specific, helps exclude LP (Wickham's striae) and psoriasis

**Q10. Which age group and sex are typical, and what triggers are described?**
- Children 5–15 years (median ~4 years), girls 2–3× more; triggers — viral infections, vaccinations (BCG, MMR, hepatitis B), trauma, drugs, hypersensitivity; seasonal clustering in spring/summer

**Q11. What are the morphological variants?**
- Classic pink/ skin-coloured papules, hypopigmented (alba) variant (common in dark skin), vesicular, nail-only lichen striatus, bilateral/ multiple bands

**Q12. How to explain prognosis to parents?**
- Self-limiting in 6–12 months, occasionally up to 2–3 years; hypopigmentation may persist months more; recurrence uncommon; no systemic disease; treatment only for itch/ cosmetic concerns

**Q13. What is the immunopathogenesis?**
- Clone of keratinocytes along Blaschko lines (mosaic) becomes targeted by CD8+ T cells after a trigger (loss of immune tolerance to the clone) — explains linear distribution and self-limiting course

**Q14. What is the course of nail lichen striatus?**
- Nail involvement (longitudinal ridging, splitting, onycholysis, nail thinning) occurs when the band reaches the nail matrix; may persist longer than skin lesions but usually resolves completely without scarring

**Q15. Is lichen striatus associated with atopy?**
- Yes — more common in atopic children; may occur in spring/summer clusters (possibly viral trigger); occasionally after vaccinations (BCG, hepatitis B) or infections

## Quick spotter facts
- Child with sudden unilateral band of tiny flat papules on a limb along Blaschko's line — lichen striatus
- Peri-eccrine infiltrate on histology

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lichenoid disorders; Linear dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis (LWNH)?**
- Sporadic mosaic disorder of pigmentation with streaks and whorls of macular hyperpigmentation following Blaschko's lines, appearing at birth or in the first weeks of life; progresses in first 1–2 years then stabilises
- Mosaic chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 7, 18, X-chromosome mosaicism) in some

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Brown macules in linear streaks and whorls ('marble-cake' pattern) on trunk and limbs, sparing face, palms, soles, mucosa, eyes; no preceding inflammation, vesicles or verrucous stages
- Usually isolated, but may have associated anomalies (CNS — seizures, developmental delay; cardiac defects, skeletal asymmetry) — 'LWNH syndrome'

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Increased basal layer melanin, prominent melanocytes; no pigment incontinence (differentiates from incontinentia pigmenti stage 3)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Incontinentia pigmenti (X-linked dominant, girls; inflammatory vesicular → verrucous → hyperpigmented → atrophic stages; pigment incontinence; eye, teeth, CNS)
- Linear epidermal naevus (raised, verrucous), hypomelanosis of Ito (hypopigmented whorls — the 'negative' counterpart), Goltz syndrome (focal dermal hypoplasia), segmental pigmentation disorder, chimerism, X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder

**Q5. Management.**
- Reassurance; screen for systemic anomalies (development, neurology, cardiac, skeletal); genetic consultation/karyotype of skin fibroblasts if systemic features
- No effective treatment; camouflage; lasers rarely help

**Q6. What are Blaschko's lines and why does LWNH follow them?**
- Lines of embryonic migration/proliferation of ectodermal cells — V on the back, S-shaped on the trunk sides, linear on limbs; a post-zygotic mutation in a melanocyte or keratinocyte clone becomes visible along these lines (cutaneous mosaicism)

**Q7. Name other disorders following Blaschko's lines.**
- Incontinentia pigmenti, hypomelanosis of Ito, epidermal naevus/ILVEN, nevus sebaceous, lichen striatus, linear LP, linear porokeratosis, Goltz syndrome, CHILD syndrome, X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (Conradi–Hünermann), segmental Darier's disease, blaschkitis

**Q8. What investigations are needed when LWNH has extracutaneous features?**
- Neurological assessment, EEG if seizures, MRI brain; echocardiography; skeletal survey for asymmetry; ophthalmology; karyotype on cultured skin fibroblasts (blood karyotype may be normal in mosaicism) — genetic counselling

**Q9. Does pigment fade?**
- Pigmentation is usually stable after early childhood, sometimes fades partially with age; no malignant potential

**Q10. Differentiate LWNH from incontinentia pigmenti in detail.**
- IP: X-linked dominant (IKBKG), girls; 4 stages (vesicular → verrucous → hyperpigmented → atrophic/ hypopigmented); eosinophilia; pigment incontinence; teeth, hair, nail, eye, CNS defects
- LWNH: sporadic, both sexes, no vesicles/ warty stage, no eosinophilia, basal hypermelanosis without incontinence

**Q11. What is hypomelanosis of Ito?**
- 'Negative' of LWNH — hypopigmented streaks/ whorls along Blaschko lines from birth/ early infancy; chromosomal mosaicism; associated CNS (seizures, intellectual disability), musculoskeletal and eye anomalies in ~30–60% — needs evaluation

**Q12. What is segmental pigmentation disorder?**
- Block-like (checkerboard) hyper- or hypopigmented patch with sharp midline demarcation (not Blaschkoid) from birth, stable; benign, no systemic association

**Q13. Explain the concept of cutaneous mosaicism types (Happle).**
- Type 1 (Blaschko lines narrow/ broad bands), type 2 (checkerboard), type 3 (phylloid — leaf-like), type 4 (patchy without midline separation), type 5 (lateralisation — CHILD); segmental type 1 and 2 manifestations of autosomal dominant disorders (superimposed mosaicism)

**Q14. Can LWNH be familial or syndromic?**
- Mostly sporadic; rare familial cases and associations with chromosomal mosaicism (trisomy 7, 14, 18, 20, X), neurological, cardiac and skeletal anomalies; genetic testing on skin fibroblasts if systemic features

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Swirls of brown pigment along Blaschko lines from infancy without preceding blisters — LWNH
- No pigment incontinence (vs IP)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Mosaic pigmentary disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lipodermatosclerosis — viva
posts.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lipodermatosclerosis** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Define lipodermatosclerosis (LDS).**
- Chronic sclerosing lobular/septal panniculitis of the lower legs due to chronic venous insufficiency (sclerosing panniculitis, hypodermitis sclerodermiformis); a C4b sign in CEAP classification
- Middle-aged and older women, obesity, venous hypertension

**Q2. Describe acute and chronic phases.**
- Acute: painful, warm, erythematous, indurated plaque on medial lower leg above the malleolus — often mistaken for cellulitis (bilateral, not febrile, no response to antibiotics)
- Chronic: woody, bound-down induration with hyperpigmentation (haemosiderin), sharply demarcated from normal skin above; circumferential fibrosis with oedema above produces an 'inverted champagne-bottle' or 'inverted bowling-pin' leg
- Associated: varicose veins, stasis eczema, atrophie blanche, venous ulcers (risk ↑)

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Venous hypertension → capillary leakage of fibrinogen → pericapillary fibrin cuffs, tissue hypoxia → fat necrosis and fibrosis; fibrinolytic dysfunction; TGF-β1-driven fibrosis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Early: septal lymphocytic infiltrate, ischaemic fat necrosis in centre of lobules
- Late: septal fibrosis/sclerosis, lipomembranous (membranocystic) fat necrosis (feathery eosinophilic membranes lining cystic spaces), haemosiderin, stasis changes (lobular proliferation of thick-walled capillaries)
- Biopsy discouraged — poor healing and ulcer risk; diagnosis is clinical

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acute: cellulitis (unilateral, fever, raised markers), erythema nodosum, morphoea, DVT, panniculitis (lupus profundus, pancreatic)
- Chronic: morphoea profunda, necrobiosis lipoidica, pretibial myxoedema (Graves'), scleroderma, eosinophilic fasciitis, elephantiasis nostras

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Venous duplex ultrasound for reflux/obstruction, ABPI before compression, Doppler to exclude DVT; blood counts/CRP to exclude infection

**Q7. Management.**
- Compression therapy (graduated stockings 30–40 mmHg; bandages initially) — mainstay; leg elevation, exercise, weight loss
- Treat venous reflux: endovenous ablation, sclerotherapy, surgery
- Drugs: pentoxifylline, stanozolol/danazol (anabolic steroids — fibrinolytic; side effects limit use), oxandrolone, aspirin; intralesional triamcinolone for acute painful areas; NSAIDs/analgesia
- Avoid trauma and biopsy; treat stasis eczema

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic progressive condition; acute pain improves with compression; increased risk of venous ulceration

**Q9. What is the role of ultrasound/ duplex in LDS?**
- Confirms superficial venous reflux (great/ small saphenous), deep venous insufficiency or post-thrombotic changes; guides endovenous ablation which improves symptoms and reduces ulceration

**Q10. Why is biopsy discouraged and what if needed?**
- Biopsy wounds in sclerotic, poorly perfused skin heal poorly and may ulcerate; if diagnosis uncertain (e.g. morphoea, panniculitis, malignancy), take a narrow elliptical/ punch biopsy from the margin with compression afterwards

**Q11. Describe the pain management in acute LDS.**
- Graduated compression (start gently as tolerated), NSAIDs, intralesional triamcinolone into painful indurated areas, pentoxifylline, anabolic steroids (stanozolol/ oxandrolone) in resistant cases, ultrasound therapy

**Q12. What is the link between obesity and LDS?**
- Obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure and venous hypertension, reduces calf muscle pump efficiency, worsens lymphatic drainage — LDS is common in obese women even without varicose veins; weight reduction is part of management

**Q13. What is elephantiasis nostras verrucosa and its link?**
- Chronic non-filarial lymphoedema (from venous disease, recurrent cellulitis, obesity, LDS) with cobblestone papillomatous verrucous hyperkeratosis of feet/legs; managed with compression, skin care, keratolytics, oral retinoids, treat infections

**Q14. What is the CEAP clinical class of LDS and its significance?**
- C4b (with atrophie blanche) — advanced chronic venous disease with high risk of ulceration (C5–C6); indicates need for duplex assessment and treatment of reflux

**Q15. What is atrophie blanche and livedoid vasculopathy?**
- Atrophie blanche: ivory-white stellate atrophic scars with telangiectasia and pigmentation around ankles — end result of venous disease or livedoid vasculopathy
- Livedoid vasculopathy: thrombo-occlusive (not inflammatory) disease of dermal vessels with painful purpuric ulcers on ankles (summer), healing as atrophie blanche; associations — thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, raised lipoprotein(a), hyperhomocysteinaemia); treat with antiplatelets/ rivaroxaban, pentoxifylline, IVIG

## Quick spotter facts
- Inverted champagne-bottle leg with woody induration — lipodermatosclerosis
- Bilateral 'cellulitis' not responding to antibiotics — think acute LDS
- Avoid biopsy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Venous disease; panniculitis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lipoma — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lipoma** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is a lipoma?**
- Commonest soft-tissue tumour: benign, slowly growing, encapsulated tumour of mature adipocytes in subcutis; soft, rubbery, mobile, lobulated, painless swelling with 'slip sign' (edge slips under the palpating finger), skin normal; trunk, neck, upper limbs, adults 40–60 y

**Q2. Variants.**
- Angiolipoma (multiple small tender subcutaneous nodules in young men, forearms — painful)
- Spindle-cell/pleomorphic lipoma (posterior neck/shoulder of older men)
- Hibernoma (brown fat), lipoblastoma (children), chondroid lipoma, intramuscular lipoma
- Naevus lipomatosus superficialis (Hoffmann–Zurhelle — soft yellowish papules on buttocks/thighs, fat in dermis)
- Lumbosacral lipoma in infants — marker of spinal dysraphism (with dimple, hair tuft, haemangioma — MRI spine)

**Q3. Syndromes with multiple lipomas.**
- Familial multiple lipomatosis, Madelung's disease (benign symmetric lipomatosis — 'horse-collar' neck fat; alcoholic men), Dercum's disease (adiposis dolorosa — painful lipomas in obese post-menopausal women), Gardner syndrome, Cowden/PTEN hamartoma syndromes, Proteus syndrome, MEN1, Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba, encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Epidermoid/pilar cyst (punctum, firmer, attached to skin), liposarcoma (large >5 cm, deep, rapidly growing, firm — imaging/biopsy), neurofibroma, angiolipoma, hibernoma, lymph node, hernia, haematoma, abscess, soft-tissue sarcoma, ganglion

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Clinical; ultrasound (well-circumscribed hyperechoic/isoechoic mass with striations); MRI for large (>5 cm), deep, subfascial, rapidly growing or painful lesions; histology after excision (MDM2 amplification by FISH to distinguish atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma)

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance if small/asymptomatic
- Surgical excision (enucleation through small incision; squeeze technique), liposuction for large/multiple (risk of incomplete removal), intralesional deoxycholic acid or steroid injection (shrinks small lipomas)
- Discuss indications and complications of excisional surgery (PYQ): indications — cosmetic, symptomatic, diagnostic uncertainty; complications — haematoma, seroma, infection, wound dehiscence, nerve injury, recurrence, scar/keloid

**Q7. Clinical features of lipoma.**
- Soft, rubbery, mobile, painless, lobulated subcutaneous swelling with 'slip sign' (edge slips under examining finger), normal overlying skin, slowly growing; sites — trunk, neck, upper limbs; 1–10 cm; adults 40–60 y

**Q8. What is angiolipoma?**
- Small (<2 cm) multiple tender/ painful subcutaneous nodules in young adults (forearms, trunk); vascular component with fibrin thrombi on histology; may be familial; excision for pain

**Q9. Syndromes with multiple lipomas — details.**
- Familial multiple lipomatosis (AD — numerous painless lipomas on limbs/ trunk), Dercum disease (adiposis dolorosa — painful lipomas in obese post-menopausal women), Madelung disease (benign symmetric lipomatosis — 'horse collar' neck fat in alcoholic men), Gardner syndrome, Proteus syndrome, Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba (PTEN), MEN1, Cowden

**Q10. Imaging role.**
- Ultrasound — well-defined hyperechoic/ isoechoic compressible mass; MRI for deep, large (>5 cm), or atypical lesions — fat signal suppressed on fat-saturation; atypical features (thick septa, nodules) → biopsy for liposarcoma

**Q11. Complications of lipoma excision.**
- Haematoma, seroma, infection, scarring, recurrence (incomplete capsule removal, intramuscular lipoma), nerve injury (forehead lipomas under frontalis — supraorbital nerve)

**Q12. Lipoma in children — consider what?**
- Lipoblastoma (rapidly growing in infants), spinal dysraphism with lumbosacral lipoma (midline lumbosacral fat pad with dimple/ hair tuft — do MRI spine), PTEN hamartoma syndrome

**Q13. Histopathology of lipoma and variants.**
- Mature adipocytes of uniform size in lobules with a thin fibrous capsule; angiolipoma (vessels with fibrin thrombi — painful, multiple, young adults), spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma (back of neck of older men — CD34+, 13q deletion), hibernoma (brown fat), myelolipoma, chondroid lipoma, lipoblastoma (children)

**Q14. When should you suspect liposarcoma?**
- Size >5 cm, deep (subfascial) location, rapid growth, thigh/retroperitoneum, firm, pain, recurrence; MRI — thick septa, nodularity, enhancement; MDM2 amplification (atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma) — needs core biopsy before surgery

**Q15. Excision techniques.**
- Elliptical excision with enucleation, squeeze technique through small incision, liposuction-assisted removal for large lesions; injection lipolysis (deoxycholic acid) experimental

## Quick spotter facts
- Soft lobulated mobile subcutaneous swelling with slip sign — lipoma
- Painful multiple small nodules in young men — angiolipomas
- Lumbosacral lipoma in infant — MRI spine

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tumours of fat). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Lymphogranuloma venereum — viva
posts.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Lymphogranuloma venereum** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. What is LGV? Agent?**
- Systemic STI of lymphatic tissue caused by invasive Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2 (commonest; L2b in MSM proctitis outbreaks), L3
- Obligate intracellular; elementary body (infectious) and reticulate body (replicative)

**Q2. Describe the three stages.**
- Primary (3–30 days): small painless papule, herpetiform ulcer or urethritis/cervicitis — transient, often unnoticed
- Secondary (2–6 weeks later): inguinal syndrome — painful, usually unilateral inguinal/femoral lymphadenitis, matted, may suppurate with multiple sinuses (unlike single opening in chancroid); fever, malaise, arthralgia, erythema nodosum/multiforme; anorectal syndrome in receptive anal sex/women — haemorrhagic proctocolitis
- Tertiary (late): genitoanorectal syndrome — chronic lymphatic obstruction and fibrosis: esthiomene, elephantiasis of genitals, rectal stricture, fistulae, perianal lymphorrhoids, frozen pelvis

**Q3. What is the groove sign?**
- Enlarged inguinal nodes above and femoral nodes below the inguinal (Poupart's) ligament separated by a groove — seen in ~20%; suggestive but not diagnostic

**Q4. What is esthiomene? (PYQ)**
- Chronic progressive hypertrophy and ulceration ('eating away') of the vulva due to lymphatic obstruction from LGV — elephantiasis with ulcers, fistulae; also seen with donovanosis, TB, filariasis
- Management: long antibiotic course + reconstructive surgery (vulvectomy/plastic)

**Q5. What is the Frei test?**
- Historical intradermal skin test with LGV antigen (delayed hypersensitivity) — obsolete because of poor specificity and safety

**Q6. Investigations.**
- NAAT (PCR) of ulcer swab, bubo aspirate or rectal swab for C. trachomatis with genotyping for L serovars (best)
- Serology: complement fixation titre ≥1:64 or microimmunofluorescence ≥1:256 supports LGV
- Culture in McCoy cells (rarely done); Giemsa — Gamna–Favre inclusion bodies
- Exclude syphilis, HIV, chancroid

**Q7. Differential diagnosis of inguinal bubo.**
- Chancroid (painful single opening), syphilis (painless rubbery), donovanosis pseudobubo, herpes (tender small nodes), TB lymphadenitis, plague, cat-scratch disease, lymphoma/metastatic nodes, filariasis, pyogenic lymphadenitis from leg infection, incarcerated hernia

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days (drug of choice)
- Alternatives: erythromycin 500 mg four times daily for 21 days (pregnancy), azithromycin 1 g weekly for 3 weeks
- NACO black kit (doxycycline 21 days + azithromycin 1 g) for bubo
- Aspirate fluctuant nodes through healthy skin; do not incise (sinus formation); surgery for late strictures/elephantiasis
- Treat contacts in last 60 days

**Q9. Differentiate LGV proctitis from inflammatory bowel disease.**
- LGV: MSM/receptive anal sex, rapid onset, rectal pain, tenesmus, mucopurulent bloody discharge, PCR positive, rapid response to doxycycline
- Crohn's: chronic, skip lesions, perianal fistula, granulomas, no infection
- Histology can look similar — always test rectal swab

**Q10. Complications?**
- Rectal stricture, rectovaginal fistula, lymphoedema/elephantiasis of genitals ('saxophone penis'), esthiomene, infertility, rarely SCC; systemic — hepatitis, pneumonitis, meningitis

**Q11. Describe the pathogenesis of LGV.**
- L serovars infect macrophages and travel through lymphatics → lymphadenitis with stellate abscesses (necrosis with surrounding palisading histiocytes) → suppuration, sinus formation, chronic lymphatic obstruction and fibrosis → elephantiasis and strictures

**Q12. Histopathology of LGV lymph node.**
- Stellate (star-shaped) abscesses with central neutrophils and necrosis surrounded by palisaded epithelioid histiocytes — also seen in cat-scratch disease, tularaemia, Yersinia, fungal infections

**Q13. What is 'saxophone penis'?**
- Late LGV lymphoedema of the penis and scrotum producing a deformed, swollen, twisted penis — also from filariasis or chronic HS; needs reconstructive surgery

**Q14. LGV in MSM — current epidemiology.**
- Outbreaks of L2b proctitis among men who have sex with men (Europe, North America) often with HIV co-infection; may be asymptomatic rectal carriage; test rectal swabs with NAAT and genotype

**Q15. What is the follow-up and partner management?**
- Clinical follow-up until resolution (bubo/ proctitis); test-of-cure NAAT for rectal infection after 3–4 weeks in some guidelines; treat all partners within 60 days with doxycycline 7 days (or full LGV course if symptomatic); screen for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis

## Quick spotter facts
- Groove sign — LGV
- Esthiomene — chronic ulcerating vulval elephantiasis
- Doxycycline 21 days (black kit)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (LGV); NACO National Technical Guidelines on RTI/STI (syndromic management, colour-coded kits). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Macular and lichen amyloidosis — viva
posts.summary: Nutritional & metabolic · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Macular and lichen amyloidosis** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What is amyloidosis? Classify cutaneous amyloidosis.**
- Extracellular deposition of insoluble fibrillar proteins with β-pleated sheet structure that show apple-green birefringence with Congo red
- Primary localised cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA): keratinocyte-derived (amyloid K) — macular, lichen (papular), biphasic (both), nodular (AL — plasma-cell light chains; risk of systemic progression ~7%), poikiloderma-like, bullous, anosacral, familial (OSMR, IL31RA mutations)
- Secondary localised: in tumours (BCC, seborrhoeic keratosis), PUVA, after injections (insulin amyloid)
- Systemic amyloidosis with skin involvement: AL (primary/myeloma — periorbital 'pinch purpura', waxy papules, macroglossia), AA (secondary — chronic inflammation; skin rarely involved), β2-microglobulin (dialysis), ATTR (familial/senile)

**Q2. Describe macular amyloidosis.**
- Grey-brown rippled (reticulate) pigmentation on the upper back (interscapular), arms, shins; mild to moderate itch
- Common in Asians, Middle East, Latin Americans; women; friction (nylon scrubs, loofahs, towels — 'friction melanosis' overlap)

**Q3. Describe lichen amyloidosis.**
- Very itchy, discrete firm hyperkeratotic hyperpigmented papules often in a rippled/linear pattern coalescing into plaques on shins (commonest), extensor forearms, thighs, upper back; men > women
- Associations: atopic dermatitis, MEN 2A (RET), familial (OSMR/IL31RA), chronic friction/scratching, lichen planus, hepatitis/biliary cirrhosis

**Q4. Pathogenesis.**
- Keratinocyte damage (friction, scratching, UV, genetic) → apoptotic keratinocyte filaments (cytokeratins, especially CK5) altered into amyloid by dermal macrophages/fibroblasts → deposits in papillary dermis
- Itch–scratch cycle perpetuates (IL-31/OSMR pathway)

**Q5. Describe stains used for amyloid (PYQ).**
- Congo red — salmon pink on light microscopy; apple-green birefringence under polarised light (gold standard)
- Crystal violet / methyl violet — metachromasia (purple-red)
- Thioflavin T / S — yellow-green fluorescence under UV (sensitive)
- Sirius red, PAS (weakly positive, diastase resistant), Alcian blue, Pagoda red, DFF (dylon), cotton dyes (Pagoda red, Dylon) — high sensitivity in skin
- Immunohistochemistry: anti-cytokeratin (34βE12 — PLCA), anti-κ/λ (AL), anti-AA, anti-TTR
- Electron microscopy: non-branching 7.5–10 nm fibrils
- Lugol's iodine (gross specimen — mahogany brown, turning blue with sulphuric acid)

**Q6. Histopathology of macular/lichen amyloidosis.**
- Small globular eosinophilic deposits in dermal papillae (macular — subtle, needs special stains), with pigment incontinence (melanophages)
- Lichen: larger deposits filling and expanding papillae + hyperkeratosis, acanthosis (features of chronic rubbing)
- Nodular: diffuse deposits throughout dermis, around vessels, with plasma cells (AL type)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
