- Macular: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, notalgia paraesthetica (localised itchy patch under scapula — T2–T6 nerve entrapment), friction melanosis, ashy dermatosis, lichen planus pigmentosus, prurigo pigmentosa, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, tinea versicolor
- Lichen: lichen simplex chronicus, hypertrophic LP, prurigo nodularis, pretibial myxoedema, colloid milium, lichen myxoedematosus

**Q8. Investigations.**
- Clinical + dermoscopy (central white/brown hub with radiating pigmentation); biopsy with special stains
- If nodular amyloidosis or systemic signs: serum and urine protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, serum free light chains, CBC, renal function, urine protein, echocardiography, abdominal fat-pad aspirate; MEN 2A screening (calcitonin, metanephrines, RET) in familial lichen amyloidosis with family history of medullary thyroid cancer

**Q9. Management.**
- Avoid friction (no nylon scrubbers), break itch–scratch cycle, sedating antihistamines, emollients, menthol/pramoxine
- Potent topical steroids under occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone (lichen), tacrolimus, calcipotriol, DMSO (dimethyl sulphoxide), capsaicin
- Keratolytics (salicylic acid, urea) for lichen papules; acitretin 0.5 mg/kg/day for extensive lichen amyloidosis
- Phototherapy (NB-UVB, PUVA), cyclosporine, dupilumab/nemolizumab (itch — case reports)
- Procedures: dermabrasion, CO2/Er:YAG laser, Q-switched Nd:YAG (macular pigment), fractional lasers
- Nodular: excision, laser; follow up for systemic AL

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Benign chronic course; recurrence common; nodular type needs monitoring for systemic amyloidosis

**Q11. What is nodular amyloidosis and why follow up?**
- Single or multiple waxy yellow-pink nodules/ plaques on face, legs, genitals; AL (light-chain) amyloid from local plasma cell clone; ~7% progress to systemic AL amyloidosis or are associated with Sjögren's — need SPEP/ immunofixation and annual review

**Q12. Systemic AL amyloidosis skin signs.**
- Pinch purpura (periorbital 'raccoon eyes' after coughing/ proctoscopy), waxy translucent papules (eyelids, flexures), macroglossia, nail dystrophy, alopecia, scleroderma-like induration, carpal tunnel syndrome; heart/ kidney involvement determines prognosis

**Q13. What is biphasic amyloidosis?**
- Coexistence of macular and lichen amyloidosis in the same patient — supports the view that they are a spectrum of the same keratinocyte-derived process

**Q14. Friction melanosis vs macular amyloidosis.**
- Friction melanosis: dark pigmentation over bony prominences (clavicles, scapulae, spine) from nylon towels/ scrubbers, no amyloid on special stains; macular amyloidosis: rippled pigmentation with amyloid deposits — both improved by stopping friction

**Q15. What is notalgia paraesthetica?**
- Localised itchy, sometimes burning hyperpigmented patch medial to the scapula (T2–T6) due to dorsal spinal nerve entrapment/ degenerative spine disease; may show secondary macular amyloid; treat with capsaicin, lidocaine, gabapentin, physiotherapy, botulinum toxin

## Quick spotter facts
- Rippled grey-brown interscapular pigmentation — macular amyloidosis
- Itchy rippled papules on shins — lichen amyloidosis
- Congo red apple-green birefringence

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous amyloidosis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Melasma — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Melasma** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define melasma.**
- Acquired, chronic, relapsing, symmetrical hypermelanosis of sun-exposed skin (mostly face) with light- to dark-brown irregular macules and patches; common in women of reproductive age with Fitzpatrick types III–V (Indian, Hispanic, Asian)

**Q2. Aetiological factors.**
- UV and visible light (high-energy visible/blue light — esp. in darker skin), heat
- Hormonal: pregnancy (chloasma/'mask of pregnancy'), oral contraceptives, hormone replacement, thyroid autoimmunity
- Genetic: family history in ~50%
- Others: cosmetics (perfumes — photosensitising), phototoxic drugs (anticonvulsants), stress, ovarian disorders

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Not merely melanocyte hyperactivity: photo-aged dermis (solar elastosis), increased vascularity (VEGF, endothelin-1), mast cells, disrupted basement membrane (pendulous melanocytes, dermal melanin drop), increased α-MSH, SCF/c-KIT, Wnt signalling, sebocyte factors — 'photoageing disorder of susceptible skin'

**Q4. Clinical patterns.**
- Centrofacial (forehead, cheeks, nose, upper lip, chin — commonest, ~60%), malar (cheeks and nose), mandibular (jawline), extrafacial (forearms, V of neck — older women)
- By depth (old Wood's lamp classification): epidermal (enhanced contrast — better prognosis), dermal (no enhancement — poor), mixed (commonest); now replaced by dermoscopy/RCM

**Q5. Discuss causes of facial hyperpigmentation (PYQ).**
- Melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (acne), Riehl's melanosis (pigmented contact dermatitis — cosmetics, kumkum), lichen planus pigmentosus, ashy dermatosis, nevus of Ota/Hori's naevus (acquired bilateral naevus of Ota-like macules), freckles/lentigines, drug-induced (minocycline, amiodarone, antimalarials, phenytoin, chlorpromazine, clofazimine), exogenous ochronosis (hydroquinone misuse), acanthosis nigricans (face), periorbital hyperpigmentation, frictional melanosis, phytophotodermatitis, Addison's disease, haemochromatosis, erythromelanosis follicularis faciei, maturational dyschromia, topical steroid-induced dyspigmentation

**Q6. How do you assess severity?**
- MASI (Melasma Area and Severity Index — area, darkness, homogeneity in forehead 30%, right malar 30%, left malar 30%, chin 10%; 0–48), modified MASI (area + darkness; 0–24), MELASQOL (quality of life)
- Dermoscopy: brown pseudo-network (epidermal), blue-grey granules (dermal), telangiectasia, sparing of follicles

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Increased epidermal melanin (basal and suprabasal), enlarged dendritic melanocytes (not necessarily increased number), dermal melanophages, solar elastosis, increased vessels and mast cells, basement membrane damage

**Q8. Discuss treatment of melasma (PYQ: depigmenting agents — indications, side effects).**
- Strict photoprotection: broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF ≥30 with UVA protection and tinted (iron oxide) for visible light, reapplied every 2–3 h; physical protection; stop OCP/ photosensitising cosmetics
- First-line topical: triple combination cream (Kligman's modified — hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) nightly for up to 8–12 weeks then maintenance with non-steroid agents (avoid prolonged unsupervised use — steroid damage, ochronosis)
- Hydroquinone 2–4% (tyrosinase inhibitor; side effects — irritation, contact dermatitis, exogenous ochronosis with long-term high strength, confetti depigmentation)
- Non-hydroquinone agents: azelaic acid 15–20%, kojic acid, arbutin, tranexamic acid (topical), cysteamine 5%, niacinamide 4%, thiamidol, licorice extract, vitamin C, retinoids, methimazole, glutathione (topical)
- Oral tranexamic acid 250 mg twice daily for 3–6 months (plasmin inhibitor — reduces melanocyte stimulation and vascularity; check for thromboembolic risk, avoid in pregnancy/OCP use/clotting disorders); Polypodium leucotomos
- Procedures (adjuncts, cautious in dark skin): chemical peels — glycolic acid 20–70%, salicylic 20–30%, lactic, Jessner's, TCA low strength; microneedling with tranexamic acid; lasers — low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG (laser toning), picosecond, fractional non-ablative, PDL for vascular component; risk of rebound and mottled hypopigmentation

**Q9. What is exogenous ochronosis?**
- Blue-black/slate-grey speckled pigmentation with 'caviar-like' papules on sites of long-term hydroquinone (or phenol, resorcinol, antimalarial) use — inhibits homogentisic acid oxidase locally; histology — yellow-brown banana-shaped fibres in dermis; very difficult to treat (stop agent, sunscreens, Q-switched lasers, CO2)

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Chronic and relapsing (especially with sun exposure); pregnancy melasma may fade after delivery; dermal component resistant; maintenance therapy and sun protection lifelong

**Q11. Describe dermoscopic patterns of melasma and their use.**
- Light brown homogeneous pseudo-network (epidermal), dark-brown dots/ globules, blue-grey granules (dermal), telangiectatic vessels (vascular component — consider tranexamic acid/ PDL), sparing of follicles; guides therapy and prognosis — better than Wood's lamp

**Q12. Chemical peels for melasma — which and how?**
- Glycolic acid 20–70% (start low, 2–4 weekly), salicylic acid 20–30%, lactic acid, mandelic acid, Jessner's, modified Jessner's, TCA 10–15%, yellow (retinoic acid) peel; series of 4–6 peels with home triple combination and sunscreen; risk of PIH and irritation in dark skin — prime with hydroquinone 2 weeks before

**Q13. Laser toning — what is it and risks?**
- Low-fluence Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064 nm (large spot, multiple passes, weekly) — sub-cellular selective photothermolysis of melanosomes; risks: mottled hypopigmentation (confetti), rebound hyperpigmentation, relapse; combine with topicals, not first line

**Q14. What is the role of glutathione (oral/IV) for melasma?**
- Antioxidant that shifts eumelanin to pheomelanin; oral/ topical glutathione has modest evidence; IV glutathione for skin lightening is not approved (FDA/ CDSCO warnings) — risks of liver/ kidney toxicity, SJS, anaphylaxis; should not be advised

**Q15. Melasma in men — features.**
- ~10% of cases; similar patterns (malar commonest), sun exposure and family history main factors; lower hormonal association; treat similarly

**Q16. What are the quality-of-life tools and counselling points?**
- MELASQOL (10-item, 7-point scale); counsel chronicity, maintenance with sunscreen (including visible light), realistic expectations, avoid unsupervised steroid-containing creams (topical steroid damaged face), and avoid OTC hydroquinone misuse

## Quick spotter facts
- Symmetrical brown facial patches in a woman, worse with sun/pregnancy — melasma
- Triple combination + sunscreen first line; oral tranexamic acid
- Long hydroquinone misuse → exogenous ochronosis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Melasma); Indian/Pigmentary Disorders Society consensus on melasma. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Miliaria — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Miliaria** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is miliaria?**
- Eruption caused by obstruction of eccrine sweat ducts with leakage of sweat into the epidermis/dermis — common in hot humid climates, neonates (immature ducts), febrile patients, occlusive clothing/dressings, bedridden patients

**Q2. Classify miliaria by the level of duct obstruction.**
- Miliaria crystallina (sudamina): obstruction in stratum corneum — tiny clear superficial dew-drop vesicles without inflammation, rupture easily; neonates, fever
- Miliaria rubra (prickly heat): intra-epidermal (spinous layer) — itchy/prickly red papules and papulovesicles on trunk, flexures, neck; commonest
- Miliaria pustulosa: miliaria rubra with sterile/superficial pustules
- Miliaria profunda: dermo-epidermal junction — non-itchy skin-coloured firm papules after repeated episodes in tropics; associated with anhidrosis and heat exhaustion ('tropical anhidrotic asthenia')

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Excess sweating + occlusion → maceration of stratum corneum → keratin plugs and PAS-positive material (extracellular polysaccharide from Staphylococcus epidermidis biofilm) block the duct → sweat leaks out → inflammation

**Q4. Discuss the composition of sweat (PYQ).**
- Eccrine sweat is hypotonic: water (~99%), sodium chloride (Na 10–90 mmol/L — reabsorbed in the duct), potassium, urea, lactate, ammonia, bicarbonate, amino acids, antimicrobial peptides (dermcidin, cathelicidin), immunoglobulin A; pH 4–6.8
- Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L in cystic fibrosis (diagnostic sweat test)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Neonates: erythema toxicum neonatorum, transient neonatal pustular melanosis, neonatal acne/cephalic pustulosis, candidiasis, herpes, staph folliculitis, impetigo
- Adults: folliculitis, Pityrosporum folliculitis, Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis — sweat-induced), insect bites, varicella (crystallina), drug eruption (AGEP)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Cool environment, air conditioning, fans, loose cotton clothing, reduce sweating and occlusion, frequent cool baths
- Calamine lotion, mild topical steroids for rubra, anhydrous lanolin (prevents duct blockage in profunda), menthol/camphor lotions; antiseptics/antibiotics for pustulosa
- Avoid heavy creams/ointments; treat fever

**Q7. Describe the physiology of sweating and thermoregulation.**
- Eccrine glands (2–4 million) secrete in response to hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre via sympathetic cholinergic fibres (acetylcholine on M3 receptors); primary isotonic secretion in the coil, sodium reabsorbed in the duct (hypotonic final sweat — defective in cystic fibrosis: high sweat chloride); emotional sweating on palms/soles/axillae; evaporation is the main cooling mechanism in heat

**Q8. What is tropical anhidrotic asthenia?**
- Widespread miliaria profunda in hot climates leading to anhidrosis of trunk with compensatory facial sweating, heat intolerance, weakness, risk of heat stroke; occurs in soldiers/ workers in tropics; move to cool environment, treat miliaria

**Q9. Drug-induced miliaria.**
- Bethanechol, isotretinoin, doxorubicin, clonidine; occlusive dressings/ topical agents; also post-febrile and in patients confined to bed

**Q10. Miliaria in neonates — differentials.**
- Erythema toxicum neonatorum (eosinophils, day 2–3), transient neonatal pustular melanosis (pigmented collarettes, at birth), neonatal acne, neonatal candidiasis, staphylococcal pustulosis, herpes simplex — Gram stain/ Tzanck smear help

**Q11. What is periporitis staphylogenes?**
- Secondary staphylococcal infection of miliaria (pustulosa) forming multiple sweat-gland abscesses in infants (scalp, face, neck, buttocks) — needs systemic antibiotics and cooling

**Q12. Treatment details.**
- Cooling, light cotton clothes, air-conditioning, tepid baths; calamine lotion, mild topical steroid for inflamed rubra; anhydrous lanolin (profunda — unplugs ducts), antiseptics for pustulosa; avoid heavy occlusive emollients; vitamin C supplementation (anecdotal)

**Q13. Describe the clinical types in detail.**
- Miliaria crystallina (sudamina): obstruction in stratum corneum — tiny clear superficial dew-drop vesicles without inflammation; neonates in the first week, febrile patients; rupture easily
- Miliaria rubra (prickly heat): obstruction in mid-epidermis (spinous layer) — itchy/prickly red papules and papulovesicles (non-follicular) on trunk, flexures, covered areas; miliaria pustulosa when pustular
- Miliaria profunda: obstruction at dermo-epidermal junction — skin-coloured papules, no itch, after repeated miliaria rubra in tropics; anhidrosis → heat exhaustion (tropical anhidrotic asthenia)

**Q14. Histopathology.**
- Crystallina: subcorneal/intracorneal vesicle; rubra: spongiotic vesicle in the epidermis around the sweat duct (acrosyringium) with PAS-positive plug and periductal infiltrate; profunda: dermal oedema and lymphocytes around the duct in upper dermis

**Q15. Prevention in neonates and adults.**
- Avoid overheating and over-swaddling; light cotton clothes, air-conditioning/fans, cool baths, avoid occlusive creams (heavy emollients), anhydrous lanolin to clear plugs (profunda)

## Quick spotter facts
- Dew-drop vesicles in febrile neonate — miliaria crystallina
- Prickly red papules in summer — miliaria rubra

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of eccrine sweat glands). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Milium / colloid milium — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Milium / colloid milium** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What are milia?**
- Small (1–2 mm), superficial, white-yellow, keratin-filled epidermoid cysts (arising from vellus hair follicles or eccrine ducts) — very common on face (eyelids, cheeks, nose) of all ages, especially newborns (~40–50%)

**Q2. Classify milia and explain their clinical features (PYQ).**
- Primary: congenital/neonatal (face, palate — Epstein pearls; gingiva — Bohn's nodules; resolve in weeks), benign primary milia in children/adults (eyelids, cheeks), milia en plaque (cluster on erythematous plaque — retroauricular/eyelid), multiple eruptive milia, nodular grouped milia, genodermatoses (Bazex–Dupré–Christol, Rombo, Gorlin, oro-facial-digital syndrome type I, Marie–Unna hypotrichosis, pachyonychia congenita)
- Secondary: after blistering diseases (EB dystrophica, porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid, EBA), trauma, burns, dermabrasion, laser resurfacing, radiotherapy, potent topical steroids (atrophy), drugs (cyclosporine, penicillamine)

**Q3. Histopathology of milia.**
- Small epidermoid cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with granular layer, containing laminated keratin

**Q4. Treatment of milia.**
- Neonatal: self-resolve — no treatment
- Extraction/de-roofing with a sterile needle or No.11 blade and expression; electrodesiccation, CO2 laser; topical retinoids for multiple; minocycline for milia en plaque

**Q5. Add a note on colloid milium (PYQ).**
- Rare degenerative condition with deposition of homogeneous eosinophilic 'colloid' material in the papillary dermis giving translucent, yellowish-brown or amber, dome-shaped papules that ooze gelatinous material on puncture
- Types: adult colloid milium (commonest — sun-exposed face, dorsa of hands, neck in middle-aged outdoor workers; chronic UV, petroleum/hydroquinone exposure; derived from elastic fibres/solar elastosis), juvenile colloid milium (before puberty; derived from keratinocytes — keratin; may be familial; associated with ligneous conjunctivitis), nodular colloid degeneration (single nodule, face/trunk), pigmented colloid milium (hydroquinone-related, ochronosis-like)
- Histology: fissured homogeneous eosinophilic material in papillary dermis with clefts, grenz zone; stains weakly with Congo red/PAS (may mimic amyloid); juvenile type keratin-positive
- Differential: lichen/nodular amyloidosis, syringomas, sebaceous hyperplasia, lipoid proteinosis, milia, hydrocystomas, xanthomas, molluscum
- Treatment: photoprotection; dermabrasion, cryotherapy, CO2/Er:YAG/fractional lasers, diathermy, curettage — recurrences common

**Q6. What are the types of colloid milium?**
- Adult type (commonest): sun-exposed face/dorsa of hands, middle-aged men with heavy sun exposure or petroleum/hydroquinone exposure — degenerated elastic fibres (elastotic)
- Juvenile (childhood, before puberty — keratinocyte-derived, amyloid-like, familial/ligneous conjunctivitis association), nodular colloid degeneration (single large nodule), pigmented colloid milium (hydroquinone-related ochronosis-like)

**Q7. Histopathology of colloid milium.**
- Fissured homogeneous pale eosinophilic colloid masses in the papillary dermis with clefts, separated from the epidermis by a thin grenz zone; adult type — elastic origin; juvenile — derived from keratinocytes (keratin positive); Congo red may be weakly positive

**Q8. What is milia en plaque?**
- Multiple milia grouped on an erythematous oedematous plaque, usually behind the ears/eyelids — associated with DLE, lichen planopilaris, pseudoxanthoma elasticum; treated by extraction, retinoids, minocycline, surgery

**Q9. Which conditions cause secondary milia?**
- Subepidermal blistering diseases healing with milia — epidermolysis bullosa (dystrophic), porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid, EBA, bullous LP; after dermabrasion, laser resurfacing, burns, potent topical steroids, radiotherapy

**Q10. Describe the clinical features of primary milia.**
- Multiple 1–2 mm firm white-yellow keratin cysts on eyelids, cheeks, nose, genitalia; congenital milia in ~40–50% neonates (nose, resolve in weeks); Epstein pearls (palate) and Bohn's nodules (gums) are oral counterparts

**Q11. What genodermatoses have milia?**
- Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome (milia, follicular atrophoderma, BCCs, hypotrichosis), oral-facial-digital syndrome type I, Rombo syndrome, Loeys–Dietz, pachyonychia congenita (steatocystomas), dystrophic EB, Brooke–Spiegler

**Q12. Technique of milia extraction.**
- Clean with alcohol, nick the surface with a no. 11 blade or 26 G needle, express the keratin with a comedone extractor/ curette; topical retinoids for multiple; electrodesiccation or erbium laser

**Q13. Clinical features of colloid milium.**
- Translucent yellow-brown, firm 1–4 mm papules on sun-exposed face (cheeks, nose, forehead), dorsa of hands, back of neck; exudes gelatinous material when punctured; often heavy outdoor workers (farmers) in India

**Q14. Treatment of colloid milium.**
- Strict sun protection, dermabrasion, CO2/ Er:YAG laser ablation, fractional lasers, cryotherapy, curettage, diathermy; recurrence possible

**Q15. Differential diagnosis of milium-like lesions.**
- Syringoma (eyelids — skin-coloured flat papules), sebaceous hyperplasia, closed comedones (whiteheads), molluscum (umbilicated), xanthelasma (yellow plaques), trichoepithelioma, calcinosis cutis, steatocystoma

## Quick spotter facts
- Tiny white keratin cysts on eyelids — milia
- Translucent amber papules on sun-exposed face oozing gel — colloid milium

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cysts; colloid milium). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Molluscum contagiosum — viva
posts.summary: Viral infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Molluscum contagiosum** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What is molluscum contagiosum?**
- Common benign self-limiting infection of the epidermis by molluscum contagiosum virus (poxvirus, genus Molluscipoxvirus; MCV-1 commonest, MCV-2 more in adults/HIV)
- Largest DNA virus pathogenic to humans; replicates in the cytoplasm

**Q2. Who gets it and how does it spread?**
- Children (direct contact, shared towels, swimming pools), sexually active adults (genital/pubic area), immunosuppressed (HIV, transplant) and atopic children
- Autoinoculation by scratching (Koebner) and shaving

**Q3. Describe the lesion.**
- Firm, smooth, pearly white or skin-coloured dome-shaped papules 2–5 mm with central umbilication; cheesy core can be expressed
- Children: trunk, flexures, face, limbs; adults: genitals, thighs, lower abdomen
- Giant molluscum (>1 cm), and many facial lesions — think HIV (CD4 <100)
- Molluscum dermatitis (eczema around lesions), 'BOTE' sign — inflamed lesions (Beginning Of The End) signalling regression

**Q4. What are molluscum bodies?**
- Large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson–Paterson bodies) in the keratinocytes of a lobulated, cup-shaped, endophytic epidermal proliferation
- Seen on squash smear of the expressed core (Giemsa/Wright) or biopsy

**Q5. Differential diagnosis?**
- Warts (no umbilication), milia, syringoma, sebaceous hyperplasia (adults, face), keratoacanthoma and BCC (single large lesion), epidermoid cyst
- In HIV: cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, penicilliosis (talaromycosis) — umbilicated papules on face; must do smear/biopsy
- Varicella (early), juvenile xanthogranuloma, Spitz naevus

**Q6. How do you investigate?**
- Clinical (dermoscopy shows central white-yellow polylobular structure with crown of peripheral vessels)
- Squash preparation for molluscum bodies; biopsy for atypical lesions
- In adults with genital lesions — screen for HIV and other STIs; in extensive facial lesions — HIV test

**Q7. Treatment options.**
- Watchful waiting in children (usually clears in 6–18 months; immunity develops)
- Physical: curettage, enucleation/expression with a needle (with topical anaesthetic), cryotherapy, electrocautery, laser (pulsed dye)
- Chemical: 10–20% KOH solution, cantharidin 0.7% (FDA-approved for molluscum in 2023), podophyllotoxin (adults, not in pregnancy), tretinoin, salicylic acid, trichloroacetic acid; berdazimer gel (nitric oxide donor, FDA 2024)
- Imiquimod is no longer favoured in children (trials showed no benefit)
- HIV: ART (immune reconstitution clears them); cidofovir in refractory

**Q8. Why treat genital molluscum in adults?**
- To prevent sexual transmission and autoinoculation, and it signals sexual exposure (screen for STIs)

**Q9. What is the course and prognosis?**
- Each lesion lasts ~2 months; the infection lasts months to years; heals without scars unless treated aggressively or secondarily infected
- Recurrence common; immunosuppressed — persistent, extensive lesions

**Q10. What is molluscum dermatitis and how do you manage it?**
- Eczematous patch around molluscum lesions (often signals immune response); treat with mild topical steroid/emollient; it often precedes clearance

**Q11. Which poxviruses affect human skin?**
- Molluscipoxvirus — molluscum contagiosum
- Orthopoxvirus — smallpox (eradicated), vaccinia, cowpox, mpox (monkeypox — 2022 global outbreak; umbilicated pustules on genitals, lymphadenopathy, tecovirimat)
- Parapoxvirus — orf, milker's nodule
- Yatapoxvirus — tanapox

**Q12. Histopathology in detail.**
- Lobulated endophytic (cup-shaped) epidermal hyperplasia; keratinocytes contain large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions (Henderson–Paterson bodies) that become basophilic as they move up; central crater opening to the surface; inflamed lesions show dense mixed infiltrate

**Q13. Dermoscopy in detail.**
- Central polylobular white-yellow amorphous structures (orifice) with peripheral 'crown' of fine linear/ hairpin vessels that do not cross the centre

**Q14. Cantharidin — mechanism and use.**
- Blistering agent from blister beetle (protein phosphatase inhibitor) → acantholysis and intraepidermal blister that sheds the lesion; 0.7% applied to lesions in clinic, washed off after 4–6 h (24 h max); painless application, blister in 24–48 h; avoid face/ genitals; FDA-approved formulation 2023 (VP-102)

**Q15. Molluscum in atopic children — special points.**
- More numerous lesions (scratching, barrier defect), molluscum dermatitis common, risk of eczema herpeticum-like spread if steroid misuse; treat eczema around lesions with mild steroid, avoid aggressive destruction

## Quick spotter facts
- Pearly umbilicated papules with cheesy core — molluscum
- Henderson–Paterson bodies (molluscum bodies)
- Many giant facial mollusca — test for HIV; rule out cryptococcosis/histoplasmosis

## Note
Cantharidin (2023) and berdazimer (2024) approvals are newer than the textbooks — please confirm before using in a viva.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Morphea (localised scleroderma) — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Morphea (localised scleroderma)** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Define morphoea.**
- Localised scleroderma — inflammatory sclerosing disease of the skin and underlying tissues (fat, fascia, muscle, bone) without Raynaud's, sclerodactyly or internal organ involvement; does not progress to systemic sclerosis

**Q2. Classify morphoea (Padua / Laxer–Zulian classification).**
- Circumscribed (plaque) — superficial or deep (morphoea profunda)
- Linear — trunk/limbs, or head (en coup de sabre, progressive hemifacial atrophy/Parry–Romberg)
- Generalised — ≥4 plaques >3 cm in ≥2 of 7 anatomical sites; includes isomorphic/symmetric types
- Pansclerotic — circumferential involvement of limbs including bone, children, risk of SCC in ulcers
- Mixed (e.g. linear + circumscribed)
- Others: guttate, keloidal/nodular, bullous, atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini, eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman) — related

**Q3. Clinical features of plaque morphoea.**
- Oval indurated plaques with ivory-white shiny centre and a violaceous/lilac border (active inflammation — 'lilac ring'); later hyper- or hypopigmented atrophic patches with loss of hair and sweating
- Trunk (bra-line, waist), proximal limbs

**Q4. Linear morphoea — why important in children?**
- Commonest type in children; along a limb, may cross joints → contractures, limb-length discrepancy, muscle atrophy, growth failure
- En coup de sabre (frontoparietal 'sword-cut' depression of scalp/forehead with scarring alopecia) — may have neurological (seizures, headache) and ocular involvement
- Needs early systemic therapy (methotrexate) and physiotherapy

**Q5. Pathogenesis.**
- Unknown: endothelial injury and inflammation (Th1/Th17 early, Th2 later) → TGF-β-driven fibroblast activation and collagen deposition
- Triggers: trauma (Koebner), radiation (post-radiation morphoea of breast), infections (Borrelia burgdorferi in Europe — debated), drugs, vaccinations; autoimmune association (ANA, anti-ssDNA, anti-histone in linear/generalised)

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Clinical diagnosis; biopsy (deep incisional) if doubt
- ANA, anti-ssDNA, anti-histone (correlate with deep/active linear disease), eosinophilia (in eosinophilic fasciitis), CBC
- MRI (deep tissue/brain in en coup de sabre), ultrasound and thermography for activity; LoSCAT (localised scleroderma cutaneous assessment tool — mLoSSI activity and LoSDI damage)

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Early (inflammatory): perivascular and interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate at dermal–subcutaneous junction, swollen collagen
- Late (sclerotic): thick hyalinised collagen bundles parallel to the surface throughout dermis, loss of adnexa (trapped eccrine glands without surrounding fat), square 'punch biopsy' sign, reduced CD34 dendritic cells

**Q8. Differential diagnosis.**
- Systemic sclerosis (Raynaud's, sclerodactyly), lichen sclerosus (overlap), post-inflammatory pigmentation, vitiligo, scleredema, lipoatrophy (steroid injection), necrobiosis lipoidica, eosinophilic fasciitis (groove sign, peau d'orange, eosinophilia), radiation fibrosis, morphoeic BCC, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis

**Q9. Management.**
- Limited plaque disease: potent topical steroids, tacrolimus, calcipotriol (± betamethasone), imiquimod; intralesional steroid for active border
- Phototherapy: UVA1 (medium dose) or PUVA/bath PUVA for widespread plaques; NB-UVB for superficial
- Systemic (linear, generalised, pansclerotic, deep, functionally threatening, en coup de sabre): methotrexate 15 mg/m²/week (max 25 mg) + systemic corticosteroids (pulse IV methylprednisolone or oral) for 3 months, continue MTX ≥12–24 months; mycophenolate if MTX fails; tocilizumab, abatacept, JAK inhibitors for refractory
- Physiotherapy for contractures; surgical correction/fat grafting for atrophy once inactive

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Plaque morphoea usually softens over 3–5 years leaving pigmentation; linear and deep forms cause lasting deformity; relapse in ~25–30% (especially childhood linear)

**Q11. Describe generalised and pansclerotic morphoea.**
- Generalised: ≥4 indurated plaques >3 cm in ≥2 body sites (trunk, thighs) — may be isomorphic (bra/ waistband areas) or symmetrical; more systemic symptoms (fatigue, arthralgia), ANA positive
- Pansclerotic: disabling, circumferential involvement of limbs/ trunk including bone, sparing fingertips; children; non-healing ulcers with SCC risk; aggressive immunosuppression needed

**Q12. What is morphoea profunda (deep morphoea)?**
- Sclerosis of deep dermis, subcutis, fascia — bound-down, ill-defined induration with overlying normal or slightly pigmented skin ('cobblestone'/ groove), arms/legs/trunk; overlaps with eosinophilic fasciitis; treat systemically

**Q13. What is atrophoderma of Pasini and Pierini?**
- Considered an abortive/ burnt-out superficial morphoea: well-defined slightly depressed grey-brown patches with 'cliff-drop' borders on the back of young adults, no induration; benign slow course; doxycycline/ hydroxychloroquine reported

**Q14. Extracutaneous involvement in morphoea.**
- Arthralgia/ arthritis, joint contractures, limb-length discrepancy, myalgia (linear/ deep types)
- Neurological (en coup de sabre/ PRS): seizures, headache, brain lesions on MRI
- Ocular: uveitis, episcleritis, eyelid atrophy — eye screening in children with head/face linear morphoea

**Q15. How do you assess disease activity?**
- Clinical: new lesions or extension, erythema/ violaceous border, warmth, induration progression (LoSCAT — mLoSSI for activity, LoSDI for damage)
- Imaging: infrared thermography (warmth — false positives in atrophic lesions), high-frequency ultrasound, MRI for deep disease; laser Doppler flowmetry

**Q16. Morphoea and lichen sclerosus overlap — significance.**
- Up to 5–10% of morphoea patients have extragenital LS, and genital LS coexists in some — examine genitals in all morphoea patients (genital LS needs specific treatment and has SCC risk)

## Quick spotter facts
- Ivory-white indurated plaque with lilac ring — morphoea
- En coup de sabre — linear morphoea on forehead
- Methotrexate + steroids for linear disease

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Morphoea); Padua consensus classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Mycetoma (Madura foot) — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Mycetoma (Madura foot)** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Define mycetoma. What is the classic triad?**
- Chronic, progressive, granulomatous, subcutaneous infection caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or aerobic filamentous bacteria (actinomycetoma) after traumatic implantation (thorn prick)
- Triad: painless subcutaneous swelling (tumefaction), multiple sinuses, discharge of grains (granules)

**Q2. Where is the 'mycetoma belt'? Who gets it?**
- Between latitudes ~15° S and 30° N — Sudan, Mexico, India, Senegal, Venezuela
- Barefoot farm workers and herdsmen, young adult males 20–40 years; foot commonest (~70%), then hand, back, scalp, buttocks (carrying sacks/wood)
- In India: Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat; actinomycetoma (Nocardia, Actinomadura) is more frequent in many Indian series, eumycetoma (Madurella) in drier areas

**Q3. Name the causative organisms.**
- Eumycetoma: Madurella mycetomatis (commonest worldwide, black grains), Trematosphaeria grisea, Falciformispora, Scedosporium boydii (white), Acremonium, Fusarium, Exophiala
- Actinomycetoma: Nocardia brasiliensis, N. asteroides, Actinomadura madurae (white/yellow), A. pelletieri (red grains), Streptomyces somaliensis (yellow)

**Q4. What do grain colours tell you?**
- Black grains — always eumycetoma (Madurella, Trematosphaeria, Exophiala)
- Red — Actinomadura pelletieri
- Yellow — Streptomyces somaliensis, Nocardia
- White/pale — Actinomadura madurae, Nocardia, Scedosporium, Acremonium, Fusarium

**Q5. Compare eumycetoma and actinomycetoma.**
- Eumycetoma: slower, well-defined, encapsulated, late bone involvement with few large (>1 cm) punched-out cavities, coarse grains 0.5–2 mm (black/pale), septate hyphae with chlamydospores, treated with azoles + surgery
- Actinomycetoma: faster, ill-defined and inflammatory, early bone involvement with many small cavities ('moth-eaten'), lymph nodes more often, fine grains (20–100 µm) of thin branching Gram-positive filaments (Nocardia acid-fast), responds to antibiotics

**Q6. How do you investigate?**
- Grains from sinus discharge, deep biopsy or FNAC — naked eye colour, KOH mount (eumycetoma: broad septate hyphae), Gram/modified ZN (actinomycetoma: thin filaments)
- Culture: Sabouraud dextrose agar (fungi); brain-heart infusion/LJ (actinomycetes); PCR/sequencing (ITS) for species
- Histopathology: suppurative granulomas around grains (type 1 neutrophils, type 2 macrophage/giant cells, type 3 epithelioid granuloma); Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon around grains
- Imaging: X-ray (soft-tissue swelling, periosteal reaction, lytic cavities); USG (hyper-reflective grains); MRI 'dot-in-circle' sign — extent before surgery

**Q7. What is the Splendore–Hoeppli phenomenon?**
- Radiating, eosinophilic, club-like material (antigen–antibody complexes) around organisms
- Seen in mycetoma, botryomycosis, sporotrichosis (asteroid bodies), actinomycosis, schistosomiasis, entomophthoromycosis (basidiobolomycosis)

**Q8. What is the dot-in-circle sign?**
- On MRI/USG: small hypointense dot (grain) within hyperintense spheres (granulomatous inflammation) — highly suggestive of mycetoma

**Q9. Treatment of actinomycetoma.**
- Combination antibiotics for months (to prevent resistance)
- Welsh regimen: amikacin 15 mg/kg/day IV + cotrimoxazole (35 mg/kg/day) for 21 days, followed by 15 days of cotrimoxazole alone; repeat 3–4 cycles; cotrimoxazole maintenance afterwards (modified Welsh — add rifampicin 10 mg/kg)
- Two-step regimen (Indian): intensive — penicillin + gentamicin + cotrimoxazole for 5–7 weeks; maintenance — amoxicillin + cotrimoxazole until 2–5 months after cure
- Modified two-step: gentamicin 80 mg IV twice daily + cotrimoxazole DS twice daily for 4 weeks, then cotrimoxazole + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily until 6 months after clinical cure
- Alternatives: dapsone, minocycline, amoxicillin-clavulanate, imipenem, linezolid; monitor renal function and hearing with aminoglycosides

**Q10. Treatment of eumycetoma.**
- Itraconazole 200–400 mg/day (drug of choice) for many months (often 9–12+), combined with surgical debridement/excision of the reduced lesion
- Alternatives: terbinafine 250–1000 mg/day, voriconazole, posaconazole; fosravuconazole under trial
- Amputation for advanced bony disease not responding

**Q11. What are the criteria of cure?**
- Healing of sinuses, disappearance of swelling, normal skin, no grains on FNAC/biopsy, no cavities on USG, return of normal bone on imaging; continue therapy months after clinical cure

**Q12. Differential diagnosis.**
- Botryomycosis (bacterial grains), chronic osteomyelitis, actinomycosis (jaw, sulphur granules, anaerobic Actinomyces israelii), tuberculosis (scrofuloderma, TB of bone), chromoblastomycosis, sporotrichosis, Kaposi sarcoma, soft-tissue tumours, Madura-like cellulitis, filarial lymphoedema

**Q13. How is actinomycosis different from actinomycetoma?**
- Actinomycosis: endogenous anaerobic Actinomyces israelii (commensal of mouth/gut), cervicofacial ('lumpy jaw'), thoracic, abdominal; sulphur granules; treat with long penicillin
- Actinomycetoma: exogenous aerobic actinomycetes (Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces), implantation on foot

**Q14. Complications and prognosis?**
- Bone destruction, deformity, disability, secondary bacterial infection, lymphatic spread, rarely visceral spread (back mycetoma → spine, lung)
- Actinomycetoma — good cure rates with combination therapy; eumycetoma — high relapse, often surgery/amputation needed

**Q15. Classify subcutaneous mycoses (PYQ short note).**
- Mycetoma, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis, phaeohyphomycosis, entomophthoromycosis (basidiobolomycosis, conidiobolomycosis), rhinosporidiosis (now Mesomycetozoea), lobomycosis, subcutaneous zygomycosis

**Q16. What is phaeohyphomycosis?**
- Infection by dematiaceous (brown-black) fungi that appear as pigmented septate hyphae/yeast-like cells in tissue (no muriform cells, no grains) — subcutaneous cysts (Exophiala), sinus, cerebral forms; treat with excision + itraconazole

## Quick spotter facts
- Swelling + sinuses + grains — mycetoma
- Black grains = always fungal
- Dot-in-circle sign on MRI

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 19A (Subcutaneous mycoses — mycetoma, Tables 19A.8–19A.10). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Neurofibromatosis type 1 — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Neurofibromatosis type 1** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Define NF1 (von Recklinghausen disease).**
- Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder (1 in 3000) due to loss-of-function NF1 gene mutations (17q11.2) encoding neurofibromin — a RAS-GTPase activating protein (tumour suppressor); ~50% new mutations; complete penetrance with variable expressivity

**Q2. Revised NIH diagnostic criteria (2021).**
- ≥2 of: ≥6 CALMs (>5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal); axillary or inguinal freckling; ≥2 neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform; optic pathway glioma; ≥2 Lisch nodules or ≥2 choroidal abnormalities; distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid wing dysplasia, anterolateral tibial bowing, pseudarthrosis of long bone); heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant (≥50% VAF in normal tissue)
- Child of a parent meeting criteria needs only one feature

**Q3. Describe the cutaneous features.**
- CALMs (first sign — infancy), freckling (Crowe's sign — axillary/inguinal, 3–5 years), cutaneous neurofibromas (soft, skin-coloured to violaceous, 'button-hole' sign — invaginate on pressure; appear at puberty, increase in pregnancy), subcutaneous neurofibromas (firm, along nerves, painful), plexiform neurofibromas (congenital, 'bag of worms', overgrowth, risk of malignant change), juvenile xanthogranulomas (with risk of JMML), naevus anaemicus, glomus tumours, pruritus

**Q4. Systemic features and complications.**
- Eyes: Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas — >90% adults), optic pathway glioma (15% children — visual loss, precocious puberty)
- Skeletal: scoliosis, sphenoid wing dysplasia, tibial pseudarthrosis, short stature, macrocephaly, osteoporosis
- Nervous: learning disabilities/ADHD (~50%), epilepsy, aqueductal stenosis, brain tumours (gliomas), unidentified bright objects on MRI
- Vascular: hypertension (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma), moyamoya
- Malignancy: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST — 8–13% lifetime; pain, rapid growth, hardening of plexiform neurofibroma), GIST, breast cancer (women <50), JMML, rhabdomyosarcoma, phaeochromocytoma

**Q5. Classify neurofibromatosis.**
- NF1 (classic), NF2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas — merlin, 22q; now called NF2-related schwannomatosis; few CALMs, cataracts, meningiomas), schwannomatosis (SMARCB1/LZTR1), segmental (mosaic) NF1, Legius syndrome (SPRED1 — CALMs + freckling, no neurofibromas)
- Riccardi classification (8 types) — historical

**Q6. Histopathology of a neurofibroma.**
- Unencapsulated dermal tumour of loosely arranged spindle cells with wavy 'S-shaped' nuclei in a pale myxoid/collagenous stroma with mast cells; S100 positive (Schwann cells), CD34 fibroblasts

**Q7. Management.**
- Multidisciplinary yearly review: skin, BP, growth, development, scoliosis, eyes (annual ophthalmology up to 8 y), neurology; MRI when symptomatic; genetic counselling (50% transmission)
- Cutaneous neurofibromas: excision, CO2 laser, electrodesiccation (cosmetic/symptomatic)
- Plexiform neurofibromas: selumetinib (MEK inhibitor — approved for symptomatic inoperable PN in children ≥2 y), mirdametinib (newer); surgery
- MPNST: wide excision, radiotherapy; whole-body MRI surveillance in high-risk; breast screening from 30 y in women

**Q8. Describe neurocutaneous syndromes (PYQ).**
- Phakomatoses: NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge–Weber, von Hippel–Lindau, ataxia-telangiectasia (oculocutaneous telangiectasia, ataxia, immunodeficiency, lymphoma; ATM), incontinentia pigmenti, hypomelanosis of Ito, neurocutaneous melanosis, PHACE, epidermal naevus syndromes, Klippel–Trenaunay, Wyburn-Mason

**Q9. Genetics of NF1.**
- Autosomal dominant, complete penetrance but variable expressivity; ~50% new mutations; NF1 gene on 17q11.2 encodes neurofibromin (RAS-GTPase activating protein — tumour suppressor); loss → RAS/MAPK overactivity (basis for MEK inhibitors); segmental (mosaic) NF1 when post-zygotic

**Q10. What is a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)?**
- Sarcoma arising in a plexiform neurofibroma in ~8–13% lifetime; warning signs — persistent pain, rapid growth, change in consistency (hard), new neurological deficit; FDG-PET/MRI and biopsy; treatment — wide excision, radiotherapy; poor prognosis

**Q11. Which skeletal features occur?**
- Scoliosis (dystrophic, early, rapidly progressive), sphenoid wing dysplasia (pulsating exophthalmos), long-bone bowing and pseudarthrosis of tibia (congenital), short stature, macrocephaly, osteoporosis, non-ossifying fibromas

**Q12. Describe surveillance in a child with NF1.**
- Annual examination: skin, growth, head circumference, BP (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma), spine (scoliosis), development/learning (ADHD, learning disability), puberty (precocious puberty from optic glioma); annual ophthalmology till 8 years for optic pathway glioma; MRI only when symptoms; breast cancer screening in women from 30 years

**Q13. Selumetinib — what and when?**
- Oral MEK1/2 inhibitor approved for children (≥2–3 y) with symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas — reduces volume and pain; side effects: acneiform rash, paronychia, GI upset, raised CK, ocular (retinal) toxicity; mirdametinib also approved recently (confirm availability)

**Q14. What are the types of neurofibromas?**
- Cutaneous (dermal) — soft, sessile/ pedunculated, 'button-hole' sign (invaginate on pressure), appear from puberty, increase in pregnancy
- Subcutaneous — firm, tender nodules along peripheral nerves (higher MPNST risk)
- Plexiform — congenital, diffuse, 'bag of worms', overlying hyperpigmentation/ hypertrichosis, can cause disfigurement and overgrowth; ~10% MPNST lifetime
- Spinal/ internal neurofibromas

**Q15. What is the button-hole sign?**
- Pressing a soft cutaneous neurofibroma pushes it into the dermis through a defect felt like a button-hole; it pops out on release — differentiates from other soft tumours (lipomas, skin tags)

**Q16. Describe the eye findings in NF1.**
- Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas — >90% adults), optic pathway glioma (15% children, usually <7 y — visual loss, proptosis, precocious puberty), choroidal abnormalities (bright patchy nodules on NIR imaging — newer criterion), plexiform neurofibroma of eyelid (S-shaped lid), glaucoma, sphenoid wing dysplasia

**Q17. What are the neurological and cognitive features?**
- Learning disabilities (~50–60%), ADHD, autism spectrum features, macrocephaly, epilepsy, hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis), headaches, 'unidentified bright objects' (T2 hyperintensities) on MRI, optic glioma, other gliomas (brainstem), Moyamoya

**Q18. What tumours are associated with NF1?**
- Optic pathway glioma, other gliomas, MPNST, gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST), phaeochromocytoma, carcinoid (duodenal somatostatinoma), juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (with JXG), rhabdomyosarcoma, breast cancer (women <50 — screen from 30 y), glomus tumours of digits

**Q19. What is the relationship between NF1, JXG and JMML?**
- Children with NF1 and juvenile xanthogranulomas were once thought to have a markedly higher risk of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia; current evidence suggests the added risk is small — routine haematological screening is not mandatory, but examine for hepatosplenomegaly and check CBC if symptomatic

**Q20. What is Legius syndrome and segmental NF?**
- Legius: SPRED1 mutation — CALMs and axillary freckling, macrocephaly, learning issues but no neurofibromas, Lisch nodules or tumours; genetic test differentiates from NF1
- Segmental (mosaic) NF1: features confined to one body segment from post-zygotic mutation; risk of transmitting full NF1 if gonadal mosaicism

**Q21. NF2 — key differences.**
- NF2 (now 'NF2-related schwannomatosis'): NF2 gene (merlin) chromosome 22; bilateral vestibular schwannomas (hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance), meningiomas, ependymomas, juvenile posterior subcapsular cataract; few CALMs, cutaneous schwannomas (plaque-like); bevacizumab for vestibular schwannomas

**Q22. Describe the management of cutaneous neurofibromas.**
- Surgical excision of symptomatic/ disfiguring lesions, CO2 laser/ electrodesiccation for multiple small ones, radiofrequency ablation; MEK inhibitors (selumetinib) shrink some cutaneous neurofibromas — topical MEK inhibitors under trial; psychological support

**Q23. Pregnancy in NF1.**
- Neurofibromas may increase in number and size; higher risk of hypertension, pre-eclampsia, caesarean delivery; prenatal or pre-implantation genetic diagnosis available; 50% transmission risk

**Q24. Cardiovascular features.**
- Hypertension (essential, renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, coarctation), NF1 vasculopathy (stenoses, aneurysms, Moyamoya), pulmonary stenosis (also Noonan overlap — NF1–Noonan syndrome)

**Q25. Histopathology of plexiform neurofibroma vs MPNST.**
- Plexiform: tortuous expanded nerve fascicles with myxoid stroma, S100/SOX10-positive Schwann cells, CD34+ fibroblasts
- MPNST: hypercellular fascicles of atypical spindle cells, mitoses, necrosis, loss of S100/SOX10 and H3K27me3

**Q26. How do you counsel parents of a child with NF1?**
- Explain AD inheritance (50% risk to each child), variable severity even within a family, regular annual reviews, signs needing urgent review (vision changes, new pain, rapid lump growth, headaches, precocious puberty, BP rise), school support for learning difficulties, NF support groups

**Q27. What is the role of mosaic and NF1 microdeletion syndrome?**
- Whole-gene 17q11.2 microdeletion (5–10%): more severe — earlier and more numerous neurofibromas, facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability, overgrowth, higher MPNST risk
- Missense 'p.Met1149' or 'p.Arg1809' variants — mild phenotype without neurofibromas (pigmentary only)

**Q28. Differential diagnosis of multiple neurofibroma-like tumours.**
- Multiple lipomas (familial lipomatosis), schwannomatosis (painful schwannomas — SMARCB1/LZTR1), Proteus syndrome, Cowden syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia 2B (mucosal neuromas), multiple dermatofibromas, cutaneous leiomyomas (Reed syndrome)

**Q29. What is the prognosis/life expectancy in NF1?**
- Life expectancy reduced by ~10–15 years mainly due to MPNST, other malignancies, and vascular disease; most patients live productive lives with surveillance

**Q30. Why is NF1 called a RASopathy?**
- Neurofibromin is a RAS-GAP; its loss increases RAS-GTP and downstream MAPK/ mTOR signalling — like other RASopathies (Noonan, Costello, cardiofaciocutaneous, Legius); explains overlapping features and use of MEK inhibitors

## Quick spotter facts
- CALMs + axillary freckles + neurofibromas + Lisch nodules — NF1
- Button-hole sign
- Selumetinib for plexiform neurofibroma

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Neurofibromatosis); NIH 2021 revised diagnostic criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nevus comedonicus — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus comedonicus** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. What is nevus comedonicus?**
- Rare organoid epidermal (follicular) naevus with clusters of dilated follicular openings plugged with dark keratin (comedo-like), arranged in a linear/Blaschkoid band, usually unilateral on face, neck, trunk or upper limbs; present at birth or childhood; NEK9 mosaic mutation

**Q2. Clinical variants.**
- Non-inflammatory (comedones only)
- Inflammatory: cysts, pustules, abscesses, scarring (acne-like) — often from puberty
- Nevus comedonicus syndrome: with CNS (seizures), skeletal (scoliosis, polydactyly), ocular (cataract) anomalies — epidermal naevus syndrome

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Wide, deep invaginations of epidermis filled with laminated keratin; rudimentary hair shafts or sebaceous lobules; follicular rupture with inflammation in inflammatory type

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acne vulgaris/comedonal (not linear), chloracne, Favre–Racouchot syndrome (solar comedones in elderly), familial dyskeratotic comedones, Dowling–Degos (comedo-like papules), linear porokeratosis, porokeratotic eccrine naevus (palms/soles), verrucous epidermal naevus

**Q5. Management.**
- Comedo extraction, topical retinoids, keratolytics (salicylic, lactic acid), ammonium lactate
- Inflammatory: oral antibiotics, isotretinoin
- Definitive: surgical excision; dermabrasion, CO2/Er:YAG laser, electrocautery

**Q6. What is the genetic basis?**
- Post-zygotic mosaic mutation of NEK9 (also FGFR2 in some) in the follicular unit — a follicular hamartoma; NEK9 mutations also seen in nevus comedonicus syndrome

**Q7. What is nevus comedonicus syndrome?**
- Nevus comedonicus with extracutaneous anomalies — CNS (seizures, developmental delay, EEG abnormalities), ocular (cataract), skeletal (scoliosis, hemivertebrae, syndactyly) — an epidermal naevus syndrome; needs neurological/orthopaedic assessment

**Q8. Complications.**
- Inflammatory variant with recurrent cysts, abscesses, sinuses and scarring (acne conglobata/hidradenitis-like), secondary infection; rarely malignancy in long-standing lesions

**Q9. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Multiple keratin plugs ('comedo-like openings') — dark-brown to black round plugs, clustered in a linear distribution

**Q10. Describe the clinical features.**
- Grouped dilated follicular openings filled with dark keratin plugs (comedo-like), linear/ unilateral along Blaschko lines on face, neck, trunk, upper arms; present at birth or childhood (50% by age 10)

**Q11. Treatment options in detail.**
- Topical retinoids (tretinoin, tazarotene), keratolytics (salicylic acid, ammonium lactate), comedone extraction, oral isotretinoin for inflammatory variant, Er:YAG/ CO2 laser, dermabrasion, surgical excision of small lesions

**Q12. Histopathology in detail.**
- Wide, deep invaginations of epidermis filled with laminated keratin plugs (dilated follicular ostia) with absent or rudimentary hair shafts; small sebaceous glands may open into base; secondary inflammation and cysts

**Q13. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Acne vulgaris/ comedonal acne (bilateral, symmetrical, adolescents), chloracne (halogenated hydrocarbons), familial dyskeratotic comedones, Favre–Racouchot (solar comedones around eyes in elderly), linear porokeratosis, epidermal naevus, Dowling–Degos (comedo-like papules)

**Q14. What is Favre–Racouchot syndrome?**
- Nodular elastosis with cysts and comedones on periorbital/ malar skin of elderly sun-exposed smokers; treat with retinoids, comedone extraction, sun protection, smoking cessation

**Q15. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

## Quick spotter facts
- Linear cluster of comedones on a child's neck — nevus comedonicus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Epidermal naevi — organoid). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nevus depigmentosus — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus depigmentosus** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is nevus depigmentosus (achromic naevus)?**
- Congenital, stable, well-circumscribed hypopigmented (not depigmented) macule or patch with irregular serrated ('splashed paint') border; present at birth or noticed in early childhood (by age 3) as pigmentation of surrounding skin increases; grows in proportion with the child
- Mosaic disorder of melanosome transfer — normal or slightly reduced melanocyte number with reduced melanin synthesis/transfer

**Q2. Clinical types.**
- Isolated (single round/oval or irregular patch — commonest on trunk, proximal limbs)
- Segmental (band-like along a dermatome-like/Blaschkoid segment, does not cross midline)
- Systematised (whorled/streaky along Blaschko's lines — overlaps hypomelanosis of Ito; check for neurological, ocular, skeletal anomalies)

**Q3. How do you differentiate it from vitiligo and nevus anaemicus?**
- Vitiligo: acquired, chalk-white (depigmented), bright Wood's lamp fluorescence, sharp convex borders, progressive, leucotrichia, absent melanocytes
- Nevus depigmentosus: congenital/stable, off-white (hypopigmented), Wood's lamp — off-white without bright fluorescence, serrated border, normal hairs, melanocytes present
- Nevus anaemicus: pharmacological vasoconstriction (increased α-adrenergic sensitivity); pale patch disappears on diascopy (blends with blanched surrounding skin) and does not redden on rubbing; normal Wood's lamp

**Q4. Other differentials.**
- Ash-leaf macules (tuberous sclerosis — multiple, look for other signs), piebaldism, pityriasis alba, indeterminate leprosy (sensation), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, segmental vitiligo, hypopigmented MF, tinea versicolor

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Clinical with Wood's lamp, dermoscopy; biopsy rarely — normal/slightly reduced melanocytes with reduced melanin (Fontana–Masson), abnormal melanosome aggregates in melanocytes on EM
- Screen for systemic features in systematised type; check sensation to exclude leprosy

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance; cosmetic camouflage
- Phototherapy poorly effective; surgical options — suction blister grafting, non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (melanocyte–keratinocyte transplant) give good results due to stability; excimer laser in some

**Q7. What is the histopathology in detail?**
- Normal epidermis with reduced melanin on Fontana–Masson; melanocyte number normal or slightly reduced (S100/ Melan-A); EM — normal melanosomes aggregated within melanocytes, reduced transfer to keratinocytes

**Q8. What is the association with systemic anomalies?**
- Usually isolated; systematised type may overlap with hypomelanosis of Ito and rarely shows neurological/ musculoskeletal/ ocular associations — examine and refer as needed

**Q9. What surgical options and outcomes?**
- Stability makes surgical repigmentation suitable: suction blister epidermal grafts, mini-punch grafts, non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (MKTP) — reported good repigmentation, though perifollicular/ marginal hypopigmentation may persist; excimer/ NB-UVB adjunct

**Q10. Differentiate ND from ash-leaf macule.**
- Ash-leaf macules: multiple (≥3), lance-ovate, from birth, with other TSC signs (angiofibromas, shagreen patch, seizures) — Wood's lamp highlights; ND usually single, irregular serrated margin, no systemic features

**Q11. Differentiate ND from nevus anaemicus at bedside.**
- Diascopy: nevus anaemicus disappears (blends with blanched surrounding skin), ND remains
- Rubbing/ heat: nevus anaemicus does not become erythematous (vasoconstriction), ND shows normal erythema
- Wood's lamp: nevus anaemicus not accentuated; ND shows off-white accentuation

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. Describe the pathogenesis.**
- Functional defect of melanocytes in a mosaic clone — reduced melanosome production and defective transfer to keratinocytes (aggregated melanosomes within melanocytes on EM); melanocyte number normal or slightly reduced

**Q14. Diagnostic criteria (Coupe's criteria).**
- Leucoderma present at birth or early in life; no alteration in distribution throughout life; no alteration in texture or sensation of the affected area; no hyperpigmented border

**Q15. Dermoscopy of nevus depigmentosus vs vitiligo.**
- ND: faint, reduced pigment network with irregular/serrated edges and preserved perifollicular pigment, no leucotrichia; vitiligo: absent network, perifollicular pigmentation (repigmenting), white glow, leucotrichia, trichrome/ starburst pattern in active disease

## Quick spotter facts
- Stable congenital off-white patch with serrated border, Wood's lamp not bright — nevus depigmentosus
- Nevus anaemicus disappears on diascopy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nevus of Ota / Ito / Hori — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus of Ota / Ito / Hori** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Write a short note on nevus of Ota (PYQ).**
- Dermal melanocytosis (oculodermal melanocytosis) with blue-grey to brown mottled patch in the distribution of the 1st and 2nd branches of the trigeminal nerve (forehead, temple, periorbital, malar), unilateral in ~90%; ipsilateral scleral (blue-grey) and ocular involvement in ~2/3
- Asian and Indian women more; onset at birth (50%) or around puberty (second peak); GNAQ/GNA11 mutations
- Mucosa (palate, nasal), tympanic membrane may be involved

**Q2. Tanino classification.**
- Type I mild (Ia orbital, Ib zygomatic), II moderate (V1+V2 area), III intensive (scalp, forehead, nose), IV bilateral

**Q3. Complications.**
- Glaucoma (ipsilateral — regular eye checks), uveal/ choroidal melanoma (especially in white patients), CNS melanoma (rare), sensorineural hearing loss; associated with Sturge–Weber/Klippel–Trenaunay (phakomatosis pigmentovascularis)

**Q4. What is nevus of Ito and Hori's naevus?**
- Nevus of Ito: same dermal melanocytosis in the distribution of posterior supraclavicular and lateral cutaneous brachial nerves (shoulder, supraclavicular, scapula, upper arm)
- Hori's naevus (acquired bilateral naevus of Ota-like macules — ABNOM): acquired in middle-aged Asian women, bilateral blue-brown speckled macules on malar areas, forehead, eyelids; no ocular/mucosal involvement; often misdiagnosed as melasma

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Elongated, dendritic, pigmented melanocytes scattered among collagen bundles in the upper and mid dermis (dermal melanocytes) — superficial, deep or diffuse types; epidermis normal

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Melasma (bilateral brown, no blue-grey or eye involvement), Mongolian spot (sacral, fades), blue naevus, lichen planus pigmentosus, drug pigmentation (minocycline), PIH, port-wine stain (early), ecchymosis

**Q7. Management.**
- Q-switched lasers (Nd:YAG 1064 nm — preferred in dark skin, alexandrite 755 nm, ruby 694 nm) or picosecond lasers — multiple sessions (5–10) 2–3 months apart; excellent response (selective photothermolysis of dermal melanin); risk of PIH/hypopigmentation, recurrence
- Ophthalmology review (glaucoma, melanoma) at baseline and periodically; camouflage

**Q8. Describe the clinical features of nevus of Ota.**
- Unilateral (90%) blue-grey/ brown speckled macular pigmentation in V1–V2 trigeminal distribution (forehead, temple, periorbital, malar, nose), with scleral/ conjunctival pigmentation in ~2/3; bimodal onset — infancy and puberty; women and Asians (incl. Indians) more

**Q9. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Arrested migration of neural-crest melanocytes in the dermis; GNAQ/GNA11 mutations; hormonal influence (appears/ darkens at puberty, pregnancy)

**Q10. Hori's naevus (ABNOM) vs melasma.**
- Hori's: bilateral speckled blue-brown/ grey macules on malar region, temples, eyelids, nasal ala in Asian women 20–40 y, no ocular involvement; dermal melanocytosis on histology — Q-switched lasers effective
- Melasma: brown confluent symmetrical patches with epidermal ± dermal pigment, worse with sun; different treatment (lasers worsen)

**Q11. What is Mongolian spot vs nevus of Ota?**
- Mongolian (dermal melanocytosis) spot: blue-grey patch over lumbosacral region in Asian/ African neonates, fades by childhood; extensive/ persistent spots associated with lysosomal storage disorders (GM1 gangliosidosis, Hurler) and phacomatosis pigmentovascularis

**Q12. Malignant transformation risk.**
- Rare melanoma of skin, orbit, uveal tract, leptomeninges (CNS) — especially with ocular involvement; annual eye and skin examination

**Q13. Q-switched laser protocol tips.**
- Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064 nm (dark skin), alexandrite 755 nm, ruby 694 nm; 4–10 sessions at 2–3 monthly intervals; endpoint — immediate whitening; side effects — transient PIH, hypopigmentation, recurrence (rare); picosecond lasers fewer sessions

**Q14. What lasers are used and why?**
- Q-switched (nanosecond) ruby 694 nm, alexandrite 755 nm and Nd:YAG 1064 nm (best for dark skin) and picosecond lasers — selective photothermolysis of dermal melanin; multiple sessions every 2–3 months; complications: hyper/hypopigmentation, textural change; excellent response, earlier treatment in childhood needs fewer sessions

**Q15. Why examine the eyes?**
- Ocular melanocytosis (sclera, conjunctiva, iris) in ~2/3; risk of glaucoma (~10%) and uveal/ choroidal melanoma — yearly ophthalmological follow-up with intraocular pressure measurement

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral blue-grey patch on V1/V2 with scleral pigmentation — nevus of Ota
- Q-switched Nd:YAG laser
- Bilateral acquired malar blue-brown macules — Hori's naevus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermal melanocytoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nevus sebaceous (of Jadassohn) — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus sebaceous (of Jadassohn)** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Write a short note on nevus sebaceous (PYQ).**
- Congenital hamartoma of the pilosebaceous–apocrine unit and epidermis (organoid epidermal naevus) — postzygotic HRAS/KRAS mutations; scalp (commonest), face, neck; ~0.3% of newborns

**Q2. Describe the three stages (clinical and histological).**
- Infancy/childhood: smooth, slightly raised, yellow-orange, waxy, hairless (alopecic) oval/linear plaque on the scalp; histology — immature hair follicles, small sebaceous glands
- Puberty (hormonal): becomes verrucous, thicker, more yellow, pebbly/cobblestoned; histology — papillomatous epidermal hyperplasia, abundant mature sebaceous glands, ectopic apocrine glands, absent terminal hairs
- Adulthood: development of secondary adnexal neoplasms — trichoblastoma (commonest), syringocystadenoma papilliferum, sebaceoma, apocrine tumours; BCC (true BCC uncommon, ~1%), rarely SCC, adnexal carcinomas

**Q3. What is Schimmelpenning syndrome (linear nevus sebaceous syndrome)?**
- Extensive nevus sebaceous with CNS (seizures, intellectual disability, hemimegalencephaly), ocular (colobomas, lipodermoids), skeletal (hypophosphataemic rickets), cardiac and urogenital anomalies; part of epidermal naevus syndromes

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Aplasia cutis congenita (atrophic/membranous, not waxy), epidermal naevus, juvenile xanthogranuloma, mastocytoma, solitary trichoepithelioma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum, congenital triangular alopecia, juvenile xanthogranuloma

**Q5. Management.**
- Observation with periodic examination vs prophylactic full-thickness surgical excision (often before puberty for cosmetic reasons/alopecia, and because secondary tumours may arise) — decision individualised (malignancy risk lower than once thought)
- Biopsy any new nodule or ulcer; CO2 laser/PDT for those unsuitable for surgery (risk of recurrence)

**Q6. What is the genetic basis?**
- Post-zygotic HRAS (≈ 90%) or KRAS mutations — RAS mosaicism; same mutations in Schimmelpenning syndrome and phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica

**Q7. Which tumours develop in nevus sebaceous?**
- Mostly benign, after puberty: trichoblastoma (commonest — previously misdiagnosed as BCC), syringocystadenoma papilliferum (second commonest), sebaceoma, apocrine adenoma/hidrocystoma, tricholemmoma
- Malignant (rare <1–2%): BCC, SCC, sebaceous carcinoma, apocrine carcinoma, porocarcinoma — usually in adults

**Q8. Clinical appearance at birth vs puberty.**
- Birth/infancy: smooth, hairless, yellow-orange, waxy, slightly raised plaque on scalp (linear/oval) — alopecic; Puberty: verrucous, pebbly, thicker (sebaceous gland hyperplasia under androgen influence); adulthood: tumour development (nodules within)

**Q9. Timing of excision — current view?**
- Prophylactic excision in childhood is no longer mandatory as malignant change is rare; excise for cosmesis, symptoms, or new nodules/ulceration; observation with periodic examination is acceptable; if excising, before adolescence gives smaller scars under local anaesthesia

**Q10. Histopathology by stage in detail.**
- Infancy: immature hair follicles, small sebaceous glands, papillomatous epidermis
- Puberty: hyperplastic, mature sebaceous glands opening directly onto surface, papillomatosis, ectopic apocrine glands in deep dermis, absent mature hair follicles
- Adulthood: secondary neoplasms (trichoblastoma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum)

**Q11. What is syringocystadenoma papilliferum?**
- Benign adnexal (apocrine) tumour, often arising in nevus sebaceous of scalp — papule/ plaque with crust and moist surface; histology — cystic invaginations with papillary projections lined by double layer of cells, plasma cell-rich stroma

**Q12. Dermoscopy of nevus sebaceous.**
- Yellow-white globules ('aggregated yellow-white globules') without hair follicles, brown globules/ papillary structures in older lesions; new nodules with arborising vessels suggest secondary BCC/ trichoblastoma

**Q13. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Aplasia cutis congenita (membranous, scarring), epidermal naevus, juvenile xanthogranuloma, solitary mastocytoma, congenital triangular alopecia, syringocystadenoma papilliferum, seborrhoeic keratosis (adults)

**Q14. Extracutaneous features in Schimmelpenning syndrome.**
- CNS (seizures, intellectual disability, hemimegalencephaly, Dandy–Walker), eye (colobomas, epibulbar dermoids), skeletal (rickets — hypophosphataemic via FGF23, bone cysts), cardiac, urogenital — mosaic HRAS/KRAS mutations

**Q15. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

## Quick spotter facts
- Yellow-orange waxy hairless plaque on scalp of a newborn — nevus sebaceous
- Trichoblastoma is the commonest secondary tumour

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Organoid naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nevus spilus (speckled lentiginous nevus) — viva
posts.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus spilus (speckled lentiginous nevus)** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. What is nevus spilus?**
- Speckled lentiginous naevus: a light-brown café-au-lait-like background patch studded with darker brown-black macules or papules (lentigines, junctional/compound naevi, sometimes blue or Spitz naevi); present at birth or appearing in childhood; considered a type of congenital melanocytic naevus (HRAS/BRAF mosaic)

**Q2. Clinical types.**
- Macular type (flat speckles — lentigines/junctional naevi) and papular type (raised speckles — compound/dermal naevi)
- Size from small to giant/segmental (zosteriform)
- Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica (papular nevus spilus + nevus sebaceous — HRAS), phacomatosis pigmentovascularis (with vascular malformation), speckled lentiginous naevus syndrome (neurological anomalies)

**Q3. Malignant potential.**
- Low; melanoma reported especially in large/giant or segmental lesions and the papular type — monitor speckles for change; biopsy atypical components

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Café-au-lait macule with lentigines (NF1/Legius — axillary freckling), agminated lentigines/naevi, congenital melanocytic naevus, Becker's naevus, partial unilateral lentiginosis, LEOPARD/Noonan

**Q5. Management.**
- Observation with photographs and dermoscopy; excision of any atypical speckle
- Cosmetic: Q-switched/picosecond lasers (background and speckles), excision of small lesions; caution — laser may complicate monitoring

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Background macule: lentigo-simplex-like basal hyperpigmentation with slightly increased melanocytes; dark speckles: junctional, compound or intradermal naevi, sometimes Spitz/blue naevi

**Q7. What is phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica?**
- Co-existence of speckled lentiginous naevus (papular type) and nevus sebaceous (HRAS mosaicism), sometimes with neurological and skeletal anomalies

**Q8. What is phacomatosis pigmentovascularis?**
- Co-existence of vascular malformation (port-wine stain/ cutis marmorata) with pigmentary naevi — dermal melanocytosis (cesioflammea), nevus spilus (spilorosea), or both; GNA11/GNAQ mosaicism; may have Sturge–Weber/KT features

**Q9. How should you follow a large nevus spilus?**
- Photography and dermoscopy annually; examine dark speckles for change; biopsy any enlarging, irregular or nodular area — melanoma risk is low but higher in large/zosteriform/papular types

**Q10. Describe the clinical presentation.**
- Tan CALM-like background patch (present at birth or early childhood) with numerous smaller darker brown-black macules/ papules ('speckles') developing over time; 1–20 cm; trunk and limbs; may be zosteriform/ segmental

**Q11. Macular vs papular types.**
- Macular type: speckles are flat (lentigines/ junctional naevi) — associated with phacomatosis pigmentovascularis
- Papular type: speckles are raised (compound/ intradermal naevi) — associated with phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica; possibly slightly higher melanoma risk

**Q12. Genetics.**
- Post-zygotic HRAS (papular) and other RAS/ RAF mosaic mutations — explaining the clonal background and speckles

**Q13. Lasers in nevus spilus.**
- Q-switched/ picosecond lasers lighten background and speckles (variable, recurrence); avoid treating atypical speckles without histology; follow-up for changes

**Q14. Describe melanoma types and Breslow/ Clark levels (often linked question).**
- Types: superficial spreading (commonest in West), nodular, lentigo maligna melanoma, acral lentiginous (commonest in Indians — soles, palms, nails), mucosal, desmoplastic, amelanotic
- Breslow thickness (mm, from granular layer to deepest cell) — main prognostic factor: T1 ≤1 mm, T2 1–2, T3 2–4, T4 >4 mm (a/b by ulceration); Clark levels I–V (anatomical) now largely replaced
- Margins: in situ 0.5–1 cm, ≤1 mm 1 cm, 1–2 mm 1–2 cm, >2 mm 2 cm; sentinel node biopsy for >0.8 mm or ulcerated

**Q15. Dermoscopy of nevus spilus.**
- Background — light-brown reticular network/ homogeneous pattern; speckles — darker reticular/ globular patterns of naevi; atypical features in a speckle (irregular network, blue-white veil) need biopsy

## Quick spotter facts
- Café-au-lait patch with dark speckles — nevus spilus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Melanocytic naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nipple eczema — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nipple eczema** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What are the causes of nipple/areolar eczema?**
- Atopic dermatitis (minor criterion of Hanifin–Rajka) — commonest, usually bilateral, adolescent girls
- Irritant (friction — 'jogger's nipple', breastfeeding — saliva, pumps), allergic contact (nursing creams, lanolin, fragrances, bra materials), Candida during breastfeeding, scabies (areolae in women), seborrhoeic

**Q2. Why is unilateral persistent nipple eczema a red flag?**
- Paget's disease of the nipple — intra-epidermal spread of underlying ductal breast carcinoma; unilateral, slowly progressive, well-defined, crusted/eroded, may have nipple retraction, discharge, lump
- Any unilateral nipple eczema not responding to 3–4 weeks of topical steroid needs biopsy and breast imaging

**Q3. Differentiate eczema from Paget's disease of nipple.**
- Eczema: bilateral, itchy, ill-defined, starts on areola, fluctuates, responds to steroids, nipple intact
- Paget's: unilateral, little itch, sharply demarcated, starts on nipple then areola, persistent, steroid-unresponsive, nipple may be destroyed/retracted; histology — large pale Paget cells (CK7+, CEA+, HER2+)

**Q4. Other differentials.**
- Psoriasis, erosive adenomatosis of nipple, Bowen's disease, hyperkeratosis of nipple and areola (naevoid), tinea, herpes, scabies

**Q5. Management of nipple eczema in breastfeeding women.**
- Emollient (pure petrolatum), mild topical steroid applied after feeds and wiped before the next feed; treat Candida in mother and baby (oral thrush) with topical azole/nystatin; correct latch; avoid allergenic nursing creams

**Q6. Work-up in a non-healing case.**
- Patch test (if contact allergy), KOH, skin biopsy, mammography/ultrasound for Paget's

**Q7. What is hyperkeratosis of nipple and areola?**
- Rare benign verrucous thickening and pigmentation — naevoid, associated with ichthyosis/AD/ CTCL or oestrogen therapy; keratolytics, retinoids, cryotherapy

**Q8. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q9. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
