- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q10. Breastfeeding nipple pain — differentials.**
- Poor latch/ trauma (fissures), candidiasis (burning, shooting pain, shiny pink nipple — treat mother and baby), bacterial infection (S. aureus — fissures with crusts), vasospasm/ Raynaud's of nipple (blanching, pain after feeds — nifedipine), contact dermatitis (creams, pump parts), eczema, herpes

**Q11. Nipple involvement in atopic dermatitis — features.**
- Bilateral scaly, fissured, itchy erythema of areola and nipple in adolescent girls/ young women; part of Hanifin–Rajka minor criteria; responds to mild steroids/ tacrolimus and emollients

**Q12. Imaging and biopsy in suspected Paget's disease.**
- Mammography + ultrasound ± MRI breast to find underlying carcinoma (present in >90%); punch/ wedge biopsy of nipple skin; refer to breast surgeon — mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy

**Q13. Management of nipple fissures and pain.**
- Correct breastfeeding latch/ positioning (lactation consultant), expressed breast milk or lanolin-free emollient, short course of mild steroid after feeds, treat infection (mupirocin, oral flucloxacillin), nipple shields temporarily

**Q14. What is the histopathology of Paget's disease of the nipple?**
- Large round pale cells with abundant clear/amphophilic cytoplasm and large nuclei scattered singly and in nests throughout the epidermis (pagetoid spread), sparing the basal layer partially; CK7+, CEA+, EMA+, HER2 often +, CK20− (unlike secondary extramammary Paget's)

**Q15. Differentiate mammary from extramammary Paget's disease.**
- Mammary: nipple/areola, almost always underlying ductal carcinoma
- Extramammary: apocrine-rich skin (vulva, perianal, scrotum, axilla) — primary intraepidermal adenocarcinoma (CK7+, GCDFP-15+) or secondary to underlying colorectal (CK20+) or urothelial (uroplakin+) cancer; 'strawberries and cream' red plaques with white scale; treat with Mohs/excision, imiquimod, PDT

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral, steroid-resistant nipple 'eczema' — biopsy for Paget's disease

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Eczemas, breast dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Nummular (discoid) eczema — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nummular (discoid) eczema** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What is nummular eczema?**
- Chronic eczema with coin-shaped (nummular) well-demarcated plaques, very itchy
- Two age peaks: young women (15–25) and elderly men (50–65); also in atopic children

**Q2. Morphology.**
- Starts as tiny papulovesicles that coalesce into round plaques 1–10 cm, oozing and crusting in acute stage, scaly and lichenified later; may show central clearing (mimicking tinea)
- Sites: legs and dorsa of hands and feet, extensor forearms, trunk

**Q3. Aetiological associations.**
- Xerosis and barrier damage, atopy, S. aureus colonisation (infective eczema), contact allergy (nickel, chromate, fragrances, neomycin), venous stasis, alcohol, drugs (isotretinoin, interferon, TNF inhibitors), dental/focal infection (older theory)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Tinea corporis (active edge, KOH), psoriasis (silvery scale, nails, other sites), impetigo, Bowen's disease (single, slowly growing), mycosis fungoides, granuloma annulare, contact dermatitis, lichen simplex

**Q5. What is infective (infectious eczematoid) dermatitis? (PYQ)**
- Eczema around a discharging infected focus (otitis externa, ulcer, fistula) from exudate; spreads peripherally; treat infection + steroid
- Significance of bacteria in eczema — S. aureus colonises >90% of AD lesions; superantigens drive inflammation and steroid resistance

**Q6. Investigations.**
- KOH, swab culture, patch test (especially if refractory), biopsy if atypical, blood sugar

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Emollients, potent topical steroid (ointment) ± occlusion; combined steroid–antibiotic for short term when infected; oral antibiotics (cephalexin, cloxacillin) for widespread infected lesions
- Tacrolimus, coal tar, NB-UVB, systemic agents (methotrexate, cyclosporine) for widespread resistant disease; sedating antihistamines
- Treat xerosis, stop alcohol

**Q8. Prognosis?**
- Chronic and relapsing; often recurs at previous sites

**Q9. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q10. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q11. Histopathology of nummular eczema.**
- Acute/ subacute spongiotic dermatitis with spongiotic vesicles, parakeratosis with serum crusts and neutrophils, acanthosis; chronic lesions psoriasiform with lichenification

**Q12. Nummular eczema with isotretinoin and other drugs.**
- Reported with isotretinoin (xerosis), interferon, ribavirin, TNF inhibitors, gold, methyldopa; withdraw/ treat xerosis aggressively

**Q13. Nummular eczema vs psoriasis — clinical tips.**
- Nummular: oozing/ crusting in acute stage, poorly marginated periphery with satellite vesicles, intense itch, legs/ dorsa of hands, no nail pitting
- Psoriasis: silvery dry scale, sharp margins, extensors/ scalp, nail pitting, Auspitz sign, less itch

**Q14. Systemic therapy options.**
- Short courses of prednisolone, methotrexate 7.5–15 mg/week, cyclosporine, azathioprine, NB-UVB; dupilumab (atopic background), oral antibiotics for impetiginised disease

**Q15. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Dotted vessels in a patchy distribution with yellow crusts/ serocrusts and white scales — compared with psoriasis (uniform dotted vessels with white scales on a red background)

**Q16. Role of patch testing.**
- Contact sensitisation (nickel, chromate, cobalt, fragrance, neomycin, preservatives in emollients) found in up to a third of chronic nummular eczema — patch test when persistent or atypical distribution (e.g. hands, feet, lower legs)

## Quick spotter facts
- Coin-shaped oozing itchy plaques on legs — nummular eczema; do KOH to exclude tinea

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Eczemas). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Palmoplantar keratoderma — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Palmoplantar keratoderma** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. Define palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK).**
- Persistent abnormal thickening (hyperkeratosis) of the palms and soles, inherited or acquired

**Q2. Discuss classification of palmoplantar keratodermas (PYQ).**
- Inherited — by pattern: diffuse (whole palm/sole — Unna–Thost/Vörner (epidermolytic, KRT9/KRT1), mal de Meleda (SLURP1 — transgrediens, glove-and-stocking, malodour, AR), Bothnian (aquaporin 5, aquagenic whitening), Greither's), focal/striate (pressure areas, linear — desmoglein 1, desmoplakin, keratin 1/16; pachyonychia congenita — KRT6/16/17; Howel–Evans), punctate (multiple small keratotic papules/pits — AAGAB; Buschke–Fischer–Brauer)
- With associated features (syndromic): Papillon–Lefèvre (CTSC — periodontitis with early tooth loss, psoriasiform plaques, pyogenic infections), Vohwinkel (GJB2 mutilating — pseudoainhum, honeycomb keratoderma, starfish knuckle keratoses, deafness; loricrin variant with ichthyosis), Naxos (plakoglobin — woolly hair, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy), Carvajal (desmoplakin — woolly hair, left ventricular cardiomyopathy), Clouston (hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia), Richner–Hanhart (tyrosinaemia type II — painful focal PPK, corneal ulcers, intellectual disability), Huriez (scleroatrophic — SCC risk), Olmsted (periorificial plaques, mutilating), Howel–Evans
- Acquired: keratoderma climactericum (menopausal women — heels), psoriasis, eczema, lichen planus, PRP, tinea pedis/manuum, reactive arthritis (keratoderma blennorrhagicum), arsenical keratoses, crusted scabies, secondary syphilis, myxoedema, drugs (capecitabine, venlafaxine, lithium, BRAF inhibitors), CTCL/Sézary, paraneoplastic (tripe palms, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex — SCC of upper aerodigestive tract), lymphoedema, aquagenic keratoderma, chronic arsenicosis

**Q3. Write a short note on Howel–Evans syndrome (PYQ).**
- Autosomal dominant tylosis with oesophageal cancer (TOC) — RHBDF2 mutation; focal PPK (pressure areas of soles) beginning in late childhood, oral leukoplakia, follicular papules, and very high lifetime risk (~95% by 65 y) of oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma — needs annual upper GI endoscopy

**Q4. What is 'transgrediens'?**
- Extension of keratoderma beyond the palms/soles to the dorsal surfaces (e.g. mal de Meleda, Greither's, Olmsted) — vs 'non-transgrediens' confined to palmoplantar skin (Unna–Thost)

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Family history, pattern, associated features (hair, teeth, nails, hearing, heart), KOH (tinea), biopsy (epidermolytic vs non-epidermolytic), genetic testing; ECG/echo in woolly-hair syndromes; endoscopy (Howel–Evans); screen for malignancy in acquired adult onset

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Mechanical paring, soaks, keratolytics (salicylic acid 5–20%, urea 10–40%, lactic acid), topical retinoids, calcipotriol
- Systemic retinoids (acitretin 10–25 mg/day) — effective but painful sensitivity if over-treated (epidermolytic types), lowest effective dose
- Treat hyperhidrosis and secondary fungal/bacterial infections, proper footwear and orthotics; surgical release of constricting bands (pseudoainhum)
- Treat cause in acquired PPK (psoriasis, hypothyroidism, drug withdrawal, tumour)

**Q7. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q8. What is Mal de Meleda?**
- Autosomal recessive SLURP1 mutation: diffuse transgrediens PPK extending to dorsa of hands/feet ('glove and sock'), malodour, hyperhidrosis, constriction bands (pseudoainhum), perioral erythema, nail changes; acitretin helps

**Q9. What is epidermolytic PPK (Vörner) vs Unna–Thost?**
- Vörner (KRT9, sometimes KRT1): diffuse yellow waxy PPK with sharp red border, epidermolytic histology — commonest hereditary PPK
- Unna–Thost (KRT1): diffuse non-epidermolytic PPK — similar clinically; histology distinguishes

**Q10. What is pachyonychia congenita?**
- Autosomal dominant KRT6A/6B/16/17: painful focal plantar keratoderma (blistering calluses), hypertrophic thickened wedge-shaped nails, oral leukokeratosis, follicular keratoses, steatocystomas (KRT17), natal teeth; pain management, paring, botulinum toxin, rapamycin (experimental)

**Q11. Treatment in detail.**
- Keratolytics (salicylic acid 10–20%, urea 40%, lactic acid), mechanical debridement, topical retinoids, vitamin D analogues; oral acitretin (diffuse non-epidermolytic and syndromic types — lower dose in epidermolytic due to fragility); treat hyperhidrosis and secondary infection (fungal); surgical excision with grafting in severe cases

**Q12. Explain the clinical examination of PPK.**
- Pattern (diffuse/ focal/ punctate/ striate), transgrediens (extension beyond palms), associated features — nails, teeth, hair, hearing, eyes, hyperhidrosis, malodour, constriction bands, family history; screen for oesophageal cancer (tylosis) and cardiac disease (Naxos/ Carvajal — woolly hair)

**Q13. Clinical patterns of hereditary PPK.**
- Diffuse (whole palm/sole — Unna–Thost/Vörner epidermolytic KRT9, Mal de Meleda — transgrediens, SLURP1), focal (pressure points — striate/ nummular; DSG1, DSP, KRT6/16 pachyonychia), punctate (many tiny keratotic papules — AAGAB punctate PPK type I)

**Q14. Name syndromic PPKs and their extracutaneous features.**
- Papillon–Lefèvre (periodontitis with loss of teeth — CTSC), Vohwinkel (mutilating — starfish keratoses, pseudoainhum, deafness — GJB2 or loricrin), Naxos and Carvajal (woolly hair + cardiomyopathy — plakoglobin/desmoplakin), Howel–Evans (tylosis + oesophageal cancer — RHBDF2), Richner–Hanhart (tyrosinaemia II — eyes, intellect), Clouston (hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia — GJB6), Olmsted (periorificial plaques — TRPV3), pachyonychia congenita (KRT6A/6B/16/17)

**Q15. Acquired PPK — causes.**
- Keratoderma climactericum (menopausal women), hypothyroidism, myxoedema, arsenic (punctate), paraneoplastic (tylosis, tripe palms, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex — SCC of upper aerodigestive tract), psoriasis, eczema, LP, PRP, Reiter's (keratoderma blennorrhagicum), dermatophytosis, secondary syphilis, crusted scabies, HIV, drugs (lithium, venlafaxine, BRAF inhibitors), lymphoedema, chronic friction

## Quick spotter facts
- Focal PPK + family history of oesophageal cancer — Howel–Evans (tylosis)
- PPK + early loss of teeth — Papillon–Lefèvre
- PPK + woolly hair + cardiomyopathy — Naxos/Carvajal

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Palmoplantar keratodermas). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Parapsoriasis — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Parapsoriasis** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. What does 'parapsoriasis' mean today?**
- Group of chronic, scaly, psoriasis-like but treatment-resistant dermatoses described by Brocq (1902)
- Current use: small-plaque parapsoriasis (SPP) and large-plaque parapsoriasis (LPP); pityriasis lichenoides (PLEVA/PLC) were formerly called 'parapsoriasis guttata/varioliformis' and are now classified separately

**Q2. Describe small-plaque parapsoriasis.**
- Round/oval, well-defined, slightly scaly, pink-yellowish patches <5 cm on trunk and proximal limbs of middle-aged men
- Digitate dermatosis variant — finger-like elongated patches along skin lines of the flanks ('hug sign')
- Benign course; rarely (≈ 0–10%) progresses to mycosis fungoides; some regard it as abortive MF

**Q3. Describe large-plaque parapsoriasis.**
- Patches >5 cm, irregular, on 'bathing-trunk' area (buttocks, hips, thighs), breasts, flexures; mild scaling and itch
- Poikilodermatous variant (atrophy, telangiectasia, mottled pigmentation — 'poikiloderma vasculare atrophicans')
- Progresses to mycosis fungoides in ~10–30% (some say it is patch-stage MF) — needs long-term follow-up and repeated biopsies

**Q4. How do you differentiate parapsoriasis from early mycosis fungoides?**
- Clinically difficult; MF suspected with progressive size >5 cm, poikiloderma, sun-protected distribution, plaques/infiltration, persistent itch
- Histology: MF shows epidermotropism of atypical cerebriform lymphocytes without much spongiosis, Pautrier microabscesses, lymphocytes lined along the basal layer; immunohistochemistry (CD4>CD8, loss of CD7) and TCR gene rearrangement (clonality)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Psoriasis, nummular eczema, pityriasis rosea (self-limiting), tinea corporis, drug eruption, pityriasis lichenoides chronica, MF, secondary syphilis, seborrhoeic dermatitis

**Q6. Treatment.**
- SPP: emollients, topical steroids, NB-UVB (most effective), PUVA; can be left alone with follow-up
- LPP: phototherapy (NB-UVB/PUVA), potent topical steroids, topical nitrogen mustard/bexarotene; biopsy any change
- Follow-up every 6–12 months (LPP) for MF transformation

**Q7. What is pityriasis lichenoides?**
- Spectrum of clonal T-cell lymphoproliferative inflammatory disorders: PLEVA (Mucha–Habermann — acute crops of papules with haemorrhagic crusts/necrosis healing with varioliform scars; febrile ulceronecrotic variant is an emergency) and PLC (chronic red-brown papules with mica-like scale that peels off)
- Histology: interface dermatitis with wedge-shaped infiltrate, extravasated RBCs, necrotic keratinocytes
- Treatment: erythromycin/doxycycline, NB-UVB, methotrexate for severe

**Q8. Dermoscopy of parapsoriasis vs psoriasis vs MF.**
- Parapsoriasis/ early MF: fine short linear vessels, orange-yellow structureless areas, 'spermatozoa-like' vessels (MF), fine white scales
- Psoriasis: regular dotted vessels — helps but biopsy needed

**Q9. Histopathology of small-plaque parapsoriasis.**
- Mild spongiosis, focal parakeratosis, sparse superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, minimal exocytosis without atypia — no epidermotropism or Pautrier microabscesses

**Q10. Discuss phototherapy in parapsoriasis.**
- NB-UVB 2–3×/week — clears ~70–80% of SPP; PUVA for LPP/ thicker lesions; maintenance phototherapy reduces relapse; regular follow-up with biopsies of persistent/ infiltrated lesions

**Q11. What is PLEVA and the febrile ulceronecrotic variant?**
- PLEVA: crops of erythematous papules with haemorrhagic crust/ necrosis, children/young adults, heal with varioliform scars; FUMHD (Febrile Ulceronecrotic Mucha–Habermann Disease): high fever, extensive ulceronecrotic lesions, systemic involvement, potentially fatal — needs methotrexate, steroids, IVIG

**Q12. What are the clinical features of pityriasis lichenoides chronica?**
- Red-brown flat papules with adherent 'mica-like' scale that detaches as a whole, on trunk and limbs, crops over months–years, leave hypopigmentation (common in dark-skinned children); treat with erythromycin/ azithromycin, NB-UVB

**Q13. Is digitate dermatosis the same as SPP?**
- Yes — a variant of SPP: finger-like elongated yellowish patches along cleavage lines of flanks (looks like a 'hug' from fingers); benign, chronic; rarely progresses to MF

**Q14. Describe the staging of mycosis fungoides (because LPP may evolve).**
- TNMB staging (ISCL/EORTC): T1 patches/plaques <10% BSA, T2 ≥10%, T3 tumours, T4 erythroderma; nodes, viscera, blood (Sézary cells) — stages IA–IVB; early stages (IA–IIA) have near-normal life expectancy

**Q15. What is the treatment of early mycosis fungoides?**
- Skin-directed: topical steroids, nitrogen mustard (mechlorethamine gel), bexarotene gel, imiquimod; NB-UVB (patches) or PUVA (plaques), local radiotherapy; advanced — total skin electron beam, interferon-α, bexarotene, methotrexate, mogamulizumab, brentuximab (CD30+), ECP, HDAC inhibitors, allogeneic transplant

## Quick spotter facts
- Finger-like patches on flanks — digitate dermatosis (SPP)
- Large poikilodermatous patches in bathing-trunk area — LPP, watch for MF

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Parapsoriasis; cutaneous lymphoma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Paronychia — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Paronychia** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Describe the anatomy of the nail unit (PYQ).**
- Nail plate (hard keratin produced by the matrix), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium — seals the space), lateral nail folds, nail matrix (proximal — forms dorsal plate; distal — forms ventral plate; lunula is the visible distal matrix), nail bed (adheres to plate, longitudinal ridges, rich vasculature), hyponychium (beneath free edge), onychodermal band
- Growth: fingernails ~3 mm/month (replace in 6 months), toenails ~1 mm/month (12–18 months)

**Q2. Define acute and chronic paronychia.**
- Acute: painful bacterial infection of the nail fold (S. aureus, Streptococcus, Pseudomonas; HSV — herpetic whitlow) after trauma, hangnail, nail biting, manicure, ingrown nail — red, hot, swollen, tender fold, pus
- Chronic: inflammation of proximal nail fold >6 weeks with loss of cuticle, rounded bolstered red fold, intermittent discharge, transverse ridging/dystrophy of nail — wet work (housewives, cooks, bartenders), diabetes, contact irritants/allergens, Candida colonisation (secondary)
- Drug-induced paronychia with pyogenic granuloma: isotretinoin, EGFR inhibitors, taxanes, antiretrovirals (indinavir)

**Q3. Differentiate bacterial and fungal chronic paronychia (PYQ).**
- Bacterial: acute onset, severe pain, throbbing, pus, rapid course, single digit, Gram-positive cocci
- Candidal/chronic: insidious, mild pain/itch, no frank pus, loss of cuticle, several fingers, wet workers, KOH yeast, nail plate ridging and discolouration (greenish-black — Pseudomonas co-infection)

**Q4. Management of acute paronychia.**
- Warm soaks (water or dilute vinegar/antiseptic) 3–4 times daily; topical mupirocin/fusidic acid
- Oral antibiotics (cloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate; clindamycin/doxycycline for MRSA) if cellulitis
- Abscess: incision and drainage by elevating the nail fold; partial nail avulsion if subungual pus
- Herpetic whitlow — antivirals, do not incise

**Q5. Management of chronic paronychia.**
- Avoid wet work and irritants; cotton-lined rubber gloves; keep hands dry; don't push back cuticles
- Topical potent steroid (± antifungal) as first line (inflammatory/eczematous mechanism), tacrolimus; topical azoles/thymol 4% in alcohol for Candida
- Oral itraconazole/fluconazole when Candida is confirmed and extensive
- Refractory: intralesional steroids, en bloc excision of proximal nail fold (eponychial marsupialisation)
- Patch test if allergic contact dermatitis suspected

**Q6. Discuss ingrown toenails and their management (PYQ).**
- Onychocryptosis — lateral nail plate embeds into lateral nail fold of great toe: tight shoes, improper trimming (curved cut), hyperhidrosis, trauma, retinoids; stages — inflammation, abscess/granulation, chronic hypertrophy of fold
- Conservative: proper nail cutting (straight across), cotton wisp/dental floss under corner, gutter splint, taping, warm soaks, topical steroid/antibiotic
- Surgical: partial nail avulsion with lateral matricectomy (phenol 88% chemical matricectomy — lowest recurrence), electrocautery/laser matricectomy, wedge resection; avoid total avulsion alone

**Q7. Describe the anatomy and growth of the nail unit (linked PYQ).**
- Components: nail plate (keratin — hard keratins), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium), lateral folds, matrix (proximal — dorsal plate; distal — ventral plate; lunula is visible distal matrix), nail bed, hyponychium
- Growth: fingernail ~3 mm/month (complete regrowth 4–6 months), toenail ~1 mm/month (12–18 months); faster in summer, dominant hand, pregnancy, psoriasis; slower in elderly, illness, yellow nail syndrome

**Q8. Candida in chronic paronychia — role.**
- Candida is often isolated but is thought to be secondary colonisation; chronic paronychia is primarily an irritant/ allergic inflammatory disorder of the nail fold in wet workers — topical steroids are more effective than antifungals alone; combine both

**Q9. What surgical options for refractory chronic paronychia?**
- En bloc excision of proximal nail fold (crescentic excision) ± nail avulsion, Swiss roll technique (reflection of nail fold and healing by secondary intention); intralesional steroid into the fold

**Q10. Ingrown toenail — staging and treatment.**
- Stage 1: erythema, oedema, pain; Stage 2: pus/ infection; Stage 3: granulation tissue and lateral nail fold hypertrophy
- Conservative: cotton wisp/ dental floss under nail edge, taping, gutter splint, warm soaks, correct cutting (straight across), proper footwear; antibiotics if infected
- Surgical: partial nail avulsion with lateral matricectomy (phenol 88% chemical, electrocautery, CO2 laser, surgical wedge excision)

**Q11. Paronychia in children (thumb-suckers) — organisms.**
- Mixed oral flora including anaerobes and Candida; treat with amoxicillin-clavulanate/ clindamycin and topical antifungal; discourage thumb-sucking

**Q12. Drug-induced paronychia.**
- Retinoids (isotretinoin), EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, erlotinib, gefitinib), MEK inhibitors, taxanes, methotrexate, indinavir — painful periungual inflammation with pyogenic granuloma-like lesions; dose modification, topical steroids, antiseptic soaks, doxycycline, silver nitrate/ timolol for granulation

**Q13. What causes acute paronychia?**
- Bacterial infection through breach of nail fold/cuticle: S. aureus (commonest), Streptococcus pyogenes, Pseudomonas, anaerobes (mouth flora in nail biters/thumb-suckers); herpetic whitlow (HSV) is a viral mimic; drugs causing paronychia with pyogenic granulomas — retinoids, EGFR inhibitors, taxanes, HIV protease inhibitors (indinavir)

**Q14. What is a felon?**
- Deep infection of the distal pulp space (closed compartments) — throbbing pain, tense swelling; needs urgent incision and drainage and antibiotics to prevent osteomyelitis/necrosis

**Q15. What are the complications of chronic paronychia?**
- Nail plate dystrophy (transverse ridges, discolouration — green with Pseudomonas, brown/black with Candida), cuticle loss, onycholysis, secondary bacterial infection, persistent swelling, rarely SCC of nail fold (in non-healing cases — biopsy)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bolstered proximal fold with lost cuticle in a wet worker — chronic paronychia
- Phenol matricectomy for ingrown toenail

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nail disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Parry–Romberg syndrome — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Parry–Romberg syndrome** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What is Parry–Romberg syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Progressive hemifacial atrophy — slowly progressive, usually unilateral atrophy of the skin, subcutaneous fat, muscle and bone of the face, typically in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve; considered part of the linear morphoea spectrum (often coexists with en coup de sabre)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Onset in childhood/adolescence (first or second decade), females more
- Progressive sinking of one side of face — cheek, temple, around eye (enophthalmos), lip, tongue, gums; minimal skin induration (unlike en coup de sabre), sometimes hyperpigmentation; deviation of mouth and nose to affected side
- Progression for 2–10 years then 'burns out'
- Associated: ipsilateral hair loss/whitening, heterochromia of iris, uveitis, dental root atrophy, delayed eruption, trigeminal neuralgia, facial pain, migraine, seizures (with intracranial calcification or white-matter lesions on MRI)

**Q3. How do you differentiate it from en coup de sabre?**
- En coup de sabre: paramedian forehead/frontal scalp linear band, sclerotic/indurated skin, scarring alopecia
- Parry–Romberg: lower face (below forehead), atrophy of deeper tissues predominantly with little skin sclerosis
- Both may coexist and share neurological complications

**Q4. Investigations.**
- MRI brain (ipsilateral white-matter hyperintensities, calcification, atrophy) and EEG if neurological symptoms; ophthalmology review
- Facial imaging (CT/MRI) to assess bone/fat loss; photographs and measurements to track progression
- ANA, anti-ssDNA (may be positive)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Linear morphoea/en coup de sabre, facial lipodystrophy (HIV/acquired partial lipodystrophy — bilateral), Rasmussen encephalitis, lupus profundus, hemifacial microsomia (congenital, non-progressive), steroid-induced lipoatrophy, Barraquer–Simons syndrome (bilateral, cephalocaudal)

**Q6. Management.**
- Active phase: methotrexate with systemic corticosteroids (pulse methylprednisolone) as in linear morphoea; mycophenolate; hydroxychloroquine (adjunct)
- After disease is inactive (≥1–2 years stable): reconstructive surgery — autologous fat grafting (most common), dermal fillers (hyaluronic acid), free flaps, bone grafts/implants; orthodontic and dental care
- Antiepileptics for seizures; eye care

**Q7. Prognosis.**
- Self-limiting progression with permanent facial asymmetry; psychosocial impact large

**Q8. What scoring helps follow the disease?**
- Serial standardised photographs, 3D imaging/ facial measurements, LoSCAT (modified Localised Scleroderma Skin Severity Index and Damage Index), MRI of face/brain for deep and neurological activity

**Q9. What dental and ocular complications occur?**
- Dental: root resorption, delayed eruption, malocclusion, jaw hypoplasia on affected side
- Ocular: enophthalmos, uveitis, heterochromia, eyelid atrophy, retinal vasculitis, optic neuritis — need ophthalmic follow-up

**Q10. What is the pathogenesis?**
- Not fully known — considered an autoimmune localised scleroderma variant (linear morphoea spectrum); other theories: sympathetic nervous system dysfunction, trigeminal neuritis, infection (Borrelia), trauma; histology of skin shows sclerosis/ atrophy with perivascular lymphocytes

**Q11. Histopathology findings.**
- Early: perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate in dermis/ subcutis; late: dermal sclerosis or simply atrophy of dermis and subcutaneous fat with loss of adnexa, sometimes muscle atrophy; similar to linear morphoea

**Q12. What is the role of autologous fat grafting?**
- Lipofilling (Coleman technique — harvesting fat by liposuction, purification by centrifugation, micro-injection in layers) restores volume once disease is inactive; may need multiple sessions; some evidence of improved skin quality from adipose stem cells; complications — resorption, cysts, asymmetry

**Q13. How is disease inactivity determined before reconstruction?**
- Stable facial measurements and photographs for ≥1–2 years, no new symptoms, MRI without active inflammation, off systemic therapy or on stable dose — then reconstructive surgery

**Q14. Prognosis for neurological involvement.**
- Seizures may persist and need long-term antiepileptics; brain lesions often stable; rarely progressive neurological deficits; neurological involvement can predate skin changes

**Q15. Classify facial hemiatrophy by severity (Guerrero-Santos).**
- Type I: skin and subcutaneous tissue (mild); II: plus muscle; III: plus cartilage/ bone — moderate; IV: severe with skeletal deformity — guides reconstructive planning

## Quick spotter facts
- Unilateral progressive facial sinking in a child without much skin sclerosis — Parry–Romberg
- Treat active phase like linear morphoea; reconstruct after burnout

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Morphoea — progressive hemifacial atrophy). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pearly penile papules — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pearly penile papules** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What are pearly penile papules (PPP)?**
- Common normal anatomical variant (angiofibromas — hirsuties coronae glandis) in 15–45% of men (more in uncircumcised, young adults): small (1–3 mm), smooth, dome-shaped or filiform, pearly white to skin-coloured papules arranged in one or several symmetrical rows around the corona and sulcus of the glans; asymptomatic, not infectious, not sexually transmitted

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Angiofibroma: dense fibrous stroma with stellate fibroblasts and dilated thin-walled vessels covered by normal or slightly thinned epidermis (same as facial angiofibroma)

**Q3. Discuss non-venereal genital lesions (PYQ).**
- Normal variants: PPP, Fordyce spots (ectopic sebaceous glands — yellow papules on shaft/labia), vestibular papillae (women — symmetrical filiform papules of vestibule; female counterpart of PPP), Tyson's glands, median raphe cysts, angiokeratomas of scrotum (Fordyce)
- Dermatoses: psoriasis, lichen planus (annular on glans), lichen sclerosus (BXO), lichen nitidus, seborrhoeic dermatitis, Zoon's balanitis (plasma cell balanitis — glistening red-orange plaque on glans of uncircumcised elderly), fixed drug eruption, contact dermatitis, candidal balanoposthitis, scabies nodules, vitiligo
- Neoplastic: erythroplasia of Queyrat, bowenoid papulosis, SCC, extramammary Paget's, Kaposi sarcoma

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Genital warts (condyloma acuminata — irregular, random distribution, cauliflower surface, acetowhite), molluscum contagiosum (umbilicated, scattered), Fordyce spots (shaft, yellow), sebaceous hyperplasia, lichen nitidus, ectopic sebaceous glands, angiokeratomas

**Q5. Why does it matter in clinics?**
- Commonly mistaken for genital warts by patients and doctors → anxiety ('venereophobia'), unnecessary destructive treatment; dermoscopy shows uniform papules with central comma/dotted vessels without the mosaic pattern of warts

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance and education (no treatment needed)
- For cosmetic/psychological distress: CO2 laser vaporisation, fractional CO2, pulsed-dye laser, radiofrequency, cryotherapy (variable) — warn about scarring and recurrence

**Q7. Discuss non-venereal genital dermatoses (expanded list).**
- Normal variants: PPP, Fordyce spots, Tyson's glands, median raphe cysts
- Inflammatory: psoriasis, LP, LS (BXO), seborrhoeic/ contact dermatitis, Zoon's balanitis, FDE, aphthae/ Behçet's, candidal/ irritant balanoposthitis
- Infections (non-STI): tinea cruris, scabies nodules, erythrasma
- Neoplastic/ premalignant: erythroplasia of Queyrat, bowenoid papulosis, SCC, extramammary Paget's, angiokeratomas of Fordyce (scrotum), sebaceous/ epidermoid cysts, lymphangioma

**Q8. What are angiokeratomas of Fordyce?**
- Multiple small dark-red/ purple papules on scrotum/ vulva of older adults — dilated superficial vessels with hyperkeratosis; benign; differentiate from angiokeratoma corporis diffusum (Fabry disease — 'bathing trunk' distribution, pain crises, renal failure)

**Q9. Treatment options when requested.**
- Reassurance is best; for persistent anxiety — CO2 laser ablation, cryotherapy, radiofrequency; avoid podophyllin/ imiquimod (ineffective, irritating)

**Q10. Psychosexual aspects — venereophobia.**
- Anxiety that normal genital variants are STIs; counsel, examine and test as needed, explain benign nature, consider psychiatric referral for persistent illness anxiety (venereophobia, Dhat syndrome in Indian context)

**Q11. What is Zoon's balanitis?**
- Plasma cell balanitis — well-defined, glistening orange-red plaque with 'cayenne pepper' spots on glans/ inner prepuce of uncircumcised older men; histology — dense plasma cell infiltrate; differentiate from erythroplasia of Queyrat (biopsy); circumcision curative

**Q12. Dhat syndrome — what is it?**
- Culture-bound syndrome in South Asia: young men attribute fatigue, anxiety, sexual weakness to loss of semen in urine/ nocturnal emissions; associated depression/ anxiety; manage with explanation, sex education, treat underlying psychiatric disorder

**Q13. What is the prevalence and natural history?**
- Present in ~15–45% of men (more in uncircumcised, young adults); appear after puberty, may fade with age; not sexually transmitted, not related to hygiene, benign and permanent

**Q14. Dermoscopy of PPP vs genital warts.**
- PPP: regular 'cobblestone' or grape-like arrangement of uniform papules with central dotted/comma vessels in rows along the corona
- Warts: irregular papillomatous lesions with glomerular/ hairpin vessels and white network, mosaic pattern

**Q15. Female counterpart?**
- Vestibular papillomatosis — symmetrical, soft, separate-based papillae on the inner labia minora/vestibule; normal variant (may be confused with warts — acetowhite test can falsely be positive)

## Quick spotter facts
- Symmetrical rows of pearly dome papules around the corona — PPP (normal variant, angiofibroma)
- Do not treat as warts

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Normal variants of genitalia; non-venereal genital lesions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pediculosis — viva
posts.summary: Infestations · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pediculosis** (Infestations)_

**Q1. Name the lice that infest humans.**
- Pediculus humanus capitis (head louse), Pediculus humanus corporis (body louse), Pthirus pubis (crab/pubic louse)
- Obligate blood-sucking ectoparasites; wingless, dorsoventrally flattened, six legs with claws

**Q2. Describe the life cycle.**
- Egg (nit) cemented to the hair shaft close to scalp → hatches in 7–10 days → three nymph stages over ~9–12 days → adult lives ~30 days; female lays 5–10 eggs/day
- Lice die away from host in 1–2 days (head louse)

**Q3. Clinical features of pediculosis capitis.**
- Children (girls more), itching of scalp esp. occiput and behind ears, excoriations, secondary impetigo, occipital/cervical lymphadenopathy
- Nits: ovoid grey-white 0.8 mm, firmly attached, cannot be flicked off (unlike dandruff/hair casts)
- Heavy infestation: matted hair ('plica polonica'), id-like papular eruption on neck

**Q4. Differentiate nits from hair casts and dandruff.**
- Nits: eccentrically cemented oval structures on one side of hair, not movable
- Hair casts (pseudonits): tubular keratin sheaths encircling the hair, slide freely along the shaft
- Dandruff: loose flakes easily shaken off; also piedra (hard nodules — fungal), trichorrhexis nodosa, hair spray droplets

**Q5. Describe pediculosis corporis.**
- Body lice live in clothing seams, visit skin to feed — seen in poverty, homelessness, refugees, overcrowding
- Itching, excoriations, hyperpigmented thickened skin ('vagabond's disease'), maculae caeruleae
- Vector of epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii), trench fever (Bartonella quintana), relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis)
- Treatment: hygiene and laundering of clothing at ≥60 °C — no need to treat the body usually

**Q6. Describe pediculosis pubis.**
- Sexually transmitted; pubic, perianal, axillary hair, beard, eyelashes (children — consider abuse)
- Itching, lice and nits at hair roots, maculae caeruleae (slate-blue macules from louse saliva on thighs and trunk)
- Screen for other STIs; treat partners

**Q7. Investigations.**
- Wet combing with a fine-toothed comb (most reliable to detect live lice)
- Dermoscopy: live nymphs, viable nits (oval with operculum) vs empty nits (translucent with flat cut end)
- Live louse = active infestation; nits >1 cm from scalp may be old

**Q8. Treatment of head lice.**
- Topical pediculicides — 2 applications 7–10 days apart (second kills newly hatched nymphs):
- Permethrin 1% cream rinse (10 min), dimeticone 4% (physical — no resistance; preferred where resistance is common), malathion 0.5%, ivermectin 0.5% lotion (single application), spinosad 0.9%, benzyl alcohol 5%, abametapir
- Oral ivermectin 400 µg/kg on days 1 and 8 for resistant cases (>15 kg)
- Wet combing every 3–4 days for 2 weeks; remove nits with fine comb/vinegar rinse; wash pillowcases, combs, hats in hot water; treat all affected household members

**Q9. Treatment of eyelash infestation (phthiriasis palpebrarum).**
- Occlusive petrolatum twice daily for 8–10 days, mechanical removal, or oral ivermectin; pediculicides not used near the eyes

**Q10. Why is lindane no longer used?**
- Neurotoxicity (seizures) especially in children and with misuse; banned/withdrawn in many countries including India (please confirm current status)

**Q11. Causes of treatment failure?**
- Resistance (kdr mutations to permethrin), wrong application, reinfestation from untreated contacts, no second application, misdiagnosis of dead nits as active infestation

**Q12. Ivermectin lotion and spinosad — details.**
- Ivermectin 0.5% lotion: single 10-min application to dry hair, no nit combing needed (lice hatching from eggs cannot feed), ≥6 months age
- Spinosad 0.9%: neurotoxic to lice and ovicidal, single application (repeat in 7 days if live lice), ≥6 months/4 years depending on country, contains benzyl alcohol

**Q13. Mechanism of dimeticone.**
- Silicone oil coats lice and blocks spiracles/ water excretion (physical suffocation and osmotic disruption) — no resistance; 4% lotion, two applications 7 days apart; flammable — avoid flames

**Q14. Head lice in schools — policy advice.**
- 'No-nit' policies are not recommended (nits alone don't mean active infestation); children can return after first treatment; screen family members; educate about not sharing combs/ hats

**Q15. Myiasis and tungiasis — related infestations (PYQ).**
- Myiasis: fly larvae in skin/ wounds (furuncular — Dermatobia; wound myiasis — Chrysomya bezziana in India); treat by suffocation (petrolatum), extraction, ivermectin, wound care
- Tungiasis: Tunga penetrans flea embedded in toes/ periungual — white papule with central black dot; extract with sterile needle, tetanus prophylaxis

## Quick spotter facts
- Nits firmly cemented on one side of hair shaft
- Maculae caeruleae — pubic lice
- Body louse — vector of epidemic typhus, trench fever, relapsing fever

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Infestations). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pellagra — viva
posts.summary: Nutritional & metabolic · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pellagra** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What is pellagra?**
- Systemic disease due to deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3 — nicotinic acid/nicotinamide) or its precursor tryptophan, with photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia and death if untreated — the '4 Ds'
- 'Pelle agra' = rough skin (Italian)

**Q2. Discuss the causes of pellagra (PYQ).**
- Dietary: maize/jowar (sorghum)-based diets — niacin in maize is bound (niacytin) and maize has little tryptophan; sorghum has excess leucine which inhibits tryptophan–niacin conversion; poverty, famine, food faddism
- Alcoholism (commonest in India today), malabsorption (Crohn's, chronic diarrhoea, gastrectomy), anorexia nervosa, HIV, haemodialysis
- Drugs: isoniazid (competes with pyridoxine — needed for conversion), 6-mercaptopurine/azathioprine, 5-fluorouracil, pyrazinamide, ethionamide, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, chloramphenicol
- Carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin), Hartnup disease (defective neutral amino-acid transport — SLC6A19), deficiency of riboflavin/pyridoxine (cofactors)

**Q3. Describe the cutaneous features.**
- Symmetric, sharply demarcated photosensitive dermatitis on sun-exposed sites — dorsa of hands/forearms (gauntlet or glove), feet (boot), face (butterfly-like), neck (Casal's necklace — band around neck in C3/C4 dermatome), V of chest
- Acute: erythema, burning, blistering like sunburn; chronic: dry rough scaly hyperpigmented (dark-brown/'varnished') thickened skin with fissures; sharp upper border
- Perineal/genital involvement (friction), angular cheilitis, glossitis (red smooth swollen 'beefy' tongue), stomatitis, vulvitis/vaginitis

**Q4. Systemic features.**
- GI: diarrhoea, abdominal pain, nausea, anorexia (atrophy of mucosa)
- Neuropsychiatric: insomnia, irritability, depression, apathy, confusion, memory loss, psychosis, dementia, peripheral neuropathy; encephalopathy in alcoholics
- Weakness, weight loss; death if untreated

**Q5. How do you diagnose pellagra?**
- Clinical diagnosis with rapid response to niacin (therapeutic test)
- Supportive: low urinary N-methylnicotinamide and 2-pyridone (<1.5 mg/24 h), low serum tryptophan/niacin; check other deficiencies (B1, B2, B6, B12, folate, zinc), LFT (alcohol), 5-HIAA for carcinoid
- Histology non-specific: pallor of upper epidermis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, psoriasiform hyperplasia (similar to necrolytic migratory erythema, acrodermatitis enteropathica — 'deficiency dermatitis')

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Photosensitive drug eruption, polymorphic light eruption, chronic actinic dermatitis, airborne contact dermatitis, porphyria cutanea tarda, lupus (SCLE/DM), Hartnup disease, kwashiorkor, necrolytic migratory erythema, Bloom/Cockayne syndromes (children), carcinoid flushing

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Nicotinamide 100 mg every 6 h (or 300 mg/day) for 3–4 weeks then maintenance (nicotinamide preferred — no flushing); high-protein balanced diet; vitamin B-complex supplements (B1, B2, B6 deficits coexist), zinc
- Photoprotection, emollients for skin; stop alcohol/offending drug; treat carcinoid/malabsorption
- Response: mental symptoms improve within 24–48 h, skin in 1–2 weeks

**Q8. Discuss cutaneous manifestations of vitamin deficiencies (PYQ).**
- Vitamin A: xerosis, phrynoderma, night blindness, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia
- B2 (riboflavin): angular cheilitis, magenta tongue, seborrhoeic-like dermatitis, oral-ocular-genital syndrome
- B3 (niacin): pellagra
- B6: seborrhoeic dermatitis-like, cheilitis, glossitis, neuropathy
- B12/folate: hyperpigmentation (knuckles, palms), glossitis, angular cheilitis, canities
- Biotin: periorificial dermatitis, alopecia (raw egg-white avidin)
- Vitamin C (scurvy): perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding, poor healing, woody oedema
- Vitamin K: purpura, ecchymoses
- Zinc: acrodermatitis enteropathica-like; essential fatty acids: xerosis, alopecia

**Q9. Discuss the role of zinc in dermatology (PYQ).**
- Cofactor for >300 enzymes (metalloproteinases, DNA/RNA polymerase, superoxide dismutase); needed for wound healing, immunity, keratinisation
- Deficiency: acrodermatitis enteropathica (inherited SLC39A4/ZIP4 defect; acquired — prematurity, low breast-milk zinc, TPN, malabsorption, alcoholism, nephrotic syndrome): periorificial and acral eroded psoriasiform dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhoea, paronychia, irritability, infections
- Therapeutic uses: acrodermatitis enteropathica (1–3 mg/kg/day elemental zinc), acne, warts, rosacea, leg ulcers, leishmaniasis, hidradenitis, erosive pustular dermatosis, as adjuvant in leprosy reactions

**Q10. Explain the biochemistry of niacin and tryptophan.**
- Niacin forms NAD and NADP (coenzymes for >400 redox reactions); synthesised from tryptophan (60 mg tryptophan → 1 mg niacin) in a pathway requiring riboflavin (B2), pyridoxine (B6) and iron; RDA ~14–16 mg niacin equivalents/day

**Q11. Why does isoniazid cause pellagra?**
- INH is structurally similar to niacin and binds pyridoxine (vitamin B6), inhibiting kynureninase — blocks tryptophan → niacin conversion; slow acetylators at higher risk; prevent with pyridoxine supplementation

**Q12. What is Hartnup disease?**
- Autosomal recessive defect of neutral amino-acid transporter (SLC6A19) in gut and kidney → tryptophan malabsorption and aminoaciduria; intermittent pellagra-like photosensitive rash, cerebellar ataxia, psychiatric symptoms in childhood, triggered by poor nutrition/ illness; diagnosis — urinary neutral amino acids; treatment — nicotinamide, high-protein diet, sun protection

**Q13. What is the Casal's necklace and why at that site?**
- Sharply demarcated band of erythema and pigmentation around the neck (C3–C4 dermatome) due to sun exposure at the collar line; may extend down as a V-shaped 'cravat'; pathognomonic of pellagra

**Q14. Pellagra in alcoholics — special points.**
- Combined deficiency (poor intake, malabsorption, impaired liver storage and conversion); presents with encephalopathy (confusion, delirium) often misattributed to alcohol withdrawal — 'alcoholic pellagra encephalopathy'; give thiamine plus nicotinamide and B-complex; check for Wernicke's

**Q15. Prevention in India.**
- Diversified diet, cereal-legume combinations, fortification, treat alcoholism, pyridoxine with INH, screen vulnerable groups (prisoners, psychiatric inpatients, homeless, chronic diarrhoea)

## Quick spotter facts
- Photosensitive dermatitis + Casal's necklace + diarrhoea + dementia — pellagra
- Maize diet, alcohol, isoniazid, carcinoid, Hartnup
- Nicotinamide — mind improves first

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nutritional dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Perioral dermatitis — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Perioral dermatitis** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is perioral dermatitis?**
- Common facial eruption of young women (and children) with small erythematous papules, papulovesicles and pustules on a red, scaly background around the mouth, sparing a narrow zone at the vermilion border; may involve nasolabial folds and periocular areas (periorificial dermatitis)

**Q2. Causes/triggers.**
- Topical (and inhaled/nasal) corticosteroids — the most important; heavy moisturisers/foundation, fluorinated toothpaste, cosmetics, sunscreens; OCPs, hormonal changes; Demodex, Candida, fusobacteria (unclear); barrier dysfunction/atopy
- Granulomatous periorificial dermatitis (childhood — Afro-Caribbean children, yellow-brown papules; FACE — facial Afro-Caribbean childhood eruption)

**Q3. Differential diagnosis.**
- Rosacea (older, central face, flushing, telangiectasia), acne (comedones), seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy scale, nasolabial), contact dermatitis (allergic — patch test), steroid rosacea, Demodex folliculitis, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, sarcoidosis (granulomatous form), impetigo, lip-licking dermatitis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Spongiotic dermatitis with perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, sometimes rosacea-like; granulomatous variant shows non-caseating granulomas around follicles

**Q5. Treatment.**
- 'Zero therapy': stop all topical steroids and facial cosmetics (warn about rebound flare for 1–2 weeks; taper from potent to hydrocortisone if severe), use gentle cleanser
- Topical: metronidazole 0.75–1% gel/cream, erythromycin, clindamycin, azelaic acid 15–20%, pimecrolimus/tacrolimus (also for steroid withdrawal), ivermectin 1%
- Oral: doxycycline 40–100 mg or minocycline for 6–12 weeks (adults); erythromycin/azithromycin in children and pregnancy; isotretinoin (resistant)
- Recurrence is common if steroids are restarted

**Q6. Describe the clinical features in detail.**
- Young women (also children): grouped small (1–2 mm) erythematous papules, papulovesicles and pustules on a red, mildly scaly base around the mouth, nasolabial folds and chin, characteristically sparing a narrow zone of skin next to the vermilion border; periocular/perinasal variants ('periorificial dermatitis'); burning more than itching

**Q7. What is granulomatous periorificial dermatitis?**
- Childhood variant (prepubertal, often darker skin) with yellow-brown monomorphic papules around mouth, nose, eyes; histology granulomatous; treat with topical metronidazole/erythromycin, oral erythromycin (children <8 y) or azithromycin

**Q8. Why do topical steroids worsen it?**
- Steroids give initial improvement (vasoconstriction, anti-inflammation) but cause rebound flare on stopping and perpetuate barrier damage, follicular overgrowth of Demodex/fusiform bacteria — steroid addiction; must stop all facial steroids (taper potent ones or switch to hydrocortisone/tacrolimus) — 'zero therapy'

**Q9. What doses of oral tetracyclines are used?**
- Doxycycline 50–100 mg/day or minocycline 50–100 mg/day for 6–12 weeks, tapering; erythromycin/azithromycin in children and pregnancy

**Q10. Differentiate perioral dermatitis from rosacea and acne.**
- POD: young women, perioral/ periocular micro-papules and pustules, spares vermilion border zone, no telangiectasia/ flushing, no comedones; steroid/ cosmetic triggers
- Rosacea: central face, flushing, telangiectasia, older adults
- Acne: comedones, wider distribution, adolescents

**Q11. Topical treatment options.**
- Topical metronidazole 0.75–1%, azelaic acid 15–20%, erythromycin/ clindamycin, pimecrolimus 1% (good for steroid-induced), ivermectin 1%; avoid occlusive moisturisers and fluorinated toothpastes

**Q12. Children's periorificial dermatitis — management.**
- Stop topical/ inhaled steroids if possible (nasal/ inhaled steroid spacers), topical metronidazole/ erythromycin, oral erythromycin or azithromycin (avoid tetracyclines <8 y); resolves over weeks

**Q13. What are the triggers from cosmetics and dental products?**
- Heavy moisturisers/ foundation (occlusion), fluorinated toothpaste, chewing gum, sodium lauryl sulphate, sunscreens; hormonal (OCP), stress

**Q14. What is 'zero therapy' and rebound?**
- Stopping all topical products including steroids and cosmetics (cleanse with water only) — initial flare (rebound) in 1–2 weeks, then improvement; reassure and support with oral tetracyclines/ topical non-steroid agents

**Q15. Prognosis.**
- Resolves in weeks to months with treatment; recurs if steroids or heavy cosmetics restarted

## Quick spotter facts
- Papulopustules around the mouth sparing the vermilion border in a steroid-cream user — perioral dermatitis
- Zero therapy + doxycycline

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Rosacea and related disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Phrynoderma — viva
posts.summary: Nutritional & metabolic · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Phrynoderma** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What is phrynoderma?**
- 'Toad skin' — follicular hyperkeratotic papules with a central keratotic plug, classically linked to vitamin A deficiency but now considered a marker of multiple nutritional deficiencies (vitamin A, B-complex, E, essential fatty acids, protein-energy malnutrition)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Dry rough skin with symmetric, firm, skin-coloured to brown follicular papules (2–6 mm) with central horny spines; first on extensor elbows, knees, then thighs, buttocks, shoulders, extensor forearms, back
- School-age children commonest, especially in low-income settings; may coexist with xerophthalmia (night blindness, Bitot's spots, xerosis conjunctivae, keratomalacia), angular cheilitis, glossitis

**Q3. Discuss features of vitamin A deficiency and hypervitaminosis A (PYQ).**
- Deficiency: xerosis, phrynoderma, hair dryness, night blindness (earliest), conjunctival/corneal xerosis, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia, increased infections (measles severity)
- Hypervitaminosis A (acute — polar bear liver, mega-doses; chronic — retinoid excess): headache, raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumour cerebri), vomiting; skin — dryness, peeling, cheilitis, alopecia, pruritus, hyperpigmentation; bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, hypercalcaemia, teratogenicity

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Follicular hyperkeratosis with keratotic plugs distending the follicle, atrophy of sebaceous glands, mild perifollicular infiltrate

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Keratosis pilaris (outer arms/thighs, atopic, finer, lifelong), lichen spinulosus (grouped spiny papules in plaques), pityriasis rubra pilaris (knuckle papules, orange keratoderma), Darier's disease (greasy seborrhoeic papules), follicular eczema, lichen nitidus, scurvy (perifollicular haemorrhage + corkscrew hair), frictional lichenoid eruption, follicular mucinosis

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Serum retinol (<20 µg/dl deficiency), CBC, total protein/albumin, other vitamins/zinc as indicated; eye examination
- Clinical response to supplementation supports diagnosis

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Vitamin A: WHO therapy for xerophthalmia — 2 lakh IU (200,000 IU) orally on day 1, day 2 and after 2 weeks (1 lakh IU for 6–12 months, 50,000 IU <6 months)
- Balanced diet with green leafy vegetables, yellow/orange fruits, dairy; B-complex, vitamin E, essential fatty acid (safflower oil) supplements; treat underlying malnutrition, malabsorption
- Topical keratolytics: urea 10–20%, salicylic acid, lactic acid; emollients
- National programme: biannual vitamin A prophylaxis for children 9 months–5 years (India)

**Q8. Discuss skin changes in kwashiorkor (PYQ).**
- Protein deficiency with adequate calories (1–5 y after weaning): 'flaky-paint' / 'crazy-pavement' dermatosis (hyperpigmented patches that peel leaving pink/hypopigmented areas), especially pressure areas, buttocks and legs
- Hair: dry, sparse, easily pluckable, hypopigmented (reddish-brown), 'flag sign' (alternating bands of light and dark hair indicating periods of poor and good nutrition)
- Oedema (pitting), moon face, hepatomegaly (fatty liver), apathy, growth failure; marasmus: wasting, loose wrinkled skin, 'monkey facies', no oedema

**Q9. Describe Bitot's spots and xerophthalmia staging (WHO).**
- XN night blindness, X1A conjunctival xerosis, X1B Bitot's spots (foamy triangular grey-white patches on temporal bulbar conjunctiva), X2 corneal xerosis, X3A/B corneal ulceration/ keratomalacia, XS corneal scar, XF xerophthalmic fundus

**Q10. Why is vitamin A important for skin?**
- Retinoic acid regulates epidermal differentiation (keratin expression), sebaceous gland function and immunity; deficiency → squamous metaplasia and follicular hyperkeratosis; excess → peeling, cheilitis, alopecia

**Q11. What is the role of essential fatty acid deficiency?**
- Linoleic acid deficiency (TPN without lipids, fat malabsorption) causes dry scaly dermatitis, follicular papules, alopecia, poor wound healing — triene:tetraene ratio >0.4; corrected by oral/ IV lipid or topical sunflower/ safflower oil

**Q12. Phrynoderma in adults — causes.**
- Alcoholism, malabsorption (coeliac, Crohn's, chronic pancreatitis, bariatric surgery), chronic liver disease, restrictive diets/ anorexia, HIV

**Q13. Response to treatment.**
- Follicular papules improve over 4–8 weeks with vitamin/ nutritional supplementation and keratolytics; night blindness reverses within days of vitamin A

**Q14. Which other nutrients are linked to phrynoderma?**
- Vitamin B-complex (especially B2, B6), vitamin E, vitamin C and essential fatty acid deficiency, protein-energy malnutrition; in India many cases respond to B-complex and EFA supplementation even with normal vitamin A levels

**Q15. Prevention at the community level.**
- Nutrition education (green leafy vegetables, yellow fruits), mid-day meal programmes, biannual vitamin A supplementation for children (9 months–5 years), deworming, treatment of diarrhoea and infections

## Quick spotter facts
- Toad-like follicular spiny papules on elbows/knees of a malnourished child — phrynoderma
- Flag sign — kwashiorkor hair

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nutritional dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Piebaldism — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Piebaldism** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define piebaldism.**
- Rare autosomal dominant congenital disorder of melanocyte migration/differentiation (KIT proto-oncogene loss-of-function; also SNAI2) with stable depigmented patches present from birth and a white forelock

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- White forelock (poliosis) with triangular/diamond-shaped depigmented patch on the mid-forehead in ~80–90%
- Symmetrical depigmented patches on ventral trunk, mid-extremities (sparing hands, feet and back), often with islands of normal or hyperpigmented skin inside and at margins
- Eyebrows/eyelashes may be white; lesions stable throughout life (no progression, may partially repigment)
- No systemic involvement (vs Waardenburg — deafness, heterochromia, dystopia canthorum)

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Absent or markedly reduced melanocytes in depigmented skin (confirmed by DOPA/immunostains); normal melanocytes at hyperpigmented islands

**Q4. Differentiate piebaldism from vitiligo.**
- Piebaldism: present at birth, stable, specific distribution (forehead, ventral trunk, mid-limbs), white forelock, hyperpigmented islands, family history (AD), no Koebner or progression, no autoimmune association
- Vitiligo: acquired, progressive or relapsing, any site (acral, periorificial), Koebner, autoimmune associations, responds to medical therapy

**Q5. Other differentials.**
- Waardenburg syndrome, nevus depigmentosus, Ziprkowski–Margolis (X-linked albinism–deafness), Tietz syndrome, hypomelanosis of Ito, tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf), Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (acquired poliosis)

**Q6. Management.**
- Genetic counselling (50% risk to offspring), sun protection of depigmented skin, camouflage
- Medical therapy (phototherapy) is ineffective because melanocytes are absent; surgical — suction blister grafts, mini-punch grafts, non-cultured epidermal cell suspension work well because disease is stable

**Q7. What is the white forelock and differential diagnosis of poliosis?**
- Localised patch of white hair (poliosis) — piebaldism, Waardenburg syndrome, vitiligo, alopecia areata regrowth, halo naevus, Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada, Alezzandrini syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, NF1, post-inflammatory/ radiation, Marfan (rare)

**Q8. Explain grafting outcomes in piebaldism.**
- Excellent and stable repigmentation with mini-punch grafting, suction blister grafts, non-cultured melanocyte–keratinocyte transplant because the disorder is stable and recipient sites lack inflammation; post-graft NB-UVB may enhance

**Q9. What is Woolf/ Tietz syndrome?**
- Tietz (MITF): generalised hypopigmentation (albinoid) with congenital profound deafness, AD
- Ziprkowski–Margolis (Woolf): X-linked albinism–deafness with piebald-like patches

**Q10. Is piebaldism associated with Hirschsprung disease?**
- Classic piebaldism is not; but piebaldism-like pigmentation with Hirschsprung disease suggests Waardenburg type 4 (Shah–Waardenburg — EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10) — check bowel symptoms and hearing

**Q11. What is the role of camouflage?**
- Waterproof cosmetic cover creams, dihydroxyacetone self-tanners, micropigmentation/ tattooing for small stable areas, hair dye for forelock; sunscreen for depigmented skin to prevent sunburn

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. Explain the molecular basis.**
- KIT encodes the tyrosine kinase receptor for stem cell factor; loss-of-function (dominant-negative mutations are more severe) prevents melanoblast migration from the neural crest and survival in ventral and midline areas — hence the distribution

**Q14. What is the role of SCF/KIT in other disorders?**
- Gain-of-function KIT mutations: mastocytosis (D816V), gastrointestinal stromal tumours, acral and mucosal melanomas — treated with KIT inhibitors (imatinib), whereas piebaldism is loss-of-function

**Q15. Why are hyperpigmented islands seen?**
- Melanocytes that do reach these areas can be hyperfunctional; CALM-like macules in piebaldism may cause confusion with NF1 (piebaldism with CALMs — check KIT vs NF1/SPRED1)

## Quick spotter facts
- White forelock + ventral depigmentation from birth, stable — piebaldism (KIT)
- Responds to grafting, not phototherapy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Genetic hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pigmented purpuric dermatosis — viva
posts.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pigmented purpuric dermatosis** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. What are pigmented purpuric dermatoses (PPD)?**
- Group of chronic benign capillaritides — lymphocytic inflammation of superficial dermal capillaries with RBC extravasation and haemosiderin deposition, giving petechiae ('cayenne pepper' spots) on a brown background; mainly lower legs; not associated with systemic disease or platelet defects

**Q2. Name the clinical variants.**
- Schamberg's disease (progressive pigmentary purpura — commonest): irregular orange-brown patches with cayenne-pepper petechiae on shins/ankles of men
- Purpura annularis telangiectodes of Majocchi: annular patches with telangiectatic punctae, young women, legs
- Pigmented purpuric lichenoid dermatosis of Gougerot and Blum: lichenoid rust-brown papules coalescing into plaques, middle-aged men
- Lichen aureus: solitary golden-brown patch, often unilateral on leg/trunk, persistent, children/young adults
- Eczematid-like purpura of Doucas and Kapetanakis: itchy, scaly, eczematous, widespread
- Others: itching purpura of Lowenthal, granulomatous PPD (Asians), linear, transitory

**Q3. Aetiology / associations.**
- Mostly idiopathic; exacerbated by venous hypertension, exercise, standing, gravitational dependency
- Drugs: aspirin, NSAIDs, paracetamol, carbamazepine, furosemide, thiamine, glipizide, chlordiazepoxide, sildenafil, medroxyprogesterone; contact allergens (textile dyes, rubber, khaki clothing)
- Associations: diabetes, hyperlipidaemia (granulomatous variant), hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis; some persistent PPD can evolve into/mimic mycosis fungoides (clonal T cells)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate around papillary dermal capillaries with endothelial swelling, extravasated RBCs and haemosiderin-laden macrophages (Perls' stain), no fibrinoid necrosis (not true vasculitis); lichenoid infiltrate in Gougerot–Blum and lichen aureus; spongiosis in eczematid type

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Stasis dermatitis/haemosiderosis (venous disease), drug-induced purpura, leukocytoclastic vasculitis (palpable), thrombocytopenic purpura, scurvy (perifollicular), MF (purpuric MF — biopsy, clonality), Kaposi sarcoma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, cholesterol/hyperglobulinaemic purpura (Waldenström)

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Dermoscopy: red globules/dots over copper-orange background with brown network
- CBC with platelets, coagulation profile, blood sugar, lipids, LFT, HCV; review drugs; biopsy in atypical/persistent cases; TCR clonality if MF suspected

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Reassurance; stop suspect drugs; treat venous insufficiency (compression stockings, elevation)
- Topical steroids (moderate–potent) or tacrolimus for itch/inflammation
- Oral vitamin C 500 mg BD + rutoside (flavonoid) 50 mg BD — improves capillary fragility; pentoxifylline, griseofulvin, colchicine (case reports)
- NB-UVB/PUVA — particularly for widespread or MF-like disease
- Lasers (PDL) for cosmetically disturbing lesions

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Chronic, relapsing–remitting over years; benign; pigmentation may persist; follow persistent widespread lesions for MF

**Q9. Describe lichen aureus in detail.**
- Solitary or few golden-brown to rust-coloured lichenoid patches/ plaques, often on legs, trunk, arms; children and young adults; persistent for years; may follow a perforator vein; dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate with haemosiderin; treatment — topical steroids/ calcineurin inhibitors, PUVA

**Q10. What is granulomatous PPD?**
- Variant in Asians with PPD lesions and histological granulomas (perivascular histiocytes); associated with hyperlipidaemia — check lipids; resistant to therapy

**Q11. What is the role of venous insufficiency?**
- Raised venous pressure increases capillary fragility and extravasation; PPD lesions often limited to legs below knee in patients with varicose veins — compression and venous treatment help

**Q12. Describe the Gougerot–Blum variant.**
- Pigmented purpuric lichenoid dermatosis — small rust-brown lichenoid papules coalescing into plaques on legs of middle-aged men; dense lichenoid infiltrate — overlaps with lichen aureus; resistant; PUVA/ topical steroids

**Q13. Drug-induced PPD — mechanism and examples.**
- Hypersensitivity capillaritis to drugs: aspirin, paracetamol, NSAIDs, carbamazepine, furosemide, chlordiazepoxide, glipizide, medroxyprogesterone, thiamine, sildenafil, interferon; resolves after withdrawal (may take months)

**Q14. Why is PPD not a true vasculitis?**
- Histology shows lymphocytic capillaritis with extravasated RBCs and haemosiderin, but no fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls or leukocytoclasia; lesions are non-palpable petechiae (except lichenoid variants) without systemic involvement

**Q15. What is the link with mycosis fungoides?**
- Persistent, extensive or lichenoid PPD can show clonal T cells and may coexist with or progress to MF (pigmented purpuric MF); biopsy with TCR gene rearrangement and follow-up in atypical, persistent cases

## Quick spotter facts
- Cayenne-pepper petechiae on orange-brown patches of shins — Schamberg's PPD
- Golden-brown solitary patch — lichen aureus
- Vitamin C + rutoside

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Pigmented purpuric dermatoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pitted keratolysis — viva
posts.summary: Bacterial infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pitted keratolysis** (Bacterial infections)_

**Q1. What is pitted keratolysis?**
- Non-inflammatory superficial infection of the thick stratum corneum of the soles (occasionally palms) producing small crateriform pits; usually asymptomatic but malodorous

**Q2. Causative organisms?**
- Kytococcus sedentarius (formerly Micrococcus), Corynebacterium species, Dermatophilus congolensis, Actinomyces
- They produce keratin-degrading proteases (keratinases) and sulphur compounds (thiols, thioesters) that cause the smell

**Q3. Predisposing factors?**
- Hyperhidrosis, occlusive footwear (soldiers, athletes, farmers in wet fields, policemen, sailors)
- Hot humid climate, prolonged water immersion

**Q4. Describe the clinical features.**
- Multiple 1–7 mm punched-out pits on the weight-bearing areas (heels, balls of the feet, toes); may coalesce into crateriform / shallow erosions
- More prominent when the sole is wet (white macerated look)
- Malodour (bromhidrosis), hyperhidrosis, sliminess, sometimes soreness or itching (painful plaque-like variant)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis?**
- Tinea pedis (scaling, KOH positive), plantar warts (pinpoint black dots, interrupted dermatoglyphics), punctate palmoplantar keratoderma, basal cell naevus syndrome pits (palms), arsenical keratoses, erythrasma of toe webs, juvenile plantar dermatosis

**Q6. Investigations?**
- Clinical; Wood's lamp may show coral-red fluorescence (corynebacteria)
- Gram stain of shaved keratin shows Gram-positive filaments and cocci; culture rarely needed
- Histology: crater in stratum corneum with organisms at the base (seen with PAS/Gram stain)

**Q7. Treatment?**
- Topical antibiotics: erythromycin, clindamycin, fusidic acid, mupirocin; benzoyl peroxide (also deodorises); azole creams (imidazoles act on Gram-positives too)
- Control sweating: aluminium chloride hexahydrate 20%, iontophoresis, botulinum toxin; absorbent cotton socks changed daily, open/breathable footwear, avoid prolonged occlusion
- Oral erythromycin in extensive or resistant cases

**Q8. Why does pitted keratolysis smell?**
- Bacterial breakdown products — sulphur-containing thiols, thioesters and sulphides

**Q9. What is the natural course if untreated?**
- Persists as long as predisposing factors (sweating, occlusion) continue; may resolve when feet are kept dry; recurrence common after stopping treatment unless footwear and sweating are managed

**Q10. Which occupational groups need prevention advice?**
- Soldiers, athletes, sailors, rice-field farmers, factory workers in boots, police — moisture-wicking socks changed twice daily, antiperspirants (aluminium chloride), antiseptic foot soaps, alternate footwear to allow drying

**Q11. Explain why topical azoles work in pitted keratolysis.**
- Imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole) have activity against Gram-positive bacteria (Kytococcus, Corynebacterium, Dermatophilus) in addition to fungi; benzoyl peroxide is also antibacterial and drying

**Q12. Differentiate from plantar pitting of basal cell naevus syndrome.**
- Gorlin pits are on palms/ soles as small shallow 'pink' pits from childhood with jaw cysts and BCCs, not related to sweat/ smell; pitted keratolysis pits are on weight-bearing sole with malodour and sweating

**Q13. Corynebacterial infections of skin — the triad.**
- Erythrasma (C. minutissimum), pitted keratolysis (Kytococcus/ Corynebacterium), trichomycosis (C. tenuis) — often coexist in hyperhidrotic patients; all respond to topical antibacterials/ azoles and drying measures

**Q14. Dermoscopy of pitted keratolysis.**
- Multiple well-demarcated crateriform depressions with visible walls; organisms seen as filaments in the pit walls on high magnification (Gram stain of shaving)

**Q15. Why might pitted keratolysis be painful?**
- Rare painful plaque-like variant — deep pits in thick plantar skin with soreness on weight bearing, especially in soldiers/athletes; responds to topical antibiotics plus hyperhidrosis control

## Quick spotter facts
- Pits on soles + foul smell + sweaty feet — pitted keratolysis
- Organism: Kytococcus sedentarius

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (ch. Pyodermas); Rook's Textbook of Dermatology for cross-check. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pityriasis alba — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis alba** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is pityriasis alba (PA)?**
- Common benign condition of children and adolescents (3–16 y) with ill-defined, slightly scaly hypopigmented patches on the face (cheeks), sometimes neck, upper arms; low-grade eczematous dermatitis — minor criterion of atopic dermatitis
- More noticeable in darker skin and after summer (surrounding skin tans)

**Q2. Clinical stages.**
- Initially mildly erythematous with slightly raised border → hypopigmented patch with fine branny scale → smooth hypopigmented patch
- Asymptomatic or mild itch; 1–4 cm, multiple; extensive PA on trunk (variant) in adults

**Q3. Aetiology.**
- Atopy, xerosis, sun exposure (UV), frequent bathing/soaps, possibly Malassezia and low serum copper; post-inflammatory hypopigmentation from reduced melanosome transfer due to inflammation/oedema

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Non-specific mild spongiotic dermatitis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, reduced melanin, normal or slightly reduced melanocytes

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Pityriasis versicolor (KOH positive, upper trunk), vitiligo (chalk-white, sharp, Wood's bright), indeterminate leprosy (sensation, nerve), nevus depigmentosus (congenital stable), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, seborrhoeic dermatitis, hypopigmented MF (persistent trunk patches in adults), progressive macular hypomelanosis, tinea faciei

**Q6. Management.**
- Reassurance — self-limiting (months to years), repigments
- Emollients, gentle soap substitute, sunscreen to reduce contrast
- Mild topical steroid (hydrocortisone 1%) short course or calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus) for scaly/inflamed patches; calcitriol; excimer laser for persistent extensive PA

**Q7. Dermoscopy of pityriasis alba.**
- Ill-defined white structureless area with fine white scale, preserved but reduced pigment network, no leucotrichia; helps differentiate from vitiligo (absent network, sharp border) and PV (scale in furrows)

**Q8. What sun-protection and bathing advice is given?**
- Use sunscreen to reduce contrast with tanned skin, limit hot baths and harsh soaps, use moisturisers after bathing, avoid scrubbing; most cases resolve in months to years

**Q9. Why is there a seasonal pattern?**
- More noticeable in summer due to tanning of surrounding normal skin and more sun-induced xerosis/ inflammation; scaling may be more in winter (xerosis)

**Q10. Role of topical calcineurin inhibitors.**
- Tacrolimus 0.1%/ pimecrolimus 1% twice daily for 6–12 weeks improves hypopigmentation and scaling (anti-inflammatory, enhance melanocyte migration); safe on face for long durations, no atrophy

**Q11. What investigations are occasionally needed?**
- KOH (to exclude PV/ tinea), sensation testing (leprosy), Wood's lamp; biopsy only in persistent extensive trunk disease in adults to exclude hypopigmented mycosis fungoides

**Q12. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

**Q13. What is the association between PA and atopic dermatitis?**
- PA is a minor criterion in Hanifin and Rajka criteria; children with AD and xerosis get PA more frequently, especially after sun exposure and frequent bathing; treating xerosis prevents it

**Q14. What is extensive pityriasis alba?**
- Widespread non-scaly hypopigmented macules on trunk/limbs in adults without atopy — overlaps with progressive macular hypomelanosis; poor response to topical agents; NB-UVB/PUVA helps

**Q15. What is progressive macular hypomelanosis?**
- Ill-defined, non-scaly, hypopigmented coalescing macules on the trunk of young adults (especially darker skin); associated with Cutibacterium acnes (red follicular fluorescence on Wood's lamp); treated with benzoyl peroxide + clindamycin and NB-UVB, doxycycline

## Quick spotter facts
