- Ill-defined scaly hypopigmented cheek patches in atopic child — pityriasis alba
- Check sensation to exclude leprosy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypopigmentation). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pityriasis rosea — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis rosea** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define pityriasis rosea (PR).**
- Acute, self-limiting papulosquamous eruption with a herald patch followed by a secondary eruption of oval scaly patches along skin cleavage lines, usually in adolescents and young adults (10–35 y); resolves in 6–8 weeks

**Q2. Aetiology.**
- Reactivation of human herpesvirus 7 (and HHV-6) — supported by DNA/mRNA in lesions, clustering, prodrome, seasonal pattern (spring/autumn), rare recurrence
- PR-like drug eruptions: ACE inhibitors (captopril), gold, metronidazole, isotretinoin, terbinafine, NSAIDs, imatinib, beta-blockers, vaccines (influenza, BCG, COVID-19)

**Q3. Describe the clinical course.**
- Prodrome in some (malaise, sore throat, headache)
- Herald patch (mother patch) in ~80%: single larger (2–10 cm) oval salmon-pink patch with a peripheral collarette of fine scale (scale attached at the edge, free towards centre) on trunk
- 1–2 weeks later: crops of smaller similar oval patches with long axis along Langer's lines — 'Christmas tree' pattern on back, 'V' on chest; mostly trunk and proximal limbs (bathing suit distribution); face, palms spared
- Itch mild–moderate; resolves in 6–8 weeks (up to 12), may leave hypo/hyperpigmentation in dark skin

**Q4. Name the atypical variants.**
- Inverse PR (flexures, face, distal limbs — commoner in children and dark skin)
- Papular (common in Indian/African children), vesicular, urticarial, purpuric/haemorrhagic, pustular, erythema multiforme-like, giant (pityriasis rosea gigantea of Darier), localised/unilateral, oral lesions
- Herald patch only, multiple herald patches, relapsing PR, persistent PR (>12 weeks)

**Q5. Why is PR in pregnancy important?**
- PR in the first 15 weeks of pregnancy is associated with miscarriage/premature delivery (HHV-6/7 reactivation) — consider acyclovir and obstetric follow-up

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Secondary syphilis (palms/soles, mucosa, lymphadenopathy, no herald patch — always do VDRL in sexually active adults with atypical PR)
- Tinea corporis (herald patch confusion — KOH), guttate psoriasis, nummular eczema, pityriasis versicolor, PR-like drug eruption, pityriasis lichenoides chronica, seborrhoeic dermatitis, MF (persistent), viral exanthems

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Non-specific subacute spongiotic dermatitis with focal mounds of parakeratosis, extravasated RBCs in papillary dermis, superficial perivascular lymphocytes, dyskeratotic cells

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — self-limiting; emollients, calamine, mild topical steroids, oral antihistamines for itch
- Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (or 400 mg TDS) early in extensive/symptomatic disease — shortens course in some trials
- Erythromycin (older evidence, inconsistent)
- NB-UVB/sunlight for extensive itchy cases (may increase post-inflammatory pigmentation)

**Q9. What is the collarette scale?**
- Fine scale attached at the periphery with free edge pointing inwards — seen in PR, also in some tinea, healing bullous impetigo, AGEP desquamation

**Q10. Describe the herald patch in detail.**
- Single, larger (2–10 cm) oval salmon-coloured patch with central wrinkled 'cigarette-paper' appearance and peripheral collarette scale, usually on trunk, appearing ~1–2 weeks before the secondary eruption; absent in ~20%

**Q11. Dermoscopy of PR.**
- Yellowish background with peripheral whitish collarette scale and dotted/ irregular vessels — helps distinguish from guttate psoriasis (uniform dotted vessels with central scale)

**Q12. What are the features of PR in children and dark skin?**
- More papular, vesicular, inverse (face, axillae, groin), prominent post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation/ hypopigmentation, oral lesions; often itchy; may be mistaken for scabies or secondary syphilis

**Q13. Describe PR-like drug eruptions.**
- Drugs: ACE inhibitors (captopril), gold, bismuth, isotretinoin, metronidazole, omeprazole, terbinafine, imatinib, NSAIDs, clonidine, adalimumab; vaccines (influenza, hepatitis B, COVID-19)
- Clues: no herald patch, more itch, larger lesions, eosinophils on histology, persists until drug stopped

**Q14. Recurrent and persistent PR.**
- Recurrence in ~2–3%; persistent PR (>12 weeks) — reconsider diagnosis (pityriasis lichenoides chronica, MF, drug eruption, secondary syphilis) and biopsy

**Q15. Explain acyclovir use in PR.**
- High-dose acyclovir (800 mg five times daily × 7 days) in the first week shortens course and reduces itch in several RCTs — rationale: HHV-6/7 reactivation; useful in extensive symptomatic disease and pregnancy (with obstetric advice)

## Quick spotter facts
- Herald patch + Christmas-tree pattern — pityriasis rosea
- Always exclude secondary syphilis (VDRL)
- HHV-6/7

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Pityriasis rosea). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pityriasis rubra pilaris — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis rubra pilaris** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. What is pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP)?**
- Rare chronic papulosquamous disorder with follicular keratotic papules, orange-red scaly plaques with islands of sparing, and palmoplantar keratoderma; can progress to erythroderma
- Bimodal age: childhood and adults (5th–6th decade)

**Q2. Classify PRP (Griffiths).**
- Type I — classic adult (commonest ~50%): starts on head/upper trunk → spreads caudally to erythroderma with islands of sparing; resolves in ~80% within 3 years
- Type II — atypical adult: ichthyosiform lower-leg scaling, alopecia, eczematous areas, long duration (20 years)
- Type III — classic juvenile: like type I, resolves in 1–2 years
- Type IV — circumscribed juvenile: knees and elbows plaques (commonest in children), variable course
- Type V — atypical juvenile: familial, early onset, scleroderma-like hands, chronic; CARD14 gain-of-function
- Type VI — HIV-associated: with acne conglobata, hidradenitis, lichen spinulosus; responds to ART

**Q3. Describe the clinical features of classic adult PRP.**
- Follicular hyperkeratotic papules ('nutmeg-grater' feel) especially on the dorsa of proximal phalanges (knuckles), elbows, knees
- Coalescing salmon/orange-red plaques with fine scale spreading cephalocaudally; well-defined islands of normal skin ('nappes claires')
- Orange-red waxy palmoplantar keratoderma ('keratodermic sandal')
- Scalp: diffuse branny scaling; face: red, ectropion; nails: yellow-brown discolouration, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages (no pits)

**Q4. Pathogenesis.**
- Unknown in most; abnormal keratinisation, vitamin A metabolism (low retinol-binding protein — old theory), IL-23/Th17 axis (rationale for IL-17/23 biologics), CARD14 mutations in familial type V; triggers — infections, UV, drugs, malignancy (paraneoplastic in elderly)

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis in horizontal and vertical directions — chequerboard pattern; follicular plugging with 'shoulder parakeratosis', thick granular layer, broad short rete ridges, sparse perivascular infiltrate; acantholysis (focal) can occur
- Distinguish from psoriasis: no Munro microabscesses, no thinning of suprapapillary plate, granular layer preserved

**Q6. Differentiate PRP from psoriasis.**
- PRP: orange-red colour, follicular papules on knuckles, islands of sparing, waxy orange palmoplantar keratoderma, fine scale, no nail pits, no Auspitz sign, histology chequerboard
- Psoriasis: red with silvery scale, plaques on extensors, pits/oil-drop nails, Auspitz sign, PsA, Munro microabscesses

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Topical: emollients, keratolytics (urea, salicylic acid, lactic acid), topical steroids, calcipotriol
- Systemic first line: oral retinoids — isotretinoin 0.5–1 mg/kg/day or acitretin 0.5–0.75 mg/kg/day for 4–6 months
- Methotrexate 10–25 mg weekly (alone or with retinoid), cyclosporine, azathioprine
- Biologics for refractory: TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab), IL-17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), IL-23 inhibitors
- Phototherapy may aggravate (photosensitivity) — use with caution; vitamin A historically
- Treat erythroderma complications; HIV testing in atypical cases

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Type I and III often remit within 3 years; types II, V chronic; erythrodermic disease needs intensive care

**Q9. Describe dermoscopy of PRP.**
- Central keratin plugs surrounded by yellow-orange background, linear/ dotted vessels at periphery, islands of sparing — differs from psoriasis (dotted vessels)

**Q10. What is the HIV-associated PRP (type VI)?**
- Associated with acne conglobata, hidradenitis suppurativa, lichen spinulosus (follicular spines — 'elongated follicular spines'); poor response to usual therapy; improves with antiretroviral therapy

**Q11. Explain juvenile circumscribed PRP (type IV).**
- Commonest in children: well-demarcated follicular hyperkeratotic orange-red plaques on elbows and knees, palmoplantar keratoderma, no progression to erythroderma; variable remission; topical keratolytics, steroids, calcipotriol

**Q12. What is CARD14-associated papulosquamous eruption (CAPE)?**
- Autosomal dominant gain-of-function CARD14 mutations giving early-onset (infancy) PRP/ psoriasis-like eruption (familial type V PRP), with facial and ear involvement, poor response to conventional therapy but excellent response to ustekinumab (IL-12/23)

**Q13. How do retinoids help PRP and what are dosing pearls?**
- Normalise follicular keratinisation; isotretinoin 0.5–1 mg/kg/day or acitretin 25–50 mg/day for 3–6 months; response in weeks; combine with methotrexate in resistant cases (watch hepatotoxicity); avoid phototherapy (photo-aggravation)

**Q14. What is the role of IL-17/IL-23 biologics in PRP?**
- Reports and small series show good responses to secukinumab, ixekizumab, ustekinumab, guselkumab and risankizumab in refractory adult PRP (IL-23/Th17 axis similar to psoriasis); used after retinoid/methotrexate failure

**Q15. Paraneoplastic and drug-induced PRP.**
- Rare associations with internal malignancy (adult type I) — age-appropriate screening; drug-induced PRP-like eruptions with imatinib, ponatinib, sorafenib, insulin, vaccines (including COVID-19)

## Quick spotter facts
- Islands of sparing + orange keratoderma + follicular knuckle papules — PRP
- Chequerboard ortho/parakeratosis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Pityriasis rubra pilaris). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pityriasis versicolor — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pityriasis versicolor** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is pityriasis versicolor? Agent?**
- Chronic, recurrent, superficial infection of stratum corneum by Malassezia (lipophilic yeast, normal skin flora) in its mycelial phase — mostly M. globosa, also M. furfur, M. sympodialis
- Not contagious; endogenous overgrowth

**Q2. Predisposing factors?**
- Hot humid climate, sweating, oily skin, adolescents and young adults (high sebum), oily applications, occlusion, malnutrition, steroids, immunosuppression, pregnancy, genetic predisposition

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Multiple round/oval scaly macules coalescing into patches on upper trunk, neck, upper arms, face (children); minimal itch
- Colour: hypopigmented (most common in Indian skin), hyperpigmented (fawn/brown), erythematous — hence 'versicolor'
- Evoked scale sign (Besnier's sign) — stretching or scratching produces fine branny scale

**Q4. Why are lesions hypopigmented?**
- Azelaic acid and other dicarboxylic acids from Malassezia inhibit tyrosinase; pityriacitrin screens UV; damage to melanocytes and smaller melanosomes; persists for weeks after cure

**Q5. Why hyperpigmented in some?**
- Larger melanosomes and thicker keratin layer with inflammatory infiltrate

**Q6. Investigations.**
- KOH mount: short hyphae and round spores — 'spaghetti and meatballs'
- Wood's lamp: yellow-gold fluorescence (not always)
- Scotch tape test with methylene blue/Parker ink; culture needs olive oil-supplemented media (rarely needed)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Hypopigmented: pityriasis alba, vitiligo (depigmented, no scale), indeterminate leprosy (sensation), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, progressive macular hypomelanosis (no scale, red fluorescence of follicles), nevus depigmentosus, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Hyperpigmented/red: pityriasis rosea, tinea corporis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, erythrasma, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis, secondary syphilis, café-au-lait

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Topical: ketoconazole 2% shampoo/lotion applied for 5–10 min daily for 3–5 days; selenium sulphide 2.5%; azole creams; terbinafine cream; zinc pyrithione; 20% sodium hyposulphite
- Oral for extensive or recurrent: itraconazole 200 mg/day for 5–7 days, fluconazole 300 mg weekly for 2 weeks (or 400 mg single dose); oral terbinafine is not effective; griseofulvin not effective
- Counsel that pigment takes months to normalise — not treatment failure

**Q9. Prophylaxis for recurrence?**
- Ketoconazole/selenium shampoo once or twice monthly or weekly in summer; or itraconazole 400 mg once a month during humid months

**Q10. Other Malassezia-related diseases?**
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis, Malassezia (Pityrosporum) folliculitis, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (debated), atopic head-and-neck dermatitis, catheter-related fungaemia in neonates on lipid infusions

**Q11. Describe Malassezia biology.**
- Lipophilic (lipid-dependent except M. pachydermatis) dimorphic yeast — commensal yeast phase on seborrhoeic skin; transforms to mycelial (hyphal) pathogenic form in heat, humidity, sebum, immunosuppression; produces azelaic acid, indoles (pityriacitrin, malassezin), lipases

**Q12. Culture of Malassezia.**
- Needs lipid-supplemented media — Sabouraud agar with olive oil overlay, Dixon's or Leeming–Notman agar; 32–37 °C; species identification by morphology/ Tween assimilation/ MALDI-TOF/ PCR

**Q13. Selenium sulphide — mechanism and use.**
- Cytostatic on epidermal cells and antifungal (reduces sebum fatty acids); 2.5% lotion/ shampoo applied for 10 min daily for 7 days, then monthly prophylaxis; side effects irritation, hair discolouration, oily scalp

**Q14. Classify antifungal drugs (PYQ).**
- Polyenes: amphotericin B (systemic, deep mycoses), nystatin (topical/ oral Candida)
- Azoles — imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole) and triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) — inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis)
- Allylamines: terbinafine, naftifine (squalene epoxidase inhibitors); benzylamine — butenafine
- Echinocandins: caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin (β-1,3-glucan synthase)
- Others: griseofulvin (microtubule — mitotic inhibitor), flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis), ciclopirox (chelator), amorolfine (morpholine — Δ14 reductase/ Δ7-Δ8 isomerase), tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), potassium iodide, efinaconazole, tavaborole

**Q15. Pityriasis versicolor in children and atypical sites.**
- Facial PV in children (hypopigmented forehead/ cheeks — mimics PA, vitiligo), flexural/ inverse PV, genital PV; check KOH; topical azoles

## Quick spotter facts
- Spaghetti and meatballs on KOH
- Evoked scale (Besnier's) sign
- Oral terbinafine doesn't work in PV

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections — Malassezia). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Porokeratosis — viva
posts.summary: Disorders of keratinisation · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Porokeratosis** (Disorders of keratinisation)_

**Q1. What is porokeratosis?**
- Group of clonal disorders of keratinisation characterised clinically by annular plaques with a thread-like raised keratotic rim and histologically by the cornoid lamella; defects in the mevalonate pathway (MVK, PMVK, MVD, FDPS genes) with second-hit somatic mutation in lesions

**Q2. Describe the types and clinical features (PYQ).**
- Porokeratosis of Mibelli (classic): one or few plaques with a raised furrowed keratotic ridge and atrophic centre, childhood, limbs
- Disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis (DSAP): commonest; multiple small (5–10 mm) annular brownish lesions on sun-exposed extensor limbs, adults; worsens in summer/immunosuppression
- Disseminated superficial porokeratosis (non-actinic — also sun-protected sites; immunosuppressed)
- Linear porokeratosis (along Blaschko's lines — highest malignancy risk)
- Porokeratosis palmaris et plantaris disseminata (palms/soles then generalised)
- Punctate porokeratosis (palms/soles), genitogluteal/ptychotropic, hypertrophic verrucous, eruptive (paraneoplastic/inflammatory), porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct naevus (PEODDN)

**Q3. What is a cornoid lamella?**
- Thin column of tightly packed parakeratotic cells angled away from the centre, arising from an invagination of epidermis with absent/reduced granular layer and dyskeratotic cells at its base — corresponds to the raised rim
- Also seen focally in actinic keratosis, verrucae, seborrhoeic keratosis (not diagnostic alone)

**Q4. Malignant potential.**
- SCC (also BCC, Bowen's) develops in ~7–11% — highest in linear and large long-standing lesions (Mibelli), lowest in DSAP; immunosuppression increases risk

**Q5. Enumerate disorders of transepidermal elimination (PYQ).**
- Primary perforating disorders: Kyrle's disease, perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, elastosis perforans serpiginosa (Down syndrome, penicillamine, Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan), acquired perforating dermatosis (diabetes + chronic renal failure)
- Secondary: granuloma annulare (perforating), necrobiosis lipoidica, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, calcinosis cutis, chondrodermatitis, gout, foreign bodies, chromoblastomycosis, porokeratosis

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- DSAP vs actinic keratosis, lichen planus (annular/atrophic), tinea corporis, granuloma annulare, seborrhoeic keratosis, Bowen's, elastosis perforans serpiginosa; linear porokeratosis vs linear epidermal naevus/linear LP

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Photoprotection, regular skin surveillance (biopsy any nodules/ulcers)
- Topical: 5-FU, imiquimod, vitamin D analogues, retinoids, diclofenac, lovastatin 2% + cholesterol 2% (topical statin–cholesterol — targets mevalonate pathway; newer effective option)
- Physical: cryotherapy, CO2/Er:YAG/fractional lasers, PDT, curettage, excision of small lesions
- Oral acitretin for extensive disease/chemoprevention

**Q8. Describe the clinical types in detail.**
- Porokeratosis of Mibelli (single/ few annular plaques with raised keratotic ridge, childhood, limbs)
- Disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis (DSAP — many small annular lesions on sun-exposed limbs, adults, worse in summer)
- Disseminated superficial porokeratosis (non-sun-exposed, immunosuppression)
- Linear porokeratosis (Blaschko — highest SCC risk)
- Porokeratosis palmaris et plantaris disseminata, punctate porokeratosis, porokeratosis ptychotropica (genital/ gluteal cleft), eruptive pruritic papular porokeratosis

**Q9. Why does porokeratosis appear in immunosuppressed patients?**
- Organ transplant recipients, HIV, chemotherapy, haematological malignancy — reduced immune surveillance allows clonal expansion of abnormal keratinocytes; often disseminated; regular SCC surveillance

**Q10. Histopathology of the cornoid lamella in detail.**
- Thin column of parakeratotic cells angled away from the centre of the lesion, overlying an epidermal invagination with absent/ reduced granular layer and dyskeratotic cells beneath; corresponds to the raised ridge; also seen focally in other lesions (cornoid lamellation — not specific alone)

**Q11. Describe the process of keratinisation and the cornified envelope (PYQ).**
- Basal keratinocytes (K5/K14) divide and move up: spinous (K1/K10, desmosomes), granular (keratohyaline granules — profilaggrin, loricrin; lamellar bodies — lipids), cornified layer (flattened anucleate corneocytes)
- Cornified envelope: cross-linked proteins (involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins) by transglutaminases (TGM1, TGM3, TGM5) with covalently bound lipid envelope (ceramides); intercellular lipid lamellae (ceramides, cholesterol, FFA) — 'bricks and mortar' barrier
- Desquamation via kallikreins (KLK5/7) degrading corneodesmosomes, regulated by LEKTI (SPINK5)

**Q12. Treatment options in detail.**
- Photoprotection; topical 5-FU, imiquimod, tacrolimus, retinoids, vitamin D analogues, diclofenac; statin + cholesterol creams; cryotherapy, CO2/ Er:YAG laser, PDT, curettage/ excision for single lesions; oral acitretin for extensive

**Q13. What is the genetic basis?**
- Mevalonate pathway genes — MVK, PMVK, MVD, FDPS (germline heterozygous mutation + second-hit/ UV-induced somatic mutation); explains DSAP worsening with UV and topical cholesterol/lovastatin therapy

**Q14. Dermoscopy of porokeratosis.**
- White-yellow 'double-edged' track-like peripheral rim (cornoid lamella) — 'white track' around a central brown/pink atrophic area with dotted vessels

**Q15. What is the newer topical treatment?**
- Topical 2% cholesterol + 2% lovastatin (or simvastatin) — corrects mevalonate pathway deficiency (bypasses toxic metabolite accumulation and supplies cholesterol); effective in DSAP and linear porokeratosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Annular plaque with thread-like keratotic ridge — porokeratosis; cornoid lamella
- Linear porokeratosis — highest SCC risk
- Topical lovastatin–cholesterol

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Porokeratosis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Prurigo nodularis — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Prurigo nodularis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What is prurigo nodularis (PN)? (PYQ)**
- Chronic, intensely itchy, firm hyperkeratotic nodules (few mm–2 cm) due to chronic scratching; the nodular type of 'chronic prurigo' (itch >6 weeks + scratch lesions)
- Middle-aged and elderly; symmetrical on extensor limbs, upper back (spares mid-back — 'butterfly sign'), buttocks

**Q2. Aetiological associations — work-up for a cause.**
- Dermatological: atopic dermatitis (most common association, 'atopic PN'), xerosis, insect bites, contact dermatitis
- Systemic: chronic kidney disease, liver disease (cholestasis, hepatitis C), diabetes, thyroid disease, iron deficiency, HIV, lymphoma/malignancy, gluten enteropathy
- Neurological: small fibre neuropathy, notalgia paraesthetica
- Psychiatric: depression, anxiety, OCD, substance use

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Neuroimmune circuit: itch–scratch cycle, increased dermal nerve fibres with reduced intraepidermal nerve density, neuropeptides (substance P, CGRP), IL-31, IL-4/13 (Th2), mast cells, eosinophils, periostin and fibrosis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Marked hyperkeratosis, irregular/pseudoepitheliomatous acanthosis, fibrosis with vertical collagen, thickened dermal nerves (neural hyperplasia), increased mast cells and eosinophils

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Hypertrophic lichen planus, nodular scabies, insect-bite reactions, pemphigoid nodularis, multiple keratoacanthomas, perforating disorders (acquired reactive perforating collagenosis in diabetics/CKD), dermatitis artefacta, lichen amyloidosis, nodular prurigo of pregnancy, epidermolysis bullosa pruriginosa

**Q6. Investigations (screen for systemic disease).**
- CBC with eosinophils, renal and liver function, thyroid, blood sugar/HbA1c, iron studies, HIV, hepatitis B/C, chest X-ray, total IgE; biopsy (± DIF to exclude pemphigoid nodularis), skin scraping for scabies; age-appropriate cancer screening if indicated

**Q7. Management (step-wise).**
- Break the cycle: emollients, cooling lotions (menthol, polidocanol), keep nails short, occlude lesions
- Topical: super-potent steroid under occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone, calcipotriol, tacrolimus, capsaicin
- Phototherapy: NB-UVB, UVA1, PUVA; cryotherapy for individual nodules
- Systemic: gabapentin/pregabalin, antidepressants (paroxetine, mirtazapine, amitriptyline), naltrexone/opioid modulators, methotrexate, cyclosporine, thalidomide (neuropathy risk)
- Biologics: dupilumab (approved for PN), nemolizumab (anti-IL-31RA; approved for PN 2024); JAK inhibitors under study

**Q8. What is the butterfly sign?**
- Sparing of the mid-upper back (area patient cannot reach) — indicates lesions are from scratching

**Q9. Prognosis?**
- Very chronic; nodules persist months–years even after itch control; severe impact on sleep and mood

**Q10. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q11. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q12. Explain the neural changes and itch mediators.**
- Hypertrophy of dermal nerves with decreased intraepidermal small-fibre density (small fibre neuropathy), increased NGF, substance P and CGRP; IL-31, IL-4/IL-13 (Th2), IL-17/22, oncostatin M; mast cells and eosinophils — targets for dupilumab, nemolizumab

**Q13. Dupilumab in PN — dose and evidence.**
- Approved for PN in adults: 600 mg loading then 300 mg every 2 weeks SC; PRIME trials — significant itch reduction (≥4-point WI-NRS) and nodule clearance; conjunctivitis main side effect

**Q14. Chronic prurigo classification (EADV).**
- Chronic prurigo = chronic pruritus (≥6 weeks) + history/ signs of repeated scratching + multiple localised/ generalised pruriginous lesions; subtypes — papular, nodular, plaque, umbilicated, linear

**Q15. What is uraemic pruritus and its treatment?**
- Common in CKD stage 5/ dialysis; xerosis, PN-like lesions; treat with emollients, UVB phototherapy, gabapentin/ pregabalin (renal dosing), difelikefalin (kappa-opioid agonist IV after dialysis), nalfurafine, optimise dialysis, kidney transplant

**Q16. Cholestatic pruritus — treatment ladder.**
- Cholestyramine, rifampicin, naltrexone (opioid antagonist), sertraline; newer — IBAT inhibitors (odevixibat, maralixibat in paediatric cholestasis), fibrates; UV-B; treat cause (stent biliary obstruction)

## Quick spotter facts
- Symmetric itchy hyperkeratotic nodules sparing mid-back — prurigo nodularis
- Screen kidney, liver, thyroid, HIV, malignancy

## Note
Nemolizumab approval for PN is newer than the textbooks — confirm current Indian availability.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Prurigo); EADV prurigo task-force concept of chronic prurigo. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pseudoxanthoma elasticum** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE)?**
- Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder of ectopic mineralisation (calcification) and fragmentation of elastic fibres in skin, eyes (Bruch's membrane) and arteries — ABCC6 mutations (liver transporter; low plasma pyrophosphate — calcification inhibitor); ENPP1/GGCX in PXE-like disorders

**Q2. Cutaneous features.**
- Onset in childhood/adolescence: small yellowish papules coalescing into cobblestoned 'plucked chicken skin' / 'Moroccan leather' plaques on the sides of the neck (first site), axillae, antecubital and popliteal fossae, groin, periumbilical (flexural areas); later lax redundant folds; oral mucosa (lower lip) yellow papules; perforating PXE (periumbilical, multiparous women)

**Q3. Systemic features.**
- Eyes: angioid streaks (breaks in calcified Bruch's membrane — grey-brown lines radiating from optic disc), 'peau d'orange' fundus, choroidal neovascularisation → haemorrhage → central vision loss
- Cardiovascular: premature atherosclerosis, intermittent claudication (peripheral arterial disease), reduced pulses, hypertension, angina, MI, stroke; GI haemorrhage (gastric arteries), mitral valve prolapse

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Fragmented, clumped, curled and calcified elastic fibres in the mid and deep reticular dermis — highlighted by Verhoeff–van Gieson (elastic) and von Kossa (calcium) stains; perforation of elastic fibres in perforating PXE

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- PXE-like papillary dermal elastolysis, solar elastosis, cutis laxa, late-onset focal dermal elastosis, perforating calcific elastosis, D-penicillamine-induced elastosis, amyloidosis, xanthomas, lax skin syndromes, Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome, white fibrous papulosis of neck

**Q6. Diagnostic criteria (Plomp 2010).**
- Major: characteristic skin lesions with histology (fragmented calcified elastic fibres); angioid streaks/peau d'orange (retina); two pathogenic ABCC6 mutations
- Minor: one ABCC6 mutation, PXE in a first-degree relative

**Q7. Management.**
- No cure; multidisciplinary follow-up: annual eye examination (Amsler grid self-monitoring; intravitreal anti-VEGF — bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept for choroidal neovascularisation), cardiovascular risk control (no smoking, lipid/BP control, exercise), avoid contact sports (eye trauma), caution with aspirin/anticoagulants (GI bleeding)
- Dietary calcium in normal amounts; magnesium supplementation and etidronate (bisphosphonate — reduced arterial calcification in trial) under study
- Cosmetic: excision of lax skin folds (plastic surgery), fillers; genetic counselling

**Q8. Describe skin findings in detail.**
- Small yellowish papules coalescing into 'plucked chicken skin' or cobblestone plaques on flexural sites — sides of neck (first), axillae, antecubital and popliteal fossae, groin, periumbilical; later lax redundant skin folds; oral mucosa (inner lip) yellow papules; 'perforating' PXE with calcified elastic extrusion

**Q9. Systemic features in detail.**
- Cardiovascular: premature atherosclerosis, intermittent claudication, angina, hypertension (renovascular), mitral valve prolapse, GI haemorrhage (gastric — submucosal vessel calcification), cerebrovascular events; ocular: angioid streaks, choroidal neovascularisation (central vision loss)

**Q10. What is periumbilical perforating PXE?**
- Acquired localised PXE in multiparous obese black women — hyperpigmented plaques with keratotic papules around umbilicus; elastic fibre calcification with transepidermal elimination; no systemic disease

**Q11. Acquired PXE-like changes — causes.**
- Penicillamine (elastosis perforans serpiginosa and PXE-like), saltpetre exposure, calcium salts, chronic kidney disease (calcific elastosis), β-thalassaemia/ sickle cell (PXE-like phenotype with angioid streaks)

**Q12. Management in detail.**
- No cure; multidisciplinary — ophthalmology (Amsler grid self-monitoring, anti-VEGF intravitreal for neovascularisation), cardiovascular risk control (statins, BP, stop smoking, exercise), avoid NSAIDs/ anticoagulants where possible (GI bleeding), avoid contact sports; cosmetic surgery for redundant skin; trials of oral pyrophosphate, etidronate (slows arterial calcification)

**Q13. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

**Q14. Explain the molecular basis.**
- Autosomal recessive ABCC6 mutations (liver transporter) → low plasma inorganic pyrophosphate (anti-mineralisation factor) → ectopic calcification of elastic fibres in skin, retina (Bruch's membrane), arteries; PXE-like phenotype with GGCX mutations (with clotting factor deficiency) and ENPP1 (GACI)

**Q15. Describe ocular findings.**
- Angioid streaks (breaks in calcified Bruch's membrane radiating from optic disc), peau d'orange of retina, comet tails; complications — choroidal neovascularisation → haemorrhage and loss of central vision; treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections; avoid contact sports/ head trauma

**Q16. What special stains are used?**
- Von Kossa (calcium — black), Verhoeff–van Gieson (fragmented, curled, clumped elastic fibres in mid/deep dermis), Alizarin red; elastic fibres look 'raveled wool'

## Quick spotter facts
- Plucked-chicken yellow papules on sides of neck + angioid streaks — PXE (ABCC6)
- Calcified fragmented elastic fibres (von Kossa)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of elastic tissue). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Psoriasis — viva
posts.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 32 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Psoriasis** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define psoriasis.**
- Chronic, immune-mediated, genetically determined, inflammatory multisystem disease with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales, nail and joint involvement, and metabolic/cardiovascular comorbidity; relapsing–remitting course

**Q2. Epidemiology.**
- Worldwide 2–3%; India 0.44–2.8%; men slightly more in India
- Bimodal onset: type I (<40 years, HLA-Cw6/C*06:02, family history, severe) and type II (>40 years, sporadic)

**Q3. Describe the genetics.**
- Polygenic; PSORS1 on chromosome 6p21 (HLA-C*06:02 — strongest), other loci: IL23R, IL12B, TNFAIP3, CARD14 (PSORS2), IL36RN (GPP), LCE3B/C deletion, ERAP1
- Concordance ~70% in monozygotic vs ~20% in dizygotic twins

**Q4. Explain the immunopathogenesis.**
- Triggers (trauma, infection, drugs) → keratinocyte stress releases LL-37 (cathelicidin) + self-DNA/RNA → activates plasmacytoid dendritic cells (IFN-α) → myeloid dendritic cells produce IL-23 and IL-12 → Th17 and Tc17 cells produce IL-17A/F, IL-22 → keratinocyte hyperproliferation, antimicrobial peptides, chemokines (CXCL1/8 → neutrophils) — self-amplifying loop
- TNF-α (from DCs, macrophages, T cells) amplifies; IL-36 important in pustular psoriasis
- Basis for targeted therapy: TNF, IL-12/23 p40, IL-23 p19, IL-17A/F/RA, IL-36R, PDE4, TYK2

**Q5. How is epidermal cell kinetics deranged in psoriasis? (PYQ)**
- Keratinocyte cell cycle shortens from ~311 h to ~36 h; epidermal turnover time from ~28 days to 3–5 days; germinative cell population doubled with all cells cycling (growth fraction ~100% vs 60%)
- Result: immature retained-nuclei cells (parakeratosis), thin/absent granular layer, acanthosis

**Q6. Name the trigger (aggravating) factors.**
- Physical trauma (Koebner), streptococcal throat infection (guttate), HIV (severe), stress, smoking, alcohol, obesity, cold dry weather, hypocalcaemia (pustular)
- Drugs: lithium, β-blockers, antimalarials (chloroquine/HCQ), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, interferons, terbinafine, imiquimod, TNF inhibitors (paradoxical), sudden withdrawal of systemic steroids (pustular flare), checkpoint inhibitors

**Q7. Classify psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Plaque (vulgaris, ~90%): chronic stable plaque, small/large plaque, rupioid, ostraceous, elephantine, annular
- Guttate (children/young adults after strep throat)
- Inverse/flexural (no scales, glazed), sebopsoriasis, scalp, palmoplantar (non-pustular), nail, genital
- Pustular: generalised (von Zumbusch, annular, exanthematic, impetigo herpetiformis of pregnancy, juvenile), localised (palmoplantar pustulosis, acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau)
- Erythrodermic
- Psoriatic arthritis
- Special: linear, napkin, drug-induced, HIV-associated

**Q8. Describe clinical signs in a plaque.**
- Well-demarcated, erythematous, indurated plaques with loose silvery-white micaceous scales on extensors (elbows, knees), scalp, lumbosacral area, umbilicus, natal cleft; symmetrical
- Grattage test (Auspitz sign): candle-grease sign (scraping produces more silvery scales), Burkley's membrane (thin moist glistening membrane after removal), then Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding from tips of dilated papillary capillaries due to thin suprapapillary plate)
- Woronoff's ring (pale halo around healing plaques, PG inhibition — after UV/steroids), Koebner phenomenon (lesions at sites of trauma in 7–14 days)

**Q9. Describe isomorphic (Koebner) response (PYQ).**
- Appearance of lesions of an existing dermatosis at sites of trauma (scratch, surgery, tattoo, burn, injection) — true Koebner (psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo); pseudo-Koebner by autoinoculation (warts, molluscum); reverse Koebner (lesion clears at trauma site); Wolf's isotopic response (new different disease at site of a healed one — e.g. after zoster)
- All-or-none phenomenon; occurs in 25% of psoriatics; positive Koebner suggests unstable disease

**Q10. Describe nail changes in psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Matrix involvement: pits (commonest — coarse, irregular), leukonychia, red spots in lunula, crumbling, transverse ridges (Beau's lines)
- Nail bed: oil-drop/salmon patch, onycholysis with erythematous border, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages
- Nail psoriasis is common (up to 50%; 80–90% in PsA) and strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis (DIP joints)
- Assessed by NAPSI (Nail Psoriasis Severity Index, 0–8 per nail)
- Treatment: intralesional triamcinolone (matrix), topical calcipotriol-steroid, tazarotene; systemic — methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, apremilast, biologics (IL-17, TNF best)

**Q11. Histopathology of psoriasis.**
- Confluent parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), spongiform pustules of Kogoj (neutrophils in spinous layer — pustular), hypogranulosis, regular (psoriasiform) acanthosis with club-shaped rete ridges, thinning of suprapapillary plates, dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae, perivascular lymphocytes

**Q12. Comorbidities associated with psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Psoriatic arthritis (~20–30%)
- Metabolic syndrome: obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
- Cardiovascular disease — severe psoriasis is an independent risk factor for MI and stroke (shorter life by ~5 years)
- Crohn's disease, uveitis, depression/anxiety, alcohol use, smoking, lymphoma (CTCL), chronic kidney disease, OSA
- Screen: BMI, BP, blood sugar, lipid profile, LFT, joint symptoms (PEST questionnaire), mood

**Q13. What is psoriatic arthritis? Give CASPAR criteria.**
- Seronegative spondyloarthropathy; patterns (Moll and Wright): asymmetric oligoarthritis (commonest), DIP-predominant, symmetric polyarthritis, arthritis mutilans (telescoping fingers), spondylitis/sacroiliitis; plus enthesitis, dactylitis
- CASPAR: inflammatory articular disease + ≥3 points from — current psoriasis (2) or personal/family history (1), nail dystrophy (1), negative RF (1), dactylitis (1), juxta-articular new bone formation on X-ray (1)
- X-ray: pencil-in-cup deformity, erosions with new bone formation

**Q14. How do you assess severity?**
- PASI (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, 0–72): erythema, induration, scaling (0–4) × area (0–6) in head (0.1), upper limbs (0.2), trunk (0.3), lower limbs (0.4)
- BSA (hand = 1%), PGA, DLQI; rule of tens — BSA >10% or PASI >10 or DLQI >10 = moderate–severe
- Treatment goals: PASI 75/90/100 response; PASI 90 now standard target with biologics

**Q15. Discuss the management of stable plaque psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Limited (<10% BSA): topical therapy — emollients, keratolytics (salicylic acid 3–6%), topical steroids (potent for body, mild for face/flexures), vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol, calcitriol) and fixed combination with betamethasone (gel/foam), coal tar, dithranol (short-contact), tazarotene, tacrolimus for face/flexures, roflumilast cream, tapinarof
- Moderate–severe or special sites/failure: phototherapy — NB-UVB 311 nm (2–3 times weekly, 20–30 sessions), PUVA (oral 8-MOP + UVA), targeted excimer laser 308 nm
- Systemic conventional: methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, apremilast
- Biologics and small molecules for those who fail/cannot take conventional drugs (or PsA)
- General: weight loss, stop smoking/alcohol, treat comorbidities, counsel chronicity

**Q16. Methotrexate — mechanism, dose, monitoring.**
- Folate antagonist (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor) — antiproliferative and immunomodulatory (adenosine release)
- Dose: 7.5–25 mg once weekly (oral/SC) after test dose 2.5–5 mg; folic acid 5 mg/day except methotrexate day
- Baseline: CBC, LFT, RFT, viral markers (HBV, HCV, HIV), chest X-ray, pregnancy test; monitor CBC/LFT every 2–4 weeks initially then 2–3 monthly; liver fibrosis assessment — FibroScan, PIIINP, rather than routine biopsy
- Adverse effects: bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia — risk with renal failure, NSAIDs, cotrimoxazole), hepatotoxicity/fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis/pneumonitis, mucositis, teratogenicity (stop 3 months before conception both sexes), nausea; antidote — folinic acid (leucovorin)

**Q17. Cyclosporine and acitretin key points.**
- Cyclosporine: calcineurin inhibitor (blocks IL-2 transcription in T cells); 2.5–5 mg/kg/day; fastest acting conventional drug — for erythrodermic/unstable/pregnancy-short-term; side effects: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, hypertrichosis, gingival hyperplasia, hyperlipidaemia, drug interactions (CYP3A4), malignancy; limit to 1 year, monitor BP and creatinine (reduce if >25% rise)
- Acitretin: retinoid (RAR agonist) — normalises keratinisation; 0.3–0.5 mg/kg/day (25–50 mg); best for pustular, palmoplantar, erythrodermic and in HIV; combine with phototherapy (Re-PUVA); not immunosuppressive; teratogenic — avoid pregnancy for 3 years after stopping (alcohol converts to etretinate); side effects: cheilitis, xerosis, hair loss, hyperlipidaemia, hepatotoxicity, DISH

**Q18. Discuss the role of biologics (PYQ).**
- TNF-α inhibitors: etanercept (fusion protein), infliximab (chimeric IV), adalimumab (human; biosimilars in India), certolizumab pegol (no Fc, minimal placental transfer — pregnancy)
- IL-12/23 p40: ustekinumab
- IL-17: secukinumab, ixekizumab (IL-17A), brodalumab (IL-17RA), bimekizumab (IL-17A and F)
- IL-23 p19: guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab — high efficacy with 8–12 weekly dosing
- Anti-CD6: itolizumab (Indian)
- IL-36R: spesolimab (generalised pustular psoriasis flares)
- Screening: TB (IGRA/Mantoux + CXR — TB reactivation esp. with TNF), HBV, HCV, HIV, CBC, LFT; avoid live vaccines
- Specific cautions: TNF — demyelination, heart failure (NYHA III/IV), lupus-like, paradoxical psoriasis; IL-17 — inflammatory bowel disease, Candida infections; IL-23 — very safe profile

**Q19. Oral small molecules.**
- Apremilast — PDE4 inhibitor (raises cAMP, reduces TNF/IL-23/IL-17) 30 mg BD after titration; no lab monitoring; side effects — diarrhoea, nausea, headache, weight loss, depression
- Deucravacitinib — allosteric TYK2 inhibitor 6 mg once daily; acne, URTI, raised CPK
- Oral JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) mainly for PsA

**Q20. Discuss recent advances in management (PYQ).**
- IL-23 and IL-17A/F biologics with PASI 90–100 in most patients; biosimilars reduce cost (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, ustekinumab)
- TYK2 inhibitor (deucravacitinib), oral IL-23R peptide (icotrokinra, in development/approval)
- Topical: tapinarof (aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist), roflumilast cream/foam (PDE4), calcipotriol-betamethasone foam/cream (PAD technology)
- Spesolimab and imsidolimab for GPP
- Treat-to-target approach, early aggressive therapy to modify comorbidity risk

**Q21. Generalised pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) — features and management.**
- Sudden fever, malaise, sheets of sterile pustules on painful erythema, lakes of pus; leucocytosis, hypocalcaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, raised liver enzymes; risk of sepsis, ARDS
- Triggers: steroid withdrawal, pregnancy, infection, hypocalcaemia, drugs; IL36RN, CARD14, AP1S3 mutations
- Treatment: admit, supportive care; acitretin (drug of choice in adults, not in women of child-bearing potential), cyclosporine (rapid), methotrexate, infliximab, spesolimab (IV, rapid pustule clearance); impetigo herpetiformis — cyclosporine/prednisolone, early delivery if severe

**Q22. Psoriasis in pregnancy and children — what treatments?**
- Pregnancy: emollients, topical steroids, NB-UVB (first choice for extensive), cyclosporine if severe, certolizumab; avoid methotrexate, acitretin, PUVA, tazarotene
- Children: topical agents, NB-UVB, methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin (short-term), etanercept, adalimumab, ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab approved in children

**Q23. Differential diagnosis of psoriasis plaque.**
- Lichen simplex chronicus, nummular eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis (scalp), tinea corporis (KOH), pityriasis rosea (guttate), PRP, lichen planus hypertrophic, mycosis fungoides, secondary syphilis (palms/soles), Bowen's disease (single), DLE, reactive arthritis (keratoderma blennorrhagicum)

**Q24. What are the dermoscopic features of psoriasis?**
- Regularly distributed red dotted (pinpoint) vessels on a light-red background with diffuse white scales
- Scalp: red dots/globules, twisted red loops, white scales; nails: red-dot lunula, oil spots, splinter haemorrhages
- Helps to differentiate from eczema (patchy dotted vessels, yellow crusts) and LP (Wickham's striae)

**Q25. Describe scalp psoriasis and its treatment.**
- Well-demarcated thick silvery plaques extending beyond the hairline (forehead, ears, nape), itch; non-scarring; pityriasis amiantacea (asbestos-like scales binding hair tufts) is a pattern
- Treatment: keratolytics (salicylic acid 3–6% oil/ointment, coal tar shampoo), steroid lotions/foam/shampoo (clobetasol), calcipotriol–betamethasone gel; systemic/biologics for severe (IL-17 agents work well)

**Q26. Describe inverse (flexural) and genital psoriasis.**
- Sharply demarcated, glazed red plaques without much scale (moisture) in axillae, groin, inframammary, natal cleft, umbilicus; fissures in folds; genitals — glans/vulva
- Treat with low-potency steroids short-term, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus), calcitriol; rule out candidiasis/ tinea; IL-17 inhibitors effective for genital disease

**Q27. Describe palmoplantar psoriasis and palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP).**
- Palmoplantar psoriasis: thick hyperkeratotic fissured plaques with sharp borders on palms/soles — disabling
- PPP: crops of sterile yellow pustules evolving to brown macules on thenar/hypothenar eminences and heels; strong link with smoking (stop smoking), thyroid disease, SAPHO syndrome; treat with potent steroids under occlusion, acitretin, PUVA (hand/foot soaks), methotrexate, apremilast, cyclosporine

**Q28. What is acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau?**
- Localised pustular psoriasis of fingertips/toes — pustules around and under the nail, nail loss, osteolysis of distal phalanx; very resistant; treat with acitretin, potent topicals, biologics (IL-17/IL-36), cyclosporine

**Q29. Discuss phototherapy in psoriasis.**
- NB-UVB (311 nm): first-line phototherapy — 3 times/week, start 70% of MED or by skin type, increase 10–20% per session; clearance in ~20–30 sessions; safe in pregnancy and children
- PUVA: oral 8-MOP 0.6 mg/kg (or 5-MOP) 2 h before UVA, twice weekly; more effective for thick plaques/palmoplantar; risks — nausea, phototoxic burns, cataract (eye protection 24 h), photoageing, SCC (dose-dependent >200 sessions), melanoma
- Excimer 308 nm targeted for localised plaques/scalp; combinations — Re-PUVA, NB-UVB + acitretin/ calcipotriol

**Q30. What is the Goeckerman and Ingram regimen?**
- Goeckerman: crude coal tar applied to plaques followed by UVB exposure daily — classical inpatient regimen
- Ingram: dithranol (anthralin) in Lassar's paste + tar bath + UVB; short-contact dithranol now preferred at home (staining, irritation)

**Q31. Psoriasis in HIV — what is special?**
- Can be the presenting feature; severe, explosive, erythrodermic, inverse and reactive-arthritis overlap; poor response to usual therapy
- Treat with ART (improves psoriasis), acitretin (not immunosuppressive), phototherapy (with caution); avoid methotrexate/cyclosporine; biologics used cautiously with controlled viral load

**Q32. What is drug-induced and paradoxical psoriasis?**
- Drug-induced/aggravated: lithium, β-blockers, antimalarials, NSAIDs, interferon, terbinafine, tetracyclines, imiquimod, checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1)
- Paradoxical psoriasis with TNF inhibitors (palmoplantar pustular common) — switch class (IL-12/23, IL-23) if severe

## Quick spotter facts
- Grattage: candle-grease → Burkley's membrane → Auspitz sign
- Munro microabscess, spongiform pustule of Kogoj
- Nail pits + oil-drop sign + DIP arthritis

## Note
Biologic approvals and Indian availability change often — confirm before quoting newer agents (icotrokinra, imsidolimab).

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Psoriasis); Indian psoriasis guidelines (IADVL); AAD-NPF 2019–2020 guidelines. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pyoderma faciale (rosacea fulminans) — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pyoderma faciale (rosacea fulminans)** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is rosacea fulminans (pyoderma faciale)?**
- Sudden, severe, explosive variant of rosacea in young women (20–40 y) with confluent nodules, pustules, abscesses and draining sinuses on the central face on a background of intense erythema; no comedones; usually no systemic symptoms (unlike acne fulminans)

**Q2. Triggers / associations.**
- Pregnancy, emotional stress, OCP/ hormonal changes, inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, UC), high-dose vitamin B6/B12, interferon/EGFR inhibitors, history of mild rosacea/flushing

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Rapid-onset (days–weeks) painful, coalescing papules, pustules and fluctuant nodules on cheeks, chin, forehead, nose; marked erythema/oedema; may scar
- Fever or arthralgia are uncommon (consider acne fulminans or neutrophilic dermatosis if present)

**Q4. Classify neutrophilic dermatoses (PYQ).**
- Sweet syndrome, pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet's, neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis, subcorneal pustular dermatosis, bowel-associated dermatosis–arthritis syndrome, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatitis, erythema elevatum diutinum, neutrophilic dermatosis of dorsal hands, autoinflammatory syndromes (PAPA, PASH, SAPHO), rosacea fulminans/acne fulminans (overlap)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acne fulminans (adolescent boys, trunk, systemic symptoms, comedones), acne conglobata, gram-negative folliculitis, halogenoderma (iodides/bromides), deep fungal infection, cutaneous TB, pyoderma gangrenosum, Sweet syndrome

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Oral prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 1–2 weeks to settle inflammation, then add oral isotretinoin 0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day for 3–4 months while tapering steroid
- Topical/intralesional steroids, gentle care, drainage of fluctuant nodules
- Pregnancy: oral steroids, azithromycin/erythromycin, topical metronidazole/azelaic acid; isotretinoin only after delivery (contraception)
- Treat underlying IBD

**Q7. Classify neutrophilic dermatoses (expanded).**
- Pyoderma gangrenosum, Sweet syndrome, Behçet's, subcorneal pustular dermatosis, neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis, bowel-associated dermatosis–arthritis syndrome, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatitis, erythema elevatum diutinum, neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis, rosacea fulminans, autoinflammatory syndromes (PAPA, PASH)

**Q8. Why is rosacea fulminans considered on the rosacea spectrum?**
- Arises on a background of rosacea in some patients, central facial distribution, flushing, absence of comedones, responds to rosacea-type therapy and isotretinoin; but some regard it as a separate neutrophilic dermatosis

**Q9. Isotretinoin protocol in rosacea fulminans.**
- Start prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg for 1–2 weeks to control inflammation, then add isotretinoin 0.2–0.5 mg/kg/day while tapering steroid over 2–3 weeks; continue isotretinoin until lesions clear (3–4 months)

**Q10. Associations reported.**
- Pregnancy, IBD (Crohn's, UC), thyroid disease, stress, high-dose vitamin B6/B12, interferon, erythema nodosum; may precede IBD — ask about GI symptoms

**Q11. Scarring and later treatment.**
- Sinus tracts and nodules can leave scars — early aggressive treatment reduces scarring; later fractional/ ablative lasers, subcision, fillers

**Q12. What is Sweet syndrome — brief features?**
- Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis: tender red juicy plaques/ nodules ('pseudovesicular'), fever, neutrophilia; associations — infections, AML, drugs (G-CSF), pregnancy, IBD; dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis; dramatic response to steroids, potassium iodide, colchicine

**Q13. How is it different from acne fulminans and acne conglobata?**
- Rosacea fulminans: young women, face only (central), sudden fluctuant nodules and sinus tracts with intense red/cyanotic background, no comedones, no systemic symptoms, no trunk
- Acne fulminans: adolescent males, trunk and face, ulcerative haemorrhagic nodules with fever, arthralgia, osteolytic bone lesions, raised ESR; acne conglobata: comedones (double), nodules, sinuses on trunk/face without systemic upset

**Q14. Histopathology.**
- Dense perifollicular and dermal neutrophilic abscesses with granulomatous inflammation, sinus tracts, without bacteria on culture (sterile)

**Q15. Pregnancy-related rosacea fulminans — management.**
- Commonly triggered in pregnancy; systemic steroids (prednisolone) + topical metronidazole/azelaic acid; erythromycin/azithromycin; isotretinoin only after delivery and lactation

## Quick spotter facts
- Explosive central facial nodules/abscesses on red background in a young woman, no comedones — rosacea fulminans
- Steroids first, then isotretinoin

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Rosacea). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) — viva
posts.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma)** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. What is pyogenic granuloma (PG)?**
- Common acquired benign vascular tumour (lobular capillary haemangioma) of skin and mucosa; neither infective ('pyogenic') nor granulomatous — misnomer; children and young adults, pregnant women (granuloma gravidarum/epulis on gingiva)

**Q2. Triggers / associations.**
- Minor trauma (often), pregnancy and OCPs (hormonal), burns, ingrown toenails
- Drugs: systemic retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin — periungual), EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, gefitinib — periungual), BRAF/MEK inhibitors, capecitabine, antiretrovirals (indinavir), cyclosporine, taxanes
- Multiple/satellite PG after removal; within port-wine stains

**Q3. Describe the lesion.**
- Rapidly growing (weeks) solitary bright red, friable, sessile or pedunculated papule/nodule (5–10 mm), with glistening or eroded surface and a collarette of scale at its base
- Bleeds profusely with minor trauma; sites — fingers, lips, face, gingiva, scalp, nail folds

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Exophytic polypoid lesion with lobules of proliferating capillaries separated by fibrous septa, a central feeding vessel, surface ulceration with inflammation, epidermal collarette at the base (inward-growing rete ridges)
- GLUT-1 negative (vs infantile haemangioma)

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Amelanotic melanoma (most important — any atypical/recurrent PG should be biopsied and sent for histology), SCC/keratoacanthoma, Kaposi sarcoma, bacillary angiomatosis (HIV — Bartonella), glomus tumour, cherry angioma, infantile haemangioma, Spitz naevus, metastasis, granulation tissue (ingrown nail), angiosarcoma, eccrine poroma

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Shave excision with curettage and cautery of the base (electrodesiccation) — lowest recurrence when the feeding vessel is cauterised; send tissue for histopathology
- Surgical excision with closure (recurrence lowest), cryotherapy, laser (pulsed-dye, CO2, Nd:YAG), silver nitrate cautery for small lesions
- Topical timolol 0.5% (children, periungual), imiquimod, sodium tetradecyl sulphate sclerotherapy
- Pregnancy-related: may regress after delivery; drug-induced: dose reduction, topical timolol

**Q7. Write short notes on glomus tumour (PYQ).**
- Benign tumour of the glomus body (modified smooth muscle cells regulating thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunts — Sucquet–Hoyer canal)
- Solitary: subungual blue-red spot with severe paroxysmal pain, cold sensitivity and point tenderness — Love's pin test, Hildreth's test (pain abolished by tourniquet), cold sensitivity test; X-ray may show bony erosion; MRI
- Multiple glomuvenous malformations (glomangiomas) — autosomal dominant (glomulin), less painful, children
- Treatment: surgical excision

**Q8. Dermoscopy of pyogenic granuloma.**
- Reddish homogeneous area with white rail-lines (fibrous septa) crossing the lesion and a white collarette at the periphery; ulceration; vessels may obscure — any atypical vascular pattern needs histology to exclude amelanotic melanoma

**Q9. What are the variants of pyogenic granuloma?**
- Cutaneous, mucosal (gingival, lip, nasal — epulis), intravenous PG (within a vein — subcutaneous nodule), subcutaneous, disseminated/ eruptive (after burns or drugs), satellite lesions after excision

**Q10. Periungual pyogenic granulomas from drugs — management.**
- Due to retinoids, EGFR inhibitors, taxanes, protease inhibitors; treat with topical timolol/ steroid under occlusion, silver nitrate, cryotherapy, nail-fold care, dose modification; partial nail avulsion for ingrowing component

**Q11. Differentiate PG from Kaposi sarcoma.**
- KS: violaceous plaques/ nodules, often multiple, on legs, face, oral palate, HIV/ elderly men/ transplant; slow growth; histology — slit-like vascular spaces, spindle cells, HHV-8 (LANA-1) positive
- PG: solitary rapidly growing bright red friable papule with collarette; HHV-8 negative

**Q12. Why do PGs recur after shave excision?**
- Residual feeder vessel/ lobular tissue at the base or deep dermis; recurrence ~10–15% (may produce satellite lesions); prevent by deeper curettage and cautery of base or full-thickness excision

**Q13. Glomus tumour vs other painful skin tumours (mnemonic).**
- Painful tumours — 'BLEND AN EGG': Blue rubber bleb naevus, Leiomyoma, Eccrine spiradenoma, Neuroma, Dermatofibroma, Angiolipoma, Neurilemmoma (schwannoma), Endometrioma, Glomus tumour, Granular cell tumour

**Q14. What is granuloma gravidarum?**
- PG on the gingiva in pregnancy (epulis gravidarum) — hormones (progesterone/oestrogen) and gingivitis; often regresses after delivery; excise if bleeding or interfering with eating

**Q15. What is bacillary angiomatosis and why differentiate?**
- Bartonella henselae/quintana infection in HIV (CD4 <100) — multiple PG-like red papules/nodules, systemic (liver — peliosis, bone); Warthin–Starry stain shows bacilli; treated with erythromycin/doxycycline for months — not with excision alone

## Quick spotter facts
- Rapidly growing bleeding red papule with collarette — pyogenic granuloma
- Always send for histology — exclude amelanotic melanoma
- Subungual painful blue spot + cold sensitivity — glomus tumour

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Vascular tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis — viva
posts.summary: Oral & mucosal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Recurrent aphthous stomatitis** (Oral & mucosal disorders)_

**Q1. Define recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS).**
- Commonest oral mucosal disease: recurrent, painful, round/oval ulcers with a yellow-grey fibrinous base and erythematous halo on non-keratinised mucosa, in otherwise healthy people; affects ~20% of population; starts in childhood/adolescence

**Q2. Classify RAS.**
- Minor (Mikulicz) aphthae ~80%: <1 cm, 1–5 ulcers, heal in 7–14 days without scar
- Major (Sutton's, periadenitis mucosa necrotica recurrens) ~10%: >1 cm, deep, last 2–6 weeks, heal with scarring, can involve soft palate, fauces, tongue
- Herpetiform ~10%: crops of 10–100 pinpoint ulcers that coalesce, heal in 1–2 weeks; not caused by HSV
- Simple vs complex aphthosis (almost constant ulcers — look for systemic disease)

**Q3. Aetiology / precipitating factors.**
- Genetic predisposition (family history), local trauma (brushing, dental appliances), stress, hormonal (luteal phase), smoking cessation, food hypersensitivity (chocolate, nuts, tomato, cinnamon), sodium lauryl sulphate toothpaste
- Nutritional deficiencies: iron, vitamin B12, folate, zinc, vitamin D
- Systemic associations (aphthous-like ulcers): Behçet's disease, coeliac disease, Crohn's disease/UC, HIV, cyclic neutropenia, PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis), MAGIC syndrome, Sweet syndrome, drugs (NSAIDs, nicorandil, methotrexate, beta-blockers, mTOR inhibitors)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of oral ulcers.**
- Herpetic stomatitis/recurrent intraoral herpes (keratinised mucosa — hard palate, gums; vesicles first)
- Hand-foot-mouth disease, herpangina, traumatic ulcer, Behçet's disease, pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid, erosive LP, EM/SJS, SLE (palatal, painless), tuberculosis, syphilis, deep fungal, SCC (persistent, indurated — biopsy any ulcer >3 weeks), drug (nicorandil), neutropenia, agranulocytosis

**Q5. What is Behçet's disease? Criteria.**
- Variable-vessel vasculitis along the old Silk Road (Turkey, Middle East, Japan); HLA-B51
- International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD 2014): oral aphthosis 2, genital aphthosis 2, ocular lesions (uveitis, retinal vasculitis) 2, skin lesions (pseudofolliculitis, erythema nodosum) 1, neurological 1, vascular (thrombosis, aneurysm) 1, positive pathergy test 1 — ≥4 points = Behçet's
- Pathergy test: 20–22 G needle prick on forearm → papule/pustule at 48 h
- Treatment: colchicine, topical steroids, apremilast (oral ulcers), azathioprine, TNF inhibitors (eye, vascular, neuro), interferon-α

**Q6. Investigations in recurrent/complex aphthae.**
- CBC, serum ferritin, B12, folate, zinc, vitamin D; coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), HIV; stool/endoscopy if GI symptoms; serial neutrophil counts for cyclic neutropenia; biopsy for atypical/persistent ulcers; pathergy and eye exam if Behçet's suspected

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Avoid triggers (SLS toothpaste, trauma, offending foods); correct deficiencies
- Topical: corticosteroids (triamcinolone in orabase, clobetasol gel, betamethasone mouthwash, beclomethasone spray), anaesthetics (lignocaine gel, benzydamine), antiseptics (chlorhexidine 0.2%), tetracycline/doxycycline mouthwash (herpetiform), amlexanox, sucralfate, hyaluronic acid gel
- Systemic (severe/major/complex): colchicine 0.5–1.5 mg/day, dapsone, pentoxifylline, short prednisolone course, apremilast, thalidomide (major aphthae in HIV — teratogenic, neuropathy), TNF inhibitors for refractory/ Behçet's
- Laser (low-level/CO2) for pain relief

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Minor aphthae become less frequent with age; major aphthae chronic; look for systemic disease when ulcers are complex or start in adulthood

**Q9. What is the pathogenesis?**
- Immune dysregulation — T-cell (CD8 cytotoxic, Th1 — TNF-α) mediated destruction of oral epithelium, triggered by trauma, microbial antigens (streptococcal HSP), stress, hormones, nutritional deficiencies; genetic predisposition (HLA, cytokine polymorphisms)

**Q10. Oral ulcer in HIV — differential and management.**
- Major aphthae (large, painful), HSV, CMV (biopsy), histoplasmosis, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, necrotising gingivitis; thalidomide (major aphthae), topical/ intralesional steroids, treat infections, optimise ART

**Q11. What is MAGIC syndrome?**
- Mouth And Genital ulcers with Inflamed Cartilage — overlap of Behçet's disease and relapsing polychondritis

**Q12. Treatment of Behçet's disease in detail.**
- Mucocutaneous: topical steroids, colchicine (0.5–1.5 mg/day — EN and genital ulcers), apremilast 30 mg BD (oral ulcers), dapsone, thalidomide
- Eye: azathioprine, cyclosporine, TNF inhibitors (infliximab/ adalimumab), interferon-α
- Vascular/ neuro: high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide/ TNF inhibitors; anticoagulation controversial in venous thrombosis

**Q13. Oral lesions of nutritional deficiency.**
- Iron: angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis; B12/ folate: beefy red tongue, aphthae; riboflavin: magenta tongue; niacin: red swollen tongue (pellagra); zinc: erosive stomatitis; vitamin C: bleeding swollen gums (scurvy)

**Q14. Histopathology of an aphthous ulcer.**
- Non-specific ulcer with fibrinopurulent membrane, mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, neutrophils), perivascular lymphocytes at the edge; no viral cytopathic effect, no granulomas, no vasculitis — biopsy mainly to exclude other causes

**Q15. What is PFAPA syndrome?**
- Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis and cervical Adenitis — children <5 y; episodes every 3–8 weeks lasting 3–6 days; normal growth; single dose of prednisolone aborts attacks; tonsillectomy can cure; colchicine prophylaxis

## Quick spotter facts
- Round shallow yellow-based ulcers with red halo on non-keratinised mucosa — aphthae
- Oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + pathergy — Behçet's
- Any oral ulcer >3 weeks — biopsy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Oral mucosal disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (RAPK)?**
- Rare autosomal dominant disorder (ADAM10 loss-of-function) of slightly depressed, angulated, reticulate brown freckle-like macules on the dorsa of hands and feet, starting in childhood/adolescence and slowly spreading proximally; worse with sun exposure
- Palmar and plantar pits (breaks in dermatoglyphics) — characteristic

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Epidermal atrophy with thin elongated rete ridges, increased basal pigmentation and melanocytes at the tips of rete — atrophic lentigo-like pattern

**Q3. Differential diagnosis.**
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (hypo + hyperpigmented mottling on dorsa, Japanese — ADAR1)
- Dowling–Degos disease (flexural; overlap cases exist)
- Acropigmentation of Dohi, freckles, lentigines, Peutz–Jeghers, Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn, dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis, acral pigmentation of B12 deficiency, Addison's

**Q4. Enumerate reticulate pigmentary disorders.**
- Dowling–Degos disease (flexural reticulate pigmentation, comedo-like pits — KRT5, POFUT1, POGLUT1)
- Reticulate acropigmentation of Kitamura (dorsa of hands/feet, palmar pits — ADAM10)
- Galli–Galli disease (DDD with acantholysis)
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (Dohi — acral mottled hypo/hyper — ADAR1) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria
- Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn syndrome and dermatopathia pigmentosa reticularis (KRT14 — absent dermatoglyphics)
- Dyskeratosis congenita (reticulate pigmentation, nail dystrophy, oral leukoplakia — telomere genes)
- Incontinentia pigmenti stage 3, X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder, Haber syndrome, confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (acquired)

**Q5. Treatment.**
- No definitive therapy; photoprotection; topical azelaic acid/hydroquinone or adapalene; Q-switched/Er:YAG laser (case reports); genetic counselling

**Q6. What is the pathogenesis?**
- ADAM10 (a disintegrin and metalloprotease 10) loss-of-function → impaired Notch signalling in skin, affecting melanocyte homeostasis and epidermal differentiation

**Q7. Clinical clues helping diagnosis.**
- Onset first/second decade, autosomal dominant family history, freckle-like angulated macules that are slightly atrophic/depressed, on dorsa of hands and feet, gradually extending to forearms, neck and face; palmar pits and interruptions of dermatoglyphics; darkens with sun

**Q8. How does dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria differ?**
- DSH (Dohi): both hyper- and hypopigmented small macules (mottled) on dorsa of hands and feet, ADAR1 mutation, East Asians, no palmar pits; RAPK: only hyperpigmented atrophic angulated macules with palmar pits

**Q9. Is there any malignant association?**
- No — benign cosmetic disorder; overlap with Dowling–Degos disease (shared features in some families) is recognised

**Q10. Dermoscopy of RAPK.**
- Brown reticular pigment network with irregular brown dots/ globules on dorsa of hands; palmar pits seen as small depressions interrupting dermatoglyphics

**Q11. Explain the significance of palmar pits as a sign — other causes.**
- Palmar pits: RAPK, basal cell naevus (Gorlin) syndrome, Darier's disease (punctate keratoses/ pits), Cowden syndrome (acral keratoses), punctate palmoplantar keratoderma, arsenical keratoses, pitted keratolysis (soles)

**Q12. What are the dyschromatoses?**
- Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria (DSH — ADAR1, acral mixed hyper/hypopigmented macules from childhood, Japanese/Chinese) and dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (ABCB6/SASH1 — generalised mottling); RAPK is hyperpigmentation only

**Q13. Explain the role of photoprotection.**
- Lesions darken with sun exposure; sunscreens and gloves reduce contrast; pigment otherwise stable and benign

**Q14. Differentiate RAPK from acral pigmentation in vitamin B12 deficiency.**
- B12 deficiency: diffuse hyperpigmentation of knuckles, palms, soles and nails (vegetarians, pernicious anaemia), with anaemia, glossitis, neuropathy — reversible with B12; RAPK is reticulate, genetic, with palmar pits

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Angulated reticulate pigmented macules on dorsa of hands with palmar pits — RAPK (ADAM10)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Reticulate pigmentary disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Rosacea — viva
posts.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 18 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Rosacea** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. Define rosacea.**
- Chronic inflammatory disease of central facial skin with flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, papules, pustules and phymatous changes; adults 30–50 y, fair skin (under-recognised in dark skin), women more (men more phymas)

**Q2. Diagnostic phenotypes (ROSCO approach).**
- Diagnostic (1 is enough): persistent centrofacial erythema with periodic intensification; phymatous changes
- Major (2 needed if no diagnostic): flushing/transient erythema, inflammatory papules and pustules, telangiectasia, ocular manifestations (lid margin telangiectasia, blepharitis, keratitis, conjunctivitis, scleritis)
- Minor: burning, stinging, oedema, dryness
- Older subtypes (NRS 2002): erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, ocular; variant — granulomatous

**Q3. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Neurovascular dysregulation (TRPV1/TRPA1 channels — heat, spices, alcohol trigger flushing; PACAP, CGRP)
- Innate immune dysfunction — high kallikrein-5 cleaves cathelicidin into pro-inflammatory LL-37; TLR2 upregulated; mast cells (MMP-9)
- Demodex folliculorum overgrowth and Bacillus oleronius; UV damage, matrix degeneration
- Triggers: sun, heat, hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol, exercise, stress, cold wind, topical steroids, cosmetics

**Q4. Clinical features of phymas.**
- Rhinophyma (bulbous nose — men, sebaceous hyperplasia and fibrosis), gnathophyma (chin), metophyma (forehead), otophyma (ears), blepharophyma (eyelids)

**Q5. Ocular rosacea.**
- In up to 50%; may precede skin; meibomian gland dysfunction, blepharitis, chalazia, conjunctival hyperaemia, dry eye, keratitis, corneal ulcers/perforation — refer to ophthalmology; treat with lid hygiene, doxycycline, cyclosporine eye drops

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Acne vulgaris (comedones, younger), SLE (malar rash spares nasolabial folds, no pustules, systemic), seborrhoeic dermatitis (scale), perioral dermatitis, steroid-induced rosacea, carcinoid syndrome/mastocytosis (flushing), photosensitivity, Demodex folliculitis, polycythaemia, dermatomyositis, sarcoidosis/lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei (granulomatous)

**Q7. Treatment by phenotype.**
- General: avoid triggers, gentle skin care, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, green-tinted cosmetics
- Persistent erythema: topical brimonidine 0.33% gel or oxymetazoline 1% cream (α-agonist vasoconstrictors — rebound erythema risk)
- Telangiectasia/erythema: PDL 585/595 nm, IPL, KTP laser
- Papules/pustules: topical ivermectin 1% (anti-Demodex — very effective), metronidazole 0.75–1%, azelaic acid 15%, minocycline foam 1.5%; oral doxycycline 40 mg modified-release (sub-antimicrobial) or 100 mg, minocycline; low-dose isotretinoin (0.1–0.3 mg/kg) for refractory
- Flushing: β-blockers (carvedilol, propranolol), clonidine, botulinum toxin, SSRIs (paroxetine)
- Phymas: isotretinoin early; surgical — CO2/Er:YAG laser resurfacing, electrosurgery, decortication
- Ocular: lid hygiene, doxycycline, topical cyclosporine, ophthalmology

**Q8. What is steroid-induced rosacea?**
- Rosacea-like eruption/flare with erythema, telangiectasia, papulopustules and atrophy after prolonged topical steroid use on the face (common in India — fairness creams with steroid); rebound on stopping; treat by stopping steroid (taper), tacrolimus, doxycycline, ivermectin

**Q9. Granulomatous rosacea and lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei (LMDF).**
- Granulomatous rosacea: firm yellow-brown monomorphic papules on cheeks, perioral, periocular with background erythema — granulomas on histology; differentiate from LMDF (central face/ eyelids, caseating granulomas, heals with pitted scars, no erythema background) and sarcoidosis/ lupus vulgaris
- Treatment: doxycycline/ minocycline, isotretinoin, dapsone

**Q10. Rosacea in dark skin — clues.**
- Erythema hard to see — look for papules/ pustules, burning/ stinging, dryness, oedema, granulomatous papules, ocular symptoms, flushing history; often misdiagnosed as acne or seborrhoeic dermatitis

**Q11. Phyma treatments.**
- Rhinophyma: early — isotretinoin (shrinks sebaceous hyperplasia); established — surgical decortication (scalpel, electrosurgery, CO2/ Er:YAG ablation, dermabrasion), radiofrequency; excellent cosmetic results; rule out BCC/ angiosarcoma in rhinophyma tissue

**Q12. Ocular rosacea — treatment.**
- Lid hygiene (warm compresses, lid scrubs), artificial tears, topical azithromycin/ metronidazole, cyclosporine eye drops, oral doxycycline (sub-antimicrobial) or azithromycin; ophthalmology referral for keratitis/ scleritis

**Q13. Rosacea severity scores.**
- Investigator's Global Assessment (IGA 0–4), Clinician's Erythema Assessment (CEA 0–4), lesion counts, RosaQoL, Rosacea Tracker; National Rosacea Society standard grading

**Q14. Skin care advice in rosacea.**
- Gentle non-soap cleansers, moisturisers with ceramides, mineral sunscreen daily, green-tinted primers for camouflage, avoid scrubs/ astringents/ alcohol toners/ menthol/ camphor, avoid triggers diary; patch-test new products

**Q15. What is the role of Demodex and microbes?**
- Increased density of Demodex folliculorum (>5 mites/cm²) in papulopustular rosacea; mites and their bacterium Bacillus oleronius trigger TLR2-mediated innate inflammation; basis of topical ivermectin 1% (anti-Demodex + anti-inflammatory)

**Q16. What drugs treat persistent erythema and flushing?**
- Topical α-adrenergic agonists — brimonidine 0.33% gel (α2), oxymetazoline 1% cream (α1) — temporary vasoconstriction (rebound erythema possible)
- Vascular lasers/IPL (PDL 585/595 nm, KTP 532 nm) for telangiectasia and erythema; oral β-blockers (carvedilol, propranolol) or clonidine for flushing; botulinum toxin (microinjections)

**Q17. What is the dose of oral doxycycline in rosacea?**
- Doxycycline 40 mg modified-release once daily (sub-antimicrobial anti-inflammatory dose — inhibits MMPs and cathelicidin) or 50–100 mg/day for 8–12 weeks; minocycline 100 mg; azithromycin or metronidazole alternatives; low-dose isotretinoin (0.25 mg/kg or 10 mg/day) for refractory papulopustular and early phyma

**Q18. Rosacea and comorbidities.**
- Associations reported: GI disorders (SIBO, H. pylori, IBD), cardiovascular risk, depression/anxiety, migraine, Parkinson's disease, dementia — evidence variable; triggers to avoid: heat, sunlight, spicy food, hot drinks, alcohol, exercise, stress, cosmetics with alcohol/menthol, topical steroids

## Quick spotter facts
- Central facial erythema + flushing + papulopustules without comedones — rosacea
- Ivermectin 1% cream; brimonidine/oxymetazoline for erythema
