- Rhinophyma — men

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Rosacea); ROSCO 2017/2019 phenotype approach. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Scabies — viva
posts.summary: Infestations · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Scabies** (Infestations)_

**Q1. What is scabies? Describe the mite.**
- Intensely itchy contagious infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis
- Female ~0.4 mm, burrows in stratum corneum, lays 2–3 eggs/day for 4–6 weeks; eggs hatch in 3–4 days; larva → nymph → adult in ~10–14 days
- Average 10–15 mites per patient in classic scabies; thousands to millions in crusted scabies; mites survive off host 24–36 h (longer in cool humid)

**Q2. How is it transmitted?**
- Prolonged skin-to-skin contact (family, sexual, care homes); fomites matter mainly for crusted scabies
- Incubation 3–6 weeks in first infestation; 1–3 days in re-infestation (already sensitised)

**Q3. Why does itching start late and get worse at night?**
- Itch is a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity to mite, eggs and faeces (scybala) — takes weeks to develop
- Nocturnal itch: warmth of bed increases mite activity and itch perception

**Q4. Clinical features of classic scabies.**
- Generalised itching, worse at night, with other family members affected
- Burrows (pathognomonic): grey wavy thread-like lines 2–10 mm with a vesicle/dot at the end — web spaces of fingers, wrists, sides of fingers
- Papules, papulovesicles on finger webs, flexor wrists, elbows, anterior axillary folds, periumbilical, waist, buttocks, inner thighs, genitals (penile/scrotal nodules), areolae in women
- Circle of Hebra: imaginary circle through axillae, elbows, wrists, umbilicus, buttocks, genitals
- Head and neck spared in adults (involved in infants, elderly, immunosuppressed)

**Q5. Scabies in infants — how is it different?**
- Face, scalp, palms and soles involved; vesicles, pustules, nodules (axillae, groin); irritability, poor feeding; often misdiagnosed as eczema or infantile acropustulosis

**Q6. What is crusted (Norwegian) scabies?**
- Hyperinfestation in the immunosuppressed (HIV, HTLV-1, steroids, transplant), elderly, Down syndrome, leprosy, neurological disease with sensory loss
- Thick grey hyperkeratotic crusts and fissures on hands, feet, extensors, scalp, nails; little itch; highly contagious (millions of mites); can cause outbreaks in hospitals
- Treatment: oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15 (± 22, 29) + topical permethrin/benzyl benzoate with keratolytics; isolation and environment cleaning

**Q7. Name other variants.**
- Nodular scabies (persistent itchy nodules on genitals/axillae; hypersensitivity; may last months after cure — intralesional/topical steroid)
- Bullous scabies (mimics bullous pemphigoid in elderly), scabies incognito (steroid-modified), scabies of the clean (few lesions), animal scabies (Sarcoptes from dogs — no burrows, self-limiting)
- Secondary: impetiginisation (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis — major problem in endemic communities), eczematisation, urticarial

**Q8. How do you confirm the diagnosis?**
- Clinical diagnosis using IACS 2020 criteria: confirmed (mite/eggs/faeces seen on microscopy or dermoscopy), clinical (burrows, male genital lesions, or typical lesions + itch + contact history), suspected
- Mineral oil scraping of a burrow → microscopy for mite, eggs, scybala
- Dermoscopy: 'delta-wing jet with contrail' sign (mite's head-legs triangle + burrow)
- Burrow ink test (ink fills the burrow)
- Skin biopsy rarely — mite in stratum corneum ('pigtail' of keratin), eosinophils

**Q9. Differential diagnosis.**
- Papular urticaria/insect bites, atopic dermatitis, prurigo, dermatitis herpetiformis, pediculosis, folliculitis, bullous pemphigoid (elderly), infantile acropustulosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (infants), drug eruption, secondary syphilis (genital nodules)

**Q10. Treatment of classic scabies.**
- Permethrin 5% cream: apply from neck down (include scalp/face in infants and elderly) to entire body including under nails, web spaces, genitals; wash after 8–14 h; repeat after 7 days — first line, safe from 2 months of age and in pregnancy
- Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose, repeated after 7 days (two doses; not ovicidal) — not for <15 kg children or pregnancy/lactation
- Alternatives: benzyl benzoate 25% (dilute for children; 3 applications), crotamiton 10% (weak, antipruritic), sulphur 5–10% in petrolatum (infants, pregnancy; 3 consecutive nights), malathion 0.5%; lindane — avoid (neurotoxic)

**Q11. General measures for successful treatment.**
- Treat all household and close contacts at the same time, even without symptoms
- Wash clothes, bed linen and towels in hot water (≥50–60 °C) and dry in sun, or seal in a plastic bag for 72 h
- Cut nails; re-apply to hands if washed
- Antihistamines, emollients, mild steroids for post-scabetic itch; antibiotics for secondary infection

**Q12. What is post-scabetic itch and how do you differentiate it from treatment failure?**
- Itch can persist 2–4 weeks after successful treatment due to ongoing hypersensitivity to dead mite antigens — no new burrows, gradually decreasing
- Failure/reinfestation: new burrows or lesions after 2–4 weeks, contacts not treated, incorrect application, resistance — re-treat (consider ivermectin + permethrin)

**Q13. What is mass drug administration in scabies?**
- WHO strategy for endemic communities (prevalence >10%): ivermectin MDA (two doses 7 days apart) — reduces scabies and impetigo; scabies added to WHO NTD list in 2017

**Q14. Mechanism of action of permethrin and ivermectin.**
- Permethrin: synthetic pyrethroid — blocks sodium channels in mite nerve membranes → paralysis and death; poorly absorbed, low toxicity
- Ivermectin: binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle → hyperpolarisation, paralysis; does not cross human blood–brain barrier (P-glycoprotein); not ovicidal hence second dose

**Q15. Scabies in pregnancy and infants?**
- Permethrin 5% (safe), sulphur ointment; avoid ivermectin and lindane
- Infants under 2 months: sulphur 5% or crotamiton; apply to whole body including head

## Quick spotter facts
- Burrows in finger webs + nocturnal itch + family affected — scabies
- Delta-wing jet sign on dermoscopy
- Crusted scabies — millions of mites, little itch, highly contagious

## Note
Lindane withdrawal in India and ivermectin age/weight limits — please confirm with current guidance.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Infestations — scabies); WHO / IACS guidance on scabies. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Sebaceous hyperplasia — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Sebaceous hyperplasia** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is sebaceous hyperplasia?**
- Common benign enlargement of sebaceous glands around a central dilated follicular duct — 2–6 mm soft yellowish papules with central umbilication (dell) on forehead, cheeks, nose of middle-aged/elderly (UV, ageing — reduced androgen-driven turnover)
- Also: neonatal (maternal androgens — tiny yellow papules on nose; resolve), transplant recipients on cyclosporine, familial premature form, juxtaclavicular beaded lines

**Q2. Discuss the variations of sebaceous glands (PYQ).**
- Ectopic sebaceous glands (not associated with hair follicles): Fordyce spots (lips, buccal mucosa, genitalia), Montgomery tubercles (areola), Tyson's glands (prepuce), Meibomian glands (eyelids), glands of Zeis
- Physiological changes: large in neonates (maternal androgens), small in childhood, enlarge at puberty; reduced in old age
- Disorders: sebaceous hyperplasia, nevus sebaceous, steatocystoma multiplex (cysts with sebaceous lobules in wall — KRT17), sebaceous adenoma/sebaceoma/epithelioma and sebaceous carcinoma (eyelid — aggressive), Muir–Torre syndrome (sebaceous neoplasms + keratoacanthomas + visceral cancers — mismatch repair genes MSH2/MLH1)

**Q3. Dermoscopy and histopathology.**
- Dermoscopy: yellow-white lobular globules ('cumulus clouds/popcorn') with crown vessels that do not cross the centre (vs arborising vessels crossing the BCC surface)
- Histology: enlarged mature sebaceous lobules arranged around a dilated central duct opening to the surface; no atypia

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Nodular BCC (pearly, arborising vessels, slowly growing — biopsy if doubt), sebaceous adenoma (Muir–Torre if multiple/young), molluscum contagiosum, milia, xanthelasma, syringoma, trichoepithelioma, fibrous papule of the nose, colloid milium, rhinophyma (diffuse)

**Q5. When should you think of Muir–Torre syndrome?**
- Sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma or sebaceous carcinoma (not ordinary sebaceous hyperplasia), especially if multiple, outside head and neck, or in younger patients — check mismatch repair protein immunohistochemistry (MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, PMS2) and screen for colorectal and other visceral cancers

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Benign — reassurance
- Light electrodesiccation, cryotherapy, shave excision, curettage, CO2/Er:YAG/pulsed-dye laser, PDT, trichloroacetic acid; oral isotretinoin (low dose) for multiple lesions (relapse after stopping)

**Q7. Describe the Muir–Torre syndrome sebaceous tumours.**
- Sebaceous adenoma (commonest), sebaceoma (sebaceous epithelioma), sebaceous carcinoma, keratoacanthomas with sebaceous differentiation; associated visceral malignancy — colorectal (most), endometrial, urological; MSH2/MLH1 mismatch repair defects — immunohistochemistry loss of MMR proteins in skin tumour; colonoscopy screening

**Q8. What is sebaceous carcinoma?**
- Aggressive adnexal carcinoma, commonest periocular (Meibomian glands — upper eyelid; mimics chalazion/ blepharoconjunctivitis — 'masquerade syndrome'), elderly Asian women; pagetoid spread; metastasis to nodes; treat with wide excision/ Mohs, conjunctival map biopsies; Muir–Torre association

**Q9. Treatment options for sebaceous hyperplasia.**
- Electrodesiccation/ cautery, cryotherapy, CO2 or pulsed-dye laser, photodynamic therapy, trichloroacetic acid, shave excision; oral isotretinoin (low-dose) for multiple lesions (relapse after stopping)

**Q10. Describe the sebaceous gland structure and secretion.**
- Holocrine glands (entire cell disintegrates to release sebum) attached to hair follicles (pilosebaceous unit) except free glands (Fordyce, Meibomian, Tyson's, Montgomery); sebum — triglycerides, wax esters, squalene, cholesterol esters; androgen-dependent

**Q11. Juxta-clavicular beaded lines and other variants.**
- Sebaceous hyperplasia variants: juxta-clavicular beaded lines (parallel rows of papules on neck/clavicles), linear/ diffuse sebaceous hyperplasia, familial premature sebaceous hyperplasia, nevus sebaceous (hamartoma)

**Q12. Describe radiofrequency/ electrosurgery modalities used for benign lesions.**
- Electrodesiccation (monoterminal, superficial dehydration), electrofulguration (sparking, no contact), electrocoagulation (biterminal, deeper), electrosection (cutting — radiofrequency 'radiosurgery' 3–4 MHz gives fine cuts with less thermal damage); precautions — pacemakers (use bipolar), alcohol-based prep (fire), smoke plume (HPV), avoid on keloid-prone skin

**Q13. Pathogenesis.**
- Age-related decrease in androgen levels slows sebocyte turnover → enlarged sebaceous lobules around a dilated duct; also associated with chronic sun damage, cyclosporine (transplant patients), HIV, X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia; premature/familial forms; neonatal (maternal androgens) — yellow papules on nose of newborns

**Q14. Differentiate from BCC clinically and by dermoscopy.**
- Sebaceous hyperplasia: yellowish umbilicated papule with central pore, 'crown vessels' (vessels at the periphery not crossing the centre), cumulus-like yellow lobules ('bunch of popcorn')
- BCC: pearly translucent, arborising vessels crossing the lesion, blue-grey ovoid nests, ulceration

**Q15. What are Fordyce spots?**
- Ectopic sebaceous glands opening directly onto mucosa — vermilion border, buccal mucosa, labia minora, glans/shaft of penis; tiny yellow-white papules; normal variant (Montgomery tubercles on areola, Tyson's glands on penis are related)

## Quick spotter facts
- Yellow umbilicated papules on forehead of elderly man — sebaceous hyperplasia (crown vessels)
- Sebaceous adenoma → think Muir–Torre

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Sebaceous gland disorders and tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Seborrhoeic dermatitis — viva
posts.summary: Eczemas · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Seborrhoeic dermatitis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define seborrhoeic dermatitis.**
- Chronic relapsing inflammatory dermatosis in sebum-rich areas (scalp, face, chest, flexures), characterised by red patches with greasy yellowish scales; dandruff (pityriasis capitis) is its mildest form

**Q2. Who gets it? (bimodal)**
- Infants (first 3 months — cradle cap, napkin/flexures; self-limiting) and adults (30–60 years, men more)
- Higher prevalence and severity in HIV (30–80%), Parkinson's disease and other neurological disorders (facial immobility, sebum pooling), Down syndrome, depression, alcoholism, after neuroleptics

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Malassezia yeasts (M. globosa, M. restricta) metabolise sebum triglycerides into irritant free fatty acids (oleic acid) → inflammation in susceptible individuals (barrier defects)
- Sebum quantity is not necessarily increased; host immune response, stress, cold dry weather contribute

**Q4. Clinical features in adults.**
- Scalp: diffuse fine scaling to thick adherent greasy scales with erythema, may extend to forehead hairline (corona seborrhoica)
- Face: eyebrows, glabella, nasolabial folds, beard, eyelids (blepharitis), ears (retroauricular fissuring, external canal)
- Trunk: petaloid (annular) lesions on presternal/interscapular areas, pityriasiform type
- Flexures: axillae, groin, submammary, umbilicus — intertrigo-like
- Seborrhoeic erythroderma (rare)

**Q5. Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis vs infantile atopic dermatitis.**
- Seborrhoeic: onset first weeks, greasy yellow scales, scalp/flexures/napkin area involved, little itch, baby comfortable, resolves by 6–12 months
- Atopic: onset after 2–3 months, cheeks/extensors, napkin area spared, very itchy, irritable baby, family history, chronic course

**Q6. What is Leiner's disease?**
- Historical term — generalised seborrhoeic-like erythroderma in infants with diarrhoea, failure to thrive and recurrent infections; now linked to immunodeficiency (C3/C5 dysfunction, SCID, Omenn)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Scalp: psoriasis (sharply defined, silvery scale, beyond hairline, nails), tinea capitis, atopic dermatitis, pityriasis amiantacea, LCH (infants), head lice
- Face: rosacea, lupus (malar), contact dermatitis, tinea faciei, perioral dermatitis
- Trunk: pityriasis versicolor, pityriasis rosea, secondary syphilis, Darier's disease
- 'Sebopsoriasis' — overlap

**Q8. Why test for HIV in severe seborrhoeic dermatitis?**
- Sudden onset, extensive, severe or treatment-resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis in a young adult may be an early marker of HIV infection

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Scalp: antifungal shampoos (ketoconazole 2%, ciclopirox 1%, selenium sulphide 2.5%, zinc pyrithione) 2–3 times weekly with 5 min contact; keratolytics (salicylic acid, coal tar) for thick scales; short course of steroid lotion/ foam (betamethasone, clobetasol shampoo)
- Face/body: ketoconazole 2% cream, mild steroid (hydrocortisone/desonide) for short periods, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/pimecrolimus) as steroid-sparing, roflumilast 0.3% foam (newer topical PDE4 inhibitor)
- Blepharitis: lid hygiene with dilute baby shampoo
- Infants: emollient/olive oil to soften crusts, gentle brushing, mild shampoo; ketoconazole cream if needed
- Severe/extensive: oral itraconazole 200 mg/day for 7 days then 2 days/month maintenance, fluconazole; isotretinoin low dose; phototherapy NB-UVB
- Maintenance shampoo once weekly to prevent relapse

**Q10. Histopathology.**
- Psoriasiform and spongiotic dermatitis with parakeratosis around follicular ostia ('shoulder parakeratosis'), neutrophils in scale crusts; yeasts in scale

**Q11. Describe the histopathology of eczema by stage (PYQ).**
- Acute: marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesicles, papillary oedema, perivascular lymphocytes ± eosinophils
- Subacute: spongiosis + parakeratosis + acanthosis, crusts
- Chronic: compact hyperkeratosis, irregular/ psoriasiform acanthosis, hypergranulosis, minimal spongiosis, vertical collagen in papillae (lichenification)

**Q12. Dermoscopy of scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis vs psoriasis.**
- Seborrhoeic: yellowish greasy scales, arborising thin red lines and atypical vessels, structureless red areas, honeycomb pigment
- Psoriasis: silvery-white scales, regularly distributed red dots/ globules and twisted red loops

**Q13. Seborrhoeic dermatitis in neurological disease — why?**
- Parkinson's disease (increased sebum, facial immobility, autonomic dysfunction), post-stroke, spinal cord injury, facial nerve palsy (on affected side), syringomyelia — sebum pooling and Malassezia proliferation

**Q14. Drugs that induce seborrhoeic dermatitis-like eruptions.**
- Neuroleptics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine), lithium, buspirone, methyldopa, cimetidine, interferon, gold, psoralens, EGFR/ BRAF inhibitors, dupilumab (head-neck dermatitis)

**Q15. Classify topical corticosteroids by potency (WHO/ British).**
- Super-potent (class I): clobetasol propionate 0.05%, halobetasol, betamethasone dipropionate in optimised vehicle
- Potent: betamethasone dipropionate/ valerate 0.1%, mometasone furoate 0.1%, fluticasone 0.05%, fluocinolone 0.025%, halcinonide
- Moderate: clobetasone butyrate 0.05%, triamcinolone 0.1%, desonide, hydrocortisone butyrate
- Mild: hydrocortisone 1–2.5%
- Ointments more potent than creams of same molecule; avoid potent on face, flexures, genitals, infants

**Q16. Seborrhoeic blepharitis — management.**
- Scaling of eyelid margins with crusts and redness; warm compresses, lid scrubs with diluted baby shampoo/ commercial lid cleansers twice daily, topical ketoconazole cream cautiously on eyelid skin, artificial tears; ophthalmology referral if keratitis

## Quick spotter facts
- Greasy yellow scales on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds — seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Severe sudden seb derm in young adult — test HIV; also Parkinson's

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Seborrhoeic dermatitis). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Seborrhoeic keratosis — viva
posts.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Seborrhoeic keratosis** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What is seborrhoeic keratosis (SK)?**
- Commonest benign epidermal tumour of middle-aged and elderly; well-demarcated, 'stuck-on', verrucous, waxy, light-brown to black papules/plaques on trunk, face, scalp, limbs (not palms/soles); FGFR3 and PIK3CA activating mutations; familial tendency

**Q2. Clinical variants.**
- Common, reticulated (adenoid), irritated/inflamed, clonal, dermatosis papulosa nigra (multiple small dark papules on face of dark-skinned people — very common in India, from adolescence), stucco keratosis (grey-white keratotic papules on ankles/legs of elderly), melanoacanthoma, inverted follicular keratosis, flat SK (resembles solar lentigo)

**Q3. Dermoscopy.**
- Comedo-like openings, milia-like cysts, cerebriform (brain-like) pattern with fissures and ridges ('fat fingers'), hairpin vessels with white halo, sharp moth-eaten border, network-like structures

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Exophytic acanthotic proliferation of basaloid keratinocytes above the level of surrounding epidermis ('string sign'), horn cysts and pseudo-horn cysts, papillomatosis, variable melanin
- Types: acanthotic (commonest), hyperkeratotic, reticulated, clonal (Borst–Jadassohn phenomenon — intraepidermal nests), irritated (squamous eddies), melanoacanthoma

**Q5. Write short notes on Borst–Jadassohn phenomenon (PYQ).**
- Intraepidermal nests of morphologically distinct cells within the epidermis — 'intraepidermal epithelioma'; seen in clonal SK, hidroacanthoma simplex (intraepidermal poroma), Bowen's disease (clonal), Paget's disease, melanoma in situ

**Q6. What is the sign of Leser–Trélat?**
- Sudden eruption of multiple SKs or rapid increase in size/number — paraneoplastic sign of internal malignancy (GI adenocarcinoma — stomach, colon; lymphoma), often with malignant AN and pruritus; also reported with erythroderma, pregnancy, HIV, drugs (cytarabine — inflamed SKs)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Melanoma (especially pigmented, irritated SK), pigmented BCC, solar lentigo, melanocytic naevus, wart, AK, SCC (irritated SK), dermatosis papulosa nigra vs skin tags/syringomas

**Q8. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — benign, no malignant potential
- Removal for irritation, cosmetic reasons or diagnostic doubt: cryotherapy, curettage (± light cautery), shave excision, electrodesiccation/radiofrequency, CO2/Er:YAG laser, TCA application; topical hydrogen peroxide 40% (FDA approved)
- Dermatosis papulosa nigra: light electrodesiccation/curettage, scissor snip, lasers — caution for PIH in dark skin
- Biopsy if any doubt (melanoma)

**Q9. What are stucco keratoses and inverted follicular keratosis?**
- Stucco keratoses: small grey-white 'stuck-on' keratotic papules on ankles/ dorsa of feet of elderly — easily scraped
- Inverted follicular keratosis: endophytic SK variant on face with squamous eddies — mimics SCC

**Q10. Histological types of SK.**
- Acanthotic (commonest), hyperkeratotic (papillomatous), reticulated/ adenoid, clonal (nests — Borst–Jadassohn), irritated (squamous eddies, inflammation), melanoacanthoma (pigmented with melanocytes), SK with atypia — horn cysts and pseudohorn cysts are characteristic

**Q11. Explain the principles of cryotherapy (PYQ).**
- Liquid nitrogen (−196 °C): rapid freezing causes intracellular ice crystals, cell dehydration, vascular stasis and ischaemic necrosis; slow thaw maximises damage; techniques — spray, cotton-tipped applicator, cryoprobe; lethal temperature for benign lesions −20 to −30 °C, malignant −50 °C (double freeze–thaw)
- Side effects: pain, blistering, hypo/ hyperpigmentation (avoid in dark skin cosmetic areas), scarring, nerve damage over superficial nerves, alopecia

**Q12. When should an SK be biopsied?**
- Atypical features — rapid growth, bleeding, irregular pigmentation, inflammation without trauma, dermoscopic melanoma features (atypical network, blue-white veil), lesions on mucosa; melanoma 'masquerading' as SK is a known pitfall

**Q13. Newer topical therapy for SK.**
- Hydrogen peroxide 40% topical solution (FDA approved for raised SK, since withdrawn commercially), tazarotene, calcipotriol, imiquimod — limited efficacy; ablative lasers (CO2/ Er:YAG) and curettage remain standard

**Q14. What is the genetic basis of SK?**
- Somatic activating mutations of FGFR3 (≈ 40–50%) and PIK3CA, also RAS; age and UV-related; not malignant (benign clonal neoplasm)

**Q15. What is dermatosis papulosa nigra?**
- Variant of SK in darker skin (Africans, Indians): multiple small dark-brown/black papules on malar face, forehead, neck from adolescence; familial; treated (cosmetic) with light electrodesiccation, curettage, scissor snip, lasers — risk of pigmentary change

## Quick spotter facts
- Stuck-on waxy verrucous plaque with milia-like cysts and comedo-like openings — SK
- Sudden eruption of SKs — Leser–Trélat

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Benign epidermal tumours). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Sporotrichosis — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Sporotrichosis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. What is sporotrichosis? Agent?**
- Subacute/chronic subcutaneous mycosis caused by the thermally dimorphic Sporothrix schenckii complex (S. schenckii, S. brasiliensis, S. globosa — commonest in Asia/India)
- Mould in environment (25 °C), yeast in tissue (37 °C)

**Q2. How is it acquired and who gets it?**
- Implantation from soil, plants, thorns (rose — 'rose gardener's disease'), sphagnum moss, hay, wood splinters; zoonotic from cat scratches (S. brasiliensis — Brazil epidemic)
- Gardeners, farmers, florists, forestry workers; in India — sub-Himalayan belt (Himachal, north-east, Uttarakhand), Kangra valley

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Lymphocutaneous (~75%): papulonodule at inoculation site (hand/forearm) ulcerates (sporotrichoid chancre) → secondary nodules along the lymphatic chain ascending the limb
- Fixed cutaneous: single plaque/verrucous/ulcerated lesion without lymphatic spread — common on face in children in endemic areas (more immune host)
- Disseminated cutaneous and systemic (osteoarticular, pulmonary — inhalation, meningeal) in immunosuppressed (HIV, alcoholism, diabetes)

**Q4. What is the sporotrichoid pattern and its differentials?**
- Nodules in a linear chain along lymphatics
- Causes: sporotrichosis, Mycobacterium marinum (fish-tank granuloma), Nocardia brasiliensis, leishmaniasis (L. braziliensis), tularaemia, cat-scratch disease, other mycobacteria, blastomycosis — remember 'SLNM'

**Q5. How do you investigate?**
- Histopathology: pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, mixed suppurative granuloma ('sporotrichoid granuloma' with central neutrophils, middle histiocytes, outer lymphocytes); organisms scanty — small cigar-shaped yeasts, asteroid bodies (Splendore–Hoeppli) with PAS/GMS
- Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 °C — the gold standard (moist white colonies becoming dark; sleeve/flower-like conidia); conversion to yeast at 37 °C
- PCR; sporotrichin skin test (epidemiology)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day (drug of choice) — continue 2–4 weeks after lesions resolve (usually 3–6 months)
- Saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI): start 5 drops thrice daily increased to 40–50 drops thrice daily — cheap and effective in India; side effects: metallic taste, salivary gland swelling, acneiform rash, GI upset, hypothyroidism; avoid in pregnancy
- Terbinafine 250–500 mg/day alternative; local hyperthermia (warm compresses) as adjunct — fungus does not grow above 37 °C
- Amphotericin B for disseminated/pulmonary/meningeal disease, then itraconazole

**Q7. Differential diagnosis of fixed cutaneous sporotrichosis.**
- Lupus vulgaris, TBVC, chromoblastomycosis, leishmaniasis, pyoderma, blastomycosis, SCC, atypical mycobacterial infection

**Q8. Why is the fixed type common on the face of children?**
- Repeated exposure in endemic areas produces strong immunity, which limits lymphatic spread

**Q9. What is an asteroid body?**
- Central yeast surrounded by radiating eosinophilic Splendore–Hoeppli material — seen in sporotrichosis (also sarcoidosis has 'asteroid bodies' of a different kind inside giant cells)

**Q10. Which drug is used in pregnancy?**
- Avoid azoles and iodides; local heat therapy; amphotericin B for severe disease

**Q11. Potassium iodide — mechanism and protocol.**
- Exact mechanism unclear — enhances immune/ neutrophil function, halogenation of fungal proteins, reduces granuloma formation; SSKI (1 g/ml): 5 drops thrice daily increased by 5 drops/dose weekly to 40–50 drops thrice daily (adults) in milk/ juice; continue 4 weeks after clinical cure
- Side effects: metallic taste, nausea, salivary/ lacrimal gland swelling, acneiform eruption (iododerma), hypothyroidism (Wolff–Chaikoff), hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow); avoid in pregnancy/ thyroid disease

**Q12. Disseminated/ systemic sporotrichosis — features.**
- In HIV, alcoholism, diabetes: multiple ulcerated nodules, osteoarticular (knee, ankle — arthritis), pulmonary (inhalation — cavitation like TB), meningitis; amphotericin B followed by itraconazole; HIV — lifelong suppression until immune recovery

**Q13. Feline (cat-transmitted) sporotrichosis.**
- Sporothrix brasiliensis epidemic in Brazil — scratches/ bites from infected cats with ulcerated lesions; higher virulence, more disseminated/ ocular disease; zoonotic control by treating cats with itraconazole

**Q14. Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis vs M. marinum infection.**
- M. marinum: fish-tank/ swimming pool exposure, nodule on fingers/ dorsum hand, sporotrichoid spread; histology tuberculoid granuloma with AFB; culture at 30 °C; treat with clarithromycin + ethambutol/ doxycycline/ rifampicin
- Sporotrichosis: soil/ plant exposure, culture fungus at 25 °C, responds to itraconazole/ SSKI

**Q15. Classify antifungal drugs (PYQ).**
- Polyenes: amphotericin B (systemic, deep mycoses), nystatin (topical/ oral Candida)
- Azoles — imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole) and triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) — inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis)
- Allylamines: terbinafine, naftifine (squalene epoxidase inhibitors); benzylamine — butenafine
- Echinocandins: caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin (β-1,3-glucan synthase)
- Others: griseofulvin (microtubule — mitotic inhibitor), flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis), ciclopirox (chelator), amorolfine (morpholine — Δ14 reductase/ Δ7-Δ8 isomerase), tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), potassium iodide, efinaconazole, tavaborole

## Quick spotter facts
- Ascending nodules along lymphatics from a hand ulcer — sporotrichosis
- SSKI — cheap drug that works
- Asteroid bodies

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch. 19A (Subcutaneous mycoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Squamous cell carcinoma — viva
posts.summary: Premalignant & malignant tumours · 28 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Squamous cell carcinoma** (Premalignant & malignant tumours)_

**Q1. Define cutaneous SCC (cSCC).**
- Malignant tumour of epidermal keratinocytes with invasion into the dermis, capable of local destruction and metastasis (2–5% overall; higher in high-risk tumours); second commonest skin cancer worldwide; in India often arises on chronic scars/ulcers and in genital or oral mucosa

**Q2. Describe SCC: types and risk factors (PYQ).**
- Risk factors: cumulative UV exposure, fair skin, age, chronic immunosuppression (organ transplant — 65–250× risk; azathioprine, voriconazole), HPV (periungual/genital — 16, 18; β-HPV in EDV), ionising radiation, arsenic, tar, mineral oils, PUVA, smoking (lip), chronic inflammation and scars (burns — Marjolin's ulcer, lupus vulgaris, DLE, chronic ulcers, osteomyelitis sinus, lichen sclerosus, erosive LP, DEB, HS), Kangri cancer (Kashmir — abdominal wall from fire pot), Kang cancer, dhoti cancer (waist), chutta cancer (reverse smoking — palate), betel/tobacco chewing (oral), xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, BRAF inhibitors (keratoacanthoma-like)
- Precursors: actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease (SCC in situ), actinic cheilitis, leukoplakia/erythroplakia, erythroplasia of Queyrat (glans), bowenoid papulosis, arsenical keratoses, porokeratosis

**Q3. Clinical types.**
- In situ: Bowen's disease — slowly enlarging, well-defined, red scaly plaque (lower legs of elderly women, trunk); erythroplasia of Queyrat (velvety red plaque on glans of uncircumcised men)
- Invasive: indurated keratotic nodule or plaque, ulcer with raised everted indurated edges, cutaneous horn, verrucous/exophytic, bleeding; sun-exposed sites (ear, lip, scalp, dorsum of hand) or on scars
- Variants: keratoacanthoma (well-differentiated SCC variant — rapidly growing crateriform nodule with central keratin plug in weeks, may regress), verrucous carcinoma (low-grade — oral florid papillomatosis, Buschke–Löwenstein (genital), epithelioma cuniculatum (plantar)), spindle-cell, acantholytic, adenosquamous, desmoplastic (aggressive)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Irregular nests and strands of atypical squamous cells invading the dermis from the epidermis, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, dyskeratosis, mitoses
- Broders' grading by differentiation: well (>75% differentiated), moderately, poorly (<25%), undifferentiated
- Keratoacanthoma: symmetric cup-shaped crater filled with keratin, glassy eosinophilic cells, buttresses ('lipping') at edges

**Q5. High-risk features.**
- Diameter ≥2 cm, depth >6 mm or beyond subcutaneous fat, poor differentiation, perineural invasion (nerve ≥0.1 mm), desmoplastic/acantholytic subtype, location — ear, lip, temple, H-zone, genital; arising in scar/chronic ulcer or radiation site; immunosuppression; recurrent tumour; rapid growth
- Staging: AJCC 8th (head and neck) and Brigham and Women's Hospital (T1–T3 by risk factors)

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Keratoacanthoma, BCC, AK (hypertrophic), wart, seborrhoeic keratosis (irritated), amelanotic melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, prurigo nodule, chronic infections (TBVC, chromoblastomycosis, deep fungal, mycetoma, leishmaniasis — pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia mimics SCC)

**Q7. Investigations.**
- Biopsy (incisional/excisional) including deep tissue; examine regional lymph nodes; FNAC/USG of nodes; CT/MRI for deep invasion, perineural spread or nodal disease; sentinel lymph node biopsy (selected high-risk)

**Q8. Management.**
- Low-risk: surgical excision with 4–6 mm margins; curettage and electrodesiccation for small low-risk; cryotherapy for in situ
- High-risk: wide excision with ≥6 mm margins or Mohs surgery; adjuvant radiotherapy for perineural invasion/positive margins/nodal disease; nodal dissection for nodal metastasis
- Bowen's disease: 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT, cryotherapy, curettage, excision
- Advanced/metastatic or unresectable: immune checkpoint inhibitors — cemiplimab (first approved), pembrolizumab; EGFR inhibitor cetuximab; platinum chemotherapy (older)
- Prevention: sun protection, treat precursors, nicotinamide, acitretin in transplant recipients, switch immunosuppressant to sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor)
- Follow-up: 3–6 monthly for 2 years then yearly; skin and node examination

**Q9. Discuss cutaneous markers of internal malignancy (PYQ).**
- Paraneoplastic dermatoses: acanthosis nigricans (malignant), tripe palms, Leser–Trélat sign, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex (SCC upper aerodigestive tract), erythema gyratum repens (lung), necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma), hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita, dermatomyositis, paraneoplastic pemphigus, Sweet syndrome/pyoderma gangrenosum (haematological), Trousseau's migratory thrombophlebitis (pancreas), carcinoid flushing, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, pachydermoperiostosis, ichthyosis acquisita (lymphoma), extramammary Paget's
- Genetic syndromes with skin markers: Gardner, Muir–Torre (sebaceous tumours), Cowden (trichilemmomas), Peutz–Jeghers, Birt–Hogg–Dubé, Gorlin, MEN 2B (mucosal neuromas), Howel–Evans, Carney complex

**Q10. Describe precursor lesions of SCC.**
- Actinic keratosis (most common precursor), Bowen's disease (SCC in situ), actinic cheilitis (lower lip), erythroplasia of Queyrat (glans), leukoplakia/ erythroplakia (oral), bowenoid papulosis, arsenical keratoses, chronic radiation dermatitis, chronic scars/ ulcers (Marjolin), porokeratosis, LS, erosive LP, HPV-related warts in immunosuppressed

**Q11. What is Bowen's disease and its management?**
- Intraepidermal SCC (full-thickness atypia): slowly enlarging, well-demarcated, red scaly plaque on sun-exposed skin (legs of elderly women), or trunk (arsenic); ~3–5% progress to invasive SCC
- Treatment: 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT (excellent for large/leg lesions with poor healing), cryotherapy, curettage, excision; erythroplasia of Queyrat — glans (higher progression)

**Q12. What is keratoacanthoma?**
- Rapidly growing (weeks) dome-shaped nodule with central keratin-filled crater on sun-exposed skin of elderly; may involute spontaneously in months leaving scar; considered a well-differentiated SCC variant — treat as SCC (excision); multiple KAs — Ferguson-Smith (TGFBR1), Grzybowski (eruptive), Muir–Torre; drug-induced (BRAF inhibitors — vemurafenib)

**Q13. Describe the TNM staging principles of cSCC (AJCC 8th, head and neck).**
- T1 <2 cm; T2 2–4 cm; T3 >4 cm or minor bone erosion, perineural invasion, or deep invasion (beyond subcutaneous fat or >6 mm); T4 gross bone/skull base invasion
- N staging by node size/number/extranodal extension; M1 distant metastasis
- Brigham and Women's Hospital (BWH) staging uses high-risk factors (≥2 cm, poorly differentiated, perineural invasion of nerve ≥0.1 mm, invasion beyond fat) — better prognostic discrimination

**Q14. Which areas carry higher metastatic risk?**
- Lip and ear (mucocutaneous junctions), temple, scalp, genitals (penile/vulval), SCC arising in chronic scars/ulcers (Marjolin) or radiation sites, perineural invasion, immunosuppressed patients — metastasis rates 10–30% vs ~2–5% overall

**Q15. Surgical management and margins.**
- Low-risk SCC: excision with 4–6 mm clinical margins; high-risk: ≥6–10 mm margins or Mohs micrographic surgery (complete margin control); assess regional nodes clinically/ ultrasound; sentinel lymph node biopsy in selected high-risk tumours
- Adjuvant radiotherapy for perineural invasion, close/positive margins, nodal disease with extracapsular extension

**Q16. Systemic treatment of advanced SCC.**
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1) — cemiplimab (first-line for locally advanced/ metastatic cSCC — response ~45–50%), pembrolizumab; cetuximab (EGFR) for those unfit for immunotherapy; platinum chemotherapy older option; transplant recipients — reduce immunosuppression, switch to sirolimus (mTOR inhibitors have anti-tumour effect)

**Q17. SCC in organ transplant recipients — why and how to manage?**
- Immunosuppression (azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors) + UV + HPV → SCC 65–250× higher, more aggressive, multiple, SCC:BCC ratio reversed (~4:1)
- Management: strict sun protection, regular skin checks (3–12 monthly), early treatment of AKs (field therapy), nicotinamide, acitretin chemoprevention (10–25 mg/day), reduce/switch immunosuppression (sirolimus/everolimus)

**Q18. Penile and vulval SCC — risk factors.**
- Penile: phimosis, poor hygiene, uncircumcised, HPV 16/18, lichen sclerosus (BXO), smoking, PUVA; presents as ulcer/ growth on glans/ prepuce; inguinal nodes
- Vulval: HPV-related (younger — usual VIN) and HPV-independent (older — LS/differentiated VIN, p53 mutation); itchy lump/ ulcer

**Q19. Oral SCC and its premalignant lesions in India.**
- High burden due to tobacco chewing (gutka, khaini), betel quid, smoking, alcohol; premalignant — leukoplakia (white plaque not rubbed off), erythroplakia (highest risk), oral submucous fibrosis (areca nut — trismus, blanching), erosive LP; buccal mucosa commonest site in India; biopsy persistent lesions >2 weeks

**Q20. Verrucous carcinoma — what is it?**
- Well-differentiated low-grade SCC variant — slow-growing exophytic cauliflower-like mass with 'pushing' borders; sites — oral (oral florid papillomatosis), anogenital (Buschke–Löwenstein), plantar (epithelioma cuniculatum — sinus tracts like rabbit burrows); rarely metastasises; wide excision (radiotherapy may cause anaplastic transformation)

**Q21. Histological grading (Broders).**
- Grade 1: >75% differentiated (keratin pearls, intercellular bridges); 2: 50–75%; 3: 25–50%; 4: <25% (poorly differentiated, spindle cell)
- Variants: acantholytic, spindle cell (sarcomatoid — cytokeratin+), desmoplastic (high-risk), adenosquamous, clear cell

**Q22. Differentiate keratoacanthoma from SCC clinically and histologically.**
- KA: rapid growth over weeks, symmetrical crateriform with central keratin plug, may regress; histology — symmetrical cup-shaped architecture with 'lipping' buttresses, glassy eosinophilic keratinocytes, intraepithelial neutrophilic microabscesses
- SCC: slower, irregular, ulcerated, infiltrative strands with atypia; often impossible to separate — treat KA as SCC

**Q23. Prevention and chemoprevention.**
- Sun protection (sunscreens reduce SCC — Nambour trial), avoid tanning, treat AK, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily, acitretin in transplant recipients and XP, HPV vaccination (anogenital), stop tobacco/areca nut (oral), avoid arsenic-contaminated water

**Q24. What is Marjolin's ulcer?**
- SCC arising in chronic scars (burns commonest), chronic osteomyelitis sinuses, venous ulcers, pressure sores, lupus vulgaris, DLE, hidradenitis; long latency (decades); aggressive with high nodal metastasis — biopsy any non-healing ulcer with raised edge/ growth

**Q25. Examination of a patient with suspected SCC — what do you check?**
- Lesion: size, site, edge (raised/ everted), base, induration, fixation to deeper structures, bleeding, perineural symptoms (pain, numbness, facial weakness)
- Regional lymph nodes (parotid, cervical, axillary, inguinal), whole-skin exam for other cancers/ AKs, oral cavity, immune status

**Q26. Prognosis.**
- Overall 5-year cure >90% for primary low-risk SCC after excision; recurrent, perineural, poorly differentiated, immunosuppressed and nodal disease have worse outcome (nodal metastasis 5-year survival ~50%)

**Q27. Cutaneous markers of internal malignancy (expanded).**
- Paraneoplastic dermatoses: acanthosis nigricans (malignant), tripe palms, Leser–Trélat sign, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica of Bazex (upper aerodigestive SCC), erythema gyratum repens (lung), necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma), hypertrichosis lanuginosa acquisita, dermatomyositis, paraneoplastic pemphigus, Sweet syndrome (AML), pyoderma gangrenosum (myeloma), Trousseau sign (migratory thrombophlebitis — pancreatic), carcinoid flushing, Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilical metastasis), extramammary Paget's, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, pachydermoperiostosis/ clubbing (lung)

**Q28. Bazex syndrome — explain.**
- Acrokeratosis paraneoplastica: psoriasiform violaceous scaly plaques on ears, nose, fingers/ toes and nails (acral) in men >40 with SCC of upper aerodigestive tract (pharynx, larynx, oesophagus) or lung; improves with tumour treatment

## Quick spotter facts
- Ulcer with raised everted indurated edge on old burn scar — Marjolin's SCC
- Keratin pearls, Broders' grading
- Kangri cancer — Kashmir

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Squamous cell carcinoma; keratoacanthoma); Brigham and Women's / AJCC staging concepts. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Stevens–Johnson syndrome / TEN — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Stevens–Johnson syndrome / TEN** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define SJS and TEN and classify by BSA.**
- Severe life-threatening mucocutaneous reactions, mostly drug-induced, with extensive keratinocyte death (epidermal necrosis) and detachment
- SJS: <10% body surface area (BSA) detachment; SJS–TEN overlap: 10–30%; TEN: >30% (Bastuji-Garin classification)
- Lesions: widespread dusky/purpuric macules, flat atypical targets, blisters; ≥2 mucosal sites

**Q2. Common culprit drugs (India).**
- Antiepileptics — carbamazepine (commonest in India), phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine
- Allopurinol (high risk, HLA-B*58:01), sulphonamides (cotrimoxazole), nevirapine, NSAIDs (oxicams), fluoroquinolones, β-lactams, anti-TB drugs, sulfasalazine, dapsone
- Onset typically 4–28 days after starting the drug (first exposure)
- Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a non-drug cause in children; ~5% idiopathic

**Q3. What are the HLA associations?**
- HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) in Han Chinese, Thai, Malay and some Indian populations — US FDA advises screening before starting carbamazepine in at-risk ancestry
- HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol; HLA-A*31:01 with carbamazepine DRESS/SJS in Europeans and Japanese; HLA-B*13:01 with dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome

**Q4. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Drug (or metabolite) presented by specific HLA → activates drug-specific cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and NK cells (p-i concept, altered peptide repertoire)
- Keratinocyte apoptosis/necroptosis by granulysin (key mediator; levels correlate with severity), perforin–granzyme B, Fas–FasL, TNF-α, annexin A1
- Massive keratinocyte death → full-thickness epidermal necrosis and subepidermal split

**Q5. Clinical features.**
- Prodrome 1–3 days: fever, sore throat, conjunctivitis, malaise, painful skin (cutaneous pain is an early warning)
- Rash starts on face and upper trunk → spreads; dusky erythematous/purpuric macules and flat atypical targets that coalesce, flaccid blisters, sheets of detached skin ('wet cigarette paper')
- Nikolsky sign and Asboe-Hansen sign positive on erythematous skin
- Mucosa (>90%): haemorrhagic crusting of lips, oral erosions, purulent conjunctivitis/pseudomembranes, genital erosions; also respiratory and GI epithelium

**Q6. Write a short note on Nikolsky sign (PYQ).**
- Shearing pressure on apparently normal/ perilesional skin causes separation of the epidermis
- Positive in pemphigus (intraepidermal acantholysis), SSSS, TEN (on erythematous skin), also EB, bullous impetigo; negative in bullous pemphigoid
- Variants: Nikolsky I (marginal — at blister edge), Nikolsky II (on normal skin away), Asboe-Hansen (bulla spread), pseudo-Nikolsky (TEN — on erythematous skin only)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- EM major (typical/raised targets, acral, HSV, less mucosal and no extensive detachment)
- SSSS (children, superficial split, no mucosa, sterile blister, tender erythema, flexural accentuation)
- GBFDE, AGEP (pustules), DRESS, linear IgA bullous dermatosis (drug — vancomycin), paraneoplastic pemphigus, bullous lupus/TEN-like lupus, GVHD grade IV, toxic shock syndrome, phototoxic reaction, burns, Kawasaki disease, MIRM

**Q8. How do you identify the culprit drug?**
- Detailed drug chart with exact start dates; ALDEN algorithm (Algorithm of Drug causality for Epidermal Necrolysis — time delay, drug presence, prechallenge/rechallenge, dechallenge, drug notoriety, other causes; score ≥6 very probable)
- In vitro tests (lymphocyte transformation test, ELISpot granulysin) — research; rechallenge contraindicated; patch test low sensitivity

**Q9. Investigations.**
- Skin biopsy (frozen section for rapid diagnosis): full-thickness epidermal necrosis, subepidermal split, sparse dermal infiltrate; DIF negative (excludes autoimmune bullous)
- CBC, renal function, electrolytes, bicarbonate, glucose, LFT, albumin, CRP, blood/skin/urine cultures, chest X-ray, ABG
- Mycoplasma serology/PCR in children; HLA testing if relevant

**Q10. What is SCORTEN? (prognostic score)**
- Calculated within 24 h of admission and at day 3; one point each: age ≥40 years; associated malignancy; heart rate ≥120/min; epidermal detachment >10% BSA on day 1; serum urea >10 mmol/L (≈28 mg/dL BUN); serum glucose >14 mmol/L (252 mg/dL); serum bicarbonate <20 mmol/L
- Predicted mortality: 0–1: ~3%; 2: ~12%; 3: ~35%; 4: ~58%; ≥5: >90%

**Q11. Supportive management (the backbone).**
- Immediately stop the culprit (and all non-essential drugs) — earlier withdrawal improves survival
- Admit to burns unit/ICU if SCORTEN ≥3 or >10% detachment; barrier nursing, warm room (30–32 °C), air-fluidised bed
- Fluids: lower than burns (≈ 2 ml/kg/%BSA + maintenance), guided by urine output 0.5–1 ml/kg/h; electrolytes; nutrition by nasogastric tube (high-protein, early)
- Skin care: leave blisters in place (biological dressing), non-adherent dressings (paraffin gauze, silicone, Mepitel), avoid adhesive tapes, silver dressings; no prophylactic systemic antibiotics — cultures and treat sepsis
- Eyes: daily ophthalmology review, lubricants, topical steroid/antibiotic drops, lysis of synechiae, amniotic membrane transplantation for severe ocular disease
- Mouth: oral rinses, white soft paraffin to lips; genital care (prevent synechiae — vaginal moulds); analgesia; DVT prophylaxis; stress ulcer prophylaxis; respiratory monitoring

**Q12. Specific (immunomodulatory) therapy.**
- Cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day for 7–10 days then taper — preferred first-line in our protocol and many Indian/European centres (inhibits CD8 T cell activation; studies show reduced mortality vs predicted SCORTEN)
- Systemic corticosteroids: early short pulse (e.g. dexamethasone/methylprednisolone) — controversial; many Indian centres use within the first 72 h
- Etanercept (TNF-α blocker) 25–50 mg SC single/two doses — RCT showed faster healing and lower mortality vs steroids
- IVIG (2–3 g/kg over 3–4 days) — conflicting evidence; combinations (steroid + IVIG) used
- Plasmapheresis, N-acetylcysteine (adjunct) — limited data
- Thalidomide is contraindicated (increased mortality in RCT)

**Q13. What are the acute and long-term complications?**
- Acute: sepsis (commonest cause of death — S. aureus, Pseudomonas), fluid/electrolyte imbalance, hypothermia, acute kidney injury, hypoalbuminaemia, ARDS/bronchial sloughing, GI bleeding, hepatitis, DVT/pulmonary embolism, ileus
- Long-term (in ~50%): eyes — dry eye, symblepharon, trichiasis, entropion, corneal scarring, blindness; skin — dyspigmentation, scarring, eruptive naevi, nail loss, hypohidrosis; mucosal — oral, oesophageal, urethral, vaginal strictures; lungs — bronchiolitis obliterans; psychological (PTSD)

**Q14. How do you prevent recurrence and educate?**
- Give a drug-allergy card/medical alert bracelet listing culprit and structurally related drugs (e.g. aromatic antiepileptics cross-react: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine — use levetiracetam/valproate)
- Report to pharmacovigilance (PvPI — ADR monitoring centre in India)
- HLA screening before high-risk drugs in at-risk groups; first-degree relatives may share HLA risk
- Start allopurinol at low dose, avoid unnecessary use (asymptomatic hyperuricaemia)

**Q15. How do you classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions?**
- Immediate (type I, IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Delayed T-cell (type IV): IVa — eczematous (Th1), IVb — DRESS/maculopapular with eosinophils (Th2), IVc — SJS/TEN, FDE (cytotoxic T cells), IVd — AGEP (neutrophil, IL-8)
- Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs): SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP, GBFDE

**Q16. Compare DRESS with SJS/TEN briefly.**
- DRESS: latency 2–8 weeks, morbilliform rash with facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia/atypical lymphocytes, internal organ involvement (liver commonest), HHV-6 reactivation; RegiSCAR score; systemic steroids mainstay with slow taper
- SJS/TEN: latency 4–28 days, epidermal necrosis and mucositis, cytotoxic T cell mediated, SCORTEN for prognosis

**Q17. Prognosis.**
- Mortality: SJS ~1–5%, overlap ~10–15%, TEN 25–35% (higher in elderly, extensive disease, delayed drug withdrawal)
- Re-epithelialisation usually in 2–3 weeks; mucosal and ocular sequelae may be lifelong

**Q18. What is the latency period and why is it important?**
- Usually 4–28 days after starting a new drug (first exposure); rechallenge can cause reaction within 48 h; drugs started >8 weeks earlier or used safely for years are unlikely culprits (except dose change) — key in ALDEN

**Q19. Describe the eye care protocol in SJS/TEN.**
- Daily ophthalmology review from admission: preservative-free lubricants hourly, topical steroid drops (prednisolone acetate) and antibiotic drops, glass-rod sweeping/lysis of conjunctival adhesions, scleral shells/ symblepharon rings
- Amniotic membrane transplantation within first week for significant ocular surface sloughing — reduces chronic sequelae; long-term follow-up for dry eye, trichiasis, limbal stem cell deficiency

**Q20. What are the oral, genital and respiratory care measures?**
- Mouth: warm saline/ antiseptic (chlorhexidine) mouthwashes, anaesthetic gels/ benzydamine, steroid mouthwash, white soft paraffin to lips; soft or nasogastric feeds
- Genital: daily examination, potent topical steroid ointment, non-adherent dressings, vaginal dilators/ moulds to prevent synechiae; urinary catheter if needed
- Respiratory: monitor oxygen saturation, chest X-ray, early intubation if bronchial involvement (poor prognosis)

**Q21. What fluid regimen is used?**
- Less than burns because dermis is intact: about 2 ml/kg/% BSA detached in first 24 h (plus maintenance) or titrated to urine output 0.5–1 ml/kg/h; prefer crystalloids, add albumin if low; avoid fluid overload; peripheral lines through unaffected skin

**Q22. Why are prophylactic antibiotics not given?**
- They select resistant organisms and increase drug-reaction risk; instead take skin/ blood/ urine/ catheter-tip cultures every 48 h and treat promptly when sepsis signs appear (fever may be absent — watch for hypothermia, falling BP, confusion, rising glucose, falling urine output)

**Q23. Discuss the cyclosporine regimen and evidence.**
- 3–5 mg/kg/day orally in two divided doses for 7–10 days then taper over a month — inhibits T-cell activation and granulysin release; multiple cohort studies and meta-analyses show lower mortality than predicted by SCORTEN; first-line in our protocol; monitor BP, renal function, electrolytes

**Q24. What is the role of systemic corticosteroids?**
- Controversial: early short high-dose pulses (dexamethasone 1.5 mg/kg/day for 3 days or methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 3 days) may halt progression when given within 72 h; prolonged steroids increase sepsis and mortality; commonly combined with IVIG or cyclosporine in Indian practice

**Q25. What are the HLA screening recommendations?**
- HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine/ oxcarbazepine in patients of Han Chinese, Thai, Malaysian, Indonesian and some Indian ancestry; HLA-B*58:01 before allopurinol in Han Chinese, Korean, Thai, and those with CKD; HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir (hypersensitivity syndrome)

**Q26. Which drugs cause SJS/TEN in HIV patients?**
- Nevirapine (first 6–8 weeks), cotrimoxazole (prophylaxis), anti-TB drugs, fluconazole; HIV increases SJS/TEN risk up to 1000-fold; manage carefully when restarting ART (avoid nevirapine permanently)

**Q27. Paediatric SJS/TEN — causes and differences.**
- Drugs: sulphonamides, antiepileptics (phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, lamotrigine), paracetamol (debated), NSAIDs; infections — Mycoplasma (MIRM), HSV; lower mortality than adults; ocular sequelae equally serious

**Q28. Discuss SJS/TEN in pregnancy.**
- Risk to mother and fetus (preterm birth); supportive care in burns/ICU; avoid teratogenic immunomodulators; IVIG and steroids preferred; neonatal TEN possible; vaginal synechiae may complicate delivery

**Q29. How do you differentiate SSSS from TEN histologically and clinically?**
- SSSS: children/renal failure, tender erythema starting periorificially and flexures, superficial peeling, no mucosal involvement, Nikolsky positive on normal skin; split at granular layer (frozen section of peeled skin — only stratum corneum and granular layer); antibiotics
- TEN: drug history, mucosa involved, full-thickness epidermal necrosis on frozen section, deeper detachment; stop drug, burns-unit care

**Q30. What is the pharmacovigilance pathway in India?**
- Report the ADR to the nearest ADR Monitoring Centre under Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI, Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission) via suspected ADR reporting form/ ADR PvPI app or toll-free helpline; causality (WHO-UMC/Naranjo) documented

## Quick spotter facts
- Painful skin + purpuric flat targets + ≥2 mucosae after carbamazepine — SJS/TEN
- SCORTEN 7 points (age ≥40, cancer, HR ≥120, BSA >10%, urea >10, glucose >14, bicarbonate <20)
- HLA-B*15:02 — carbamazepine

## Note
Cyclosporine first-line follows our department decision; steroid use varies between centres.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (SJS/TEN); SCORTEN; ALDEN; Indian SJS-TEN consensus. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Striae distensae — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Striae distensae** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What are striae distensae?**
- Linear dermal scars with epidermal atrophy due to stretching and changes in dermal connective tissue (stretch marks)
- Early: striae rubrae (red/purple, raised, inflamed); late: striae albae (white, atrophic, wrinkled, depressed)

**Q2. Causes.**
- Physiological: puberty (adolescent growth spurt — thighs, buttocks, breasts, lower back), pregnancy (striae gravidarum — up to 90%, abdomen, breasts, thighs; PYQ in physiological changes of pregnancy), weight gain/obesity, body-building
- Pathological: Cushing's syndrome (wide >1 cm, purple, also on unusual sites), prolonged topical or systemic corticosteroids (especially potent steroids under occlusion in flexures — groin, axilla, inner thighs), Marfan syndrome, Ehlers–Danlos, anorexia nervosa recovery, chronic liver disease, HIV (protease inhibitors), diabetes

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Mechanical stretch + hormonal influence (glucocorticoids, oestrogen, relaxin) → fibroblast dysfunction, fragmentation and loss of elastic fibres and fibrillin, reduced collagen synthesis → rupture of dermal connective tissue
- Genetic predisposition (family history, fibrillin/elastin/collagen gene variants)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Early: dermal oedema, perivascular lymphocytes, elastolysis
- Late: thinned epidermis with flattened rete ridges, thin straight collagen bundles parallel to skin surface (like a scar), reduced and curled elastic fibres, loss of adnexa

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Linear focal elastosis (yellow palpable striae on lower back of elderly men), anetoderma, atrophic scars, linear atrophoderma of Moulin, linear morphoea
- Cushing's striae vs physiological: wide, deep purple, beyond usual sites (shoulders, axillae), with other Cushingoid features — screen with cortisol tests

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Prevention: no strong evidence; massage with emollients (centella asiatica, hyaluronic acid) may help in pregnancy
- Striae rubrae respond better: topical tretinoin 0.05–0.1% (not in pregnancy/lactation), hyaluronic acid, pulsed-dye laser 585/595 nm, IPL
- Striae albae: microneedling (± PRP), fractional non-ablative (1550 nm) or ablative (CO2, Er:YAG) lasers, radiofrequency, microdermabrasion, excimer laser (repigmentation), chemical peels (glycolic/TCA)
- Counsel: improvement (not complete removal) is the realistic goal; treat cause (stop steroids, Cushing's)

**Q7. How do striae of Cushing's syndrome differ?**
- Wide (>1 cm), deep purple-red, depressed, on abdomen, flanks, thighs, axillae, breasts; associated central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, thin skin, bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia — confirm with overnight dexamethasone suppression test, 24-h urinary cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol

**Q8. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Rubrae: pink-red streaks with linear/dotted vessels; Albae: white, atrophic linear bands with absent pigment network and skin markings parallel to the long axis

**Q9. Topical steroid-induced striae — prevention.**
- Avoid potent steroids on flexures, face, groin, and under occlusion; limit duration; use fingertip units; prefer calcineurin inhibitors on thin skin; striae once formed are permanent

**Q10. What are the risk factors for striae gravidarum?**
- Young maternal age, family history, high pre-pregnancy BMI and weight gain, large baby/ macrosomia, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy, lighter skin type; appear in second half of pregnancy on abdomen, breasts, hips, thighs

**Q11. What is the role of topical tretinoin and its limitations?**
- Tretinoin 0.05–0.1% nightly improves early striae rubrae (stimulates collagen synthesis, fibroblast activity); contraindicated in pregnancy and avoided during breastfeeding; little effect on mature striae albae

**Q12. Explain fractional lasers in striae.**
- Fractional photothermolysis creates microscopic thermal zones → neocollagenesis and remodelling; non-ablative 1550 nm (fewer side effects) and ablative CO2/Er:YAG (better efficacy, more PIH in dark skin); 3–6 sessions; combine with PRP/ radiofrequency

**Q13. Striae in adolescents — counselling.**
- Very common during growth spurts (boys — lumbosacral, thighs; girls — breasts, thighs, buttocks); harmless, fade to white with time; rule out steroid misuse (gym supplements, topical creams) and Cushing's if severe/ atypical

**Q14. Linear focal elastosis — what is it?**
- Elastotic striae: palpable yellow linear bands on lower back of elderly men — increased, fragmented elastic fibres in dermis (differs from striae with reduced elastin); considered a keloidal repair of striae

**Q15. Striae in Marfan syndrome — significance.**
- Striae in unusual sites (shoulders, lower back) without weight change is a minor criterion in Marfan syndrome (FBN1); look for tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic root dilatation

## Quick spotter facts
- Wide purple striae on unusual sites — think Cushing's/steroids
- Striae rubrae respond better than striae albae

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermal disorders; physiological skin changes in pregnancy). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Systemic lupus erythematosus** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Define SLE.**
- Chronic multisystem autoimmune disease with autoantibodies (especially to nuclear antigens) and immune-complex–mediated tissue injury of skin, joints, kidneys, serosa, blood, CNS; women of child-bearing age (F:M ~9:1)

**Q2. Pathogenesis.**
- Genetic (HLA-DR2/DR3, complement C1q/C2/C4 deficiency, TREX1, IRF5, STAT4) + environmental triggers (UV, drugs, EBV, oestrogen, smoking) → impaired clearance of apoptotic cells → exposure of nuclear antigens → loss of tolerance → autoantibodies → immune complexes deposit → complement activation and inflammation
- Type I interferon signature (plasmacytoid DCs) — basis for anifrolumab; B-cell hyperactivity (BAFF/BLyS — belimumab)

**Q3. Discuss the latest classification of SLE (PYQ).**
- 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria: entry criterion ANA ≥1:80 on HEp-2 cells (ever); then additive weighted criteria in 7 clinical and 3 immunological domains; classify as SLE with ≥10 points and ≥1 clinical criterion (each counted only highest in a domain)
- Clinical: constitutional (fever 2); haematological (leucopenia 3, thrombocytopenia 4, autoimmune haemolysis 4); neuropsychiatric (delirium 2, psychosis 3, seizure 5); mucocutaneous (non-scarring alopecia 2, oral ulcers 2, subacute cutaneous or discoid lupus 4, acute cutaneous lupus 6); serosal (effusion 5, acute pericarditis 6); musculoskeletal (joint involvement 6); renal (proteinuria >0.5 g/24 h 4, class II/V nephritis 8, class III/IV nephritis 10)
- Immunological: antiphospholipid antibodies 2; complement — low C3 or C4 3, low C3 and C4 4; SLE-specific antibodies — anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith 6
- Earlier: 1997 ACR (4 of 11) and 2012 SLICC (4 of 17 with ≥1 clinical and ≥1 immunological, or biopsy-proven lupus nephritis with ANA/anti-dsDNA)

**Q4. Describe the cutaneous manifestations of lupus (Gilliam classification — PYQ).**
- LE-specific: acute cutaneous LE (ACLE — malar 'butterfly' rash sparing nasolabial folds, generalised photosensitive eruption, TEN-like ACLE), subacute cutaneous LE (SCLE — annular/papulosquamous, anti-Ro, drug-induced), chronic cutaneous LE (CCLE — DLE, lupus profundus/panniculitis, chilblain lupus, lupus tumidus, hypertrophic/verrucous DLE, mucosal DLE, LP–LE overlap)
- LE-non-specific: vascular — Raynaud's, livedo reticularis, vasculitis (urticarial, leukocytoclastic), periungual telangiectasia, thrombophlebitis, Degos-like lesions; non-scarring alopecia (lupus hair — frontal broken hairs), oral ulcers (painless palatal), bullous SLE, calcinosis, rheumatoid nodules, sclerodactyly, erythema multiforme-like (Rowell's)
- Risk of SLE: ACLE ~100% association, SCLE ~50% meet criteria (mild), DLE ~5–10% (higher if widespread)

**Q5. Discuss the systemic manifestations (renal and cardiac — PYQ).**
- Constitutional: fever, fatigue, weight loss
- Musculoskeletal: non-erosive polyarthritis (Jaccoud's arthropathy — reducible deformities), avascular necrosis (steroids), myositis
- Renal (lupus nephritis, 40–60%) — ISN/RPS classes: I minimal mesangial, II mesangial proliferative, III focal (<50% glomeruli), IV diffuse (≥50% — most common and severe; 'wire loop' lesions), V membranous, VI advanced sclerosing; monitor urine protein, sediment, creatinine; biopsy if proteinuria >0.5 g/day
- Cardiac: pericarditis (commonest), myocarditis, Libman–Sacks (non-infective verrucous) endocarditis on mitral valve, premature atherosclerosis/CAD; congenital heart block in neonatal lupus (anti-Ro)
- Lungs: pleuritis/effusion, pneumonitis, alveolar haemorrhage, shrinking lung, pulmonary hypertension
- Haematological: anaemia (chronic disease, AIHA), leucopenia/lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, APS
- Neuropsychiatric: seizures, psychosis, cognitive dysfunction, stroke, neuropathy
- GI: serositis, mesenteric vasculitis, hepatitis; eyes: retinal vasculitis (cytoid bodies), sicca

**Q6. Describe the various immunological tests (PYQ).**
- ANA by IIF on HEp-2 — most sensitive (>95%) screening; patterns: homogeneous (dsDNA, histone), speckled (Sm, RNP, Ro, La), nucleolar (scleroderma), centromere (limited SSc), rim/peripheral (dsDNA)
- Anti-dsDNA — specific (~95%); titre correlates with nephritis/activity
- Anti-Sm — most specific (~99%), low sensitivity
- Anti-histone — drug-induced lupus (>95%)
- Anti-Ro (SS-A)/La (SS-B) — SCLE, neonatal lupus, Sjögren's, ANA-negative lupus
- Anti-U1 RNP — MCTD
- Antiphospholipid: anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant
- Complements C3, C4 (low in active disease), CH50; anti-C1q (nephritis); Coombs test; ESR high with normal CRP (unless infection/serositis)

**Q7. Write a short note on the LE cell phenomenon (PYQ).**
- Neutrophil that has phagocytosed the denatured nuclear material (homogeneous haematoxylin body) of another cell opsonised by antinuclear (anti-histone/DNA) antibodies — described by Hargraves (1948)
- Positive in ~70–80% of SLE but also in drug-induced lupus, RA, hepatitis; now replaced by ANA/anti-dsDNA testing

**Q8. Write a short note on the lupus band test (PYQ).**
- DIF showing continuous granular band of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, ± IgA) and complement (C3) along the dermo-epidermal junction
- Lesional skin: positive in DLE (~70–90%) and SLE lesions
- Non-lesional skin: sun-protected (buttock/inner arm) positive in ~50% SLE (associated with nephritis and active disease); sun-exposed non-lesional positive in ~70–80% SLE
- False positives: rosacea, PMLE, normal sun-exposed skin (usually only IgM)

**Q9. What is the antiphospholipid syndrome? (lupus anticoagulant — PYQ)**
- Arterial/venous thrombosis and/or pregnancy morbidity (recurrent miscarriage <10 weeks, fetal death >10 weeks, pre-eclampsia/placental insufficiency) with persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies (12 weeks apart)
- Lupus anticoagulant: paradoxically prolongs phospholipid-dependent clotting tests in vitro (aPTT, dilute Russell viper venom time) not corrected by mixing with normal plasma but corrected by adding excess phospholipid — but causes thrombosis in vivo
- Skin: livedo reticularis/racemosa, ulcers, necrosis, splinter haemorrhages, Degos-like lesions, anetoderma, catastrophic APS
- Treatment: warfarin (INR 2–3) for thrombosis; aspirin + LMWH in pregnancy

**Q10. How do you assess disease activity?**
- SLEDAI-2K, BILAG, ECLAM; CLASI for skin (activity and damage); SLICC/ACR damage index

**Q11. Management of SLE.**
- All: photoprotection, hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg/day (≤5 mg/kg real body weight) for every patient unless contraindicated — reduces flares, damage, thrombosis; annual eye screening after 5 years (baseline)
- Mild (skin, joints): HCQ, NSAIDs, low-dose prednisolone, topical steroids/tacrolimus
- Moderate: prednisolone ≤7.5 mg/day long-term target, methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate
- Severe organ (nephritis class III/IV, CNS): IV methylprednisolone pulses, mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus), belimumab add-on, voclosporin, obinutuzumab
- Biologics: belimumab (anti-BLyS), anifrolumab (type I IFN receptor antibody — also good for skin), rituximab (off-label)
- Manage comorbidities: cardiovascular risk, bone health, infections (vaccines), APS anticoagulation, pregnancy planning (disease quiet ≥6 months; continue HCQ, aspirin)

**Q12. What is drug-induced lupus?**
- Classic: procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, minocycline, quinidine, methyldopa, TNF inhibitors, chlorpromazine; slow acetylators
- Features: arthralgia, serositis, fever; renal/CNS/skin rare; anti-histone antibodies; anti-dsDNA usually negative (except anti-TNF); resolves on withdrawal
- Drug-induced SCLE: terbinafine, hydrochlorothiazide, calcium channel blockers, PPIs, ACE inhibitors, taxanes, griseofulvin, anti-TNF — anti-Ro positive

**Q13. What is neonatal lupus?**
- Transplacental maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies → annular erythematous lesions (periorbital 'raccoon eyes'), photosensitive, resolves by 6 months; congenital heart block (permanent — needs pacing), hepatobiliary disease, cytopenias
- Mother may be asymptomatic; future pregnancies risk ~15–20%; HCQ during pregnancy reduces heart block risk

**Q14. Write a note on mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD — PYQ).**
- Overlap of SLE, SSc, polymyositis/DM features with high titre anti-U1 RNP antibodies
- Raynaud's (nearly all), puffy/swollen hands (sausage fingers), sclerodactyly, arthritis, myositis, oesophageal dysmotility, pulmonary hypertension (main cause of death); renal and CNS disease uncommon
- Treatment according to organ involvement; steroids responsive features (myositis, serositis)

**Q15. Describe acute cutaneous lupus (ACLE) in detail.**
- Localised: malar 'butterfly' rash — symmetrical erythema/oedema across cheeks and nasal bridge, sparing nasolabial folds and eyelids, photosensitive, heals without scarring
- Generalised: photosensitive morbilliform eruption, erythema on dorsa of hands between knuckles (spares joints), periungual erythema
- TEN-like ACLE: widespread epidermal necrosis in active SLE (rare)

**Q16. What is SCLE and its features?**
- Subacute cutaneous LE: photosensitive non-scarring annular-polycyclic or papulosquamous (psoriasiform) plaques on upper trunk, V of neck, extensor arms (face often spared); ~50% meet SLE criteria (mild, often musculoskeletal); anti-Ro/SSA in 70–90%; HLA-DR3
- Drug-induced SCLE — terbinafine, thiazides, CCBs, PPIs, ACE inhibitors, TNF inhibitors, taxanes, leflunomide, griseofulvin, checkpoint inhibitors

**Q17. Describe lupus panniculitis and chilblain lupus.**
- Lupus profundus/panniculitis: firm deep nodules on face, upper arms, buttocks, breasts healing with lipoatrophy; lobular lymphocytic panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis; DLE above in ~1/3; differentiate from subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma
- Chilblain lupus: tender purple papules/plaques on fingers, toes, nose, ears in cold damp weather; familial form TREX1/SAMHD1 (type I interferonopathy)

**Q18. What is lupus tumidus?**
- Highly photosensitive, smooth, red, urticarial/ succulent plaques without scale or follicular plugging on face/upper trunk, heal without scarring; dermal mucin and perivascular lymphocytes without interface change; rarely systemic; strong response to antimalarials and sun protection

**Q19. How is SLE skin involvement scored?**
- CLASI (Cutaneous LE Disease Area and Severity Index): activity (erythema, scale/hypertrophy, mucous membrane lesions, recent hair loss, non-scarring alopecia) and damage (dyspigmentation, scarring/atrophy, scarring alopecia) by anatomical areas

**Q20. What are the haematological and immunological criteria pitfalls?**
- Lymphopenia/ leucopenia common (not due to drugs), Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia, ITP (may precede SLE by years — check ANA in young ITP); low C3/C4 with active nephritis; anti-dsDNA rises before flares; high ESR with normal CRP — CRP rise suggests infection or serositis

**Q21. Discuss neuropsychiatric lupus.**
- 19 ACR syndromes: headache, seizures, cognitive dysfunction, mood/anxiety, psychosis, cerebrovascular disease (APS), aseptic meningitis, myelopathy, demyelination, chorea, neuropathies
- Mechanisms: vasculopathy, APS thrombosis, autoantibodies (anti-NMDA, anti-ribosomal P — psychosis), cytokines; MRI, CSF, EEG; treat with steroids + cyclophosphamide/rituximab (inflammatory) or anticoagulation (thrombotic)

**Q22. How do you manage lupus nephritis briefly?**
- Biopsy-guided: class III/IV ± V — induction with IV methylprednisolone pulses then oral prednisolone + mycophenolate (2–3 g/day) or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus 500 mg every 2 weeks × 6), add belimumab or voclosporin/obinutuzumab; maintenance MMF or azathioprine ≥3–5 years; HCQ, ACE inhibitor/ARB, BP and lipid control; class V — MMF/calcineurin inhibitor + antiproteinuric
- Targets: proteinuria <0.5–0.7 g/day by 12 months

**Q23. What is the role of hydroxychloroquine — mechanism and dose?**
- Raises lysosomal pH in antigen-presenting cells, inhibits TLR7/9 signalling and type I IFN, reduces antigen presentation; antithrombotic, lipid-lowering, glucose-lowering
- Dose ≤5 mg/kg real body weight/day (usually 200–400 mg); side effects — retinopathy (screen), GI upset, skin pigmentation (blue-grey shins/palate), rash (DRESS rarely), cardiomyopathy and QT prolongation (rare), haemolysis in G6PD (rare), psoriasis flare; safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding

**Q24. Anifrolumab — what is it?**
- Human monoclonal antibody against type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1); 300 mg IV every 4 weeks for moderate–severe SLE on standard therapy — particularly good for skin (CLASI) and joints; herpes zoster and respiratory infections more frequent

**Q25. Pregnancy in SLE — counselling points.**
- Plan when disease is quiescent ≥6 months on pregnancy-compatible drugs (HCQ, azathioprine, low-dose prednisolone, tacrolimus); stop MMF, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide ≥3 months earlier
- Risks: flares, pre-eclampsia, fetal loss, preterm birth, neonatal lupus/congenital heart block (anti-Ro — fetal echocardiography weeks 16–26), APS complications; low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks, LMWH if APS

**Q26. What is the Sjögren's syndrome overlap and its skin features?**
- Secondary Sjögren's in ~15–20% of SLE; sicca (dry eyes/mouth), parotid enlargement, anti-Ro/La; skin — xerosis, annular erythema (Asian), purpura (hypergammaglobulinaemic, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis), Raynaud's; risk of lymphoma (MALT)

**Q27. Differentiate the malar rash of SLE from other causes.**
- SLE: spares nasolabial folds, photosensitive, non-scaly, transient with flares
- Rosacea (papules, pustules, flushing, involves nasolabial folds), seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy scale in nasolabial folds), DM (heliotrope, involves nasolabial folds, violaceous), contact/photo-dermatitis, erysipelas (unilateral, fever), pellagra, tinea faciei, PMLE

**Q28. What is SLE-associated alopecia?**
- Non-scarring: diffuse telogen effluvium during flares, 'lupus hair' (frontal short broken hairs), alopecia areata-like; scarring alopecia from DLE plaques — permanent; early treatment of scalp DLE prevents scarring

**Q29. Mention mucosal lesions of lupus.**
- Painless palatal ulcers/erythema (hard palate — a classification criterion), buccal DLE-like white radiating lesions, lip DLE, nasal septal ulceration/perforation, conjunctival lesions

**Q30. Prognosis and causes of death in SLE.**
- 10-year survival >90% now; bimodal mortality — early from active disease (nephritis, CNS) and infections, late from cardiovascular disease (accelerated atherosclerosis) and treatment complications; poor prognosis: nephritis, young male, low socioeconomic status, African/Asian ancestry, APS

## Quick spotter facts
- Malar rash sparing nasolabial folds — ACLE
- 2019 EULAR/ACR: ANA ≥1:80 entry + ≥10 points
- Anti-Sm most specific; anti-dsDNA tracks nephritis; anti-histone — drug lupus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Lupus erythematosus); 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE classification criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) — viva
posts.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Classify scleroderma (PYQ).**
- Localised scleroderma (morphoea) — skin ± underlying tissue, no internal organ disease: plaque, generalised, linear (including en coup de sabre and Parry–Romberg), deep, pansclerotic, mixed
- Systemic sclerosis (SSc): limited cutaneous (lcSSc — skin thickening distal to elbows/knees ± face; includes CREST), diffuse cutaneous (dcSSc — proximal limbs and trunk), SSc sine scleroderma (internal disease + antibodies without skin thickening), overlap syndromes
- Scleroderma-like disorders: scleredema, scleromyxoedema, nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, eosinophilic fasciitis, chronic GVHD, porphyria cutanea tarda, phenylketonuria, drug/toxin-induced (bleomycin, taxanes, vinyl chloride, silica, toxic oil, L-tryptophan)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis.**
- Triad: vasculopathy (endothelial injury → intimal proliferation, obliteration, Raynaud's, ischaemia) + immune activation (autoantibodies, T/B cells, IL-6, type I IFN) + fibrosis (TGF-β, PDGF, CTGF → myofibroblasts producing excess collagen in skin and organs)

**Q3. Describe skin features.**
- Raynaud's phenomenon (first symptom in >90%)
- Oedematous (puffy fingers) → indurated → atrophic phases
- Sclerodactyly (tapered, tight, shiny fingers with flexion contractures), digital pitting scars, ulcers on fingertips and knuckles, resorption of terminal phalanges (acro-osteolysis)
- Face: mask-like expressionless face, beaked nose, microstomia with radial perioral furrowing (purse-string mouth), loss of wrinkles
- Salt-and-pepper pigmentation (perifollicular retention with depigmentation), telangiectasias (matted), calcinosis cutis, nailfold capillary changes, pruritus (early)

**Q4. Write a short note on Raynaud's phenomenon (PYQ).**
- Episodic vasospasm of digital arteries on exposure to cold/stress — triphasic colour change: white (ischaemia/pallor) → blue (cyanosis) → red (reactive hyperaemia), with pain/numbness
