- Primary (Raynaud's disease — young women, symmetrical, no ulcers, normal nailfold capillaries, ANA negative) vs secondary (SSc, SLE, MCTD, DM, Sjögren's, cryoglobulinaemia, vibration tools, thoracic outlet, drugs — β-blockers, ergots)
- Treatment: keep warm, gloves, stop smoking; calcium channel blockers (nifedipine SR, amlodipine) first line; losartan, fluoxetine, topical nitrates, PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil), IV iloprost, bosentan (prevents new digital ulcers), botulinum toxin, sympathectomy

**Q5. Write a short note on CREST syndrome (PYQ).**
- Limited cutaneous SSc variant: Calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia (mat-like on face, hands)
- Anti-centromere antibodies (~50–90%); slower course; late complications — pulmonary arterial hypertension, primary biliary cholangitis

**Q6. Write a short note on calcinosis cutis (PYQ).**
- Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in skin
- Types: dystrophic (normal calcium/phosphate; damaged tissue — SSc, DM, lupus, tumours, trauma), metastatic (high Ca × P product — CKD, hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D, milk-alkali), idiopathic (scrotal calcinosis, subepidermal calcified nodule, tumoral calcinosis), iatrogenic (calcium gluconate extravasation, EEG paste), calciphylaxis (vascular calcification in CKD — painful necrosis, high mortality)
- Treatment: treat cause; diltiazem, bisphosphonates, warfarin (low dose), probenecid, colchicine (inflammation), sodium thiosulphate, excision, CO2 laser, lithotripsy

**Q7. What are the systemic features?**
- GI (90%): oesophageal dysmotility (dysphagia, reflux, Barrett's), watermelon stomach (GAVE), small bowel bacterial overgrowth, pseudo-obstruction, wide-mouthed colonic diverticula, faecal incontinence
- Lungs: interstitial lung disease (leading cause of death — dcSSc, anti-Scl-70), pulmonary arterial hypertension (lcSSc, anti-centromere)
- Kidney: scleroderma renal crisis — sudden hypertension, AKI, microangiopathic haemolysis (dcSSc, anti-RNA polymerase III, high-dose steroids >15 mg/day) — ACE inhibitors are life-saving
- Heart: myocardial fibrosis, arrhythmias, pericarditis
- Musculoskeletal: tendon friction rubs (dcSSc — poor prognosis), arthralgia, myopathy; also sicca, hypothyroidism, erectile dysfunction

**Q8. Antibodies and their associations.**
- Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70): dcSSc, ILD
- Anti-centromere: lcSSc/CREST, PAH, digital loss
- Anti-RNA polymerase III: rapid diffuse skin, renal crisis, cancer association (synchronous)
- Anti-U3 RNP (fibrillarin): PAH, myositis, young men of African descent
- Anti-PM/Scl: overlap with myositis; anti-Th/To: lcSSc with ILD/PAH

**Q9. Give the 2013 ACR/EULAR classification criteria.**
- Skin thickening of fingers of both hands extending proximal to MCP joints — sufficient alone (9 points)
- Otherwise add: skin thickening of fingers — puffy fingers 2 or sclerodactyly distal to MCP 4 (higher counted); fingertip lesions — digital ulcers 2 or pitting scars 3; telangiectasia 2; abnormal nailfold capillaries 2; PAH and/or ILD 2; Raynaud's 3; SSc-related antibodies (anti-centromere, Scl-70, RNA pol III) 3
- Total ≥9 = definite SSc (excludes scleroderma-like disorders)

**Q10. Investigations in SSc.**
- ANA (nucleolar/centromere/speckled), specific antibodies; nailfold capillaroscopy (giant capillaries, haemorrhages, avascular areas — 'scleroderma pattern': early, active, late)
- HRCT chest, PFT with DLCO, 6-minute walk, echocardiography ± right-heart catheterisation for PAH, NT-proBNP
- Renal function, BP, urine; upper GI endoscopy/manometry; skin score (modified Rodnan skin score, 17 sites 0–3, max 51)

**Q11. Management of SSc (organ-based).**
- Skin: methotrexate, mycophenolate (first choice for dcSSc skin + ILD), cyclophosphamide, rituximab, IVIG, autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplant for rapidly progressive dcSSc; physiotherapy
- Raynaud's/digital ulcers: as above (CCB, PDE5i, iloprost, bosentan)
- ILD: mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R), nintedanib (antifibrotic), rituximab, lung transplant
- PAH: endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan), PDE5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues, riociguat
- Renal crisis: ACE inhibitor (captopril) titrated quickly, dialysis; avoid high-dose steroids
- GI: PPIs, prokinetics, rotating antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth
- Calcinosis and telangiectasia: as above; pulsed-dye laser for telangiectasia

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- 10-year survival ~70%; dcSSc worse; deaths mainly from ILD, PAH, cardiac disease; renal crisis mortality reduced by ACE inhibitors

**Q13. How do you examine a patient with suspected SSc (clinical case approach)?**
- Hands: puffy fingers, sclerodactyly, digital pits/ulcers/gangrene, calcinosis, flexion contractures, nailfold capillaries (hand lens/dermoscope), resorbed tips, tendon friction rubs
- Face: microstomia (measure inter-incisor distance), radial furrows, beaked nose, mat telangiectasia, salt-and-pepper pigmentation, expressionless face
- Skin score: modified Rodnan skin score (17 sites, 0–3); proximal extent decides limited vs diffuse
- Systemic: BP (renal crisis), chest (basal 'velcro' crackles — ILD; loud P2 — PAH), dysphagia, reflux, joint contractures, muscle weakness

**Q14. Describe the modified Rodnan skin score.**
- Skin thickness by palpation (0 normal, 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 severe — cannot pinch) at 17 sites: fingers, hands, forearms, upper arms, thighs, legs, feet (bilateral) + face, anterior chest, abdomen; maximum 51; used to classify and monitor dcSSc (peaks in first 3–5 years then softens)

**Q15. What is nailfold capillaroscopy and its patterns?**
- Non-invasive examination of nailfold capillaries (videocapillaroscopy/ dermoscope with oil)
- Scleroderma pattern (Cutolo): early — few giant capillaries and haemorrhages, preserved density; active — many giant capillaries and haemorrhages, moderate loss; late — severe capillary loss, avascular areas, ramified/bushy capillaries
- Useful to differentiate primary vs secondary Raynaud's and predict progression to SSc

**Q16. What is scleroderma renal crisis — features and treatment?**
- Abrupt onset of severe hypertension (sometimes normotensive), acute kidney injury, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, headache, retinopathy, pulmonary oedema; usually within 4 years of dcSSc; risk — anti-RNA polymerase III, rapidly progressive skin, prednisolone >15 mg/day
- Treatment: ACE inhibitor (captopril titrated quickly) even if creatinine rising, add CCB/ARB for BP, dialysis if needed (renal recovery possible over 2 years); avoid nephrotoxins; monitor BP at home

**Q17. Discuss digital ulcer management.**
- Prevention: stop smoking, keep warm, CCB, PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil), bosentan for recurrent ulcers (prevents new ulcers)
- Active ulcers: IV iloprost (prostacyclin analogue) 3–5 days, PDE5 inhibitors, analgesia, wound care (moist dressings), treat infection (osteomyelitis risk), digital sympathectomy/ botulinum toxin, fat grafting; amputation for gangrene

**Q18. Explain the pathogenesis of oesophageal involvement.**
- Smooth-muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the lower two-thirds of oesophagus with neural damage → hypomotility, incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter → reflux, heartburn, dysphagia, strictures, Barrett's oesophagus, aspiration (worsens ILD); manometry shows absent peristalsis; treat with PPIs, prokinetics, head-end elevation, small meals

**Q19. Interstitial lung disease in SSc — screening and treatment.**
- Commonest cause of SSc-related death; risk — dcSSc, anti-Scl-70, African descent; screen all at diagnosis with HRCT and PFT (FVC, DLCO), then PFT every 6–12 months
- HRCT: NSIP pattern (ground glass with reticulation, basal), UIP less often
- Treatment: mycophenolate (SLS-II), cyclophosphamide (SLS-I), tocilizumab (early progressive), rituximab, nintedanib (antifibrotic — slows FVC decline), lung transplant

**Q20. What is pulmonary arterial hypertension in SSc?**
- Late complication of lcSSc (anti-centromere), progressive dyspnoea, loud P2, right heart failure; screening annually with echo, PFT (DLCO/FVC ratio), NT-proBNP (DETECT algorithm); right heart catheterisation (mPAP >20 mmHg, PVR >2 WU) confirms; treat with ERA + PDE5i combination, prostacyclins, riociguat; poor prognosis

**Q21. What is eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome)?**
- Scleroderma-like disorder: acute symmetrical painful swelling then induration of limbs (sparing hands/face and fingers), peau d'orange, groove sign (venous furrows on elevating limb), after strenuous exercise; peripheral eosinophilia, hypergammaglobulinaemia; no Raynaud's; full-thickness biopsy to fascia/ MRI shows fascial thickening
- Treatment: prednisolone ± methotrexate; associated haematological disorders (aplastic anaemia) occasionally

**Q22. Name other scleroderma mimics and how to differentiate.**
- Scleredema (Buschke) — diabetes/post-streptococcal/ paraprotein; upper back and neck woody induration, no Raynaud's
- Scleromyxoedema — paraproteinaemia (IgG-λ), waxy papules, 'Shar-Pei' sign, doughnut sign on knuckles, systemic (dermato-neuro syndrome); IVIG
- Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis — gadolinium in renal failure, limbs, brawny induration
- Chronic sclerodermoid GVHD, porphyria cutanea tarda (sclerodermoid), POEMS, phenylketonuria, stiff skin syndrome, morphoea

**Q23. What are the newer and future treatments in SSc?**
- Autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for early rapidly progressive dcSSc with poor prognosis (SCOT, ASTIS trials — improved survival, treatment-related mortality risk)
- Rituximab, tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R), abatacept, JAK inhibitors, nintedanib, anti-fibrotic research (lenabasum failed); CAR-T cell therapy (CD19) in refractory SSc — early reports

**Q24. Describe musculoskeletal involvement.**
- Arthralgia, synovitis, tendon friction rubs (leathery creak over tendons — dcSSc, poor prognosis), flexion contractures, acro-osteolysis (resorption of distal phalanges), calcinosis, myopathy/myositis (overlap with anti-PM/Scl, anti-Ku)

**Q25. What is the prognosis by subtype?**
- dcSSc: 10-year survival ~50–70%; early (first 5 years) high risk of renal crisis, ILD, myocardial involvement
- lcSSc: slower course, 10-year survival ~70–90%; late PAH and GI complications

**Q26. Raynaud's phenomenon — primary versus secondary (table).**
- Primary: young women, symmetrical, mild, no ulcers/pitting, normal nailfold capillaries, ANA negative, normal ESR
- Secondary: older onset (>30 y), asymmetric, severe, painful, digital ulcers/gangrene, abnormal capillaroscopy, ANA/SSc antibodies, raised ESR, features of CTD

**Q27. What are the cutaneous signs of SSc on dermoscopy and imaging?**
- Dermoscopy/ capillaroscopy as above; high-frequency ultrasound for skin thickness; plain X-ray hands — calcinosis, acro-osteolysis; thermography for Raynaud's

**Q28. Describe mixed / overlap syndromes involving SSc.**
- SSc–myositis overlap (anti-PM/Scl, anti-Ku), SSc–SLE, SSc–RA, SSc–Sjögren's, MCTD (anti-U1-RNP); management targets the dominant organ involvement

**Q29. Counselling points for an SSc patient.**
- Chronic disease with organ-based screening (yearly echo/PFT), stop smoking, protect hands from cold (gloves, warm clothes), skin care with emollients, physiotherapy/stretching to prevent contractures, oral hygiene/dental care (microstomia), small meals for reflux, home BP monitoring in dcSSc, pregnancy planning when disease stable (avoid in early dcSSc)

**Q30. What drugs/toxins cause scleroderma-like disease?**
- Bleomycin, taxanes (docetaxel), gemcitabine, pentazocine (injection-site fibrosis), vitamin K injections (Texier's disease), appetite suppressants, L-tryptophan (eosinophilia–myalgia syndrome), toxic oil syndrome (rapeseed oil), vinyl chloride, silica (Erasmus syndrome), organic solvents, epoxy resins, checkpoint inhibitors

## Quick spotter facts
- Sclerodactyly + microstomia + salt-and-pepper pigmentation — SSc
- Anti-Scl-70 → ILD; anti-centromere → CREST/PAH; anti-RNA pol III → renal crisis
- Renal crisis — ACE inhibitor

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Scleroderma); 2013 ACR/EULAR SSc classification criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Tattoo & tattoo reactions — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tattoo & tattoo reactions** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Classify tattoos.**
- Decorative/professional (cosmetic — permanent make-up of eyebrows, lips, eyeliner), amateur (Indian 'godna' — traditional), traumatic (asphalt/road-rash, gunpowder, coal miners, pencil lead), medical (radiotherapy marks, nipple-areola reconstruction, micro-pigmentation of scalp/vitiligo camouflage)
- Temporary: henna (natural, brownish-red) and 'black henna' (PPD-added — strong sensitiser)

**Q2. Pigments and colours.**
- Black — carbon (Indian ink), iron oxide, logwood
- Red — mercuric sulphide (cinnabar), cadmium selenide, ferric oxide, organic azo dyes (now most common)
- Yellow — cadmium sulphide; green — chromium oxide; blue — cobalt aluminate; white — titanium dioxide, zinc oxide; brown — ferric oxide; purple — manganese

**Q3. Classify tattoo reactions.**
- Acute: inflammatory (normal healing), infections — bacterial (S. aureus, Pseudomonas, non-tuberculous mycobacteria like M. chelonae from contaminated ink), viral (hepatitis B/C, HIV, HPV warts, molluscum), fungal; leprosy and syphilis historically
- Hypersensitivity: allergic contact dermatitis (red pigment commonest — cinnabar/azo), photo-allergic (yellow — cadmium), lichenoid, granulomatous (sarcoidal — may be first sign of systemic sarcoidosis), pseudolymphomatous
- Koebner phenomenon: psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo, DLE in tattoo
- Neoplastic: keratoacanthoma, SCC, BCC, melanoma (coincidental)
- Others: MRI-related burning/swelling (iron oxide), pigment migration to lymph nodes (mimics metastasis), 'blow-out' (pigment spread into fat), keloid

**Q4. Why is 'black henna' dangerous?**
- Contains paraphenylenediamine (PPD) to darken and speed colour — causes severe allergic contact dermatitis (blisters, hypopigmentation/keloid in the tattoo shape) and lifelong sensitisation to hair dyes, textile dyes, sunscreens (PABA), local anaesthetics (benzocaine), sulphonamides (cross-reacting para-amino compounds)

**Q5. Histopathology of tattoo reactions.**
- Pigment granules in macrophages and extracellularly in dermis; patterns: lichenoid interface, spongiotic, granulomatous (sarcoidal/foreign-body), pseudolymphomatous, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia

**Q6. How do you evaluate a tattoo reaction?**
- History — colour involved, timing, sun exposure, systemic symptoms
- Biopsy; culture for mycobacteria if papulopustules within weeks; patch test (pigment series, PPD); chest X-ray/ACE for sarcoid; HBV/HCV/HIV serology for amateur tattoos

**Q7. Treatment of tattoo reactions.**
- Topical/intralesional steroids, tacrolimus; hydroxychloroquine/allopurinol for granulomatous; systemic therapy for sarcoidosis
- Excision or laser removal for persistent allergy (caution — Q-switched laser can release allergen and trigger systemic reaction)
- Antimicrobials as per culture (NTM — clarithromycin)

**Q8. Methods of tattoo removal.**
- Q-switched lasers (nanosecond) and picosecond lasers — selective photothermolysis/ photoacoustic shattering of pigment, cleared by macrophages; wavelength by colour: black — 1064 nm Nd:YAG/755 nm alexandrite; red — 532 nm KTP; green — 755/694 nm ruby
- Multiple sessions 6–8 weeks apart; the R20 method (repeated passes) and perfluorodecalin patches
- Side effects: hypo/hyperpigmentation, paradoxical darkening of cosmetic tattoos (white/flesh — titanium/iron oxide turns black), scarring, allergic reactions
- Older: excision, dermabrasion, salabrasion, CO2 laser — scar

**Q9. What is paradoxical darkening?**
- Laser reduction of ferric oxide (rust, flesh, white tones) to black ferrous oxide — common with cosmetic lip/eyebrow tattoos; test spot first

**Q10. Infections from tattooing — prevention.**
- Use licensed studios with sterile single-use needles/ ink caps, gloves, hand hygiene, autoclaving; risks — hepatitis B/ C, HIV, NTM (contaminated ink/ dilution water), syphilis, leprosy (historically), warts; check hepatitis B vaccination

**Q11. Granulomatous tattoo reaction and sarcoidosis.**
- Papules/ nodules within tattoo (often black or red) with sarcoidal granulomas; may be first sign of systemic sarcoidosis (lungs, eyes — uveitis, 'tattoo-associated uveitis'); investigate with chest X-ray, ACE, eye exam; treat with intralesional steroids, HCQ, methotrexate

**Q12. MRI and tattoos.**
- Iron-oxide pigments may cause burning/ swelling during MRI (heating, ferromagnetic artefacts) — rare, mild; inform radiographer; cold compress

**Q13. Laser removal complications in detail.**
- Blistering, pinpoint bleeding, textural change, hypopigmentation (dark skin — 1064 nm safer), hyperpigmentation, scarring, allergic reaction from pigment release (anaphylaxis rare), paradoxical darkening (white/ flesh/ red-brown ferric oxide), ink darkening of cosmetic tattoos, incomplete removal (green/ blue harder)

**Q14. Legal and ethical aspects.**
- Minors require parental consent (varies by state/ country); document medical history (bleeding disorders, keloid tendency, pregnancy, immunosuppression, active skin disease) before tattooing

**Q15. Cosmetic tattoos (permanent make-up) — specific issues.**
- Eyebrow microblading, lip liner, eyeliner — allergic granulomas, infections, migration, unnatural colour change with time, paradoxical darkening on laser removal; eyelid tattoo risks corneal injury

## Quick spotter facts
- Reaction confined to red part of tattoo — allergy to mercury/azo red pigment
- Black henna — PPD sensitisation
- Granulomas in tattoo — look for sarcoidosis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tattoos, foreign-body reactions). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Telogen effluvium — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 16 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Telogen effluvium** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define telogen effluvium (TE).**
- Diffuse, non-scarring increased shedding of telogen (club) hairs occurring 2–4 months after a triggering event that pushes many anagen follicles prematurely into telogen; commonest cause of diffuse hair loss in women

**Q2. Describe the causes and types (PYQ).**
- Acute TE (<6 months): high fever (typhoid, dengue, malaria, COVID-19), major surgery, childbirth (post-partum TE — 2–4 months after delivery), crash dieting/protein deficiency, severe emotional stress, haemorrhage, stopping OCPs, drugs (retinoids, anticoagulants, β-blockers, antithyroid, anticonvulsants)
- Chronic TE (>6 months): iron deficiency, thyroid disease, malnutrition (zinc, protein, vitamin D, biotin rarely), chronic illness (SLE, renal/hepatic failure, HIV), idiopathic chronic TE in middle-aged women (thick hair initially)
- Headington's functional types: immediate anagen release, delayed anagen release (post-partum), short anagen, immediate telogen release (minoxidil initiation), delayed telogen release

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Sudden increase in hair fall (handfuls while combing/washing) with diffuse thinning, especially bitemporal recession; hair pull test positive (>10% club hairs) all over scalp; no scarring, normal scalp
- Club hairs with depigmented bulb seen on pull test

**Q4. Write a short note on anagen effluvium (PYQ).**
- Abrupt cessation of mitotic activity in anagen follicles → tapered, fractured dystrophic hairs shed within days–weeks (1–4 weeks) of insult; ~80–90% of scalp hair lost
- Causes: chemotherapy (commonest), radiation, thallium/arsenic/mercury poisoning, boric acid, colchicine overdose, severe AA, pemphigus, protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor)
- Usually reversible; regrowth may differ in colour/texture; scalp cooling reduces chemotherapy-induced alopecia; topical minoxidil may speed regrowth

**Q5. How do you differentiate TE, AGA and diffuse AA?**
- TE: sudden shedding after trigger, positive pull test diffusely, uniform hair diameter on trichoscopy, many empty follicles/upright regrowing hairs, frontal ≈ occipital density
- AGA: gradual thinning, pattern distribution, hair diameter diversity >20%, frontal < occipital density, pull test usually negative
- Diffuse AA: rapid diffuse loss, exclamation-mark hairs, yellow and black dots, dystrophic anagen hairs on pull test

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Detailed history of triggers 2–4 months earlier; hair pull test, trichogram (telogen >20–25%), trichoscopy
- CBC, serum ferritin, TSH/free T4, vitamin D, B12, zinc, protein/albumin, LFT/RFT, ANA if indicated, VDRL (if moth-eaten), hormonal profile if signs of hyperandrogenism; biopsy for chronic TE vs early AGA

**Q7. Management.**
- Identify and remove/correct the trigger; reassurance — acute TE recovers in 3–6 months; cosmetic improvement takes 12–18 months
- Correct deficiencies: iron (ferritin), vitamin D, protein-rich diet; treat thyroid disease
- Topical minoxidil 2–5% may shorten duration (initial shedding); avoid harsh hair treatments
- Chronic TE: counselling (stable hair density over time), minoxidil, low-dose oral minoxidil

**Q8. Classify alopecia (linked PYQ).**
- Non-scarring: AGA, alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction (early), tinea capitis (non-inflammatory), syphilis, nutritional/ endocrine, hair shaft disorders
- Scarring (cicatricial) — primary: lymphocytic (DLE, LPP, FFA, CCCA, pseudopelade of Brocq), neutrophilic (folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis), mixed (acne keloidalis, erosive pustular dermatosis); secondary: burns, radiation, trauma, infections (kerion, favus), tumours, morphoea, sarcoid

**Q9. Acute vs chronic telogen effluvium.**
- Acute TE: shedding 2–3 months after trigger (fever, surgery, childbirth, crash diet, haemorrhage, drugs, COVID-19), lasts <6 months, full recovery expected
- Chronic TE: diffuse shedding >6 months in middle-aged women, often fluctuating, bitemporal recession, no miniaturisation, no clear trigger in many — must exclude AGA (female pattern) and nutritional/ thyroid causes

**Q10. Trichoscopy in TE.**
- Normal hair density pattern with many empty follicles, short regrowing hairs (upright regrowing), no significant variation in shaft diameter between frontal and occipital regions (unlike AGA), no exclamation marks

**Q11. What is the trichogram?**
- Plucking 50–100 hairs and examining roots: normal anagen:telogen 85–90:10–15; TE shows >20–25% telogen (club) hairs; anagen effluvium — dystrophic anagen hairs; AA — dystrophic/ telogen

**Q12. Post-COVID-19 telogen effluvium.**
- Common 1–3 months after COVID-19 infection (fever, stress, inflammation); self-limiting over 6–9 months; reassure, correct deficiencies, topical minoxidil may hasten regrowth

**Q13. Counselling in TE.**
- Reassure that hair follicles are intact and regrowth will occur (takes 6–12 months for cosmetic density); avoid unnecessary supplements and harsh treatments; diet with adequate protein, iron; manage stress

**Q14. What is the hair pull test and how is it interpreted?**
- Grasp ~50–60 hairs near the scalp and pull gently from proximal to distal — >10% (≥6 hairs) extracted indicates active shedding (TE, active alopecia areata, anagen effluvium); club (telogen) roots in TE

**Q15. What is the normal hair cycle?**
- Anagen (growth, 2–6 years, ~85–90% of scalp hairs), catagen (involution, 2–3 weeks, ~1%), telogen (rest, ~3 months, ~10–15%), exogen (shedding) and kenogen (empty follicle); normal loss 50–100 hairs/day

**Q16. What are the mechanisms of TE (Headington's functional types)?**
- Immediate anagen release (fever, drugs, surgery — premature entry into telogen; shedding after 2–3 months), delayed anagen release (post-partum — prolonged anagen then synchronised shedding), short anagen syndrome, immediate telogen release (minoxidil initiation — early shedding of telogen), delayed telogen release (seasonal shedding in animals/ humans)

## Quick spotter facts
- Diffuse shedding 3 months after typhoid/childbirth, positive pull test — telogen effluvium
- Anagen effluvium — chemotherapy, within weeks

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hair loss). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Tinea capitis — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tinea capitis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Who gets tinea capitis and why mostly children?**
- Prepubertal children (3–7 years); rare after puberty because sebum fatty acids (fungistatic) increase
- Adults: post-menopausal women, immunosuppressed

**Q2. Classify tinea capitis by hair invasion (PYQ).**
- Ectothrix: arthroconidia outside the shaft, cuticle destroyed — Microsporum (M. canis, M. audouinii; fluoresce green) and T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum (non-fluorescent large-spored)
- Endothrix: arthroconidia inside the shaft, cuticle intact — T. tonsurans, T. violaceum (commonest in India), T. soudanense; 'black dot' type; non-fluorescent
- Favic: T. schoenleinii — hyphae and air spaces inside hair; dull green fluorescence

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Non-inflammatory: grey patch (Microsporum — scaly round patches with broken dull hairs), black dot (endothrix — hairs break at scalp surface), seborrhoeic/diffuse scaling type (mimics dandruff), alopecia areata-like
- Inflammatory: kerion (boggy, tender, pustular mass with loose hairs, lymphadenopathy — zoophilic species; may scar), agminate folliculitis
- Favus: yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula) around hairs, mousy odour, scarring alopecia

**Q4. What is a kerion? Should it be incised?**
- Intense delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to zoophilic/geophilic dermatophytes producing a painful boggy swelling with pus-discharging follicles
- Do not incise (it is not bacterial abscess); treat with systemic antifungal ± short oral steroid for severe inflammation; can cause scarring alopecia

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Wood's lamp: green (Microsporum), dull green (favus), none (Trichophyton)
- KOH mount of plucked hairs and scales — ecto/endothrix spores
- Culture of hairs/scales (brush or cotton swab method) to identify species — important for choice of drug and to trace animal source
- Trichoscopy: comma hairs, corkscrew hairs, zig-zag hairs, Morse-code hairs, broken/black dots, bar-code hairs

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis (silvery scales, hairs intact), alopecia areata (no scaling, exclamation-mark hairs), trichotillomania (bizarre shapes, hairs of varying length), pityriasis amiantacea, atopic dermatitis, impetigo/folliculitis (kerion), discoid lupus, lichen planopilaris, secondary syphilis (moth-eaten alopecia)

**Q7. Treatment — choose the drug by organism.**
- Oral therapy is always needed (topicals do not penetrate the follicle)
- Griseofulvin (ultra-micro/micro) 20–25 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks (or longer) with fatty meal — best for Microsporum
- Terbinafine by weight for 2–4 weeks (Trichophyton) — <20 kg 62.5 mg, 20–40 kg 125 mg, >40 kg 250 mg/day; Microsporum needs longer
- Itraconazole 5 mg/kg/day 4–6 weeks or pulses; fluconazole 6 mg/kg/day 3–6 weeks
- Adjunct: ketoconazole 2%/selenium sulphide 2.5% shampoo twice weekly for patient and family to reduce spore shedding
- Examine and treat household contacts and pets; children can attend school once on treatment

**Q8. Side effects of griseofulvin.**
- Headache, GI upset, photosensitivity, urticaria, lupus flare, porphyria precipitation, enzyme inducer (reduces OCP and warfarin effect), disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; avoid in pregnancy and men should avoid fathering a child for 6 months

**Q9. Endpoint of treatment?**
- Mycological cure (negative KOH and culture), not just clinical improvement

**Q10. What is tinea capitis in adults like?**
- Often atypical, diffuse scaling or mimics seborrhoeic dermatitis, folliculitis decalvans or DLE; usually Trichophyton (T. violaceum, T. tonsurans)

**Q11. What is the id reaction in tinea capitis?**
- Itchy papulovesicular eruption on face/trunk after starting treatment of kerion — immune hypersensitivity, not drug allergy; continue antifungal, topical steroid

**Q12. Prognosis of kerion?**
- Heals with variable permanent scarring alopecia if treatment is delayed

**Q13. Describe favus in detail.**
- Trichophyton schoenleinii: yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula) formed of hyphae and keratin around hair shafts, mousy odour, scarring alopecia; hair shows hyphae and air bubbles inside (favic invasion), dull green Wood's fluorescence; endemic in parts of Kashmir, Middle East, Africa

**Q14. Classify antifungal drugs (PYQ).**
- Polyenes: amphotericin B (systemic, deep mycoses), nystatin (topical/ oral Candida)
- Azoles — imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole) and triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) — inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis)
- Allylamines: terbinafine, naftifine (squalene epoxidase inhibitors); benzylamine — butenafine
- Echinocandins: caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin (β-1,3-glucan synthase)
- Others: griseofulvin (microtubule — mitotic inhibitor), flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis), ciclopirox (chelator), amorolfine (morpholine — Δ14 reductase/ Δ7-Δ8 isomerase), tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), potassium iodide, efinaconazole, tavaborole

**Q15. Treatment of carriers and prevention.**
- Asymptomatic carriers (family, classmates) — ketoconazole/ selenium shampoo twice weekly; disinfect combs, brushes, pillow covers, caps; avoid sharing; treat pets (M. canis) — vet

## Quick spotter facts
- Black dots in a patch of alopecia — endothrix (T. violaceum/tonsurans)
- Boggy pustular scalp mass — kerion (don't incise)
- Scutula + mousy odour — favus

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Tinea corporis / cruris / faciei — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 17 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tinea corporis / cruris / faciei** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Define dermatophytosis. Classify fungal infections (common PYQ).**
- Dermatophytosis: infection of keratinised tissues (stratum corneum, hair, nails) by dermatophytes — keratinophilic moulds (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton; newer genera Nannizzia, Arthroderma)
- Fungal infections: superficial (pityriasis versicolor, tinea nigra, piedra), cutaneous (dermatophytosis, candidiasis), subcutaneous (mycetoma, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis), systemic (histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis), opportunistic (aspergillosis, mucormycosis)

**Q2. Classify dermatophytes by habitat.**
- Anthropophilic (human): T. rubrum, T. interdigitale (anthropophilic), T. tonsurans, T. indotineae, E. floccosum — chronic, less inflammatory
- Zoophilic (animals): M. canis, T. mentagrophytes, T. verrucosum — acute, inflammatory
- Geophilic (soil): M. gypseum (Nannizzia gypsea) — inflammatory

**Q3. What is the current dermatophytosis situation in India?**
- Epidemic of chronic, recurrent, extensive and steroid-modified tinea since ~2014
- Main agent now Trichophyton indotineae (ITS genotype VIII of T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale complex) — anthropophilic, spreads within families
- Causes: rampant use of topical steroid–antifungal–antibiotic combinations, incomplete treatment, hot humid climate, tight synthetic clothes, crowding, fomites; terbinafine resistance via squalene epoxidase (SQLE) gene mutations (e.g. Phe397Leu, Leu393Phe)

**Q4. Clinical features of tinea corporis.**
- Annular/arcuate plaques with raised, scaly, active edge (papules, vesicles) and central clearing; itchy; on trunk, limbs
- Variants: tinea imbricata (T. concentricum — concentric rings), bullous, Majocchi's granuloma, kerion-like, tinea profunda, pseudo-imbricata (after steroids)

**Q5. What is tinea incognito (steroid-modified tinea)?**
- Altered appearance after topical/systemic steroids — loss of active edge, less scale, more widespread, pustules, pseudo-imbricata (concentric rings), purpura, striae, bizarre shapes
- KOH often richly positive; mimics eczema, psoriasis, lupus, rosacea (on face)

**Q6. Describe tinea cruris and tinea faciei.**
- Cruris: groin, inner thighs, may spread to buttocks, pubis; scrotum usually spared (unlike candidiasis); men more
- Faciei: non-bearded face, photo-aggravated, often misdiagnosed as lupus or rosacea; may lack scale

**Q7. How do you do a KOH mount and what do you see?**
- Scrape the active edge with a blunt scalpel onto slide, add 10–20% KOH (40% for nails), warm gently, coverslip
- Branched septate hyaline hyphae ± arthroconidia
- Variants: KOH with DMSO, chlorazol black E, Parker ink, calcofluor white (fluorescence) to improve sensitivity

**Q8. Culture media and their uses (Sabouraud's — PYQ).**
- Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) with chloramphenicol and cycloheximide (Mycosel/Mycobiotic) — routine dermatophyte culture at 25–30 °C for up to 4 weeks
- Dermatophyte test medium (DTM) — phenol red turns red with dermatophytes
- Potato dextrose agar (pigment, sporulation), urease test (T. interdigitale positive, T. rubrum negative), hair perforation test, trichophyton agars (vitamin requirements)
- Antifungal susceptibility testing (CLSI M38) and SQLE mutation PCR in resistant cases

**Q9. Differential diagnosis of annular lesions.**
- Nummular eczema, psoriasis, pityriasis rosea (herald patch, collarette), granuloma annulare (no scale), annular lichen planus, erythema annulare centrifugum (trailing scale), subacute cutaneous lupus, Hansen's (BT), seborrhoeic dermatitis, secondary syphilis, sarcoidosis, mycosis fungoides, erythrasma (groin)

**Q10. Topical treatment principles.**
- Apply twice daily to lesion plus 2 cm margin, continue 2 weeks after clinical cure (usually 4–6 weeks)
- Azoles (luliconazole 1%, sertaconazole 2%, eberconazole, clotrimazole, ketoconazole), allylamines (terbinafine 1%, naftifine), amorolfine 0.25%, ciclopirox 1%
- Avoid steroid–antifungal combinations (fixed-dose combination creams)

**Q11. Systemic treatment — Indian consensus.**
- Indications: extensive, multiple sites, recurrent/chronic, failed topical, immunosuppressed
- Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day (5 mg/kg) for 4–8 weeks — currently the most used first-line drug in India; take after a fatty meal, avoid antacids/PPIs
- Terbinafine 250–500 mg/day for 4–6 weeks (higher doses for resistant strains, though failure common with SQLE mutations)
- Griseofulvin, fluconazole (150–300 mg weekly) — less preferred now
- Combination (itraconazole + terbinafine) and voriconazole/posaconazole only for documented refractory cases; continue until clinical and mycological cure

**Q12. What are general measures for recurrence prevention?**
- Treat all family members, wash and sun-dry clothes, iron clothes, loose cotton clothing, don't share towels, keep folds dry, weight loss, stop steroid creams, adherence to full course
- Antifungal powders/soaps as adjuncts; treat tinea pedis/onychomycosis reservoirs

**Q13. What is Majocchi's granuloma?**
- Follicular and dermal invasion by dermatophyte (often T. rubrum) after steroid use or shaving of legs — perifollicular papulopustules/nodules; needs systemic antifungal

**Q14. Why do we see more azole-preferred practice than terbinafine in India today?**
- T. indotineae shows high terbinafine minimum inhibitory concentrations due to SQLE mutations; itraconazole still mostly effective, though rising MIC reports exist

**Q15. Side effects and interactions of itraconazole and terbinafine.**
- Itraconazole: CYP3A4 inhibitor — interactions (statins, warfarin, midazolam, cyclosporine), contraindicated in congestive heart failure (negative inotropy), hepatotoxicity rare, needs acidic stomach
- Terbinafine: taste disturbance, hepatotoxicity (rare), drug rash, SCLE flare, CYP2D6 inhibition (tricyclics, beta-blockers)

**Q16. What is the id reaction (dermatophytid)?**
- Distant sterile eruption (vesicles on palms/fingers, papules) due to hypersensitivity to fungal antigen, usually with inflammatory tinea (kerion, tinea pedis); KOH negative at id site; settles when primary infection is treated

**Q17. Name the specific special forms of tinea.**
- Tinea imbricata (T. concentricum — tribal populations, Pacific/NE India; concentric rings)
- Tinea nigra (Hortaea werneckii — brown macule on palm; not dermatophyte)
- Tinea manuum (one-hand, two-feet syndrome)
- Tinea barbae, tinea capitis, tinea pedis, tinea unguium

## Quick spotter facts
- Active scaly edge + central clearing + KOH hyphae — tinea corporis
- T. indotineae + SQLE mutation = terbinafine-resistant tinea (India)
- Scrotum spared in tinea cruris (involved in candidiasis)

## Note
Doses follow the Indian expert consensus on dermatophytosis (IADVL Task Force); check the department's current protocol.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections); Indian expert consensus on dermatophytosis (2018–2023). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Tinea pedis & onychomycosis — viva
posts.summary: Fungal infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tinea pedis & onychomycosis** (Fungal infections)_

**Q1. Clinical types of tinea pedis.**
- Interdigital (commonest; 4th web space; maceration, fissuring, scaling) — dermatophyte complex with bacteria (Gram-negative 'dermatophytosis complex')
- Moccasin (chronic hyperkeratotic, T. rubrum; diffuse fine scaling of soles and sides)
- Vesiculobullous (inflammatory, instep, T. mentagrophytes/interdigitale)
- Acute ulcerative (Gram-negative superinfection)
- 'Two feet, one hand' syndrome — tinea pedis with tinea manuum of one hand

**Q2. Risk factors for tinea pedis.**
- Occlusive footwear, sweating, communal bathing/swimming pools, sports, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression

**Q3. Differential diagnosis of tinea pedis.**
- Interdigital: erythrasma (coral-red), candidal intertrigo, Gram-negative infection, soft corn
- Plantar: psoriasis, keratoderma, contact dermatitis (dorsum), dyshidrotic eczema, juvenile plantar dermatosis, pitted keratolysis

**Q4. Define onychomycosis. Organisms?**
- Fungal infection of the nail unit — dermatophytes (tinea unguium; T. rubrum, T. interdigitale) ~ 70–90% in toenails, non-dermatophyte moulds (Scopulariopsis, Fusarium, Aspergillus, Neoscytalidium) and Candida (fingernails, chronic paronychia)

**Q5. Classify onychomycosis by clinical pattern (PYQ).**
- Distal lateral subungual (DLSO) — commonest; invasion via hyponychium; subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, yellow discolouration
- Proximal subungual (PSO) — through proximal nail fold; white under proximal nail; marker of HIV/immunosuppression (T. rubrum) or moulds (Fusarium with paronychia)
- Superficial white (SWO) — chalky white patches on the nail surface (T. interdigitale, moulds); superficial black variant
- Endonyx — milky white nail without hyperkeratosis (T. soudanense, T. violaceum)
- Total dystrophic — end stage
- Mixed patterns; Candida onychomycosis (with chronic paronychia; CMC — total dystrophy)
- Dermatophytoma — yellow/white longitudinal streak or patch (fungal ball) — poor response

**Q6. How do you sample a nail for diagnosis?**
- Clean with alcohol; take subungual debris from the most proximal part of the affected area (DLSO), scrape the surface (SWO), punch/drill proximal plate (PSO)
- KOH 20–40% (± DMSO), wait or warm; culture on SDA with and without cycloheximide (moulds need the latter)
- Nail clipping histology with PAS — most sensitive single test
- PCR; dermoscopy (spiked/jagged proximal border of onycholysis, longitudinal streaks, 'aurora borealis' pattern)
- Non-dermatophyte mould is accepted as cause only when repeatedly isolated / seen in direct microscopy

**Q7. Differential diagnosis of nail dystrophy.**
- Nail psoriasis (pits, oil-drop sign, onycholysis with red border, salmon patch), lichen planus (pterygium, thinning), traumatic onychodystrophy (shoe pressure), yellow nail syndrome, onychogryphosis, eczema, subungual tumours (SCC, melanoma), pachyonychia congenita, Darier's disease

**Q8. Systemic treatment of onychomycosis.**
- Terbinafine 250 mg/day — 6 weeks fingernails, 12 weeks toenails (drug of choice for dermatophyte)
- Itraconazole pulse: 200 mg twice daily for 1 week every month — 2 pulses fingernails, 3–4 toenails (also covers Candida and some moulds); or continuous 200 mg/day
- Fluconazole 150–450 mg once weekly for 6–12 months (fingernails 6, toenails 9–12)
- Efficacy assessed at 12–18 months as nail grows out (toenail grows ~1 mm/month)

**Q9. Topical treatment of onychomycosis.**
- For mild DLSO (<50% nail, no matrix involvement), SWO, children, or with oral therapy
- Amorolfine 5% lacquer weekly; ciclopirox 8% lacquer daily; efinaconazole 10% solution; tavaborole 5% (US approvals)
- Adjuncts: nail avulsion (chemical with 40% urea or surgical), debridement, laser and photodynamic therapy (limited evidence)

**Q10. What are the poor prognostic factors?**
- Matrix involvement, >50% nail affected, dermatophytoma, lateral edge disease, thick nail plate (>2 mm), slow growth, elderly, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, non-dermatophyte moulds

**Q11. What is Scytalidium/Neoscytalidium infection?**
- Non-dermatophyte mould causing moccasin-like tinea and onychomycosis in tropics; resistant to most antifungals; cycloheximide sensitive (grows only on media without it)

**Q12. Prevention of recurrence?**
- Treat tinea pedis, dry feet and web spaces, antifungal powder in shoes, change socks, avoid barefoot in communal areas, discard old footwear, treat family members, periodic topical (amorolfine) use

**Q13. Onychomycosis Severity Index (OSI).**
- Score = area involved (1–5) × proximity to matrix (1–5) + 10 if dermatophytoma or >2 mm subungual hyperkeratosis: 1–5 mild, 6–15 moderate, 16–35 severe — guides choice of topical vs systemic therapy

**Q14. Classify antifungal drugs (PYQ).**
- Polyenes: amphotericin B (systemic, deep mycoses), nystatin (topical/ oral Candida)
- Azoles — imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole, luliconazole, sertaconazole) and triazoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) — inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (ergosterol synthesis)
- Allylamines: terbinafine, naftifine (squalene epoxidase inhibitors); benzylamine — butenafine
- Echinocandins: caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin (β-1,3-glucan synthase)
- Others: griseofulvin (microtubule — mitotic inhibitor), flucytosine (DNA/RNA synthesis), ciclopirox (chelator), amorolfine (morpholine — Δ14 reductase/ Δ7-Δ8 isomerase), tolnaftate, Whitfield's ointment (benzoic + salicylic acid), potassium iodide, efinaconazole, tavaborole

**Q15. Lasers and devices in onychomycosis.**
- Nd:YAG 1064 nm (long-pulsed/ Q-switched), diode 870/930 nm — thermal effect on fungi; modest efficacy; PDT; iontophoresis; used as adjuncts to antifungals

## Quick spotter facts
- Proximal white subungual onychomycosis — screen for HIV
- Terbinafine 6 weeks fingernail / 12 weeks toenail
- Dermatophytoma — streak in nail, needs removal + oral therapy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Superficial fungal infections, nail infections). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Trichotillomania — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Trichotillomania** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Write a note on trichotillomania (PYQ).**
- Body-focused repetitive behaviour (DSM-5 obsessive-compulsive and related disorder) — recurrent pulling of one's own hair resulting in hair loss, with repeated attempts to stop and significant distress/impairment
- Two peaks: preschool children (habit, benign, often outgrown) and adolescents/young women (chronic, psychiatric comorbidity)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Bizarre, irregular-shaped patches of incomplete alopecia (often on vertex/frontoparietal of the side of the dominant hand) with hairs of varying lengths, broken stubs, no inflammation, scalp normal
- 'Tonsure' pattern (Friar Tuck sign — vertex loss sparing the periphery)
- Eyebrows, eyelashes, pubic hair may be involved
- Trichophagia (eating hair) → trichobezoar (Rapunzel syndrome — tail extending into small bowel) — ask about GI symptoms
- Associated: anxiety, depression, OCD, skin picking, nail biting, ADHD

**Q3. Trichoscopy and histopathology.**
- Trichoscopy: broken hairs at different lengths, flame hairs, V-sign (two hairs broken at the same level), tulip hairs, hook hairs, trichoptilosis (split ends), coiled hairs, black dots, haemorrhages; no exclamation-mark hairs or yellow dots (as in AA)
- Histology: increased catagen/telogen follicles, trichomalacia (distorted soft hair shafts), pigment casts, perifollicular haemorrhage, empty follicles, minimal inflammation

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Alopecia areata (smooth patch, exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots), tinea capitis (scaling, KOH), traction alopecia, pressure alopecia, secondary syphilis, loose anagen syndrome, hair shaft defects (monilethrix, trichorrhexis nodosa)

**Q5. Discuss trichorrhexis nodosa (PYQ).**
- Commonest hair shaft defect: nodes (beaded swellings) where the cortex frays into brush-like fibres — 'two brooms pushed together' — hair breaks easily
- Acquired (physical/chemical trauma — combing, bleaching, straightening — proximal in Afro-textured hair, distal in others) or congenital (argininosuccinic aciduria, Menkes, trichothiodystrophy)

**Q6. Write a short note on Menkes kinky hair (PYQ).**
- X-linked recessive ATP7A mutation — defective copper transport (low serum copper and caeruloplasmin) → pili torti (twisted flattened hair), steely brittle hypopigmented hair, pudgy cheeks, hypothermia, seizures, neurodegeneration, death in early childhood; treat early with copper histidinate injections

**Q7. Management.**
- Non-confrontational explanation; involve parents (children); habit-reversal training (awareness, competing response) and CBT — first line
- Pharmacotherapy: N-acetylcysteine 1200–2400 mg/day (evidence in adults), SSRIs (comorbid depression/anxiety), clomipramine, olanzapine/aripiprazole (low dose), naltrexone
- Barriers: short haircut, gloves, bandana; psychiatric referral for chronic cases
- Childhood habit type often resolves spontaneously

**Q8. Classify alopecia (linked PYQ).**
- Non-scarring: AGA, alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction (early), tinea capitis (non-inflammatory), syphilis, nutritional/ endocrine, hair shaft disorders
- Scarring (cicatricial) — primary: lymphocytic (DLE, LPP, FFA, CCCA, pseudopelade of Brocq), neutrophilic (folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis), mixed (acne keloidalis, erosive pustular dermatosis); secondary: burns, radiation, trauma, infections (kerion, favus), tumours, morphoea, sarcoid

**Q9. Trichoscopy signs in detail.**
- Broken hairs at different lengths, trichoptilosis (split ends), flame hairs (wavy proximal hair residues), V-sign (two hairs broken at same level), tulip hairs, hook hairs, coiled hairs, black dots, hair powder (sprinkled shaft fragments), absence of exclamation-mark hairs (seen in AA) — though overlap possible

**Q10. Histopathology findings.**
- Increased catagen/ telogen hairs, trichomalacia (distorted, soft hair shafts), pigment casts in follicular canal, perifollicular haemorrhage, empty follicles, no significant inflammation, normal follicle density

**Q11. What psychiatric comorbidities and treatments?**
- Comorbid anxiety, depression, OCD, skin picking, ADHD; treatment — habit reversal training (first line), CBT, N-acetylcysteine (1200–2400 mg/day), SSRIs, clomipramine, olanzapine/ aripiprazole in resistant; children — often self-limiting 'baby trich' with parental guidance

**Q12. What is the 'hair pull test' and 'hair window' in trichotillomania?**
- Pull test is negative (hairs firmly anchored); 'hair growth window' — shaving or occluding a small area shows normal regrowth when the patient cannot pull — confirms diagnosis

**Q13. What are the DSM-5 criteria?**
- Recurrent pulling of hair resulting in hair loss; repeated attempts to decrease/stop; clinically significant distress or impairment; not due to another medical condition or psychiatric disorder (e.g. BDD); classified under obsessive-compulsive and related disorders

**Q14. What is trichobezoar and Rapunzel syndrome?**
- Trichophagia (eating pulled hair) forms a hair-ball in the stomach (trichobezoar) — abdominal pain, vomiting, obstruction; Rapunzel syndrome — tail of bezoar extending into small intestine; needs endoscopic/surgical removal

**Q15. What is 'tonsure pattern' and 'Friar Tuck sign'?**
- Patch of hair loss on the vertex/crown with a fringe of normal hair at the periphery — typical of chronic trichotillomania (hair at the margins is harder to pull)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bizarre patch with hairs of different lengths, flame hairs and V-sign — trichotillomania
- Trichophagia → Rapunzel syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Psychocutaneous disorders; hair disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 27 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Tuberous sclerosis complex** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. Define tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).**
- Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder (1 in 6000) with hamartomas in skin, brain, kidneys, heart, lungs and eyes, due to mutations in TSC1 (hamartin, 9q34) or TSC2 (tuberin, 16p13 — more severe) → loss of inhibition of mTORC1 (mammalian target of rapamycin) → cell growth; ~2/3 de novo
- Classic Vogt triad: seizures, intellectual disability, facial angiofibromas (epiloia) — present in <50%

**Q2. Describe the clinical features, criteria and diagnosis (PYQ) — 2021 criteria.**
- Major (11): hypomelanotic macules (≥3, ≥5 mm), angiofibromas (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas (≥2), shagreen patch, multiple retinal hamartomas, multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines, subependymal nodules (≥2), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), angiomyolipomas (≥2)
- Minor (5): 'confetti' skin lesions, dental enamel pits (>3), intraoral fibromas (≥2), retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, non-renal hamartomas, sclerotic bone lesions
- Definite TSC: 2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor features, or identification of a pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant; possible: 1 major or ≥2 minor (LAM + angiomyolipomas alone = need another feature)

**Q3. Write a short note on adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) (PYQ).**
- Misnomer — they are angiofibromas (not sebaceous adenomas): symmetrical, smooth, red-pink, dome-shaped papules on nasolabial folds, cheeks and chin (sparing upper lip), appearing at 2–5 years and increasing at puberty; ~75–90% of TSC
- Histology: dermal fibrosis with stellate fibroblasts, dilated capillaries, absent elastic tissue, atrophic follicles
- Treatment: topical sirolimus (rapamycin 0.1–1%) — first line; PDL, CO2/Er:YAG laser ablation, shave excision, electrosurgery

**Q4. Write a short note on the shagreen patch (PYQ).**
- Connective tissue naevus (collagenoma): irregular, slightly elevated, skin-coloured to yellowish-brown plaque with orange-peel ('pig-skin'/shagreen leather) surface, usually on the lumbosacral area; appears in early childhood (~50% of TSC)
- Histology: thickened, densely packed collagen bundles in dermis

**Q5. Other skin signs.**
- Hypomelanotic macules (earliest sign — at birth; ash-leaf shape, polygonal 'thumbprint', confetti macules on limbs; best seen with Wood's lamp; poliosis)
- Fibrous cephalic plaque (forehead — yellowish-brown plaque, often first facial sign)
- Ungual fibromas (Koenen's tumours — periungual/subungual flesh-coloured papules after puberty, toenails > fingernails; longitudinal groove in nail)
- Intraoral (gingival) fibromas, dental enamel pits, molluscum pendulum, café-au-lait macules (not specific)

**Q6. Systemic manifestations.**
- CNS: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA (obstructive hydrocephalus), seizures (infantile spasms — West syndrome), intellectual disability, autism, TAND (TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders)
- Kidney: angiomyolipomas (bleeding — leading cause of death in adults), cysts (TSC2/PKD1 contiguous gene syndrome), renal cell carcinoma
- Heart: rhabdomyomas (fetal/neonatal — regress), arrhythmias (WPW)
- Lungs: lymphangioleiomyomatosis (women — pneumothorax, chylothorax), multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia
- Eyes: retinal hamartomas ('mulberry'), achromic patches

**Q7. Investigations and surveillance.**
- MRI brain (every 1–3 years until 25 y — SEGA), EEG, renal MRI (every 1–3 years), echocardiography and ECG (infancy), HRCT chest (women ≥18 y), ophthalmology, dental exam, neuropsychiatric assessment; genetic testing; examine parents

**Q8. Management.**
- mTOR inhibitors: everolimus (SEGA, angiomyolipomas, refractory seizures), sirolimus (LAM; topical for angiofibromas)
- Vigabatrin for infantile spasms; other antiepileptics; epilepsy surgery
- Embolisation/nephron-sparing surgery for bleeding angiomyolipomas
- Skin: topical sirolimus, lasers, excision of ungual fibromas and shagreen patches if symptomatic
- Genetic counselling (50% risk; germline mosaicism in apparently unaffected parents)

**Q9. Classify multiple tumour syndromes (PYQ).**
- With adnexal tumours: Cowden (trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, oral papillomas — PTEN; breast/thyroid/endometrial cancer), Muir–Torre (sebaceous neoplasms + visceral cancers — mismatch repair), Brooke–Spiegler/familial cylindromatosis (CYLD — cylindromas, spiradenomas, trichoepitheliomas), Birt–Hogg–Dubé (fibrofolliculomas, renal tumours, pneumothorax — FLCN), Gorlin (BCCs), Rombo, Bazex–Dupré–Christol
- With fibrous/neural/vascular tumours: TSC, NF1/NF2, Gardner (epidermoid cysts, osteomas, desmoids, colonic polyps — APC), MEN 2B (mucosal neuromas), Carney complex, Reed syndrome (multiple cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas + renal cell carcinoma — fumarate hydratase), blue rubber bleb, Maffucci

**Q10. Explain the genetics and molecular basis.**
- Autosomal dominant; TSC1 (hamartin, 9q34) or TSC2 (tuberin, 16p13 — more severe, ~70%); two-thirds are de novo
- Hamartin–tuberin complex inhibits Rheb → mTORC1; loss → mTOR overactivation → cell growth, hamartomas in skin, brain, kidney, heart, lung — basis of mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus)
- TSC2–PKD1 contiguous gene deletion → early severe polycystic kidney disease

**Q11. Give the 2021 updated diagnostic criteria (International TSC Consensus).**
- Major (11): hypomelanotic macules (≥3, ≥5 mm), angiofibromas (≥3) or fibrous cephalic plaque, ungual fibromas (≥2), shagreen patch, multiple retinal hamartomas, multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines, subependymal nodules (≥2), subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma, lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), angiomyolipomas (≥2)
- Minor (7): 'confetti' skin lesions, dental enamel pits (>3), intraoral fibromas (≥2), retinal achromic patch, multiple renal cysts, non-renal hamartomas, sclerotic bone lesions
- Definite: 2 major or 1 major + ≥2 minor, or pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant; possible: 1 major or ≥2 minor (LAM + AML alone doesn't count as definite)

**Q12. Describe the hypomelanotic macules in detail.**
- Earliest skin sign — at birth/infancy in ~90%: ash-leaf (lance-ovate), polygonal, thumbprint, confetti (tiny 1–3 mm on extremities); better seen with Wood's lamp; also poliosis (white hair tuft)
- Histology: normal melanocyte number with reduced melanin and smaller melanosomes

**Q13. Facial angiofibromas — treatment.**
- Appear at 3–10 years, increase at puberty: red papules on nasolabial folds, cheeks, chin (sparing upper lip)
- Topical sirolimus (rapamycin) 0.1–1% gel/ointment daily — first-line, best when started early; maintenance needed
- Procedures: pulsed-dye laser (erythema), CO2/ Er:YAG ablation, shave/ electrosurgery, dermabrasion for established fibrotic lesions; recurrence common

**Q14. What are ungual fibromas (Koenen tumours)?**
- Flesh-coloured firm papules emerging from proximal nail fold (periungual) or under the nail (subungual) — appear after puberty; produce longitudinal nail groove; more on toes; treated by excision when painful; single lesion can occur after trauma in normal people

**Q15. Describe the neurological features.**
- Epilepsy in ~85% (infantile spasms in ~1/3 — vigabatrin first-line; drug-resistant epilepsy common; everolimus, cannabidiol, epilepsy surgery), cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA (near foramen of Monro — hydrocephalus; everolimus/ surgery), TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders (TAND — intellectual disability, autism, ADHD, anxiety)

**Q16. Renal and pulmonary features.**
- Angiomyolipomas (~80% adults) — risk of haemorrhage when >3 cm (Wunderlich syndrome); treat with everolimus or embolisation; renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma (rare), CKD
- Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) — women of reproductive age, cystic lung disease, pneumothorax, chylous effusion; sirolimus stabilises lung function

**Q17. Cardiac rhabdomyomas — relevance.**
- Detected antenatally (often the first clue to TSC on fetal echo); usually regress in infancy; may cause arrhythmias (WPW) or outflow obstruction in neonates

**Q18. Ophthalmic and dental features.**
- Retinal astrocytic hamartomas ('mulberry' or flat translucent), retinal achromic patches; dental enamel pits (best seen with dental dye), gingival fibromas — oral exam essential

**Q19. What is the fibrous cephalic plaque?**
- Raised, yellow-brown/ skin-coloured rubbery plaque on forehead/scalp (collagenoma) — often the first visible lesion after hypomelanotic macules; counts as major criterion with angiofibromas

**Q20. Surveillance recommendations.**
- Brain MRI every 1–3 years until age 25 (SEGA), EEG in infants (subclinical seizures), TAND screening yearly, abdominal MRI every 1–3 years for AML, BP and renal function yearly, chest HRCT in women at 18 y (LAM), ECG/echo at baseline, dermatology and dental review yearly, ophthalmology baseline

**Q21. Differential diagnosis of facial angiofibromas.**
- Acne vulgaris (comedones, pustules), rosacea, trichoepitheliomas (Brooke–Spiegler), Birt–Hogg–Dubé fibrofolliculomas, MEN1 angiofibromas, multiple syringomas, sebaceous adenomas (Muir–Torre), tricholemmomas (Cowden)

**Q22. What is the histopathology of angiofibroma and shagreen patch?**
- Angiofibroma: dermal fibrosis with stellate/ plump fibroblasts, dilated vessels, perifollicular fibrosis, atrophic follicles
- Shagreen patch: connective tissue naevus (collagenoma) — thickened dense collagen bundles, reduced elastic fibres

**Q23. Systemic mTOR inhibitors — use and side effects.**
- Everolimus: SEGA, renal AML (>3 cm), refractory epilepsy; sirolimus: LAM; also improve skin lesions
- Side effects: stomatitis/ mouth ulcers, acne-like eruptions, hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, infections, impaired wound healing, proteinuria, pneumonitis

**Q24. Genetic counselling in TSC.**
- 50% risk to offspring of affected parent; de novo in ~2/3 but parents should be examined (mild features, gonadal mosaicism ~2%); prenatal/ pre-implantation testing possible

**Q25. How does TSC present at different ages?**
- Fetus/newborn: cardiac rhabdomyoma, hypomelanotic macules
- Infancy: infantile spasms, developmental delay, ash-leaf macules
- Childhood: angiofibromas, shagreen patch, autism/ learning difficulties
- Adolescence/adult: ungual fibromas, renal AML, LAM in women

**Q26. Classify multiple tumour/ hamartoma syndromes with skin markers.**
- TSC (angiofibromas), NF1 (neurofibromas), Cowden/ PTEN hamartoma (trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, oral papillomas — breast/thyroid/endometrial cancer), Birt–Hogg–Dubé (fibrofolliculomas — renal cancer, pneumothorax), Gorlin (BCCs, palmar pits), Muir–Torre (sebaceous tumours — colorectal cancer), Gardner (epidermoid cysts, osteomas — colon polyps), MEN1 (angiofibromas, collagenomas), MEN2B (mucosal neuromas), Carney complex (lentigines, myxomas), Brooke–Spiegler (cylindromas, trichoepitheliomas)

**Q27. What is the prognosis?**
- Variable; main causes of morbidity/mortality — renal disease (AML haemorrhage, CKD), status epilepticus/ SUDEP, SEGA, LAM; most live into adulthood with surveillance

## Quick spotter facts
- Facial angiofibromas + ash-leaf macules + shagreen patch + Koenen's tumours — tuberous sclerosis (mTOR)
- Topical sirolimus for angiofibromas; everolimus for SEGA/AML

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Tuberous sclerosis); 2021 International TSC Consensus diagnostic criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Twenty-nail dystrophy (trachyonychia) — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Twenty-nail dystrophy (trachyonychia)** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. What is trachyonychia?**
- Roughness of the nail plate due to matrix inflammation — opalescent, rough, sandpapered nails with excessive longitudinal ridging (opaque type) or shiny nails with multiple small regular pits (shiny type); when all 20 nails are involved — 'twenty-nail dystrophy'
- Commoner in children; usually benign and self-limiting

**Q2. Causes.**
- Idiopathic (isolated)
- Alopecia areata (most common association — especially children), lichen planus (most common histological cause), psoriasis, eczema/atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis vulgaris, IgA deficiency, vitiligo, sarcoidosis, pemphigus vulgaris, incontinentia pigmenti, selective IgA deficiency

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Spongiotic changes of matrix (most common — AA, eczema, idiopathic), lichenoid (LP), psoriasiform — nail matrix biopsy rarely justified because benign course and risk of scarring

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Onychomycosis (KOH), nail psoriasis (pits are coarse/irregular, oil-drop, onycholysis), LP with pterygium, brittle nails (onychoschizia), Darier's disease (red and white longitudinal bands with V-notching), chemical damage (nail cosmetics), ageing ridges

**Q5. Discuss nail pitting with causes (PYQ).**
- Pits = small depressions due to focal parakeratosis from the proximal matrix shed as the nail grows
- Psoriasis (coarse, deep, irregular, random), alopecia areata (fine, shallow, regular geometric grid), eczema/atopic (coarse, irregular, with transverse ridging), lichen planus, Reiter's/reactive arthritis, pityriasis rosea, secondary syphilis, sarcoidosis, normal individuals (a few pits)
- Rosenau's depressions (larger pits — psoriasis)

**Q6. Enumerate skin diseases with nail changes (PYQ).**
- Psoriasis (pits, oil-drop, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinters), LP (pterygium, thinning, ridging), AA (pits, trachyonychia), eczema (pits, Beau's lines, shiny nails from rubbing), Darier's (red–white bands, V-nicks), pemphigus (paronychia, onychomadesis), EB (dystrophy/anonychia), SJS/TEN (shedding), DM (cuticular changes), SLE (red lunulae, periungual erythema), SSc (pterygium inversum, ulcers), yellow nail syndrome, pachyonychia congenita, nail–patella syndrome (triangular lunulae, absent patella, iliac horns, nephropathy)

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Reassurance — spontaneous improvement over years (children especially)
- Cosmetic: nail hydration (emollients, nail oils), avoid trauma, nail lacquer
- Active treatment rarely needed: potent topical steroid ± occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone to matrix, tazarotene; systemic therapy only if associated disease needs it (JAK inhibitors improve AA nails)

**Q8. Describe the anatomy and growth of the nail unit (linked PYQ).**
- Components: nail plate (keratin — hard keratins), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium), lateral folds, matrix (proximal — dorsal plate; distal — ventral plate; lunula is visible distal matrix), nail bed, hyponychium
- Growth: fingernail ~3 mm/month (complete regrowth 4–6 months), toenail ~1 mm/month (12–18 months); faster in summer, dominant hand, pregnancy, psoriasis; slower in elderly, illness, yellow nail syndrome

**Q9. Associated conditions in detail.**
- Idiopathic (commonest in children), alopecia areata (most common association), lichen planus, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, eczema, vitiligo, ichthyosis vulgaris, IgA deficiency, sarcoidosis, Down syndrome

**Q10. Treatment options in detail.**
- Reassurance and cosmetic measures (nail polish, buffing) in children (spontaneous improvement); emollients/ nail hardeners; topical steroids/ tacrolimus to proximal nail fold, intralesional triamcinolone into matrix, short systemic steroids, oral retinoids, cyclosporine, JAK inhibitors (alopecia areata-associated)

**Q11. Enumerate nail signs of systemic disease.**
- Clubbing (cardiopulmonary, IBD, cirrhosis), koilonychia (iron deficiency), Beau's lines (systemic illness), Muehrcke's lines (hypoalbuminaemia), Terry's nails (cirrhosis, CHF, diabetes), half-and-half (Lindsay's — CKD), Mees' lines (arsenic, thallium), splinter haemorrhages (endocarditis, trauma), yellow nails (yellow nail syndrome), blue lunulae (Wilson's, argyria, zidovudine), periungual telangiectasia (CTD)

**Q12. What is nail lichen planus and why urgent treatment?**
- Thinning, ridging, splitting, red lunula, dorsal pterygium (permanent scarring), anonychia — early systemic/ intralesional steroids prevent irreversible matrix damage

**Q13. Describe the two clinical types.**
- Opaque (rough, sandpaper-like) trachyonychia: severe, longitudinal ridging, opaque grey nails with brittleness and koilonychia
- Shiny trachyonychia: milder, many small regular pits that reflect light, nails shiny

**Q14. Is it always 20 nails?**
- No — not all nails need be involved; the term 'trachyonychia' is preferred; usually childhood; spontaneously improves in many (≈ 50% in 6 years), especially idiopathic and alopecia-areata-associated

**Q15. What is the best investigation?**
- Diagnosis clinical; nail matrix biopsy only when diagnosis influences treatment (lichen planus — risk of scarring/ pterygium); trichoscopy/scalp exam for alopecia areata; KOH to exclude onychomycosis

## Quick spotter facts
- Rough sandpapered ridged nails on all 20 nails of a child with AA — trachyonychia
- Fine geometric pits — AA; coarse irregular pits — psoriasis

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nail disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Urticaria & angioedema — viva
posts.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Urticaria & angioedema** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define urticaria and angioedema.**
- Urticaria: transient itchy wheals — central swelling with surrounding flare, each lasting <24 h and leaving no mark — due to dermal oedema
- Angioedema: deeper swelling of dermis/subcutis/mucosa, more painful than itchy, lasting up to 72 h
- Either or both may occur

**Q2. Classify urticaria (PYQ).**
- Acute (<6 weeks) vs chronic (≥6 weeks)
- Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU): no specific trigger — autoimmune (type I autoallergic with IgE against self antigens like TPO/IL-24; type IIb autoimmune with IgG against IgE/FcεRI) or unknown
- Chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU): physical — symptomatic dermographism (commonest), cold, delayed pressure, solar, heat, vibratory; non-physical — cholinergic, contact, aquagenic
- Others/related: urticarial vasculitis, autoinflammatory syndromes (CAPS, Schnitzler), urticaria pigmentosa (mastocytosis), hereditary angioedema (no wheals)

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Mast cell degranulation (immunological IgE/autoantibody, complement C5a, neuropeptides, drugs like opioids/contrast, NSAIDs via COX-1 inhibition) → histamine, prostaglandin D2, leukotrienes, PAF, cytokines → vasodilation and vascular leak
- Bradykinin-mediated angioedema (no wheals, no itch): hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency, ACE inhibitors

**Q4. Causes of acute urticaria.**
- Idiopathic (~50%), infections (viral URTI in children — commonest), drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs, opioids, contrast), foods (nuts, shellfish, eggs, milk), insect stings, latex, blood products

**Q5. Investigations — guideline approach.**
- Acute: none routinely unless a specific allergen is suspected
- Chronic spontaneous: limited — CBC with differential, ESR/CRP, total IgE and IgG anti-TPO (predict response to omalizumab/cyclosporine), ± basophil activation test/autologous serum skin test
- Further tests only if history suggests: thyroid function, H. pylori, stool for parasites, tryptase, skin biopsy (wheals >24 h — urticarial vasculitis), complement C4 and C1-INH for angioedema without wheals
- Provocation tests for CIndU: FricTest for dermographism, ice-cube/TempTest for cold, exercise/hot-bath for cholinergic, weighted rods for delayed pressure, phototest for solar

**Q6. Write a short note on cold urticaria (PYQ).**
- Wheals on cold exposure (cold air, water, drinks — lips/throat swelling), develop on rewarming
- Primary (acquired idiopathic) or secondary (cryoglobulins, cold agglutinins, infections — EBV, HIV, hepatitis)
- Ice-cube test: 5 min on forearm, read after 10 min — wheal positive; TempTest for threshold
- Risk: anaphylaxis/drowning with whole-body immersion (swimming) — carry epinephrine
- Treatment: avoid cold, high-dose non-sedating antihistamines, omalizumab; familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (NLRP3) is different — fever, rash, arthralgia after cold; treat with IL-1 blockers

**Q7. What is cholinergic urticaria?**
- Tiny (1–3 mm) itchy wheals with large flares after rise in core body temperature — exercise, hot shower, spicy food, emotion; young adults; sweat allergy and hypohidrosis implicated
- Exercise/hot-water test; non-sedating antihistamines, propranolol, omalizumab; exercise-induced anaphylaxis is a separate entity (food-dependent — wheat ω-5 gliadin)

**Q8. Differentiate urticaria from urticarial vasculitis.**
- Urticarial vasculitis: individual lesions last >24 h, burn/pain more than itch, leave purpura/bruising/pigmentation, systemic features (arthralgia, fever, kidney, eye, lung), low complement in hypocomplementaemic form (anti-C1q, SLE association)
- Biopsy: leukocytoclastic vasculitis; treatment — dapsone, colchicine, HCQ, steroids, immunosuppressants

**Q9. Management of chronic urticaria — the stepwise guideline.**
- Avoid triggers (NSAIDs, alcohol, tight clothing, physical triggers), treat underlying cause if found
- Step 1: standard-dose second-generation H1 antihistamine daily (cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, bilastine, desloratadine, rupatadine) — not on demand
- Step 2: increase up to 4-fold dose after 2–4 weeks if not controlled
- Step 3: add omalizumab (anti-IgE) 300 mg SC every 4 weeks (may increase dose/frequency if needed)
- Step 4: cyclosporine 3.5–5 mg/kg/day (with antihistamine) if omalizumab fails
- Short oral steroid courses (≤10 days) only for severe exacerbations; montelukast, dapsone, HCQ, H2 blockers have weak evidence
- Newer: dupilumab and the BTK inhibitor remibrutinib approved for CSU in some countries (confirm in India)

**Q10. Assessment tools.**
- UAS7 (urticaria activity score over 7 days: wheals 0–3 + itch 0–3 per day, max 42), UCT (urticaria control test, ≥12 controlled), AAS (angioedema activity), CU-Q2oL (quality of life)

**Q11. What is hereditary angioedema (HAE)?**
- Autosomal dominant deficiency (type I — low C1-INH level, ~85%) or dysfunction (type II — normal/high level but non-functional) of C1 esterase inhibitor; HAE with normal C1-INH (factor XII, plasminogen mutations, oestrogen-dependent)
- Recurrent non-itchy, non-pitting swellings of skin, gut (colic, vomiting), larynx (fatal asphyxia) without wheals; triggers — trauma, dental work, stress, oestrogens, ACE inhibitors
- Screening: low C4 (also during attacks); C1-INH level and function
- Treatment: antihistamines/steroids/adrenaline do NOT work; acute — C1-INH concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 antagonist), ecallantide, fresh frozen plasma; prophylaxis — lanadelumab (anti-kallikrein), berotralstat, C1-INH, danazol, tranexamic acid

**Q12. What is ACE-inhibitor angioedema?**
- Bradykinin accumulation from reduced breakdown — face, lips, tongue swelling without wheals; may occur after years of use; commoner in Black patients; stop the drug (also avoid ARBs cautiously); icatibant in severe cases

**Q13. How do you treat acute urticaria and anaphylaxis?**
- Acute urticaria: non-sedating antihistamine (up to 4×) ± short prednisolone course
- Anaphylaxis: adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 ml of 1:1000) IM in anterolateral thigh (child 0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg), repeat after 5 min if needed; airway, oxygen, IV fluids, then antihistamine and steroid; observe ≥6–12 h; prescribe adrenaline auto-injector

**Q14. What is dermographism?**
- Wheal along a line of firm stroking within minutes (Darier's sign is the same in mastocytosis lesions); symptomatic dermographism is the commonest CIndU — FricTest; antihistamines

**Q15. Prognosis of CSU.**
- About 50% remit in 1–5 years; severe disease, angioedema, autoimmunity and positive ASST predict longer course

**Q16. Explain mast cell activation and mediators in detail (PYQ: chemical mediators of urticaria).**
- Preformed (granule): histamine (H1 — wheal, flare, itch), tryptase, chymase, heparin, TNF-α
- Newly synthesised: prostaglandin D2, leukotrienes C4/D4/E4, PAF
- Cytokines/chemokines: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, IL-31 — late-phase and itch
- Triggers: IgE–FcεRI cross-linking (allergen/ autoantibodies), complement C5a, MRGPRX2 receptor (opioids, neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, icatibant, contrast — pseudo-allergic), substance P, physical stimuli

**Q17. Discuss physical urticarias other than cold and cholinergic.**
- Symptomatic dermographism (commonest — linear wheals after scratching)
- Delayed pressure urticaria (deep painful swellings 4–8 h after pressure — soles, buttocks, shoulder straps; poor antihistamine response — dapsone, omalizumab)
- Heat urticaria (local wheals after heat contact), solar urticaria (within minutes of sun/visible light — phototesting, omalizumab, hardening), vibratory angioedema (ADGRE2), aquagenic urticaria (small perifollicular wheals after water contact)

**Q18. What is NSAID-exacerbated urticaria?**
- COX-1 inhibition shifts arachidonic acid to leukotriene pathway — aspirin/NSAIDs worsen chronic urticaria in 20–30% of CSU patients; advise paracetamol or selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib/etoricoxib) instead; NSAID-induced urticaria/angioedema can occur in non-CSU patients too

**Q19. Describe the role of diet in chronic urticaria.**
- True food allergy rarely causes chronic urticaria; pseudoallergen-free diet (avoid additives, preservatives, colouring, natural salicylates) for 3–6 weeks may help some patients; avoid unnecessary restriction

**Q20. Omalizumab — mechanism and use in CSU.**
- Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody — binds free IgE → reduces FcεRI on mast cells/basophils → less activation; 300 mg SC every 4 weeks (can up-dose to 450–600 mg or every 2 weeks); response in ~70%, faster in type I autoallergic CSU (high IgE); safe in pregnancy; anaphylaxis rare

**Q21. Cyclosporine in CSU.**
- 3.5–5 mg/kg/day for 3–6 months for omalizumab non-responders (better in type IIb autoimmune CSU — low IgE, positive basophil test/ ASST); monitor BP, creatinine; taper slowly

**Q22. What is autologous serum skin test (ASST)?**
- 0.05 ml of patient's own serum injected intradermally vs saline and histamine controls; red wheal ≥1.5 mm larger than saline at 30 min = positive — suggests autoimmune (functional histamine-releasing autoantibodies) urticaria; stop antihistamines 2–3 days before; supports diagnosis but not essential

**Q23. What is urticaria in pregnancy and children — treatment?**
- Pregnancy: loratadine or cetirizine (best data), avoid up-dosing beyond needed; omalizumab acceptable if severe
- Children: second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine, levocetirizine, desloratadine, fexofenadine, bilastine) dosed by age/weight; acute urticaria usually viral; chronic urticaria — screen thyroid autoimmunity, coeliac if indicated

**Q24. What is Schnitzler syndrome?**
- Chronic non-itchy urticarial rash + monoclonal IgM (or IgG) gammopathy + recurrent fever, bone pain, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, raised CRP; neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis on biopsy; responds dramatically to IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab); risk of lymphoproliferative disease

**Q25. Autoinflammatory urticaria-like syndromes.**
- Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS — NLRP3: FCAS, Muckle–Wells, NOMID/CINCA) — urticarial rash from infancy, fever, conjunctivitis, deafness, amyloidosis; adult-onset Still's disease (evanescent salmon rash), Schnitzler — treat with IL-1 inhibitors

**Q26. What is mastocytosis and how to differentiate from urticaria?**
- Clonal mast cell disease (KIT D816V); urticaria pigmentosa/ maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis — brown macules/ papules that urticate on rubbing (Darier's sign), mastocytoma (child), systemic forms — flushing, anaphylaxis, raised baseline tryptase (>20 ng/ml)
- Urticaria: transient wheals without residual pigment, normal tryptase

**Q27. Angioedema without wheals — approach.**
- Ask about drugs (ACE inhibitors, gliptins, NSAIDs, oestrogens), family history, abdominal attacks; check C4 (low in HAE/acquired C1-INH deficiency), C1-INH level/function, C1q (low in acquired — lymphoproliferative/ autoimmune); normal complements → idiopathic histaminergic (responds to antihistamines) or ACE-inhibitor/ HAE with normal C1-INH

**Q28. Contact urticaria — differentiate from chronic urticaria.**
- Contact urticaria: wheals only at contact site within minutes–1 h, triggered by specific substances (latex, foods, cosmetics, plants), may progress to generalised urticaria/ anaphylaxis (immunological); diagnosis by open/prick tests; avoidance

**Q29. What is the urticaria activity score (UAS7) cutoff?**
- UAS7 = sum over 7 days of daily wheal score (0–3) + itch score (0–3), maximum 42: 0 urticaria-free, 1–6 well controlled, 7–15 mild, 16–27 moderate, 28–42 severe; UCT ≥12 = well controlled (4-week recall)

**Q30. Prognosis of chronic inducible urticaria.**
