- Often persists longer than CSU (years); dermographism and cold urticaria may last 5–10 years; avoidance and regular antihistamines control most

## Quick spotter facts
- Individual wheal <24 h and leaves no mark = urticaria; >24 h with bruising = urticarial vasculitis
- Angioedema without wheals + abdominal pain + low C4 — HAE (no response to antihistamines)
- Step up: antihistamine ×4 → omalizumab → cyclosporine

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Urticaria); EAACI/GA²LEN/EuroGuiDerm/APAAACI urticaria guideline 2022. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Vesicobullous diseases (pemphigus / pemphigoid) — viva
posts.summary: Vesicobullous diseases · 31 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Vesicobullous diseases (pemphigus / pemphigoid)** (Vesicobullous diseases)_

**Q1. Classify vesiculobullous disorders (PYQ).**
- Genetic: epidermolysis bullosa (simplex, junctional, dystrophic, Kindler), Hailey–Hailey, Darier's (rarely bullous), bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma, porphyrias
- Autoimmune intraepidermal: pemphigus vulgaris, foliaceus (endemic fogo selvagem, pemphigus erythematosus/Senear–Usher), IgA pemphigus, paraneoplastic pemphigus, drug-induced pemphigus, pemphigus vegetans, herpetiformis
- Autoimmune subepidermal: bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid, pemphigoid gestationis, linear IgA bullous dermatosis/chronic bullous disease of childhood, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous SLE, anti-p200 (anti-laminin γ1) pemphigoid
- Infections (bullous impetigo, SSSS, herpes, varicella), drug (SJS/TEN, FDE), physical (burns, friction, cold, insect bites), metabolic (diabetic bullae, porphyria), others (bullous LP, bullous mastocytosis)

**Q2. Explain the pathogenesis of pemphigus (desmoglein compensation theory).**
- IgG (mainly IgG4) autoantibodies against desmogleins (desmosomal cadherins) → loss of keratinocyte adhesion (acantholysis) via steric hindrance and signalling (p38 MAPK)
- Dsg1 expressed mostly in superficial epidermis, Dsg3 in deep epidermis and mucosa (where Dsg1 is scant)
- Mucosal-dominant PV: anti-Dsg3 only (mucosa fails, skin protected by Dsg1); mucocutaneous PV: anti-Dsg3 + anti-Dsg1 (suprabasal split in skin and mucosa); PF: anti-Dsg1 only (subcorneal split in skin; mucosa protected by Dsg3)
- Same theory explains bullous impetigo/SSSS (exfoliative toxin cleaves Dsg1)
- Genetic: HLA-DRB1*04:02, DQB1*05:03; triggers — drugs (thiol drugs like penicillamine, captopril), UV, burns, pregnancy, stress, diet (garlic, thiols)

**Q3. Clinical features of pemphigus vulgaris.**
- Age 40–60; oral erosions first in ~70% (buccal mucosa, palate, gingiva) — may precede skin by months; painful, slow-healing
- Flaccid blisters on normal skin of scalp, face, axillae, groin, trunk → rupture to painful erosions that bleed and enlarge; heal without scars (hyperpigmentation)
- Nikolsky sign and bulla spread (Asboe-Hansen) positive
- Other mucosae: conjunctiva, nose, larynx (hoarseness), pharynx, oesophagus, genitals, anus; nails — paronychia, haemorrhages

**Q4. Clinical features of pemphigus foliaceus.**
- Superficial flaccid blisters rarely seen; scaly crusted erosions with 'cornflake' scales in seborrhoeic distribution (face, scalp, upper trunk); no mucosal involvement; may become erythrodermic
- Pemphigus erythematosus (Senear–Usher): localised PF of malar area with lupus serology/ DIF overlap
- Endemic PF (fogo selvagem — Brazil) linked to black fly bites
- Drug-induced: thiol drugs more often PF pattern

**Q5. What is paraneoplastic pemphigus?**
- Associated with lymphoproliferative neoplasms (non-Hodgkin lymphoma, CLL, Castleman disease, thymoma)
- Severe intractable stomatitis (lips, tongue), polymorphic skin lesions (PV-like, BP-like, EM-like, lichenoid, GVHD-like), conjunctivitis; bronchiolitis obliterans (often fatal)
- Antibodies to plakins (envoplakin, periplakin, desmoplakin), Dsg3, A2ML1; IIF on rat bladder epithelium positive
- Poor prognosis; treat tumour, rituximab, IVIG

**Q6. Tzanck smear in pemphigus.**
- Scraping from base of a fresh bulla stained with Giemsa: acantholytic cells — rounded keratinocytes with large hyperchromatic nuclei, perinuclear halo and condensed peripheral cytoplasm ('fried-egg' appearance) — screening test only; also seen in SSSS, Hailey–Hailey, Darier's, herpes

**Q7. Describe the role of immunofluorescence (PYQ).**
- DIF (perilesional skin in Michel's medium) — gold standard: pemphigus — intercellular IgG/C3 in fish-net/chicken-wire pattern (PF more upper epidermis); BP — linear IgG/C3 along BMZ; DH — granular IgA in dermal papillae; LABD — linear IgA; lupus — granular IgG/IgM/C3 at BMZ (lupus band)
- IIF (patient serum): pemphigus on monkey oesophagus (PV) or guinea-pig oesophagus (PF) — titre correlates with activity; salt-split skin — roof binding (BP, LABD) vs floor binding (EBA, anti-laminin 332 MMP, anti-p200, bullous SLE)
- ELISA: anti-Dsg1, Dsg3 (indices track disease activity, guide stopping therapy), BP180 (NC16A), BP230, collagen VII; BIOCHIP multiplex

**Q8. Histopathology of PV, PF and BP.**
- PV: suprabasal cleft with acantholysis, basal cells attached to the floor like a 'row of tombstones', eosinophilic spongiosis early
- PF: subcorneal/granular layer split with acantholysis
- BP: subepidermal blister with eosinophils (cell-rich), eosinophilic spongiosis in urticarial phase; cell-poor in some

**Q9. Write a short note on Nikolsky sign (PYQ).**
- Dislodgement of the epidermis by lateral pressure on apparently normal skin — indicates intraepidermal loss of cohesion
- Positive: pemphigus (PV, PF), SSSS, TEN (on erythematous skin), EB (some), bullous impetigo; negative in BP, DH, EBA
- Variants: marginal Nikolsky (extension of blister edge), direct (on normal skin away from lesions), Asboe-Hansen (bulla-spread) sign, Sheklakov's sign

**Q10. Clinical features of bullous pemphigoid (BP).**
- Commonest autoimmune blistering disease; elderly (>70); IgG against BP180 (collagen XVII, NC16A domain) and BP230 in hemidesmosomes
- Prodromal (non-bullous) phase: itchy urticarial or eczematous plaques for weeks–months
- Tense, large, clear or haemorrhagic blisters on normal or erythematous skin of flexures, lower abdomen, thighs; heal without scars (milia occasionally); mucosa involved in 10–30% (mild)
- Associations: neurological disease (dementia, Parkinson's, stroke), drugs (DPP-4 inhibitors — gliptins, especially vildagliptin; loop diuretics, spironolactone, PD-1 inhibitors), psoriasis (and its phototherapy)

**Q11. Differentiate pemphigus vulgaris from bullous pemphigoid.**
- PV: middle age, mucosa almost always, flaccid fragile blisters, erosions predominate, Nikolsky +, suprabasal acantholysis, intercellular IgG on DIF, anti-Dsg3/1, more severe, needs immunosuppression
- BP: elderly, mucosa rarely, tense intact blisters, intense itch, Nikolsky –, subepidermal blister with eosinophils, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ, anti-BP180/230, can respond to topical steroids

**Q12. Management of pemphigus.**
- General: admit severe disease; barrier nursing, fluid–electrolyte, nutrition, wound care (non-adherent dressings, saline/potassium permanganate soaks), pain control, oral care (steroid mouthwash, lignocaine), treat infections, eye/ENT care
- Severity: PDAI (Pemphigus Disease Area Index) or ABSIS
- First line: systemic prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day with steroid-sparing adjuvant (azathioprine 2–2.5 mg/kg after TPMT check, or mycophenolate mofetil 2–3 g/day) — as in our treatment ladder
- Rituximab (anti-CD20) — highly effective: rheumatoid arthritis protocol 1 g IV on day 1 and day 15 (or lymphoma protocol 375 mg/m² weekly × 4), with short steroid; maintenance 500 mg at 6 months/relapse — international guidelines now place it first-line for moderate–severe PV (Ritux 3 trial)
- Other options: dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP — Pasricha; Indian regimen), IVIG 2 g/kg/cycle monthly (useful in infections/refractory/pregnancy), cyclophosphamide, plasmapheresis/immunoadsorption, dapsone (PF), methotrexate, newer: BTK inhibitors, FcRn blockers (efgartigimod) under study
- Prophylaxis while on steroids: calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonate, PPI, deworming (ivermectin/albendazole — strongyloides), TB screening, blood sugar/BP monitoring, PCP prophylaxis with rituximab in some, HBV screening before rituximab

**Q13. Discuss pulse therapy (PYQ).**
- Administration of supra-pharmacological doses of drugs intermittently to achieve faster response and reduce long-term side effects
- Dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP, Pasricha 1984): dexamethasone 100 mg in 500 ml 5% dextrose IV over 2 h on 3 consecutive days + cyclophosphamide 500 mg IV on day 1, repeated every 4 weeks; plus oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg daily between pulses
- Phases: I — pulses + daily cyclophosphamide until complete remission; II — continue pulses for 9 months; III — oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg daily for 9 months; IV — no treatment (follow-up)
- Side effects: hyperglycaemia, hypertension, arrhythmia, electrolyte disturbance, infections; cyclophosphamide — haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna, hydration), infertility/amenorrhoea, bone marrow suppression, malignancy
- Other pulses: methylprednisolone pulse 1 g × 3 days, dexamethasone–azathioprine pulse, oral mini-pulse (OMP) for vitiligo/LP

**Q14. Comment on the role of diet in pemphigus (PYQ).**
- Thiol-containing foods (garlic, onion, leek, chives) and phenol/tannin-rich foods (tea, betel nut, mango, cassava) and isothiocyanates (mustard) reported to trigger acantholysis in susceptible persons — advise moderation
- Practical: soft bland high-protein diet for oral lesions, avoid spicy/hard foods; diabetic and low-salt diet while on steroids; adequate calcium and vitamin D

**Q15. Management of bullous pemphigoid.**
- Localised/mild: super-potent topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% (whole body 30–40 g/day in extensive disease — as effective as oral steroids with fewer deaths, French trial)
- Doxycycline 200 mg/day ± nicotinamide (BLISTER trial — non-inferior, safer than prednisolone in elderly)
- Moderate–severe: prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day with taper; adjuvants — methotrexate (low dose, elderly), azathioprine, mycophenolate, dapsone
- Refractory: rituximab, IVIG, omalizumab, dupilumab (approved for BP in some countries — confirm), stop culprit drug (gliptin)
- Care: skin — drain tense blisters with sterile needle leaving roof, wound care; monitor steroid complications in elderly

**Q16. Discuss differential diagnosis of bullae in children (PYQ).**
- Infective: bullous impetigo, SSSS, varicella, HSV, hand-foot-mouth disease
- Genetic: epidermolysis bullosa, incontinentia pigmenti (vesicular stage), bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, Hailey–Hailey (adolescents), bullous mastocytosis, porphyria (CEP, EPP)
- Immune: chronic bullous disease of childhood (linear IgA — 'string of pearls'/cluster of jewels around genitals and face), childhood BP, juvenile PV (rare), DH, bullous SLE
- Others: insect bite bullae, burns/scalds (child abuse), friction blisters, fixed drug eruption, SJS/TEN, Kawasaki (desquamation), phytophotodermatitis

**Q17. Write short notes on pemphigoid gestationis (PYQ).**
- Rare autoimmune subepidermal blistering disease of pregnancy (2nd–3rd trimester) or puerperium; IgG1 against BP180 (complement-fixing); HLA-DR3/DR4 association; linked to molar pregnancy and choriocarcinoma
- Itchy urticarial papules/plaques starting around the umbilicus then tense blisters spreading to trunk and limbs (face, mucosa spared); flares at delivery; recurs in subsequent pregnancies (earlier and more severe) and with OCP
- DIF: linear C3 (± IgG) at BMZ — distinguishes from polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (DIF negative, starts in striae, spares umbilicus)
- Fetal: small-for-gestational-age, prematurity, transient neonatal blisters (passive antibodies)
- Treatment: potent topical steroids, oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day; antihistamines; IVIG/cyclosporine for refractory

**Q18. Name the dermatoses of pregnancy.**
- Pemphigoid gestationis, polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPPP), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (itch without primary lesions, raised bile acids — fetal risk, ursodeoxycholic acid), atopic eruption of pregnancy (commonest — eczema/prurigo, early onset)

**Q19. What is dermatitis herpetiformis?**
- Cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease); IgA against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3)
- Intensely itchy grouped papulovesicles/excoriations on extensors (elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp, shoulders), symmetrical
- Histology: neutrophilic microabscesses in dermal papillae; DIF: granular IgA in dermal papillae (diagnostic)
- Treatment: strict lifelong gluten-free diet (reduces lymphoma risk), dapsone (rapid itch relief — check G6PD), sulfapyridine

**Q20. Prognosis and remission definitions in pemphigus.**
- Mortality fell from ~75% pre-steroid era to <5–10% now (mostly infections and steroid complications)
- Complete remission off therapy: no new lesions for ≥2 months off all systemic therapy; complete remission on minimal therapy: prednisolone ≤10 mg/day (and/or minimal adjuvant) for ≥2 months; relapse: ≥3 new lesions/month not healing in 1 week (consensus definitions)

**Q21. What are the variants of pemphigus vulgaris?**
- Pemphigus vegetans — Neumann type (erosions heal with vegetations, more severe) and Hallopeau type (pustules evolve to vegetations, milder) in flexures, scalp
- Pemphigus herpetiformis (itchy annular vesicles like DH, anti-Dsg1/3), drug-induced (thiol — penicillamine, captopril; non-thiol — rifampicin, NSAIDs), IgA pemphigus (subcorneal pustular dermatosis type — desmocollin 1; intraepidermal neutrophilic type)

**Q22. What is the pemphigus disease area index (PDAI)?**
- Validated activity/damage score: skin (12 sites, 0–10 each), scalp (0–10), mucosa (12 sites, 0–10) activity + damage (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation) — total activity 0–250; mild <15, moderate 15–45, significant >45
- ABSIS (Autoimmune Bullous Skin Disorder Intensity Score) is an alternative

**Q23. What is the rituximab protocol and monitoring?**
- RA protocol: 1 g IV on day 1 and day 15 (premedicate — paracetamol, antihistamine, methylprednisolone 100 mg); lymphoma protocol 375 mg/m² weekly × 4
- Before: HBsAg/anti-HBc (reactivation), HCV, HIV, TB screen, CBC, immunoglobulins, pregnancy test; avoid live vaccines
- After: CD19/CD20 B-cell counts, anti-Dsg titres; maintenance 500 mg at 6 months (and/or 12, 18) if Dsg ELISA remains high; side effects — infusion reactions, infections, hypogammaglobulinaemia, late neutropenia, PML (rare)

**Q24. What is mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP)?**
- Subepidermal autoimmune blistering disease mainly of mucosae (oral — desquamative gingivitis 85%, ocular — conjunctival scarring, symblepharon, blindness; nasal, laryngeal, oesophageal, genital) with scarring
- Antigens: BP180 (C-terminal), laminin 332 (associated with malignancy), α6β4 integrin (ocular)
- Treatment by risk: low-risk (oral/skin only) — topical steroids, dapsone, tetracyclines; high-risk (ocular, laryngeal, oesophageal) — cyclophosphamide/rituximab, IVIG, systemic steroids; ophthalmology follow-up

**Q25. What is epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA)?**
- Autoantibodies (IgG) against type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils) — mechanobullous type (trauma-induced blisters on extensors healing with scars and milia, nail loss) and inflammatory BP-like type; association with Crohn's disease
- Diagnosis: DIF linear IgG at BMZ with u-serrated pattern, salt-split skin floor binding, ELISA collagen VII
- Treatment difficult: colchicine, dapsone, steroids, rituximab, IVIG

**Q26. What is linear IgA bullous dermatosis?**
- Linear IgA deposits at BMZ against LAD-1/BP180 (97/120 kDa) — children (chronic bullous disease of childhood: annular 'string of pearls'/'cluster of jewels' blisters around genitals, face) and adults (drug-induced — vancomycin commonest, also captopril, NSAIDs, lithium)
- Treatment: dapsone (rapid), sulfapyridine, steroids; stop drug

**Q27. What are the salt-split skin findings and their use?**
- Incubating normal skin in 1 M NaCl splits through lamina lucida; IIF with patient serum: roof (epidermal) binding — BP, pemphigoid gestationis, MMP (BP180), LABD; floor (dermal) binding — EBA, anti-laminin 332 MMP, anti-p200 pemphigoid, bullous SLE

**Q28. Describe the steroid side effects to monitor in pemphigus patients.**
- Metabolic: hyperglycaemia, hypertension, weight gain, dyslipidaemia, hypokalaemia
- Bone: osteoporosis, avascular necrosis of femoral head; eyes: cataract, glaucoma; GI: peptic ulcer; infections: TB, fungal, strongyloides hyperinfection, PCP; skin: striae, acne, atrophy; psychiatric; HPA suppression (taper slowly)
- Prophylaxis: calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonate, PPI, albendazole/ivermectin, isoniazid prophylaxis if latent TB, regular sugar/BP checks

**Q29. Why does pemphigus flare in pregnancy and how is it managed?**
- Hormonal/immune changes — flares in first trimester and postpartum; neonatal pemphigus from transplacental IgG (transient blisters, resolve in weeks)
- Treatment: lowest dose prednisolone, topical steroids, IVIG (safe), azathioprine (if needed); avoid mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate; rituximab avoided (B-cell depletion in neonate)

**Q30. What is the role of anti-desmoglein ELISA?**
- Quantitative anti-Dsg1 and anti-Dsg3 IgG: confirms diagnosis, defines phenotype (mucosal vs mucocutaneous vs foliaceus), monitors activity — Dsg3 index correlates with mucosal, Dsg1 with skin activity; persistently high titres after remission predict relapse; useful to decide rituximab maintenance and stopping therapy

**Q31. Bullous diseases associated with neurological disorders — explain.**
- Bullous pemphigoid is strongly associated with dementia, Parkinson's disease, stroke, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis — shared BP180/BP230 antigen isoforms expressed in the CNS; neurological disease often precedes BP by years

## Quick spotter facts
- Row of tombstones — PV
- Fish-net intercellular IgG — pemphigus; linear IgG/C3 BMZ — BP; granular IgA in papillae — DH
- Dsg compensation: Dsg3 only = mucosal PV; Dsg1 only = PF

## Note
Our treatment ladder: 1st line steroid + azathioprine; 2nd rituximab/MMF; 3rd DCP/IVIG (her decision). Rituximab first-line in international guidelines is mentioned for viva awareness.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Autoimmune vesiculobullous disorders); Indian consensus on pemphigus (IADVL/ IJDVL) and rituximab use. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Vitiligo — viva
posts.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 30 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Vitiligo** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. Define vitiligo.**
- Acquired, chronic depigmenting disorder characterised by well-defined milky-white (amelanotic) macules and patches due to selective loss of functional melanocytes from the epidermis and/or hair follicles
- Prevalence ~0.5–2% worldwide; India 0.5–2.5% (higher in Gujarat, Rajasthan); no sex predilection; ~50% begin before 20 years

**Q2. Describe melanogenesis briefly and the role of melanocytes in depigmentary disorders (PYQ).**
- Melanocytes (neural crest origin) in basal layer, ratio ~1:36 keratinocytes (epidermal melanin unit); tyrosine → DOPA → dopaquinone (tyrosinase) → eumelanin (brown-black, via TRP-1, TRP-2/DCT) or pheomelanin (red-yellow, with cysteine); melanosomes (stages I–IV) transferred to keratinocytes via dendrites
- Regulation: MC1R (α-MSH), SCF/c-KIT, endothelin-1, HGF, bFGF, UV via p53-POMC; Wnt/β-catenin, MITF master regulator
- Depigmentary disorders: absent melanocytes (vitiligo, piebaldism, Waardenburg), normal melanocytes with reduced melanin (albinism — tyrosinase defect, nevus depigmentosus — transfer defect, pityriasis alba, PIH), destroyed melanocytes (chemical leucoderma, leprosy, scars)

**Q3. Discuss current concepts in aetiopathogenesis (PYQ).**
- Convergence theory — combination of: (1) genetic susceptibility (polygenic — NLRP1, PTPN22, TYR, HLA-A*02, FOXP3; ~20% family history); (2) melanocyte intrinsic defects — oxidative stress (H2O2 accumulation, low catalase), unfolded protein response, impaired adhesion (melanocytorrhagy — reduced E-cadherin, DDR1); (3) autoimmunity — innate (HSP70i, NK cells, IL-1β, NLRP inflammasome) and adaptive — melanocyte-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells producing IFN-γ → keratinocyte CXCL9/10 → CXCR3 recruitment (JAK–STAT pathway — basis of JAK inhibitors); resident memory T cells explain relapse at same sites; reduced Tregs
- Other theories: neural (segmental — neurochemical mediators), biochemical (tetrahydrobiopterin, catecholamines), viral, intrinsic adhesion defect

**Q4. Classify vitiligo (VGICC 2012).**
- Non-segmental vitiligo (NSV — 'vitiligo'): acrofacial, mucosal (≥2 sites), generalised (vulgaris), universal (>80% BSA), mixed (NSV + SV), rare variants (punctata, minor/hypochromic, follicular)
- Segmental vitiligo (SV): uni-, bi- or plurisegmental — early onset, rapid spread then stable, leukotrichia common, poor response to medical therapy but excellent to grafting
- Unclassified/undetermined: focal (isolated macule not segmental, <2 years), mucosal (single site)

**Q5. How do you assess activity and stability?**
- Signs of activity: Koebner phenomenon (type IIb — experimentally induced; VIDA), confetti-like depigmentation, trichrome/quadrichrome/pentachrome patches, inflammatory vitiligo (raised red border), ill-defined borders, new lesions/enlargement in last 3–12 months
- VIDA (Vitiligo Disease Activity score): +4 active in ≤6 weeks, +3 in 6 weeks–3 months, +2 in 3–6 months, +1 in 6–12 months, 0 stable ≥1 year, −1 stable with spontaneous repigmentation ≥1 year
- Extent: VASI (Vitiligo Area Scoring Index — hand units × % depigmentation), VETF, F-VASI/T-VASI; VitiQoL for quality of life
- Dermoscopy: active — trichrome, starburst/comet-tail, micro-Koebner; stable — sharp border, perifollicular pigmentation (repigmenting), reversed pigment network

**Q6. What is the Wood's lamp finding and its use?**
- 365 nm UVA: bright chalk-white (blue-white) fluorescence of depigmented skin with sharp border — accentuates lesions in fair skin, distinguishes depigmentation (vitiligo) from hypopigmentation (dull off-white), helps monitor activity and repigmentation

**Q7. Associated diseases.**
- Autoimmune thyroid disease (commonest — Hashimoto's, Graves'), alopecia areata, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, psoriasis, myasthenia gravis, inflammatory bowel disease, APS (autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes)
- Eye: uveitis, retinal pigment changes; ear: sensorineural hearing loss (rare)
- Syndromes: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada (uveitis, meningism, dysacusis, vitiligo, poliosis), Alezzandrini (unilateral facial vitiligo, poliosis, retinitis, deafness)

**Q8. Differential diagnosis.**
- Congenital: piebaldism (white forelock, stable from birth), nevus depigmentosus (off-white, stable), Waardenburg, tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf), hypomelanosis of Ito
- Acquired hypopigmentation: pityriasis alba, pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, indeterminate/ tuberculoid leprosy (sensory loss), idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, progressive macular hypomelanosis, hypopigmented MF
- Depigmentation: chemical leucoderma (para-tertiary butyl phenol, monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, bindi/footwear adhesives — confetti macules at contact site), DLE, lichen sclerosus, morphoea, scars, halo naevus, leucoderma in melanoma (immunotherapy-related)

**Q9. Histopathology.**
- Absence of melanocytes and melanin in lesional epidermis (confirmed with Fontana–Masson, MART-1/Melan-A, HMB-45 immunostaining); active border — superficial perivascular and lichenoid lymphocytes (CD8)

**Q10. Investigations.**
- Clinical diagnosis with Wood's lamp; thyroid function and anti-TPO antibodies (annually if positive), CBC, fasting glucose, vitamin B12 if indicated; biopsy only if doubtful

**Q11. Discuss therapeutic options in vitiligo (PYQ).**
- Halting activity: oral mini-pulse (OMP) — betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg on 2 consecutive days per week for 3–6 months (Pasricha), short oral steroids; methotrexate, minocycline, azathioprine, cyclosporine for rapidly progressive disease
- Topical: potent/mid-potency corticosteroids (limited/extra-facial), calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1% — face, neck, genitals), ruxolitinib 1.5% cream (topical JAK — FDA 2022 for NSV ≥12 y), calcipotriol (with steroid), topical PUVA/psoralen + sunlight (PUVAsol)
- Phototherapy: NB-UVB (311 nm, 2–3 times/week — first line for generalised; ≥6–12 months; best on face, neck, trunk; poor on acral and lips), excimer laser/light 308 nm (targeted, localised), PUVA (older)
- Systemic JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, ritlecitinib, upadacitinib) with phototherapy — emerging
- Antioxidants (Polypodium leucotomos, vitamin E, ginkgo biloba, α-lipoic acid), afamelanotide (with NB-UVB) — adjuncts
- Depigmentation for extensive (>50–80%) recalcitrant disease: monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone 20%, 4-methoxyphenol, Q-switched ruby/alexandrite laser, cryotherapy
- Camouflage (cosmetic cover, dihydroxyacetone, micropigmentation/tattooing for lips), counselling, support groups

**Q12. Discuss surgical management of vitiligo (PYQ).**
- Indications: stable vitiligo (no new lesion/extension for ≥1 year; positive minigraft test — repigmentation spread from a test graft after 3 months), segmental and focal vitiligo, resistant areas after medical therapy; avoid in keloid tendency and active disease
- Tissue grafts: punch/mini-punch grafting (1–1.5 mm; cobblestoning side effect), split-thickness skin grafting (thin STSG — good for large areas), suction blister epidermal grafting (best cosmetic match, no scarring at recipient), hair follicle grafts (leucotrichia)
- Cellular grafts: non-cultured epidermal cell suspension (melanocyte–keratinocyte transplantation, MKTP/ReCell), non-cultured extracted hair follicle outer root sheath cell suspension, cultured melanocytes
- Post-operative NB-UVB/PUVAsol improves results; complications — infection, cobblestoning, colour mismatch, Koebner at donor site, graft rejection; lips and acral areas respond less

**Q13. What is leucotrichia's significance?**
- White hairs in vitiligo patches indicate loss of the follicular melanocyte reservoir — poor prognosis for medical repigmentation (repigmentation normally starts perifollicularly); surgical approaches preferred

**Q14. Prognostic factors.**
- Good: recent onset, younger age, face/neck/trunk lesions, perifollicular repigmentation, dark hair in patches, NSV of short duration
- Poor: acral and lip (lip-tip) vitiligo, mucosal, leucotrichia, long duration, segmental (medically), Koebner positivity, family history, associated autoimmunity, universal type

**Q15. Genetic causes of hypomelanosis (PYQ).**
- Absent melanocytes: piebaldism (KIT), Waardenburg (PAX3, MITF, SOX10, EDNRB/EDN3), Tietz syndrome
- Abnormal melanin synthesis: oculocutaneous albinism (OCA1 TYR, OCA2 OCA2/P gene, OCA3 TYRP1, OCA4 SLC45A2), phenylketonuria
- Melanosome biogenesis/transfer: Hermansky–Pudlak (bleeding, pulmonary fibrosis), Chédiak–Higashi (giant granules, infections), Griscelli (silvery hair)
- Mosaic: hypomelanosis of Ito, nevus depigmentosus; tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules), incontinentia pigmenti (stage 4)

**Q16. Discuss Waardenburg syndrome (PYQ).**
- Autosomal dominant neural-crest disorder: white forelock, congenital sensorineural deafness, heterochromia iridis/ brilliant blue eyes, depigmented patches (piebald-like)
- Types: WS1 (PAX3, dystopia canthorum — lateral displacement of inner canthi), WS2 (MITF/SOX10, no dystopia — deafness commoner), WS3/Klein–Waardenburg (PAX3, limb anomalies), WS4/Shah–Waardenburg (EDNRB/EDN3/SOX10 — with Hirschsprung disease)

**Q17. What is the Koebner phenomenon in vitiligo and how is it classified?**
- Development of vitiligo at sites of trauma; VIDA/ Koebner classification (Van Geel): type 1 — history of Koebner (1a: aligned on a scar, 1b: induced by repeated friction/pressure); type 2 — clinical observation (2a: lesions at friction sites, 2b: linear/scratch-induced); type 3 — experimentally induced
- Presence suggests active, extending disease and poorer response; avoid friction (tight clothes, rubbing)

**Q18. What is inflammatory vitiligo and other unusual presentations?**
- Inflammatory: raised erythematous border, itching — active disease
- Trichrome (white, light-brown intermediate zone, normal), quadrichrome (perifollicular repigmentation), pentachrome (blue-grey PIH), confetti (tiny 1–5 mm macules — rapidly progressive), blue vitiligo (PIH in vitiliginous skin), hypochromic/minor vitiligo (dark skin, partial loss), follicular (leucotrichia with little skin involvement)

**Q19. Explain the oral mini-pulse (OMP).**
- Pasricha regimen: betamethasone or dexamethasone 5 mg (0.1 mg/kg in children) orally on two consecutive days per week (e.g. Saturday–Sunday) for 3–6 months to arrest spread
- Advantages: fewer side effects than daily steroids; side effects — weight gain, insomnia, acne, menstrual irregularity, agitation; not for repigmentation alone — combine with phototherapy/topicals

**Q20. NB-UVB protocol in vitiligo.**
- Twice or thrice weekly (non-consecutive days); start 200–250 mJ/cm² (or fixed by type) and increase 10–20% per session until faint erythema persisting <24 h; continue at least 6 months and up to 12–24 months if repigmenting; ≥25% repigmentation by 3 months predicts response
- Best response: face, neck, trunk; poor: hands, feet, lips, bony prominences; side effects — erythema, itching, xerosis, tanning of normal skin (contrast); combine with tacrolimus/ calcipotriol

**Q21. What are JAK inhibitors' role in vitiligo?**
- IFN-γ signals via JAK1/2–STAT1 to induce CXCL9/10, which recruits CD8 T cells; blocking JAK reduces the inflammation
- Topical ruxolitinib 1.5% cream twice daily (≥12 y, NSV, ≤10% BSA) — facial repigmentation F-VASI75 in ~30% at 24 weeks, rising with longer use
- Oral JAK inhibitors (ritlecitinib, upadacitinib, povorcitinib) in trials/off-label (tofacitinib, baricitinib) — work best with light exposure; monitor infections, lipids, thrombosis

**Q22. What are the patterns of repigmentation?**
- Perifollicular (commonest — from follicular melanocyte reservoir, with phototherapy), marginal (from the edge), diffuse, combined; perifollicular gives best cosmetic result; acral/ glabrous skin lacks follicles hence poor response

**Q23. What is the minigraft (test graft) test?**
- 4–5 punch grafts (1–1.2 mm) placed in the recipient patch; if pigment spreads ≥2–3 mm around grafts within 3 months without Koebner at donor site, disease is stable and suitable for surgery

**Q24. Describe suction blister epidermal grafting technique.**
- Raise blisters on donor site (thigh) using suction syringes/cups (200–400 mmHg) for 1–3 h; recipient site dermabraded or laser-ablated or frozen to raise blister; donor blister roofs transferred and dressed for 7 days; good colour match, no scarring; post-op NB-UVB/PUVAsol

**Q25. Discuss chemical leucoderma.**
- Depigmentation from contact with melanocytotoxic chemicals — phenols/catechols: para-tertiary butyl phenol (adhesives, bindi, footwear, rubber), monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, hair dyes (PPD), detergents, alta, deodorants
- Clues: confetti macules at contact site, history of exposure, may spread beyond (becomes vitiligo in susceptible); stop exposure, treat as vitiligo

**Q26. What are the side effects of topical steroids and tacrolimus in vitiligo?**
- Steroids: atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, acneiform, hypertrichosis — use intermittent (e.g. 5 days a week or 15 days on/off) and avoid face long-term
- Tacrolimus: burning/stinging initially, folliculitis, alcohol flushing; no atrophy — preferred for face, eyelids, flexures, genitals; continue twice weekly for maintenance (prevents relapse)

**Q27. Psychosocial aspects and stigma in India.**
- Confusion with leprosy ('safed daag'), marriage difficulties, depression, anxiety, reduced quality of life; use VitiQoL/DLQI; counselling, camouflage, support groups, patient education that it is not contagious

**Q28. Vitiligo in children — special points.**
- Higher segmental proportion, family history, associated halo naevi, atopy; prefer topical calcineurin inhibitors and mid-potency steroids, NB-UVB from ~6–7 years (cooperative), OMP in active spreading disease; screen thyroid

**Q29. What is the VASI and how is it calculated?**
- Vitiligo Area Scoring Index = Σ (hand units, 1 HU ≈ 1% BSA) × (residual depigmentation: 100, 90, 75, 50, 25, 10, 0%) over body regions (hands, upper limbs, trunk, lower limbs, feet; face separately — F-VASI); range 0–100; VASI50/75 used in trials

**Q30. Melanocyte–keratinocyte transplantation (MKTP) — steps.**
- Harvest thin split-thickness skin (1/10 of recipient area) from thigh, trypsinise (0.25% trypsin 37 °C, 50 min) to separate epidermis, prepare cell suspension in medium/patient's serum, apply to dermabraded/laser-ablated recipient area, cover with collagen dressing; repigmentation over 3–6 months; can treat up to 10 times donor area

## Quick spotter facts
- Chalk-white sharply defined patch with Wood's lamp accentuation — vitiligo
- Trichrome, confetti and Koebner — active disease
- Stability ≥1 year before grafting

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Vitiligo); Vitiligo Global Issues Consensus Conference (VGICC) 2012 classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Warts (verruca) — viva
posts.summary: Viral infections · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Warts (verruca)** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What are warts? Name the virus.**
- Benign epidermal proliferations caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) — non-enveloped double-stranded circular DNA virus, Papillomaviridae; >200 types
- Infects basal keratinocytes through micro-abrasions; replicates as cells differentiate; causes koilocytes

**Q2. Classify cutaneous and mucosal warts with HPV types.**
- Common warts (verruca vulgaris): HPV 2, 4 (27, 57)
- Plantar (myrmecia, deep): HPV 1; mosaic plantar: HPV 2
- Plane (flat) warts: HPV 3, 10
- Butcher's warts: HPV 7
- Anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata): HPV 6, 11 (low risk) — high-risk 16, 18, 31, 33 cause intraepithelial neoplasia
- Epidermodysplasia verruciformis: HPV 5, 8 (beta-HPV)
- Oral: focal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck's disease) HPV 13, 32; recurrent respiratory papillomatosis HPV 6, 11
- Bowenoid papulosis and Buschke–Löwenstein tumour (giant condyloma, HPV 6, 11)

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Common: rough hyperkeratotic papules, fingers/hands/knees; periungual (nail biters); filiform on face/neck
- Plantar: inward-growing painful papule with surrounding callus; interrupted dermatoglyphics; black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on paring
- Plane: flat-topped smooth skin-coloured or brown papules on face/backs of hands; linear in scratch lines (Koebner/pseudo-Koebner)
- Anogenital: soft papillomatous, sessile or pedunculated papules (cauliflower-like)

**Q4. How do you differentiate a plantar wart from a corn (clavus)?**
- Wart: interrupts skin lines, black dots on paring, pain on lateral squeeze (pinching), multiple, not necessarily on pressure points
- Corn: skin lines pass through, central translucent core, no black dots, pain on direct pressure, at pressure points

**Q5. Histopathology of a wart?**
- Hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis in columns over papillomatous peaks, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges bending inwards ('arborisation')
- Koilocytes (vacuolated keratinocytes with pyknotic nucleus and perinuclear halo) in upper spinous/granular layer, coarse keratohyaline granules, dilated capillaries in dermal papillae
- Myrmecia: large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Common: seborrhoeic keratosis, actinic keratosis, SCC/keratoacanthoma, molluscum, TBVC, lichen planus hypertrophic, acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf
- Plane: lichen planus, lichen nitidus, syringomas, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, milia
- Genital: pearly penile papules, Fordyce spots, vestibular papillae, condyloma lata (secondary syphilis — moist, flat), molluscum, bowenoid papulosis, seborrhoeic keratosis

**Q7. Treatment options — classify.**
- Destructive: chemical — salicylic acid 12–26%/lactic acid (first line, cheap), trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin 20–25%/podophyllotoxin 0.5% (genital; not in pregnancy), cantharidin, glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde
- Physical — cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen, every 2–3 weeks), electrocautery/radiofrequency ablation, curettage, CO2/Er:YAG laser, pulsed-dye laser
- Antiproliferative: 5-fluorouracil, bleomycin intralesional, cidofovir, retinoids (plane warts)
- Immunotherapy: imiquimod 5% (genital), sinecatechins, contact sensitisers (DPCP, SADBE), intralesional antigens (MMR, Candida, PPD, Mw vaccine, vitamin D3), oral zinc, cimetidine (weak evidence)

**Q8. What is intralesional immunotherapy? Mention the principle.**
- Injecting an antigen (MMR vaccine, Candida antigen, PPD, Mycobacterium w/MIP, vitamin D3) into one or a few warts induces a Th1 cell-mediated response that clears distant untreated warts too
- Useful for multiple, recalcitrant warts; side effects — pain, flu-like illness; avoid in immunosuppressed and pregnancy (live vaccines)

**Q9. Management of anogenital warts.**
- Patient-applied: podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution/0.15% cream (3 days on, 4 off, up to 4 cycles), imiquimod 5% (3 nights/week up to 16 weeks), sinecatechins 15%
- Provider: cryotherapy, TCA 80–90%, podophyllin 25%, electrocautery, excision, laser
- Pregnancy: cryotherapy/TCA/excision — avoid podophyllin, imiquimod relatively avoided
- Screen for other STIs, examine partner, Pap smear in women; condom use
- In children — consider sexual abuse but also non-sexual (vertical, autoinoculation, hetero-inoculation)

**Q10. What is epidermodysplasia verruciformis? (short note)**
- Rare inherited (mostly autosomal recessive — TMC6/EVER1, TMC8/EVER2, CIB1) susceptibility to beta-HPV (5, 8)
- Widespread plane-wart-like papules and pityriasis versicolor-like macules from childhood
- ~30–60% develop SCC on sun-exposed skin in 4th–5th decade — strict photoprotection; acquired form in HIV/transplant

**Q11. Which HPV vaccines are available? Schedule?**
- Bivalent (16, 18), quadrivalent (6, 11, 16, 18), nonavalent (adds 31, 33, 45, 52, 58), Indian quadrivalent Cervavac (Serum Institute, 2022)
- Best before sexual debut — 9–14 years: 2 doses 6 months apart; ≥15 y: 3 doses (0, 1–2, 6 months); WHO now also allows single dose
- India: HPV vaccination for girls 9–14 years announced for national programme

**Q12. Why are warts common and recalcitrant in transplant recipients?**
- Impaired cell-mediated immunity; HPV persists and lesions progress to SCC (beta-HPV with UV as co-factor)

**Q13. What is Buschke–Löwenstein tumour?**
- Giant condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6/11) — locally destructive, verrucous carcinoma-like; treat with wide surgical excision

**Q14. What is bowenoid papulosis?**
- Multiple small reddish-brown flat papules on genitals of young adults (HPV 16) — histology of SCC in situ, behaviour usually benign; partners risk cervical neoplasia

**Q15. Prognosis of untreated common warts?**
- About two-thirds of warts in children resolve spontaneously within 2 years; regression may show blackening

## Quick spotter facts
- Black dots + interrupted dermatoglyphics — plantar wart
- Koilocytes — HPV
- HPV 5, 8 — epidermodysplasia verruciformis with SCC risk

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections — HPV). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Xanthomas — viva
posts.summary: Nutritional & metabolic · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Xanthomas** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What are xanthomas?**
- Yellowish papules, plaques, nodules or tendon swellings formed by lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in skin/tendons — often markers of hyperlipidaemia (primary or secondary) but can occur with normal lipids (normolipaemic)

**Q2. Describe the clinical types and lipid associations.**
- Eruptive xanthomas: crops of small red-yellow papules with erythematous halo on buttocks, extensors — high triglycerides (types I, IV, V; uncontrolled diabetes) — risk of acute pancreatitis
- Tuberous xanthomas: firm yellow nodules on elbows, knees, buttocks — types II, III (dysbetalipoproteinaemia)
- Tendinous xanthomas: smooth nodules in Achilles tendon, extensor tendons of hands — type IIa familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL receptor defect), also cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, sitosterolaemia
- Planar: xanthelasma palpebrarum (eyelids — commonest; ~50% have normal lipids), palmar crease xanthomas (xanthoma striatum palmare — type III dysbetalipoproteinaemia, pathognomonic), intertriginous (finger webs — homozygous FH), diffuse plane xanthomas (normolipaemic — paraproteinaemia/myeloma)
- Verruciform xanthoma (oral/genital), xanthoma disseminatum (non-LCH histiocytosis, normolipaemic, with diabetes insipidus)

**Q3. Classify primary hyperlipoproteinaemia (Fredrickson — PYQ).**
- Type I: raised chylomicrons (lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II deficiency) — eruptive xanthomas, lipaemia retinalis, pancreatitis, hepatosplenomegaly; childhood
- Type IIa: raised LDL (familial hypercholesterolaemia — LDLR, APOB, PCSK9) — tendon, tuberous xanthomas, xanthelasma, arcus, premature CAD
- Type IIb: raised LDL + VLDL (familial combined) — xanthelasma, tuberous
- Type III: raised IDL/chylomicron remnants (dysbetalipoproteinaemia — apo E2/E2) — palmar crease and tubero-eruptive xanthomas
- Type IV: raised VLDL (familial hypertriglyceridaemia) — eruptive xanthomas; associated diabetes, obesity
- Type V: raised VLDL + chylomicrons — eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis

**Q4. Secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia.**
- Diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, cholestasis (primary biliary cholangitis — planar xanthomas), obesity, alcohol, pancreatitis
- Drugs: oral retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin), oestrogens, corticosteroids, cyclosporine, protease inhibitors, β-blockers, thiazides, olanzapine

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Dermal collections of foam cells (macrophages with lipid vacuoles), Touton giant cells (wreath of nuclei), extracellular cholesterol clefts (tuberous/tendinous), inflammation in eruptive xanthomas
- Lipids dissolved during processing — frozen section + Oil Red O / Sudan stains show lipid

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Fasting lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides), lipoprotein electrophoresis, apo E genotype (type III)
- Blood sugar/HbA1c, thyroid function, renal function, urine protein, LFT
- Serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation for plane xanthomas with normal lipids
- Cardiovascular risk assessment (ECG, lipid targets); family screening for FH

**Q7. Write short notes on Tangier's disease (PYQ).**
- Autosomal recessive ABCA1 deficiency → almost absent HDL; cholesterol esters accumulate in reticuloendothelial tissues — enlarged orange-yellow tonsils (pathognomonic), hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, premature atherosclerosis, corneal clouding

**Q8. Treatment of xanthomas.**
- Treat underlying lipid disorder: diet, weight loss, exercise, glycaemic control, treat hypothyroidism; statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors (FH), fibrates/omega-3 for hypertriglyceridaemia — eruptive xanthomas regress in weeks with TG control
- Local for xanthelasma/persistent lesions: TCA 50–70% application, surgical excision, CO2/Er:YAG/Q-switched/fractional lasers, radiofrequency, cryotherapy, intralesional pingyangmycin/bleomycin
- Tendon xanthomas regress slowly with aggressive lipid lowering; surgery only if functional problems

**Q9. Significance of xanthelasma.**
- Commonest xanthoma; ~50% normolipaemic but independently linked with myocardial infarction and atherosclerosis risk (Copenhagen study) — always check lipids and CV risk

**Q10. What is xanthelasma treatment in detail?**
- TCA 50–100% careful application (risk of scarring/ hypopigmentation), surgical excision (blepharoplasty for large), CO2/ Er:YAG ablation, Q-switched Nd:YAG, radiofrequency, cryotherapy; recurrence ~40%; treat dyslipidaemia

**Q11. What are normolipaemic plane xanthomas?**
- Diffuse yellow-orange plaques on eyelids, neck, trunk, flexures with normal lipids — associated with monoclonal gammopathy, multiple myeloma, lymphoma, Castleman disease; check SPEP/ immunofixation

**Q12. What is necrobiotic xanthogranuloma?**
- Indurated yellow-red plaques, especially periorbital, with atrophy/ ulceration; strongly associated with IgG paraproteinaemia/ myeloma; histology — palisading granulomas with necrobiosis, cholesterol clefts, Touton giant cells; treat with IVIG, chlorambucil, treat myeloma

**Q13. What is cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis?**
- Autosomal recessive CYP27A1 defect (bile acid synthesis) → cholestanol accumulation: tendon xanthomas (Achilles) with normal cholesterol, juvenile cataracts, chronic diarrhoea, progressive neurological dysfunction; treat with chenodeoxycholic acid

**Q14. Lipid-lowering drugs — skin-relevant points.**
- Statins (HMG-CoA reductase) — myopathy, lichenoid/ DM-like eruptions rarely; fibrates for high TG (eruptive xanthomas); ezetimibe; PCSK9 inhibitors (FH); niacin — flushing (aspirin pre-treatment)

**Q15. Juvenile xanthogranuloma — differentiate from xanthoma.**
- JXG: non-Langerhans histiocytosis in infants/ children — solitary or multiple yellow-orange-red papules/ nodules on head/neck, normal lipids, spontaneous regression in 3–6 years; 'setting sun' dermoscopy; Touton cells; eye involvement (iris — hyphaema, glaucoma); association with NF1 ± JMML

## Quick spotter facts
- Crops of yellow papules with red halo on buttocks — eruptive xanthomas (high TG → pancreatitis risk)
- Palmar crease xanthomas — type III
- Achilles tendon xanthoma — familial hypercholesterolaemia

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Xanthomas and lipid disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Xeroderma pigmentosum — viva
posts.summary: Genodermatoses · 25 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Xeroderma pigmentosum** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)?**
- Rare autosomal recessive disorder of nucleotide excision repair (NER) of UV-induced DNA damage (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, 6-4 photoproducts) — complementation groups XPA–XPG and variant (XPV — POLH, defective translesion synthesis); commoner with consanguinity (India, Middle East, Japan)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Infancy: acute exaggerated sunburn on minimal exposure (in ~50% — XPA, XPB, XPD, XPF, XPG), photophobia
- Early childhood: freckling (lentigines) on sun-exposed skin by 2 years, xerosis, poikiloderma (atrophy, telangiectasia, mottled hyper/hypopigmentation)
- Skin cancers: >10,000-fold risk of NMSC before 20 years (median age of first NMSC ~9 y) and ~2000-fold melanoma risk; also tongue tip SCC
- Eyes: photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, ectropion, corneal clouding, ocular surface tumours
- Neurological (~25%, XPA, XPD): progressive neurodegeneration — sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, areflexia, ataxia, intellectual decline; De Sanctis–Cacchione syndrome (XP + dwarfism, hypogonadism, severe neurological)
- Internal malignancies: CNS tumours, leukaemia, lung

**Q3. Enumerate disorders caused by defective DNA repair (PYQ).**
- Xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome (cachectic dwarfism, photosensitivity without cancer, pigmentary retinopathy — ERCC6/8), trichothiodystrophy (brittle sulphur-deficient hair with tiger-tail banding under polarised light — PIBIDS), XP–Cockayne overlap, UV-sensitive syndrome, Bloom syndrome (BLM helicase — photosensitive malar telangiectatic erythema, short stature, immunodeficiency, cancers; high sister chromatid exchange), Rothmund–Thomson (RECQL4 — poikiloderma from infancy, sparse hair, skeletal defects, osteosarcoma), Werner syndrome (adult progeria — WRN), ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM), Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita (telomere maintenance), Muir–Torre/Lynch (mismatch repair)

**Q4. Write a short note on Rothmund–Thomson and Bloom syndromes (PYQ).**
- Rothmund–Thomson (poikiloderma congenitale): AR RECQL4; erythema and blistering of cheeks at 3–6 months spreading to extremities → poikiloderma, sparse hair/eyebrows, juvenile cataracts, short stature, radial ray defects, dental anomalies; osteosarcoma and skin cancers
- Bloom: AR BLM; growth retardation, narrow face, photosensitive butterfly telangiectatic erythema, CALMs, immunodeficiency, infertility, very high risk of leukaemia/lymphoma and other cancers early in life

**Q5. Diagnosis.**
- Clinical; DNA repair assays — unscheduled DNA synthesis in cultured fibroblasts after UV, host-cell reactivation, comet assay; post-UV cell survival; molecular genetic testing for the complementation group; prenatal diagnosis possible

**Q6. Management.**
- Rigorous lifelong UV protection: avoid daylight (night activities — 'children of the night'), UV-protective clothing, face shields, UV-blocking films on windows, broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreens, sunglasses; vitamin D supplementation
- Skin surveillance every 3–6 months by dermatologist; early excision of premalignant/malignant lesions; field therapy (5-FU, imiquimod), PDT; oral retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin) for chemoprevention; nicotinamide; T4 endonuclease V liposome lotion (experimental)
- Eye: methylcellulose drops, protective eyewear; neurological and audiological follow-up; genetic counselling
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors highly effective for advanced cancers in XP (high mutational burden)

**Q7. Describe the genetic complementation groups.**
- Autosomal recessive defects of nucleotide excision repair (NER): XP-A to XP-G (XPA — severe neurological disease, Japan; XPC — commonest worldwide, no neurology; XPD — overlaps with trichothiodystrophy/Cockayne), plus XP variant (POLH — translesion DNA polymerase η, normal NER, milder, adult onset)

**Q8. What cancers develop and at what age?**
- Median age of first NMSC ~9 years (vs ~60 in general population) — BCC, SCC, melanoma (≈ 2000-fold risk for NMSC, 2000× melanoma before age 20); ocular (conjunctival SCC, corneal clouding), tongue tip SCC; internal cancers (CNS, lung, leukaemia) somewhat increased

**Q9. Neurological features.**
- In ~25% (mainly XPA, XPD): progressive sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, intellectual decline, ataxia, areflexia, peripheral neuropathy — De Sanctis–Cacchione syndrome (with dwarfism and hypogonadism)

**Q10. Explain nucleotide excision repair and why its defect causes skin cancer.**
- UV (mainly UVB) produces cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts in DNA; NER recognises (XPC, XPE), unwinds (XPB, XPD — TFIIH), excises (XPG, XPF–ERCC1) the damaged segment and polymerase fills the gap
- Defect → unrepaired UV lesions → C→T and CC→TT 'UV signature' mutations in p53, PTCH1, oncogenes → early skin cancers; neurons (oxidative DNA damage repaired by NER) degenerate → neurological disease

**Q11. Describe the cutaneous course of XP.**
- Severe sunburn on minimal exposure in ~50% (XPA, XPD) from infancy; others show early freckling (by age 2) without burning (XPC, XPE)
- Progressive photoageing: xerosis, poikiloderma (hypo/hyperpigmentation, telangiectasia, atrophy), actinic keratoses, keratoacanthomas, BCC, SCC, melanoma (lentigo maligna) in childhood on face, lips, tip of tongue

**Q12. Ocular involvement.**
- Photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, corneal opacification, ectropion, loss of eyelashes, conjunctival/ corneal SCC and melanoma of exposed eye; protection with UV-blocking glasses, lubricants

**Q13. How is XP diagnosed?**
- Clinical features + cellular tests: unscheduled DNA synthesis (UDS) in cultured fibroblasts after UV, UV-sensitivity/ host-cell reactivation assays, recovery of RNA synthesis; molecular genetic testing (complementation group); prenatal diagnosis possible

**Q14. Photoprotection measures in XP (practical).**
- Avoid all daylight UV — stay indoors in daytime, UV-blocking films on windows and car glass, UV meters, protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats with UV-protective face shields, gloves, high SPF broad-spectrum sunscreens reapplied, wrap-around UV sunglasses; 'children of the night' — schooling arrangements
- Vitamin D supplementation (deficiency due to sun avoidance)

**Q15. Treatment of skin lesions in XP.**
- Frequent (3–6 monthly) full-skin examinations; early excision of suspicious lesions (Mohs for facial tumours), cryotherapy/ curettage for small lesions; field therapy for AKs — 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT (caution), chemical peels/ dermabrasion; oral retinoids (isotretinoin/ acitretin) for chemoprevention; nicotinamide; T4 endonuclease V liposome lotion (experimental); immunotherapy (PD-1 inhibitors) for advanced cancers — XP tumours respond well (high mutation burden); radiotherapy can be used when needed (repair of ionising-radiation damage is intact) but with caution

**Q16. Differentiate XP from other photosensitive genodermatoses.**
- Cockayne syndrome (CSA/CSB — photosensitivity without increased cancer, cachectic dwarfism, 'bird-like' face, progeria, cataracts, retinal pigmentation, neurodegeneration)
- Trichothiodystrophy (XPD/TTDN1 — brittle sulphur-deficient hair with 'tiger-tail' banding on polarised light, ichthyosis, intellectual disability, photosensitivity, no cancer increase)
- Bloom syndrome (BLM — telangiectatic facial erythema, short stature, immunodeficiency, cancers — leukaemia), Rothmund–Thomson (RECQL4 — poikiloderma from infancy, skeletal defects, osteosarcoma), porphyrias (EPP — burning pain), Hartnup disease, Kindler syndrome

**Q17. Genetic counselling in XP.**
- Autosomal recessive — 25% recurrence; high in consanguineous communities (India, Middle East, North Africa); carrier testing for siblings; prenatal diagnosis

**Q18. Prognosis.**
- Without protection, median survival historically ~32 years (mainly metastatic skin cancer, neurological degeneration); strict photoprotection from early childhood markedly reduces cancers

**Q19. What is the De Sanctis–Cacchione syndrome?**
- Severe XP (usually XPA) with microcephaly, progressive intellectual disability, dwarfism, hypogonadism, sensorineural deafness, spasticity/ ataxia — neurological XP

**Q20. XP variant — how is it different?**
- Defect in DNA polymerase η (POLH) for translesion synthesis; NER normal; milder, later onset (2nd–4th decade) skin cancers, no neurological disease; cellular test — UV sensitivity in presence of caffeine

**Q21. Role of dermatology team in school and social life.**
- Educate teachers/ family, organise indoor activities, UV-safe classrooms (film on windows, LED lighting low-UV), psychological support, support groups ('XP Family Support')

**Q22. Internal and other cancers in XP.**
- ~10–20 fold increased internal cancers — CNS tumours (gliomas), lung (smokers), haematological (leukaemia), thyroid; avoid smoking and other carcinogens

**Q23. What anaesthesia/ procedural precautions?**
- Light sources in operating theatres and surgical lamps can emit UV — use filters/ LED; minimise fluorescent exposure; ophthalmic procedures need UV protection

**Q24. Why are lip, tongue tip and eyes common tumour sites?**
- Highly sun-exposed mucosal sites without melanin protection and with frequent UV exposure (lower lip, anterior tongue, conjunctiva/ cornea) — SCC of tongue tip is almost exclusive to XP in children

**Q25. Chemopreventive retinoid regimen.**
- Isotretinoin 0.5–2 mg/kg/day reduced new skin cancers by ~60% in XP (Kraemer study) but with significant toxicity; lower doses (0.5 mg/kg) or acitretin used; tumours recur on stopping — long-term use with monitoring

## Quick spotter facts
- Freckling and poikiloderma with multiple skin cancers in a child of consanguineous parents — XP (NER defect)
- Children of the night — strict UV protection

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of DNA repair). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._

posts.title: Yellow nail syndrome — viva
posts.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
posts.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Yellow nail syndrome** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Write a note on yellow nail syndrome (PYQ).**
- Rare disorder with the triad: yellow slow-growing nails, lymphoedema (usually lower limbs) and respiratory involvement (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, recurrent bronchitis/pneumonia) — two of three features enough for diagnosis
- Adults (median ~50 y); impaired lymphatic drainage (functional lymphatic abnormality) with microvasculopathy

**Q2. Describe the nail changes.**
- Diffusely yellow to yellow-green thickened nails, increased transverse and longitudinal curvature (overcurved), loss of cuticle, absent lunula, onycholysis, very slow growth (<0.25 mm/week; normal ~0.5–1.2 mm), onychomadesis; all 20 nails often affected

**Q3. Associations.**
- Malignancies (lung, breast, lymphoma), autoimmune disease (RA, thyroid), immunodeficiency, nephrotic syndrome, AIDS, drugs (penicillamine, bucillamine, gold, titanium dental implants/joint prostheses — titanium exposure hypothesis)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of yellow nails.**
- Onychomycosis (KOH/culture), psoriasis, ageing, nicotine staining (proximal spared), carotenaemia (skin also yellow), tetracycline/ antimalarial pigmentation, jaundice (sclera), pachyonychia congenita, nail varnish staining, diabetes (yellowish nails)

**Q5. Investigations.**
- Chest X-ray/HRCT, pleural fluid analysis (exudative, lymphocytic, sometimes chylous), sinus imaging, lymphoscintigraphy, nail clipping KOH/culture, screen for associated malignancy/autoimmunity

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Nails: oral vitamin E (α-tocopherol 800–1200 IU/day) ± oral itraconazole/fluconazole pulse (increase nail growth), zinc, topical vitamin E; nails may improve spontaneously (~30%)
- Lymphoedema: compression, physiotherapy, skin care
- Respiratory: pleurodesis/decortication for recurrent effusions, antibiotics and physiotherapy for bronchiectasis; octreotide (chylous effusions)
- Remove titanium implants if implicated

**Q7. Describe the anatomy and growth of the nail unit (linked PYQ).**
- Components: nail plate (keratin — hard keratins), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium), lateral folds, matrix (proximal — dorsal plate; distal — ventral plate; lunula is visible distal matrix), nail bed, hyponychium
- Growth: fingernail ~3 mm/month (complete regrowth 4–6 months), toenail ~1 mm/month (12–18 months); faster in summer, dominant hand, pregnancy, psoriasis; slower in elderly, illness, yellow nail syndrome

**Q8. Associations in detail.**
- Primary/ idiopathic; secondary — malignancies (lymphoma, breast, lung), immunodeficiencies, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, nephrotic syndrome, drugs (penicillamine, gold, bucillamine, titanium implants — 'titanium yellow nail')

**Q9. Treatment in detail.**
- Nails: oral vitamin E 1000–1200 IU/day, oral itraconazole/ fluconazole pulse therapy (stimulate growth), zinc; topical vitamin E; nails may improve spontaneously (~30%)
- Lymphoedema: compression, physiotherapy
- Pleural effusion: thoracentesis, pleurodesis, octreotide (chylous)
- Sinusitis/ bronchiectasis: antibiotics, physiotherapy
- Remove titanium implants if implicated

**Q10. Differential diagnosis of yellow nails in detail.**
- Onychomycosis (subungual debris, KOH +), psoriasis, ageing, smoking (nicotine stain), nail polish staining, carotenaemia, jaundice, tetracyclines, diabetes (glycation), lymphoedema-associated nail changes, PXE

**Q11. What is the prognosis?**
- Chronic disease; nail changes may remit in ~1/3; respiratory complications determine morbidity; life expectancy mildly reduced in some series

**Q12. Investigations in detail.**
- Chest X-ray/ CT (pleural effusion, bronchiectasis), pleural fluid analysis (exudate, lymphocyte-rich, sometimes chylous), sinus imaging, lymphoscintigraphy (lymphatic hypoplasia), nail KOH/ culture to exclude onychomycosis, screen for malignancy/ autoimmune disease/ thyroid, review titanium exposure

**Q13. Pathogenesis.**
- Functional/ anatomical lymphatic abnormality (lymphatic hypoplasia or impaired drainage) leading to slow nail growth (<0.25 mm/week) and thickened, discoloured nails, pleural effusions and lymphoedema; may be primary or secondary

**Q14. Classic triad and its frequency.**
- Yellow nails + lymphoedema (usually lower limbs) + respiratory involvement (pleural effusion — chylous/exudative, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, recurrent pneumonia); full triad in only about one-third; two of three are enough for diagnosis

**Q15. Nail findings in detail.**
- Thick, hard, yellow to green, excessively curved transversely and longitudinally, loss of cuticle, onycholysis, very slow growth, absence of lunulae; all 20 nails often affected

## Quick spotter facts
- Yellow overcurved slow-growing nails + lymphoedema + pleural effusion — yellow nail syndrome
- Vitamin E + itraconazole
